en: Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Now, concerning the vows of the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī-vrata):
whatever has fallen away from dharma may at any time indeed become the object of one's speech.
That very Hemādri, in due order, has described a multitude of vows for the thirteenth lunar days.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, deliverer from the ocean of worldly existence,
tell me of some vow that bestows beauty and good fortune.
O Keśava, please describe to me in detail that by which Anaṅga was gratified and granted his fruit— namely, a form and beauty like his own.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, it is heard that the god Anaṅga is the wielder of the trident and the bearer of the Pināka bow; when he is fully worshipped, what is there on earth that a man does not obtain?
Therefore, I shall tell you this regarding the vows of the Trident-bearer,
which has not been declared to anyone— the supreme vow among all vows.
O Pāṇḍava, having crossed over [this world] with devotion on this thirteenth lunar day called Anaṅgā, whatever a mortal man desires in this world, he obtains it without a doubt.
O Pārtha, what is the use of many vows that yield fruit only upon being uttered?
This thirteenth day is meritorious, bestowing the fruit of all vows.
Therefore, one who desires abundant merit should strive diligently in this rite;
for the thirteenth day known as Anaṅgā instantly destroys the multitude of sins.
She who pacifies all that is evil, she who bestows all auspiciousness,
and she who grants incomparable happiness, good fortune, beauty, and charm.
O Pāṇḍava, because Kāma was formerly burnt by the fire from the eye of the Three-eyed One and reduced to ashes in this world, yet remains through his mere resolve (saṅkalpa),
he is called Anaṅga; for this reason, it is called Anaṅgatrayodaśī.
Furthermore, O Pārtha, it is heard that there is a well-known etymological explanation of its name according to the Purāṇa; listen as I tell it to you.
The Blessed Lord Śambhu is bodiless, a form of radiant energy, and beyond the reach of the senses;
because that very God is present in this [day], it is therefore called Anaṅgatrayodaśī (the Thirteenth Day of the Bodiless One).
Renowned, fully attained, eternal, and bestowing all fruits—
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should remain composed.
Having bathed in a river, a pond, at home, or even from a well,
and having worshipped Mahādeva, the moon-adorned one, according to the prescribed rite.
The self-arisen *liṅga* that exists as a reality established in non-existence is called "Anaṅga" (the Bodiless); the practitioner should worship it with devotion.
Having established [the deity] with auspicious nectars such as curd, milk, ghee, honey, and sugar,
one should subsequently bathe it with scented water.
With incense, lamps, and food offerings, with flowers available at that time, with various kinds of fruits and edible foods, and with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
Then, having uttered the names [of the deities] that have been heard, an oblation should be performed with sesame seeds and unbroken rice;
one should drink milk-rice made from *aśvattha*, *jāti*, and *nāraṅga* fruits, mixed with honey.

The offerings of wood, flowers, fruit, and food, as well as their consumption, follow the sequence beginning with the *aśvattha* tree and so forth. This is likewise for the subsequent months. First, one should worship Anaṅga together with Madhumatī; having worshipped him by the name Anaṅga and consumed honey, one should sleep at night.
Through the practice of consuming honey, a sweet voice arises;
the devoted practitioner attains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
O Hero, one should worship the Lord of Yogis with *udumbara* flowers, auspicious pomegranates, sweetmeats, sandalwood, and *madayantī*.
Having bathed [the image] with milk and other substances, O Pārtha, and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one should touch it while reciting "O Lord of Yoga" and consume sandalwood paste at night.
By consuming sandalwood, one becomes gentle, cool, and fragrant;
such a devotee shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
In the month of Māgha, one should worship with *nyagrodha*, *saktanda*, *mātuliṅga*, and *sumālikā* flowers;
and one should worship the Yogin together with Madayantī, [offering] *sumālika*, *somalaka*, pearls, and *bhauti*.
Having recollected "Smara" in Māgha, one should consume water containing pearls.
By the power of consuming [this], a stainless intellect arises,
and the bodies of women become rich in beauty, delighting the minds and eyes.
His eyes are like those filled with pearls, his limbs are as long as lotus petals, and he is pure;
by consuming sandalwood, he becomes gentle, peaceful, and fragrant.
One obtains the complete fruit of the sacrifice known as Bahuśrama by means of jujube fruits (*badarī*) in the month of Phālguna, using water from the Girī and Jīvīraṇa rivers.
One should worship Vīreśa with *kakkola* at night, accompanied by cooling substances;
one should mutter the name of the Hero (*vīra*) during the night and consume *kakkola* at night.
By that, a fragrant scent arises from his body and mouth;
through it, he becomes an abode for a multitude of virtues, resembling molten gold.
Having obtained the fruit of a gomedha sacrifice, one is glorified in the world of Śakra;
[this occurs] in the month of Caitra with *krañja*, *damana*, grapes, *vaḍhaka*, and cooling substances.
Camphor is cooling. O Pārtha, at night, one should have the Lord of Devas, named Rūpa, consume camphor along with Subhagā, according to the previously mentioned procedure during the sacrifice.
Possessing camphor-like brilliance in the sight of his beloveds and endowed with the weight of fragrance,
he brings delight to the eyes of all people like the moon.
O Pārtha, that man who performs this act with devotion is born [again];
he attains the fruit of a human sacrifice—of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship Mahārūpa together with Indrāṇī using mango blossoms, arka flowers, cooked rice, grains of parched barley, nutmegs, and fruits.
O Bhārata, if one should consume the unsurpassed nutmeg at the time of night,
all his desires on earth become fruitful.
Having obtained the fruit of a thousand cows, one is glorified in the world of Rudra;
likewise, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, [one should worship] with jambū and bilva leaves, śrīphalas, and cakes.
Having fully worshipped Pradyumna accompanied by Lalitā as the Lord of the Lavanga, one should consume lavanga at night; thereby, one shall obtain beauty.
Having obtained the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice, O Bhārata, he rejoices in heaven during the month of Āṣāḍha with apāmārga, nīpa, coconut, and kadamba trees.
At night, one should worship Umāpati with sesame seeds and Tilottamā;
reciting the mantra of Umāpati, the wise man should consume water mixed with sesame seeds.
Like Tilottamā, he becomes unsurpassed in the perfection of beauty;
O scion of the Kuru lineage, he obtains the fruit of the white lotus by offering jasmine, water-lilies, plantains, fruits, and sweetmeats in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
With *sumana* and jasmine flowers, one should worship the wielder of the trident (*Śūlapāṇi*) while dressed in white garments;
having consumed fragrant water, one should sleep at night free from envy.
One becomes fragrant, enriched with all happiness, and long-lived;
the supreme fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice shall be his.

In the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship Sadyojāta, accompanied by Gaurī, with offerings of *pālāśa* leaves, *cāmpeya* flowers, sugar, and clarified butter; likewise, one should worship with *ājyapura*, which is a *ghṛtapūra* (a cake fried in ghee).
Having consumed aloe-wood (agaru), one becomes a preceptor on earth and enjoys the fruit of the gift of a golden Tulāpuruṣa.
In the month of Āśvina, one should worship the Lord of the Thirty-three with Apāmārga, Karkandhu, jaggery, and pūrakas, along with golden water and gold.
By consuming golden water, one becomes golden-hued;
one certainly attains the fruit of the Naramedha sacrifice.
With *ūrjā*, *kadambaka*, *droṇa*, *kuṣmāṇḍa*, salt,
and fruits, one should worship Vidyādhipati together with Madanā.
[6] It should be known that this consists of fruits called *amṛtaphala* together with edible salt. One endowed with supreme faith should consume the salt therein;
from consuming this, one becomes possessed of beauty and charm.
In the event that even offerings of food (naivedya) are unavailable, one should provide sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).

Here, regarding the brushing of teeth, flowers, food offerings, and the consumption [of the remains], which were prescribed in sequence for each verse, this alternative rule (anukalpa) is stated for the absence of each respective item.
In all cases of breaking the fast (pāraṇa), one should feed the most excellent twice-born (dvijottama) brahmins.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee, the self-controlled man should eat together with his kinsmen;
provided there is no obstacle to his vow on that day, nor is he incapacitated by birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Having fasted on that day, one should perform the concluding rite (pāraṇā) once more;
thus, at the end of the year, according to one's capacity, [the image] should be adorned with jewels and other ornaments.
Then, having consecrated a golden image of Umāmaheśvara during the night,
[one should worship it] with flowers, incense, perfumes, various food offerings, and fruits.
Then, at the time of dawn, having performed the fire-oblation and the offering of bali,
he should bestow all of this which is about to be described upon a twice-born man.
One should have an image of Śiva made of gold, possessing the form of a *liṅga* and yet bodiless (*anaṅga*).
Having placed it upon copper vessels, one should set it down atop the water-pot (*kalaśa*).
Having covered it with a white cloth and worshipped it with flowers and food offerings,
O learned one, it should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who is a devotee of Śiva.
One who possesses the capacity should give a bed, a milch cow with her calf,
and the gift of an umbrella and sandals, along with water-filled jars.
Twelve [lamps] should be prepared here, adorned with garlands and sandalwood paste,
covered with white cooked rice, and offered to the Brahmins.
Twelve jars filled with perfumes should be offered to the Lord alone,
along with a five-colored canopy resounding with the tinkling of banners and bells.
And one should fasten a beautiful, auspicious bell in the temple of Śiva;
on that very day, O Pārtha, one should worship while exerting oneself.
[He worshipped] the God of gods, the Lord of the Trident, with flowers, food offerings, and lamps,
as well as with various performances such as singing, instrumental music, and dancing.
In this [occasion], gifts should be bestowed according to one's own wealth,
for this auspicious day is considered equal to an eclipse of the sun.
And one should offer food according to one's ability, possessing the six flavors with sweetness preeminent, to the devotees of Śiva; indeed, such things should be given especially.
One should not insult that which has been honored, nor cast it aside, nor speak untruth;
having thus performed that festival, the unsurpassed sacrifice to Śiva.
Then, having established the deity within his heart, he should himself eat, accompanied by his circle of servants, while maintaining peaceful conduct and humility;
having thus performed [the rite] according to the rules, a man becomes one who has fulfilled his duty.

Or a woman, O tiger among kings, having performed this supreme vow, obtains this very fruit; there is no need for hesitation in this matter. Having thus performed it properly, a man who is permeated by a spirit of devotion [attains the goal].
One is liberated from all heaps of sins, even including the killing of a Brahmin;
having attained fame in this world, upon death, one is indeed glorified in heaven.
Having returned here due to the remainder of his merit, he shall become a sovereign king;
by the power of this vow, he shall become Madana incarnate.
He is enriched with good fortune, wealth, and happiness; his mind is peaceful and he has conquered his senses.
Surrounded by sons and grandsons, he shall live for a hundred autumns,
becoming devoted to the worship of Śiva with his mind fixed on Śiva alone.
By remembering Śiva at the time of death, one attains union with Śiva;
for she who, in the past, out of desire, fasted on the bright lunar day for the sake of obtaining a celestial body.
Having fasted while reciting that [mantra] along with the names of its deities,
one proceeds to the supreme, divine station of the Moon-crested Lord.
Thus ends the vow of Anaṅga-trayodaśī as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should depict Anaṅga upon a cloth,
measuring exactly one *hasta* in size, dark like the sprouts of blue *dūrvā* grass.
Endowed with both delight and grace, bearing the bow and arrows of Puṣya,
he should be depicted well-established upon the canvas, surrounded by all the hosts of Apsarases.
Having worshipped with various flowers, garments, food offerings, and lamps,
as well as with various kinds of delightful incense and the sound of diverse musical instruments;
One should worship [the deity] within a beautiful flower-pavilion in a lovely garden;
the preceptor should be diligently honored with various offerings and devotion.
By means of clothing, gold, food, and drink, according to one's ability and with devotion,
a person attains the state of being desired by all and becomes beloved by everyone.
A woman shall obtain good fortune in this world and in the next;
she should perform worship every month according to the prescribed sequence.
Or on a single day, O child, or throughout the year,
one should worship Madana, the abode of the mind, Manmatha, who is dear to Rati,
as well as Anaṅga, Kandarpa, and Makaradhvaja.
Likewise, having worshipped the Mind-born One known as Kusumāyudha,
as well as Viṣamabāṇa and the twelfth, Mālatīpriya.
One should always worship Anaṅga with effort during the month of Bhādrapada;
thus, one should perform this Kāmavrata according to these very rules.
Thus ends the Anaṅgavrata as declared in the Kālottara.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Śrīvatsa, O Puruṣottama, tell me of the propitiation of Yama."
Just as one does not go to the terrible hell that is the end of hells.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, having bathed in the waters of the Sravaṇā at the city of Dvāravatī,
I saw a sage approaching named Mudgala by name."
Having bowed down with marks of respect to that excellent sage, who was blazing like the sun and illuminated by his ascetic power, Yudhiṣṭhira then questioned him as follows.
Filled with wonder, that sage Mudgala recounted this vow named Yamādarśana, which removes the fear of living beings.
Mudgala said:
I shall relate the account of what was seen by me in my own small hut;
suddenly, free from disease, I fell upon the surface of the earth.
And I see my body being seized on all sides by fierce men;
that man, no larger than a thumb, is being dragged away by force.
Bound tightly by the messengers of Yama and carried away by them with great speed,
I see in an instant Yama, with his tawny eyes, in the assembly hall.
Black and white, with a fierce face, accompanied by death and disease,
and attended by personified forms of wind, bile, phlegm, and the rest.
By desire, grief, fever, vomiting, splenic disorders, abdominal distension, fistula-in-ano, consumption,
urinary disorders, and various eye diseases;
But his own body, O Kṛṣṇa, was covered with terrible wounds such as those of the Jvālāgardabhaka and others, and with many kinds of diseases of various forms that were terrifying.
And he was surrounded on all sides in battle by personified hells of terrible appearance, as well as by Rākṣasas and Piśācas.
He was surrounded by Viṣāraka, Vasiṣṭha, and others, as well as the scribes Citragupta and the rest, and by the guardians of the directions beginning with Āditya, who serve as witnesses to karma.
And by messengers such as Raudramukha and others, who ride upon lions, serpents, and other mounts,
who hold nooses, goads, and other weapons in their hands, and whose faces are contorted with frowns.
With massive bodies and extremely terrifying, they are the overseers of the most wicked sinners;
[the hells] consist of forests of sword-leaves, glowing coals, pits of caustic liquid, and those filled with blood.
Amidst the breaking of bones, the cutting of flesh, and the flowing of blood, he who stands there appears as Yama; no other person is he.
Filled with wrath, Dharmarāja said to all his servants: "Let him be released! Why has he been brought here by you of distracted minds?"
"Let Mudgala, the son of Bhīṣmaka and a Kṣatriya from the city of Kuṇḍinī, be brought here; let the sage, whose life is exhausted, be abandoned."
Having been told this, they departed from there; then, returning once more, those wise servants of Yama, filled with great wonder, spoke to Dharmarāja.
Our lifespan having been exhausted there, we did not perceive anyone as we departed;
bewildered in mind, we did not know—forgive us, O Lord of the Worlds!
Yama said: Generally, those by whom the thirteenth day— which destroys the agony of hell— has been observed are not seen by men who are the servants of Dharma.
Those who have died in Ujjayinī, Prayāga, or even Bhairava, and those by whom sesame, food, cows, gold, and so forth, as well as daily fodder for cattle, have been given;
The servants said:
"O Lord, O son of the Sun, tell us what that vow is like;
and what must be performed therein regarding the four aims of human life?"
Yama said:
For one year continuously, beginning with the month of Mārgaśīrṣa in the forenoon,
on the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) during a weekday other than Monday or Tuesday.
In my name,
one should summon thirteen twice-born men who are knowers of the truth of the Purāṇas and Vedas, who are of good conduct, and who possess clear insight.
One should seat the virtuous, who have the sun as their sole refuge and are devoted to the welfare of all beings,
facing eastward upon a clean and auspicious cloth.
Having clothed them in undergarments, one should diligently and with devotion massage them,
beginning from the head, rubbing them with sesame oil.
One should bathe them with fragrant decoctions and pleasantly warm water;
having bathed each one individually, all these best of the twice-born.
Once they have bathed comfortably and sipped water for purification, the observer of the vow, devoted to devotion, should himself,
along with his servants, perform service for them with a concentrated mind.
And he should place thirteen well-consecrated balls of molasses (guḍapūpa), each separately, facing them as they sit facing the east.
One should repeatedly offer well-cooked food along with its condiments,
according to one's pleasure, according to satiety, according to desire, and without being asked.
Having observed the object to be given, those who desire their own welfare should,
having become pure, perform the consecration here with sesame seeds and rice.
Then, with each [offering] measuring one *prastha*, accompanied by a copper vessel,
provided with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), covered, and containing pure water-pots;
With excellent leather garments, cloths, and flowers,
the messengers should honor those best of Brahmins individually with this mantra.
One should cause those Brahmins of equal appearance to sit according to the distinction of rows;
[these include] Yama, Śanaiścara, Mṛtyu, and Vināyaka with staff in hand.
He is non-existence, dissolution, peace, the queller of suffering, and the ender;
he is the guardian of the world, the possessor of wealth, the fierce, the terrible, the one with a formidable face, and Śiva.
"May he, with a face brightened by grace toward me, grant the gift of fearlessness.
Having spoken thus, the practitioner, having given what is to be given, should again [perform the rite].
He should follow the twice-born who have been satisfied and honored according to the rules of his own *gṛhya-sūtra*.
Any man whatsoever who should perform this vow even once in this manner—
[13] Even when that man has died, O messengers, he does not go to the abode of Yama;
unseen by others, he arrives at the solar orb by means of a celestial chariot.
Therefore, he goes to the city of Viṣṇu and from there proceeds to the city of Śiva;
by that Mudgala, the vow was performed exactly as prescribed, even if it were deficient.
"Therefore, O bull among Kṣatriyas, he does not come to my world.
Mudgala said:
"Having heard these words of Yama, my messengers have departed for some other place."
And I, having heard everything, was filled with wonder in my mind.

Then, having regained his own body, he rose up as if from sleep; thereafter, having entered into the state of Hari, he came here to see you. What was heard by me there has now been told by me to you here.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Having spoken thus, O King, Mudgala departed for his own hermitage.
"O son of Kuntī, you too should perform this [act] here upon the surface of the earth."
Then, having abandoned the uncertain realm of Yama, the abode of Death,
those other men or women as well, O Yudhiṣṭhira, [attain] heaven in this manner.
Those on the surface of the earth who, on each thirteenth day,
shall perform [the rite] by means of a single meal, a meal at night, or even by fasting;
By means of this vow known as Yamādarśana, which is indeed the highest of all vows,
they are liberated from all sins and [ascend] in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
They shall go to the delightful city of Indra, which is filled with hosts of Apsarases,
being fanned by yak-tail whisks and praised by gods and asuras alike.
Adorned with rows of umbrellas and the sounds of singing and musical instruments,
they were not seen by those messengers of Yama of terrible form, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Unafflicted by hundreds of diseases, beyond the range of piśācas and the like,
unstruck by various terrible weapons, and uninjured.
Freed from the path of Yama's sight, endowed with every happiness,
adorned with all ornaments, and possessing gentle countenances upon their own heads.

Having bathed thirteen sages, fed them with ghee and milk-rice, and honored them with offerings of sesame seeds and rice, those who have cultivated their own karma dwell in heaven for a very long time.
O Pārtha, those who observe this vow on the thirteenth day never at any time behold the face of Yama.
Thus ends the vow of the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight known as Yamādarśana, as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
On the thirteenth day of the lunar fortnight, on Thursday, having bathed in the afternoon and offered libations to the gods, ancestors, and sages with sesame seeds and rice, he should proceed.
He who, having worshipped Narasiṃha, observes a fast,
is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Narasiṃha-trayodaśī-vrata as declared in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O tiger among the Yadus, tell me of the vow that destroys [the loss of] fragrance."
It bestows a sharp intellect and likewise destroys the misfortune of the body.
[15] Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, in former times, the great sage Jātūkarṇa was asked this very question by the queen, the high-minded Kālanandana.
Seated and delighted, he spoke to her as she listened;
with palms joined in reverence, the queen spoke quickly to Jātūkarṇya.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyaiṣṭha,
having bathed in the waters of a sacred river, one should worship [the deity] born in an auspicious place.
The white mandāra, the arka, the red karavīra,
the nimba, and likewise the durlabha— these are beloved by the Sun-god.
O Pāṇḍava, having looked at the sun in the sky with this mantra while offering lamps, food offerings, flowers, and so forth, one should bathe and recite it within the heart.
O Sūrya, you who arise from the white Mandāra and the white Arka;
O Karavīra, salutations to you; O Nimba tree, let there be homage to you.
O best of kings, in this manner, whichever man— or woman endowed with devotion— worships these three trees individually every year with devotion.
In her body, neither foul odor nor misfortune arises;
she shall have no fear of childlessness in this world, nor any defect resulting from barrenness.

O King, extreme good fortune—difficult for other women to attain—is born [for those who perform this]; it has been declared that those who practice these rites shall destroy both foul odor and misfortune.
O Bhārata,
those who worship the Nimba tree— which is as meritorious as the rays of the rising sun— with offerings of flowers, unbroken rice grains, and lamps, enjoy happiness entirely freed from all defects.
[16] They become fortunate women, endowed with the increase and prosperity of all sensual pleasures, and free from the defect of misfortune.
Thus ends the vow for the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī-vrata*) as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, which destroys foul odors and misfortune.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By those entering into wildernesses, forest fastnesses, and rivers..."
And also in crossing the ocean, and in battles, O crusher of foes.
O Lord, which deity should one remember there as the one who provides protection?
And how, O God, does a person act for the sake of obtaining protection?
Kṛṣṇa said: A person who remembers the goddess Umā Durgā, the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the source of all blessings, does not encounter suffering.
One who constantly remembers her, the mistress of the world, who dwells in the heart of every being as the imperceptible mark of the perceptible, does not experience fear.
But when I came to this earth to learn the sacred scriptures, O Bhārata, I went to the presence of my preceptor Saṃdīpani together with Bala.
And having attained knowledge, I promised the sacrificial fees;
then, perceiving my divine nature, he cultivated me accordingly.
"Prabhāsa-tīrtha, this son of mine who has died is being offered by you;
therefore, I have meditated upon the Goddess who delivers one from all calamities."
[17] At that time, the goddess Maṅgalā was also renowned as Aṅkāvaṅkā.
O Pārtha, for one who worships this triad, there is auspiciousness everywhere.
The three— Saṃhitāntarakṛt, Valabhadra, and Maṅgalā— are there;
from that time onwards, the people residing there have always worshipped me,
as well as Valabhadra and Sarvamaṅgalā who stands between them.
On my left is Nārāyaṇa; from him I am Kapāla. Thus, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, month after month, I maintain my vow.
Furthermore, by means of eating once a day, eating only at night, or fasting;
and with perfumes, flowers, and lamps, as well as honey, molasses, wine, and spirituous liquors.
O King of kings, he who worships with devotion using parched grain, rice-pudding, and offerings of cooked rice quickly becomes liberated from all sins.
Whoever remembers this triad shall surely overcome all calamities;
or else, being in a distant land, one should have three images fashioned.
Whether it be made of clay, of gold, inscribed, or even painted as a picture—
by worshipping it according to the prescribed rite, one enjoys the full fruit of all of them.
Whoever always worships this triad on the third day of the bright fortnight with offerings of flowers, meat, and wine—
in his dwellings, the most terrifying [omens] shall perish.
The fears produced by enemies, snakes, and living beings [are] instantly [dispelled].
Thus concludes the vow of Sarvamaṅgalā on the thirteenth lunar day, as described in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
[18] Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Great King, having fasted on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight,
beginning from the month of Vaiśākha, O Lord, one should worship Kāmadeva.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give to a brahmin an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food, as well as a pair of fragrant garments.
Having performed this desired vow for a year, a person dwells in heaven for a very long time;
having returned to the human state, he becomes free from disease.
Endowed with happiness and endowed with beauty.
Thus ends the Kāmadeva-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Great King, having fasted on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, [one should worship] Mahārāja.
Starting from the month of Phālguna, a person should worship constantly.

One should present the great king Dhanada with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and an abundance of food; and at the conclusion of the vow, one should bestow gold upon a preeminent Brāhmaṇa.

Reflecting thus, he then wandered through the lonely forest.

As he went along thinking, "Where shall I see her?", O Pāṇḍava, he saw a cow with her calf running here and there in the midst of the grass.

"Where else shall I see such a one as that on this very earth? O King, Kauṇḍinya became distraught and lost all hope for his life.
Sighing long and hot breaths, O Bhārata, that twice-born man fell upon the earth; then, regaining consciousness and crying out "Ananta!", he rose up.
"Surely I shall see my life again," thus resolved in his mind,
O best of the Bharatas, he rose up and woke from his sleep upon that tree.
Out of compassion, the infinite God appeared before his very eyes in the form of an old brahmin and said to him, "Come, come!"

He beheld himself seated upon that auspicious divine lion-throne,

Having thus offered salutations with these and other words, he then spoke again to that twice-born man.

therefore, one should perform it in whatever manner possible, avoiding stinginess regarding wealth.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived and the vow is fully completed,
the practitioner of the vow, observing celibacy and remaining humble, [should perform the rite] on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight.
[37] Having undertaken the discipline of eating but one meal a day, endowed with devotion,
and having bathed in a river, a natural pond, or likewise at a sacred bathing place or spring;
With all medicinal herbs, all fragrant substances, sesame paste, and likewise with *āmalaka* fruits,
one should properly gratify the ancestors and the deities according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Then, having returned home and prepared a very beautiful altar,
one should draw a mandala there, beautifully adorned with five colors.
It should be well-filled with fresh stalks and be auspicious on all sides;
upon it, one should place a new, flawless, and beautiful water-pot.
Even a poor man, O King, having prepared an infinite [offering] with great effort, should place it upon a copper vessel together with a copper plate.
Having prepared a very spacious bed, the observer of the vow should place Ananta there,
along with Vāsudeva accompanied by Lakṣmī, and with a mace and a plow.
And having honored the teacher with garments as well as ornaments.
Then, with great concentration, one should worship that god Ananta, who possesses universal forms, with devotion and with various colors and finger-rings.
He was clothed in a pair of garments, wearing a yellow sacred thread,
and anointed with fragrant sandalwood mixed with camphor and agallochum.
Then one should anoint the limbs [with this], saying: "May Madhusūdana be pleased."
The mantra for the unguent:
Then, having taken up flowers, one should worship them individually with their names:
"Salutation to Ananta" for the feet, and to Saṅkarṣaṇa for the ankles.
[38] To the Self of the Body, [he offers] with both knees; to Viśvarūpin, the hips;
to Viśvarūpa, the penis; and to Viśvarūpin, the perineum.
To Padmanābha at the navel, to the Supreme Self (Paramātman) at the heart,
to the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha at the throat, and to the bearer of all weapons at the arms.
O Vācaspati, salutations to you; one should worship Hari in the mouth. On the forehead, [one should worship] with "To Keśava," and on the head, "Salutations to the Soul of All."
He is the self of sorrow, the self of all beings, the twinkling of an eye, and the dissolution of a moment.
O destroyer of the fear of birth, death, old age, and disease;
divine essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and most enchanting;
you who are the sustenance of all beings—please accept this incense.
The incense mantra:
You are the light of all beings, the supreme splendor among splendors;
you are the self-luminous, supreme abode—may this lamp be accepted.
The mantra for the lamp: The four kinds of delicious food are the supreme sustenance for living beings.
O Lord, this offering of food has been given by me; please accept it with pleasure.
Please accept this betel leaf, together with areca nut, enchanting camphor,
and other sanctified ingredients.
Since this pure pair of garments is dear to Vāsudeva,
may Ananta always be pleased with me by means of this cloth of pleasing color.
Having performed worship in this manner, one should then proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa);
then, having established the fire according to the ritual procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra.
[39] Then he should commence the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rule, using fuel-sticks of the Aśvattha tree, sesame seeds, rice, barley, and clarified butter.
One should offer oblations with the Puruṣasūkta, or alternatively with the hymn beginning "ato devā," or with the verse:
"Viṣṇu strode across this; in three places he planted his step."
The preceptor, being wise, should offer oblations one hundred and eight times for each [deity],
having performed everything according to the prescribed rule with these mantras.

*Anantāya svāhā! Kālāya svāhā! Saṃvatsarāya svāhā! Ahorātrāya svāhā! Ardhamāsāya svāhā! Māsāya svāhā! Ṛtubhyaḥ svāhā! Saṃvatsarāya svāhā!* Then follow the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. Having performed the entire expiation (*prāyaścitta*) with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), clarified butter, and sesame seeds, the observer of the vow should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation to Prajāpati and [the other deities]. Then, having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapālas*) and the planets in their proper order, the observer of the vow should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) accompanied by the sounds of song and musical instruments.
In the same manner, the observer of the vow should pass the remainder of the night listening to the Purāṇas;
then, at the time of dawn, having bathed, being pure, and having performed his daily rites, he should proceed.
One should worship the one of universal form according to the previously stated procedure;
having worshipped the god Hari, one should then worship the preceptor.
Having caused the recipient, together with his wife, to be clothed and adorned with garments and ornaments,
and having worshipped the cow according to the rules with mantras, one should diligently present it as a gift.
Surabhi, the mother of Viṣṇu, eternally abides in the station of Viṣṇu;
O Mother Cow, having accepted this morsel offered by me, you ought to protect me.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
For the purpose of performing the Godāna rite, one should give gold according to the prescribed rule;
having worshipped with this mantra, one should present it to the preceptor (ācārya).
Furthermore, he should inform the teacher of his period of probation (parivāsa) and honor fourteen invited Brahmins;
having honored them with garments and sacred threads, he should feed them with abundant food.
Then, free from stinginess regarding wealth, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to them according to his own ability; he should give a fee to the preceptor and ask for his forgiveness.
One should subsequently recite [the text] even if it is deficient in ritual action, deficient in devotion, deficient in material offerings,
or likewise deficient in mantra, for the sake of completing the vow.
O Vāsudeva, lift up completely me who am submerged in the great ocean of endless saṃsāra; establish me in the infinite form.
Homage to you of infinite form; homage to you!
Having thus bestowed gifts upon an infinite number of people, as well as upon brahmins,
he should likewise give wealth to the poor and the destitute.
Then, having fixed one's mind on the Imperishable, one should eat as is available together with all beloved sons, relatives, and kinsmen.
And having become pure, one should meditate upon Viṣṇu on that day as the teacher;
when this is done, O best of kings, Janārdana quickly [bestows his grace] through that ritual act.
The Blessed One, who possesses infinite forms, is always pleased;
he obtains the fruit of his vow and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Sūta said:
Having slain Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Lord of Gods and Teacher of the World,
the Lord of Ramā, whose anger was appeased, sat comfortably upon his lap.
Prahlāda, the best among the wise, while protecting his excellent kingdom,
spoke these pleasing words alone in his father’s lap.
Prahlāda said:
"Obeisance to you, O Blessed One Viṣṇu, in the form of Nṛsiṃha; obeisance!
I am your devotee, O sole Lord of the gods, and I ask you one thing according to the truth."
"O Master, although you are my enemy, devotion toward you has arisen in me in manifold ways;
tell me, O Lord, how have I become dear to you, and what is the cause?"
Nṛsiṃha said:
O one of great wisdom, listen with a one-pointed mind; I shall tell you, my child, the cause of devotion and the cause of being dear [to the Lord].
Indeed, in former times you were a Brahmin, but you have not studied at all.
By name you are indeed Vāsudeva, yet your mind is attached to courtesans;
in which birth did you not perform even the slightest meritorious deed?
O sinless one, having abandoned many other virtuous vows, you were solely intent on the company of courtesans; yet, by the power of my vow, devotion has arisen within you.
[42] Prahlāda said:
O Śrī Nṛsiṃha, let it be told first: whose son was he, and what was his vow?
And how was that performed by me while living as a courtesan?
Therefore, you ought to relate that greatness of Viṣṇu at this time.
Nṛsiṃha said:
Formerly, in the city of Avantī, there was a Brāhmaṇa who had mastered the Vedas;
his name was Suśarman, renowned throughout many worlds.
The best of the twice-born performs the daily fire-oblation and the three twilight prayers;
indeed, being self-restrained, he is devoted to all the rites pertaining to Brahman.
All the supreme gods have been worshipped by him with sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma;
yet, O friend, how much evil has been committed by him while possessing such means?
His wife was Suśīlā, renowned throughout the three worlds;
she was devoted to her husband, possessed of virtuous conduct, and entirely dedicated to her spouse.
From that best of the twice-born, five sons were likewise born of her;
they were of virtuous conduct, highly learned, and devoted to their father.
Among them, you were the youngest, intent on consorting with prostitutes;
thus, while it was being forbidden, you drank liquor.
Gold was stolen by them, and they have committed much evil together;
you laugh constantly in the house of a wanton woman, even though you are forbidden.
The *vilāsinī* is a courtesan. Once, a great quarrel occurred between her and him in that house; because of that state of conflict, you did not take your meal.
[43] Unbeknownst to him, he performed my vow, the supreme among all vows;
by means of his practice of renunciation, he kept a vigil throughout that night.
A certain lover of a courtesan was born, but none equal to you;
you observed vigils at night and renounced enjoyments many times over.
By the performance of this vow, the deities rejoice in heaven;
for in ancient times, Brahmā indeed performed this unsurpassed rite for the purpose of creation.
By the power of my vow, that world of mobile and immobile beings was fashioned by the Lord in ancient times for the purpose of slaying Tripura.
O sinless one, in ancient times, the three cities were swiftly brought down by the power of this vow, as well as by many other gods and sages.
This supreme vow was ordained by kings of great wisdom;
through the power of this vow, they all attained perfection.
Even a Vaiśya woman became dear to me, moving happily throughout the three worlds.
"O child, such is my vow, renowned throughout the three worlds;
this vow has been undertaken by the playful woman through a quarrel."
O Prahlāda, because of that, unsurpassed devotion has indeed arisen in you toward me,
even though it was prompted by Dūti and Vilāsinī who recognized my day of religious observance.
She who caused the quarrel and yet observed my vow has been born as an apsaras, having enjoyed manifold pleasures.
O Prahlāda, having abandoned the playfulness of karma, you are filled with great wonder;
yet the Blessed One remains for the sake of his task, and likewise, the envious one remains separate.
Having performed all your duties, you shall depart quickly;
for that man who shall certainly perform this vow, [it will bear fruit].
There is no returning for them from me, even after hundreds of kalpas;
one who is childless obtains sons, and my devotee becomes endowed with great luster.
A poor man obtains wealth such as that of Kubera;
one desiring splendor obtains splendor, and in kingdoms, he obtains supreme sovereignty.
One who desires long life shall obtain it, indeed such as that of Śiva himself;
this vow of women is excellent, bestowing sons as well as good fortune.
It ensures that they remain free from widowhood, destroys grief for sons,
bestows wealth and grain, and auspiciously brings about excellence within one's lineage.
From that, there shall arise for them the divine happiness of a sovereign ruler;
whether they be women or men, they perform this supreme vow.
To them I grant happiness endowed with both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O child, what is the use of saying more? Great indeed is the fruit of this vow.
Neither I nor Śaṅkara am able to describe the fruit of my vow;
even Brahmā, with his four manifested forms, would not find the limit of its greatness.
Prahlāda said:
O Blessed One, by your grace I have heard this unsurpassed vow. The fruit of this vow is truly the cause of my devotion to you.
O Lord, through this specific lineage, the destruction of my sins has come from you;
now I desire to hear the supreme procedure for this vow.
In which month and on which day does this occur, O Lord?
O God, you should explain this to me now in detail.
O Lord, out of compassion for me, please tell me in its entirety, O Master, the procedure by which one may indeed enjoy the complete fruit.
[45] Nṛsiṃha said:
"Excellent, excellent, O highly fortunate one! Listen now with a one-pointed mind as I describe to you in its entirety the supreme ritual procedure for this vow."
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
one should perform this meritorious vow, which brings about my own birth and destroys all sins.

Year after year, this most excellent and highly secret [rite], which brings me satisfaction, should be performed by those humans who fear worldly existence. By performing it alone, one obtains the fruit of twelve thousand twelfth-day observances (dvādaśīs).
I speak as a friend to those high-souled men who are born under the conjunction of the Svāti asterism on a Saturday.
Through the conjunction of Siddhi and Yoga, as well as Vaṇija and Karaṇa,
it is obtained by the power of destiny through the union of merit and good fortune.
Having killed [an enemy] on a day endowed with all these [factors], it brings about the destruction of ten million;
even on a day possessing any one of these yogas, that day destroys sin.
This supreme vow must be performed exclusively on my day;
otherwise, one goes to hell for as long as the moon and sun endure.
In whatever manner the commission of sin may occur in the Kali age,
in that very same manner it is destroyed through the power of that vow.
By the power of my vow, the minds of the wicked shall not be so inclined;
having reflected thus, one should perform my vow in the month of Mādhava.
And the observance must be performed, beginning with the cleansing of the teeth:
"O Śrī Nṛsiṃha, you who are most fierce, having shown compassion toward me..."
[46] "And today I shall perform the vow; lead it to completion without obstacles.
This is the mantra for the observance.
One established in the vow must not associate with evildoers.
Those who desire the fullness of their results must not engage in false speech.
One established in a vow must not engage in conversation with women or with those who have been slain;
on this entire auspicious day of mine, my great form should be remembered.
Then, at the time of midday, one should perform [the rite] in clear water such as that of a river,
or in a house, or in a pure and auspicious natural pond or lake.
Having performed his bath with a Vedic mantra, the wise man [should apply] earth,
cow dung, and likewise the fruit of the dhātrī tree.
Having bathed with sesame seeds, which destroy all sins, and having put on clean garments, those great-souled ones should perform their daily rites.
Then, having returned home and remembering me with the yoga of devotion,
one should smear the ground with cow dung and fashion an auspicious eight-petaled lotus.
Having placed there a water-pot (kalaśa) provided with copper and jewels,
one should set upon it a vessel completely filled with rice.
And there, an image of me and likewise an image of Lakṣmī should be installed, made of gold weighing one pala,
or half of that, or even half of that again.
It should be performed according to one's capacity, free from stinginess regarding wealth;
having bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should then perform the worship.
Then, having summoned that brahmin teacher— who was free from greed, endowed with virtuous conduct, peaceful, self-controlled, and a master of his senses— [he addressed him].

[47] Having seen this, the wise one should cause worship to be performed by that very person in accordance with the scriptures; following the instructions of the preceptor, he should perform the worship according to the prescribed rule.
One should have a pavilion constructed there, adorned with clusters of flowers.
With a restrained mind, one should worship with flowers blooming in their proper season,
using the sixteen services, as well as the mantras and the names.
Then he should be worshipped according to the prescribed rites with Purāṇic mantras:
"O Nṛsiṃha, Supreme Lord, for the sake of your satisfaction, I offer cool, divine sandalwood mixed with moon-like saffron."
Thus ends the mantra for sandalwood paste.
O Lord, with flowers produced in their season, such as *tulasī* and others, I worship You, Nṛsiṃha, together with Lakṣmī; salutations be unto You!
The Flower Mantra:
O Great Viṣṇu, I offer this incense made of black agallochum, which is most dear to all the gods, for the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus ends the incense mantra.
The lamp is declared to be the remover of sin and the destroyer of the mass of darkness;
splendor is obtained through the lamp, therefore I offer this lamp to you.

Thus ends the mantra for the lamp. O Beloved of Ramā, I offer to you this beautiful food-offering, which bestows happiness and is provided with various kinds of eatables and delicacies; please effect the destruction of all my sins.
[48] Thus ends the mantra for the food offering (*naivedya*).
O Nṛsiṃha, Acyuta, Lord of Gods, Beloved of Lakṣmī, Master of the World!
By this presentation of the *arghya* offering, may all my heart's desires be fulfilled.
Thus is the *arghya* mantra:
"O yellow-robed one of mighty arms, O destroyer of Prahlāda’s fear,
by being worshipped according to reality, become the bestower of the fruits as described."
This is the mantra of prayer.
At night, one should keep vigil with the sounds of singing and musical instruments,
by reciting Purāṇas, through dances, and by listening to auspicious stories.
Then, at the time of dawn, having performed his bath without weariness,
he should diligently worship me according to the previously described procedure.
O sinless one, with a mind intent on well-being, one should perform the Vaiṣṇava Śrāddha in my presence;
thereafter, the gifts that are to be given shall be described.
Indeed, for the sake of conquering both worlds, a golden lion that brings me satisfaction must be given to the twice-born who possess worthy vessels.
Cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold should be given along with auspicious fruits;
a bed provided with a cotton mattress should be given together with the seven types of grain.
Other things also should be given according to one's ability for my satisfaction;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth out of a desire for the stated fruit.
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
even those who are destitute should perform this rite and give what they can according to their means.
O Vrata, all castes indeed have the right to perform this;
however, it must be performed especially by my devotees who are solely intent upon me.
O Lord of Gods, deliver those men born in my lineage who are intent on spiritual perfection from the difficult-to-cross ocean of worldly existence.
For me, who am submerged in the ocean of sin, overwhelmed by the waters of the waves of disease and suffering, and overcome by living beings while fallen into great misery;
Grant me the support of Your hand, O Lord of the World reclining upon Śeṣa!
O Śrī Nṛsiṃha, beloved of Ramā, You who are the refuge of Your devotees.
O Janārdana, whose hand holds the discus and who dwells in the Ocean of Milk,
O Lord of Gods, through this vow, grant me both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus ends the mantra of supplication.
Having prayed in this manner and then having dismissed the deity according to the prescribed rite,
one should present all the offerings and other items to the preceptor.
Having fully satisfied the Brahmins with sacrificial fees, he should dismiss them;
then, at midday, the man, being composed, should eat together with his kinsmen.
Whoever listens with devotion to this vow that destroys sin,
by the mere act of hearing it, he dispels even the murder of a Brahmin.
That man who recites this supreme, secret,
and purifying [text] shall attain all his desires and obtain the fruit of this vow.
Thus ends the Narasiṃha-caturdaśī-vrata in the manifestation of Narasiṃha within the glorious Narasiṃha Purāṇa.
[50] Śiva said:
Now, O Six-faced One, hear briefly concerning the Liṅga-vows here;
indeed, one whose vows are praised should properly undertake the vow beginning from the month of Kārttika.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, one should worship Śiva;
furthermore, a great ritual bath and a great worship should be performed.
For all those observing the *liṅga-vrata*, one should likewise subsist on food taken only at night.
Having performed worship with effort using garments, food offerings (*naivedya*), and other articles,
one should fashion a *liṅga* made of rice-flour (*śālipiṣṭa*) measuring one cubit (*aratni*).
Ratni is the performer of excellent deeds.
One should place a prastha of sesame seeds and gold upon the linga;
indeed, incense made of kunduru, as well as sandalwood and agallochum, should be offered.
It should be given to one whose form is Śiva; having gone [to him], one attains imperishable auspiciousness.
A linga should be given to a brahmin who is of the nature of Śiva,
especially on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
after having duly worshipped the linga with a great ritual bath as before.
Having smeared Śiva with saffron alone, one should worship him with that;
first, a white sandalwood liṅga should be fashioned according to the prescribed measurement.
One should place gold and a prastha of rice on the back [of the image], and a serpent in front of Śiva;
one should arrange incense made of camphor in the four directions,
and offer a large wick and other items, as well as eight auspicious vessels of curd.
The "Eight Auspicious Verses" (Śubhāṣṭaka) refers to the "Eight Verses on Maṅgala. Having performed this according to the prescribed rite, one should present it to the Liṅga;
then, one should offer it to the Preceptor, who is designated as Īśāna-Rudra.
One should offer [the gift] to the preceptor after worshipping the *liṅga* with the words, "May Rudra, the Lord, be pleased. In this same manner, it should be inferred for the other months as well.
O Six-faced One, by means of this vow one attains union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, one should worship Śiva as before.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should burn a hundred pieces of guggulu incense all around Śiva.
One hundred palas of milk-rice (pāyasa),
mixed with ghee and sugar, measuring one prastha.
A *prastha* measure of rice;
the food offering (*naivedya*) should be placed before [the deity], along with banners (*patākā*) numbering according to the *śaktis*.
The *śaktis* are eight.
Furthermore, with that [offering], one should place a white liṅga made from the flour of *pāli* on a banner; one should also place an *āḍhaka* of sesame seeds, gold, and a liṅga to the right.
One should offer this vow to Rudra, known as Śaṅkara;
having worshipped Śiva on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should observe it.
A linga made of rice grains, unbroken rice, a prastha of sesame seeds,
and gold should be placed with great care on the right side of Śiva.
One should burn a prastha measure of mudga rice with ghee in the east, and offer incense of agaru, sihvaka, and candana before Śiva.
Having thus invoked the fierce Vrata according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the oblation;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should worship the Guru with devotion according to one's ability.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phalguna, having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite,
one should offer guggulu resin with ghee as incense and four large wicks.
Various kinds of sweetmeats (modakas) soaked in ghee should be offered, along with milk, according to the previously mentioned procedure; likewise, one should present the linga to Śarva.
Having worshipped with "Salutation to Śarva," the preceptor should be given abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Having done this, O Mahāsena, one attains absorption in that [divinity] at some point;
having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Then, having completed [the rite] for Bhavarudra, one should worship the preceptor;
thus should this be performed with diligence by one desiring the imperishable world.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
having diligently worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, preceded by a great ceremonial bath;
Having smeared it with saffron, one should anoint Śiva with sandalwood paste;
having fashioned a linga made of flour, it should be adorned with golden flowers.
One should place a prastha of sesame seeds, gold, and other sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
two large wicks should be offered, along with a garland of lamps fed with ghee.
One should offer two hundred palas of guggulu mixed with clarified butter;
one should burn agarwood, śihvaka, and candana, each weighing one pala.
Then, having worshipped Śiva with devotion using *damanaka* flowers,
one should offer a golden *tila*-linga to Bhava-Rudra.
The gurus, numbering eleven,
should be honored with diligent effort through gifts of land and clothing, and by the distribution of gold and other riches.
This vow, known as the "Supreme Vow," is beneficial when observed for a year;
he who performs it with devotion shall go to the highest state.
His ancestors rejoice, and he is glorified in the world of Rudra for ten thousand divine years; at the end of that time, he becomes a lord of wealth.
[53] Furthermore, those who possess self-knowledge have gone to dissolution in the eternal Śiva;
O Mahāsena, he who acts like Śiva is also worshipped.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having performed the daily rites, one should constantly recite the Śiva-mantra;
having anointed [the deity] with sandalwood paste, one should worship with jasmine flowers.
Saffron and laghucandana incense should be offered before Śiva.

Light incense and heavy incense should be offered; a row of lamps, as well as a *ghārikā* lamp, a small bell, and a banner; and savory cakes from the *agāla* tree, along with milk products combined with ghee.
Broken vessels and vessels of ghee should be given outside of that;
he who acts thus, desiring imperishable sovereignty and liberation, shall enjoy it.
He also delivers his ancestors— ten preceding and ten succeeding generations—
especially on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rite, preceded by a great ceremonial bath,
and having smeared the God with sandalwood paste, one should offer the four-fold mixture (*catuḥsama*).
Candana, kāśmīra, and granthila, O Śikhidhvaja—
this is called the "fourfold equal" (catuḥsama) body-unguent, which is dear to Śiva.
One should offer incense made of rice, saffron, camphor, and small blue lotuses,
followed by many rays of light as an offering of food.
The rays are camphor; there, these are called the *liṅgas*. And likewise, the *ghorikas*, the *laḍḍukas*, the *ghṛtapūra*, and the *paṭatrika*.
Having diligently offered milk for the Lord to drink out of affection,
one should present a golden liṅga made of flour and betel leaves.
Afterwards, one should honor the preceptor with a canopy, banners, a fan, and likewise a mirror, as well as with vehicles and abundant food.
Thus, he who performs this correctly goes to the supreme state;
his ancestors rejoice throughout the entire world of Rudra.
For thousands of millions of eons and hundreds of millions of eons,
one should observe the vow on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Having performed both the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, one should then perform the optional (kāmya) rites:
namely, bathing, worship, recitation, meditation, and fifthly, the fire offering (homa).
Thus it is eternally proclaimed, O Six-faced One, that [this practice] should be performed day after day in the presence of the True One;
likewise, on occasions such as the eighth lunar day, the worship should be doubled.
Likewise, the rite of ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa) is established as a constant subsidiary (nityāṅga) observance;
as are initiation (dīkṣā), consecration (pratiṣṭhā), the ritual grasping (grahaṇa), and the solstice-observance (ayana).
The eighty-six auspicious [days] are declared to be the cause;
likewise, it should be known that the optional vows (kāmyavrata) are to be performed as the supreme goal.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord as before with unguents,
incense made from the powder of *vānara*, and likewise an offering of milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
One should offer a monkey, a lion,
water purified with cloth, and a lunar libation to the deity;
one should also present a betel-box, a bell, and gold.
With devotion and according to the prescribed rite, one should offer a fan, sandals, a silk cloth, incense, a censer, and food offerings to Bhīmarudra with great reverence.
Devoted to the worship of the teacher and free from deceit, they should perform this;
by means of this foremost vow, O Śivā, they attain supreme dissolution.

He also delivers his ancestors—ten preceding and ten succeeding generations. His ancestors rejoice in the worlds of Rudra for eighty thousand divine years, O Six-faced One; thereafter, he goes to the Sun.
One should observe the vow on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada;
one should perform a bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and apply a light ointment.
One should offer circular incense made from camphor and red resin (or red lead), combined with other types of incense; in its absence, it should be mixed with clarified butter.
There were many varieties such as *khaṇḍaka* and others, along with *modakas*,
*kiraṇas*, *ghārikās*, and *vaṭakas*, as well as the auspicious white *śikhariṇī*.
Having made a golden liṅga from a prastha of ground śāli rice,
along with betel, clothing, a seat, and sandals,
and having placed his knees upon the ground, he should offer food to the wielder of the Pināka bow.
As before, the worship of the Guru must be performed, free from deceit;
the man, together with his kinsmen, attains union with Śiva.
His ancestors rejoice like Rudra in the worlds of Rudra,
by observing this vow on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja.
The bathing should be performed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), and the anointing with one pala of yellow pigment (rocanā); one should worship with the "unmatta" substances and with the moon.
With a hundred rows of lamps, one should offer boiled rice with ghee as food,
along with prepared pieces of cake and auspicious thickened milk.
One should offer to Śiva husked areca nuts, cloves, nutmegs, and betel nuts, as well as fragrant substances, emblems, and gold.
The teacher, moreover, is to be honored thereafter with gold, garments, food, and vehicles;
he attains union with Śiva in the realm of Śaṅkara along with his ancestors.
[56] Listen to the vow for the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika. A great ablution must be performed, as well as an anointing with the fourfold unguent.
One should also provide a hundred rows of lamps and four great wicks.

At the gate, one should place a Vaijayantī banner; in the middle, and in the cardinal and intermediate directions, one should offer a moon-shaped ornament made of cloth, and in the cardinal and middle directions, a casket.
A moon-patterned canopy, a light *raśāla* lattice-work, and a casket; cooling camphor and the finest incense named *samugāka*.
In each of the intermediate directions, there is an offering of *guggulu* resin with clarified butter, one hundred times each.
One hundred and eight oblations of rice flour, prepared in a wooden trough (droṇa), should be offered in the east.
Upon its back is a linga made of flour, measuring twelve finger-breadths in height,
adorned with a golden garland and decorated with strings of pearls.
Having offered [the food] with supreme devotion and effort to the Eternal One,
one who is composed should speak thus for the sake of his own consumption and for the sake of being thoroughly liberated from bondage:
"O Mahādeva, let this be yours; let this alone be the bestower of success.
Having properly offered it according to the rule, the vow is correctly performed as prescribed."
One who desires it attains incomparable sovereignty, and one seeking eternal liberation;
even a betrayer of kindness and a slayer of a Brahmin shall attain the state of Rudra.
By worshipping the Guru with supreme devotion and with gold, garments, food, vehicles, jewels, pearls, and so forth, one is born [in a noble state].
An elephant-vehicle should be given, or one originating from a horse by its very nature;
when this is performed, the vow of the *liṅga* becomes complete.
Thus ends the vow of the *liṅga* as declared in the *Kālottara*.
Now, however, I shall proclaim the supreme vow of the *pratimā*,
including the great ablution (*mahāsnāna*) and a hundred rows of lamps with great wicks (*mahāvarti*).
One should offer anointment with saffron and incense indeed with guggulu;
the food offering (naivedya) should consist of milk and ghee, offered exactly one hundred and eight times.
She is the size of a palm tree, has twenty-four eyes and four arms,
and is adorned with various ornaments, holding a trident, a sword, a skull-topped staff, a bow, and arrows.
One should fashion a beautiful image made of rice flour upon the back of a bull;
there, one should represent Śiva being fanned with chowries.
One should diligently offer to the preceptor a mirror, betel, a fan, sandals, a seat, the Vaijayantī banner, and a vehicle.
It should be performed every month on the fourteenth day,
beginning from the month of Kārttika until the end of Āśvayuja.
This is declared to be the supreme vow, known as the Pratimā-vrata;
even one who has killed a Brahmin or a preceptor, or is burdened by the five great sins, [is purified by it].
Even one who is a betrayer of friends, ungrateful, or a violator of trust,
shall attain the state of Rudra, accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Indeed, he rejoices in the world of Śiva for thousands of millions upon millions of years.
At the conclusion of that, he is born as a king—alone, heroic, and wise;
through the power of Śiva-initiation, he attains knowledge and sovereignty.
One attains the supreme state by which one is not born again;
thus should he instruct him, and then cause the gift of land to be performed for him.
[58] One should diligently cause a great elephant, a great horse, or even a great vehicle to be given; at the conclusion of that, one shall attain the vow.
Thus ends the vow of the image as spoken in the Kālottara.
Nandikeśvara said:
"Listen attentively, O Brahmin; I shall describe the Māheśvara vow."
Renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Śivacaturdaśī.
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, eating but one meal, I, having come to you for refuge, pray to you, the Lord of the Gods.
Having fasted on the fourteenth day and worshipped Śaṅkara,
one should fashion a golden bull and feed others on the following day.
Having thus observed the vow and slept, the man, rising in the morning and having performed his ablutions and recitations, should thereafter worship Śaṅkara together with Umā with white lotuses,
perfumes, incense, and ointments.
The form of Umāmaheśvara is to be understood as that described for the Aviyoga-dvādaśī vow:
"Salutation to Śiva" for the feet; "Salutation to the Soul of All" for the speech;
"Salutation to the Three-eyed One" for the forehead; and "Salutation to Hari" for the eyes.
One should worship the face with "To Indumukha," the neck with "To Śrīkaṇṭha," the two ears with "To Sadyojāta," the two arms with "To Vāmadeva," and the heart with "To Aghorahṛdaya."
One should offer the two breasts with "tatpuruṣāya," and likewise the abdomen with "īśānāya."
One should worship the right side with "Salutation to Anantadharma," the left side with "Salutation to Jñānabhūta," and the two thighs with "Salutation to Anantavairāgyasiṃha."
The wise one should worship the knees with "Salutation to the Lord of Infinite Conduct," the shanks with "Salutation to the Primal One," and the ankles with "Salutation to the Self of Space."
One should worship the hair and the back of Him whose form is the self of Vyomakeśa;
one should also worship Pārvatī with "Salutation to Puṣṭi" and "Salutation to Tuṣṭi."

Then, one should present to a Brāhmaṇa a golden bull, accompanied by a water-pot, adorned with white garlands and garments, endowed with the five jewels, and provided with various kinds of edible foods.
"May Sadyojāta, the wielder of the Pināka bow, the God of gods, be pleased here.
Then, being pure, one should satisfy the Brahmins with food according to one's ability.
Having consumed the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya), he should sleep on the ground facing north;
then, on the fifteenth day, having honored the Brahmins, he should eat while remaining silent.
In the same way, one should perform all this on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight;
on all fourteenth days, one should perform the worship as previously described.
But as for those specific months, learn them here in their proper order;
one should recite this in sequence during the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa.
It should be understood that these [offerings] are at the end of the Āśvina month:
"Salutation to you, Śaṅkara; salutation to you, Karavīraka;
salutation be to Tryambaka, and thereafter to Sthāṇu."
Homage to you, O Paśupati; homage again to you, O Śambhu!
Homage to you, O Supreme Bliss; homage to the bearer of the crescent moon!
"Obeisance to Bhīma"—thus have I come to you for refuge.
[60] Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with *kuśa* grass;
The consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as bilva, water from the five horns of a cow,
and black sesame seeds, is prescribed to be performed in sequence according to the rules.
It is traditionally taught that on the fourteenth day of every month, one should partake of a single morsel [of food] offered with mandāra,
mālatī, and madhuraka flowers,
as well as with sinduvāra, aśoka, mallikā, and pāṭala blossoms.
On the fourteenth day, one should worship the Lord of Pārvatī with *arkapuṣpa*, *kadamba*, *śatapatrī*, and likewise with *utpala* flowers— one by one.
Furthermore, when the month of Kārttika has arrived, he should gratify the twice-born with various kinds of food and edibles, as well as with garments, garlands, and ornaments.
Having performed the ritual release of a blue bull according to the procedure prescribed in the Śruti,
a man [should offer] a golden image of Umā-Maheśvara along with a bull and a cow.
One should give a bed equipped with all its furnishings, accompanied by a water-pot, together with eight pearls and provided with white eyes and a cloth.
Furthermore, having bathed [the image] placed upon a copper vessel together with rice grains,
one should offer it to a peaceful Brahmin who is devoted to Vedic vows.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, that which pertains to the Sāmaveda should be given; it should never be given to one who observes the "heron-vow" (hypocrisy).
One should give to a learned Śrotriya who recognizes virtues, to a teacher, and to one who knows the ultimate reality.
Having worshipped him who has no deficient limbs, who is gentle, who always brings about auspiciousness,
and who is accompanied by his wife, with garlands, garments, and ornaments;
When a guru is present, the gift should be given to the guru; in his absence, it should be given to a twice-born.
One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth; by doing so, one falls downward due to that fault.
The man who performs the Śivacaturdaśī according to this rite obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed here or in the hereafter by fathers or even by mothers, all that shall go to destruction.
Long life, health, and the increase of one's family—
these shall be inexhaustible here; and in the hereafter, the state of having four arms and lordship over the Gaṇas for ten million kalpas in heaven.
Having dwelt for a hundred [years], one attains the state of Śambhu.
Neither Bṛhaspati, nor Indra, nor even the Grandfather [Brahmā] is capable of describing its fruit;
neither the host of Siddhas nor I am capable of it.
Even if there were millions of tongues for the purpose of speaking...
He who reads this, or always remembers it, or even listens to it without envy— this Śiva-Caturdaśī [vow] grants liberation from all sins, just as the ocean does for the immortals.
Tens of millions of celestial nymphs praise that blameless one; what need is there to mention the conduct of one who always practices it?
And whatever woman performs [this] with devotion,
having first sought permission from her husband, her teacher, or her son, she too,
by the grace of the Supreme Lord, [attains the same].
He goes to the supreme state of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
Thus ends the Śivacaturdaśī vow as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Now, O Brahman, hear of another supreme and excellent vow that bestows prosperity.
O highly fortunate one, on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], for the pacification of all diseases and afflictions.
For one afflicted by fever, abdominal tumors, splenic disorders, colic, leprosy, or diarrhea,
this [rite] must always be performed in the mortal world for the sake of dispelling that suffering.
Having bathed and maintained his resolve, free from all desires,
he should worship the Sun while repeatedly reciting the Gāyatrī.
Beginning from before sunrise until the sun has set,
one should remain composed, abstaining from food and having conquered anger.
When the sun has set, O observer of noble vows, one should worship the god Puruṣottama after fasting and bathing according to the prescribed rules on the sacred festival day.

On the *parvan*, that is, on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*). And this vow of the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight (*śuklacaturdaśīvrata*) is mentioned in the Purāṇa within the section on vows for the bright fortnight.
Having worshipped the Supreme Self, the Imperishable (*acyuta*), as is appropriate, one should practice the recitation of the *gāyatrī* there in the presence of the God of gods.
According to one's own capacity, one should offer a thousand, ten thousand, or even a hundred [flowers],
and likewise prepare a vessel made of copper or clay.
Having filled it with ghee measuring five *prasthas*,
one should likewise place gold, silver, pearls, red grains, and sesame seeds.
Having placed that inside [the vessel], the wise one should prepare it provided with two new garments;
then, having established it before him at the conclusion of the worship, the high-minded one [should proceed].
There, having begun with Mārtaṇḍa and worshipped him according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform circumambulation and prostration, filled with joy through the recitation of hymns of praise.
May he who stands here, possessing a light skillful at piercing through dense darkness,
pacify from this moment the suffering arising from various diseases for me.
And the lotus-eyed Puruṣa is established within the interior of all.
"O Acyuta, may you dispel my supreme fear and affliction"—
with this mantra, he opened that garment.
One should cause oneself to be shown there so that it is clearly perceived,
and then have it bestowed upon a poor Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas.
Having given the sacrificial fee to the teacher, one should provide a feast for the Brahmins;
one should eat together with one's relatives and also release oneself from the observances.
Acting thus in this world, a man becomes free from all diseases;
possessing the beauty of gentle limbs and conduct, he attains long life.
Just as water quenches a well-kindled fire that one approaches with longing,
so too, O Brahmin, may this vow here pacify the fire of disease.
O observer of noble vows, for men here who are severely afflicted by various diseases,
no means of pacifying them through their power exists other than through this vow.
Thus ends the Gāyatrī-vrata as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa:
"On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, when the lunar day coincides with a Sunday,
one should worship the Sun, the wielder of the trident (Śūlin), according to the prescribed rite while observing a fast."
The meaning is: according to the procedure previously stated in the section on the *liṅga-vrata*.
One should then worship with saffron as an unguent for the body and with fragrant flowers.
One should prepare milk-rice mixed with ghee in the measure of one prastha;
a gift of land should then be diligently bestowed upon a devotee of Śiva.
By means of this foremost of vows, one shall attain the status of a lord of the earth;
this is called the Bhūmivrata, which a protector of the earth should cause to be performed.
Thus ends the vow concerning the lunar stations as taught in the Kālottara.
When the conjunction of Jupiter and the Maghā constellation occurs on the fourteenth day,
one should fast and worship Maheśvara, the God of gods, on that day.
Following the procedure for the great ablution, preceded by the great wicks,
one should worship with sandalwood unguent and white flowers.
Incense, however, should be offered with fruit, combined with a small amount of camphor;
one should also cause white garments and a cow to be given to the preceptor.
Consuming *jātī* nutmeg and keeping a vigil at night is beneficial;
this very vow is known as the increaser of longevity, prosperity, and fame.
Thus ends the Devavrata as declared in the Kālottara.
Furthermore, if the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight falls on a Sunday during the month of Āśvina,
a special ritual bath for Śiva, the Supreme Self, must be performed.
One should worship with body-unguents made of yellow pigment (rocanā) and red flowers;
likewise, one should offer cow's ghee and milk as the food offering (naivedya).
[65] One should bestow a gift of gold upon a brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva;
furthermore, the practitioner must perform the ritual consumption of saffron.
This secret vow should be performed with devotion by men desiring sons;
indeed, sons endowed with all auspicious marks are born to them.
Thus ends the Sūryavrata as declared in the Kālottara.
Īśvara said:
[It is prescribed] for children, the elderly, the sick, those devoted to worldly enjoyments, and among women and the ignorant.
I shall describe the procedure for them, O son, so that they may be liberated.

On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna, one should perform with great devotion the Śiva-vrata, which grants all desires— especially for the poor, the helpless, and those who are unable [to perform other rites].
At night, however, there should be a special worship accompanied by a great ceremonial bath;
furthermore, two great lamps should be offered, as well as one hundred and eight [other lamps].
One should worship Śiva Paśupati with incense made of guggulu mixed with clarified butter,
along with various pieces of sugar-candy and many kinds of diverse foods.
O son, just as it is offered with devotion without regard for wealth,
one should perform a vigil at night before Śiva and chant the name of Śiva.
The auspicious five-syllabled mantra of Śiva.
Thus, one who observes the vow of Śambhu, having performed worship at dawn, should offer the oblation:
"Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire world."
Śiva is victorious everywhere; he who is Śiva, I am indeed that very one.
Whatever good deed has been performed by me through action, mind, or speech— [may it be for his sake].
[66] O Mahādeva, whatever deficiency or excess there may be regarding the substance, the mantra, or the ritual action—
O Supreme Lord, O Parameśvara, accept all of that.
O Śiva, whatever has been performed by me— whether daily, occasional, or for a specific purpose—
all that, O Supreme Lord, is offered by me unto you.
O Lord, Master of the knowers of the Vedas, you likewise abide as the soul of all parts;
whatever portion of my dwelling is deficient, and whatever is further in excess, [may it be made equal].
Out of compassion for all beings, O God, Lord of the World, please grant this:
I have never performed any vow, nor given any gift, at any time.
O Śambhu, by this preeminent vow, everything— including the observances and the giving of gifts— has been accomplished by me through your grace and at your command.
O Lord, this excellent vow has been offered by me to you;
it is likewise [observed] by those who are impoverished, by those who are afflicted, and by the wise and the yogis.
By children, the simple-minded, and the elderly, as well as by men and women afflicted by disease,
a vigil should be diligently observed before Śiva during the month of Phālguna.
