Those who do not specifically worship the Lord of Beings (Bhūtapati) on this day of the spirits (bhūtadivasa) are themselves overcome by those very spirits.
Therefore, on the *bhūtā* (fifteenth) day of the month of Phālguna, one should worship the Lord of Beings (*Bhūtapati*).
All the vows prescribed for the eighth and fourteenth days have indeed been performed by him through that very [observance].

Skanda said: "O Lord, what rite for the conclusion of the vow (udyāpana) should be performed by men? What is the procedure, what are the materials required, and how should it be done? Please tell me."
[67] Īśvara said:
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, according to the truth, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds:
the auspicious Śivarātri vow must be observed for fourteen years.
Having taken a single meal on the thirteenth day and observed a fast on the fourteenth,
and having prepared all the necessary materials, one should have a pavilion constructed there.
Covered with cloths and flowers, and adorned with fine silken fabrics,
one should cause a divine Bhadramandala to be drawn there in the center, starting from the linga.
Alternatively, one should arrange a Sarvatobhadra pavilion within the tent,
provided with primary and secondary decorations and illuminated everywhere with lamps.
There, one should choose a pure preceptor together with the officiating priests;
those Brahmins, being forms of Śiva, are to be honored with sandalwood paste and flowers.
Having been authorized by those brahmins, he should commence the worship of Śiva;
he should then place upon it a water-filled jar that is free from blemishes.
One should have [the vessel] made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay;
having wrapped it with a pair of cloths, one should worship it with cloth-foliage.
Or with half that amount, or again with half of that half,
one should worship the form of Umāmaheśvarī seated upon a bull.
Come, O Lord of the gods of gods, out of a desire for the welfare of the mortal world;
I worship you according to the prescribed rite—be gracious and well-disposed toward me.
The invocation mantra:
O wise one, prepare a stainless footstool made of gold;
adorned with various jewels, you must prepare a seat for the sandals.
One should contemplate the Lord situated within the heart, resembling pure crystal;
one should meditate with the heart upon the Imperishable One, clad in a tiger skin.
O Lord of Gods, accept this *arghya* consisting of fragrant water, flowers, and sweet-smelling sandalwood; grant me unwavering devotion.
Take this fine *dukūla* cloth, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain;
O Lord of Umā, may you always remain gracious.
O Supreme Lord, O Best of Gods, accept this divine sandalwood paste from the Malaya mountains as an unguent.
The sacred thread, innate and fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times,
which bestows long life, auspiciousness, and luster— please accept this sacrificial thread from me.
O Lord, these fragrant garlands and other offerings—indeed, these flowers were taken by me for the purpose of worship; please accept them.
This incense, the essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, is to be smelled by all the gods; may this incense be accepted.
O Lord of Gods, accept this lamp, consisting of clarified butter joined with a wick and ignited by fire, which dispels the darkness of the three worlds.
O God, please accept this food offering; make my devotion unwavering.
Grant me my desired boon, and in the hereafter, grant me the supreme goal.
"O Lord, this fruit has been placed by me before you;
by this, may I obtain the attainment of fruition in birth after birth."
Please accept this most divine betel nut,
accompanied by betel leaves and blended with camphor.
O Fire, you who possess golden seed and dwell within the womb of Hiraṇyagarbha;
since you bestow the fruit of infinite merit, grant me peace.
Having worshipped Soma, Maheśvara, and his retinue,
one should perform the fire-oblation with effort according to the rules, using the Raudra mantras.
One should worship the Brahmins with devotion and feed fourteen of them,
as well as the preceptor together with his wife, honoring them with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
One should give them individually the sacred thread, garments, and so forth,
as well as a cow with her calf, along with clothing and adorned with various ornaments.
One should give [it] to the most excellent teacher, saying, "May Śiva be pleased with me.
Then, that image, together with its water-pot, its cloth, and mounted upon a bull—
One should present her, adorned with all ornaments, to the preceptor, saying:
"Whatever vow has been performed by me, whether it be complete or incomplete."
"May everything reach completion through your grace," he prayed,
and having thus entreated those brahmins, he bowed down to them again and again.
Then, with their respective name-mantras, one should offer individual jars to them:
Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Bhava, Sarva, and Umāpati.
Rudra, Paśupati, Śambhu, Varada, Śiva,
Īśvara, Mahādeva, Hara, and Bhīma— these are the fourteen names.
Skanda said:
O Lord of Beings, I have heard many kinds of such injunctions;
please explain, step by step, the procedure for worship along with the mantras.
Śiva said:
Listen to the essence of all dharma— the worship of Śiva on Śivarātri—
by means of which vow and ritual action one attains the merit of heaven.
Having performed his bath and become pure, provided with washed garments,
he should bathe the Lord of the Gods with mantras originating from the Vedas.
Then, O son, worship should be performed according to the prescribed rite:
"Homage to you, Lord of Sacrifice and Master of the World; homage to you, Sovereign of the Three Realms."
"O Maheśa, accept this worship offered by me at the first stage.
Thus, at the first watch. Second:
Salutations to the unmanifest, the subtle; salutations to you, O Destroyer of Tripura!
Accept this worship, O Lord of Gods, along with the sacrificial fee offered according to my capacity.
The third mantra, offered according to one's ability:
"I am bound by various snares, the bonds of worldly existence."
O Śaṅkara, lift me up, for I have been cast down by the snares of delusion.
The fourth [chapter]: Then, at the conclusion of the worship, one should offer every month an *arghya* consisting of flowers, sandalwood paste, unbroken rice, *durvā* grass, and *kuśa* grass.
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, and the remover of all sins;
O Lord, accept this *arghya* offered by me on the night of Śivarātri.
The mantra for the *arghya* offering during the first watch:
"O Śaṅkara, I have committed many sins;
O Beloved of Umā, accept this *arghya* on Śivarātri and be gracious to me."
The mantra for the *arghya* offering during the second watch:
"O Lord of Pārvatī, I am consumed by the burdens of suffering and poverty;
protect me, O Mahādeva! Accept this *arghya*; salutations be unto you!"
Thus ends the *arghya* mantra for the third watch.
"O Lord of Gods, do you not know? Grant me devotion;
O Lord of the Universe, grant me the status of a servant at Your pair of lotus feet."

Thus ends the mantra for the offering of the fourth watch. O Śiva, whatever has been performed by me— whether daily, occasional, or for a specific desire— all that is now offered to you, O Supreme Lord.

The Prayer: O you who perform the worship of Śiva for one year, perform it for me! For those who possess even a slight degree of devotion, they surely go to the world of Śiva at least once, however it may be.
Even that hunter went [there], having become a lord of the Kṛtins.
Thus ends the vow for the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇacaturdaśīvratam*) in the *Kālottara*.
Sūta said:
[To the one] seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, the God of gods, the Teacher of the World...
Having five wheels, ten arms, three eyes, and holding a trident in his hand.
Holding a skull and a khaṭvāṅga staff, bearing a bow and a shield, he is auspicious;
wielding the Pināka bow, he is formidable, bestowing boons and granting fearlessness.
[72] Richly adorned with the splendor of serpents upon his ash-smeared limbs,
having the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, resembling a dark blue cloud, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Having prostrated before the Lord of Umā as he was being worshipped, all the gods [beheld him];
there the Blessed One sports, surrounded by his own attendants.
Having dismissed all the deities, he remained together with Umā;
seeing that Lord of the gods of gods, she laughed, her eyes wide with joy.
There, Pārvatī questioned the preeminent god as he stood alone.
Pārvatī said:
"Out of your grace, tell me that supreme vow which is to be kept secret;
O Lord of the gods, you have already described various vows to me."
O Lord, I have been made to wander again by you through many acts of charity, numerous sacred fords, and various other places.
O Lord, I wish to hear that which is the supreme among vows, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation; please tell it to me, O Master.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the best of all vows,
which has not been told to anyone— a mystery that bestows liberation.
I shall relate that by which even Yama himself would go to destruction when it is told; listen with a one-pointed mind.
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight between the months of Māgha and Phālguna should be known as Śivarātri; it is the most excellent among all sacrifices.
Neither by gifts, nor by sacrifices, nor by other rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees—
even having performed a thousand such sacrifices— is there anything equal to Śivarātri.
That Kṛṣṇā is the destroyer of strife and the eradicator of the path to Yama;
those who observe the auspicious night of Śiva do not go to the city of Yama.
O Goddess, O fair-faced one, it truly, truly bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one who intends to perform the Śiva-vow should practice it with a single-minded focus.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, how may one go to Śiva, bypassing the city of Yama?
O Master, make this very great wonder manifest before my eyes."
Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, to this auspicious ancient narrative as it occurred,
which destroys the command of Yama and bestows the abode of Śiva.
In former times, there was a certain Niṣāda who was fond of meat;
he lived in a border region, was a forest-dweller, and subsisted on living creatures.
A meat-eater, always supporting his family on his back,
stout and corpulent, a bow-bearer with a left-leaning body and a blue tunic.
With his left arm protected by a leather guard and finger-protectors bound on,
holding a bow in the left hand and an excellent arrow in the right.
That Niṣāda, a slayer of living beings, has gone out into the difficult forest;
his livelihood depends on living creatures for the maintenance of his family.
As he was departing, his mother also gave him her blessings,
being delighted by the distinct bursting of her womb.
May Śakra protect your head, and Dhanada likewise your arms;
may Candra protect your heart, and Bṛhaspati your face;
may Vahni protect your belly, and the Lord of the South (Yama) your hips.
May Death protect you, as well as the Sun and everything else;
go to the forest, which is filled and surrounded by many beasts of prey.
That great forest resounded with the long-drawn roars of tigers;
[there were creatures] with large tusks, massive bodies, long tongues, and terrifying faces.
Tigers were seen there, and the forest was brought under control by creeping plants;
in that great, difficult, and terrifying forest, which was thick with trees.
In a mountain cave filled with various forest-dwelling creatures,
the Niṣāda, engaged in that very means of livelihood, would go into the forest and, while sustaining his body,
look here and there toward all directions.
They ran here and there, their minds greedy for meat, following every footprint, every trail, and every lair of deer and boars.
All that forest has now passed behind the Niṣāda here;
indeed, no beasts of prey, nor deer, boars, or citralas can be found there.
Standing there in despair, the hunter said, "The sun has set," and he beheld a lake there with pure and stainless water.
Seeing the lake crowded with swans and cranes and adorned with ruddy geese,
he reflected upon the slaughter of living beings therein.
"O Goddess, having reflected for a very long time, I shall undoubtedly commit the taking of life at night"; having thus deliberated, he went toward the pond.
Having reached the shore there, he wandered here and there in the four directions and, for the sake of his protection, caused a hermitage to be built.
On its bank stands a palm tree with lush grass and many leaves;
in its midst, O lady of excellent complexion, a great liṅga resides.
And in its midst, O lady of beautiful countenance, was a great tree, a bilva;
having taken leaves from that tree for the purpose of clearing the path, [he proceeded].
Those [offerings] thrown upon the head of the Liṅga on its southern side—
there is no daytime meal for that well-disposed person, even regarding meat.
Having entered there, he found no sleep caused by the hunter;
by the power of its fragrance, deer and boars were driven away.
The deer did not remain there, following the path of their wounds from the arrows;
then the night waned, and the orb of the sun rose.
Despairing, the hunter emerged from the midst of the net;
then, afflicted by hunger, the hunter set out on the path toward home.
Meanwhile, all those boys, following their father’s path, looked about;
seeing even the Niṣāda, they asked, "How is it that night has already arrived?"
"O father, no food has been brought; the children have gone away in despair.
They are weeping with piteous cries: 'Give us food!'"
Then his father became silent, distressed with his face cast down;
"O Lord, please eat," his wife spoke these words.
Having fasted for a day and night, the wood was set ablaze for you;
and he took his meal with whatever was provided by his wife.
But the Niṣāda, devoid of dharma, evil-minded, and a slayer of living beings,
kept a vigil at night on Śivarātri without desire, O fair-faced one.
[76] But because worship with bilva leaves had been performed upon the top of the liṅga,
when he died in the course of time, he was seized by the servants of Yama.
Ten million excellent celestial chariots were dispatched by Śiva with this command:
"Let the hunter, who has been seized by the servants of Yama, be brought here quickly."
There is no doubt that the impurity of one who was previously a hunter and used to slaughter living beings is utterly consumed on Śivarātri.
Having heard these divine words, those attendants prepared to depart,
while praising the supreme god Śiva— the peaceful and untainted one.
As they all proceeded, they saw a hunter being struck with many iron rods as well as with fists.
All the other hosts raised a great clamor;
being struck by one another, those servants of Yama spoke thus.
The servants of Yama said:
"We shall not release this Niṣāda, the slayer of living beings,
as long as Yama does not see him and he has not become purified thereby."
The servants of Śiva said:
"O servants of Yama, this man was formerly a most wicked hunter;
however, he observed Śivarātri in the forest despite having no desire to do so."
Therefore, by the command of Śiva, we have all arrived here in celestial chariots;
until we behold Śiva, we shall certainly not release this man.
Then they began to strike with swords, mallets, and spears;
that great battle commenced between those who were each desirous of victory over the other.
Some, with the joints of their limbs broken, and others fallen into a swoon,
the servants of Yama, their bodies shattered, utter cries of lamentation.
Crying out, "Save us! Save us! they went to the abode of Yama;
Niṣāda too was led by the hosts to where the god Maheśvara dwells.
Upon merely being seen by the Lord, the Niṣāda attained the status of a Gaṇa;
he stood there with a divine body, adorned with celestial ornaments.
To him, Maheśa gave a celestial chariot that fulfills all desires,
crowded with Rudra-maidens and adorned with garlands of flowers.
Accompanied by various musical instruments and adorned with various jewels,
he sports for a very long time, until the dissolution of all beings.
Having thus obtained this boon, he sports under the dominion of Yama;
then, following the King of Dharma, the messengers of Yama arrive.
With all their limbs reddened with blood, they weep with shattered heads;
their bodies are mangled and their limbs torn apart on every side.
Having seen this, Dharma said: "Who is this that has been joined with his time?
I shall send forth the god Kāma; let this indeed be told."
And by whom has this various slaughter been committed against you?
The messengers of Yama said:
"Listen, O King, to how the battle with Śiva’s attendants occurred,
and how that sinful Niṣāda, the slayer of living beings, was led away."
But while being seized by us, he was forcibly carried away by the hosts of Śiva.
Hearing that, Dharma became enraged: "That most wicked one has fallen under my power!"
"How does one go to the city of Śiva? O Citragupta, consider this! Citragupta replied:
"By whom the book has been examined and no good deed whatsoever was performed..."
He does not perceive the increase of Dharma, nor does he discern what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma;
this is my firm conviction, O Lord, and I speak the truth, the absolute truth.
Śiva said:
Having thus learned of the Niṣāda’s conduct as reported by Citragupta,
Dharmarāja spoke these words of welcome:
The King of Dharma said:
"I shall not concern myself with this creature after today;
having gone there, I will present him to the service of Śiva."
Having been addressed thus, Citragupta and Yama then departed quickly;
and having gone to the Lord of the Gods, Yama began to offer praise.
Yama said:
Homage to you, the Lord of the World, the destroyer of great power;
homage to the manifest destroyer of Time, the one who reveals the nature of Time.
Homage to you, the three-eyed one; homage to you, the wielder of the trident;
homage to you, the bearer of the skull-bowl; homage to you, the holder of the khaṭvāṅga staff.
Homage to the one with hands like *ḍamuru* flowers, who holds a spear and a serpent;
homage be to the blue-throated one, who wears an elephant hide.
Homage to the Lord of the three worlds, the destroyer of great sins;
homage to the annihilator of the Kālakūṭa poison, the consumer of desire.
O Lord, you purify that which is unpurifiable; this is a great wonder to me, since even a Niṣāda, a sinner living in a house, has been delivered by you.
"O Destroyer of Tripura, I shall certainly not entertain thoughts of evil," having said this to the God of gods, he prostrated himself like a staff.
Placing the staff-emblem at the tip of his foot, he became silent.
Īśvara said:
"For what reason, O Dharmavardhana, do you cast aside your staff and seal?
By whom have you been offended, my child, and by whom has your pride been crushed?"
The King of Dharma said:
"O Lord of the Gods of gods, your attendants went to the place where that sinner was,
and my servants, O God, were slaughtered by them in many ways and most cruelly."
O Lord, that Niṣāda was a man of evil deeds and wicked conduct, a killer of living beings;
he did not acquire any merit from the time of his birth.
"O Lord of the gods of gods, that which was done by your attendants in many ways was improper;
that sinner was seized and led to the city of Śiva, yet he was not handed over to me."
"Therefore, O Lord, I have come; having abandoned my seal (mudrā), I am wandering.
Śiva said:
"O Gaurī, while Yama was speaking thus, I laughed and said: 'It was done by me.'"
And the Niṣāda, a man of evil deeds, may live by the slaughter of living beings.
Once, having gone to the forest, he obtained nothing at all;
then, at the end of the day, hopeless and afflicted by hunger and thirst, he went to the edge of the water.
Then, in the middle of the night, he established a hermitage within Mahājālī;
in the center of that enclosure stands a great liṅga that has existed for a long time.
Holding bilva leaves in his mouth, he cast them from the road;
by some chance of fate, they were carried by the wind onto the top of the linga.
O King of Pretas, although tender bodies were cast down against his will,
he observed Śivarātri while remaining awake for the sake of immortality.
By the power of Śivarātri, he has come under my command;
he has attained the divine and imperishable state of a Gaṇa within the teaching of Śiva, which bestows liberation.
Liberated like Rudra, he eternally enjoys pleasures in heaven;
at the end of those enjoyments, he goes to the supreme Śiva, the ultimate cause.
By the power of Śivarātri, he has come under my teaching.
Therefore, O Mahādharma, always take up this staff and the seal;
those mortals who are most wicked never come into my presence.
From this day forward, O Lord of Dharma, do not show contempt;
seize, seize the seal of Great Dharma and the staff as you please!
O Great Yama, protect the truth for the sake of upholding your own dharma;
take your water-pot as a staff and go quickly to your own home.
Punishing the evildoer and indeed protecting the one who follows his own dharma—
having been addressed thus, Dharmarāja went to his own auspicious home.
Thus, O Goddess, has the great vow of Śivarātri been described by me.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord, a hunter who was devoid of desire attained immortality after performing this rite.
O Lord of Gods, this is a marvel, but it is a much greater marvel to me."
I wish to hear about that Śiva-vow which one performs out of desire according to the vision of the scriptures; you should deign to speak of it.
Śiva said:
Listen, O illustrious goddess, you who speak so charmingly in every way;
I shall describe the power of Śivarātri, which destroys even those of sinful deeds.
Whether it be the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Māgha or at the beginning of Phālguna,
that lunar day should be known as meritorious and the destroyer of all sins.
O Goddess, this should always be given to one who is peaceful in soul, free from anger, ascetic, and devoid of malice, and who follows the feet of the Guru.
Otherwise, O Great Goddess, the man or the devoted wife who gives this [gift] year after year shall go to hell.
I survey the entire world: who would worship me with devotion, having performed the recitation of Śiva-mantras, as well as fire-offerings, ritual worship, and illuminations?
One who keeps vigil on Śivarātri should behold Śiva with a concentrated mind;
such a person, O Goddess, is my devotee who fasts on Śivarātri.
Having attained an imperishable and divine status among the Gaṇas and the eternal teaching of Śiva,
he enjoys all pleasures born of immortality.
Thus, for twelve years, the nourisher of Śivarātri—
whatever man keeps me awake during that night— shall attain heaven.
Without having honored me, one does not know this; it is declared that he who worships Śiva and keeps vigil on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] fulfills this vow.
A man who desires imperishable enjoyments in heaven, equal to a god, should never drink the milk from his mother’s breast.
By performing the procedure taught in the scriptures, one attains the complete fruit.
One should undertake twelve such fasts either at the beginning of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, or on the day of the Festival of Lights (Dīpotsava), or during the month of Māgha.
Having kept a vigil at night, with the quarters of the sky illuminated by lamps,
he should remain devoted to Śiva through the diversion of song and instrumental music, as well as through worship and the recitation of prayers.
In this manner, for twelve years,
O lady rich in asceticism, one should [serve] the preceptor who knows the scriptures of Śiva, and especially Brāhmaṇas.
Having addressed the ascetics with supreme devotion and returned home,
he should choose a preceptor and take hold of his two feet.
"Come to my home, dear one; make our home fulfilled.
Having thus addressed them at night, [he did so] again at the clear dawn.
Having worshipped the *liṅga*— both stationary and mobile— the householder should bathe it with the five divine nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and with fragrant unguents and other such preparations.
One should bathe [the image] with a thousand or a hundred water-pitchers;
or one may bathe it with fifty, or even half of that, using cool water.
Then, having anointed both the stationary and the moving [images] with sandalwood paste,
one should worship them with lotuses, jasmine flowers, and bilva leaves.
Having likewise lit lamps in all directions,
thick with camphor,
as well as food offerings and various edibles such as milk, sugar-candies, and *maṇḍakas*.
There was jaggery and other such items, as well as sweetmeat balls and much food that was highly pleasing to the palate.
One should likewise offer these to the guru, the deity, and the ascetics;
having worshipped the guru before the deity and having prepared an auspicious mandala.
And very fine garments, as well as a bed with its furnishings.
One should indeed give twelve cows, as well as clothing and other such items;
or else, one should simply offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and perform oblations with sesame seeds.
Having given [the gifts], one should feed all the teachers and ascetics;
afterwards, one should indeed ask for forgiveness, saying: "May Maheśvara be pleased with me."
And likewise, one should honor the teacher who is devoted to the Śiva-vow with various perfumes and other offerings, as well as all the others who have gathered there.
One should worship with sacrificial fees, water-pots, and fresh food;
having done this, O Great Goddess, one shall not again obtain a body.
O Goddess, when that man dies, he shall go to the world of Śiva;
from that place, he does not waver even for hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Then, at the turn of time, he went in person to see the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū),
accompanied by the world-protectors (lokapālas) in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires.
Then he should behold Mahādeva, surrounded by various hosts;
having seen him, he praises Śiva, the Lord of Gods and Sovereign of the three worlds.
Homage to you, O Lord of the World; on your forehead is the moon-crested one.
Homage to you, who are joined with Umā, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Homage to you, O burner of desire, who pervades the three worlds; homage to you!
O God Śaṅkara, I am afraid of Time; homage to you, O fierce Time!
Thus praised, Bhairava grants the desired boon.
Bhairava said:
"I am pleased with you, my devotee, because of your fasting on Śivarātri."
I grant you a boon that is difficult even for gods and dānavas to obtain.
These maidens are most divine, possessing three eyes and four arms;
they are endowed with beauty and youth, and have full, elevated breasts.
Golden-hued and of great splendor, they were endowed with the brilliance of the sun;
they were clothed in divine garments and anointed with sandalwood and agallochum.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, their faces illuminated by earrings—
such high-minded women of slender waists have been given by me.
Possessing ten million celestial palaces and adorned with every ornament, sport, O fortunate one; you are my son, a leader of my retinue.
"O you who go everywhere, today I am pleased with you, my devotee who delights in the vows of Śiva, as you traverse this world and the next, including all that is moving and unmoving."
In the world of Rudra, however, there are maidens who have three eyes and four arms,
who are exceedingly devoted to their husbands, just as I am with Umā.
Together with them, O illustrious one, enjoy the pleasures as you desire for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
By the power of this vow, attain union with Śiva before [death];
become all-pervading and merge into the supreme state.
There is nothing higher than the highest, superior to the Śivarātri vow;
he who does not worship Rudra, the Lord of Devas and Sovereign of the Three Worlds.
A living being wanders through thousands of births; of this there is no doubt.
When one is united with that state, one attains the status of a Rudra-gaṇa;
there, whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, recited, worshipped, or used for honoring the guru [becomes inexhaustible].
But for one who keeps a vigil on Śivarātri, all that becomes inexhaustible;
even a man who is devoid of the vow may [attain this] through some particular merit.
One who keeps a vigil there attains equality with Rudra;
[the merit is equal to that of] a solar eclipse at Kurukṣetra, Himavat, or Kurujāṅgala.
Likewise, that which is given with devotion on Śivarātri becomes inexhaustible;
for he who observes the fast of Śivarātri while his vows remain unbroken [attains this].
He attains all desires and rejoices together with Rudra;
likewise, that which is given on the day of Śivarātri becomes inexhaustible.
Indeed, he who observes the fast on Śivarātri with unbroken vows sports in the presence of Śiva, his heart’s desires for all things fulfilled.
Blessed are those men in the world who are devoted to Śivarātri;
even if the oceans were to dry up and even if the Himavat mountain were to waste away.
Mount Meru, Mandara, Laṅkā, Śrīśaila, and the Vindhya—
all these may move at various times, but the vow of Śiva is indeed immovable.
Therefore, on that thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, a devoted man, eating but once a day,
should undertake the religious observance with this mantra.
"O Lord of the World, by your grace, may this Śivarātri vow— which yields great fruit— be performed by me without obstacle."
"O Lord, a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda, being composed in mind, should likewise undertake this vow, reciting: 'I take refuge in Night, the mother, and in the two earthen [elements].'"
With this mantra, "The Śivarātrivrata," a Śūdra or others should take up the observance among Brāhmaṇas and the rest:
"I take refuge in the Night, the mother, the dwelling-place of all beings,
the auspicious, the blessed, the dark one, the night of the entire world."
I have taken refuge in the auspicious night, which brings rest, which governs all, and which is garlanded with planets and constellations; O blessed one, may we reach its end.

The meaning is that one should undertake the vow with these two mantras established in the *Ṛgveda*: "O auspicious one, may I reach the further shore" and "O best of those possessing the *aśman* mantra.

Having worshipped Śiva and seen the Guru, having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), being pure and self-possessed, one should perform the vow after making this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) both on the preceding day and in the morning.
Then, during the final portion of the day, one should indeed recite one's own Gāyatrī without weariness.

One should perform a bath with black sesame seeds either at home or in a beautiful body of water; at the onset of night, the observer of the vow should go to the temple of Śiva. At the end of the day, he should perform an ablution and worship Śiva by name.
One should perform the recitation of the book with incense, food offerings, and fragrances, with dance, song, and lamps, and with the sounding of conchs and discs.
In the second watch of the night, one should worship Śaṅkara by name;
one should honor the Supreme Lord according to the previously mentioned procedure.
In the third watch, one should likewise worship the deity named Maheśvara;
when the fourth watch has arrived, one should worship the one named Rudra.
Thus, endowed with devotion, one should keep vigil during the night;
one obtains the complete fruit—this is the truth, O fair-faced one.
[87] At dawn, one should perform ritual bathing, recitation, and fire-offerings, and feed those who are devoted to Śiva;
one should also present white water-pots along with sacrificial fees according to one's capacity.
One should worship with devotion the Brāhmaṇas established in the Māheśvara vow and cause the Śiva-śāstra to be recited; such a person shall go to the abode of Śiva.
Those of meritorious deeds who observe the fast will certainly go to heaven;
so too shall he who recites this narrative of the Śiva-vow in the presence of Śiva.
And he rejoices in the world of Śiva for as long as the fourteen Indras endure;
thus has the great vow of Śivarātri been described regarding heaven.
He attains the world of Śiva and rejoices together with Śiva.
Thus ends the Śivarātrivrata, including its concluding rite (udyāpana), as declared in the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
[It was spoken] on the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, variegated with various minerals,
filled with diverse trees and creepers, and adorned with many jewels.
In that place, crowded with throngs of Apsarases and frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
the Blessed One sports there, surrounded by his own hosts.
There, the Gaṇas, Nandin and the others, sport in the presence of Śiva;
there is great curiosity there, resounded by the five kinds of sounds.
With lutes, flutes, and drums, as well as the fivefold [instruments],
that mountain was filled with celestial maidens and was exceedingly beautiful.
By virtue of their grace, they dwell there upon Kailāsa, which is made of gold, exceedingly beautiful, filled with rows of banners, delightful, and frequented by all the deities.
Having dismissed all the deities, he sports together with Umā;
while Mahādeva was staying there, Umā questioned Śaṅkara.
Umā said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, honored by all the worlds;
having bestowed your grace, O Lord of gods, tell me, O Master.
Homage, homage to Mahādeva! You always remain established in your own nature;
why, then, does agitation arise within my great consciousness?
"O Mahādeva, indeed no auspicious vow has been performed by me.
Having shown favor, O Lord of Gods, let a vow be told to me, O Master."
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, to the supreme secret, the best of all vows,
which has not been told to anyone— a mystery that bestows liberation.
I shall proclaim that which, when told, would cause even Yama himself to go to destruction; listen always with a one-pointed mind.
The fourteenth day of the dark fortnight between the months of Māgha and Phālguna is to be known as Śivarātri, the lunar day that is the most excellent of all sacrifices.
There is nothing equal to Śivarātri, even after performing a thousand sacrifices consisting of gifts, fire-offerings, austerities, and other rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
They are not among those who stand before Yama, O Goddess, by whom this [work] has been composed which bestows auspiciousness;
it grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, how may one go to Śiva, bypassing the city of Yama?
This alone is a great marvel; O Master, grant me proof of this."
Śiva said:
Listen with diligence, O Goddess, to this auspicious ancient tale,
which subdues my command and bestows the world of Śiva.
Those by whom this bestower of auspiciousness has been performed do not go to the city of Yama;
listen, O Goddess, beloved of Śiva, to the great wonder that has occurred.
In the land of Videha there was a king renowned by the name Sudharmā, who was ever supremely righteous and devoted to the protection of his subjects.
All kings on earth remained under his control;
indeed, in his kingdom, no one at all became diseased or miserable.
O beautiful daughter of the gods, the king protects the virtuous like his own sons;
such was the auspicious beloved of that king, who was distinguished by these qualities.
His wife was named Tilottamā, endowed with all virtues,
possessed of beauty and grace, and established in perpetual youth.
The wife of that lord of the earth was like a conversation between swans and cuckoos; she possessed the gait of an elephant in rut, and her character was exactly in accord with her beauty.
She who is devoted to her husband’s pleasure and welfare is indeed dear to him;
and those other beautiful wives, numbering hundreds of thousands, are likewise beloved.
All of them, endowed with excellent qualities, remained as maidservants;
and thus, O beautiful goddess, as time passed in this manner, at a certain point—
After this, the destroyer of enemies, whose soul was devoted to his own duty, departed;
meanwhile, having seen the goddess Tilottamā, who was endowed with all excellent qualities.
Then, seeing King Ripumardana approaching,
he rose up himself and offered him the royal throne.
Then the queen, remaining under his control, sat down beside the king and saluted him, repeatedly saying, "May it be well with you."
And having heard "Śivā" uttered by the king and the queen at that time— this is the ellipsis—
he recollected his former karma, which had been performed in another birth.
Then, remembering that, he cast away the betel leaf held in his hand.
The king formed a resolve in his mind to worship Śiva;
then that goddess said, "Grant me this: what is the reason for this abandonment?"
"If you say to me, 'I shall not die before you,' then that king [will grant your wish]. Then, the queen was determined to die.
Having understood it, he spoke of her conduct in a previous birth:
"Listen attentively to my words, O beautiful goddess."
Having heard the words spoken by you, which were endowed with the name of Śiva,
all my conduct in my previous birth, whatever was performed there, has been remembered by me.
Listen, my dear, and be attentive; I shall tell you.
In former times, I was a Vaiśya, pure and devoted to my own duty.
O Goddess, as time passed, by the power of her previous births,
a thought of theft arose even in her who was devoted to her own duties.
Having departed at night, I went forth to commit theft.
At that auspicious time, O Goddess, it was the month of Māgha;
furthermore, during that very dark fortnight, there occurred the Śiva-yoga.
The lunar day was the fourteenth, and it is remembered as Śivarātri;
