"O Lord of Deer, our breaking of the fast with you as our husband will be praiseworthy;
we too shall come along with you, O best of deer."
Likewise, O beloved, we do not recall ever having done anything displeasing to you,
whether in flowering forest groves or at the confluences of rivers.
And we have descended into the mountain ravines;
therefore, my beloved, there is no purpose for life without you.
For those who are wretched and deprived of a husband, life is devoid of purpose;
indeed, a father gives in limited measure, a brother gives in limited measure, and a son gives in limited measure.
Who would not honor a brother who is a giver of the immeasurable—
even a woman endowed with wealth and surrounded by many sons and friends?
O deer, she will be an object of pity for her circle of kinsmen, being deprived of her husband;
for there exists no other sorrow for women like that of widowhood.
Blessed are those women who die before their husbands;
for a lute is not played without strings, nor is a chariot drawn without wheels.
A woman, even if surrounded by a hundred sons, is not honored if she has no husband;
likewise, one who is destitute, addicted to vice, aged, diseased, or mentally deranged is not honored.
Whether fallen or even wretched, a husband is always the refuge of women;
there is no dharma equal to the husband, and there is no friend equal to the husband.
"There is no protector equal to a husband; for women, the husband is the supreme refuge.
Having lamented thus, they all resolved upon death.
Accompanied by their children and tormented by grief for their husband,
the deer heard their words and became lost in thought within his heart.
In every way, I must indeed go into the presence of the hunter;
for the preservation of truth is paramount in all things, whereas otherwise my family would perish.
If I go there, my family will perish;
yet if I do not go there, my truthfulness will likewise be lost.
Better is the death of a son, or likewise of a wife or oneself;
for by violating the truth, a man will surely go to hell until the end of the world.
Therefore, truth must always be protected by men who seek their own welfare;
by truth the earth is sustained, and by truth the sun gives heat.
[111] By truth the winds blow; by truth the supreme grows. Having reflected thus upon the heart-pleasing dharmas, he died.
He departed from the hermitage at that very moment with those doe-like women;
having bathed in that lake, he indeed performed the renunciation of his actions.
Having paid homage to that linga and meditating on the auspicious Śiva in his heart,
he should renounce bathing, drinking, sexual intercourse, and sensual enjoyment.
Desiring desire, anger, and likewise greed, as well as the delusion that destroys liberation,
he went toward the hunter, even while longing for food, drink, and other such things.
His wife and sons likewise followed closely behind him,
having resolved upon death and taking up the supreme fast unto death (anāśaka).
Surrounded by his wife and sons, the deer came to that place where the hungry hunter stood together with his children.
Having come to that place together with his family, the deer,
guarding his truthful words, spoke these words to the hunter:
The deer said:
"O hunter, kill me first; afterwards, kill my wives in order, and after that, my young ones. Let them be slain; do not delay."
O hunter, there is no fault whatsoever in your killing of deer;
we shall all go to heaven, purified by the sword, without a doubt.
"Even for you and your family, there will be sustenance for life.
Having heard these words spoken by the deer, the hunter then—
Having reproached himself, he spoke these words to the deer.
The hunter said:
"O great-souled deer, go, go to your own dwelling!"
I have no need for material gain; whatever is destined to be, that shall come to pass.
Indeed, from the killing of living beings, as well as from threatening or binding them, arises evil;
I shall never, under any circumstances, commit such evil for the sake of my family.
Compassion is the root of all dharmas, truth is their branch, and self-restraint is their fruit;
for you are now my teacher, the instructor of these dharmas.
"Go, go, O deer, together with your family;
for I have laid down my weapons, having taken refuge in truth and righteousness."
Having heard those words of the hunter, the deer spoke to him again:
"Having performed the renunciation of my actions, I have come here into your presence."
"Kill him! Kill him quickly! No sin shall be yours.
I was previously bound by a word given by me; because of that, I am dying."
"By me and my family, greed has been abandoned in our own lives.
Having heard these words, the hunter spoke this speech:
You are my guru, you are my father and mother; you are my kinsman, friend, and well-wisher.
I shall lay down my weapons, and I shall renounce my power of illusion and the rest.
Whose wife, whose son, and whose family, O deer? Each must experience their own karma; go, O deer, as you please.
Having spoken thus, the hunter quickly unstrung his bow along with its arrows,
circumambulated the deer, paid homage to them, and asked for their forgiveness.
He beheld the hunter before him, whose speech was like milk;
in that interval, the celestial drums resounded in the sky.
A most enchanting rain of flowers fell from the sky,
and celestial messengers arrived in a chariot of secret splendor.
The divine messenger said:
"O hunter of great being, who strikes fear into all creatures! Ascend this most excellent celestial chariot and go to the third heaven in your own body."
By the power of Śivarātri, your sin has gone to destruction;
likewise, both the fast and the night vigil have been accomplished.
Since worship was performed for Śiva during every watch [of the night], even though out of ignorance, you shall be liberated from all sins; go now to the abode of Rudra.
O Great Being, King of Beasts, accompanied by all your wives—
united with your two consorts— do not attain a state that is not celestial.
"By your name, this triad shall attain renown in the world.
Having heard these words, the hunter and likewise the deer—
Having ascended their celestial chariots, they reached the station of the stars;
yet, O Pārvatī, the path of the two female deer is visible even today.
Attached to its rear, two stars resembling jewels are seen;
this constellation, known by the name of the Hunter (Mṛgaśiras), is auspicious when it is visible.
That which is joined with the three stars of Tārā is called Mṛgaśīrṣa;
two young children are in front, and the third, the doe (mṛgī), is behind.
Having arrived there behind him at the onset of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
the king of beasts is seen even today, as is the excellent bear moving through the sky.
[114] Waking at night without desire, as well as fasting and worship—this was performed by the king of hunters; its fruit has been fully described.
Those men who, with a spirit of devotion, shall observe the auspicious Śivarātri vow, accompanied by fasting and kept awake throughout the night;
Indeed, even Brahmā becomes as if dull-witted when attempting to describe their fruit;
there is no vow equal to Śivarātri for removing the fear of sin.
By performing which one is liberated from all sins, of this there is no doubt;
it is the very fruit obtained by men who bathe at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.

O Pārvatī, by merely hearing [this], that fruit which arises from performing austerities at Dvārakā in Vaiśākha, from serving [the deity] in Āṣāḍha, from offering the funeral rice-balls (piṇḍa) at Gayā, and from [worship] before Lord Mādhava in Kārtika, is surely attained.
Thus ends the majesty of the Śivarātri vow in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the glorious Liṅga Purāṇa.
The sages said:
It is known as Śivarātri; at what time does it occur?
What is its fruit, and of what nature is it? Tell us the truth in detail.
Sūta said:
O twice-born ones, the fourteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha—
its night is proclaimed as Śivarātri.
In that place, Hara always manifests within all lingas;
it is especially renowned among all the immortals as Sevaṃkaṇeśvara.
The sages said:
How did Śivarātri originate, or by whom was it established? Why does it yield such great fruit? Tell us everything in detail.
Sūta said:
I shall first relate that ancient narrative,
the dialogue between Bhartṛyajña and King Aśvasena.
Formerly, the lord of Ānarta was known as Aśvasena;
he was constantly devoted to dharma and had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
In former times, Bhartṛyajña was asked this out of curiosity by him,
as he observed the Kali age increasing day by day.
Bhartṛsena said:
O virtuous sage, tell me of some vow to be performed in this Kali age—
a merit born of association with the wicked that destroys all sins.
In ancient times, during the Kṛta Yuga, mortals were always pure and possessed of great longevity;
but what has become of this in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, and especially now that the Kali Yuga has arrived?
Therefore, having abandoned the annual vow, prescribe some rite that lasts for a single day;
one should do today what is to be done tomorrow, and in the forenoon what belongs to the afternoon.
"For death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or not.
Having heard those words of his, the noble-minded Vārtṛyajña—
Having reflected for a very long time and having perceived with his divine eye, he said:
"O King, there is a meritorious vow known as Śivarātri."
O Great King, that which occurs on a single day destroys all sins;
whatever gift is given, whatever oblation is offered, and likewise whatever mantra is recited on that day [is of infinite merit].
Everything becomes inexhaustible when the night vigil is performed;
one without a son obtains sons, and one without wealth shall obtain wealth.
Whether desiring long life for one of short lifespan or the destruction of enemies— whatever desire one contemplates while performing this vow, that shall be attained.
Whatever [desire] a mortal may attain, if free from desire he attains liberation;
likewise, he is released from the sins committed during the year—of this there is no doubt.
If one should keep a vigil while reciting this with a single-minded focus,
whatever signs there may be— whether moving or stationary—
the god Hara, from whom [all things] proceed, will manifest within that very night.
Therefore, she was proclaimed as Śivarātri, beloved of Hara;
he was then entreated by all the gods with the desire to bestow grace upon the worlds.
O Blessed One, in this Kali age, for one who is possessed of all sins,
there is a vow on earth dedicated to Vināyaka for the sake of liberation from the sins of the year.
Purified by this worship, mortals shall attain purity;
then whatever is given or offered by them reaches us.
Whatever is given by those who are impure, all that arises from what has been given;
yet, due to the Kali age, only a very small portion remains for us.
Whatever is given by human beings, even if it be abundant, [is offered] to Śaṅkara.
The Blessed One said:
"O Lord of the Gods, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha,
I shall descend to the earth at night— not by day— in the Kali age."
One who desires prosperity and seeks purification from all sins should worship all lingas, whether mobile or immobile.
O best of gods, that person who performs worship to me on that night with these mantras shall become free from sin.

Oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta; Oṃ, obeisance to Vāmadeva; Oṃ, obeisance to Tatpuruṣa; Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna. Having worshipped the five faces with perfumes, flowers, and unguents, as well as with garments, lamps, and food offerings, one should then present the arghya water.

By means of this mantra, my devotee, having meditated upon me dwelling in the mind as the Beloved of Gaurī, the Lord of Devas, whose hair is adorned with serpents and other creatures, [attains success].
"For the sake of purification from the sins of the year, may this water-offering (argha) be accepted by me.
Then, one should honor the Brahmin with food, clothing, and other gifts.
Having offered it to him and performed a circumambulation, one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth;
thereafter, one should keep a vigil with the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
O Lord of the Gods, he who performs this vow here shall likewise do so with narrations of the Dharma, with dances, and with water-sprinkling.
"It shall serve as an expiation for the purification of all sins.
Having heard that, all the thirty gods bowed down to the Moon-crested Lord.
Greatly delighted, the best of kings returned to their own abodes;
they indeed dispatched Nārada, the most excellent of sages, throughout the earth.
Then, for the sake of awakening the people and for the occasion of Śivarātri,
he too went to the surface of the earth and proclaimed it everywhere.
From the time that the greatness of Śivarātri was proclaimed by the Trident-bearer (Śiva),
it has been known as Śivarātri upon the surface of the earth.
It bestows all desires, is meritorious, and destroys all malevolent beings;
there I shall relate to you an excellent ancient narrative.
This is what occurred here in the Naimiṣa forest concerning a certain hunter:
there was a certain hunter who was such by birth alone, and not by his actions.
Overcome by vice, this thief of others' wealth has never observed a vow,
nor given a gift, nor performed recitation.
However, he had merely seized the wealth of people through deceit;
then, after some time, Śivarātri arrived.
In the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, there is a merit-bestowing sanctuary of the trident-bearing God of gods, which destroys all sins.
Then, O tiger among men, a vigil was commenced by the people throughout the night, accompanied by women adorned with beautiful ornaments.
Remaining awake with his wealth, that thief reflected:
"If I go now, perhaps some woman adorned with ornaments might appear."
Or perhaps they will be asleep; then, having arrived from my journey, I shall kill Śvāśya, take his ornaments, and depart.
Having thus resolved in his mind, he went into his presence;
having climbed a *karṇikāra* tree, he remained there hidden.
Gazing in all directions, the woman emerged,
especially distressed by the cold, as he was intent upon the act of theft.
Having fallen asleep for only a short while, she did not realize that she had departed;
thus, beneath her, the *liṅga* born of Hara was left behind by the *avadhūta*.
At that very time, however, the sun of sharp rays rose up,
turning its face away from the wicked, from thieves, and from those filled with lust.
Then the men and women,
having prostrated before Maheśvara, that supreme and profoundly peaceful one, together with Umā, departed each to their own abode.
And that thief, hopeless, emaciated by hunger, and overwhelmed by the cold,
descended from that tree and sat down somewhere near the fire of the Dharma.
Then, after a long time,
he passed away and was born in the house of the lord of Darpaṇa, having become one who remembers his former births.
By the power of his fast, by staying awake during that night,
and likewise by the worship of that Liṅga on Śivarātri.
Then, having obtained the great kingdom of his father and grandfather,
he caused a temple for that Liṅga to be constructed and its purification performed.
Year after year, having arrived on Śivarātri,
one should remain intent on fasting and keep vigil through the sounds of singing and musical instruments.

Having honored them with discourses explaining the Dharma, with the sounds of conciliatory words, and with the previously mentioned gestures of the eyes, one should offer the water of respect (arghya) according to the prescribed rite.
Having gratified the Brahmins with their desires, he went to his own realm, the Victor. Then, after some time, the Śivarātri festival arrived;
there, in that palace, sages led by Śāṇḍilya arrived.
Then Śāṇḍilya, Bharadvāja, Javakrīta,
Jālava, Pulastya, Pulaha, Gārgya, and many other kings likewise [approached].
That King Bṛhatsena, the son of the lord of Daśārṇa,
also arrived to keep vigil before that liṅga.
Then, having worshipped the god and prostrated before those sages,
he sat down in front of them, permitted by the best of the twice-born.
O King, as he danced, his long eyes were fixed upon her; he spoke of many kinds of stories concerning the royal sages of the past, and especially those of the brahmins.
Then, while he was speaking, he was questioned by those exponents of the Veda,
whose minds were filled with curiosity and whose eyes were wide open with wonder.
"O King, we all stand here filled with curiosity; if you are staying in this temple of the deity, please tell us the truth."
The king said:
"O best of Brahmins, if I know it, I shall tell you without doubt;
having worshipped before the God, I swear this by my own soul in truth."
The sages said: "Why have you abandoned your many abodes so easily to come here from your own country, O traveler, wishing to perform a vigil? Alas!"
"Since this occurs every year, you surely know the reason for it.
O lord of men, if it is not a secret to you, then tell me.
Having said this, he smiled with embarrassment and spoke with a heavy heart.
O best of the twice-born, this is indeed a supreme secret and is not to be spoken;
nevertheless, I shall explain it because it concerns the foremost of the horse-gods.
Then, O lord of men, that man indeed related the account concerning his previous birth as a thief.
In former times, during Śivarātri, there occurred the worship of the Lord with a sense of theft, as well as the keeping of the vigil and the fasting, all performed without [proper] observance.
Endowed with the recollection of his former births, the king related to them the entire account of his previous life exactly as it had occurred.
Then all those sages offered various kinds of words of praise to that best of kings, the royal seer, accompanied by ten blessings.
Having kept vigil throughout the night, they went to the hermitage;
and the king, having likewise honored those best of the twice-born at that very time, [departed].
Having kept a vigil throughout the night, he subsequently departed for his own city.
Bhartṛyajña said:
O King, thus has Śivarātri arisen upon the surface of the earth,
and its majesty has been described to you in this manner.
Therefore, O best of kings, she should be performed with every effort,
especially in the Kali age, if one desires prosperity for oneself.
This was performed by Viṣṇupa, Nala, and Nahuṣa;
by Māndhātṛ, Dhundhumāra, Sagara, and Yuyutsu.
Likewise, other rulers of the earth, endowed with perfect faith, attained their desired wishes; and the king gazed upon them with his two eyes.
And by Satyavatī, Sāvitrī, the goddess Śrī, Sītā, Arundhatī, Sarasvatī, Pārvatī, and likewise Rambhā.
[122] And by Indrāṇī, Vṛṣāṇī, Svadhā, and likewise Svāhā;
by Rati, Prīti, Prabhāvatī, and Gāyatrī, O best of kings.
All have attained their supreme desires, endowed with exceeding good fortune;
and whoever should hear or even recite these in the presence of Śiva.
He too is liberated from the sin committed that day; there is no doubt about this.
There is no water equal to the Ganges; there is no god comparable to Hara.
There is no vow equal to Śivarātri; this truth has been spoken by me.
Meru is composed of all jewels, and the sky is filled with all wonders.
O King, Śivarātri is proclaimed to consist of all dharmas;
just as Garuḍa is among birds and the ocean among rivers,
so too is Śivarātri the most excellent and preeminent among all dharmas.
Thus ends the Śivarātrivrata in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Great King, the Caturdaśī that has passed is always extracted [as the time for the rite].
Then the extinguished fire shall once again attain existence.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How was Agni lost in former times when the task of the gods had arrived?
By whom was that fire-concealment performed there, and how indeed did you come to know it?
Kṛṣṇa said:
O great king, in ancient times the gods were defeated by Tāraka;
they questioned the Creator of the Universe, asking, "Who shall bring about his end?"
Having meditated for a long time, that Rudra, born of attachment, said:
"The infant, born from the splendors of Gaṅgā, Svāhā, and Agni, shall slay the Daitya."
Having heard this, the planets and gods, where Śambhu was together with Umā,
bowed down to him and spoke those words that had been uttered by Brahmā at that time.
And having been surpassed by Rudra, he bowed together with Umā;
praised by the immortals, he made an effort regarding that which had been spoken.
Then, for more than a hundred divine years, time passed in sexual union.
Nor is there any cessation whatsoever from that state.
And a very great fear arose among those gods, thinking:
"He who will indeed become Rudra-Umā-Sambava shall be possessed of great power."
He will slay the Daityas and the hosts of Dānavas; of this there is no doubt. After what length of time will the cessation of their seed occur?
Having reflected on this, the gods dispatched Vāyu and Agni there;
I saw them both together with you, as well as Viṣama.
And the goddess, abandoned by the gods, cursed them in anger:
"Since this fear of brahmins has been produced for me, surpassing even that of the dwellers of heaven."
Then he spoke softly to the gods and all their hosts:
"Let Agni take my vigor, which has indeed been accumulated for a very long time."
Thus addressed by Rudra, Agni vanished from the assembly of the gods;
he was neither established in heaven, nor on earth, nor in the sun, nor upon the surface of the world.
One should not exert effort in the temple of a deity, nor should one rub fire [there]. Worms, insects, and moths are on the backs of the denizens of heaven;
O swan, O peacock, O parrot, O peacock, quickly go to the multitude of conchs!
The Fire-god cursed him, saying, "Indeed, you shall become double-tongued and twice as large.
Then all the gods questioned the bird, the best among winged creatures.
O Jīvañjīvaka, tell us the truth regarding the sun:
while wandering constantly through this forest, have you ever seen fire anywhere?
He spoke not a single word that was either auspicious or inauspicious;
even when questioned again and again, he would utter no other speech.
The Fire-god, being pleased, said to him: "Live long! I shall tell you:
because nothing was spoken by you, therefore you shall have variegated body-hair."
"Live, live, live again as long as you desire and for the duration of your lifespan! O Jīvajīvaka, I grant you this second excellent boon."
Your human speech shall be clear and its meaning distinct;
if anyone is afflicted by a disease, that wise person shall perform a ritual bath.
In an instant, the lamp will become like a young partridge on Mount Śahya;
and whoever shall eat that third [offering], which is indeed censured, [shall eat] flesh.
He shall be undecaying and indeed immortal for all time;
having granted him this boon, he then attained the state of fire.
The gods also saw him right there, not having entered the bamboo;
they performed for him the birth-rites and others, their minds guided by the injunctions of the scriptures.
Then those gods, being pleased, spoke to Vaṃśa, the lord of the three worlds:
"Having become free from impurity through fervor, she will choose [sons] who have Agni as their seed."
Indeed, that which is the excellence of the bamboo staff, the lifelong celibate student,
and the merit found in the protection of the sacred fire— all that which is desired by those practicing celibacy [is attained].
That best of the twice-born attained him who was carrying a stained staff;
then, having shown favor to his lineage, they spoke these words regarding a single oblation.
"Accept the bride-price; you shall have a son.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"When Agni had vanished from the gods, by whom was the state of being Agni then assumed?"
Furthermore, after what length of time would fire attain the state of being fire?
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Brahmin, for three nights the fire is lost by one who has never possessed the state of fire;
at what time and on which lunar day (tithi) shall he regain that state of fire?
In former times, there was a great union between Utathya and Āṅgiras.
"I am indeed not superior to you in knowledge or asceticism, nor even in my son," Utathya said;
thus addressed, Angiras spoke to that sage.
Go to the abode of Brahmā, accompanied by the twice-born led by Marīci,
and joined by other sages who are the best among the Brahman-kings and royal seers.
O Brahmin, Utathya, with a distressed mind, said to those sages:
"Tell us clearly, which among us is the eldest?"
Then the sage Brahmā spoke to those two who were angry in mind:
"Go and bring the gods, the lords of the worlds, from their various abodes."
Then, having observed them together, I shall witness your marriage;
thereafter, those two, having gone together, shall bring the sages themselves.
The world-protectors, Mahendra and the others, Yama, Varuṇa, and Anila; the Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, the Viśvedevas, Bharadvāja, Atri, and Nārada.
The Gandharvas, the Vittapas, the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, the Daityas, and the Dānavas have come here;
the one of fierce rays (the Sun) has not arrived, but all the others have assembled.
Having seen all the gods, Brahmā spoke to those sages:
"Bring them here quickly, either by conciliation or else by force."
Having spoken thus, Utathya departed for the solar orb;
having gone there, he said to Mārtaṇḍa, "Come quickly and dwell here."
He then said to Utathya, "O Brahmin, how shall I proceed?
Having spoken thus, Sūrya departed for the earth once I had gone away.
Thus addressed, the sage departed for his respective assembly of the gods and related what had been said by the radiant one concerning Tapana.
Brahmā said to Aṅgiras, "Bring him here quickly.
Having been addressed by you, he went to that place where the sun blazes.
"Come, come, O Blessed Sun, back again to the abode of Utathya!
Thus addressed, the Sun went to where the gods had assembled.
Having stood for a moment, he asked, "What task has arisen?
To Mārtaṇḍa, who was thus questioning him, Brahmā replied with respect.
Go quickly, before the world is consumed by fire;
the time has come for you to depart for Goloka, which is dark blue and tawny.
Pāṭala, Harita, Śoṇa, and Śvetavaṣa have been destroyed;
as have Śākadvīpa, Kuśadvīpa, and Krauñcadvīpa with their cities.
Everything burnt by Aṅgiras shall be burnt yet again;
Aṅgiras, the Sun, shall burn the entire world for as long as it endures.
"Go now from here quickly to your own abode, O Prabhāskara.
Thus addressed by Savidhu, he ascended to his own abode.
Having approached the presence of the god-like Ravi, who resembled the fire at the end of an eon, Aṅgiras said this: "He has gone; what shall I do?"
The wise call him Angiras, a mass of ascetic merit free from blemish;
having praised him, they said, "Assume the state of fire for now upon the surface of the earth."
O best of beings, just as Agni acted previously, so too must you;
while I am praising Agni, where has he vanished and where does he abide?
Thus addressed by the gods, he then assumed the state of fire;
how he was seen by the gods as Agni has been related by him to me in its entirety.
When that task for the gods had been accomplished, the gods then said to Agni:
"O Agni, you must assume the office of the fire-god for the sinless son of Aṅgiras."
He said, "Release my place; listen to these words that bring satisfaction:
O sage, I shall become your foremost son in the first [kalpa]."
Bṛhaspati was born for the sake of honor, as were other sons of Bhava;
thus addressed, the sage was pleased and begot many sons.
Then that Aṅgiras begot sons and grandsons;
O King, Agni again obtained Agni as his guest.
Sleeping on every fourteenth day, he was born as Havyavāhana—
the bearer of oblations for the gods and for those beings who move about in households.
To each of them, this lunar day was assigned by Rudra;
this lunar day is the cause for worship by sages as well as by kings.
[128] By means of the arrows of Nala, Sandhātṛ, and Saṃvādya, as well as others such as Śāna and Puṣa,
he was the slayer of thousands of beloved ones in certain battles.

Those who were guests of ignorance, those who perished in the presence of predatory beasts, fire, or water, those who were devoured by wild animals, and those who died in the hells such as Tapana and the rest; [may they all attain liberation].
And for those who were executed by hanging or by impalement on stakes and the like,
a gift made on the auspicious fourteenth day likewise bestows the happiness of heaven.
Indeed, those men encounter various undesirable causes as well as abundant fruits to be experienced.
Thus, O King, this lunar day is recited by people as belonging to Agni;
some say it belongs to Indra, while others recite that Rudra is Agni.
O King, listen to how the fulfillment of this desire is accomplished:
by observing a fast at night alone,
through the mere knowledge of which one is liberated from all sins.
A man who is devoted to the worship of Śiva, having conquered anger and being pure,
should take the earth as his vessel and eat his meal at night.
Alms-gathering is superior to fasting; not begging is superior to alms-gathering;
eating at night is superior to not begging; therefore, one should subsist by eating at night.
The gods eat in the forenoon, likewise the sages at midday;
the ancestors eat in the afternoon, and the Guhyakas and others at twilight.
Transcending all [other] times, he should likewise eat only at night;
his food should consist of sacrificial offerings (haviṣya), he should bathe, and his diet should be light.
One should perform the fire-ritual, sleep on the ground, and eat only at night;
having prepared a mandala during the twilight hours with pure cow dung.
O King of kings, one should offer a lamp as well as the arghya water, along with flowers, perfumes, unbroken grains (akṣata), and fruits,
while meditating in the mind upon Śaṅkara with this mantra:
"The Lord of beings, the all-pervading God, the self-born, the omnipresent Śiva."
Pleased by the offering of the *arghya*, may he dispel my threefold sin.
Having given the *arghya* and fed the Brāhmaṇa, one should eat oneself while remaining silent.
Thus, at the end of the year, when the vow has been completed and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has been given,
one should present a vessel made of gold, silver, or even copper.
If one is unable [to do so], one should place an earthen vessel filled with cow's ghee upon a full water-pot,
and likewise cover it with a pair of white cloths.
Having bathed a golden image of Śiva with devotion using the five nectars and other substances,
and having placed it upon a cloth, one intent on devotion should worship it.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules with flowers, perfumes, incenses, lamps, and sandalwood, one should offer the eightfold *arghya*.
With a mind imbued with devotion, one should offer fruits, flowers, cow's milk, curd, sprouts of dūrvā grass, and sesame seeds to the deity while reciting the worship mantra.
Sandalwood, rice grains, and water constitute the eightfold *arghya*.
Water joined with the eight [substances] beginning with fruit is called the eightfold [offering].
Having held it upon one's head, one should descend to the ground on one's knees.
Incense and perfumes should be offered to Mahādeva in the proper sequence.
Having offered an oblation of edible rice and having bowed to the Supreme Lord,
one should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), avoiding any stinginess regarding one's wealth.
And it should be given to a twice-born who is learned in the Vedas and knows the Purāṇas;
he who gives all this with such devotion has been described [in this way].
Freed from all sins, accompanied by sons and grandsons,
and endowed with wealth and grain, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
At the time of death, by remembering Śiva, a person shall go to the world of Śiva;
staying there with supreme joy for four yugas.

O best of the Bharatas, he who performs at night on the auspicious eighth and fourteenth lunar days that which is prescribed by the rules of the scriptures shall become a lord of the earth in the Tretā age.
Having ascended a celestial chariot filled with the tumultuous sounds of the women of creation, he goes to the world of Maheśa with great ease.
Thus ends the vow of the fourteenth day as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In ponds filled with water and in great hermitages by the water..."
To whom do those women, nurtured by their noble families, offer the guest-offering, O Kṛṣṇa?
Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, on the fourteenth lunar day (bhūta-tithi) of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada,
one should then devotedly offer the most excellent arghya to Varuṇa.
By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and likewise by women,
with fruits, flowers, garments, lamps, lac-dye, and sandalwood;
With the seven incompatible grains, curd, flour, water, and sandalwood—
these being prepared without cooking over fire— and mixed with sesame seeds and rice.
One should worship with dates, coconuts, and likewise with *bījapūrṇātuka*—
*ātuka* being a specific kind of fruit—
as well as with grapes, pomegranates, betel nuts, and flowers.
Having drawn the god Varuṇa, the lord of aquatic creatures, within the mandala.
O Indra among kings, one imbued with devotion should worship with this mantra:
"Salutations to you, O Varuṇa; salutations to you, Lord of aquatic creatures."
O Lord of Waters, homage to you; homage to the Lord of juices.
May there be no moisture [of sin], no foul odor, and may there be no unpleasantness in my mouth.
"May Varuṇa, the lord of the Vāruṇī wine and the bestower of wealth, be equal to me.
O King, the man who worships Varuṇa with such devotion [attains this].
Having eaten food not cooked by fire at midday with a restrained mind,
O Pāṇḍava, a person of any of the four castes or even a woman [is purified] by this vow.
One should offer the *nivedya* to the Brāhmaṇa and likewise present the *naivedya*;
he who performs the Pālī-vrata in this manner, O Pārtha, remains devoted to his vow.
At that very moment, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
Just as the measure of the ocean is indeed not known by anyone, [so too is the merit of this act].
For thus, in the house of those who observe vows, it is impossible to know [the extent of] their wealth,
nor their lifespan, fame, renown, good fortune, or strength.
The greatness of the vow and its fruit are appropriate for you; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having approached the vast embankment of the river—which possesses exceedingly powerful, pure, and obstructed waters—and having formed a line with many bodies, [they stood there].
[132] For those who worship Varuṇa together with the ocean,
there shall be in their home prosperity that is priceless and unfathomable.
Thus ends the Pālī-caturdaśī vow as spoken in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, listen now to this very gift [of merit] in the assembly hall of Brahmā.
This was sung of old by Devala in the presence of the hosts of celestial sages.
Out of supreme compassion, O Pārtha, I shall fully declare to you that unsurpassed vow of Kali, which brings about grace for the worlds.
In ancient times on the summit of the celestial realm, they were honored by the gods, gandharvas, yakṣas, kinnaras, apsarases, daughters of the immortals, and daughters of the nāgas.
Having realized the worthlessness of saṃsāra, they resided in the grove of plantain trees on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada, O King.
The guest-offering (arghya) should be presented by excellent women with various kinds of fruits,
as well as with sprouted seeds, the seven types of grain, lamps, lac-dye, and sandalwood.
With curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, garments, food offerings cooked in ghee,
nutmegs, betel nuts, cloves, and plantains.
On that day, even beautiful women should offer the arghya;
listen, O lord of men, to the mantra for that very purpose.
O plantain tree, you who are always the bestower of desires, I place you within my heart; O plantain tree, grant me physical health and beauty—grant it! Salutations be to you!
O King, in this manner, whether it be a devoted man or a woman who has not yet cooked for herself with fire, or even those of the four castes, whoever should worship Rambhā—
In that family, there shall certainly be no woman who is a ruin to the lineage,
nor one who is miserable, unfortunate, deformed, wanton, or of evil conduct.
Whether she be a wanton woman, a low-caste woman, or a remarried widow, she is once again a courtesan— a female jackal howling with the sound of a donkey, a wicked woman who performs deceitful acts.
And she who never deviates from her vow of devotion to her husband shall become rich in the happiness of conjugal fortune and endowed with the glory of sons and grandsons.
May the long-lived Kīrtimatī live for a hundred years upon this earth;
for in former times, this vow was practiced by Gāyatrī while she resided in heaven.
Likewise, he was with Gaurī on Kailāsa, with Paulomī in the Nandana grove,
with Lakṣmī in Śvetadvīpa, and with Rādhā upon the circle of the earth.
With Arundhatī in the Dāruvana forest, with Svāhā on Mount Meru,
with Sītā at Citrakūṭa, and with Vedavatī in the Himalayas.
O Pārtha, O auspicious one, this excellent vow was performed by Mānumatī in the city called Nagara; it is auspicious when the month of Bhādrapada has arrived.
Whatever she does, she is never overcome by sufferings.
Those who worship the beautiful plantain tree with its blossoming stalks using flowers, unbroken grains, incense, and lamps—
in their homes, [misfortunes] never arise at any time.
For women who act ignobly are like widows, though they be not deformed.
Thus ends the Kadalī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Deities known as Śrāvaṇīs are heard of as being famous throughout the world.
Who are they, and what indeed should one do for their sake? Tell me of their dharma.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pāṇḍava, there exist meritorious deities named Śrāvaṇyas,
created by Brahmā at the beginning, and a specific duty was assigned to them among mankind.
Whatever one speaks here in this world, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
they swiftly bring it within the range of Brahmā’s hearing.
And for this reason, those [powers] of Prajāpati are always honored in the world:
the cognition of hearing from afar and the range of vision from afar.
O Pārtha, that which exists among them should be heard by men who are contented and well-nourished, through causes and effects, by means of inconceivable and logical reasons.
They cause him to hear [the Veda], and thus they become "śrāvaṇī" for the Creator; for that reason, they are so remembered.
Just as there are gods, just as there are Daityas, just as there are Vidyādharas and humans.
Just as here there are Siddhas, Gandharvas, Nāgas, Kiṃpuruṣas, birds, Rākṣasas,
and Piśācas— the eight classes of beings born from the gods.
Likewise, because they perform meritorious deeds, these [days] beginning with Indra are known as Śrāvaṇikās;
men and women together should observe the vow dedicated to them.
However, their vow-restraint is always very severe;
having smelled incense, cooked food, water, or even fragrance [they must maintain it].
Furthermore, food must be given to other women at the conclusion of their meal;

if one has eaten at the conclusion of another vow, that same vow must be performed by oneself as well, otherwise— as there will be the fault described later— the vow is extremely severe, O Pāṇḍava, even if death should occur before it is completed.
Then, seized by throat-obstruction (*galagraha*), they become speechless, emitting gurgling sounds;
vomiting foam and blood, they die in extreme agony.
It is heard, however, O Pārtha, that in ancient times there was a sinless king upon the earth.
O descendant of Bharata, his wife was the great queen named Japaśrī,
who was endowed with beauty in all her limbs and possessed of every virtue.
Devoted to the service of her husband and exceedingly dear to him,
she once went to bathe at the hermitage of a sage on the Gaṅgā.
Then he saw the virtuous Arundhatī, the wife of Vasiṣṭha,
feeding the wives of the sages with meals of food.
And so, having prostrated herself, the Great Holy Lady was questioned by the Goddess:
"O Blessed One, you are worshipped; tell me, what is this that is called a vow?"
"O auspicious one, O great virtuous lady, show compassion toward me as well.
Arundhatī said:
"Listen, blessed lady, I shall explain the vow known by the name Śrāvaṇika."
This was related by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, his own master.
This is the secret, auspicious dharma that brings about the fulfillment of all one's vows;
whether you go or stay, O Queen, I shall offer you hospitality.
Having spoken thus, O Pārtha, Jayaśrī, after being invited at her own pleasure,
ate that which was most dear to her, out of respect shown by the sage’s wife.
Having eaten and sipped water, the Supreme Goddess quickly departed for her own city;
in time, however, she forgot that vow involving the meal.
Then, when the time was fulfilled, that great virtuous woman, Jayaśrī, as she was dying,
uttered a gurgling sound with a voice faltering in her throat.
Vomiting froth mixed with saliva from their mouths again and again,
they remained for fifteen days with loathsome and terrible countenances.
Then, when the sixteenth year had arrived, having heard of Arundhatī’s conduct,
he quickly entered the inner apartments and beheld the queen.
He related to Nahuṣa what had been eaten during the Śrāvaṇī vow;
having heard that, King Nahuṣa indeed made the vow his food.
As it was said, Arundhatī gave that which was desired in its entirety, as much as was wished for; and eight auspicious water-pots were offered, dedicated to Jayaśrī.
In an instant, O lord of men, she passed away;
having been released from her mortal coil, she ascended to the realm of Śakra in a celestial chariot radiant as the sun.
Being shaken by chowries and struck by gods and asuras...
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, O Supreme Person, what should be done there by men?"
Tell me in great detail about the Śrāvaṇī-vrata, or [tell it] by means of women.
Kṛṣṣṇa said:
O lord of men, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa,
and likewise on the eighth day, a man should bathe at midday in pure water.
And he should invite women of noble family, or even just one according to his ability;
or Brahmin women of good conduct who are of the same lineage, according to his means.
Just as one should [invite] a single Brahmin there who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas,
who knows the mantras and the Itihāsas, and who is pure, tranquil, and has conquered his senses.
Having offered the arghya according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the washing of the feet.
One should adorn [the deity] with fragrant sandalwood, as well as flowers, incense, and so forth,
and with necklaces, threads, vermilion, saffron, and other ornaments.
Then one should offer excellent, well-cooked food, both solid and soft;
twelve vardhanīs should be placed before them.
The *vardhanī* is a water-vessel;
it should be without cracks, filled with water, clearly visible, and wrapped with thread.
Covered with *somalaka* flowers, adorned with garlands of blossoms,
anointed with sandalwood paste, and each provided individually with much gold.
In the midst of that, O Pārtha, the sacrificer himself should then stand upon the mandala and place a single vardhanī vessel upon his own head.
One should recite this mantra while meditating upon Keśava in the mind:
"Whatever has been done in childhood, in youth, or even in old age..."
May that debt of mine arising from the ancestors, gods, and humans be fully discharged;
this vow of mine is now fulfilled—deliver me from the ocean of existence.
"Free from debt, I wish to go to the stainless abode of Viṣṇu.
"So be it," all those women should say, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then, having summoned a brahmin, the sacrificer should say this:
"O brahmin sage, recite the mantra by which one may go to the imperishable."
Then, O son of Pāṇḍu, the virtuous twice-born man should carefully recite this mantra while placing the vardhanī vessel upon her head.
O well-formed one, burn away my debt with the head of this goddess;
[whether it be] the *kaduka*, the *nisvavṛkṣa*, or the *madhuka* from there, O mother!
Then, O Brahmin, go to Mahādeva at Śrāvya on that auspicious day of Śrāvaṇika;
having bowed your head, speak these words.
At that time, one should present the vardhanikā vessel to that brahmin;
thus, having made this agreement and having quickly given those [gifts], they went to the forests.
The agreement is that they shall speak with one voice;
having taken water-pots, the women should go to their own homes.
O best of kings, she who, having taken up her water-pot and eaten at the proper time, diligently observes the Śrāvaṇī vow in her own home;
When her time has arrived, she meets death in happiness;
endowed with wealth and grain, she is adorned with sons and grandsons.
Devoted to the service of her husband, free from mental and physical ailments,
and endowed with incomparable good fortune, the virtuous wife shall live for a hundred years.
Remembering Hari at the time of death, one goes to the abode of Hari;
born again and again among mortals, she shall become the beloved of Gaurī.
O Pāṇḍava, even a man, having observed this vow according to the prescribed rule and having made a formal agreement with other men, shall obtain this same fruit.
Those people who listen with devotion to this vow as it is being recited shall,
liberated from all sins, go to heaven without a doubt.
Indeed, those women who, for the sake of the gods, ancestors, and hosts of Siddhas, offer fresh food mixed with jaggery and ghee,
as well as water-pots containing both water and food, are worthy of being heard from.
Having wandered upon the earth, they bestow happiness and then pass away.
Thus ends the Śrāvaṇikā-vrata as spoken in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Agastya said:
"He who has not performed the Aśvamedha and other sacrifices, nor even practiced great austerity,"
And since you have not given gold and knowledge to the Brahmins, you shall become fickle.
Without bathing in all the sacred fords, without studying all the Vedas,
and without practicing self-yoga, how could one attain the desired goal?
How may there be the attainment of all desires, both in this world and the next,
and how may the realm of Śiva be reached, from which return is difficult to obtain?
Even by the floods of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, committed over many lifetimes.
O Six-faced One, tell me how one might be liberated in an instant,
even without performing the worship of Śiva according to the extensive rites described in the Purāṇas.
Tell me, what is that which brings satisfaction with little effort and which is auspicious and divine?
Skanda said:
When the vow has been performed, O Great King, all this is obtained.
O Sage, it immediately bestows heaven, liberation, and other goals, and grants satisfaction to Śaṅkara.
The fourteenth day, conjoined with the asterism of the Water-jar-born (Kumbha) and Śiva; "Water-jar-born" is an address to Agastya; the asterism of Śiva is Ārdrā.
Now, the pair of Bhādrapadās is joined with one [of them].
The meaning is: "on whichever [lunar day] falls between the pair of Pūrvābhādrapadā and Uttarābhādrapadā.
For on that [day], Rudra conquered Tripura and likewise Andhaka;
he destroyed Dakṣa and rendered him free from pride.
Therefore, because it bestows victory, this lunar day grants satisfaction to Śaṅkara.
From him, Gaurī obtained an excellent boon;
and from that very same [source], the auspicious and supreme Śiva himself was born as her son, named Nakula.
Therefore, for the sake of the supreme propitiation of Śivā, one should perform a vow for her;
Lord Śaṅkara bestows both sovereignty and liberation in this world.
And among the vows of great kings, he was one who brought satisfaction to Śiva alone;
that man performed all these many vows.
Not even by thousands of horse-sacrifices, nor by hundreds of Rājasūyas,
nor by various vows performed, nor by the highest practices of yoga.
The fruit obtained by the Great King through the observance of his vow is not equal to that of giving ten billion tawny cows to virtuous Brahmins who are worthy recipients.
Between one who would give this [gift] and one who would perform this [rite], the latter is superior;
for by worshipping Śambhu even once, he is not surpassed even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
And Hari himself spoke these words:
"I am present when one has performed merit accumulated over hundreds of millions of births."
"And you, O Great King, ought to ensure that this vow is performed without obstacle.
Agastya said:
"O Guha, I have heard from you the majesty of this king of vows."
[141] Now I desire to hear the ritual procedure that grants one's desired object.

Skanda said: On the fourteenth day of Āgastya, whether under the asterism Ārdrā or Bhādrapadā, and whether it be the bright or the dark fortnight, there is no distinction, just as there is none regarding the cow.

Then, O Great King, having become one who has obtained a single birth, a man should, on the thirteenth lunar day, perform the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for all the vows according to the prescribed rule.
Then, on the fourteenth day, one should perform a bath with sesame seeds, cow urine, and cow dung;
then with clay, then with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and thereafter with pure water.
Then one should recite the Śivasankalpa mantra one thousand times.
The Śivasankalpa mantra is the Yajurvedic text beginning with "yaj jāgrato dūram" and so forth, as well-known in the Yajur Veda branch.
However, for a Śūdra, the six-syllabled mantra [removes] the effects of actions committed over ten million lifetimes.
The six-syllable mantra is "namaḥ śivāya.
By performing this, one is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt about this.
One should bathe Śambhu, together with Umā, at home with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
By bathing in Puṣkara with the five products of the cow, sugarcane extracts, fragrant waters, and medicinal herbs, one obtains the fruit of giving ten million tawny cows.
Having anointed Śambhu with gorocanā, sandalwood, saffron, cardamom, camphor, black agallochum, devadāru, musk, and other such substances;
One obtains the merit arising from the horse sacrifice and other such rites.

With the five auspicious flowers (*pañcaka*), *kuśa* grass, *śaī*, and *marica*; with *tulasī*, *śephālikā*, *atimuktaka*, and *mallikā*; with the glorious *mālatī*, white water-lilies (*kumuda*), and bees among the hundred-petaled lotuses (*śatapatra*).
Worship yields the fruit of hundreds of millions of month-long fasts.
Śrībilva, padminī, and bhṛṅgarāja;
one should offer incense made from these five ingredients, or else the prescribed ten-ingredient incense, along with guggulu smeared with ghee, before the Lord.
By giving away this entire earth filled with fuel and grain, one quickly attains that fruit which is to be obtained.
Having offered a row of lamps blazing with fragrant oil, or even lamps made from cow-ghee,
or else having bestowed blessings upon young maidens;
One shall obtain the fruit of giving ten million [gifts].
By offering milk-rice, meat-balls, rice-essence, sweetmeats, and *aśokavarti* at Kurukṣetra, one partakes in the merit of a gift of gold.
Then, the observer of the vow should place hair from the front of the neck and from the head upon a black antelope skin;
the remainder of the sentence implies "in front of Maheśvara.
There, he should humbly fashion heaps made of stone, measuring one *āṭaka* each, at various places.
But it is deficient by two *prasthas* according to the measure of a poor man's *prastha*.
One should place a wide, auspicious seat made of wood upon it; then, one should place two items thereon for the purpose of bathing with saffron and unguents.
The pair known as Umā-Maheśvara,
having wrapped it in white cloth, one should then make it very firm;
that is the "pair" (dvipa).
To the north of that, however, one should place another [image] covered with white cloth.
Another second elephant;
then the door, and in the center [the following]: a trident, an axe, a bow, a sword, a skull-bowl, a khaṭvāṅga staff, the Gaṅgā, the Moon, and the great bull.

Having established these golden [images] as well as a pair of golden cattle, one should next place a door between the two elephants. Then, between the door, the elephant, and Maheśvara, one should place the trident, the axe, the bow, and so forth.
[One should worship them] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains, incense, lamps, garments, and food offerings.
One should honor [the deity] with various foods and drinks cooked in oil, as well as with diverse fruits.
Having taught the four Vedas to ten million Brahmins and having given all the Purāṇas, one obtains that same fruit.
By reciting even once a single Ṛg verse, a single Yajus formula, a single Sāman chant, or a single Atharvan verse,
one obtains the merit of having mastered the four Vedas and a hundred supreme refuges.
Having circumambulated the Sage and prostrated like a staff before the Lord, the Master ten times,
one who desires liberation attains it at will.
The observer of the vow obtains his desire exactly as he has requested.
Then, reciting the Śivasaṃkalpa hymn while offering a thousand bilva leaves, or muttering the Tryambaka mantra, one should perform the fire oblation.
Whatever fruit one obtains by bathing at all sacred fords, by performing all sacrifices at all times, and by observing all vows— that same fruit shall be attained here.
[144] Then one should offer the *arghya* to Śiva with fragrant substances, flowers, and white unbroken grains (*akṣata*),
together with excellent diamonds, gems, rubies, pearls, and emeralds.
In a vessel made of jewels, gold, silver, or the like, or likewise in one made of bell-metal or copper,
one whose knees rest upon the ground should offer the *arghya* water that has been consecrated.
In the vessel, on the forehead, and in the hollowed palms of the twice-born.
Salutations be to You, the auspicious, the peaceful, the cause of all; salutations to You, the omnipresent, the knower of all,
the infinite Lord of all, and the giver of everything.
Homage be to the one whose form is not left out by all radiance.
Having offered the *argha* with this mantra during a solar eclipse at Kurukṣetra,
the practitioner of the vow obtains that same fruit which one gains by giving cows, land, gold, and other gifts.
Even liberation is easily attained by him, O King; what need is there to mention [sovereignty] over the realms of the gods?
Having performed the great vow for the sake of the supreme goal, Maheśa.

By means of these three recitations of yours throughout the remainder of the night, a person shall spend the entire night in wakefulness; thus, he will no longer be subject to the causes of hell and other such states.
O Kṛṣṇa, there is no fruit of unrighteous action for the great-souled ones.
Whether by day or by night, whatever thirst, hunger, or their combination may arise,
one should provide for all of this, including the black antelope skin and other requisites, with the mantra.
One should provide fifteen tawny cows, or ten, or two, or even one auspicious cow, all equipped with every necessary utensil, and dedicate them according to the mantra alone.
May the eternal Śiva, the Great Lord who destroys all impurity, be pleased with me;
he is the great king of vows, who has been gratified.
May he always grant me the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Then, having eaten again at dawn, the observer of the vow should give curd to a twice-born man who is an instructor in the ritual,
preceded by a seat made of the skin of a black antelope belonging to the Lord of Sages.
Standing with palms joined in reverence, he recites the mantra of offering.
Be gracious to me, O Lord of All, O Consort of Umā; lift me up from this ocean of worldly existence as I bow before you.
You have always been honored by me through the sovereign of all vows.
Saying "You are my refuge," I have indeed come for protection.
Having thus observed this with a preliminary salutation, the excellent teacher bestows this as prescribed;
he effects absorption into Śiva according to the scriptures.
He does not return again to the presence of the one born from the jar.
Then, having consumed the five products of the cow and observed silence while eating, the practitioner,
having severed all obstacles, attains the supreme state.
Skanda said:
"In this regard also, O Agastya, it is heard that the best of the twice-born, Viśvadeva,
was intent on the diversion of sport with Umā in the assembly of the gods."
The gods, beginning with Ravi and Brahmā, were conquered by that splendor;
their radiance overwhelmed, they went to Brahmā in fear.
Brahmā said: In former times, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) performed a great vow;
Viśvadeva beheld that which was being performed by Mudgala.

Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O King, I shall recount in detail the ancient history of Holi, which has been handed down through tradition.

Having conquered the entire earth and brought the lords of men under his control,

While that king was ruling, there was neither famine nor disease, nor untimely death among men; nor were there any wicked people who took delight in unrighteousness.

coming both by day and by night, she afflicts many children."

Having heard the words of the citizens, Raghu was filled with wonder;

Raghu said:
"O best of the twice-born, who is this Rākṣasa named Ḍhoṇḍha, and what is his power?
How is this evildoer to be restrained by me?"
He is called a *rājā* because of his protection; he is a *pati* because of his guardianship of the earth.
A king who fails to protect the earth becomes a sinner.
Vasiṣṭha said:

[she is the foremost] among unchaste women, and especially among men.
She drinks her fill of the blood that flows from the cutting of her nose.

"O lord of men, today is the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna;

Let people speak as they please, free from hesitation, according to whatever opinion each holds,

Extending and chanting his thousand names,
that wicked woman was indeed driven away by that sound and by the oblation.

and by that fierce deed, the Rākṣasī met her destruction.
From that time forth, this fire-offering (homa) has become known in this world as Aḍāḍā;

O Pārtha, because it is performed by the twice-born on this day, it is known as Holi;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this full-moon day is the essence of all lunar days.
Because she is the essence of all worlds and bestows supreme bliss,
O Pārtha, infants must be kept safely within the house when night falls.
In the courtyard of the house, which has been smeared with cow dung and provided with a quadrangular space,

what should people who desire happiness do at dawn on the first day of the month of Māgha when the sun has risen?
Kṛṣṇa said:

O Indra among kings, listen to me as this mantra is recited:

one should afterwards cause the wise man to consume the mango flower together with the sandalwood.
That worship of the mind-born [Kāma] was demonstrated by the seers.

And the mantra for consuming [the offering] is:
"This foremost blossom of the mango tree belonging to spring,
together with sandalwood, I drink today for the fulfillment of all desires."
Immediately thereafter, one should give gifts according to one's ability to the foremost of the twice-born, to the sūtas, māgadhas, and bards, saying: "May my desire be fulfilled."

O Pārtha, for one who thus performs the Phālguna festival as prescribed in the scriptures,
all their heart's desires are fulfilled without effort.
Mental anxieties and physical ailments are undoubtedly destroyed;
the person remains happy, endowed with sons and grandsons.
Meritorious, purifying, and everywhere destructive of all obstacles—
thus, O Pārtha, has this most excellent of lunar days been described to you.
When the season of frost had passed, on the morning of the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, as the spring season had arrived,
he partook of mango blossoms together with sandalwood paste.
Truly, O Pārtha, a person who is even-minded shall be happy.
This shall continue for as long as a year.
Thus ends the procedure for the Holi festival as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

It pacifies all diseases and destroys all that is inauspicious;
by performing it even once, protection shall be established for one year.
Kṛṣṇa said: Listen, O tiger among the Pāṇḍavas, to an ancient history concerning what was formerly performed by Indrāṇī for the sake of increasing Śakra’s victory.
In ancient times, there was a twelve-year war between the gods and the asuras;
therein, Śakra was defeated by the asuras along with all the foremost of the gods.
Abandoning heaven along with the gods and divested of all his ornaments,
he reached Amarāvatī and remained there, intent solely on saving his life.
Then, having brought them together, the king of the Dānavas said: "Listen, you gods and men, for the three worlds have been brought under my control."
"Worship me and praise me; I am worthy of worship by gods and asuras alike.
Whoever, even Śakra, should act otherwise, he shall meet his death at my hands."
Then, by the word of the Lord of the Dānavas, all ritual acts were destroyed,
including those consisting of the utterances of Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭ, and so forth.
The Vedas were not studied, the deities were not worshipped, and festivals were not celebrated; everything was in a state of total disorder.
Upon the destruction of Dharma, the lord of the gods suffered a loss of strength;
perceiving him to be utterly weakened, all the Dānavas rushed forward to attack.
Though he had been driven away by the hosts of asuras and had lost his kingdom, the king of the gods,
having addressed Bṛhaspati, spoke these words:
I am unable to remain here, nor can I depart, being pursued by them;
I desire to fight in every way—whatever is destined to happen, let that happen.
Life endures even through battle;
the Creator fashioned the giver [of life] only so long as it was not yet desired by the mind.
"O Brahmin, you predict victory for me; I shall fight with the Dānavas.
It is better to blaze for a moment than to smolder for a long time."
The sovereignty of the gods is dependent on karma, and human effort is also said to be karma.
"Therefore, I shall do this today; it will certainly result in the highest good.
Having heard these words of the Lord of the Gods, Bṛhaspati then spoke.
Bṛhaspati said:
"This is not the time for valor now; abandon your anger, O Purandara!
Actions devoid of proper place and time result in the opposite of what was intended."
If these deeds are obstructed, it would result in a very great calamity.
Indra said:
"O Brahmin, what is the use of much speaking? I shall fight with the Dānavas."
For men, single-mindedness is the best course at the commencement of any undertaking.
When both these qualities and defects are unified by the wise,
whatever task is undertaken, its defects turn away.
While the two were thus conversing, Śacī said to the Lord of the Gods:
"O God, today is the day of Bhūta; tomorrow morning there will be a festival."
"I shall perform a protection rite by which victory will be achieved.
And the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra carried out everything according to the words of Paulomī.
Then, on the morning of the full moon, Paulomī, having performed the auspicious rites,
bound a beautiful protective amulet upon her right hand.
Then Śakra, the slayer of the enemies of the gods, having had his protection secured and having had benedictions performed by the twice-born,
mounted the elephant Airāvata and went forth.
Having reached the army of the Dānavas and proclaimed his own name,
he struck down the heads of his enemies with sharpened arrows.
Seeing him arrive so suddenly, the Dānavas were greatly delighted;
they assailed Śakra with sharp arrows and peacock-feathered shafts.
Prahlāda, the lord of the Dānavas, said to all the Dānavas:
"By good fortune, you have today obtained the sight of this slayer of a Brahmin coming within the range of your vision."
"O Dānavas, having quickly united with this multitude of chariots—
that is, with this collection of chariots—
let an effort be made while that wicked one has not yet perished."
Then, by the words of the lord of the Dānavas, those descendants of Danu [departed].
Breaking their silence, the great-souled ones said to Śakra, "We have been slain!
Thereupon, the lord of Śacī, enraged, raised his radiant thunderbolt.
He struck down the host of Dānavas in an instant, like Time destroying all creatures;
those mighty Dānavas were being slaughtered by the Lord of the Gods.
Terrified by extreme fear and deluded by the thought that this was the end of time,
some entered the ocean while others took refuge in the dense forest.
With shaven heads and emaciated, they lived naked in the forest,
proclaiming the dharma of compassion and adhering to the vow of the Nirgranthas.
Foolish people, devoted to the doctrine of causality, deceive the multitudes of living beings;
thus Śakra returned to his own abode after having utterly defeated the Daityas.
He protected the three worlds while being honored by gods and asuras;
then, their joy destroyed by the lord of the gods, the asuras came to Śukra for refuge.
Having prostrated, they said: "I have been defeated in battle by my enemy;
for even Śakra has been defeated by this one whose prowess is inferior to that of a Brahmarṣi."
"Therefore, shame on human effort in this world; for destiny is indeed more powerful.
Śukra said:
"Do not despair, O Daityas; such is the course of affairs."
By fate, victory and defeat for living beings occur at the proper time through your agency.
An alliance with Śakra would not be appropriate now;
for by Śacī, the Lord of Śacī has been rendered invincible to all enemies.
By the power of the protective thread-binding, the great lord of the Dānavas has been conquered;
wait for one year, and thereafter prosperity will come to pass.
Released by Bhārgava himself, those Dānavas were freed from their fever;

O Yudhiṣṭhira, this power of the protective rite has been described to you;

Yudhiṣṭhira said:

For however many diverse things you speak, O Blessed One, just so am I not satiated as I hear these discourses of manifold meaning.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, when the sky was covered with clouds and the earth’s surface was lush with green grass,
at the break of day on the full moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
A wise person should perform his bath according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti;
thereafter, he should offer libations to the gods and the ancestors with the finest water.
O observer of noble vows, the Brāhmaṇa should perform the rites beginning with the Upākarma, as well as the libation to the sages, and he should perform the Śrāddha ceremony dedicated to the Vedas.
For Śūdras, bathing and giving gifts without mantras are recommended.
Then, at the time of afternoon, [one should prepare] an auspicious protective amulet-case.
One should have it fashioned with auspicious unbroken grains and white mustard seeds, adorned with gold,

One should place [the image] woven with variegated threads upon a silver plate.

Whoever performs the binding of the protective thread according to this rite shall remain free from all defects and happy for a year.
The person who, during the month of Śrāvaṇa, listens to this cooling water [mantra] while the Lord of the Gods presides, and performs this rite of protection,

He, together with his sons and grandsons, and accompanied by his circle of friends, [departed].
Thus ends the vow of the Full Moon of the Tying of the Protective Thread (*rakṣābandhana-pūrṇimā-vrata*) in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.

The sages said:
You have related this which was heard [by us]: the liberation from the bonds of Paśu, the Pāśupata vow belonging to Liṅga, which was practiced of old by the gods.

"In ancient times, the Lord created Śailādi [Sanatkumāra]."

O best of Brahmins, having fashioned a small linga and bathed it with sandalwood water,

Having fashioned an auspicious golden lotus, complete with a pericarp and filaments,

O observer of noble vows, having bathed [the deity] with white thousand-petaled lotuses, red lotuses, blue water-lilies, or whatever other flowers are available, while reciting the Gāyatrī mantra;

In the absence of those, one should worship with silver and bilva leaves;
and even in the absence of gems, one may worship with gold or silver.
If even silver is not available, one should have it made of copper or iron;
