in the white *arkakusuma* flower, Prajāpati himself is present as the four-faced one.
In the flower of the *karṇikāra* tree, wisdom (*medhā*) is directly established;
in the *karavīra*, the Lord of the Gaṇas; and in the *baka*, Nārāyaṇa himself.
Since the daughter of the mountain [Pārvatī] delights in all flowers of excellent fragrance,
therefore, with these flowers as they may be obtained, as well as incense and other offerings—
One should worship the Lord of the Gods with devotion according to one's means;
thereafter, one should devotedly offer milk-rice and the great sacrificial oblation (mahācaru).
It should be accompanied by ghee and side dishes, provided with all necessary ingredients;
it may be pure rice, or rice mixed with mung beans, or even rice with *āḍhakī* beans.
The offerings and flowers, acquired solely through righteous means,
as well as various kinds of food, were then consecrated with water.
For the sake of the stability of all the gods, the nectar was prepared from milk and clarified butter;
it was established by Viṣṇu himself, the victorious one, within the waters.
Therefore, one should worship the God; for life-breath (prāṇa) is established in food, nourishment in the offering, and the wind itself in the fan.
Mahādeva is the soul of all; indeed, the Lord of Waters resides in the fragrant water, while Mahādeva himself is directly established as Prakṛti upon the cloth.
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, one should thus worship with devotion according to the prescribed rite on every full moon day.
Truthfulness, purity, compassion, forbearance, contentment, and indeed generosity— O Brahmins, one should likewise observe a fast on the full moon day;
and at the end of the year, one should especially perform the gift of a cow and the ritual release of a bull.
One should devoutly feed Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas and have mastered them;
by that, the Liṅga is worshipped along with all ritual materials.
Or one should install it in a sacred field of Śiva, or give it to a Brāhmaṇa;
thus, in all months, the Śivaliṅga is the great vow.
O best of sages, one should perform that very act with devotion, for it is the supreme among all austerities;
[one shall travel] in celestial chariots adorned with jewels and resplendent like ten million suns.
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva, he never returns here again;
or else, within a single month, he should indeed observe this most excellent vow.
One attains the world of Śiva; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Or else, even a man devoid of wealth who meditates upon that liṅga [attains the same].
Having attained a divine station for one year as a boon, he shall go to Śiva;
he shall attain the state of a god, the state of a progenitor, and even the sovereignty of the gods.
Even a man who is capable attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas;
one seeking knowledge obtains knowledge, and one seeking enjoyment shall obtain enjoyment.
Seeking wealth, one obtains merit; those who desire long life obtain it;
and whatever desires one contemplates, one attains them all here and rejoices.
By the mere observance of this vow for one month, one shall attain Rudra at its conclusion.
This is the supreme purifier, a secret,
and the best of vows, as perceived by the Creator of the Universe.
For the benefit of the gods, asuras, and mortals here,
and for the supreme welfare of the vidyādharas through auspiciousness.
Having thus worshipped the Lord according to the prescribed rite and having bowed his head along with his servants and sons,
he performed the recitation and hymn of praise known as the *Vyapohana*.
Having circumambulated Śiva with great effort.
Long ago, for the welfare of the three worlds, this hymn was composed by the Creator,
the Grandfather himself, together with the Lord of the Gods.
But because of its great power, this is highly precious.
Having heard it from the mouth of Nandin, I shall now recite this auspicious hymn, which bestows all accomplishments, as it was spoken by the high-souled Kumāra.
This was told by Vyāsa, or heard from him with great reverence;
salutations to Śiva, the pure, the stainless, and the illustrious.
Salutation to the destroyer of Vṛṣa, to the All, to Bhava, to the Supreme Self;
He who indeed has five faces and ten arms, and is endowed with fifteen eyes.
Resembling pure crystal, adorned with all ornaments,
omniscient, omnipresent, peaceful, and firmly established above all—
may this Soma, seated upon the lotus throne, swiftly dispel my sin.
May Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Sadyojāta,
and the blessed Vāmadeva swiftly dispel all evil.
May Ananta, the Lord of all sciences, dispel my sin;
for Rudra is indeed the one Guru, and the Moon is known throughout the three worlds.
May the Blessed Lord Īśa, who consists of the three forms, who awakens devotion to Śiva, and who is fully perfected through meditation on Śiva, dispel my sin. May he,
who is solely accomplished in the meditation on Śiva, remove my evil.
May Śrīkaṇṭha, the Lord of Śrī, the illustrious one who is ever devoted to the meditation on Śiva and is himself directly enamored of Śivā, dispel my sin.
May the venerable Śikhaṇḍin, who is peaceful through the smearing of Śiva’s ashes,
devoted to the worship of Śiva, and glorious, dispel my sin.
The goddess Trailokyanāmitā, the ancient Oṃkārā,
the great goddess Dīkṣāyaṇī, and the auspicious Gaurī Haimavatī.
Ekavarṇā, Agra-jā, Māyā, and likewise Pāṭalā;
Aparṇā is the goddess Varadā, who is solely intent upon the granting of boons.
Umā, the destroyer of sins, is present in person at Kāśī;
she is the goddess who wields the khaṭvāṅga staff, whose fingertips are like delicate sprouts,
and who is surrounded by her sons, the divine Naiṣkarmaka and others.
The lotus-eyed goddess Kālikā was with Menā and Nandā;
she who is the mother of the high-souled Vītaśoka and Nandin,
and who is Śubhāvatī, Suśīrṣā, Pañcacūḍā, and the bestower of boons.
And the imperishable Prakṛti has proceeded for the sake of the creation of all beings,
expanded by means of the twenty-three principles beginning with Mahat.
The daughter of the mountain, eternally bowed to by Lakṣmī and the other Śaktis,
is the great goddess who churns the mind; she is Māyā, fond of adornment,
for by her Māyā indeed the entire world, including Brahmā and all else, both moving and unmoving, exists.
The Yoginī who eternally agitates and deludes is established in the heart;
she dwells in the eleventh world, her eyes resembling blue lotuses.
She is eternally praised with supreme devotion by all the gods,
headed by Gaṇendra, Ambhojagarbha, Indra, Yama, and Vitteśa.
She has arisen as their mother, the destroyer of all calamities;
she is the remover of the distress of devotees, auspicious, and she sports within the nature of worldly existence.
The Goddess who bestows enjoyment and liberation, who grants fearlessness to her devotees—
may that Goddess Umā herself swiftly dispel my sin.
May the illustrious Caṇḍasarvagaṇeśāna, who emerged from the mouth of Śambhu and is devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel my sin.
The Lord Sālaṅkāyanapātra, the master who stands upon the plow in the fire,
let that god, the sovereign of all hosts of beings, attain the state of Yama and the status of Manu.
The giver of all, the all-pervading, the light of all, the Lord, the Sovereign—
[he who is worshipped] by the gods together with Nārāyaṇa, along with Indra, the Moon, and the Sun.
And by all the yakṣas, gandharvas, and bhūtas who bring about prosperity,
as well as by the uragas, the ṛṣis, and the high-souled Brahmā.
May Nandin, the lord of the three worlds, who dwells within the inner apartments as a sage,
praised and ever worshipped by all, dispel our sin.
Mahākāla, of great splendor, like another Mahādeva,
devoted to the worship of Śiva and endowed with glory— may he dispel my sin.
May that bull, the tiger among sages, who is solely devoted to the meditation on Śiva and constantly engaged in the worship of Śiva, dispel my sin.
Measuring nine crores, resembling Mount Meru and Mandara,
it was adorned with divine elephants such as Airāvata and others, all endowed with celestial yoga.

Having bound the function [of the mind] within the stalk of the heart-lotus of the Lotus-eyed One and having restrained it—He who is Gajendravaktra himself, whose feet reach down to the seven netherworlds; [205]
The seven islands are his arms;
Śiva follows all sacred fords along with the seven oceans and the mines.
The god is the devourer, the god whose arms are smeared [with ashes], whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire.
The great trees, the great vidyās, and the exceedingly fierce ones have had their asuras slain;
they are [conquered] by divine dhāraṇīs consisting of Vedic riddles and endowed with the noose of yoga.

The aged one, whose eyes are like the white lotus, resides within the thicket of the heart-lotus; he who is Gajendravaktra is directly surrounded by hundreds of millions of Gaṇas, both those engaged in activity and those withdrawn from it.
May he who is fully accomplished through meditation on Śiva,
the lord of Bhṛgu, with tawny eyes and his body smeared with ashes, dispel my sin.
May that glorious one, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva, who eternally crushes all enemies with his four bodies, dispel my sin.
May Skanda— the wielder of the spear, the peaceful one, the leader of the army, whose vehicle is the elephant,
the glorious commander of Śiva’s forces— dispel my sin.
May Manu, Āśava, as well as Īśāna, Rudra, Paśupati,
Ugra, Bhīma, and Mahādeva— who is ever devoted to the worship of Śiva—
those forms of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) remove my sin.
Mahādeva, Śiva, Rudra, the hundred-headed one, Nīlalohita, Īśāna, Vijaya, Bhīma, Devadeva, and Bhavodbhava.
And Kapīśa and Divākara—
these indeed, Bhairava and the others, who are Rudras equal to Rudra himself,
having attained union with the life-force of Śiva, may they remove my impurity.
Vaikartana, Vivasvat, Mātanga, Bhāskara, Ravi,
Lokaprakāśaka, Lokasākṣin, and Trivikrama.
Āditya, as well as Sūrya, Aṃśumat, and Divākara—
may these twelve Ādityas indeed dispel my impurity.
The sky, touch, fire, taste, and the plants of the earth;
the moon, the sun, and likewise the self—the Vasus, all imbued with Śiva.
May the Vasus, Pāvaka, Cyavana, and Ṛti dispel my sin, impurity, and manifold fears.
Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, the Lord Īśāna, Hari,
and the Blessed Grandfather (Brahmā) were all intent upon meditation on Śiva.
May these— the arm that touches with its rays, the wind, and likewise the Maruts— dispel the evil committed by thought and deed.
Prāṇa, apāna, jīva, īśa, and marut are thus described.
May everyone devoted to the worship of Śiva remove my impurity—
whether they be a sky-walker, one who moves through the eight [directions], a slayer of a Brahmin, a knower of Brahman, or one of pure intellect.
Suṣeṇa, Śāśvata, Puṣṭa, and the mighty Apuṣṭa—
these indeed are the Cāraṇas of Śambhu, who are exceedingly resplendent through their worship.
May they all remove my impurity and whatever sin has been committed by me—
[he who is] the knower of mantras, the master of mantras, the wise one, the king of swans, worshipped by the Siddhas.
May the Siddhas, who possess supreme accomplishment, who bestow all accomplishments,
and who worship the state of Śiva, remove all impurity.
The Yakṣas are Yajñeśa, Dhanada, Maṇibhadra,
Pūrṇabhadra, Svairamālin, Śibi, and Puṇḍarīka.
May Narendra and Yajñeśa likewise dispel my impurity;
as well as Ananta, Kulika, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka.
Karkoṭaka, Mahāpadma, Śaṅkhapāla, and the mighty Mahābala—
having attained prostration before Śiva, they became ornaments for the god Śiva.
May they dispel impurity and evil, as well as all poisons, both stationary and mobile:
Vīṇājña, Kinnarajña, Śūrasena, and Pramardana.
May the Kinnaras— possessing excellence, enjoying sublime pleasures, and skilled in song,
and perfected through prostration to Śiva— dispel my impurity.
Disciplined by learning, a mass of splendor through knowledge, the best among those who know the Vedas;
awakened, wise, illustrious, grateful, and of great renown.
May all these Vidyādharas, who are devoted to the meditation on Śiva,
remove every impurity through the grace of Mahādeva.
Hayagrīva, Mahājṛmbha, the highly illustrious Kālanemi,
Sugrīva, Mardaka, Piṅgala, and Devamārdava.
Prahlāda, Anuhrāda, Śibi, Brāṣkala,
Jṛmbhaka and Kumbha, Māyāvī, Kārtavīrya, and Kṛtañjaya.
May these high-souled gods, who are devoted to Mahādeva,
dispel this most terrible burden of my own sin.
And Garuḍa, Hari himself, the king of birds, the crusher of the enemy hosts.
The enemy of the nāgas, golden-hued, son of Vinatā, the breaker,
the destroyer of the poison of nāgas, and indeed the vehicle of Viṣṇu.
May these golden-hued Garuḍas, the vehicles of Viṣṇu,
adorned with various ornaments, dispel my fear.
Agastya and Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras and Bhṛgu as well,
Kaśyapa and Nārada, Dadhīci and likewise Cyavana.
Upamanyu and other sages, who were devoted to Śiva and intent on the worship of Śiva, said: "May [the sin] committed by thought and deed be destroyed."
Vāyu, Anila, and Marut are synonymous;
likewise, Prāṇa, Prāṇeśa, Jīveśa, Jīva, and Maruta are one and the same.
May all those devoted to the worship of Śiva dispel my impurity—
the sky-walker, the one who moves through the eight [directions], the slayer of a Brahmin, the knower of Brahman, and the wise one.
The fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers; the Agniṣvātta and Barhiṣad ancestors, as well as the maternal grandfathers and the rest.
May those who are devoted to the meditation on Śiva dispel fear and evil;
and may Lakṣmī, Dharaṇī, Gāyatrī, and Sarasvatī do the same.
Durgā, Umā, Śacī, Jyeṣṭhā, and the Mothers worshipped by the gods; as well as those esteemed as deities, such as the Gaṇas, the Grandmothers, and others.
May those who are devoted to the meditation on Śiva dispel fear and evil;
as well as Lakṣmī, Dharaṇī, and likewise the Mothers of the Gaṇas.
May all the Mothers of beings, and the Mothers of the hosts of serpents,
through the grace of the God of gods, dispel my fear.
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Tilottamā,
Sumukhī, Durmukhī, Kāmukī, and Kāmavardhinī.
Furthermore, other auspicious divine apsarases from all the worlds,
permeated by Śiva, constantly perform the tāṇḍava dance for his welfare.
May the planets— Arka, Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, and Bṛhaspati— who delight in singing praises and worshiping Śiva, remove my impurity.
May Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and the mighty Ketu—
those who worship Śiva— dispel this terrible fear and the pain in the head.
May Aries, Taurus, Gemini, and likewise Cancer be auspicious.
And Leo, Virgo, Libra,
Scorpio, as well as Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.
May these twelve lunar mansions, devoted to the worship of Śiva,
dispel the greatest of evils through the grace of the Supreme Lord:
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, and likewise Rohiṇī.
The illustrious [asterisms] are Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Āśleṣā;
as well as Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī.
Hasta, Citrā, as well as Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā,
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, O highly fortunate one, and likewise Pūrvāṣāḍhā.
Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, as well as Śatabhiṣā,
Pūrvabhādrapadā, and likewise the auspicious Prauṣṭhapadā (Uttarabhādrapadā).
May the goddess Pauṣṇī and Kuṇḍodaka always dispel my impurity,
as well as Jvara and the mighty Śatakarṇa.
Mahākarṇa, Prabhūta, and the Lord Prītivardhana—
these beings are surrounded by hundreds of millions upon millions of spirits.
May they, who are perfected solely through meditation on Śiva, who are cool and possess the form of Indra, dispel fear and evil by the grace of Mahādeva.

His form resembles the jasmine flower and the moon; he is like the submarine fire (Vaḍavāmukha) to the jasmine and the moon, yet he is the enemy of hundreds of submarine fires and the one who pierces the submarine fire.
He possesses a magnificent body, is truly devoted, and is as white as the Ocean of Milk.
Ever abiding in the light of Rudra, together with the fierce Gaṇas,
he is the Lord Vṛṣendra, the source of emanation and the father of the entire universe.
Constantly surrounded by his mothers, Nanda and the others, and ever devoted to the worship of Śiva, may the crusher of the demon Meṣa dispel my sin.
The mother of cows, the mother of the world, who resides in the realm of Rudra—
may that highly fortunate mother of cows dispel my sin.
Virtuous and endowed with moral conduct, devoted solely to the worship of Śiva;
endowed with moral conduct and devoted solely to the worship of Śiva, she dwells in the world of Śiva.
May she, who dwells eternally in the world of Śiva, dispel my sin—
she who is omniscient in the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras, the immortal Lord of all gods.
The eldest, the Lord of All, the gentle one—this is the quartet of Mahāviṣṇu.
The first commander-in-chief delights in the scripture;
he is the crusher of rams, mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, and possesses dark, curly hair.
With eyes black and white, adorned with the moon and serpents,
he was surrounded by these pretas, piśācas, and kūṣmāṇḍas.
May she who is truly devoted to the worship of Śiva remove my sin;
likewise may Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī do so.
Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, and likewise Agnāyikā—
all these indeed are the Mothers, worshipped by all the worlds.
May the Yoginīs, being composed in meditation, dispel great sin;
and may Vīrabhadra, of great splendor, who resembles snow, the kunda flower, and the moon [grant protection].
The son of Rudra is Raudra, whose great hands hold the trident and the spear;
he has a thousand arms, is omniscient, and is himself the wielder of all weapons.
[211] Endowed with the three sacrificial fires as his eyes, the Lord who grants fearlessness to the three worlds,
the eternal protector of the Mothers, whose vehicle is the great bull.
The glorious one, created by the three worlds, was devoted to the worship of Śiva’s feet;
he was the one who severed the head of the sacrifice and destroyed the teeth of Pūṣan.
May that Gaṇeśvara— the son of Agni, who was born directly from the eye of the sky,
and whose wife is Yaśodā— dispel my sin.
May Mahālakṣmī, the eldest, the most excellent, the giver of boons, adorned with every ornament,
and the Mother of the World, dispel my sin.
May Mahāmohā, the highly fortunate one, who is surrounded by hosts of great beings and is eternally devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel my sin.
May that Goddess Lakṣmī— who is endowed with all virtues, marked by all auspicious characteristics,
and the bestower of happiness at all times— dispel my sin.
May the Great Goddess, who has ascended for the destruction [of the world], the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
the auspicious Rudrā devoted to the worship of Śiva, dispel my sin.
May Rudrāṇī, the beloved of Rudra, the leader of the hosts of Brahmāṇḍas,
and Kūṣmāṇḍa— being composed in mind— dispel my sin.
Having praised the Goddess with this, one should ask for forgiveness for everything at the conclusion;
having prostrated with the head upon the ground, [one should do so] every month before the best of the twice-born.
Whoever recites or even hears this *Vyapohana-stava*,
having shaken off all sins, is glorified in the world of Rudra.
One seeking a daughter shall obtain a daughter; one desiring victory shall obtain victory;
one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth; one desiring sons shall obtain many sons;
a seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge; and one desiring enjoyments shall attain enjoyments.
Whatever desires one may pray for, as well as the fruit of sacrifices,
the merit of gifts, and especially that of religious observances— [all these are attained].
By reciting it ten million times, a human being attains that merit; even one who has killed a cow, one who is ungrateful, a slayer of heroes, a slayer of a Brahmin,
a killer of those who have sought refuge, and a betrayer of a friend’s trust.
Even one who is a leper, of evil conduct, a slayer of mother or father,
having destroyed all his sins, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the *pāśupata* vow for the removal of impurities as declared in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the excellent *pāśupata* vow,
by performing which even Brahmā and the others are all remembered as *pāśupatas*."
Vāyu said:
I shall proclaim that secret which cuts away all sins—
the excellent Pāśupata vow, which was heard by me directly from the mouth of Śiva.
The time is the full moon day of Caitra; the place is a sanctuary of Śiva, or another auspicious location with favorable characteristics such as a sacred field or a grove.
There, on the thirteenth day of the waxing moon, having bathed well and performed his daily rites,
he should worship and prostrate before the incomparable Noble One (Atulārya) along with his preceptor.
Having performed the worship according to his own Vedic branch, he himself should wear white garments,
a white sacred thread, and white garlands and unguents.
Seated upon a seat of darbha grass and grasping a handful of darbha,
having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should face either the east or the north.
Having meditated upon the God and the Goddess according to the path of their petition,
one should form the resolve, "I shall perform this vow," and thus become initiated.
Until the fall of the body, or for twelve years,
or half of that, or half of that again, or even for twelve months.
Whether it be half of that, or half of that again, or even for one month,
or for twelve days— this is the rule for the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) of the vow.
Having kindled the fire for the purpose of the Virāj oblation,
he should offer clarified butter, fuel sticks, and the sacrificial porridge (caru) in their proper sequence.
O King, before the Pūrṇāhuti, one should intend for the purification of the principles (tattvas);
one should offer oblations with the root mantra and with *tārā*, using sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*) and other materials.
Remember these pure principles within my body as distinct from one another:
the five elements as principles, and the five sense organs.
Through the division of knowledge and action, there are five and five respectively;
the seven elements beginning with skin, and the five vital airs beginning with prāṇa.
Likewise, the mind is characterized by egoism; both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are devoid of qualities.
Passion (rāga), knowledge (vidyā), limited agency (kalā), necessity (niyati), and time (kāla);
then pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), Maheśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śakti— these they know to be the Śiva-tattvas in their proper order.
Having offered oblations with the mantras, the priest shall become free from passion by means of them;
then, having taken cow dung and formed it into balls, he should offer them as an invitation.
Having placed it before him and protected it on that day while eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), he should,
at dawn on the fourteenth day, perform all that which has been prescribed.

On that day, remaining without food, one should complete the remainder of the time. Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) according to the true principle, either in the morning or on the festival day itself, and having respectfully approached the Rudra-fire, one should take the sacred ash from the vessel.
Then, having matted his hair or shaved it off, together with his disciples, he should offer oblations into the fire; thereafter, free from shame, he may become a sky-clad ascetic (digambara),
or otherwise wear saffron-colored garments, or clothes made of skin or rags.
He should wear red garments or bark-cloth, and carry a staff and a pestle;
then, having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water twice, he should purify his own body.
Having performed the sakalīkaraṇa rite with that ash produced from the impurities of a hut,
one should, in due order, rub the limbs starting from the head down to the feet while reciting the six Atharvanic mantras beginning with "agnis".

"Fire is indeed ash; wind is ash; water is ash; the earth is ash"—having offered all-giving oblations with these six Atharvaṇa mantras, [one should apply] "this ash on the limbs" and "these on the eyes.
Then, having wiped [the face] in that very same sequence, one should perform the smearing of ash over all the limbs with the syllable *praṇava* and the word "Śiva."
Then one should fashion the *tripuṇḍra* known as the "threefold life-force";
having attained the state of Śiva, one should then practice the yoga of Śiva.
One should perform this Pāśupata vow at the three junctions of the day;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and it brings about the cessation of the state of being a bound soul (paśutva).
Having abandoned that state of being a bound animal (paśu) and having performed the Pāśupata vow,
Mahādeva, the eternal one whose form is the Liṅga, is to be worshipped.
One should imagine a golden eight-petaled lotus, adorned with the nine gems,
complete with a pericarp and filaments, as the seat.
One should visualize the sun as resembling white or black, or even white and red;
in the absence of that [visualized form], however, there is simply that which consists of mental cultivation alone.
Having placed a small crystal *liṅga* together with its pedestal in the center of the pericarp of a lotus, one who has taken refuge [in the practice] should worship it in due order.
Having installed the beautifully adorned *liṅga* according to the prescribed ritual,
one should conceive of the five-faced, radiant form upon the seat,
[purifying it] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and other auspicious substances gathered according to one’s means.
One should bathe [the deity] with thousands of full jars well-prepared,
using fragrant substances along with camphor, sandalwood, and saffron.
Having smeared the *śivaliṅga* with *sāvitraka* paste and adorned it with ornaments,
one should worship it with *bilva* leaves, lotuses, or red water-lilies (*utpala*).
With blue lotuses (*utpala*),
with other blue lotuses, and likewise with various other fragrant flowers—
these excellent flowers and flowers such as *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Having worshipped according to one's means through the procedure for the great worship (mahāpūjā),
[one should offer] incense, a lamp, as well as the water-offering (arghya) and especially the food offering (naivedya).
Having offered [the food] according to the prescribed rule, one should perform auspicious rites;
and [one should offer] desired and excellent things acquired through righteous means.

All substances should be offered, especially in this vow. (Regarding the number of *śrīpatra*, *utpala*, and *padma* flowers, the *Trikāmatā* states: O brahmins, for each of these, there should be one hundred and eight, pervading the entire area. The eightfold offering (arghya) is most excellent, and incense and lamps especially so.
In the [face] called Aghora, black agallochum; in the [face] called Sadyojāta, red [resin] and realgar;
in the [face] called Vāmadeva, sandalwood; and again, in the [mouth], black agallochum.
One should offer Pauruṣeya-guggulu in the southeast, Saugandhika in the north, and Sītā and the others at the entrance; one should especially offer incense in the northeast as well.
Sugar, honey, camphor, combined with the ghee of a tawny cow,
sandalwood, agallochum, and kuṣṭha are indeed prescribed as the garland.
Then follows the row of lamps for the Goddess, beginning with the camphor wick.
Thereafter, Aghoracandana should be offered for each wheel;
having worshipped [the goddess] Dhivakharāmukhī in sequence within the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa).
Then, one should likewise worship the limbs of Brahmā in the first enclosure;
in the second enclosure, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), who are universal monarchs (cakravartins), are to be worshipped.

In the fourth enclosure, all the lords of the hosts (gaṇeśvaras) are to be worshipped;

All the gods and goddesses, all the sky-dwellers,
those dwelling in the netherworld, and even all the hosts of sages.
All the gurus of the yogins, as well as the five Mothers,
the guardians of the fields (kṣetrapālas) together with their retinues, and all this world of the moving and the unmoving— [all these are present].
Then, at the conclusion of the preliminary worship, having fully worshipped the Supreme Lord,

The king also, having adorned himself with various flowers and ornaments, offered betel-leaf with its accompaniments along with mouth-perfumes and other items.
Having performed the worship extensively up to the end of the *nīrājana* rite, one should complete the remainder of the worship;

Whatever is beneficial and pleasing to anyone, having performed all that according to what is appropriate,

First, from her mouth, my own message was swallowed—

Endowed with all the auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament,

thereafter, one should worship Suvidyā in front of the deity.
Having offered flowers for the sake of the deity’s nourishment upon the *liṅga*,
one should protect both the water and the fire, or [perform it] by means of the deity's name.
Every day he should thus generate [the deity] and perform everything as prescribed by the priest;

He should satisfy his devoted Brahmins, those who have not yet eaten, and the poor and helpless;

Or, observing the vow of milk, subsisting on alms, or eating only once during the day;

Sleeping on ashes, sleeping on hemp, or else sleeping in the hero’s posture (vīrāsana),

On a Sunday or a Monday, on the fifteenth day of either fortnight,

One should avoid with every effort— through thought, deed, and speech— those who follow heretical paths, those who have fallen from their caste, women in their courses, those in the state of birth-impurity, and outcasts.
Patience, generosity, compassion, truthfulness, non-violence, and virtuous conduct should be present;

One should perform the ritual bath three times a day, or even the ash-bath;

What is the use of saying more here? One who observes inauspicious vows should not practice [this];
rather, through the grace [of the teacher], one should always examine the relative weight and lightness within right conduct.
One should perform extensive expiation through worship, fire-offerings, recitation, and so forth;
one should act thus without negligence until the completion of the vow. One should also perform the gift of a cow, the release of a bull, and worship of the assembly.
This general procedure for this vow has been declared according to the rules;

In Vaiśākha, one should know the Vajra-liṅga; in Jyeṣṭha, the auspicious Māravratam;

Permitted by the preceptor, facing either the east or the north,

One should consecrate that [mound] with a mantra; having spread out either a mat of split bamboo or the skin of a tiger or an ox, and having consecrated a water-pot belonging to this [deity], one should then offer an oblation to the presiding deity from this [mound] and to that [deity], and should place the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).

One should have an elephant recite [the following] in whichever direction that enemy may be; having gone to that direction, one should bring the elephant there with gold, silver, diamond, gem, pearl, conch, sandalwood, *bhadradāru*, costus, *nalada*, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), collyrium, emerald, *kuśila* stone, and with lotuses—*padma*, *kumuda*, and *utpala*. Regarding this, there are these verses:
"For protection, a new bamboo staff should be made."
It should be exactly sixteen aratnis in measure, with four joints, and pleasing to the heart.

Because he saves [them] from that enclosure, having placed grass on the tips of the staffs, he swallows each calf as it is born. Sanatkumāra said:
Now, O high-minded one, listen to that which is to be performed on the festival day (parvan).

Whatever merit or demerit has been performed on a sacred festival day (parvan),
men enjoy the fruit of that for sixty thousand years.

yet for this very reason, men are beset by afflictions that lead to inexhaustible suffering.

grants all happiness, and is auspicious— is now described here.
On the fourteenth day, having bathed with purity after cleansing his teeth, and having observed celibacy while restraining his speech, body, and mind;

Likewise, one should assign the five sense organs, as well as the intellect, the vital breath, and the mind—
all these deities— to be placed within all four pitchers.
A mortal shall cross over all calamities, even the fear of mental anguish and physical disease;
may they always protect my intellect, vital breath, mind, and consciousness.
"May they protect us always from calamities; may they grant us auspiciousness"—with this mantra, having performed worship in the kindled fire, Jātavedas.
One who is self-restrained should perform oblations with sesame seeds mixed with unbroken rice and anointed with the three sweets, using six mantras according to the rule over the consecrated fire.

and to Mṛtyu in the form of Kāla"—these are the six mantras.
Then, having offered with the weapon-mantra, with the vital breath, and also with the organs, saying "to the organs," one should discard the bali-offering with what remains of that.
Then, having seated the candidate upon a throne, the preceptor should perform the consecration before him with milk and that same water.
To a poor householder, one should give gold weighing a niṣka or a māṣa, as well as sesame seeds,

Then, for him, [he should bring] full jars mixed with turmeric powder,
as well as water-pots filled with seeds and filled with salt.
One should give four sets of four [cows] to women for the sake of supreme longevity;
having given a boon to the preceptor and performed the satiation of the Brahmins.
The wise person should spend the remainder of the day according to the rules for the fast,
and on the following day, he should perform the worship of the Blessed One.
One should eat together with one's kinsmen and relinquish restrictive observances;
he who acts thus on a festival day shall become long-lived.
When all diseases arise and all suffering comes forth,
he who performs a ritual bath on a festival day attains supreme peace.
Thus ends the Āyurvrata as declared in the Gāruḍa Purāṇa.

worship that Vighneśā, who bestows both seen and unseen rewards.

Brahmā said:
For the sake of a son, for the sake of sovereignty and learning, or even for fame and good fortune,

One should fashion an image endowed with all auspicious characteristics, made either of gold, or silver, or of a sword, or even of sandals.

Having taken her, on an auspicious lunar mansion, adorned with white garments,
provided with sprouts of barley and *śāli* rice, and decorated with drinking vessels;

having offered oblations into the fire with mantras, one should then install the goddess there.
There, on an altar provided with barley, sprouts, and so forth,
one should worship after having smeared it with yellow pigment, sandalwood, and camphor.
One should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite with various kinds of flowers, incense, perfumes, and food offerings; likewise, one should collect the seed-syllables.
Barley, wheat, mung beans, rice, sixty-day rice, and *āṭakī*;

The bow is indeed for the destruction of enemies; that very same [bow] is for one who desires that [destruction]. Food, however, should be caused to be given according to what is obtained, for the sake of all purposes and desires.
Then one should ask forgiveness from the Goddess and receive the requested knowledge—the knowledge being the mantra to be described hereafter.
For the sake of a son, one should worship children; for victory, women and the twice-born.

According to this procedure, the mantra is also written here:

*Oṃ yaḥ pṛthivyāṃ retatamehādavatayomāmakṣitāni vidyā prayacchaty aṣṭau putrān janayati vedavedāṅgapāragān | yo 'dhītya na prayacchaty aputro napuṃsako bhavati | ahaṃ vīryeṇāhaṃ balena tu oṃ namo bhagavate akṣīṇaretase svāhā.* Or, at the time of sexual union, one should meditate upon that goddess, the sovereign of the thirty [gods],
by whose seed this world is adorned and purified upon the earth.
Oṃ! To Retā, to Mahāretā, to the one of all vigor and great strength;
to Kāma, the god of desire, may he grant my desires!
One should resort to a bed consecrated with this mantra;
it bestows eight sons, provided that one does not fall into delusion.
Having thus received the vidyā, one should constantly worship the goddess;
then there arises the accomplishment of all desires, which is desired and unconquerable.
Whatever fruits and flowers grow here during the rainy season,
those one should cause to be given to the preceptor of the goddess together with her daughter.
O child, flowers and fruits should be offered according to what is available during the auspicious months of Śrāvaṇī, Āśvinī, or Kārttikī.
One who desires success must necessarily abide by this rule through fire-offerings, celibacy, and the mastery of many mantras.
A sonless man obtains sons, wealth, good fortune, and long life;
or else, by this knowledge, she becomes white and free from all defects.
By inhaling the seeds of the citron (*bījapūraka*) and the shoots of the banyan tree (*vaṭa*).
Having prepared *nāgakeśara* flowers, one obtains the fruit [of the rite].

*Bṛhatī sitā* is white *bṛhatī*. *Vaṭa-śṛṅgāṇi* are the sprouts of the *vaṭa* tree. By means of this knowledge, one attains the fruit through nasal administration (*nāvana*) and by drinking clarified butter mixed with the fruit and water.
He becomes invincible in the world, a master of the vidyādharas and lord of wealth.
This *phalasarpis* is established in the *Āyurveda*.
All this has been declared as the supreme vow for the sake of victory;
it bestows success upon all people through its observance according to the prescribed rite.
Thus ends the vow for obtaining a son as described in the Devīpurāṇa.
Kārkaṇḍeya said:
Having begun thus on the full moon day of Kārttika, [one should observe it] until the moon is perfectly full.
O King, one should always worship at sunrise and remain a night-eater (observing the vow of eating only at night).
Having prepared a salt mandala and anointed it with sandalwood paste,
one should then worship Soma together with the ten lunar mansions.

(One should offer salt prepared with *saindhava* salt. One should worship [the deity] during the month of Kārttika when it is joined with the asterisms Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī; likewise, O King, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa when it is joined with Saumya (Mṛgaśiras) and Ārdrā.
O Yādava, listen, O King: in the month of Pauṣa, it is conjoined with Āditya and Puṣya; and in Māgha and Phālguna, it is joined with Maghā and Āśleṣā.
Then the noble one should worship the Lord together with those belonging to Savitṛ.
O King, listen: in Caitra, one should worship [the deity] conjoined with Citrā and Svāti;
likewise, in Vaiśākha, one should worship him conjoined with Viśākhā and Anurādhā (Maitra).
In the month of Jyaiṣṭha, it is joined with the Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla constellations; in Āṣāḍha, it is known as the Uttarā;
in Śrāvaṇa, it is endowed with Śravaṇa; and [in Bhādrapada] with Śraviṣṭhā, which belongs to Varuṇa.
Likewise, in Bhādrapada, [he worships] Pauṣṇa joined with Ajāhivradhna;
and in Āśvayuja, he worships the Lord joined with Aśvinī and Bharaṇī.
(Three [offerings] each in Kārttika and the following months, in the order of the *kṛttikā* constellation, up to Phālguna, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada).
With an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food;
with pure *paramānna*, salt, and ghee.
Women whose husbands are living should be honored with sugarcane, products of sugarcane, milk, and milk-rice,
as well as by means of their auspicious physical characteristics.
Immediately thereafter, the self-restrained man should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) once the Brāhmaṇas have completed their vow, adorned with great silver.
A vessel made of great silver is the *kuśumbha*.
Whether it be a woman or a man, by giving a seat with a spear [as an offering],
that person shall become endowed with beauty, good fortune, charm, and wealth.
By performing this vow, one goes to the heavenly world.
And that man who, observing a fast, performs this unsurpassed vow,
obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
One especially attains whatever has been proclaimed regarding good fortune and the like;
one obtains all the desires wished for by the mind without a doubt.
He shall be as pleasing to the people as the moon,
and likewise equal to the Lord of Wealth in prosperity;
and he shall be equal to Śakra in power.
Having attained human birth, he shall become a king.
Thus ends the vow for the Full Moon of Manoratha as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the full moon day of Kārttika, [one should worship] the full moon of the cool-rayed one.
One should worship upon a sixteen-petaled lotus, specifically within the pericarp.
There, one should worship the twenty-eight lunar mansions in the filaments;
on the petals, the lunar days (tithis) themselves are to be honored, and thereafter one should worship the moonlight (jyotsnā).
Agni, Brahmā, Ambikā, Īśa, Nāga, Skanda, Viriñcana; Śiva, Durgā, Yama, Indra, Viṣṇu, Kāma, Śiva, and Indu.
And these ancestors have been declared by the sages to be the deities of the lunar days (tithis);
[they are propitiated] with perfumes, garlands, salutations, lamps, incense, and an abundance of food.
O highly fortunate one, [he was honored] with pure, excellent food, curd, salt, cakes,
and likewise with fruits produced in their season.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a pair of garments to a twice-born;
and the brahmins, O highly fortunate one, [should be honored] with cloths dyed with great silver.
Both of them should properly honor those who are worthy of worship and those who possess knowledge of the times;
observing a fast, eating only once a day, or likewise eating only at night, the knower of dharma should perform this vow while consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya).
O lord of men, this [yantra] should be diligently prepared by a man; it bestows good fortune, the splendor of beauty, charm, and the enjoyment of the love of women.
Likewise, one of undaunted spirit should perform his duty with women.
Thus ends the Saubhāgyavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a man [should worship] the orb of the moon.
Fasting on the full moon day and performing worship, one shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice.
The fruit of sacrifice is the fruit of all sacrifices.
By honoring [the deity] while eating only at night, one obtains the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice;
and by fasting and eating only at night, one obtains the fruit of the Vājimedha sacrifice.
Observing the fast and adhering to the excellent vows,
one who performs this vow for a year attains his desired goal and the worlds of the Moon.
Having observed the fast for a very long time at the proper hour,
one attains union with that Śambhu who is beyond darkness.
Thus ends the Candra-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
[237] Mārkaṇḍeya said: Having begun from the month of Proṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada), when the lunar disc is full,
Having worshipped the god Varuṇa with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, and food,
Having meditated thus upon the water of a reservoir for one year, the wise man should,
at the conclusion of the vow, give a water-cow to a twice-born.
O King, a person who gives [a gift] provided with an umbrella and sandals, and adorned with a pair of garments, attains the world of Varuṇa;
having dwelt there for a very long time, he returns as a human being.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, endowed with beauty, and likewise possessed of wealth.
Thus ends the Varuṇa-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja, preceded by the preceding [day], a man on earth—
Having observed a fast, he should likewise worship the god Surendra.
O lord of men, [he offered] Śacī, Airāvaṇa, the thunderbolt, and the citron,
together with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food.
Having given gold at the end of the year,
one attains the world of Purandara;
and having returned to human birth, one is honored by kings.
He may become either a king or a preeminent among the twice-born.
Thus ends the Śakra-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
[238] Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of men, having fasted on the fourteenth day and the full moon day, [one should proceed].
Afterwards, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
By performing this Śakra-vrata, one is liberated from the sins of a month;
therefore, one should practice it with every effort month after month.
Having reached the world of the lord of gods after a year, and having dwelt there for a very long time as a human king, he shall,
upon returning to the human state, be honored by kings.
He may become either a king or a preeminent among the twice-born.
Thus ends the Brahmakūrca vow as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
He who, fasting on the full moon day of Kārttika, gives away a well-adorned maiden—
whether his own daughter or the daughter of another— at an auspicious confluence of rivers;
"This vow, named Santānada, bestows a happy rebirth.
Thus ends the Santānada-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one who observes the *naktabhuk* vow should give a ram fashioned from gold;
likewise, on the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should behold a king and a couple.
In this manner, one who should give a maidservant adorned with garments on every full moon day—
this should be performed on every full moon day, O son of Kuntī— with abundant sacrificial fees.
This is known as the Rāśivrata, which destroys the afflictions caused by the planets;
it likewise fulfills all desires and bestows the world of Soma.

Thus ends the Rājīvavrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa. One who observes the Paryovrata on the fifteenth day and, at the conclusion of the vow, gifts a pair of cows, attains the world of Lakṣmī; this is proclaimed as the Devīvrata.
Thus ends the Devī-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. From the Kālottara:
Having fasted on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, remaining established in the observances.
For the sake of Śiva, the Ghṛtakambala rite should be performed on the full moon day.
Thereafter, one should offer a handsome black bull and cow;
such a person is honored in the world of Śiva for one hundred and fifty divine years.
Regarding the Śivadharma:
he who offers a "blanket of ghee" as far as the altar surrounding the liṅga shall obtain infinite merit on the full-moon festival of Māgha.
Having performed the vigil with song, dance, and other arts even once on the festival day,
one is honored in the world of Rudra for one hundred and fifty manvantaras.

Thus ends the ritual for the ghee-blanket as declared in the *Śivadharmottara*. Furthermore, the man who, being devoted, worships Soma on the full moon day—his good fortune shall increase; this is my firm conviction.
The root mantras are proclaimed by their own names, as are the mantras of the colors;
and Ātithīśvara is to be fashioned, as before, situated upon a lotus petal.
Soma is the lord of the lunar days (*tithi*); his form should be understood as that described in the *Caturdaśī-sthita-mahārāja-vrata*.
Worship is performed with offerings of perfumes and flowers according to one's capacity;
even when performed with abundant materials, it yields fruit through its richness in devotion.
A fire sacrifice performed with a stream of clarified butter, fuel-sticks, curd, milk, rice, and honey,
while the mind is tranquil, yields the same fruits as previously described.
This vow is to be explained like the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata. Thus ends the Somavrata as described in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
[The meal] should consist of food mixed with ghee and adorned on top with honey.
One should give one Magadhan prastha of black sesame seeds.
One should prepare two prasthas of rice separately,
served with various kinds of food, whether consisting of eggs or of meat.
Having wrapped the *liṅga* with silk born from cocoons or cotton born from pods, one who is composed should offer this oblation with mantras,
having worshipped according to the rule on the full moon day.
For thousands of millions of aeons he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
when his merit is exhausted, having returned here, he is born into a prosperous family.
"Intelligent, fortunate, illustrious, and a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences"—
thus is described the *Ghṛtabhājana-vrata* as taught in the *Śrīśivadharma*. One should fast on the full moon day for one year, remaining well-restrained.
At the end of the year, one should present a measure of all kinds of perfumes as an offering.
By means of various magnificent Mahāyāna vehicles adorned with two kinds of fragrances,
one is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred billion eons.
Having diligently attained enjoyment in the world of Īśvara as she desired,
she will eventually come to this world and obtain a king as her husband.
Thus ends the Gandha-vrata as declared in the Śivadharma.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having fasted on the fourteenth day and the full moon day, one should worship Hari.
And in the month of Caitra, the powerful Nikumbha was accompanied by the Piśācas.
He went to fight the piśācas dwelling on the island of sand;
at the end of that [journey], as they were traveling, at midday, in every house—
Worship should be performed with effort daily, according to one's capacity and in the proper sequence;
having fashioned a charming image of a Piśāca, either out of clay or out of grass.
With perfumes, garlands, garments, and captivating ornaments;
with edible foods such as *pūrikās* and cakes, meats, sacrificial offerings, and drinks.
With drinks prepared according to their respective lineages, with various kinds of food offerings,
with weapons of diverse forms, and with umbrellas, sandals, and staffs;
With dried grain cakes and solid foods prepared on a hearth,
or with flour from grains split by a sling, or with parched grains and the like, using a hide.
Having worshipped him at midday with pleasing stringed instruments as well as those suitable for Arjuna, he did so again when moonrise arrived.
One should worship him as before, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
then, having performed the rite for well-being, the Brahmin should dismiss him.
On the second day, however,
one should follow him as far as a mountain or a tree that is not far from his house.
Furthermore, upon re-entering the house, a truly great festival must be celebrated,
with the resounding noise of songs and musical instruments, as well as the clamor of the people.
Having fashioned a snake out of grass encircled with sturdy wood,
one should always play with it in villages and cities.
There, at that very moment, by means of which [rite] it occurs for wicked serpents,
they must be cut into pieces within three or four days.
"The pacification of all afflictions [is achieved] by worshipping the nine-fold [mantra] in every house;
it should be worshipped in a well-concealed place and guarded for one year.
This is the worship of Nikumbha as described in the *Itihāsa-purāṇa*.
He who, having performed the ritual release of a bull on the full moon day of Kārttika, observes the practice of eating only at night, attains the state of Śiva; this is remembered as the Vṛṣavrata.

Thus ends the Vṛṣavrata as declared in the Padmapurāṇa. [243] O best of the twice-born, one should always perform the worship of her who impels actions in the worlds on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight.
By means of garlands and unguents, with white flowers and fragrant incense,
or by the gift of red garments, or else by the offering of lamps;
Having worshipped that goddess with split pulses, various foods, and likewise with cakes, one should eat at night together with one's wife.
If one is unable to perform the worship of the Goddess on the entire fifteenth day by any means whatsoever, it must nevertheless be performed during the month of Kārttika.
O Bhārgava, that woman who worships Umā becomes a devoted wife, always delighting in dharma in this world.
And her mind never at any time gives rise to what is unwholesome.
Thus ends the vow for the full moon as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"O Rāma, having reached the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
one should indeed paint upon the wall of a garden house the two goddesses Ume and Śauca."
Quickly, at their door or within the house, one should paint various household utensils in many colors according to one's ability, and likewise draw them all around the two of them.
Having bathed and purified herself, a woman devoted to her husband should worship that first yellow garment, along with the *kaṭaumukha* and the *nāsika*.
One should worship especially with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and excellent food, as well as with sugarcane and its various products.
Having performed worship to those two, one should gaze upon that which is made of sand;
one should place white [powder] in the eye and give that milk to a twice-born man.
Thereafter, one should eat at night, avoiding sesame oil;
by worshipping these two, one shall not suffer the ruin of one's home.
A devoted wife of great fortune attains a long life;
by worshipping the full moon thereafter, she shall obtain great good fortune.
Then, O King, descendant of Yadu, by worshipping the desired planet or the lunar mansion,
one obtains safety and the fulfillment of desires for that woman.
O King, by worshipping the month, the name, the lunar mansion, and the conjunction of the full moon, one shall then attain great good fortune.
O King, by worshipping the Full Moon associated with Nṛsiṃha,
a man shall obtain all his desires along with the host of Mothers.
O King, by honoring a single mother, one obtains all desired objects;
by honoring trees, one attains the world of the Vanaspatis.
Thus ends the vow for various fruits on the full-moon day as declared in the Viṣṇudharma:
"On the full-moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one who has fasted and subdued his senses,
having performed a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), is liberated from all sins."
Thus ends the Pūrṇimā-vrata as declared in the Vahnipurāṇa.
Regarding the Candra-vrata, one should observe a fast at night on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight.
One should observe this vow for fifteen years;
it is equal to thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of royal consecrations.
"O Indra among kings, he by whom this vow is performed has fulfilled his desires.
Thus ends the Candra-vrata as declared in the Vārāha Purāṇa.
Īśvara said:
If a man feeds a married couple on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
having clothed them according to his ability, he is liberated from misfortunes.
O beautiful one, he who worships on the full moon day with offerings of perfumes and flowers will be born into the Brahmin caste for seven lifetimes.
Thus ends the vow for attaining Brāhmaṇahood as declared in the *Prabhāsakhaṇḍa*.

Thus concludes the section on Full-Moon Vows (*pūrṇimā-vrata*) within the *Vrata-khaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Mahādeva, Emperor of Emperors, sovereign of all administrative powers, and master of all branches of knowledge.
[246] Now begins the twentieth chapter: the vows for the new moon day (amāvāsyā).

In this very place resides that eminent and virtuous lord of the twice-born, Śūri Hemādri, by whom the world of the Nāgas was incessantly and excessively gratified with offerings, such that they no longer consume them, regarding them as the remnants of Rāhu’s meal upon the digit of the moon.
The collection of the New Moon vows is proclaimed by Ākhyātikīrti.
Agastya said:
O Holy One, by your grace this detailed exposition of the vow has been heard by me;
now tell me of the Ardhodaya, which is difficult to attain within the realm of the moving and the unmoving.
"O Lord, if you say that the life of living beings is merit, then what should be done, and what would be the fruit once it has been performed? Tell me, O Six-faced One."
Listen to this meritorious conjunction called Ardhodaya,
which is difficult to attain for animals, humans, and gods, and which grants all desires.
When there is a *vyatīpāta* yoga on a Sunday during the *māyā* phase of the *maghā* nakṣatra, which has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity,
they call that an *ardhodaya*, equal to a thousand suns and planets.
O observer of noble vows, this was practiced in the past by Vasiṣṭha, by the son of Jamadagni,
by Sanaka and others, and by many men of great learning.
May the son born from a jar be seen by hundreds of thousands of others,
so that he may obtain the fruit of all acts of charity, sacrifices, and pilgrimages.
[247] By him who has performed the Ardhodaya rite, the earth together with its oceans and endowed with its seven islands would have been given away with his whole being.
Whatever merit is gained from bathing and giving gifts at the sacred fords (tīrthas) such as Mānasa,
and likewise at Gaṅgā, Gayā, Prayāga, and the triad of Puṣkara;
O Brahmin, O Pot-born one, by this vow all that— or perhaps even more—
becomes equal to ten thousand excellent horse-sacrifices and whatever merit arises from sacrificial rites and charitable works.
But for those by whom the Ardhodaya rite has been performed according to the prescribed ritual,
there shall be the Horse Sacrifice in their home, as well as prosperity and imperishable progeny.
Indeed, the performer of the vow shall obtain long life and vast fame as the fruit;
[he shall dwell] in the worlds of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and the Lord of Waters.
A virtuous lord of the world, remaining as a portion of Vāyu and Kubera,
shall dwell in the worlds of the Moon and Sun, served by the guardians of the quarters.
The merit that comes from the gift of ten million cows to those residing at sacred fields and pilgrimage sites does not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit born of the Ardhodaya festival.
He is indeed the lord of the Bhūrloka, and he is the lord of the Bhuvarloka;
he is the lord of Svarloka and of the people, and the sovereign of those two worlds.
He shall dwell eternally in Maharloka for as long as the fourteen Indras endure;
thereafter, he becomes a personage of Hiraṇyagarbha who has performed his vows.
The Lord of the World, the imperishable Person of all worlds, is his witness;
by the grace of Ardhodaya, he shall dwell in the world of Brahmā.
Likewise, by this [rite], one becomes Viṣṇu, and Brahmā likewise becomes Rudra;
the world of Śiva, endowed with divine sovereignty, becomes worthy of worship through its qualities.
One should drink according to the measure of a śakra by the power of this vow;
thereafter, one shall become the sovereign of the three worlds in the form of Viṣṇu.
Bearing the conch, discus, and mace, wearing a forest garland, Hari himself— the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the Master of Lakṣmī— becomes manifest through the power of this vow.
Agastya said:
O Skanda, by what procedure should this supreme vow be performed?
For humans, the Ardhodaya occurs but rarely, and life on earth is difficult to obtain.
Skanda said:
It was performed by Vasiṣṭha in the Kṛta age, by Raghu in the Tretā,
by Dharmarāja in the Dvāpara, and by Pūrṇodara in the Kali age.
O best of the twice-born, other gods, humans,
and Daityas have also properly performed the Ardhodaya rite, which bestows the fruit of all fulfilled desires.
On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, on a Sunday,
under the Vaiṣṇava asterism (Śravaṇā), during the very rare Vyatīpāta yoga.
The Vaiṣṇava constellation is Śravaṇa.
Having bathed at the confluence in the forenoon, having become pure and composed,
a man should abide by his observances for the sake of purification from all sins.
"O gods, I shall perform the three-deity vow which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
may the three gods and the three fires be present before me this day."

Thus is the mantra of the rule. O best of the twice-born, the images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa should be made with a number of palas of gold equal to [the weight of] one, half, and half again of that [respectively].
A mountain of sesame seeds for Śambhu consists of three hundred and thirty droṇas;
here, Śambhu is Brahmā.
O Aṅgiras, Viṣṇu and Rudra should be fashioned according to the previously mentioned number.
Then one should prepare three beds, fully equipped with all necessary furnishings.
One should perform [these acts] for the sake of the three gods according to one's devotion and capacity;
indeed, three cows should be given for the pleasure of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Gifts of gold, land, grain, and so forth,
according to the extent of one's wealth, should be bestowed with faith and great effort upon the Brahmins.
At midday, however, a man, having bathed, become pure, and composed in mind,
should worship the triad of deities situated in the midst of the mountain of sesame seeds.
First is the worship of Brahmā:
Salutations to you, the creator of the universe, the Truth, the Supreme Lord;
salutations to the God, the Lord of gods, and the Lord of sacrifices.
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā for the feet; salutation to Hiraṇyagarbha for the thighs;
salutation to Dhātṛ for the knees; salutation to Parameṣṭhin for the shanks;
salutation to Vadhri for the private parts; and indeed salutation to Padmodbhava for the abdomen.

Salutation to the one whose vehicle is a swan (*haṃsavāhana*) at the region of the hips; salutation to Śatānanda on the chest; salutation, salutation, to the Lord of Sāvitrī on the arms. Oṃ, salutation to the *Ṛgveda* on the eastern face; salutation to the *Yajurveda* on the southern face; salutation to the *Sāmaveda* on the western face; salutation to the *Atharvaveda* on the northern face. Oṃ, salutation to the Four-faced One (*caturvaktra*) on the head. On the two cheeks: Oṃ, salutation to the Skull (*kapāla*).

Then, the worship of the World-Protectors (*lokapāla*) should be performed by the Brahmins with their respective mantras, [visualizing the deity] as Hiraṇyagarbha, Puruṣa, Pradhāna, and the Unmanifest Form (*avyaktarūpa*).
Be gracious, appear before me, accept this worship; homage be unto you!
This is the mantra for the prayer to Brahmā.
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, homage to you, O Garuḍa-bannered one!
O wearer of the yellow garment, salutations to you; O Janārdana, let there be homage to you.

Salutation to Ananta; salutation to Your feet, O Viśvarūpa. Salutation to Mukunda for the knees; salutation to Govinda for the thighs; salutation to Pradyumna for the private parts; salutation to Padmanābha for the navel. Salutation to Bhuvanodara for the belly; salutation to Kaustubhavakṣas for the chest. Salutation to Caturbhuja for the arms; salutation to Viśvatomukha for the face. Salutation to the thousand-headed god Ananta for the crown of the head.
O Ādityacandranayana, O Digbāhu, O Daityasūdana, O Compassionate One, accept this worship offered by me with devotion.
Thus ends the mantra for praying to Viṣṇu.
O Maheśvara, O Maheśāna, salutations to you, O Destroyer of Tripura!
Salutations to the one with cloud-like hair; salutations to you, whose banner is the bull.
Salutation to Īśāna for the feet; Candraśekhara for the shanks;
the god Paśupati for the knees; and Śaṅkara is remembered for the thighs.
To Umākānta at the secret place, to Nīlalohita at the navel,
to Kṛṣṇavāsas on the belly, and to Nāgopavītī on the chest.
To Bhogirūpa on the arm, to Nīlakaṇṭha on the neck;
to Pañcavaktra on the mouth, and to Kapardin on the head.
O you whose nature is immeasurable, who dwell in darkness, and who bring an end to the world— O Lord whose banner is the bull, accept this worship offered by me with devotion.
Thus ends the mantra for praying to Maheśvara.
In this manner, the sequence of worship has been proclaimed with these mantras, performed with diligence.
One should worship the preceptor with devotion by means of garments, ornaments, and decorations;
[the teacher's seat] should be one cubit in size, the parasol one span, and there should be a water-pot.
A pair of white garments should be given to Brahmā, who embodies all forms;
a pair of yellow garments to Viṣṇu, and a red one to Śaṅkara.
One should perform the ceremonial bath with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and worship with one's own flowers,
lotuses, tulasī leaves, and unbroken bilva leaves.
The gods should be worshipped in due order with divine offerings appropriate to that time;
this vow, which is very difficult to attain, should be performed according to one's capacity.
Since it is certain that this life of living beings is impermanent,
now hear in truth the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) which is a limb of the vow.
Having dedicated it to the three deities through rites prescribed by the scriptures:
"Homage, homage to Prajāpati Viśvarūpa and to Rudra."
Having thus established the fire with this very mantra out of devotion, one should then perform the *homa* according to one's available means:

"Svāhā to Agni Prajāpati; Svāhā to Agni Viṣṇu; Svāhā to Agni Rudra. Such is the *homa* for each deity. With the mantra "Prajāpataye na tvat... for Prajāpati; with "Idaṃ viṣṇuḥ... for Viṣṇu; and with "Tryambakaṃ... for Mahādeva—with these mantras, one performs the *homa* of clarified butter (*ghṛta-homa*).

By means of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the mantra "Svāhā to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Mahādeva," one attains and secures all desires; this oblation is the concluding rite of the vow. Then, at the conclusion of the oblation, one should give a milch cow, adorned with golden horns, silver hooves, and ornaments of bells.

One should present to the preceptor a cow with a copper-colored back, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel and all necessary utensils, along with a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), and one of excellent character.
By the power of this vow, O Brahmin, whatever has been given, offered in sacrifice, chanted, or worshipped through thousands of rituals becomes as if the duty has been fully accomplished.
All this has been related by me, the supreme vow that is difficult to attain, just as Ardhodaya was seen; what else do you wish to hear?
Thus ends the Ardhodaya-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa: Having observed the vow with self-restraint and fasting on the new moon day for one year, one should,
at the end of the year, fashion an image of Śiva out of flour and present it.
For Śiva, one should devoutly place a silver lotus, or a gold one of excellent color, upon his head; the remainder of the ritual should be performed as previously described.
Whatever sin has been committed even out of desire, such as the killing of an embryo and so forth—all that is destroyed by the gift of the trident to women; of this there is no doubt.
Accompanied by his wife, a man is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred crores of yugas by means of the Mahāpadma celestial chariot.
"As before" means she should practice non-violence, celibacy, sleeping on the ground, silence toward heretics, and so forth.
Having enjoyed various kinds of pleasures in the worlds of Īśa, Loka, and others,
and having attained them here in this world in due order, she shall obtain a husband according to her desire.
Thus ends the vow of the gift of the trident as declared in the *Śivadharmottara*.
Agastya said:
At the beginning of creation, the Pitṛs, having been created by Brahmā, then spoke to him.
O Blessed One, grant us our livelihood so that we may know it as it truly is.
Brahmā said:
"May the new moon day (amāvāsyā) be yours; on that day, let those who have been satiated by men with water, sesame seeds, and kuśa grass attain supreme satisfaction—there is no other way."
Likewise, having fasted on this day out of devotion to the ancestors, sesame seeds should be given;
may they, being long satisfied, bestow the supreme [fruit] upon him without delay.
Therefore, on this lunar day, a wise person should perform all of this.
Thus ends the Pitṛvrata as declared in the Varāha Purāṇa.
[254] Brahmā said:
The ancestors, being gratified by the offered rice-balls (piṇḍas) that have been tasted,
always bestow increase of progeny, wealth, protection, longevity, and strength.
The root mantras and the limb mantras are proclaimed by their respective names;
they are to be performed with offerings of perfume, flowers, and other gifts according to one's ability.
Even if performed with deceitful worship or through guile,
it bestows abundant results when accompanied by streams of clarified butter, sacrificial fuel, curd, milk, rice, and honey.

The oblation performed with a peaceful mind yields the previously mentioned fruits. This vow is to be explained in the same manner as the Vaiśvānara-pratipad-vrata. Thus ends the Pitṛ-vrata as described in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
He who observes the vow of subsisting on milk alone for one year on the fifteenth day—
by "fifteenth day" is meant the new moon day (amāvāsyā), according to the agreement with other Purāṇas.
At the conclusion of the year, the performer of the śrāddha should give five milch cows each,
along with saffron-colored garments and water-jars.
He goes indeed to the world of Viṣṇu and shall deliver a hundred ancestors;
in another birth he becomes a king—this is remembered as the milk-vow (payovrata).
Thus ends the Amāvāsyā-milk-vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The Prabhāsvaras, the Barhiṣads, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas."
And there are flesh-eating beings, elemental spirits, those who drink clarified butter, and those who feast at auspicious times.
O King, the hosts of ancestors are always to be honored with the offering of Soma;
O lord of men, beginning from the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra.
On that day, one should perform the śrāddha rite for as long as a year lasts,
with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, salutations, incense, lamps, and food.
And at the end of the year, O highly fortunate one, he should likewise give a milch cow to a Brahmin who is devoted to his ancestors, according to his capacity.
Having performed this desired vow for a year,
he attains those worlds;
having dwelt there for a very long time, he shall be happy.
The preeminent person attains liberation.
Thus ends the vow dedicated to the ancestors as described in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Yādava, beginning from the full moon of Caitra, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight...
Having performed the worship of the fire with perfumes, garlands, and an abundance of food.
O lord of men, one should likewise perform an oblation of sesame seeds in the name of Agni;
and at the end of the year, one should give gold to a Brahmin.
Having performed this desired vow for one year,
one obtains constant wealth and fame,
as well as an unsurpassed disposition toward dharma and beauty of form.
He, the foremost of men, [obtained] his desired objects at will.
Thus ends the Vahni-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O best of men, at the conclusion of the new moon day, one should observe a fast.
They worship the moon and the sun situated in a single zodiac sign within the two lotuses.
O Yādava, one should place the sun upon an eight-petalled lotus and the moon upon a sixteen-petalled one;
the sun should be entirely red and the moon white.

O illustrious one, one should offer oblations of sesame seeds and rice mixed with ghee and milk; O King, one should likewise worship according to the prescribed rite. At the conclusion of the vow, one should present gold to Brahmā and Indra.
Or, O illustrious one, he who desires his own prosperity should perform this vow for a year and, having completed it,
offer abundant lamps according to the prescribed rite.
Having attained the lunar station, his assembly ever increases; he shall be endowed with wealth both in the triple heaven and even here on earth.
Thus ends the Candra-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
[257] The Blessed One said:
Having reached the new moon day (amāvāsyā), [one should offer] to a Brāhmaṇa who has a family...
Whatever one may give to a knower of the Vedas, dedicating it to Śaṅkara;
May the Lord Soma, the eternal Mahādeva, be pleased;
the sin committed during seven lifetimes perishes at that very moment.
Thus ends the vow for the new moon day as declared in the Kūrma Purāṇa: By honoring three Brahmins on the new moon day with Brahmā, the Grandfather, in mind, one is liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the vow for the new moon day as declared in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*.

Thus concludes the section on new moon vows in the *Vrata-khaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Hemādri, who is the sovereign of all faculties, a master of all branches of knowledge, and the supreme king of great kings under the illustrious Mahādeva.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
Now follow the various vows for individual lunar days (*tithi-vrata*), among those vows for specific lunar days already mentioned.
Having found the opportunity, Hemādri once again took up that [work],
in which he set forth a multitude of vows that yield manifold fruits for various guests [of the dharma].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Hṛṣīkeśa, I remind you of that which was not told to me by you;
please speak of that Sāvitrī-vrata, being well-disposed toward me with grace.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall describe the supreme enhancer of the greatness of noble women,
just as the vow was formerly performed by Sāvitrī, the king’s daughter.
There was a lord of the earth named Aśvapati, a righteous soul devoted to the welfare of all beings,
who was beloved by the people of both the city and the countryside.
The lord of all, truthful in speech and with senses restrained, though childless,
undertook this vow together with his wife out of a desire for offspring.
She, the goddess Sāvitrī, beloved of Brahmā, was pleased with that which is renowned as the Sāvitrī mantra, the bestower of all desires.
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ"— this is her manifest form standing here,
the goddess who holds a water-pot in her hand, bestows boons, and speaks with a smile.
He said, "O King, you shall indeed have one daughter;
through her grace, all this has been attained by you."
She shall be addressed by the name Manmā, and she will indeed possess great fame;
O Great King, you ought not to grieve.
Having spoken thus, that goddess then vanished from sight;
after a long time, a daughter of divine form was born.
For the pleasure of Sāvitrī, she was honored with a livelihood and likewise with worship by means of the Sāvitrī mantra;
for she had been commanded by Sāvitrī herself, being indeed equal to Sāvitrī.
The Brahmins gave her the name Sāvitrī; nevertheless, she remained so [named].
Sāvitrī grew up in her father’s house like an embodied form;
after a long time had passed, she reached the bloom of youth.
People thought with amazement, "This woman of slender waist and broad hips has arrived like a golden statue; she must be a daughter of the gods."
She, whose eyes were like lotus petals, glowing as if with splendor,
also performed that Sāvitrī vow as instructed by her guru.
Then, having fasted and bathed his head, having duly worshipped the deities,
and having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules on the occasion of the moon's change (the new moon), he should cause the Brahmins to recite auspicious prayers.
Having received those flowers upon her head with her own hands, the princess,
surrounded by her companions, approached like the goddess Śrī incarnate.
Having respectfully saluted her father’s feet, the modest woman of lovely smiles,
with her hands joined in reverence, stood by the side of the king, O lady of noble form.
Seeing his own daughter, who had attained youth and possessed a divine form,
the king consulted with his ministers and spoke for the sake of recollection.
The time for giving away your daughter has arrived, yet no one chooses her from me;
though I reflect upon it, I see no suitor here who is a worthy match for her.
Nevertheless, you must be given by me; otherwise, blame would fall upon me. Act in such a way that I may not be censured by the gods and others.
"O daughter, this is well-known in the treatises on Dharma as it is being recited by me:
that maiden who sees her menses while still at her father's house and remains unconsecrated [by marriage],"
The murder of his father makes that girl a Vṛṣalī;
therefore, I send you here—perform the svayaṃvara yourself, my daughter.
"You have been approved by the elders; go quickly and do not delay.
Act in such a way that I do not become subject to reproach among the gods and others."
"So be it," said Sāvitrī, and having spoken, she quickly departed in a costly chariot,
surrounded by her ministers.
She went to the delightful penance groves of the royal sages,
there bowing at the feet of the venerable elders.
Then he wandered through sacred fords, mountains, and forests;
through various delightful regions and most enchanting hermitages.
Having accomplished her purpose at that hermitage,
she chose a boon and returned to her own abode.
Accompanied by the Sāvitrī mantra and with a deeply contented mind,
she beheld there the divine seer Nārada standing before her father.
Having bowed to the brahmin seated upon his throne, she, speaking with a smile,
related everything by which she had gone to and returned from the forest.
Sāvitrī said:
"There was among the Śālvas a righteous-souled Kṣatriya, a lord of the earth, known as Dyumatsena; by fate, he became blind."
He also had a beautiful wife named Rukmiṇī;
his kingdom was seized by his enemies through the employment of stratagems and sowing dissension.
He set out with that young wife;
his son, who was highly virtuous and increased in strength, accompanied him.
"I have mentally chosen Satyavat, who is rich in name and form, as my husband.
Nārada said:
"Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery! Sāvitrī, what is this that you have done?"
That you, out of childishness, acted toward the virtuous King Satyavat in such a manner.

That king speaks the truth; therefore he is remembered as Satyāśva (He of True Horses). Horses are always dear to him, and he makes horses out of clay. He also paints horses in pictures; for that reason, he is called Citrāśva (He of Painted Horses).
How can Rantideva be sufficiently praised for his devotion and his excellence in generosity,
being like the Brahmin Satyavāk, the skillful Śibi, and Auśīnara?
Noble like Yayāti, pleasing to behold like Soma,
and equal to the Aśvins in beauty, the son of Dyumatsena shone resplendent.
[262] There is only one fault, and no other: from this day forward, Satyavān will have his lifespan exhausted in a year and will relinquish his body.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having heard this from Nārada, the king said to his daughter:
"Daughter Sāvitrī, go and choose another bridegroom, a virtuous husband."
"In one year, he, being short-lived, will cast off his body.
Sāvitrī said:
"Kings speak but once; the wise speak but once."
A daughter is given once; these three things happen only once, each in turn.
Whether he be long-lived or short-lived, virtuous or even devoid of virtue, my husband has been chosen by me once; I shall not choose a second.
Having made a resolution with the mind, it is then expressed by speech;
afterwards it is carried out through action—this is the eternal law.
Nārada said:
"If this is desired for your daughter, then let it be performed quickly.
May there be no obstacle; Sāvitrī will bring you prosperity."
