Having spoken thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Nārada flew up into the sky and departed for the third heaven,
having produced incomparable sorrow for that king.
The king, too, agitated by suffering, remained long absorbed in meditation:
"Alas! A most grievous calamity has arisen for those like me, which is boundless."
"Alas! Having seen this suffering, it would be better to remain childless.
This was truly said by those who know the Purāṇas: 'A daughter is the sole vessel of misery.'"
[263] "Everything that was said by the gods appears false to me. Having lamented thus in many ways, he tormented himself by his own self.
Having recollected the goddess Sāvitrī, by whom a boon was granted in the past,
he sang [of] everything regarding his daughter's marriage and then performed the nuptial rites.
Having gone in person with all necessary materials to the forest frequented by sages,
at an auspicious moment, accompanied by Brahmins standing nearby who had mastered the Vedas.
Having honored that maiden and given her abundant cakes,
he spoke these words to the illustrious lady with a distressed inner soul.
O illustrious Dyumatsena, listen to my supreme words:
this daughter of mine is exceedingly dear to me, even more so than my own life.
For Satyavān, who loves the truth, is indeed a fitting husband for her;
and you, who love righteousness, are likewise a fitting father-in-law for her.
Therefore, her offenses should be forgiven; for this daughter of Vāli has been pampered by royalty.
Whatever is desired by the son-in-law, and whatever is desired by you two, [should be granted].
"That must be told to us; may it be well with you, I am departing.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Having thus taken his leave, the king departed, distressed by what Nārada had spoken."
And Sāvitrī, having obtained that husband desired by her heart, [was filled with joy].
The slender-limbed woman rejoiced exceedingly, like a meritorious person who has obtained what is to be given;
thus it was for those virtuous ones dwelling then in that hermitage.
O Bhārata,
as Sāvitrī lay there, reflecting day and night, some time passed for those who were watching her.
What was spoken by Nārada does not depart from my heart.
[264] Then, after a long time had passed, there came a time,
O King, when it was destined for Satyavat to die.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Prauṣṭhapada, at the beginning of the night,
Sāvitrī kept the words spoken by Nārada in her heart as she performed her count.
Thinking, "I must die on the fourth day," the beautiful woman undertook a three-night vow known as Sāvitrī, which yields great fruit.
Having observed the fast, that virtuous and devoted wife Sāvitrī remained steadfast;
then, having completed the three nights, she bathed and offered libations to the deities.
The sweetly smiling lady paid homage at the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law;
then Satyavat set out for the forest, taking his axe,
and Sāvitrī also followed behind her husband as he departed.
Though she was being restrained by her husband and addressed by the two elders, they both said to her: "O blessed lady, do not go to the thorny forest."
"You are delicate, O auspicious lady, and cherished by the king;
how will you be able to go through that forest filled with beasts of prey and thorny brambles?"
"Three fasts have been observed by you today; therefore, eat, O slender-waisted one.
Sāvitrī said:
"This is not the dharma for excellent women, that while her husband is hungry,"
And those who perceive the Dharma say that one should eat only by oneself.
Furthermore, I have a curiosity regarding the display of this forest;
I shall go with my husband as his companion before long.
"By the grace of your feet, do not impose a prohibition upon me.
Having understood this, that young woman, devoted to her husband, then departed.
Following her husband step by step in that delightful forest,
Sāvitrī traveled a long distance and then gathered fruits and other provisions.
Speaking pleasant words to his wife, he took sacrificial grass, *kuśa*, flowers,
and dry wood, and prepared a load of firewood.
In that manner, he split the wood with his axe as if in play;
then, as he was splitting it, a pain arose in his head.
Then, having concealed all of that, Satyavān took refuge in the shade of a banyan tree; overcome by pain, his mind was somewhat intent on describing it.
Leaning against a branch of the banyan tree, Satyavān spoke with a faltering voice:
"Sāvitrī, see how this pain afflicts my head."
I shall not say anything at all, for my mind is indeed wandering;
O beautiful one, I wish to sleep for a moment upon your lap.
"Rest, O mighty-armed one," said the sorrowful Sāvitrī;
"we shall go to our own beautiful hermitage later."
As long as he remained with his head on the ground, having placed [the child] upon his lap,
so long did hundreds and thousands of beings with terrifying faces appear.
The messengers of Yama, fierce and exceedingly terrifying, approached;
yet they were unable to remain near Sāvitrī once she cast her gaze upon them.
Having gone there, they reported all that wonder of Sāvitrī:
"By the mere casting of her glance, we were unable to run away from her."
That virtuous woman seems to burn our very bodies with her glance;
therefore, go yourself—Satyavān cannot be won back by us in any way.
Having heard this, the fierce and powerful Yama, the taker of life, rose up in anger from his excellent throne and mounted his terrible buffalo.
He arrived with great haste where that devoted wife sat;
Sāvitrī, too, was terrified as she looked here and there.
"Being on guard, how and who will lead my husband away today?"—
at that moment, the young woman saw a man who was dark-brown in complexion.
To him, who wore a crown and yellow garments and appeared like the sun itself risen,
Sāvitrī then spoke with sweet syllables after bowing down.
Who are you—whether a god or a daitya—who has come to assail me?
For I cannot be dislodged from my own duty by anyone through any power whatsoever.
Or rather, O best of men, it was as if she were about to ask [him] about a blazing flame of fire.
Yama said:
"I am Yama, the Restrainer, the terrifier of all beings.
This husband of yours, O devoted wife, has reached the end of his lifespan in your very presence."
"I was not able to conquer him by means of my servants; therefore, I have come here in person.
Having said this, [he seized] from the body of Satyavat that which was bound by the noose.
Yama forcibly dragged out the Person the size of a thumb;
then he began to proceed along the path frequented by the ancestors.
Sāvitrī too, of beautiful form, having performed an auspicious rite with her foot for the protection of her husband’s body,
then followed closely behind him.
[267] Because of her devotion to her husband, she remained unwearied as she meditated upon her own lord; with her thoughts fixed on him and her life-breath centered in him, Yama then spoke to her.
"Turn back and go, Sāvitrī; you have come here from a great distance.
This path, O large-eyed one, is not to be followed by anyone."
Sāvitrī said:
"Neither fatigue nor exhaustion ever arises for me as I follow my husband in the presence of your virtuous self."
For the virtuous, the virtuous are the refuge and none other; for women, the husband is always the refuge;
for those of the various castes and stages of life, the Vedas are the refuge; and for disciples, the teacher is the refuge.
For all living beings indeed there is a place upon the surface of the earth;
however, for women, there is no other refuge except their husband.
Pleased by these and other appropriate words endowed with righteousness and purpose, Dharmarāja spoke thus to Sāvitrī:
"I am pleased with you, O blessed one; therefore, choose boons, O lady of virtuous vows."
And she, bowing low in humility, chose five boons:
the restoration of her sight, as well as the kingdom for her high-souled father-in-law.
The life of her husband, as well as his eternal attainment of dharma;
the hundred sons of her father, and likewise a hundred for herself.
Having granted the boon, Dharmarāja then sent her back;
thereupon Sāvitrī returned to that banyan tree.
Placing his head upon her lap as before, she sat down;
O Bhārata, she massaged the limbs of her husband who was now at peace.
[268] Having risen and regained consciousness, the healthy man spoke this with urgency:
"O blessed lady, why was I not awakened? My time has passed far too quickly."
What indeed will my father say, and what will my sorrowful mother say?
For today everything has turned contrary; the time for dwelling in the forest has truly come.
Thinking, "Time has never passed for me without my mother and father," they both oppose me; thus, no further persuasion has been attempted here.
Sāvitrī said:
"How can I awaken you here while you are afflicted by a headache?
O sinless one, I did not delay here for the sake of doing anything improper to you."
Smiling, Sāvitrī rose and took up fuel for the fire upon her head;
then, taking the sacrificial wood, kuśa grass, and other necessities, the two of them went to their own hermitage.
Then the father beheld them with his own eyes with supreme joy.
Embracing him, smelling his head, and placing his son upon his lap, he said:
"By good fortune, I behold you returned together with your wife."
When asked the reason for his delay, he related it exactly as it was;
having understood the matter, the king was exceedingly delighted and honored that virtuous woman.
O highly fortunate one, Dyumnasena then obtained the kingdom enjoyed by his ancestors, with all thorns removed, and performed sacrifices.
Then the king, having approached his sons who were superior in their own virtues,
and having learned of Sāvitrī’s conduct as well as the life of her husband, [was filled with joy].
He attained the acquisition of a vast kingdom and experienced supreme joy.
This narrative of Sāvitrī destroys all sins.
O Pārtha, this [mantra] should always be recited in the morning; it bestows freedom from widowhood upon women, grants heaven and liberation, and bestows happiness and good fortune.
If this vow is performed quickly on the full moon day of the month of Bhādrapada,
its entire majesty has been recounted by me to you, O King.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, what kind of vow was that which Sāvitrī performed?
Tell me the procedure for it in that month of Bhādrapada."
"Who is the deity in that vow, what is the mantra, and what is the fruit, O All-pervading Lord?
Tell this to me, O Protector; for I am not yet satiated, O Mādhava."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Listen with devotion, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, to the Sāvitrī-vrata;
I shall describe it to you, O Yudhiṣṭhira, exactly as it was observed by that Satī."
On the thirteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth,
one should devoutly observe the vow of fasting for three nights.
If she is unable [to fast for the entire day], she who has conquered her senses should take a single meal at night on the thirteenth day;
on the fourteenth day she should eat only what is unasked for, and on the full moon day she should observe a complete fast.
Having bathed daily in a great river, a pond, or even a mountain spring—
especially on the full moon day— one should perform the ritual bath with mustard seeds, clay, and water.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having taken a measure (prastha) of sand in a vessel,
or else having taken grain such as barley, rice, sesame, and so forth;
Then, having fashioned an image of Sāvitrī in a bamboo vessel wrapped with a pair of cloths, one should likewise perform the purification of Brahmā.

[270] One should fashion an image of Brahmā out of gold, or clay, or even silver, according to one's means; the description of the form of Brahmā has been stated previously. One should offer a pair of red garments to Sāvitrī, and white ones to Brahmā.
One should thus worship Sāvitrī together with Brahmā with devotion,
using perfumes, flowers, food offerings, lamps, and auspicious sweetmeats.
It was filled with ripe kośātakas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and karkaṭī fruits,
as well as coconuts, dates, kapitthas, and pomegranates.
With *bījapūra* fruits, along with *nāraṅga*, *śākhoṭa*, and *panasa* fruits;
with fragrant coriander, cumin, and salt;
and with sprouted grains of the seven types of grain arranged in bamboo vessels.
With turmeric, auspicious neck-threads,
and saffron filaments, Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā, indeed effects her descent.
A Brāhmaṇa woman herself should worship that Sāvitrī with the mantra;
for other women, the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas is traditionally taught.
O Goddess, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, holding a lute and a book, O Mother of the Vedas, salutations to you; grant me freedom from widowhood.
Grant me beauty, grant me fame, grant me good fortune, grant it to me!
O Purifier, protect me just as you were pleased with Sāvitrī.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should cause a vigil to be held there with the sounds of singing and musical instruments and by throngs of joyful women.
One should pass that night with various meritorious narratives;
one should spend the night in celebration with stories concerning Sāvitrī.
Then, at the time of dawn, before the sun has risen,
O best of Brahmins, one should present the food offerings to Sāvitrī.
Then, [one should give] to one who knows the Sāvitrī-kalpa, to a reciter of the Sāvitrī narrative,
to one who knows the Vedas, to one established in his own duty, or to a poor householder.
O son of Kuntī, having prostrated according to the prescribed rite with this mantra,
[one should offer] [substances] mixed with dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and sesame seeds, while standing facing the eastern direction.
The brahmin, wearing clean garments, preceded by the utterance of *oṃ* and the word *svasti*, [should say]:
"This golden Sāvitrī, together with gold, is given by me."
"O Brāhmaṇa, please accept this for the sake of pleasing Brahmā.
Having thus given it to that best of the twice-born, O Yudhiṣṭhira, [he gave] that Sāvitrī.
One should take all that, including the food offering (naivedya) and so forth, to the house of a Brāhmaṇa;
one should walk ten paces oneself and then enter one's own home.
One should devoutly feed married women with sacrificial food (haviṣya) according to one's ability,
honoring them with flowers, saffron, vermilion, betel leaves, and neck-threads.
One should dismiss them with garments and ornaments according to one's ability, free from stinginess regarding wealth, saying: "May Sāvitrī be pleased."
After they have eaten well and are thoroughly satisfied, all the Brahmins should say:
"Sāvitrī, who is devoted to your excellent vows, shall be a granter of boons to you."
May you have eight sons and a husband with a long life free from disease;
may your noble lineage flourish, joined by sons and grandsons, and may that vow of yours, O observer of good vows, be fulfilled according to this rite.
Likewise, on the fifteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, at the foot of a banyan tree, a virtuous woman,
having fasted for three nights, should worship according to this rite.
Together with Satyavatī, O Yudhiṣṭhira, she, being virtuous, having hung a load of wood from a banyan tree, [worshipped] with offerings of fruit, food, and lamps.
Having kept a vigil at night preceded by song and dance,
O best of men, one should then perform the rites at dawn according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should give even that to a Brahmin, having prostrated and asked for his forgiveness;
this excellent vow, O Pārtha, has been described by me according to the prescribed rule.
Those who practice this in this world, accompanied by their sons and grandsons,
shall enjoy pleasures on earth for a long time and then go to the abode of Brahmā.
This merit-bestowing, sin-removing, auspicious rite that destroys suffering belongs to those who recite and listen to the Sāvitrī vow with devotion.
She who, having observed a fast for three days, worships her mother— the progenitor of the Vedas and the object of mindfulness— along with her husband,
likewise saves the lineage of her father as well as that of her husband, just like Sāvitrī.
Having extracted [it], she enjoys happiness for a long time upon the earth.
Thus ends the Brahma-Sāvitrī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. From the Skanda Purāṇa:
After Dharmarāja had granted his boon, Sāvitrī said:
O God, that virtuous woman who shall perform my vow with devotion, having been so instructed by her husband, shall become a recipient of all fruits.
The King of Dharma said:
Whether she be a woman, a widow, one without sons, or one deprived of her husband;
whether she has a husband or has sons—listen to this vow that must be performed.
When the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, the devoted wife,
having bathed and become pure, should sprinkle the banyan tree with abundant water.
One should devoutly wrap it with thread and honor it with fragrant flowers and auspicious unbroken grains of rice.
Saying "Salutation to Vaivasvatāya," she should circumambulate [the sacred site] clockwise;
being composed, she should perform the *nakta* rite at night for one year.
Likewise, she should worship the banyan tree (*vaṭavṛkṣa*) every fortnight.
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, one who eats light food should pass the twelfth days;
having brushed his teeth, he should then undertake the religious observance (niyama).
Having fasted for three nights, on the fourth day,
I indeed offered an oblation to the Moon and worshipped that virtuous lady.
"O Mother of the World, having honored the best of the twice-born with sweet foods according to my ability, I shall eat; O Sage, grant that I may do so without obstacle."
This is the mantra for the observance.
O best of the twice-born, having prepared a vessel made of bamboo and a *prastha* measure of sand,
one should place a vessel containing seven kinds of grain along with one *prastha* of ghee.
Having placed a golden image of Sāvitrī together with Brahmā upon two garments,
one should fast for three nights for the sake of their gratification.
One should remain at the foot of a banyan tree for as long as three days;
there, one should have a golden image of Sāvitrī fashioned together with Satya.
Having placed [the image] upon a silver couch, one should set it atop a chariot;
the auspicious chariot made of silver should be half a pala, or according to one's ability.
And likewise, [the worship] on a load of wood and at a banyan tree is very extensive;
having thus formed the pair, one should worship with freedom from envy.
O ascetic, having fashioned a circular mandala with cow dung,
perform the ceremonial bathing with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), as well as with water scented with perfumes and flowers.
Having worshipped Sāvitrī there with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, garlands, garments, and ornaments, the wise man should establish her within the mandala.
One should place a lotus made of yellow flour or else with sandalwood,
and then install the Goddess, who has a lotus-seat, upon that lotus.
Having established [the image] according to this rite, one who is free from envy should worship it.
Now, the mantra for the worship of Sāvitrī:
"Obeisance to Sāvitrī" for the feet, and "to Prasavitri" for the knees.
The hips belong to her whose eyes are like lotus petals; the belly belongs to the Sustainer of Beings.
Oṃ, salutation to Gāyatrī at the throat; she is the beloved of Brahmā on the head.
Now follows the worship of Brahmā and Satyavān:
the two feet are to be worshipped with "Salutation to Dhātṛ," and the two thighs with "Salutation indeed to Jyeṣṭha."
One should worship Parameṣṭhin in the penis and Agni in the form of the hips; having worshipped Vedhas in the belly, one should worship Padmanābha in the heart.
Having worshipped the throat for Vidhi, the face for Hiraṇyagarbha,
and the head for Brahmā, one should offer salutations to Viṣṇu in all the limbs.
Having thus worshipped them in due order according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, O King,
one should then offer the *arghya* to both with a silver vessel.
The *arghya* mantra for Sāvitrī:
Oṃ! O Goddess, who holds a lute and a book, O Mother of the Gods, salutations to you; grant me freedom from widowhood.
O devoted wife, O highly fortunate one, O you born of fire, O lady of pure smiles,
O you of firm vows and firm intellect, O you who speak so kindly to your husband!
O lady of noble vows, grant me the good fortune of non-widowhood; grant me sons, grandsons, and happiness. Accept this water offering; salutations, salutations!
Now, the *arghya* mantra for Brahmasatyavat:
"The entire universe, including gods, asuras, and humans, was created by you.
O God who upholds the vow of truth, whose form is Brahman, salutations be unto you."
Now follows the mantra for the worship of Yama:
"You are the witness of the worlds, the discernor of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
O Vaivasvata, King of Dharma, accept this *arghya*; salutations be unto you!"
O Dharmarāja, Lord of the Ancestors, source of peace for all living beings,
you who are the very form of Time, accept this water offering and grant me freedom from widowhood.
Free from envy, one should worship with fragrant flowers, food offerings, fruits, saffron, lamps, red garments, and ornaments.
[276] Now, the mantra for the prayer to Sāvitrī:
O Sāvitrī, the Gāyatrī of Brahman, who always speaks what is dear;
by that truth, protect me from the ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra.
You are Gaurī, you are Śacī, you are Lakṣmī, and you are the radiance within the lunar orb;
you alone are the Mother of the World—O fair-faced one, lift me up!
O lady of virtuous vows, grant me good fortune and the prosperity of my lineage.
Whatever evil I have committed, even throughout hundreds of births, may it all be reduced to ashes; and grant me the state of never being widowed.
Now follows the prayer-mantra of Brahmā and Satyavān: "O Lord, just as there is no separation for you from Sāvitrī,
so may there be no separation for us in birth after birth."
Now follows the mantra of prayer:
"O witness of all actions, worshipful to the world, worthy of universal homage, be gracious to me!
May this entire vow of the year be completely fulfilled for me."
O Goddess Sāvitrī, just as you obtained a virtuous husband with a lifespan of four hundred years, so may you act for me, O Goddess.
Sāvitrī, the progenitress and the constant beloved of Brahmā,
you are likewise worshipped by all the twice-born, by women, and by the hosts of sages.
O Goddess of virtuous vows, you are to be worshipped by all beings at the three junctions of the day;
this worship has been offered by me—accept it, and homage be unto you!
One should keep a vigil there with auspicious acts such as singing and dancing;
then, as each day passes, the women of the household are to be honored.
One should likewise offer vermilion, saffron, betel leaf with its sacred blade (*pavitraka*), and all these items of the "Eightfold Auspiciousness" (*saubhāgyāṣṭaka*), as well as alms-food.
Day and night, remaining free from desire and anger,
one should perform this worship of the cat in this manner for three days.
Now hear from me what must be done on the fourth day:
there should be twenty-four, sixteen, twelve, or eight couples.
One should honor [the preceptor] with gifts of clothing, cows, ornaments, coverings, and seats;
or else, one should honor a single preceptor who performs the ritual of the vow.
Endowed with all auspicious marks, having mastered the meaning of all treatises,
bathed after completing his Vedic studies and vows, he was peaceful and had conquered his senses.
Having honored him together with his wife with garments, ornaments, and decorations,
one should give a bed complete with its furnishings and a most beautiful house.
But one who is unable should, according to his capacity, arrange it little by little;
O daughter, he should have a golden image made together with her husband.
This is the mantra of visualization:
"O Goddess Sāvitrī, just as you obtained Satyavān as your husband with a lifespan of four hundred years, so do you act through me."
The mantra for the gift of an image:
Sāvitrī is the mother of the world; Sāvitrī is the father of the world.
This Sāvitrī is given by me; O Brāhmaṇa, please accept it.
Now, the mantra for receiving [the gift]:
"The beautiful Sāvitrī has been received by me, given by you;
as long as the moon and the sun endure, may you be happy together with your husband."
Then, with devotion, one should ask forgiveness from the guru and the guru’s wife.
Whatever deficiency I have committed in this vow, or whatever was poorly performed, may all that reach fulfillment through the word of you two.
The mantra for watering the *vaṭa* tree every month:
"Dharmarāja, Yama, Dhātṛ, Nīla, Kālāntaka, the Imperishable."
One should water the banyan tree month after month with these names: Vaivasvata, Citragupta, Dadhna, Bhṛtyu, Kṣaya, and Vaṭa.
"O daughter, let me dwell in a banyan tree; therefore, you should water it with great care.
Then, free from all hesitation, you should worship the Guru together with his wife."
With ornaments, garments, and captivating saffron,
[one should worship] near a banyan tree, or in a house, or upon an auspicious sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
One should perform an oblation of ghee with the Sāvitrī mantra;
O noble lady, one should devoutly offer milk-rice together with ghee.
With the *vyāhṛtis* and the mantra, one should likewise offer sesame, rice, and barley;
at the conclusion of the *homa*, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), free from stinginess regarding one's wealth.
Then, having diligently prostrated at the feet of the brahmin, she should ask for his forgiveness;
at the end of the day, the ascetic woman, being tranquil, should eat only at night.
Having offered the *arghya* water, and having beheld and bowed to Arundhatī, [one should say]:
"O Arundhatī, salutations to you, the beloved and auspicious wife of Vasiṣṭha."
O you who are worthy of homage from all the gods, O devoted wife, salutations be to you!
Having accepted everything, may this fruit together with its flower be given by me.
"Grant us sons, grant us happiness; accept this water offering, homage be to you!
Having spoken thus, she whose senses were subdued should eat together with her female companions and the Brahmins.
The woman who thus performs this unsurpassed vow [shall find that] her brothers,
fathers, sons, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen likewise [attain their goals].
Likewise, for three hundred births, she shall be long-lived and free from disease;
and together with her husband, that virtuous woman is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the Vaṭasāvitrī-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Indrāṇī said:
"O Brahmin, having seen me, Nahuṣa was exceedingly tormented by desire."
He began to assault me; therefore, I have come to you for refuge.
O Guru, is there some means, or perhaps a vow or even a gift, by which I may be liberated from my grief? Tell me that, O Great Sage.
Having heard her words, the preceptor then spoke these words;
Bṛhaspati said:
"There is a vow called Aśoka-trirātra, which is supreme for removing grief."
And that vow, which destroys grief, must be observed for three nights.
It destroys sins and removes diseases, increases sons and grandsons,
bestows long life, brings fame, and is the supreme granter of wealth and grain.
Listen to that supreme three-night vow named Aśoka, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, is divine, and destroys all illusion.
In the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Jyeṣṭha, and likewise Bhādrapada,
on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should observe the practice of eating only once a day.
Then, having risen at dawn, the observer of the vow should perform his bath;
then, having sipped water (ācamana) and become pure, he should prostrate himself again and again.
One should worship the Ashoka tree with devotion as the embodiment of Brahma and Vishnu,
O Queen of the Gods, according to this detailed sequence as declared in the Puranas.
O Aśoka, you have appeared here upon this earth for the sake of destroying grief;
O tree, who bears the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, accept this water of honor.

Herein is the fashioning of the images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra together with their Śaktis, since their offering is seen later on. Among these, the form of Brahmā and Sāvitrī is prescribed for the Putrakāma-Pūrṇimā vow; the form of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, however, for the Pūrṇimā-sthala-Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa vow; and that of Umā and Maheśvara is declared for the Aviyoga-Dvādaśī vow. Alternatively, the triad of images should be understood as that described in the general rules (paribhāṣā).
The mantra for the *arghya* offering is: "This water for the feet, prepared with meritorious water, is offered to you; salutations!"
O Aśoka tree, please accept this offering mixed with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and fruits.
The mantra for the water for the feet:
"Sandalwood, of three kinds, produced from trees and fashioned by the gods—
accept it, O best of trees, and show compassion toward me."
[281] The Mantra for Incense: O Lord of Trees, accept these flowers, such as the *mālatī* and others, which are divine; may my heart’s desires be fulfilled.
The Flower Mantra:
O Great Tree, these incenses such as guggulu and others, as well as those resembling aguru, have been offered by me with devotion; please accept them.
The incense mantra:
May this *ārātrika* lamp, fashioned from a great tree and joined with light,
which illuminates the world and is worthy of worship, truly belong to my lineage.
The lamp mantra:
You are worshipped by the divine gods, by the dānavas, and by the great serpents;
by the apsarases and the gandharvas—therefore, I worship you.
The mantra for worship:
"O Aśoka, this supreme food, provided with various kinds of edibles and consumables,
endowed with these six flavors, is offered to you by me with devotion."
Having thus worshipped that tree and prostrated before it again and again, the devotee should thereafter pray to the Aśoka tree with this mantra:
Whatever has been deficient or whatever has been done in excess in this vow,
may all that reach completion through your grace, O Best of Trees.
This is the mantra of prayer.
One should perform worship every month according to this very procedure;
indeed, one should continue for twelve months and then perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Having correctly undertaken the vow, one should fast for three nights;
one should have an *aśoka* tree fashioned out of silver, possessing various branches and endowed with fruit.
Having established it with a pair of garments, well-perfumed with fragrances and flowers,
provided with various fruits, and adorned with flower garlands;
One should listen to the Purāṇas with the diversions of song and instrumental music, and through various narratives of emotional states, as well as the fruit of this vow.
Having thus performed the vigil, one should make numerous gifts;
specifically, having honored sixteen pairs of Brahmins.
To them, however, water-pots, winnowing baskets, and garments should be given;
but for the teacher, a pair [of garments] should be honored with auspicious clothes and ornaments.
On the first day, one should likewise give gifts of cows, gifts of land, gifts of houses, and so forth; thereafter, one should bestow the Sāvitrī together with a Brahmin.
O fair-faced one, the Umāmaheśvara [image] should be given on the second day,
and the most beautiful Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa on the third day.
One should give the Aśoka tree along with its furnishings and ask forgiveness for everything;
thereafter, one should feed one's kinsmen and satisfy the poor and the helpless.
Then one should perform the breaking of the fast, and indeed break the fast again and again;
when this is done for three nights, the fruit that has been described by the wise is attained.
Listen to that, O highly fortunate lady; I shall tell it to you in brief:
the fruit which one enjoys by performing sacrifices such as the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha).
The fruit of that is multiplied ten-millionfold by [performing this rite for] three nights; of this there is no doubt.
This is likewise true for one who gives a cow, or various other gifts such as cows, buffaloes, and so forth.
Likewise, whatever merit is produced when the recollection of sacred fords is performed,
one obtains all that fruit which has been proclaimed as merit by the sages.
Having heard these words of her preceptor of immeasurable splendor,
that goddess then performed the supreme Paulomī-vrata.
By the power of that vow, she was united with Śakra;
this very vow was previously performed by the princess Sāvitrī.
By the power of this vow, a husband has been obtained along with prosperity by Anuṃdhatī,
Vedavatī, Damayantī, and Anasūyā.
All the heart's desires have been attained by Rukmiṇī and the other women;
those men on earth who read this, who hear it, and who perform the virtuous vow with devotion [shall likewise attain them].
Having been freed from evil, they go to the celestial realm in long-lasting celestial palaces and become happy.
Thus ends the Aśoka-trirātra-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O Maheśvara, tell me of some vow that brings about the state of not being widowed."
She experiences suffering for her husband, and likewise for her sons.
Childlessness is a great suffering, and having a wicked son is also suffering;
O Bull-bannered One, these indeed are the sufferings that women endure.
O best of gods,
O Śaṅkara, if there is such a thing, speak for the benefit of women so that they do not encounter widowhood in this mortal world.
She attains incomparable good fortune and a husband who is highly honored,
endowed with all excellent limbs, like another god of love.
O Śaṅkara, tell me this: who is the best among kinsmen, most worthy of worship, possessed of good conduct, endowed with wealth, and learned in all the scriptures?
Īśvara said:
Listen with a one-pointed mind, O Nandīśa, to this supreme vow called Rambhā,
by the performance of which women become fulfilled in their purpose.
O Nandin, she shall never become a widow nor ever childless.
O Lord Nandin, hear the procedure as it is performed by men.
O observer of noble vows, on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should with devotion dedicate that auspicious plantain tree to the observance of a three-night vow.
Having bathed, one should wrap [the image] with devotion and offer perfumes, flowers, and other articles;
one should perform this at night as a *nakta* fast for one year, remaining composed in mind.
In that very same manner, one should constantly water the plantain tree;
then, O observer of noble vows, having reached the twelfth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
O Nandin, having worshipped Śiva with unbroken grains (akṣata) at a river or a pond,
and having bathed, one should worship Him who bears Umā as half of His body.
Then, having observed a single meal, one should undertake the restraint for the vow, thinking:
"Having properly worshipped the Goddess of the Gods, I shall fast for three days."
[285] O Maheśvarī, by your grace, may my vow be fulfilled without obstacle. Having prepared a wonderful and most beautiful sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) for Rambhā, [I pray].
Standing near Rambhā, one should have a pavilion constructed there, provided with song and instrumental music, and adorned with garlands of flowers.
Provided with a canopy and endowed with all kinds of beauty,
one should place a plantain tree in the center, adorned with fruits, flowers, and other ornaments.
Then one should give a silver vessel of beautiful form, adorned with all ornaments and fitted with golden fruits, along with a pair of garments.
Salutations again and again to you, the plantain tree, the bestower of desires, the embodiment of wisdom;
salutations to Rambhā, the essence of delight, the granter of all happiness.
Salutations again and again to you, the plantain tree, the bestower of desires, the mocā.
The worship mantra:
O you who are meditated upon as a plantain tree, you who grant all desires when meditated upon;
O Goddess, grant me physical health and sovereignty—homage be to you!
This is the mantra of prayer:
"O one of excellent vows, one should worship with flowers, mantras, and colored threads;
with threads dyed with turmeric, accompanied by throngs of joyful women."
When a vessel filled with seven kinds of grain has been replenished to the measure of one *prastha*,
one should place Umā, Maheśvara, and Śambhu within it.
The observer of the vow should worship Hari and Rukmiṇī, who are seated upon a silver couch;
having wrapped them in a pair of garments,
he should anoint them with sandalwood paste and worship them with fragrant flowers appropriate to the season.
O Nandīśa, with these mantras and names, beginning from the feet,
one should worship the pair of feet of Gaurī, saying "to Tripurā."
Salutations again and again to the knees for Candranetrā and Aparṇā; then salutations to the waist for Manmathanāśa and Smarā, and thereafter to Girijā.
He should worship the navel with "Salutation to the Lord of All," and likewise Ambikā with "To Girijā";
in the heart, he should worship Maheśvara with "To the One Dwelling in the Heart" and "To the Trident-Bearer."
I bow to the Supreme Goddess Pārvatī with my face for the destruction of desire;
I bow to the one with matted hair who wields the trident, with my head for the granting of good fortune.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign accompanied by Umā,
with dance, instrumental music, song, and other offerings, one should then fast upon a plantain tree.
One should remain awake there with auspicious recitations from the Purāṇas;
thus, well-disposed and full of devotion, one should spend three nights honoring Nandīśa.
O Nandīśa, having drawn [the diagrams] for three days and being firm in his vows,
he should worship the couples according to the extent of his available wealth.
Having fed and honored the preceptor together with his wife,
there should then be an oblation of ghee performed with as many bilva leaves as the number of days.
Restraining his speech, the wise man should offer oblations into the fire with either speckled butter, curd, or milk, while reciting the mantra "tat savituḥ."
On the thirteenth day there are thirteen oblations, on the fourteenth fourteen, and on the fifteenth fifteen; such is the number for each day.
To the Guru, O sinless one, a white umbrella should be given, and likewise to his wife, a red garment should be offered while uttering these words.
May the bull-bannered God, together with Gaurī, be pleased with me.
The mantra for the gift:
"Just as Śacī stands by the side of Indra, O beautiful one,
may I likewise always stand by the side of my husband, O Rambhā."
Grant me beauty, grant me wealth, and likewise fame and good fortune;
grant me sons, grant me riches, and grant me all my desires.
The prayer mantra:
A tawny cow (kapilā) should be given there, together with all necessary implements;
likewise, an image of Umā and Maheśvara accompanied by a plantain tree.
Listen to how a pregnant woman or one whose child is still an infant should perform it:
she should take a single meal on the twelfth day and likewise on the thirteenth.
One should practice the Nandī-vrata by eating only at night on the fourteenth day and by fasting on the fifteenth day; thus one should observe this vow.
O Nandīśa, this vow bestows sons and grandsons. O Nandin of noble vows, for that woman who performs this vow according to this rite,
there shall be no one in her lineage who is childless or likewise a widow.
May you rejoice like Arundhatī until the dissolution of all beings;
may you, a virtuous woman, always be endowed with fame as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
This vow was formerly performed with devotion by the wives of the gods.
Through them, divine and exceedingly delightful enjoyments were obtained;
they shine in the heavenly world like the rays of the sun.
Through the majesty of the vow alone, one attains [the goal], there is no doubt;
such is the power of this vow, O high-minded Nandīśa.
Whoever should read or even hear it, that person also is honored in heaven.
Thus ends the Rambhā-trirātra vow as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Skanda said:
"O God of gods, Mahādeva, Supreme Brahman, Maheśvara!"
It bestows longevity, fame, wealth, sons, prosperity, dharma, and the perpetuation of one's lineage.
O Great Lord, tell me of the vow that destroys all sorrow,
by which sons who have been born, as well as those yet to be born, shall be free from disease and likewise happy.
Their sons and daughters-in-law appear most beautiful;
having attained incomparable good fortune, no co-wife is ever born to them.
By which, having enjoyed every happiness, one shall go to the abode of Vaikuṇṭha.
Īśvara said: O Skanda, I shall declare to you the eternal vow, the best of all vows,
by the mere performance of which one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
That which, having performed it, a human being obtains the fruit of all possible gifts is known as the "Three Nights of the Cow" (Gotrirātra), which destroys all sins.
Whether it be a woman or a man, one should observe the three-night vow on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja.
One should perform this vow near the festival of lights (dīpotsava):
having bathed in the morning on the thirteenth day and having indeed cleansed one's teeth.
Purified by devotion to Govinda, one should observe the vow for three nights, [reciting]:
"O Govinda, Lord of the worlds, sinless upholder of Govardhana!"
I shall observe the three-night vow; O Acyuta, be my refuge.
This is the mantra of the rule:
Having constructed an auspicious underground chamber— either in a cow-pen or on a path for cows—
measuring eight cubits [in length] and four cubits [in width], square and very beautiful.
Having fashioned a canopy with flower garlands and various kinds of fruits,
and having then prepared an altar in the center, one should have a mandala made there,
either named Sarvatobhadra or consisting of nine stalks.
In the center of that, one should place the god Hari, the upholder of Govardhana,
along with Rukmiṇī, Mitravindā, Śaibyā, and Jāmbavatī.
To the left of the Lord, indeed, Satyabhāmā, Rādhā, and Vāsudevāgnijit should be worshipped with a spirit of devotion.
On the right side, Nanda should be worshipped, and one should sacrifice to him first;
behind, one should worship the auspicious Balabhadra and Yaśodā.
Surabhī, Sunandā, and the cow named Subhadrā—
these four goddesses should be placed in front of Kṛṣṇa.
Sixteen auspicious images should be fashioned from gold māṣakas,
and Govardhana should be made of silver weighing one pala.
Adorned with great trees shaped like umbrellas and graced by auspicious birds,
it was crowded with cowherds and cowherdesses and endowed with massive trees.
Having thus established [the deity] with effort, one should then perform the worship:
"Oṃ, come, Blessed One Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by the cowherds and cowherdesses."
And accept the worship offered by me along with the queens, Rukmiṇī and the others.
The invocation mantra:
"Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa for the feet; obeisance to Hari for the knees;
obeisance to Baladeva for the belly; obeisance to Mukunda for the hips."
The two arms should be worshipped with "to the wielder of the discus" (cakriṇe), the throat with "to the wearer of the beautiful throat" (śrīkaṇṭhadhāriṇe),
the face with "to the lotus-faced one" (padmamukhāya), and the head with "salutation to Govinda.
One should thus worship the eight limbs of Hari using mantras beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with "namas."

Salutations to Rukmiṇī; salutations to Mitravindā; salutations to Śānti; salutations to Jāmbavatī; salutations to Surabhi; salutations to Satyabhāmā; salutations to Rādhā; salutations to Nāgnajitī; salutations to Yaśodā; salutations to Balabhadra; salutations to Nanda; salutations to Sunandā; salutations to Subhadrā; salutations to Nāgnajitī; salutations to Kāmadhenu.

The prayer mantra:

Having asked his teacher for forgiveness there, he should eat pure and consecrated food,
seated together with beloved and disciplined companions, restrained in speech, and intent upon Viṣṇu.
Having observed this vow with a pure mind during the festivals of lamps, a man brings about the increase of his entire lineage;
endowed with happiness, he enjoys an abundance of pleasures.
At the end, that person goes to the abode of Murāri.
Thus ends the Gotrirātra-vrata as described in the Skanda Purāṇa.
When the Bhārata war had concluded and the Kuru army had met its destruction,

I bow to the feet for the sake of crushing the Dānava Bali; I bow to the knees for the sake of protecting the three worlds.

The worship mantra:
O Vāsudeva, Lord of the universe, who has made Your dwelling in the Ocean of Milk!
Accept this *arghya* offered by me, and grant me prosperity forever.
The *arghya* mantra:
Having offered the *arghya* with *kūṣmāṇḍa*, coconut, citron, and pomegranate fruits,
and having performed worship, one should propitiate Kāmadhenu.
The Worship of Kāmadhenu.
Having formed a hollowed cup with the hands, one should say this before Kāmadhenu:
"May the wish-fulfilling cow, being pleased, destroy my diseases."
May my cow of plenty, being pleased, destroy my sins.
May the gracious Kāmadughā grant me happiness;
may the gracious Kāmadughā grant me sons.
Then, when the third day has arrived, three bamboo vessels [are prepared].
He has attained the state of Virūḍhaka and is fully endowed with the fruit of perfection.

one should install the deity there for the sake of completing the vow.

then, at the time of dawn, one should perform a fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rites.

furthermore, a cow should be given to the Brahmin, and having made the offering, one should follow behind.

Now, I shall tell you another ancient history as well.
From the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha, there emerged a certain auspicious discourse between a tigress and a cow, consisting of the science of ethics and born of a divine lineage of cattle.
By her own will, the cow went forth and roamed in the deep forest;
by the power of her asceticism, she was fearless toward lions, tigers, and other wild beasts.
That cow of the Lord of Munis went into a mountain cave;
there was a very powerful tiger who had been cast down by Śiva’s curse.
With large tusks and a massive body, that hero named Jalavardhana went forth with outstretched arms to experience the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Vyāghra said:
Many days have passed for me while tormented by hunger;
having seen you by the power of fate, you have been prepared as my food.
The cow said:
"O best of tigers, by the power of Vasiṣṭha, I certainly shall not be harmed by powerful, wicked creatures; you may know this for certain."
[297] O mighty-armed one, listen to these few words with a one-pointed mind;
I do not speak before you out of my own personal desire for life.
What purpose is served by a Kṣatriya who possesses an unstable body filled with impurities and excrement, yet remains devoid of service rendered to others?
Those who, indeed, through speech, mind, or action, do not provide assistance even when one's body is being destroyed— their birth is meaningless.
Those soldiers who, at the time of death in battle, possess other thoughts and utter words of weakness, go to a terrible hell; so say the ancient sages.
Those whose minds are free from the illusion of wife, son, and kinsmen,
and who are devoted to the Ancient Person (Purāṇapuruṣa), attain the supreme goal.
A boy born on a Monday resides in my house;
he has seen me arrive, and there is sorrow born of affection in my heart.
The friend will satisfy that child with milk according to her own desire;
without telling my friend, I shall quickly come into your presence.

The tiger said: "In the Vedas, Shastras, and Puranas, it is recited by the ancient sages that [one may take food] during times of distress to women, Brahmins, or cows, at a wedding, or during a conflict with a king."
Indeed, even at the risk of one's life, one must never speak an untruth except in other circumstances;
for there are those who have fallen into calamity and those who have come under the power of their enemies.
He by whom the self is protected performs that [task] without a doubt;
for before him stands the food ordained by the Supreme Lord.
The fool who does not grasp it shall indeed go to a state devoid of bliss,
[a state] that cannot be attained by gods, nor by humans, nor by yakṣas, nor by piśācas.
[298] Indeed, truth is a firmly established word for living beings who, having encountered calamity,
subsist on contentment produced by gathering water and grass.
For those fallen into distress, even untruth [is permissible]; what then need be said of cattle?
The Earth, the Ādityas, and the gods abide in truth.
"Therefore, having set aside the truth, you must speak in the presence of the Bull-bannered Lord.
Hearing those words of his, she was overcome with affection for her child.
There, indeed, he made a vow again and again in the presence of the tiger.
The cow said:
"O tiger, having been born as a twice-born man, he is then reborn as one fallen from the Vedas—
one who is devoid of Vedic study and the twilight rituals, and abandoned by truth and purity."
May I be tainted by that sin— the sin of one who sells what should not be sold and officiates at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officate— if I do not return again.
Whatever sin exists in one of evil intent, a rogue, a deceiver, or one who cheats others—if a man persists in giving gifts and bestowing them upon such a person; [that sin falls upon him].
May I be smeared with that sin if I do not return again,
or if I sell the Vedas, or eat the food of a corpse or one who is in a state of ritual impurity.
May I be smeared with that sin if I do not return again—
[the sin] of one who seizes a woman whose children have died and who fails to support her parents.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that same sin as he who would steal the property of the gods, the property of the guru, or the property of Brahman.
Whoever should seize land given by himself or given by another—
whatever sin belongs to one who is not a Vaiṣṇava, that same sin belongs to the one who acts with hypocrisy.
May I be smeared with that sin if I do not come back again—
to one whose senses are unrestrained, to a rogue, to one who slanders others' faults,
to an ungrateful person, to a miser, to one who covets another's property, and to a deceitful man.
May I be smeared with that sin if I do not return again,
being devoid of virtuous conduct and causing suffering to others.
May I be smeared with that sin if I do not return again—
O you who are contented with slandering others and devoid of all virtuous qualities!
Whatever sin lies in the killing of a Brahmin, and likewise in the murder of one's father or mother—
may that transgression fall upon me if I do not return again.
If I do not return again, may I be smeared with that same sin by which a man who has two wives abandons one of them.
Whatever sin belongs to those hunters who administer poison while remaining in their own places,
by that sin may I be tainted, if I do not return as a serpent once more.
Whatever sin belongs to the nihilists and to those ancient seekers of sense-objects—
by that sin may I be tainted, if I do not return again.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by the sin of whoever yokes three oxen to a plough in an uneven manner.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin of those who show contempt for cows and strike them with sticks.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin of one who, having given his daughter once, desires to give her a second time.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that same sin as he who creates an obstacle while this story is being told.
If I am not reborn again, may I be tainted by that sin of one who constantly reviles ascetics and is likewise devoted to reviling the Vedas—
especially one whose wife is a Brāhmaṇa woman who is pregnant.
May I be smeared with that sin if I do not return again to one who is cruel,
devoid of family dharma, and intent on non-virtuous action.
May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again—
to the fool, the heretic, the thief, and the seller of sesame seeds.
He alone eats sweet food, failing to support his wife and son;
he is self-indulgent, of evil conduct, and a plunderer of the property of the gods.
May I be smeared with that sin if I do not return again—
[the sin] of those who kill Brahmins, those who revile their gurus, and likewise those who revile their masters.
May I be smeared with that sin if I do not return again to Kurukṣetra during the great festival when the moon and the sun are eclipsed.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin of those who accept a great gift devoid of offerings to the gods and ancestors.
May I be smeared with the sin of that false witness, the liar, and the one who covets another's property,
if I do not return again.
Those who approach the wives of others, those who are betrayers of trust,
and one who is destitute of wealth or afflicted by a great disease— [these are not to be approached].
If I do not return again, may I be smeared with that sin of whatever woman, endowed with beauty and youth, does not worship me.
Now, O King of Beasts, what is the use of speaking at length before you?
If I do not come quickly, my truthfulness will not be realized.
Satisfied by those words and free from desire for food, the tiger said:
"O cow, release your extended trunk and go to your own home.
Released by the tiger, that cow returned to her own hermitage.
Seeing that the calf had grown large, she became intensely full of milk;
having satisfied the young one with her milk, she entrusted him to her companions.
Seeing them, the cows were distressed, filled with maternal affection;
seeing them, the boy was even more sorrowful, thinking, "I do not know how it may be for me."
Taking each child there in turn, they asked the reason for this;
after she had related the account to them, she spoke to that boy.
Follow me and go, for you are endowed with truthful speech;
I shall go quickly to that forest where the tiger dwells.
The friend said:
