The supreme enmity between a tiger and a cow is renowned throughout the three worlds."
When the welfare of Brahmins, women, or children is at stake, or when faced with a life-threatening danger from an enemy, the sages have declared that untruth is not at all blameworthy.
In ancient times, the Lord of the Gods slew the powerful Vṛtra, the enemy of the gods;
likewise, Viṣṇu, having made oaths, [slew] Śaṅkha, who was devoid of trust.
Therefore, remain there in your own home together with your retinue;
eminent sages reside there, for wicked beings never dwell there.
The cow said:
By truth the sun shines; by truth the moon shines;
even the four-faced Brahmā [shines] by truth; by truth the entire world [endures].
Soma might perhaps live deprived of his true speech;
by truth the world of truth exists, and truth is established in the Veda.
By the power of my truthful word, I shall go toward that tiger without fear;
and in that forest, the tiger saw the cow approaching as it was walking along.
The tiger said:
"Oh, how incomparable is my fortune! The wish-fulfilling cow has arrived; liberated from this wicked birth, I shall go into the presence of Hara."
Just as the purifying wish-fulfilling cow, which removes the impurities of the Kali age, arrived,
there appeared a tiger-like host of moons, the embodiment of all prosperity,
with hands bound by spotless jewels and a resplendent crown.
Having worshipped her thoroughly, he addressed the cow with devotion and sweet words.
I am blessed; I have accomplished my purpose through the grace of the wish-fulfilling cow;
freed from all sins, I go into the presence of Hara.
May the cows protect my merit; may the cows protect my fame;
may the cows protect my family—my wife, sons, and grandsons.
Those cows, when fully honored, bestow great abundance upon those such as me;
cows remove all sins and grant the fruit of all merit.
Homage be to the wish-fulfilling cows who purify the three worlds;
homage again and again to Nanda and the others, by whose milk the entire universe is sustained.
The Cow said:
O Great Gaṇa, choose a boon that brings joy to the worlds;
whatever desirable boon you wish for, I shall grant it to you out of devotion.
The Gaṇas said: "May the world always be happy through its trust in you and your followers, who are like wish-fulfilling cows (kāmadhenu) capable of bringing benefit to the entire universe."
May all success be attained through your grace by those who delight in your progeny or who take refuge in your progeny.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having been told, "So be it," she departed; the tiger went to the city of Śiva, and the satisfied Kāmadhenu returned to the hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.
Having performed the *gotrirātra* rite in this manner, whether a woman or a man,
O observer of excellent vows, one attains all desires for seven births.
Thus ends the narrative of the Gotrirātra-vrata as spoken by Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
One should draw nineteen lines running north and south;
the crescent moon consists of three squares, while the chain in the corner consists of five squares.
A stepped well (vāpī) may consist of eleven squares, while a bhadra consists of nine squares;
a stepped well is also recorded as having twenty-four squares, with its enclosure wall consisting of twenty.
One should fill the white moon-chain and the black creeper with blue;
the auspicious black [lotus] or the white one has a yellow pericarp as its circumference.
The Sarvatobhadra mandala is endowed with the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Thus ends the procedure for the mandala.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace many meritorious deeds have been performed by me."
O Madhusūdana, many meritorious deeds have been heard of and performed by me.
They shall be removers of all sins and bestowers of all desires;
now I wish to hear of the most excellent vow among vows.
O Mādhava, if you are pleased with me, tell me some vow of yoga by performing which a man or a woman is liberated from all sins.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O best of kings, I shall describe the most excellent of vows, which has not been told to anyone; listen to that, O supreme among monarchs.
Whatever desires they may long for, men and women obtain them exactly so; at that very moment, they are liberated from all [obstacles].
O King, by the grace of the divine wish-fulfilling cow,
one obtains good fortune, progeny, prosperity, and supreme happiness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"If you are pleased, O Blessed One, tell me the auspicious procedure for this vow, O tiger among men; by your grace, I shall perform it."
What are the mantras, what are the salutations, and which deities are proclaimed? What is the gift, and what is the mantra for the water-offering (arghya)? O best of gods, please tell me.
Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, that which was previously spoken by Nārada to Sagara and the others has been recalled by you; listen with a one-pointed mind, O King, to this vow.
One should begin on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada;
having risen at dawn on that thirteenth day, one should become pure.
One should first undertake the observance, preceded by the cleaning of the teeth;
having sipped water and taken up water, one should utter this mantra:
O Goddess, in my undertaking of the fast for this vow of three nights at the three junctions of the day, be my refuge; salutations to you who take the form of a cow.
May the great god, the Lord Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa, be gracious;
[one should worship] the golden image of the god Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa according to one's own capacity.
One should bathe the Lord of Kamalā with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the products of the cow (gavya),
and then install Him upon a Sarvatobhadra mandala or even on an eight-petaled lotus.
One should please the Earth and likewise Hari with fragrant flowers, excellent food offerings, hymns of praise, songs, and dances, as well as by the offering of coconut water as an *arghya*.
O Jagannātha, bestower of fortune, may this three-night vow of mine be brought to completion;
accept this *arghya*, salutations be unto you!
Thus ends the *arghya* mantra.
Thereafter, one should perform the *ārātrika* ceremony with devotion for the pleasure of Kṛṣṇa,
using a new water-filled jar filled with sacrificial food (*haviṣyānna*).
Having performed this for three days, O Pārtha, one should likewise settle [the image];
then, having worshipped the cow, one should perform the pouring of water and circumambulation.
In former times, having offered earrings, a water-pot, and a ritual pitcher,
along with food, clothing, perfumes, and other divine flowers accompanied by lamps;
For three days, the observer of the vow should keep a lamp of ghee burning day and night without interruption,
either in front of the cow or within the sacred circle of the deity.
Then one should perform the offering of the *arghya* with fruits such as coconut and others.
The Arghya-mantra:
Five cows were produced when the great ocean was being churned;
among them, salutations again and again to that cow who is Nandā.
By whomsoever the cow following the path has been circumambulated,
by him the earth with its seven continents has been circumambulated.
May cows be before me; may cows be behind me;
may cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows.
The wise man should offer the *ārātrika* lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), a great festival of song and instrumental music, as well as saffron, a jar, a water-pot, and a cow.
Having thus worshipped that cow with perfect devotion for three days,
one should feed her barley and grass and give her water to drink.
One should perform [the rite] with cow dung, unbroken grains, and rice; by those very means, one should effect the breaking of the fast.
Thereby, one delivers the people of that region from even that which is falling and brings misery.
One should perform a vigil at dawn, which destroys all sins;
O Pāṇḍava, one is liberated from the three kinds of sin within half a watch.
By performing this expiation for the sin committed, one is released from it within half a watch;
having had four bamboo vessels made, one should worship them.
With auspicious coconut water, grapes, dates, and pomegranates;
with sprouted grains, flowers, vermilion, cloth, saffron, and collyrium.
On the first day, one should offer an *arghya* of citron; on the second, auspicious pomegranate;
and on the third day, one should offer an *arghya* with coconut for three days.
Three bowls should be prepared, filled with sacrificial food (haviṣyānna),
for the deity Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa and for Brahmā together with his wife.
One should worship with flowers, garments, and golden threads, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
for three days, one should devotedly provide food for a married couple and a cow.
On the day of breaking the fast, she should feed Brahmins, her beloved kinsmen, and others;
she should then present that cow to the Guru, who is the very form of Viṣṇu.
Adorned with saffron, clothed in garments, and decorated with a bell and a crown,
preceded by songs, instrumental music, dance, and the recitation of peace-mantras.
O Pārtha, she who performs this supreme Gotrirātra vow in this manner shall, by the vow itself, lead even a sinner as far as the house of a Brahmin.
But for women and men, O best of kings, it is always difficult to obtain even thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of vājapeya sacrifices.
Whatever fruit one obtains by performing the vow of three nights at a cow-pen,
that same fruit is obtained at Prabhāsa, Kurukṣetra, and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
O King, one might give a hundred loads of gold to obtain that same fruit as he who has given a gift of a cow,
complete with clothing and fulfilling all desires.
Clad in the garment of the ocean, he has given away the earth;
thus, O Pārtha, does one perform this supreme three-night vow.
A man is liberated from the threefold evil committed in other existences;
O lord of men, she shall never experience the suffering caused by a husband.
He will undoubtedly experience the happiness of having sons and grandsons.
And in another birth, that woman shall not experience widowhood;
even in a future existence, widowhood will not be a source of great suffering for her.
One without a son obtains sons, and one devoid of wealth obtains wealth—
whatever has been acquired through body, mind, and indeed through action.
All that sin perishes when the vow of three nights for the sake of one's lineage is performed;
having enjoyed abundant pleasures in this world, one’s lifespan shall indeed be complete.
By the power of this vow, O King, one is glorified in Goloka;
it bestows fame, grants wealth, and brings about good fortune.
It bestows long life and health and destroys all sins;
having bathed there with devotion, O King, you should perform the vow together with your wife.
"If you desire to obtain sovereignty and eternal fame here, [then perform this]"—
having heard that, the best of the Pāṇḍavas, being composed, undertook the vow.
"By the power of this vow, a kingdom free from thorns has been obtained.
Thus ends the Gotrirātra-vrata as declared in the Śrī-Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
Listen attentively to that which you ask me;
I shall describe the most excellent vow, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires and aims.
By performing this rite, women do not become widows or remain childless;
the lifespan of their husbands increases, and they possess sons endowed with wealth.
Therefore, I shall fully proclaim that supreme vow among all vows,
by the grace of which Umā [attained] Rudra, Lakṣmī [attained] Kṛṣṇa, and Śacī [attained] Hari.
O Sage, just as Sāvitrī attained Rāma, and as Sītā [attained] Rāma,
so too did the goddess Umā in former times cast off her own body due to the wrath of Dakṣa.
Born in the house of Himavat, wearing matted hair and bark garments,
she practiced severe penance— helpless, without food, and with her senses conquered.
Standing on a single big toe, the young woman was surrounded by the five fires;
seeing her firm resolve in asceticism, Śambhu himself then departed.
"Why do you now perform such a painful act, O Gaurī? Umā said:
"So that Mahādeva may indeed become my supreme husband."
For that purpose, I am performing severe penance, difficult even for the sun to endure.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O girl, to the easy means, the supreme vow among all vows,
by the performance of which Śambhu will grant you half of his own body.
Therefore, O blessed lady, observe for three nights the vow known as the Bilva-vrata;
by performing it with devotion, this woman obtained Maheśvara as her husband.
"From him, O great sage, Kārttikeya was born, as was Gaṇeśa," thus was it said previously by Brahmā to Agasti, the best of sages.
His mind filled with wonder, he proceeded to ask about the ritual.
Agastya said:
"O best of men, at what time, on which day, and in what place [should this be performed]?"
By what rite should it be performed, and how is the lord of the forest (the sacrificial post) to be worshipped?
Brahmā said: O best of the twice-born, when the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived,
on the full moon day and during the day of the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, one should perform the supreme bath with siddhārtha seeds for the sake of spiritual perfection.
Thereafter, one should water the Śrīvṛkṣa tree and worship it with perfumes and flowers;
for one year, one should subsist on a single meal of sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Upon seeing a dog, a pig, a donkey, or similar creatures, one should abandon eating;
one should practice this rule correctly month after month.
Then, when a full year had passed, O great sage, he went to the vicinity of the bilva tree and took a prastha measure of sand in a vessel.
Alternatively, having taken grain such as barley, rice, sesame, and so forth,
one should wrap it in a pair of cloths within a vessel made of bamboo.
One should fashion a golden image of Umāmaheśvara according to one's ability and adorn it well;
one should offer a pair of red garments and an oblation consisting of food together with fruit.
With many kinds of flowers and likewise various kinds of fruits,
with jaggery, sugarcane, cumin, grains, salt, and sprouted seeds,
as well as with the seven types of grain and lamps prepared in bamboo vessels.
With necklaces, auspicious threads, and saffron filaments,
this Goddess Umā, the beloved of Hara, effects her descent.
O Abode of Śrī, salutations to you; O Beloved of Śiva, let there be obeisance to you!
Grant me non-widowhood and indeed prosperity in birth after birth.
O you who are worshipped, bestow upon me prosperity, wealth, husband and sons, health, the continuity of my lineage, good fortune, and the perfection of beauty.
A Brahmin who is peaceful and learned in the mantras should offer a thousand bilva leaves according to the prescribed rite, and therein he should also offer milk-rice (pāyasa) as an oblation.
Having fashioned a silver tree adorned with golden fruits,
one should wrap it with a yellow cloth up to one hundred and eight times.
Beginning on the thirteenth day and continuing until the lunar day is complete,
one should keep a vigil for three nights, subduing the senses through fasts.
O Lord of Ramā, O Lord of Creatures, O Sovereign of the three worlds, O Master!
O Maheśvara, together with Gaurī, accept this water offering from me, O God.
Then, when morning has arrived, having bathed with sesame and mustard seeds,
one should honor the preceptor and his wife with garments, ornaments, and flowers.
Having worshipped the preceptor with devotion, one should diligently offer these: sandals, shoes, an umbrella, a bed, and a well-adorned cow.
On that day, one desiring one's own welfare should honor sixteen, eight, or four Brahmin couples adorned with garments, ornaments, and gifts of cows,
and should provide them with sweet food to eat.
The woman who performs this vow, which destroys sin,
brings about all perfections, and is meritorious, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having remained in the presence of Śiva for as long as a hundred crores of kalpas,
she shall thereafter become a queen in the mortal world, endowed with sons and grandsons.
Thus ends the Bilva-trirātra-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa:

Having taken refuge at the root of a Bilva tree, one who is pure and fasts for three nights should mutter the name of Hari one hundred thousand times; he thereby removes even the sin of killing an embryo.
Thus ends the Haratrirātra vow as declared in the Saura Purāṇa.
Skanda said:
I shall now describe the Arundhatī vow, which always bestows good fortune.
By practicing this correctly, a woman indeed becomes a vessel of good fortune.
O bull among the gods, having reached the spring season on the third lunar day, she gives birth to one endowed with beauty and accompanied by sons and grandsons.
Having bathed according to the prescribed rules and having fasted for three nights, she,
firm in her vows, summoned four couples.
One should worship with flowers, betel leaves, sandalwood, and likewise with unbroken grains (akṣata),
as well as with saffron, agallochum, camphor, vermilion, and musk.
Having placed it upon a stone slab, accompanied by molasses, ghee, and salt,
together with a clod of earth, and wrapped in a pair of cloths.

A *loṣṭaka* is a grinding stone placed upon a flat slab of stone; this is what is meant by the "supporting lower millstone. One should invoke the Great Goddess, who is equal to the life-breath of Vasiṣṭha:
"Come, O boon-granting Goddess; O lady of virtuous vows, be present here!"
O beautiful lady, you are the foremost of all women devoted to their husbands;
come, worship the goddess Arundhatī with auspicious flowers.
Having fashioned a golden image with two arms, all its limbs beautiful, and holding a rosary and a water-pot, one should worship it with [the following] names.

One should always worship her thighs with "Salutation to you, who are worshipped by the gods," and her knees with "Salutation to you, who are worshipped by the world. One should then worship her hips with "Salutation to the Great Chaste Lady."
Salutations always for the sake of peace to the navel as the profound ether, to the wife of the Sage, then to the two breasts as the nourishers of the world, and likewise to the throat and arms.
Salutations again and again to the two hands as Varadā, and to the face as Dhṛti;
likewise, Arundhatī is to be worshipped, and Kamalapriyā is the head.
Having thus worshipped that goddess, one should offer fragrances and flowers;
having worshipped the virtuous goddess, one should then present the *arghya* offering.
O highly fortunate Arundhatī, who speaks kindly to Vasiṣṭha;
O Goddess, grant me good fortune, and grant me wealth and sons.
[314] The Arghya Mantra:
Having offered the arghya with devotion while holding a handful of flowers,
one should pray to that illustrious, great chaste lady who is worshipped by the world.
Grant me sons, grant me wealth, grant me good fortune, O lady of noble vows;
grant me grandsons and all my desires, O Goddess, salutations be unto you!
This is the mantra of supplication:
"Likewise, on each and every day, the married women (suvāsinīs) should be worshipped;
similarly, one should offer auspicious scents, unbroken rice (akṣatas), and all kinds of edible foods."
And they should likewise perform oblations with sacrificial fuel-sticks and auspicious sesame seeds,
either one hundred and eight times or for as many days as there are.
And having honored twenty-four couples with ornaments, clothing, and other gifts, according to the number sixteen.
To the preceptor together with his wife, one should give garments and ornaments,
a bed with its furnishings, and a bell-metal vessel accompanied by a lamp.
One should give a mirror, a fly-whisk, and a milch cow;
moreover, having fed [the Brahmins], one should give women winnowing-baskets along with water-jars.
Likewise, water-pots with water, as well as their clothing according to the prescribed rule,
should be given; and *polikās*, *ghṛtapūpas*, and especially *pūrikās*, as well as *somālikās*, should be offered— one of each, and likewise doubled.
The food given should be double the amount required for one's own portion. Having honored the poor and the helpless, one should personally observe the practice of eating only at night;
"dharma" is the word understood from the context.
By this very same procedure, a woman may also perform the vow.
Likewise, for a thousand births, she attains freedom from widowhood,
endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of wealth and grain.
That great satī shall live for more than a hundred years together with her husband;
having thus worshipped him, she goes to the state that is free from all suffering.
The wives of gods likewise in heaven,
as well as the wives of sages and the highly fortunate wives of kings— [all attained this through] a vow that grants all desires.
Thus ends the Arundhatī-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Now I shall further describe another excellent rite, the Dūrvā-trirātra.
It bestows happiness, prosperity, sons, and grandsons upon women.
In ancient times, this dūrvā grass arose from the body hairs of Viṣṇu;
upon it was placed the supreme churned nectar.
There, drops from the overflow of the jar of nectar fell upon the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, and uragas.
Because her body was touched by them, this dūrvā grass became ageless and immortal;
it is venerable, pure, and likewise saluted and honored by the gods.
Listen, O observer of noble vows, to the complete procedure for the Dūrvā-trirātra rite:
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
Having fasted for three nights until the lunar day is complete,
one should worship the deity Umāmaheśvara, as well as Sāvitrī and Dharma.
[316] Having established [the deity] at the root of a *dūrvā* grass plant, one should then have a pavilion constructed.

The form of Umāmaheśvara is to be envisioned during the first Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow; the form of Sāvitrī is to be envisioned on the full-moon day for those desiring a son; and the form of Dharma is to be understood from the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"He has four faces, four feet, and four arms, and is clad in white garments."
The Dharma should be depicted as white, adorned with all ornaments, and resplendent;
he holds a rosary in his right hand and a book in his left.
The mantra for sprinkling *dūrvā* grass:
"I sprinkle the root of the *dūrvā* with waters comparable to nectar. Grant me freedom from widowhood; salutations again and again to you, the *dūrvā*."
O Dūrvā grass, you are indeed born of the nectar of immortality; you are praised by gods and asuras.
Grant me good fortune and progeny, and be the accomplisher of all my purposes.
Just as you have spread across the surface of the earth with your branches and sub-branches,
so too grant me a lineage that is free from old age and death.
Having recited thus, one should sprinkle [the water] while circling it clockwise;
then, having performed the worship of the deity according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Unmarried women should be honored with bamboo vessels containing garments;
one should remain according to this ritual for as long as three days.
One should keep a vigil there with the sounds of dancing and musical instruments,
as well as the recitation of the Śānti-pāṭha, the Purāṇas, and the excellent narrative of Sāvitrī.
Then, at the clear dawn on the auspicious first day of the lunar fortnight,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) there with sesame seeds, clarified butter, sacrificial fuel sticks, and other materials.
Then, with each stalk recited over with the mantra one thousand times,
he— having cast off anger and being free from envy— should offer a stream of wealth.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmin without being stingy with one's wealth;
likewise, one should honor the teacher as the very embodiment of Umā and Maheśvara.
Cows should be given there, especially those of blue color;
if none of these colors are available, one should give a milch cow with her calf.
A cow with a copper-colored back, silver hooves, and horns adorned with gold;
decorated with ornaments of bells, possessing a tail of jewels, and yielding abundant milk.
Likewise, one should give such other cows as well during the three-night *dūrvā* rite;
[one should honor] a teacher who is learned in the Vedas, elderly, and a householder.
One should appoint there as preceptor a teacher who is omniscient and learned in the scriptures;
one should cause a garment to be given to the preceptor together with his wife.
Adornments for women measuring one cubit and one span,
as well as pairs [of deities], should likewise be honored, numbering twelve in total.
At the conclusion of the meal, ornaments, clothing, and so forth should be given;
likewise, a bed and a sturdy bamboo vessel should be provided for them.
Having given to the Brahmins gifts that bring supreme delight to women— consisting of the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka) along with fruits and milk-rice (pāyasa)— he attained great fortune.
Having fed her friends, companions, and all her kinsmen from every side,
that woman who, having fasted, observes this ancient vow—
The three-night *dūrvā* vow is purifying, meritorious, and bestows progeny;
it grants sovereignty, happiness, and good fortune, and increases the lineage of sons.
Remaining for a long time in the world of mortals, he shall thereafter attain heaven;
there he is gladdened by the gods together with his ancestors and their kinsmen.
They dwell there in delight until the dissolution of all beings;
thereafter, one should diligently offer an oblation to Arundhatī at night.
Taking a small portion of water in a conch shell, along with flowers, fruits, and sandalwood,
and placing one knee upon the ground, one should diligently offer the *arghya* oblation.
The *arghya* mantra:
O Arundhatī, virtuous goddess, who speaks kindly to Vasiṣṭha; O granter of boons, grant me always freedom from widowhood and good fortune.
Thus ends the Dūrvā-trirātra-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
"That which is the supreme merit among vows, which brings about the destruction of the suffering of birth—"
O Teacher of the World, tell me that which is sufficient for the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Brahmā said:
Listen as I speak of that which destroys the cycle of existence— including conception, birth, old age, sickness, and suffering— and which brings complete satisfaction to Viṣṇu.
In the past, your elder brothers, headed by Marīci, who were seekers of liberation, tranquil, and devoted to asceticism, gave [this] with devotion, dedicated to Hari.
O divine sage, regarding that vow of yours known as the "Hundred Kings," which is so difficult for men to perform— [please tell me] its procedure and its fruit of great exaltation.
He who performs three hundred three-night fasts dedicated to Janārdana goes to the abode of Hari, taking with him a hundred generations of his lineage.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, beginning from the ninth lunar day, the observer of the vow should constantly undertake the three-night rites according to the prescribed rule.
Full of faith, having conquered anger, bathing daily and endowed with forbearance,
one should always worship Viṣṇu through action, mind, and speech.
Having worshipped Janārdana with the mantra "Oṃ namo vāsudevāya," one should recite it one thousand and eight times every day.
One should always avoid false speech, theft, harsh words, and sinful conversation,
and one should always abstain from honey, meat, and the flavors of fermented liquors.
Devoted to the celibate life, tranquil, and intent on the welfare of all beings,
the observer of the vow should always remain dedicated to Vāsudeva according to the prescribed rule.
On the eighth day, having eaten only one meal, he should observe a fast for three days;
on the eleventh day, being pure and having bathed, he should be devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva.
On the twelfth day, one should worship the Lord Keśava with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, as well as with food offerings, incense, lamps, and so forth, along with songs and dances.

Having performed this rite for one hundred three-night periods according to this method, a person should then devoutly complete the vow with special ceremonies when the month of Kārttika arrives; this vow is unsurpassed.

There are two three-night periods every month; thus, over fifty months, there are one hundred such periods. Because of the addition of two intercalary months, this occurs in four years, with the completion taking place in the month of Kārttika.
In this manner, O King, one should give food to the twice-born as well as pairs of garments.
Thus according to the monthly rite;
likewise, listen to those [rules regarding] the sacred thread, umbrellas, and seats. Having thus honored the Brahmins and especially the preceptor, [one should proceed].
Having bowed with his head, O Lord, one should bring the entire vow to completion;
for that devoted brahmin, the fruit shall be twice that which was prescribed.
The observer of the vow is absorbed into the supreme reality, the imperishable Vāsudeva;
and having heard this meritorious vow, O best of the twice-born, those who possess such a celestial chariot go to the highest goal, completely liberated from all sins.
Thus ends the Trivikrama-trirātra-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇu-rahasya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"But within the body of Anasūyā were Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara."
By what austerity were they produced? This is my curiosity, O Keśava.
Indeed, Anasūyā is said to have been established as the foremost among virtuous women in the three worlds through her charity,
her asceticism, and her bathing at sacred fords.
Born into a preeminent lineage and honored by all the world—
O Mahāmati, tell me here how this came about through the birth of Atri.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: O Pārtha, when she has performed that great vow, she indeed attains the supreme state after three nights; she partakes of the *caru* and attains auspiciousness.
By his power, she attained the status of a virtuous wife, possessing the beauty and noble birth of a daughter,
throughout the three worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Supreme God, at what time, on which day by day, in which place, and according to what rite should it be performed? Tell me how one's caste may be established.
Nārāyaṇa said:
O Pāṇḍava, it should be performed on the thirteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha;
thereafter, one must undertake the observance with the permission of the preceptor.
Having taken a single meal on the twelfth day, one should observe three days of fasting;
there, one should have a beautiful pavilion constructed, adorned with banners.
In that regard, a birth ceremony (jāti) should be performed according to one's means, using gold;
silver flowers should be made and placed within a bamboo vessel.
There, the three gods— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara—
are to be worshipped together with their consorts, using auspicious flowers and various kinds of fruits.
In this rite, the fashioning of the forms of Viṣṇu and Śiva is to be understood as being like the Aśoka-trirātra.
One should fill a bamboo vessel with barley, rice, sesame seeds, and so forth;
having worshipped the triad of deities, [one should cover] the bamboo vessel with three cloths.
One should worship the preceptor’s couple with yellow, red, and white flowers, as well as various fruits,
garments, ornaments, and floral offerings.
One should offer sandals, shoes, a bed, an umbrella, and a well-adorned cow;
furthermore, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with barley mixed with sesame seeds and rice.
With jaggery, sugarcane, milk-rice, grains, salt, and sprouted rice,
as well as with lamps fashioned in bamboo vessels using the seven kinds of grain;
O King, listen to the fruit that arises from this vow performed with necklaces and auspicious *kiṃśuka* filaments during the night.
When worshipped, she bestows birth, wealth, sons, health, the continuity of one's lineage, good fortune, and the perfection of beauty.
Thus ends the Jātitrirātra vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Having fasted for three nights, one should offer a beautiful mansion on the full moon day of Phālguna;
one thereby attains the world of the Sun—this is known as the Dhāmavrata.
"The Sun is the deity here.
Thus is described in the *Padma Purāṇa* the Dhāmatrirātra vow.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having reached the day of the sun on the tenth lunar day, a man who has fasted for three nights should worship Trivikrama, beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
With a restrained mind, one should worship the God with three-colored flowers—
namely white, yellow, and red—
and likewise offer three kinds of unguents and incense made from the three fragrant substances.

[323] O best of men, one should offer an oblation consisting of the three essences— guggulu, kuṭuka, and śrīveṣṭika— along with the three sweets and three lamps. Furthermore, a fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with barley, sesame seeds, and mustard seeds.
O King, he should likewise give the three metals— copper, gold, and silver— to the twice-born;
for this vow not only bestows a noble lineage.
It is taught as that which brings about the attainment of one's desired wishes.
Thus ends the vow of the Three Nights of Noble Lineage (*sukulatrirātravrata*) as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"In the month of Caitra, with a restrained mind, one should worship the Lord with three white water-lilies (*kumuda*)."
Having bathed there in the river for three nights while eating only at night,
he should give five milch goats along with gold to a twice-born man.
He is never again born in the world of the living;
this is declared to be the vow of the *bastā*, which destroys all diseases.
The Sun is the deity here.
Thus is the Bastatrirātra vow described in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
O Pārtha, during the month of Bhādrapada, on the third and fourth days of the bright fortnight at sunrise, one should perform this with faith for a full year.
[324] By means of fasting, one should undertake the vow known as Goṣpada;
then, whether a man or a woman, having bathed, [should worship] with flowers, incense, and ointments.
And with curd mixed with ghee,
O Bhārata, one should anoint the horns and the tail of cows, along with garlands of forest flowers.
With devotion, one should give daily fodder for cows and clothing during the first and last watches of the day;
one should eat food not cooked by fire, avoiding oil and alkaline substances.

In the forenoon and afternoon, on the second and fifth days, at the footprints of the cows, [one should recite]: "The mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus, the sister of the Ādityas, the navel of immortality—I shall proclaim this to the wise person. She has come as one free from sin, like a desirable guest; she is life and breath. This is the *arghya* mantra.
"May cows be before me; may cows be behind me.
May cows be in my heart; I dwell in the midst of cows."

Thus ends the mantra for requesting the cows. O best of the Kurus, a person full of devotion should [recite] this mantra daily at the city gate or in the cow-pen as the cows are departing or returning.
One should offer arghya and likewise a morsel of food for the satisfaction and nourishment of the cows;
having thus worshipped them and offered the arghya, one should then proceed toward home.
On the fifth day, free from anger, he should eat cow's milk products and curd,
as well as rice flour, fruit, vegetables, sesame paste, and sprouted grains.
At the end of the day, O Indra among kings, one should sleep that night with self-restraint;
at dawn, having given a "cow's footprint" plot of land to a Brahmin who has a family.
To a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, according to his ability, he should offer a golden image and seek forgiveness from Govinda, the Lord of Cows, who has Garuḍa upon his banner.
Likewise, having fashioned an auspicious Mount Govardhana out of jaggery,

one should worship it individually with flowers, incense, and other offerings according to one's capacity; O Pārtha, just as [one worships] the Gopada, so too should one worship the Govardhana mountain.

One who is devoted to cows, having observed the cow-vow and having given a gift of land as large as a cow's footprint with devotion, should say: "May Govinda be pleased," and give it to a preeminent brahmin with devotion.
One attains good fortune, beauty, and charm, as well as abundant prosperity;
one shall obtain a household filled with calves and cows, and attain devotion to the cows.
Having enjoyed vast pleasures, O King, he shall go to the city of heaven upon death;
from there, having enjoyed divine pleasures by the remainder of his merit, he shall depart.
Having obtained a family endowed with wealth, grain, and people, and possessing the prosperity of rice, sugarcane, and milk, one who is devoted shall once again become pure in lineage.
Thus, O Pārtha, by the power of this vow, one passes through three births;
thereafter, having reached Goloka, which is free from rebirth, one never returns.
Having become like a god, he remains as long as the moon and stars exist,
wearing a divine form, garlanded, and adorned with celestial ornaments.
Served by hosts of Apsarases with the singing and instrumental music of Gandharvas,
he remains there for a hundred divine yugas and thereafter goes to the city of Viṣṇu.
Whoever performs this vow of the cow's footprint for three nights,
honors cows, and subsists on cow-products,
having fixed Govinda, the Primordial Being, in his mind—
He attains that meritorious world, the purifier of cows.
Thus ends the Gopada-trirātra-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
"O knower of dharma, you are a virtuous devotee; listen now to my Kālarātri-vrata. I shall tell it to you today, exactly as it is to be performed according to the rules."
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja, the wise man, having conquered his senses,
being truthful in speech, firm in mind and self, should abide in the observances.
First, the illustrious one should construct a pavilion on a level and auspicious portion of ground—
quadrangular, even, smooth, and adorned with banners and flags.
Having marked out the site with a cord according to the measurement of one cubit,
one should cause a beautiful pit to be constructed there in the shape of a cow, in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
Then he should gather the necessary materials: sacred *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and twenty-seven fuel sticks made from *palāśa* and *pippala* wood.
One should bring water-pitchers, jars, and new, auspicious vessels;
"gargarī" means a churning vessel.
Also, vessels filled with gold and auspicious ones made of split bamboo.
The food offering, flowers, water for the arghya, and fresh sacrificial oblations—these indeed [are required].
One should indeed gather all of this, including very beautiful condiments,
fragrant flowers, jasmine, and blue lotuses.
One should also bring many other purifying items such as fruits,
as well as various fragrances and incense, foremost among them guggulu.
Having thus gathered the refined seats, as well as the small ladle and the large sacrificial spoon,
and likewise four [priests] born of noble families, he should collect these requisites.
For the purpose of the formal acceptance (*adhivāsa*), one should designate teachers who are pure,
free from anger, and worshippers of the gods and Brahmins.
Or rather, O child, with four such teachers— born of noble families and endowed with truthfulness, purity, and forbearance— who remain steadfast in their observances?

Having worshipped [the deity] while fasting for seven nights and eating only at night for eight days, one thus completes the vow to be accomplished in a fortnight. Then, having undertaken the observances, [one should perform the rite] in that fire-pit shaped like a bow.
O child, one should indeed have the fire-oblation (homa) performed by Brahmins born of the lineage of Śaṅkara.

Those born in the lineage of Śaṅkara are those who have received Śaiva initiation. In the absence of such persons, one desiring the sacrificial ground for the fire-oblation here should have it performed by those known to be skilled, born of unimpaired lineages, and likewise [endowed with the aforementioned qualities].
When the absence of a fire-oblation (homa) occurs, the following rule applies for those equal to the Śaivas:
having first worshipped the Lord of the Gaṇas, the Protector of the Mothers, and the Bull-bannered One, one should then perform the oblation.
Skanda is the protector of the Mothers.
For the sake of accomplishing all rites, one should worship Hara—the Lord of Gods—in his own form along with the Mothers, who are of the nature of fire, for the sake of success in all actions. [328]

Bhūpāla, Kṣetrapāla, Āgneya, and Kārttika; Jātarūpa and Suvarṇa [represent] the form of Vināyaka in the Kṛṣṇacaturthī vow. However, the form of Skanda is to be understood as Kārttikeya in the Ṣaṣṭhī vow. The form of the Mothers is described in the Viṣṇudharmottara. The form of the "born" (jāta), meaning the manifested one, consists of the elephant-faced [deity] and others; with that, one should worship Deveśa and the other deities. He offers oblations of seven palāśa leaves; he should offer them at sunrise.
Furthermore, when the sun has set, one should offer oblations of *aśvattha* wood.
At midnight, with devotion, one should perform the supreme fire sacrifice (homa) for one hundred and eight times using black sesame seeds mixed with ghee.
By this mantra, right there, all that is inauspicious is destroyed;
it is the bestower of boons, well-accomplished, and the provider of nourishment and cooling relief.

Oṃ hrīṃ, homage! O you who are clothed in black; you who ride upon seven thousand koṭis of lions; you of a thousand faces; you of great strength; you who are unconquered; O Prasaṅgiri; you who banish all enemy armies; you who cut through the spells of others; you who madden all beings; you who subdue all spirits! From every evil, drink, drink! Spell, destroy, cut asunder! Devour, devour all the wicked! O you with flaming tongues, you with the terrifying mouth! Scatter all creatures! Break, break the chains! Homage be to you, O Praty-aṅgirā! Svāhā!
Having performed the fire sacrifice and offered the oblation (bali), one should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) in all directions with a mixture of rice-and-pulse gruel,
blood, and milk.
One should offer a great oblation prepared with rice mixed with sesame, wine, and milk;
one should perform this for seven days, and now listen to what occurs on the seventh day.
One should offer five oblations or ten *bali* offerings.

In the case of the seven-day *bali-homa*, on the seventh day, having performed fifty [offerings] with the *mahāvyāhṛtis* joined and unjoined, one should offer ten; this is for the sake of the ten full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*), as the count is distinct. With four [offerings], he is born into that family for three, one, or seven nights.
Or else, having stayed there for a night, one should indeed remain for the sake of worship.

Having performed the *bali* offerings and *homa* by means of fasting for seven nights, three nights, or one night according to one’s ability, one should perform worship; the fortnight should be observed by eating only at night.
O child, worship must always be performed on the fifth day according to the rules.
Listen now to the truth regarding how the Brahmins born of the sacrifice of Dharma are to be satisfied.
With Śaiva rites arising from the sacrifice of Dharma,
for seven days and then one day, he should wash the face of the Goddess with sandalwood and agallochum, out of supreme devotion.
This washing of the face, which was previously prepared with the color of sandalwood and agallochum, should be applied to the writing on the document.
Whatever image is made of clay, one should always worship it after washing it with water purified by mantras and wiping it with a clean cloth.
One should then prepare the honey-mixture (madhuparka) with honey and perform the worship.
Then, having applied the nectar once more, one should wash the face and the body;
thereafter, having circumambulated again and prostrated like a staff, one should proceed.
The Dharmapāla-udbhava is indeed to be approved through excellent praise.
This is the *Nāmastotra* of Dharmapāla for the devotee.
Having praised him there with devotion according to the rules, one should then [honour] the Brahmins in accordance with the ritual.
O child, one should worship with golden [images] and with meat that is consistent with the Dharma.
Furthermore, one should cause singing, dancing, and especially instrumental music to be performed with great effort before the Goddess in this manner.
"O child, he always accepts even a very small thing out of devotion;
it is only right that I give my entire possession to one who is devoted to me."
For the sake of my pleasure, having bathed with purity and subdued the senses, one should practice devotion endowed with self-restraint and forbearance while reciting my mantra.
One should not wear ornaments, for this [conduct] has been declared for him;
indeed, such a person shall not lead [others] to heaven, nor to austerity, nor even to liberation.
Having thus completed [the rite], he should then go home slowly;
having gone there, being pure and filled with joy, he should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should duly offer oblations into the fire for me and for one's mother, using eight young girls and eight of the best of the twice-born.
The Mother, the group of Mothers, and so forth—eight [of them].
Having fed eight twice-born men who are established in their vows and devoted to the dharma of Śiva,
one should dedicate the offering to the god Śaṅkara, his consort, and Vināyaka.
For each [of the officiants], eight and then seven [offerings] should be made, especially to the Hotṛ priest;
thereafter, one should ask for forgiveness after prostrating again and again.
All this has been fully described; it may be performed in detail with devotion.
Furthermore, out of compassion, one should feed there those who are poor, blind, and miserable.
Whatever is given to Veda-knowing Brahmins, whatever is given to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin),
and likewise whatever is given out of compassion to guests—
all that gift is indeed inexhaustible according to its value and the prescribed rule.
"Surely this has been granted by the Lord; this is the truth, there is no doubt.
Both the worthy and the unworthy must all be fed together at my festival."
Having received all women, children, and the infirm with the highest intention, he,
together with his kinsmen and endowed with supreme joy,
being self-restrained, should consume the remnants of the sacrifice like the sacrificial fire.
He who always performs the Kaumudī festival at the wrong time and during the dark fortnight [is guilty].
One should observe the festival of Akālakaumudī and Dīpālikā,
beginning on the eighth day of the month of Āśvayuja and continuing through the full-moon day;
one may do so while fasting, or by eating only at night, or again, by eating only once a day.
Having abandoned the multitude of evils, he shall go to the supreme goal.
By means of the full-moon day (pañcadaśī), this festival is a subsidiary part of the vow; for this very reason, it is an act to be performed by the gods.
O Pārtha, whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or those of Śūdra birth—
If they shall practice this vow, they too will go to the state free from affliction.
One who has sons and wealth should perform it in this manner according to the prescribed rule.
Terrible calamities do not embrace them, nor are they oppressed by enemies;
this renowned Kālī-vrata must be performed by those born of noble lineage.
Those desiring peace and prosperity, those desiring knowledge,
and those desiring *ramā*— that is, those desiring *lakṣmī* (fortune)—
should proceed with diligence, being carried by ten thousand times ten thousand lions.
He who practices this shall go to heaven in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
"O child, you ought to perform this vow, which destroys all sins, as it was then described by me; do so with supreme devotion and without weariness."
He who establishes a relationship with those of superior birth,
or with one of lower caste, shall be a doer of harm by this act.
Thus ends the Kālarātrivrata as declared in the Kālikāpurāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"In the month of Āśvina, or Māgha, or Caitra, or even Śrāvaṇa..."
The vow should be commenced on the dark lunar day and concluded on the white lunar day.
The limit of the bright fortnight is the conclusion of the white lunar half-month.

And this has been stated that it should be performed within the months itself, starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the eighth day of the bright fortnight, according to the method to be described.
One should perform [the rite] on the eighth day of the month of Āśvina during the dark fortnight by means of a single meal.
Or the goddess Maṅgalārūpiṇī, or else the slayer of Ruru.
One should worship with ninefold offerings of perfumes, garlands, and food.
O child, one should feed nine maidens and men who are devotees of the Goddess with nine varieties of fragrant food;
the ninth meal should be taken at night until the tenth lunar day has passed.
One should fast on the eleventh day; this is the rule once again.

Furthermore, the meaning of "this procedure" (*eṣa vidhiḥ*) is as follows: after the four-day period consisting of eating once a day (*ekabhakta*), eating at night (*nakta*), eating food obtained unasked (*ayācita*), and fasting (*upavāsa*) on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, another three four-day periods are to be observed until the eighth day of the bright fortnight. Having fasted according to the rule, Śakra [performed] daily giving, fire-offerings (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), worship, and the feeding of virgins.
This must be performed by one who has conquered anger and is devoted to the Goddess,
through the ninefold slaughter of sacrificial animals such as buffaloes, goats, sheep, and others.
It should be performed for the sake of the elemental spirits and vaitālas, and not out of a desire for one's own benefit.
For there, the twice-born, adorned with maidens and devoted to the Goddess,
[perform sacrifice] by means of the ninefold animal slaughter and not by the cutting of pieces.

In the Bhūtavaitāla [rite], for the sake of the Bhūtavaitālas and with the desire to accomplish one's own purpose—that is, the desire for one's own enjoyment—the [deities] are to be adorned; this is the specific rule. There should be performances by actors and dancers, spectacles, chariot processions, and vigils.
Gifts should be given according to one's capacity, and to all [the recipients] according to their respective abilities.
Those who possess the form of Mahābhairava and wear garlands of bones should be especially worshipped with beautiful garments in cities and other places,
O best of gods, for the sake of attaining all desired objects.
By this method, O Śakra, one obtains the fruit according to one's desire.
Maṅgalā, Bhairavī, Durgā, Vārāhī, Tridaśeśvarī,
Umā, Haimavatī, Kanyā, Kapālī, and Kaiṭabheśvarī.
One should indeed mutter these names: Kālī, Brāhmī, Maheśī, Kaumārī, Madhusūdanī, Vārāhī, Vāsavī, and Carcā;
one should worship and feed maidens according to the rites prescribed in the scriptures.
Clothing, ornaments, bronze vessels and the like, water-pots, and waist-bands should be given according to one's capacity by the devotees of the Goddess who desire happiness.
Alternatively, for nine nights, or indeed for seven, five, or three nights,
one should proceed in sequence by eating once a day, eating only at night, eating only what is unasked for, or fasting.

The sequence is as follows: nine nights with one meal per day, seven nights with eating only at night, five nights with food obtained unasked, and three nights by fasting. The counting begins from the ninth day, making the eighth day the conclusion. These are the options for one who was unable to perform the previous [full observance].
O Śakra, one should pass the month of Āśvina until the eighth day of the bright fortnight;
there, having prepared a mandala according to the rules, one should worship Maṅgalā.
O Śakra, one shall obtain all desires from you, who are endowed with every provision, who bestow all accomplishments, and who grant every wish.
O child, it grants wealth to one who desires wealth, bestows a kingdom upon one who desires a kingdom,
grants health, grants sons, and destroys even the greatest of sins.
It should be performed by all castes— by men, women, children, and eunuchs—
for the Goddess is always omnipresent, O Śakra, and yields great fruit.
By this method, O child, that discernment bestows the great fruit of all vows for all those whose source is the vow.
This great merit known as the Ninth has been correctly revealed to you;
it must not be told to one devoid of devotion, to a fool, or to a rationalist.
It should be given to one who is devoted, peaceful, and dedicated to Śiva and Viṣṇu;
to a man who is a devotee of the Goddess, of virtuous conduct, and intent on the worship of virgins.
Right here, one shall accomplish all desires without hesitation,
just as gold is the foremost among gifts worthy of being honored by Brahmins.
Just as Bhūrloka is among all worlds, the Jāhnavī among sacred fords (tīrthas),
the Aśvamedha among sacrifices, and Mathurā is for those desiring liberation.
Just as the serpent-eater is the best among lute-players, and as Acyuta is the foremost among the gods,
so too has the Bhīṣmapañcaka been declared the most excellent of all vows.
It was practiced by Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Garga, and others at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga and other ages;
it was practiced by Nabhoja, Amburīṣa, and others at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga and other ages.
In the Kali age, [this shall be performed] by Brahmins such as Vīrabhadra, by Śūdras, and by others.
The five days are to be honored; this great vow has been performed by the Brahmins through celibacy, recitation, fire-offerings, ritual acts, and so forth.
And likewise for those Kṣatriyas who are devoted to truth, purity, and their vows,
there shall be neither mental anxieties nor physical diseases, nor shall there be any fear of enemies.
Constantly honored throughout saṃsāra, though he is but one, he becomes great;
by hearing [this], all undertakings are accomplished—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Maṅgalā-vrata as described in the Devī-purāṇa.
[336] Now follows the Bhīṣma-pañcaka-vrata.
From the Nārada Purāṇa:
Nārada said:
"That which is this immovable merit, the supreme vow among all vows..."
The Bhīṣmapañcaka vow should be performed with great effort during the month of Kārttika.
O best of gods, out of your grace and with the desire for the welfare of the sages, please tell me clearly the ritual procedure for that and its fruit.
Brahmā said:
O best among those who observe vows, I shall proclaim a most meritorious vow.
Since Bhīṣma obtained this five-day vow from Vāsudeva,
it was therefore called the Bhīṣmapañcaka.
Who, other than Keśava, is capable of describing the virtues of this vow?
This vow is of great merit and is the destroyer of even the most heinous sins.
Therefore, men should diligently perform the Bhīṣmapañcaka rite;
having bathed properly during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, one should remain firm in their vows.
On the eleventh day, the observer of the vow should undertake the five-day rite;
having bathed according to the rules in the morning, he should likewise do so at midday.
Having smeared oneself with cow dung at a river or a mountain spring,
one should properly satisfy the ancestors in due order with barley, rice, and sesame seeds;
then, having bathed, observed silence, and put on clean garments, one who is firm in his vows [should proceed].
[337] Then one should worship Lord Hari, the remover of all sins;
with devotion, one should bathe Acyuta with honey, milk, ghee, and other such substances.
In that same manner, one should likewise [bathe] Keśava with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), with fragrant sandalwood water,
with sweet-smelling sandalwood, and then with saffron.
One should smear the Garuḍa-bannered Lord with a paste mixed with camphor and uśīra,
and worship him with appropriate flowers accompanied by fragrances and incense.
One who possesses unwaning devotion should burn guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter,
and should offer a lamp day and night for five days.
One should offer the supreme rice-milk (paramānna) as a food offering (naivedya) to the God of gods;
having thus worshipped the Lord of gods, one should praise him and bow down.
One who observes the vow should mutter "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva" one hundred and eight times,
and should offer oblations of sesame, rice, and barley smeared with clarified butter.
And with the six-syllabled mantra accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā."
"Oṃ namo viṣṇave" is the six-syllabled mantra.
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), having bowed to the one whose banner is Garuḍa,
and having recited the mantra as before, a man should sleep upon the ground.
All this ritual procedure should indeed be performed even during five days;
however, listen now to that which has been specifically prescribed for this vow, so that nothing is omitted.
On the first day, a person should worship the feet of Hari with lotuses;
on the second day, he should worship the region of the knees with bilva leaves.
And on the third day, one should worship the navel with a water-pitcher;
then one should worship the shoulder with *vāṇa*, *bilva*, and *jaya* flowers;
thereafter, one should worship the head of the Discus-bearer with *mālatī* flowers.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, with devotion and a mind fixed upon Him, one should worship the God of gods with the mantra of recitation and offer perfumes and incense.
Having worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa on the eleventh day with a concentrated mind,
one should properly consume cow dung three times and observe the fast on the eleventh day.
On the twelfth day, the observer of the vow should worship with cow’s urine accompanied by mantras;
on the thirteenth day, with milk; and likewise on the fourteenth day, with curd.
Having consumed these for the sake of purifying the body, one should fast for the remaining four days.
The consumption [of the food] is performed with the *homamantra*.
On the fifth day, however, having bathed and worshipped Keśava according to the rules,
one should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas and give them sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
Likewise, one should honor the instructor with garments and ornaments;
thereafter, one should eat at night, preceded by the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thus, having properly completed this supreme vow as it has been described—
the meritorious and renowned Bhīṣmapañcaka, which removes all sins.
By abandoning meat from birth onwards, one attains merit;
by completely renouncing it during the Bhīṣmapañcaka, one obtains the full fruit of that merit.
A drinker of intoxicants who would otherwise consume liquor until the end of his life obtains a superior fruit by abstaining from it during the Bhīṣmapañcaka.
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen to the ancient dharma of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika.
The Bhīṣmapañcaka should be understood as beginning from the eleventh day.
This is difficult for those lacking in resolve and impossible for those with childish minds;
one of evil intellect must be avoided through the firm determination of the holy life.
One should avoid liquor, meat, falsehood, and sinful speech;
[one should live] with men devoted to the worship of Kṛṣṇa, subsisting on vegetables and the food of sages.
By means of their speech, women should act so as to increase their own truthfulness and merit;
widows, however, should act for the sake of the auspicious prosperity of their sons.
O Pāṇḍava, for the sake of fulfilling all desires and for the sake of liberation itself,
one should constantly perform ablutions and acts of giving until the full moon day of Kārttika.
The Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed by those devoted to the meditation on Viṣṇu.

The Vaiśvadeva is the oblation to all the deities, and they should be contemplated as manifestations of Viṣṇu. Whichever image of each [deity] is to be made, it should have a fierce face and be extremely terrifying.
With swords in hand and exceedingly deformed, they indeed had terrifying fangs.
She should be placed upon a measure of sesame seeds and wrapped in a black cloth;
her hair is adorned with a wreath of red flowers, and she wears blazing golden earrings.
Having worshipped with supreme devotion by means of the names of Dharmarāja,
one should recite this mantra while holding a handful of flowers.
"May whatever evil was committed in another birth or again in this birth come to rest through the grace of your feet.
Having thus worshipped the golden image according to the prescribed rite,
It should be accompanied by gold and a golden sacrificial fee,
and given to the reciter with the words, "May the Dharma be pleasing to me," just as it was for Kṛṣṇa, the god of gods, whose actions are effortless.

In that same manner, an image of Hari should be given. Having performed worship according to one's ability, one should give gold and a cow to Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas, saying: "May Kṛṣṇa be pleased with me."
One should also respectfully give whatever wealth others desire;
having fulfilled one's duty and remaining established therein, one should become dispassionate and self-restrained.
With a peaceful mind and free from affliction, one shall attain the supreme state;
[the deity] is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, possessing four fangs and four arms.
Eight-footed, one-eyed, with spike-like ears and a great roar;
wearing matted hair, double-tongued, copper-faced, and clad in the skin of the king of beasts.
Mahādeva, whose form does not exist, is to be meditated upon;
this form of Mahāviṣṇu, the deity of the vow, is to be contemplated and worship offered. A lion skin—a strip from the body of the king of beasts—is [the offering].
This was told to me by Bhīṣma as he lay upon his bed of arrows.
Thus, I have explained to you this difficult-to-perform Bhīṣmapañcaka.
O tiger among kings, that vow is the most excellent Bhīṣmapañcaka;
Acyuta bestows liberation upon whoever propitiates him with devotion during it.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or an ascetic,
by performing this Bhīṣmapañcaka, one indeed attains the abode of Viṣṇu.
A killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of intoxicants, a thief, one who violates the Guru’s bed, or one who is always a liar—
each is completely liberated from their sin by properly performing the Bhīṣmapañcaka once.
Then, Viṣṇu, who bestows liberation upon men, becomes pleased with this;
for having heard this sacred Bhīṣmapañcaka being recited, [he is gratified].
The mortal who recites this is liberated from sins and becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this great vow is auspicious, meritorious, and the destroyer of evil.
By performing which, even a slayer of a Brahmin or a killer of a cow is liberated from all sins—
that which is renowned on earth as Bhīṣmapañcaka,
beginning on the eleventh day and ending on the fifteenth.
For the man devoted to eating the food of sages, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow grants the desired fruit therein, O Pāṇḍava.
Thus ends the Bhīṣmapañcaka vow.
Vyāsa said: Formerly, the Dānavas, having worshipped Janārdana, [attained] that which was ageless... [ajarbhāt].
He created that Goddess Yoganidrā for the sake of his own protection.
The Blessed Lady grants success in one part,
yet that very same [success] is attained in its entirety when she is worshipped during the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika by the command of Keśava.
Alternatively, on the fourth, eighth, or ninth day, it is easily accomplished;
likewise, on the fourteenth day, by women who have bathed well in due order.
Outside the house, however, wherever there may be a solitary fruit-bearing tree,
one should likewise worship it with an abundance of flowers, incense, and food offerings.
A woman who has sons, being disciplined in mind, speech, and body,
took with her all necessary provisions and went to an excellent village.
Then, being well-pleased and desiring to please him, she gives [the offering] to Śyena.
"Offer this seat, clothing, and so forth to the Blessed Lady.
Having said this, he goes to his own home; then all his desires are fulfilled.
"In the Kṛta Yuga, he was renowned as one like a servant or a hired laborer;
the meaning is that in the Kṛta Yuga, he was famous for being like a slave or a hireling in his state of service.
Then King Ṛtuparṇa, who had the chariot above others, [was] in his own city.
Having set it down, he gave it to Śyena to take back to his own beloved wife.
In other ages, however, one should mutter the mantra "analas" as well;
then she, having arrived on the ground, turns away facing east and goes to her own abode.
However, it is certain that whichever bird was previously summoned by him shall alone take the morsel of food.
First, that woman, being well-composed, eats at home;
afterwards, the householder eats together with his servants, kinsmen, and relatives.
The household goddess, however, should worship her husband according to that very same ritual procedure.
She should not be given as a prey for a hawk, nor should she take refuge in a tree;
rather, in a secure place within the house, the noble wife devoted to her husband should perform worship.
When the true nature of husband and wife does not exist in other ages,
then he performs only that much which constitutes the duty of his own family.
The meaning is that, even without the husband's permission, the Śyenayā [rite] should be performed by the wife in the home itself;
this is the procedure for the Śyenagrāsa as stated in the Ādityapurāṇa. The Lord said:
Henceforth, I shall declare the vows in their proper order:
on the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights alike.
Having fasted and become self-restrained with a threefold inner disposition,
one should then, being pure, especially worship Śiva in the afternoon.
One should perform recitation, fire-oblations, and so forth according to the previously stated procedure;
or one should worship the Guru with supreme devotion through the means of practice and other such rites.
Then, one should cause [the disciple] to consume three mouthfuls of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
having touched [him] while he has taken them, his subsistence shall be on sacrificial food (haviṣyānna).
By this method, one should diligently observe the vow for as long as life lasts;
thus [he honors] his father, his grandfather, and likewise his great-grandfather.
By the power of the Śiva-vow, they dwell in the worlds of Śiva;
this is the vow known as the Śiva-vow, the most excellent among all vows.
Thus ends the Śivavrata as declared in the Kālottara.
Maitreya said:
Indeed, the month of Kārttika is great, consisting of all the gods;
it is especially so during the dark fortnight, specifically for those five days.
Whatever merit is given to them on the eleventh day becomes inexhaustible and fulfills all desires; even a lamp lit by others for a mouse on that day [yields such fruit].
Having attained a human birth which is difficult to obtain, she reached the supreme goal;
and even the hunter, having worshipped Janārdana on the fourteenth day, [attained the same].

Lacking devotion due to association with others, he went to the world of Viṣṇu after giving lamps that had been offered by others on the thirteenth day of the month for those such as outcaste dog-cookers.
A certain Vaiśya woman named Līlāvatī,
having witnessed the worship of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow on the new moon day, became filled with anger and went to the imperishable heaven.
One who recites the Ajapa mantra twice daily shall become a sovereign lord of kings;
therefore, lamps should be offered at night when the sun has set.

When one who eats only at night for five days does so for the sake of auspiciousness in houses, in all cow-pens, in shrines, in sanctuaries, on the streets of the gods, in cremation grounds, and by lakes;

Those sinful ancestors for whom the rites of offering rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water have been omitted obtain the state of heaven by receiving a rice-ball on the fourteenth day or the new moon day; this is the implied conclusion.
In that regard, Śrī should indeed be worshipped by men with diligent effort.
Those who desire prosperity should strive diligently to sport there during the night,
together with their kinsmen and wives, through dancing, singing, and keeping vigil.
If one experiences joy here, his victory lasts for a year;
however, if he plays at dice, there will be loss upon losing, but certain victory upon winning.
A person shall obtain happiness and joy for an entire year;
indeed, in ancient times, Śambhu was defeated by Gaurī at dice and sent away naked.
Therefore, Śaṅkara is sorrowful while Umā is endowed with happiness;
Viṣṇu, the source of the universe, sleeps happily together with Śrī.
For this reason, during that night, there is a pleasant sleep for all people.
Nandā, Sunandā, Surabhī, Suśokhā, and likewise Sumanā emerged from the ocean while it was being churned; bathing at dawn in these rivers bestows auspiciousness.
The meaning is that at dawn, one's own body is manifested from the Kāmadhenu;
having bathed there and having worshipped with diligence, a man who has purified his defilements obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow by honoring the cow.
Having fasted on the eleventh day for four days,
a man should bathe Viṣṇu with clarified butter or even with cow's milk.
Eating only at night, one should worship Madhusūdana with milk products,
sacrificial offerings, perfumes, flowers, excellent food offerings, garments, ornaments, and earrings.
I offer this water of honor (arghya) to Janārdana, to Viṣṇu, whose arms are raised with the conch, sword, and discus, and who holds the mace and lotus in his hands, bearing the Śārṅga bow.
Even for the mountain-king, though endowed with splendor.
[346] I [shall utter] the names Śrīdhara and Śrīnivāsa— the Lord of Śrī, the very beloved who supports Śrī, the friend of Śrī, and indeed the root-source of Śrī.
Being duly worshipped by me, may he grant my desires.
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite with the names associated with Śrī,
one should perform a separate vigil for the Lord of the World together with Śrī.
May that Goddess Nandā, the splendor of Bhārgava, who is honored everywhere for her lineage, come to my home well-pleased as a granter of boons to me.
The goddess Sunandā, who is always present before the descendant of Aṅgiras,
may she, being well-pleased, true, and a granter of boons, come to my house.
May that fragrant wish-fulfilling cow, who grants all desires and who always attends upon Bharadvāja, come here to my home, honored by the gods.
May she who is Suśīlā, who devoted herself to Kaśyapa and grants all desires everywhere,
be well-pleased with me and remain forever as my wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) in my home.
May that auspicious Sumanā, who rejoiced upon reaching Vasiṣṭha,
come always to my home— she who grants desires and is worshipped by the gods.
Having thus performed the worship according to the prescribed rite, at the clear and auspicious dawn,
he— having bathed, wearing white garments, and adorned with white garlands and unguents— [should proceed].
Having performed his daily rites, joyful and adorned with earrings and armlets,
one who joyfully gives away a wish-fulfilling cow on the first day of the lunar fortnight in the morning shall become a bestower of all desires.
The *kāmadenu* (wish-fulfilling cow), however, is described in the *Vahni Purāṇa*; it should be consulted in the section on gifts (*dānakhaṇḍa*).
All this of Hari is excellent and pure, and among those, the autumn season is the most excellent.
In that [year], it was the auspicious month named Kārttika;
indeed, even therein, the new moon day (darśa) was meritorious.
In her, Hara— freed from the fear of the Daityas—
attained a broad chest and now sleeps in comfort;
she was indeed fashioned by Lakṣmī in ancient times.
Wherein even the gods are the granters of desires.
Where, on the day of sacrifice, all the excellent cows roam upon the surface of the earth as sacrificial grass,
and in whose house they describe their playful pastimes.
And in that regard, this is the truth: [it is] destruction and exhaustion.
Therefore, you should give the wish-fulfilling cow right here, dedicated to Keśava,
to a brahmin who possesses all virtuous qualities.
Having thus performed the entire vow of Hari.
O lord of the earth, a person liberates seven ancestors, seven descendants, and himself from the sin committed during seven lifetimes.
At every step, a person obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
this is proclaimed as the most excellent of all gifts.
It bestows all desires, brings fortune, destroys sin, grants everything, and is auspicious;
it [is the remedy] for all sins, even for those that are great.
O King, this expiation is praised and was declared by Brahmā;
O King, this vow must be performed by Brahmins, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, and Śūdras.
For the sake of obtaining all desired fruits, the virtuous should perform the Kamadhenu vow;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should diligently perform a sesame oblation (tilahoma) dedicated to Kāmadhenu.
Thus ends the Kāmadhenu-vrata as declared in the Vahni Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
On the new moon day of the month of Kārttika, the gods [should worship] Keśava.
Having obtained safety, they slept peacefully on the slopes of the Ocean of Milk.
Lakṣmī, freed from the fear of the Daityas, slept happily upon the chest of his arm;
and Brahmā slept upon the lotus at the hand of the four-armed one as he lay asleep.
For this reason, people should properly prepare a comfortable bed;
one should not eat there during the day, except for children and the sick.
Having worshipped Lakṣmī at the time of dusk, one should then, in due order,
offer lamp-trees according to one's capacity in the temples of the gods.
At crossroads, in cremation grounds, by rivers, mountains, and houses;
at the roots of trees, in cow-pens, at market squares, and in caves.
[349] The places of buying and selling should be adorned with garments and flowers;
immediately thereafter, in a location surrounded by rows of lamps.
Having first fed the Brahmins and distributed food to those who are hungry,
one should eat while adorned and beautified by new garments.
In ancient times, Śaṅkara engaged in a most enchanting game of dice together with his affectionate, charming, clever, and discreet kinsmen.
O Satyavat, on the first day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
Śaṅkara was conquered there, and Pārvatī obtained victory.
For this reason, Śaṅkara is sorrowful while Umā always dwells in happiness;
therefore, people should perform the *dhūta* rite there at dawn.

One should listen to songs, instrumental music, and the like, being well-anointed and well-adorned;
and one should eat especially excellent food together with praiseworthy kinsmen.
On that night, a very beautiful place for the bed should be prepared.
Adorned with perfumes, flowers, garments, jewels, and garlands,
it was encircled by rows of lamps and likewise perfumed with incense.
And that night should be passed together with beloved women;
having honored the twice-born, kinsmen, and relatives with new garments.
Thus ends the vow for a pleasant sleep as declared in the Āditya Purāṇa. [350] Now follows the great festival of Kaumudī.
In the Padma Purāṇa: On the new moon day of the month of Kārttika, one should offer a lamp in the hall of Brahmā; he shall go to the supreme abode.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), Brāhmaṇa women should be honored with unbleached garments, lamps, and offerings mixed with jaggery; thus, one shall indeed go to the city of Brahmā.
Whoever honors and adorns her on that first lunar day (pratipad) with perfumes, flowers, and new garments,
shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
This lunar day is of great merit, characterized by offerings of clarified butter;

He who feeds Brahmins on this day, and especially himself,
goes to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor.
O illustrious one, in the month of Caitra, the first lunar day (pratipadā) is meritorious and excellent;
on that day, O best of men, whatever superior person touches sesame seeds and performs a bath [attains great merit].
O King, tiger among the Kurus, no misfortune, mental afflictions, or physical diseases shall befall him; therefore, one should perform this bath.
Likewise, O King, he should perform the divine *nīrājana* rite, which destroys all diseases,
and he should adorn whatever cattle, buffaloes, and other animals he possesses along with them.
Then, with oil, cloth, and other offerings, he should lead them all beneath the archways;
thereafter, O scion of the Kuru lineage, he should provide a feast for the Brāhmaṇas.
These three lunar days were proclaimed of old, O joy of the Kurus;
they occur in the months of Kārttika, Āśvayuja, or likewise in Caitra, O King.
O King, bathing and giving gifts on the full moon day of Kārttika yield a hundredfold merit;
likewise, offerings of clarified butter bring auspiciousness, while offerings of earth destroy inauspiciousness.
In the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, Trivikrama said to Bali:
"Likewise, the merit that arises when the great festival of Śakra has taken place— "
O tiger among men, there shall be a great festival for you called the Vīrapratipadā; there, joyful, well-nourished, and beautifully adorned [people] will honor you.
By diligently honoring [the deity] with the offering of flowers and incense,
there shall be a preeminent festival there day and night.
In the same way, the Kaumudī festival shall occur now in your kingdom, and likewise in the future;
as stated in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In ancient times, having requested this earth in the form of Vāmana,
Hari formerly purchased it at Bali’s sacrifice by means of three strides.
O King, having made Bali, the lord of the Daityas and a dweller of the netherworld, a tribute,
he gave the kingdom to Indra for three days and nights.
O best of men, I shall tell you this very [mantra], marked with the name "Bali-rāja," which is for the sake of obtaining wealth and enjoyments, along with its secret [instructions].
On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, at the onset of night,
the sovereignty of the Daityas over the surface of the earth was established according to their will.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, tell me specifically about Kaumudī;
for what purpose is a gift given on that day, and who is the presiding deity?
Furthermore, O Janārdana, what should be given there, and to whom should it be given?
What is prescribed here as exhilaration, and what is proclaimed here as play?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika, at the break of dawn,
those who fear hell must certainly perform their ritual bath.
One should wave apāmārga plants or sprouts over the head,
provided they are possessed of both cold and heat and contain thorns and young leaves.
O Apāmārga, as you are being turned around again and again, take away my evil.
