This is the Brāhmaṇa mantra: [one should offer] shoots from milk-exuding trees. Thereafter, the libation (tarpaṇa) should be performed for Dharmarāja by means of his names:
"To Yama, to Dharmarāja, to Mṛtyu, and to Antaka."
To Vaivasvata Kāla, the destroyer of all beings;
to Auḍumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, and Parameṣṭhin.
Salutations indeed to Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta;
having worshipped the deities, a lamp should be offered to Naraka.
Then, at the time of dusk, one should offer beautiful lamps in the temples and monasteries of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the other deities.
In gabled chambers, in shrines, in assembly halls, and by rivers;
in walls, gardens, and ponds, as well as in city gates and pleasure groves.
And in the temples of Siddhārtha, Buddha, Cāmuṇḍā, and Bhairava;
in solitary Mandara mountains, and indeed in elephant stables.
Thus, O lord of men, at the time of dawn on the new moon day,
having bathed and then worshipped and bowed with devotion to the gods and the ancestors.
Having performed the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha with curd, milk, ghee, and so forth,
and having fed the Brahmins with various kinds of edible foods, one should ask for their forgiveness.
Then, in the afternoon, the king should have it proclaimed throughout the city:
"The world may enjoy its own kingdom free from force; let everyone act as they please."
And formerly the world was joyful, with courtyards whitened by lime and every house adorned with trees, sandalwood, and garlands.

It was enchanting with men and women intoxicated by their passion for gambling and drinking, and it was filled with the brilliance of lamps burning brightly, while people were delighted by dancing and instrumental music.
The people were delighted and thrilled by one another’s clapping of hands,
their faces brightened by betel-leaf and smeared with powdered saffron.
Adorned with garments of fine silk and ornaments of gold and rubies,
he displayed a wondrous and intense passion that aroused great curiosity.
It was crowded with young women, where people moved about resplendent in bright garments;
it was delightful, filled with rows of lamps that destroyed the bonds of darkness.
In an auspicious time free from the *pradoṣa* (dusk) and other defects, and devoid of faults such as the *doṣas*,
those who speak of travel, recreation, wandering, victory, and livelihood [should proceed].
Free from minor calamities, delivered from the fear of thieves and women,
and colored by the affection of friends, kinsmen, relatives, and well-wishers.
Then, at the time of midnight, the king himself should go to the city on foot,
slowly and slowly, to behold its beauty.
Amidst the great sound of musical instruments and blazing hand-lanterns,
he beheld the splendor of the palace with his own men who were guarding it.
Having beheld this great marvel and reflected upon his own welfare,
as well as the joy of King Bali's sovereignty, he should then return to his own home.
When night had thus advanced and the people’s eyes were blinded by sleep,
[he was not yet awakened] by men and women with sun-crystals, drums, and sandalwood.
Alakṣmī is driven out from the courtyard of one's own home by joyful women;
then, when all the people have awakened, a great festival takes place.
With garlands and lamps in her hands, overflowing with affection and tenderness,
the playful courtesan acted for her own sake, performing rites for well-being and auspiciousness.
And as she went from house to house, [she saw women] intent on massaging feet,
occupied with grinding flour and applying unguents, and busily engaged in serving their elders.
While intent on saluting the twice-born, while uttering greetings such as "a pleasant night," and while gifts were being given at will to married women.
At the time of dawn, the king should honor the people as is appropriate;
he should satisfy the gods, virtuous men, and the twice-born with sincerity alone.
Others, however, [serve] with food and drink, or by the gift of speech; these are the wise.
With garments, gifts of betel, flowers, camphor, and saffron,
and with various kinds of foods and delicacies, the lady of the inner apartments [honored him].
With villages and grants of territory, with flowers, camphor, and saffron,
and with various kinds of foods and delicacies, she gratified the women of the inner apartments.
He won over the neighboring kings with villages and unequalled gifts, as well as with wealth;
he bound those attached to his infantry with neck-ornaments and auspicious collars.
The king himself should satisfy his own kinsmen individually with gifts marked with their names;
having satisfied them as is appropriate, he should then satisfy the wrestlers, soldiers, and actors.
He saw bulls and buffaloes fighting with their enemies,
as well as elephants, horses, warriors, and well-adorned foot soldiers.
Having mounted a platform himself, he should watch actors, dancers, and wandering performers;
then he should provoke to anger and terrify cows, buffaloes, and other such animals.
O Bhārata, one should cause the bulls to rejoice with cows by making them engage in a dialogue of questions and answers; then, at the time of afternoon, in the eastern direction.
O King, one should construct a divine path-fence made of *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass, provided with many hanging tassels, at difficult passes, at pillars, and at trees.
Having displayed elephants and horses, one should lead them into his courtyard in the evening;
likewise cows, bulls, and buffaloes, adorned and resounding with the loud ringing of bells.
[356] When the fire-oblation (homa) has been performed by the best of the twice-born, one should station guardians of the path;
for the oblation performed with the mantra of Durgā bestows happiness upon all the worlds.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter, and then, O observer of noble vows, one should perform a prostration with this mantra:
"O Mārgapālī, who bestows happiness upon all the worlds, homage be to you!"
"Come back again to my vow with objects of sense such as sons and wives,
or indeed with the enjoyment of the kingdom, or with a hundred or a thousand [villages], O King."
Or, according to his own capacity, he may provide with common foods for the mother’s family,
the father’s family, and the children along with their kin.
He who gives the *mārgapālī* shall cause the entire world to cross over.

Just as in the following [sections], for the sake of the increasing fruit of giving—where one undertakes the *mārgapālī* vow by pledging hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, or hundreds of thousands of meals, and gives them to all for their satisfaction—the fruit belongs to that person. Here, the terms "village" (*grāma*) and "kingdom" (*rāṣṭra*) are indicative of ten thousand (*ayuta*) and a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*).
Furthermore, a lustration ceremony (*nīrājana*) should be performed right there, which bestows victory upon the kingdom.
In this manner, cows, elephants, and bulls pass over the surface of the *mārgapālī*.
Kings, princes, brahmins, and those of the śūdra caste—
by crossing over the Mārgapālī, may they be free from disease and endowed with happiness.
Having performed all this here, and having offered worship at night to Bali, the lord of the Daityas, the king should perform the vow directly upon a mandala drawn on the ground.
Having painted the lord of the Daityas as Bali with five-colored pigments,
complete with all ornaments and seated together with Vindhyāvatī;
And Kūṣmāṇḍa, born of victory, was formidable and surrounded by many dānavas;
his face was full of joy, and he wore a crown and large earrings.
Having had an image of the king of the Daityas made with two arms,
the king himself should then worship it in the middle of his house within a spacious hall.
Then, together with his brothers, mother, and kinsmen, he was contented;
[he offered worship] with lotuses, flowers, blossoms, white water-lilies, and red lotuses.
With perfumes, flowers, food offerings, unbroken grains, and molasses cakes;
with liquor, meat, wine, and things to be licked; and with lamps, wicks, and stolen goods.
O King of kings, with this mantra, together with his ministers and domestic priest, [he said]:
"O King Bali, obeisance to you, O Lord, son of Virocana!"
"O future Indra, O enemy of the gods, please accept this worship.
Having thus performed the worship, the king then observed a vigil during the night.
One should cause spectacles such as plays, dances, and storytelling to be performed;
and within the house, the people should likewise [arrange] upon the bed white rice grains.
Having established King Bali, one should worship him with fruits and flowers;
O descendant of Kuru, gifts are given specifically for the sake of Bali.
Those things which they call inexhaustible have been fully demonstrated by me alone;
whatever gift is given in this [field], whether it be small or great.
All that shall become inexhaustible and supremely pleasing to Viṣṇu;
indeed, the earth was recovered by Viṣṇu from Bali when he was satisfied.
A great festival was given to the Asuras that brought them benefit;
from that time forward, O Indra among kings, the auspicious Kaumudī has been observed.
[358] Who else is there who drives away all calamities, destroys all obstacles,
removes the grief of the world, and brings about wealth, nourishment, and happiness?
By the word *ku* the earth is to be known; from it come joy (*muda*) and exhilaration (*harṣa*), thus two [meanings].
Because of this, those who know the roots (*dhātu*) and those who know the etymologies (*nirgama*) remember this as *Kaumudī*.
Because people rejoice with one another through various states of being— glad, contented, and seeking happiness— therefore this is known as Kaumudī.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, because white water-lilies (kumuda) were offered to Bali by the kings on this day,
O Pārtha, it is therefore remembered as Kaumudī.
In this way, O lord of the people, for year after year, a single day and night was given to the king of the Dānavas, like a mirror upon the surface of the earth.
For that man who performs this in the kingdom, whence can there be fear of disease?
Whence, it is asked, is there no fear there? There is no fear caused by death;
there shall be abundance of food, security, health, and the highest excellence of crops.
And all people shall be free from disease and devoid of all calamities.
O King Yudhiṣṭhira, because of the performance of the Kaumudī festival here on this earth,
whatever state of mind one maintains while staying with it, so shall it be for them.
Indeed, his year passes away in the form of joy, dejection, and so forth;
weeping, he weeps for a year, and rejoicing, he rejoices for a year.
One who has eaten shall remain a healthy eater for a year, and one who is healthy shall continue to be healthy;
therefore, the Kaumudī festival should be celebrated by men with joy and contentment.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this lunar day belongs to Viṣṇu, to the Dānavas, and to the ancestors.
Those of noble mind who perform the worship of King Bali during the Festival of Lights, which brings joy to all people, [attain great merit].
O King, those who are preoccupied with hundreds of ways to increase the pleasure of giving and enjoying [wealth] attain complete joy through sheer delight.
Thus concludes the Great Festival of Kaumudī as described in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. Now follows the Great Festival of Bhūta from the Skanda Purāṇa.
When the lord of Pārvatī had departed at the conclusion of their dalliance,
the goddess, who bestows supreme purity, rose from her bed and performed her purificatory rites.
Then, as Pārvatī touched it, there appeared a stream of water resembling a lake—this is the ellipsis (*iti śeṣaḥ*). "Lake" (*saraḥ*) here means a waterfall (*nirjhara*).
She felt anxious, thinking: "Neither a son nor even a daughter has been born."
As she was thus reflecting, [a tear] arose from the water of her heart.
A lotus-eyed maiden was born, fashioned from clay,
clothed in blue garments and veiled in red.
Having smelled the head of that maiden, the daughter of the mountain who had arisen from the waters of his heart, Pārvatī embraced her and departed.
"O lady, since you have been born with your limbs smeared by the mud of the earth,
therefore there shall be a great festival known as the 'Water-Sport'."
On that day when you shall descend upon the great world of Indra,
on that day your people will celebrate a great festival.
That desire which belonged to Bhairava, to the Goddess, and to Bhava, became Mahābhairava himself; taking the girl by the hand, he stood there.
Then the blessed Ambikā, the wife and beloved of the Blessed One, spoke to the man: "Who are you, and why do you seize my daughter?"
Then Bhairava, whose face was formidable with fangs and whose form was terrifying,
spoke low to Umā like a cloud charged with lightning.
"That passion which arose so terrible between the Blessed One and Bhava—
these two born from it shall become my wife."
Seeing that couple standing there with deformed limbs and clad in shabby garments,
Soma-bhūṣa looked at them with apprehension, wondering, "Who are these two?"
Then both Bhava and Bhavapāla— the enemy of Tripura, whose matted hair is marked by the moon—
fell at his feet and spoke while standing near him.
Who are you two, and what shall I do?
Then Ambikā,
whose complexion was like ten million suns, lightning, and fire,
spoke to the Lord of the Mountains with a face full of smiles as she addressed him.
Moving here with playful ease.
That which was your desire and mine here—
terrible and fear-inducing even to the gods—
is indeed this man born from existence.
This very fire of passion of mine is directed toward a woman alone.
Then Umā spoke to the moon-born one, who was wearing the guise of a cowherd; the Lord addressed these words to the couple: "Soma-lakṣa."
For as soon as this excellent woman was meditated upon by you in meditation,
at that very moment, through my power, she became this Bhairava for you.
"O Goddess, I cannot exist without you, nor can you exist without me;
therefore, this has been given to you today by me and by Lambodara."
"O my beloved, a festival shall take place among them as proclaimed by you;
there will first come for me this great festival of Dattaka."
Therefore, O Goddess worshipped by the best of gods, the entire world consists of that [nature];
for that reason, O Pārvatī, men and women are mutually attached to one another.
In women, the heart resides in the vulva; in men, the heart resides in the penis. O lady, this entire world is marked by the vulva and the penis.
Men together with the gods, crying out "Bhaga!
Liṅga!", will strike one another down while shouting at each other.
At both the beginning and the end, there shall be a festival of terror;
for the remainder of the time, there shall be a festival of the upper terrace.
Whatever city, town, or village Bhairavī enters will become like one possessed by madness, including its women and elders.
[362] O Daughter of the Mountain, the city, though inhabited by the four castes who are not actually insane, will become like one mad, intoxicated by its delight in the Bhairava Āgamas.
Just as the deities enter the twice-born when they are appointed for the sake of the ancestors,
so too, O Bhairavī, does Bhairava enter men through his majesty.
Then, mounted upon donkeys, smeared with dung and mud,
they made their dress and ornaments from bitter *tāmbūla* creepers.
With breasts bound by the fruits thereof, making loud and manifest sounds,
their entire bodies adorned with ashes yet fouled by the mire of feces, urine, and filth.

While cymbals were being played— cymbals accompanied by cruel and nonsensical speech, meaning words that were incoherent, disconnected, and lacking consistency between what preceded and what followed—
the Bhairava, O fair-limbed lady, was being signaled by his wife.
O timid one, he will indeed enter the city, generating joy among the people;
once Bhairava has entered the city worshipped by Indra, O fearful one.
Then that festival will be both pleasing and terrible to the people. "Pleasing" means beloved; "terrible" means intense.
For those who are fearful, even their hundred years will be worn out by old age.
All those men, like Vatsaka, will likewise celebrate a festival.
Their limbs were polished with various ornaments and adorned with saffron and agallochum;
they were wrapped in many yellow garments and cloths.
With ear-ornaments and garlands, they are always garlanded and crowned;
they are always garlanded, possessed of brothers, crowned, and adorned with arm-ornaments.
Likewise, even though their hair is rough, it is [adorned] with flowers such as the *campaka*.
Slapping their limbs, they caused their beloved words to be heard.
In the streets and on the royal highways, they proclaimed here and there that noble sons were the cause of the lack of physical form in noble women.
Revealing at every step all the doubts regarding those secret and hidden matters concerning women of noble family.
Singing, dancing, and engaging in various thoughts,
they who were formerly modest have now become shameless;
even in matters that should cause shame, they revile their elders and others as well.
Mortals, delighting in worldly pleasures, will act according to their own whims;
the son will not feel shame before his mother, nor will the fire-drill [the father] feel shame before the son.
A son is not [the kinsman] of his father, nor is a father the [kinsman] of his son, nor is a grandfather;
a sister’s son is not [the kinsman] of his maternal uncle, nor is a maternal uncle the [kinsman] of his sister’s son.
In just a moment, when their own kinsmen have become shameless,
they will, like fools, threaten one another with harsh words.

Their speech was as harsh as that of Brahma-ogres; they were pale-limbed and appeared as if dead; their bodies were smeared with the remnants of broken offerings; yet their limbs were beautiful and their movements graceful.
Some carried dogs, while others were mounted on female donkeys; some wore pomegranate garb, some cowherd dress, and other base men appeared in many different guises.
Some were dressed as kings and others as themselves; some were young men appearing in the form of the elderly, while others went about disguised as barbers.
They will intensely circulate incense mixed with onions and a rain of *sīdhu* liquor according to their ability— an incense that causes aversion through the sense of smell.
And others will give a foul-smelling aquatic creature to men who are ignorant, placing it upon their noses along with impurities.
O Goddess, other men there, adorned with divine garments and ornaments,
indeed rejoice like men while reciting poetic compositions.
Just as one might neigh among horses without neighing at another,
so do the ancestors tremble for the slayer of a Brahmin.
For just as kings [are beneficial] to horses and men to elephants,
so too does the sprinkling of water for joy arise for the benefit of men.
O God, the ancestors do not eat the oblation of that man who,
out of malice, creates discord between those who are at peace.
Neither you nor I find satisfaction in that, O Pārvatī;
yet you should cease this great sorrow caused by your failure to obtain a son.
But when the terrifying event has passed, O Udaśevikā, incomparable abundance of joy will come to you, just as it has come to you now.
This palace of yours does not shine as it once did because of your grief;
it will become like that city when it is devoid of its attendants.
O Daughter of the Mountain, men and women will render houses and temples lusterless with ashes and mud.
"O Queen, the city will become like one laid waste by thieves;
it will be filled with men who resemble ghosts, covered in lumps of clay, ashes, excrement, and urine.
Then the men will cry out, 'A terrible death has occurred!'"
"Covered more thickly with grass there, and wrapped in her garment, she lies down"—
speaking thus with her voice, she said, "This Bhairava leaves us not."
Mortals will carry away that beloved one who has died— a death shrouded in secrecy—
having laid him down either on the bank of a pond or likewise on the bank of a river.
Having bathed there, freed from impurity, they shall go to the abode of Hara;
having performed the ritual bath for Bhairava, they are known as those who have reached the elevated altar through the festival.
Men will become like those observing the vows of sages, united with their beloveds;
O Pārvatī, just as those men were repeatedly ashamed and filled with modesty upon the arrival of Bhairava.
In that very same way, those who had been filled with fear once again became surrounded by ascetics devoted to solitary penance.
But that brahmin, O beautiful one, who recites this Bhairavotsava in the assembly of twice-born gods,
shall indeed increase in sons and grandsons in due time.
One shall attain the auspicious state of Mahāgaṇeśa.
Thus from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Exulting, [he proclaims], 'Bhūtamātā! in every village and in every city."
Singing, dancing, and laughing, the people run about in every direction.
He raves like a madman, falls upon the ground like one intoxicated,
runs about excessively like one enraged, and cries out aloud like a corpse.
Seized by the wind, the world contorts its face and limbs;
like a ghost, it wallows in ashes, urine, and mud.
Is this the path prescribed by the scriptures, or is it merely worldly? My mind is bewildered, O Kṛṣṇa; you alone ought to explain this to me.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, I shall tell you whatever is in your mind;
it is my conviction that you are both orthodox and full of faith.
In former times, on Mount Mandara with its beautiful caves, Hara dwelt together with Pārvatī,
filled with joy as he sported with divine playthings.
Seeing Gaurī, whose face was like the cool-rayed moon, who was joyful, and who possessed full, elevated hips and a pair of breasts shining like jars, the Teacher of the World [was moved].
Like the spreading plantain-sheath of the very root of the tree of desire, once burnt away.
Delighted, Śiva enjoyed himself upon a costly couch;
thus he took his pleasure with that most beautiful woman for a hundred divine years.
Then the goddess, having arisen, emerged from the obstruction;
the woman rose up from the voiding of urine, her belly torn open.
She was dark-complexioned, with a formidable face, tawny eyes, and red hair;
she was adorned with a garland of skulls and wore a crown of bound-off heads.
The auspicious goddess Śivā wears a skull-staff and a skeleton, her hands marked with ritual gestures;
she is clothed in a tiger skin and wears a girdle of tinkling bells.
She resounds with the sounds of the ḍamaru and maru drums, filling the sky with her cries of "phet";
and other goddesses stand at her side, following the rhythm of her song and instrumental music.
Bearing skull-bowls and staffs, and draped in elephant hides, they dance and laugh with unrestrained vigor and incomparable joy.
In that very same way, a man was born from Śaṅkara, possessing his form and ornaments,
followed by many most terrifying spirits.
With faces like those of lions and tigers, and with teeth that scraped the very sky,
Bhavānī and Bhava became one in an instant.
Seeing them, the God, his mind filled with joy, said to the greatly astonished Goddess:
"O auspicious one, look, look at these two who have arisen from my own body."
O Goddess, just as the two brothers Bhaṇḍa and Vibhīṣaṇa were [respectively] loathsome, marvelous, erotic, terrifying, and rending, so too do I consider these two [the Rasas] to be.
Nothing resembling these two appears immediately after them:
Bhrātṛbhāṇḍā, Bhūtamātā, and likewise Udakasevikā.
Having assigned three names to them, Hara then granted her a boon;
she had come with her purpose frustrated and was standing at the foot of the World-Tree.
Those who shall serve [the deity] with devotion using mouthfuls filled with water,
having anointed [the image] with sandalwood paste, and then worship it with flowers and incense;
O Goddess, he who acts in this way, permeated by devotion, should quickly feed [the deity] with saṃyāva, kṛśara, apūpa, and pāyasa.
He shall obtain an increase in sons and cattle, as well as physical health;
neither Śākinīs, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas shall enter his house.
Children play and grow up free from disease.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
At what time should the worship of Bhūtamātṛ be performed by those seeking happiness?
O tiger among men, you ought to tell me this regarding those men.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
This goddess is always the benefactor of children.
He is worshipped through various names, various rites, and at various times,
beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) in the month of Jyeṣṭha until the fifteenth day (pañcadaśī).
The designation "Jyaiṣṭha" is used with the intention of referring to the month ending in the full moon;
during that time, worship should be performed with incitements and spectacles.
The exposition of the fruits of forbidden actions is presented as a mockery of heretics by men intent on laughter, disguised in wondrous attire.
Out of greed for wealth, those who study the Vedas and are self-restrained on the path do not see one being impaled on the tip of a stake, even as they look on.
"You have seen him, who was exultant and intolerant of another's wife;
having had his hands cut off, he has been cast by the Lord into the waters of Puṣkara."
Shaded by a sun-protecting parasol, fanned by palm-leaf whisks,
and seated upon a white lion-throne, he proceeds happily toward his meritorious destination.
O people, do you not see your own sovereignty in the hand of another,
being split by saws and splashing with streams of blood?
It is said that this thief, who causes supreme distress to all, has been captured;
struck by blows from the staff, he is being led away by the police officers.
Surrounded by onlookers shouting with the beat of Yama’s drums,
he was bound and led away for execution, his face turned toward the enemy force—
he a twice-born man with sharp hair, a sharp beard, and clad in white garments.
And while he watches her being struck with slaps from a libertine and a courtesan, [he says:
"O slut, go out from this house, having fattened yourself as much as your belly could hold!"
Why does that fool perform the burdening and nourishing of these children—
both those who are terrifying and those who are not— who are themselves dependent on the childish?
Set down the lamps of ghee while performing your rhythmic dance-steps;
what kind of world-weariness has arisen in his heart, caused by his attachment to fields, women, and wealth?
Even though this child has undertaken the great vow,
as he wanders about, does he not see the red, black, and white-bodied [deities]?
She saw a variegated male and female parrot inside the hollow of a tree,
surrounded by many small chambers and rendered impassable by a multitude of arrows.
"O daughter, you have been seized— she who is characterized by the sounds 'vimukta', 'hikva', and 'hūṃ', and by her excellent striking and glances, and who has a face that is half-black."
Behold her with disheveled hair, dancing like a yoginī,
her wild tāṇḍava dance intensified by the deep sound of musical instruments.
This circle of Dindiṇas is to be visualized with the dress and ornaments of madmen;
they carry baskets at their waists and wear black woolen blankets.
The *ḍombī* woman wanders about crying out, and the lute [is played] at the house during a solar eclipse;
thus, by means of these many spectacles and performances...
One should thus cause those [afflictions] directed toward sons, brothers, and friends to depart;
on the eleventh or ninth lunar day, having lit a lamp within the two earrings.
Guarded by many protectors and preceded by the sound of musical instruments, he should be led at the time of dusk to where the Goddess is surrounded by people.
In the heroic observances (vīracaryā), the lamp is said to accomplish all aims;
thus one should carry forth the lamp until the fifteenth lunar day.
On the fifteenth day, one should perform a great festival for the Bhūtamātṛ;
one should bathe her, worship her, and offer as an oblation rice mixed with meat.
Having prostrated together with his kinsmen and asked for their forgiveness, he should return home;
O Pārtha, he thus performs this great festival year after year.
For as long as one year, no obstacle shall arise in his home.
Those who honor her with playful gestures that cause people to laugh—
let him sprinkle her, the granter of fearlessness, the sustainer of the earth’s prosperity.
Together with their brothers, servants, sons, and kinsmen, they remain free from all calamities and live happily for a great many years.
Thus ends the festival of the elements alone.
The Earth said:
"I am free from grief for father, mother, husband, brother, or son."
O Keśava, tell me that vow by which a woman becomes so.
Varāha said:
Formerly, there was a Prajāpati named Dakṣa; he had a daughter named Satī, who, being of auspicious vows, was given as a lawful wife to Mahādeva.
The sacrifice was commenced by Dakṣa, and all the gods were invited;
they were honored according to tradition, but Śaṅkara was not invited.
Treated with contempt by him, O Earth, the goddess abandoned her body and was born again as the daughter of the Himavat mountain, endowed with the memory of her former births.
There, wearing a garland of *nameru* flowers and appearing eight years of age,
she departed for asceticism despite being restrained by her father, brothers, and mother.
Having undertaken fierce asceticism on the mountain together with her friends,
she subsisted on withered leaves for a thousand years.
She remained subsisting on water for another thousand years,
and likewise, she endured a third great period without any food.
In this manner, she performed austerities for ten thousand years;
yet even so, that Lord of Gods, the wielder of the bull and the trident, was not pleased.
Thus, being weary, dejected, and emaciated from that constant state,
she, filled with rage, again resolved to enter the fire.
Then Kālī, having risen and performed her morning rites,
suddenly spoke many stories on the earth.
Surrounded by her companions who were filled with devotion,
she stood waiting for him when the celestial sage Nārada, who discerns all the worlds, arrived.
Gaurī, the daughter of Himavat, intent on the worship of Śiva and desiring her husband as a god,
remained thus for many groups of years.
"O Sage, when the god is not satisfied,
this Gaurī is then resolved to enter the fire," said Gaurī’s friend to the sage.
Having heard these words of hers, Nārada, filled with compassion,
approached her side and spoke these words, O Vasundharā.
Nārada said:
O beautiful one, enter into some ritual action by name;
hear from me that deed by which Hara is pleased in this world.
O daughter of the Mountain, perform that vow known as Saṅghāṭana.
[372] "By performing the Saṅghāṭaka vow, you shall then obtain that husband.
The Goddess said:
"O Sage, out of compassion for me, tell me that vow."
By performing that [penance], I shall indeed attain that Maheśvara as my husband.
Nārada said:
Listen with a focused mind, O blessed lady, to this Saṅghāṭaka vow;
I shall relate it to you as it was told of old by Brahmā to me.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
one should undertake the vow of eating but a single meal, having first cleansed the teeth and other organs;
then, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) in the evening, one should observe a fast on the second day.
On the third day as well, and likewise on the fourth, there should be the breaking of the fast;
and one should worship Śiva with devotion during both fasts.
Where one should offer [the oblation] at night without formal ritual procedures, one should sleep on the ground;
then, having risen in the morning and recollected the deity, one should worship him.
Without deceit, one should offer an excellent leaf-plate; one should not give blood as food. One should feed seven Brahmins, or at least feed them according to one's capacity.
Having given them a sacrificial fee and paid homage, one should dismiss them;
afterwards, the breaking of the fast should be performed—this is the ritual for the *saptasaṃghāṭaka*.
Having observed the fast for seven and a half months,
one should then perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) at the seventh conjunction (saṅghāṭa).
[373] And this vow should also be performed during the bright fortnight. By performing it thus during both fortnights, seven *saṅghāṭaka* units will be completed in three and a half months.
Listen now with a one-pointed mind to the procedure for the foremost Brahma here:
a man and a woman should be fashioned out of gold according to one's capacity and with devotion.
Richly adorned with all ornaments and seated upon a couch,
they should then be bathed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and subsequently with scented water.
One should also anoint [the image] with water containing all medicinal herbs and with saffron;
it should be covered with saffron-dyed cloths and adorned with various flower garlands.
Having placed [the image] upon a couch, one should begin the night vigil;
one should cause the vigil to be performed at night with songs, instrumental music, dances, and so forth.

Having performed the night vigil with the sounds of great auspicious instruments such as mṛdaṅgas and paṭahas, when morning has arrived, one should then invite Brahmins with devotion and provide them with food according to one's means.
One should also give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to them; a man and a woman seated upon a couch, along with all kinds of bedding, one should present everything to the instructor.
Having personally offered everything to him who is accompanied by his wife and honored with garments and other gifts, he should then ask the Brahmin for forgiveness.
Oṃ, homage to Śambhu; homage to Bhava with Umā; Oṃ, homage to Śaṅkara. Thus is the mantra for worship.
Oṃ, homage to Mayaskara, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Śiva, svāhā! Oṃ, homage to Śivataḥ, svāhā!
Thus end the mantras for the fire-oblation.
Having fed the Brahmin together with his wife, one should ask for his forgiveness.
Having offered all of that and bowed down, one should dismiss him.
O highly fortunate lady, listen as I relate with certainty the fruit that a woman obtains by completing this vow in its entirety.
For as long as a hundred kalpas, in birth after birth, may that woman be free from the suffering of misfortune arising from separation from husband and sons.
He shall be born into that family even after hundreds of other births;
that family will certainly be filled with wealth and grain.
Through the greatness of this vow, one shall be endowed with physical beauty and good fortune, as well as joined with happiness and prosperity, in birth after birth.
If a woman or a man should hear this vow while it is being recited,
they shall be liberated from all suffering and honored in the heavenly world.
Varāha said:
Having fully explained the vow according to the prescribed rules, Nārada departed with the swiftest speed; the goddess, devoted to the vow, remained behind.
By the greatness of the Saṅghāṭa vow, Gaurī quickly obtained an auspicious husband and became happy; likewise, any other woman may also become so.
[375] Having heard this, O Earth, you must observe this vow, my dear;
you will obtain everything as desired—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the Saṅghāṭaka-vrata as declared in the Varāha Purāṇa:
One should observe a single meal on both the full-moon and new-moon days;
by performing that single meal there, one does not descend into hell.
There, having bathed Hari with golden lotuses, one should worship him with diligence using the Puṇyāhavācana rite and auspicious sounds such as the word "Victory! (jaya).
Then, taking up the vessel amidst the sounds of singing, the Vedas, and other music,
one should perform a circumambulation of that powerful Viṣṇu.
Then, having addressed him according to the rules, one should worship him especially;
having fed his favorite alone and bowed down, one should ask for his forgiveness.
Having consulted with one Brahmin, honored him, and circumambulated him,
he should feed him a vessel of food mixed with ghee and ask for his forgiveness.
Having fed the most excellent Brahmins, one should gratify them with sacrificial fees;
and one should satisfy those observing vows with gifts of food, clothing, and other such items.
"Those who are wretched, blind, and miserable—[one should give to them] before the day departs.
Thus ends the Harivrata as described in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa.
Anilāda said:
Having fashioned the god Narasiṃha out of silver with four arms,
one should install him in a copper vessel and provide him with many fangs.
On his two arms were rubies, while his nails were of coral;
on the region of his breasts were topazes, and both his earrings were sapphires.
Having fashioned eyes of *rājāvarta* stone and a crest of blue *vaidūrya*,
and having made this beautiful form, one should fill that vessel— which is joined with honey—
with water mixed [with other substances], and once filled, one should burn it again.

Having placed this form in that vessel and having set it down, one should fill the vessel with honey mixed with water. Furthermore, one should place another vessel filled with honey and water upon it.
Covered with a pair of cloths, one should seat it upon the throne.
One should likewise perform its worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense.
The wise one should prepare an offering of various kinds of food;
he should worship it, joined with a canopy above, with garlands of flowers.
Or else, having undertaken the twelfth day (dvādaśī) in either the month of Kārttika or Vaiśākha, one should properly perform the offering; for by doing so, one attains that supreme state.

Relying upon the twelfth day, one should perform that festival—the "Elephant Play" (*hastikrīḍā*)—during the four days beginning with it; then, on either the full moon of Kārttika or Vaiśākha, a gift should be given.
Whether in the forest or in battle crowded with hosts of bandits, no fear arises for him who performs this even once.
Terrible calamities do not enter him; it bestows wealth, long life, progeny, beauty, and delightful good fortune.
This great playground of Hari’s sport has been correctly described to you,
as well as the righteous practices in brief that lead to the attainment of that abode.
Having heard this, one goes to the meritorious state and is liberated from all sins;
one's wealth and lifespan increase, especially during the month of Śrāvaṇa.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and adorn a pair [of a Brahmin and his wife];
he should listen to the Purāṇa during the rainy season on the following day.

Thus ends the description of Harikrīḍāyana as spoken in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa. O son of Kuntī, he who is desirous of performing sacrifice should feed the twice-born on the fifth and sixth lunar days, as well as on the eighth and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight.
"By observing this fast, one is born free from disease and endowed with beauty.
Thus is the Yamavrata as declared in the Mahābhārata.
Anilāda said:
Ah, I shall declare the Great Vow (Mahāvrata) by which one ascends to that state;
listen to the ritual procedure, which is difficult even for gods, asuras, and sages to attain.
On the full-moon day at the end of the month of Āśvayuja,
one who has purified his soul should eat milk-rice saturated with ghee at night, along with sandalwood and sugarcane products.

At the end of Āśvayuja, during the month of Kārttika— that is, on the new moon day at the conclusion of Kārttika— the practitioner, having sipped water (ācamya) and become pure, should use a tooth-stick made of bilva wood. Having consumed this sugarcane juice (aikṣava), the devotee, endowed with faith, should bow to Mahādeva.
"O Lord, O Mahādeva, by your command I wish to undertake this eternal vow; please grant me the means to accomplish it therein."
Having spoken thus and undertaking this rule, for sixteen years I shall observe the unsurpassed fast on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Then, on the first day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the following day,
having observed a fast and having consulted his teacher, he repeatedly remembered Mahādeva.
One should invite sixteen, eight, or half of that number of Brahmins who are devoted to Mahādeva and whose bodies are covered with ashes, as well as couples.
Having approached the Lord with devotion and lit sixteen lamps,
one should bow with devotion to Mahādeva, the Lord of Beasts, and make the offering.
Having taken leave [of his teacher] and gone home, remembering Mahādeva while on the ground,
he should sleep at night without food upon a bed spread with clean cloth.
Then, at the rising of the thousand-rayed sun, having bathed and taken lamps,
as well as food offerings, water for the ritual bath, and so forth, he should go to the abode of Śaṅkara.
Having gone there to the canopy, and having offered a pair of garments,
a bell, incense, and banners, one should then perform the ritual bathing.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should abandon the vow with astringent decoctions;
immediately thereafter, one should bathe [the deity] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and with ghee.
And likewise, one should bathe [the deity] again with honey, curd, and further with milk,
or else with juice, sugar, and fruits.
Then, having bathed him with sesame-water and subsequently with warm water,
one should afterwards anoint the excellent body with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
Having thus worshipped him with devotion and placed gold [upon his head], one should go home;
having placed gold upon the arm and set a golden flower there,
one should indeed offer an oblation (*naivedya*) consisting of various kinds of fragrant fruits.
Having gone home, he worshipped the omnipresent Hiraṇyaretas according to the prescribed rule.
Having established the Jātavedas fire, one should satisfy it with sesame seeds and clarified butter;
likewise, one should feed those observing vows, the preceptor, and married couples.
One should honor them according to one's ability with gifts of gold, garments, and so forth;
having thus dismissed all of them together with one's own kinsmen, one should depart.
Having first drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he should joyfully eat while remaining silent;
whatever remains as leavings of this, he should offer to Mahādeva.
Desiring one's own welfare, one should perform all that directed toward him;
at the commencement, however, both the poor and the wealthy should perform the prescribed rite.
According to one's financial capacity, both monthly and in its entirety;
or if someone has very little wealth, [they may perform it] starting from the month of Puṣya up until Kārttika.

Having performed the rite on the new moon night according to the previously stated procedure, one should then fast on the first day of the lunar fortnight and, being pure, drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Remembering Mahādeva with devotion, one should eat together with those who bear the *liṅga*;
at the end of the month of Kārttika, one should perform the entire preceding rite.
One should observe the fast on both lunar days, the first and the second;
thus, when the month of Pauṣa has arrived, one should perform the night-vow on the first day.
In the second year, one should fast on the second lunar day until the end of the month of Kārttika; likewise, one should observe one lunar day in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and another.
As before, one should abandon it in the month of Pauṣa, and one should perform this practice every year in the same manner.

The resultant meaning of this verse is as follows: On the new moon day one should eat at night (*nakta*) and on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*) one should fast; this is the first year. In the first [year], on the first new moon day one eats at night and on the second day (*dvitīyā*) one fasts; in the remaining [years], one eats at night on the *pratipad* and fasts on the *dvitīyā*. This is the second [year]. In the first month, one eats at night every day and fasts on the second and third days; in the remaining [months], one eats at night on the *dvitīyā* and fasts on the *tṛtīyā*. This is the third [year]. Having performed it thus for the remaining years, in the sixteenth year, at the emergence of the full moon of Kārttika—that is, at the time of sunrise—[one completes the vow].
Having worshipped the deity as before, one should satisfy Kṛśānu with *dhanni*;
[one should satisfy] Arcis with *dhyanni*.
One should give *gaṃ* to Mahādeva, and to a twice-born who has been initiated.
[He should give] a golden-horned cow with her calf, equipped with a bell and a bronze milking vessel,
along with sixteen Brahmins observing the Śiva-vow together with the preceptor.
Having fed them, one should honor them according to one's ability with gold, garments, and other gifts;
one should also give them individually parasols, sandals, and water-pots.
Having dismissed those sixteen couples, he should indeed feed them; having repeatedly dismissed them,
he should feed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas according to his ability.
And on that day, one should give food to others who are afflicted by hunger.
Thus, this great vow is a means of expiating even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
it bestows manifold enjoyments in the remaining worlds, beginning with Bhūr and Bhuvaḥ.
That which stands like a staircase for all four castes—
this very thing one should accomplish upon reaching youth, as it has been prescribed right here.
This ancient vow is auspicious, eternally bestowing long life, supreme beauty, and good fortune; it is prescribed for both women and men,
and it should be observed by a widow as well as by one who is not yet widowed.
Even by a young girl, that vow must be observed in order to avoid separation;
having fasted every month, she should eat together with those who observe the vow.

This should be performed according to one's ability during two, three, or four years, or throughout all the years; and at the end of the distinct years, one should perform the rite at the commencement [of the next].
While seeking the accumulation of flowers and that state of health,
if someone should die before the undertaken vow is completed;
The reciter, the listener, and those who take delight in the vow— all these obtain that fruit through the power of their noble undertaking.
"Those who are embraced by merit become oriented toward that state.
Thus is described the Mahāvrata as stated in the Kālikā Purāṇa.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Māgha, and then on the full moon day, [one should perform the rite].
One should always perform this rite correctly; thus one shall go to his state.
For this vow, when performed according to the prescribed rite, bestows beauty, grants good fortune,
and indeed yields sons and happiness.
To the proclaimer of this vow, who is disciplined and endowed with virtues, [one should offer].
[382] Then, one desiring the stages [of realization], being well-purified, should worship with sandals and other such items,
as well as a vessel joined with gold and garlands, and even a blue cow.
And in the absence of gold, one should use half a karṣa of silver;
[one should also provide] a pair of new, fine garments adorned with a profusion of flowers.
Having placed that vessel there, one should set it down in a clean location;
then, one should perform a vigil with auspicious songs, instrumental music, and other such rites.
At dawn, one should carry the vessel to the great temple of Hari;
having bathed the Lord Viṣṇu with milk and other substances, one should personally worship Him.
One should present that vessel and utter the words, "May [the deity] be pleased.
Then, with various kinds of foods and fragrant water, one should offer.
One should offer a food offering (naivedya) rich in curd, sugar-candy, clarified butter, and milk, as well as a sacrificial oblation (bali).
Then, having bowed down, one should return home and further gratify the preceptor (ācārya).
Having bowed down, he should devoutly feed the observers of the vow together with the twice-born;
he should provide excellent food for all the ascetics indeed.
And for all who are miserable, blind, and wretched, there is no obstacle;
by this very vow alone, one shall properly attain the auspicious state.
"May the long-lived and wealthy man rejoice here for a very long time"—
this is the Pātravrata as declared in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa.
[383] Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Lord of Gods, it is my conviction that the recollection of past births is difficult to attain;
therefore, I wish to hear by what action it is obtained.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Even a Śūdra, by means of Brāhmaṇas, may be born into a great family;
he shall be a donor, patient, wealthy, eloquent, handsome, and possessed of auspicious qualities.
O King, there are indeed four auspicious things with four legs;
they are beset by many obstacles and are difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined themselves.
The first [festival] is in Mārgaśīrṣa, the second likewise in Phālguna;
the third, O King of kings, is celebrated in Jyeṣṭha, and the last in Bhādrapada.
O best of men, for three months beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
that which is known as Tripuṣkara is the supreme means for producing magnanimity.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for three months beginning from the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha,
that [period] is called Tripuṣkara, which bestows strength and valor.
Likewise, O son of Pāṇḍu, at the beginning of the month of Bhādrapada, for three months—
either through the granting of boons by the gods, or by the service of the sages, or by bathing in sacred fords (tīrtha), O Lord, or by austerity, fire-offerings, and vows— [the merit is attained].
Kṛṣṇa said:
O King, four auspicious days should be observed with effort by a righteous man; through their power, a person becomes deficient in nothing and gains the memory of his past lives.
In former times, there was a Vaiśya named Śubhodaya on the banks of the Yamunā;
he observed the vow-observance (vratapada), and in due course of time, he died.
The son born to Sañjaya was renowned as Svarṇaṣṭhīvī;
through the power of his vows, he knew the thoughts of others' births, yet he was struck down by thieves.
Though he was restored to life once more by the power of Nārada,
he remembered his entire previous history exactly according to the truth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: How did Sañjaya’s son come to be called Svarṇaṣṭhīvī?
And how was he led away by the bandits toward death, yet restored to life?
Kṛṣṇa said:
O lord of men, there was a king named Sañjaya in Kuśāvatī;
he had two divine sages as his constant friends, Nārada and Parvata.
Once, having arrived at the house of Sañjaya by chance,
the two of them were honored with hospitable greetings and offerings of food and other services.
Then, while they were seated and recounting their previous adventures,
Sañjaya’s daughter Varuṇī arrived in the presence of her father.
Parvata said to the king: "This maiden is of excellent complexion;
her ankles are concealed, her thighs are well-knit, and her hips and breasts are full."
Her eyes, nails, and feet resemble lotus petals; her hair is thick, dark, soft, and glossy, with curls drawn back from her forehead. Her complexion is like the filaments of a lotus.
Graceful in her elephant-like gait, with beautiful nose and a skillful voice—oh, what beauty! Oh, what fortitude! Oh, what supreme loveliness!
With her nose like a blooming sesame flower, her form is clearly perceived;
whose auspicious and beautiful daughter is this, who so captivates my heart?
To that Brahmin who was speaking thus, his eyes wide with wonder, the king then said: "O Brahmin, Parvata is my daughter."
Then the wise Nārada, his senses agitated, spoke these words:
"O King, I desire to marry; let this maiden be given to me."
"I shall grant you the boon you desire, even one that is exceedingly difficult to obtain.
Thus addressed by Nārada, Sañjaya was then filled with joy in his heart.
With palms joined in reverence and eyes wide with joy, he said this:
"Let a son be granted to me quickly—one who is an inexhaustible mine of gold."
Whatever urine, feces, or phlegm one casts upon the ground—
may all that indeed become stable gold.
"So be it," Tāḍakā replied to Nārada;
"O you of noble vows, I give to you a son who spits gold."
Having spoken thus, Nārada, with a joyful heart, then married Satī, the slender-waisted maiden who was adorned with ornaments.
Seeing that deed of his, Parvata was overcome with anger;
with eyes blazing and lips quivering from rage, he spoke to Nārada.
"Since you previously desired this woman who was to have been married by you,
therefore you shall never go to heaven along with me."
O Nārada, that son who was granted to him by you through the granting of a boon,
he too has been struck down by thieves and shall meet his death.
Thus addressed by Parvata, Nārada spoke with a troubled mind:
"You do not understand dharma at all; you are deluded, O evil-minded one!"
O observer of noble vows, a girl who is common to all men is considered the most abundant; those learned in the scriptures perceive no fault in accepting her as a bride in this world.
Because you did not serve the elders, you curse me in anger;
yet the completion of the marriage mantras occurs at the very first step.
Since you curse me, who am innocent, without understanding this,
therefore, alas, you too shall not go to heaven without me.
Even if Sañjaya’s son should meet his death through a curse, I shall nevertheless bring him back from the realm of Yama; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus cursed one another, those two divine sages,
having been honored by Sañjaya, O Lord, departed once more toward their own hermitages.
Then, in his seventh month, a son was born to that king;
his father gave him the name Svarṇaṣṭhīvī, which was truly appropriate to his nature.

Through the fruit of his auspicious vows, he became one who remembered his past lives, possessed a form like that of the god of love, was the cause of the origin of gold, and was a knower of the nature of all beings in this world.
There, whatever— phlegm, excrement, or anything else— one casts upon the ground,
it all becomes gold through the grace of Nārada.
Therefore, that king, highly honored, performs various sacrifices such as the Rājasūya according to the rules, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
He supported his dependents, nourished his kinsmen and guests,
and constructed temples, lakes, groves, and ponds;
and having conceived affection for him, he protected that son, who was surrounded by guards.
[387] There were heaps of gold from the son of the king;
then, some bandits, having heard of that mine of gold, [arrived].
Out of greed for wealth, those highly arrogant Southerners killed him;
when he was destroyed, that [power] born from the granting of the boon was lost.
The king's gold was lost, and another portion went to ruin elsewhere;
knowing his son had been slain by bandits, the king was deeply distressed.
With his mind agitated, he lamented and fell down in a swoon;
seeing him thus lamenting, Nārada spoke to him immediately.
"O King, do not despair; listen to this story of the Bharatas.
Having said this, he related the deeds of those of great splendor.
Having heard of the deeds of those high-souled lords of men— both of the kings who had perished and of the ascetics who were endowed with sacrificial fees— the king [reflected upon them].
His grief suddenly vanished and he returned to his natural state;
Nārada, for his part, [brought back] the king’s deceased son from the abode of Yama.
He quickly brought him back, exactly as he had been wounded;
and having seen and touched his son, he was filled with a heart full of joy.
Ashamed and amazed, he then spoke with palms joined in reverence:
"O Nārada, what wonder is this, that you have become so gracious toward me?"
The son given by you was killed by bandits in such a manner that,
for six months, he has now regained his entire life once more.
He remembered his former life, which was the cause of his recollection of past births;
this is the vow, the most excellent of vows—what else shall I tell you?
Likewise, O son of Pāṇḍu, at the beginning of the month of Bhādrapada, for three months,
that is declared to be Tripuṣkara, which bestows manifold branches of knowledge.
Likewise, O lord of men, for the three months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa,
that [place] is called Viṣṇupada, which bestows all dharmas.
O Bhārata, these auspicious duties have been thus declared by the sages;
they should indeed be performed by men and women with the approval of the Brāhmaṇas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, God of gods, tell me in detail,
O Madhusūdana, about the preeminent foundation of auspicious observances."
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen attentively, O King, to the supreme expansion of auspicious things;
I shall relate that which has never before been told by me to anyone.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, at the beginning, the first four lunar days of the bright fortnight are excellent:
the second, the third, the fourth, and likewise the fifth.
Having subdued his senses, he should eat only one meal on the first lunar day (pratipad),
and then, at dawn on the second day, having performed whatever duties are to be done.
When more than one watch of the day has passed, the wise man should perform his bath,
taking up earth and cow dung while reciting these mantras.
I shall declare to you the supreme rule regarding Brahmins;
I shall explain both those to whom this should not be given and those to whom it should be given.
The mantras should indeed be given to those Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who are wise and pure, but not to those whose conduct is mixed.
Even a woman who has been abandoned by her husband, provided she always remains steadfast in her own proper conduct,
may undertake the vow together with her husband, endowed as they are with virtuous character.
The fruit of bathing in rivers, ponds, tanks, wells, or at home is known to be tenfold; indeed, it is even greater when performed with mantras.
Having taken up the clay with the mantra, one should apply it to all the limbs:
"For you, O Clay, are honored by the gods; both the defiled and the pure have been made stainless by you."
"I too have saluted you with devotion; make me pure this very day.
Reciting thus, he should offer the clay from the tip of his own hand while accompanied by the mantra.
The knower of dharma, having smeared the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), should perform the immersion in water using white mustard seeds,
black sesame seeds, vacā, and all medicinal herbs, in that order.
You are the beginning of all the gods and of the worlds, O you who consist of the universe;
salutations to the Lord of pure beings and of the essences.
May the water born from the Ganges and the ocean, as well as that of the Puṣkara, Narmadā, and Yamunā rivers, be present here; may it remain close to me in this vicinity.
Having first touched his body with clay, cow dung,
and water, and having thus bathed and immersed himself, he should stand on the bank after sipping water (ācamana) three times.
Having put on two bright garments, pure and with a restrained mind,
he should, being well-composed, offer libations to the gods, the ancestors, and human beings.
Having thus undertaken the vow, he should go home with pure observances;
he should neither laugh nor converse until the appearance of the moon.
And having bathed, one should then [perform the rite] on the second day and so forth, up to the fourth day.

[390] One should worship the deity according to the vow on the four days beginning with the second, reciting respectively: "Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa," "Obeisance to Acyuta," "Obeisance to Ananta," and "Obeisance to Hṛṣīkeśa."
On the first day, worship of the feet of the Discus-bearer (Viṣṇu) is prescribed;
on the second day, worship of the navel should be performed by men according to the rules.
On the third day, one should place the worship of Puradvipa upon the chest;
on the fourth day, one should place the worship of Jagaddhātu upon the head.
One should offer flowers, ointments, incense, and water for honor (arghya), along with ornaments,
excellent and abundant food offerings, and gifts of lamps, out of devotion.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, according to the prescribed rite, the observer of the vow,
at the end of the day during the clear hour, [should proceed].
Pervaded by that same disposition, one should offer the *arghya* with devotion to Soma;
and such as it should be offered—with *ṛg*-verses, with earth, and likewise with other materials—so is that *arghya* worthy of being given.
I shall explain that to you correctly; listen to me, Yudhiṣṭhira.
[One should worship] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, and so forth.
With jewels born of the ocean and others such as diamonds, lapis lazuli, and pearls;
with flowers, fruits, waves, dates, and coconuts.
This rule is proclaimed for all those endowed with virtuous conduct who are provided with clothing, coverings, cattle, horses, land, and gold.
For the other [deity], according to one's capacity, with fruits, flowers,
unbroken grains, and water, along with salt, clarified butter, molasses, jars of oil and milk, and sesame seeds.
A person should offer the arghya, reciting the names of the Moon in sequence— Śaśin, Candra, Śaśāṅka, and Indu— beginning from the second lunar day.
Having performed worship during the night, one should increase the offerings in accordance with the waxing of the moon;
O best of kings, one should increase the arghya every day according to the waxing of the moon.
In this manner, the *arghya* should be offered; hear now the sequence of the mantra ritual:
"You are ever new, being born again and again at the end of every month."
O lamp of the courtyard of the sky, born from the churning of the ocean of milk, you indeed nourish the gods who are thrice united with Agni through the oblation.
O Rāmānuja, who illumines the expanse of the quarters, salutations be unto you!
Having offered the *arghya* to the King of the Twice-born (the Moon), one should present it to that Brahmin.
Having withdrawn the water for the guest-offering (arghya) in due order, he should then eat while maintaining silence,
using the earth as his vessel and resting upon lotus leaves.
Having smeared the goddess Dārā upon leaves of the *pālāśa* tree, or honey-leafed plants, or on a well-washed stone surface, the knower of mantras should do so with this mantra.
"O Goddess, source of all flavors, I desire to eat at your feet;
for my benefit, please prepare food that is delicious like nectar."
Having thus recited [the mantra] and eaten food excellent in its preparation of vegetables,
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), touch the cavities of the head, and, having remembered Soma, sleep upon the ground.
On the second day, one should eat with an abundance of cow's milk products;
on the fourth, O King, with ghee; and on the fifth, one should eat kṛśara (rice and pulse porridge) mixed with jaggery on the ground.
At all auspicious occasions, śyāmāka rice should always be eaten,
prepared with cow’s ghee and accompanied by fruits and vegetables.
Then, having performed the morning bath and offered libations to the ancestors and the deities,
one should devoutly feed the Brahmins, give gifts, and bid them farewell.
Afterwards, he should eat with his servants and kinsmen according to his desire;
thus, for all three months, he remains firm in his vows regarding all auspicious matters.
A man free from envy who performs this with devotion for one year—
his fortune and victory are assured, and Soma is ever pleased with him.
The maiden who performs this obtains a worthy husband;
she becomes fortunate, auspicious, virtuous, and forever not a widow.
"One who desires a kingdom obtains a kingdom; one who desires wealth shall obtain wealth;
and one who desires sons shall obtain sons—thus spoke the Blessed Sun."
Having obtained auspicious wealth, sons, wives, and kin, as well as delightful marriages between noble families and the splendors of beds, food, drink, couches, and meals;
He becomes one who remembers his past births, O Bhārata, and a doer of auspicious deeds.
Thus ends the Bhadracatuṣṭaya-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. Sumantu said:
Listen, O Kaurava, to the rites based upon the secrets of the lunar days (tithis).
Merely by hearing it, there shall be the destruction of sins; by performing it, one obtains infinite fruit.

On the first lunar day, one should subsist on milk; on the second, one should eat flowers; on the third, food excluding salt; on the fourth, one should eat sesame-based food; on the fifth, one should subsist on milk; on the sixth, one should eat fruits; on the seventh, one should eat vegetables; on the eighth, one should eat *bilva* fruit; on the ninth, one should eat flour; on the tenth, one should eat food not cooked over fire; on the eleventh, there is a fast; on the twelfth, one should eat clarified butter; on the thirteenth, one should eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*); on the fourteenth, one should eat barley-based food; and on the full moon day, one should consume cow-urine and water boiled with *kuśa* grass. Such is the rule for the consumption of food.
Thus the various consumptions have been described; first, the *didhipu* was mentioned, but that [consumption] is prescribed for all [days] beginning with the day of *kṣīrapratipad*.

The procedure specifically prescribed for the milk-vow (*kṣīrapratipad*) is now described. On the day preceding the day of the vow, one should perform ablutions at the three periods of the day, observe a fast, recite the *pavitra* hymns, and chant the *gāyatrī* together with the *śiras*. On the day prior to that, having taken a single meal, one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) for the fast. On the day of the vow, one should give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the twice-born. This is the preliminary procedure for the dates (*tithis*). He who observes this rule for one fortnight obtains ten times the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and dwells in heaven for the duration of a Manu-period (*manvantara*), living together with Apsarases and Gandharvas who sing his praises. For four months, however, he obtains a hundredfold the fruit of both the horse-sacrifice and the royal consecration (*rājasūya*). He dwells in heaven for seventy cycles of the four ages (*caturyuga*), being praised by Apsarases and Gandharvas. This constitutes one full year, O King, for him who, according to this discipline, undertakes these lunar-day vows (*tithivratas*) on the ninth day of Āśvayuja, the third day of Vaiśākha, or the full moon of Kārttika.
Whether a celibate student, a householder, a woman, or a man, one who is pure and of disciplined mind goes to the realm of the Lord Puṣpadanta.
The Sun is the lord Puṣpadanti.
Thus is the Mahāphala-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
one who performs the five-fire penance in the month of Jyeṣṭha and gifts a golden cow at sunset goes to heaven.
It occurs on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days; this is known as the Rudra-vrata.

And as for the eighth and fourteenth days: one should perform the *pañcāgni-sādhana* (the practice of the five fires) during these four days, and on the evening of the fourth day, one should give a golden cow.
This is the Rudra-vrata as declared in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
A man [should observe it] on the two fifth days and the two first days of the month.
Having fasted and being richly perfumed, he should lie down with his beloved.
But he whose mind is as steady as a bird, free from passion and attachment,
whose mind is steady like a bird, intent on meditation upon the Sun, equanimous,
and possessed of mindfulness and virtue— listen to the fruit of his merit.
For a thousand divine years, and likewise for a hundred divine years.

"Then he meditates upon this Mahādeva; of this there is no doubt. Thus is described the Sambhoga-vrata as stated in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa. On the full moon day, the new moon day, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, [one should observe this vow].
She should remain celibate for a year, eating sacrificial food only at night.
Having fashioned a very beautiful image of Umā and Maheśa out of gold, or even one made of silver weighing half a karṣa, he should bathe it with ghee and other substances.
Having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, with pairs of beautiful garments,
with all kinds of foods to be chewed and eaten, and with canopies, banners, and chowries;
One should feed the devotees of Śiva and satisfy the poor and the helpless;
one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and ask for forgiveness with the mantras of Śiva.
Having prepared a vessel made of copper, bell-metal, or similar material, and having covered it with a white cloth,
one should fashion an image within a sanctuary in the center.
One should prepare and place a vessel as a sacred seat;
having placed that vessel upon one's head, it should be adorned with a garland of flowers.
One should lead [the image] to the temple of Śiva with the splendor of banners, conchs, and other regalia;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should present it to the Liṅga-form of Maheśvara.
One should place that vessel, adorned with ornaments, in two parts;
having circumambulated Śiva and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness.
Having completed this meritorious vow, hear now what fruit one shall obtain:
by means of magnificent, mind-captivating great vehicles that resemble twelve suns in brilliance.
He rejoices at will with the Rudras in the world of Īśvara for thousands of millions of kalpas and even beyond that many millions of kalpas.
At the conclusion of that, that highly fortunate one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Umāmaheśvara vow as declared in the Śivadharmottara.
On the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, she should remain strictly observant of celibacy.
For one year he should not eat out of a desire to conquer the enjoyment of the earth;
at the end of the year, having fashioned an image, he should perform the ritual procedure as previously described.
Having undertaken that vow with ritual baths and water offerings (*arghya*), one shall obtain the aforementioned qualities.
Here too, an image of Umāmaheśvara must be fashioned. "As before" means as described in the previous vow.
[One shall attain] celestial vehicles made of Jāmbūnada gold, adorned and possessing four gates.
Having gone to the divine city of Śiva, one shall obtain every enjoyment;
this is the vow named Umāmaheśvara, spoken by the Lord.
Out of compassion for all women and especially for men,
one should therefore perform the Umāmaheśvara vow with every possible effort.
It should be performed by men and women so that they may attain imperishable happiness;
indeed, it is for the sake of pleasing Goddess Umā, even though [the world] has perished from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Thus is described another Umāmaheśvara vow as stated in the Śivadharmottara:
"O Nārada, he who takes refuge at a bilva tree and observes a fast for twelve days becomes liberated from the sin of killing an embryo."
"Śiva is the deity here.
Thus is described the Pāpamocana-vrata as stated in the Saura Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
O best of the twice-born, whether it be a woman or a man, one who is untiringly devoted to fasting on the full moon and the new moon for one year [attains the fruit].
At the end of the year, she who observes excellent vows should present an image enriched with all kinds of perfumes; that woman shall attain union with Bhavānī, or else her own form.

"One obtains [the fruit] here; there is no doubt, this is the truth, the truth, O lords of sages. Thus ends the Bhavānī-vrata as declared in the Liṅga Purāṇa. Furthermore, there are two eighth days (Aṣṭamīs) and likewise two fourteenth days (Caturdaśīs) of the month.
The new moon day, the full moon day, and both the seventh and twelfth lunar days.
For one year, constantly abstaining from food and with senses fully subdued,
he obtains both the fruit of celibacy and the fruit of one who performs a long sacrificial session (sattra).
By abstaining from food, one obtains the fruit that comes from approaching one's wife during her season;
these are the presiding deities for the lunar days (tithis).
Thus ends the pentad of vows for pairs of lunar days as stated in the *Yama-smṛti*.
On the fourteenth and eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights,
he who, being pure and devoted to the worship of Śiva, does not eat for one year;
Whatever inexhaustible merit is proclaimed for those who constantly perform sacrificial sessions,
all that merit goes to him [who dies] in her, and he proceeds to the world of Śiva.
Thus ends the Śaiva fast-vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
By performing the night-meal (nakta) on the eighth day of the dark fortnight and continuing until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one attains enjoyments in this world and reaches Śiva in the hereafter.
Thus ends the Śiva-nakta-vrata as declared in the glorious Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
On the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights, [one should observe this vow].
Then, having eaten only at night for one year, he who worships Śiva;

"Having obtained the fruit of all sacrifices, he goes to the supreme goal. Thus is described the Mahāvrata as stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa. When the month of Pauṣa has arrived, O son, during both fortnights...
On the fourteenth day, or on the eighth, or even on the full moon day.
Having performed the daily rites according to the rules, one should then perform the optional rites;
therein, worship with special offerings should be performed by one of pure mind.
One should offer as a food offering (naivedya) one prastha of barley-gruel (yāvaka), prepared with sugar, milk, and clarified butter;
furthermore, one should feed and honor Brahmins numbering eleven (the number of Rudras).
One should have a figure made of flour paste, one span in height,
adorned with horns, a manger, and a tail.
Then a tawny cow, together with her own vehicle, should be given to the preceptor for the sake of Śiva; now hear the merit of this vow.
[399] With celestial chariots resembling ten million suns, fulfilling all desires,
crowded with hosts of Rudras, and surrounded by Rudra-maidens;
Yoked to chariots drawn by bulls and accompanied by the sounds of various songs, he—
along with twenty-one generations of his kin— goes to where Śaṅkara dwells;
and for as many births as there are hairs on those bulls, he is born among those families.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are, he is glorified in the world of Rudra;
having attained proximity, he thereafter attains union (sāyojya).
O Śivā, by this ritual method, having offered a sword made of flour according to the prescribed injunctions, one shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
Likewise, by offering a discus in the month of Phālguna, one shall attain that state;
and by offering an image of Śiva made of flour before Śiva in the month of Caitra.
He is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin and shall attain the world of Śiva;
in the month of Vaiśākha, he should offer the tip of a staff before Śiva.
One should prepare an offering made of flour measuring half a cubit and present it at the conclusion of the worship;
one is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should offer a sword made of flour to Śiva;
one is thereby liberated from ingratitude and goes to the world of Rudra.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should offer a vessel made of flour to Śiva;
one is liberated from all misdeeds accumulated in this very birth.
He who offers a banner made of flour before Śiva according to the prescribed rite in the month of Śrāvaṇa shall attain imperishable liberation.
He who offers a mace made of flour in the month of Bhādrapada attains the status of a lord of treasures and is glorified in the world of Śiva.
And in the month of Āśvayuja, having applied a colic-inducing paste made from half-ground flour;
It should be offered before Śiva; it removes the sin of foeticide.
In the month of Kārttika, one should offer a mace and a discus before Śiva.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a lotus made of flour burns away the sins committed over seven lifetimes, just as fire consumes fuel.
One should offer it to Śiva according to the prescribed rite and shall attain all sovereignty;
thus have I proclaimed all the night-vows (nakta-vratas).
Having performed the daily worship, one should perform the optional worship;
every month, worship of the Guru must be performed, as well as the offering of the vow.
At the end of the year, a great worship (mahāpūjā) must be performed according to the prescribed rules;
the preceptors should be honored with gold, garments, food, and vehicles.
Then one shall quickly attain the fruit as described for the Kṛttikās;
however, O Mahāsena, through stinginess regarding wealth, one is deprived of the merits of sacrifices and charitable works.
Thus ends the Śivavrata as taught in the Kālottara.
[401] Now follows the procedure for the raising of Indra’s Banner (śakradhvajocchāyavidhi).
In the Devīpurāṇa,
Śakra said:
"By what ritual was she obtained by those descended through the lineage of my family?"
O Lord, please explain specifically the ritual procedure for the banner-pole.
Brahmā said: O best of gods, O king of the gods, the number of grains of sand in the Gaṅgā might be determined,
but it could not be for the lineage of the Daityas who desire victory.
Some were slain by Viṣṇu, some by the god Śambhu;
some were struck down by Guha, and some were sought to be killed by me.
Many others as well were accompanied by goddesses, yet they did not meet their destruction;
such was the lord of Daityas named Suvala, who possessed the emblem of a swan and was endowed with great strength.
O Vāsava, Daṇḍaghāta was born in my lineage;
by him, O Lord, the gods were formerly conquered during the Manvantara of Bhānu.
O Vāsava, all of us together with Śakra have assembled,
yet we are not able to fight the Daityas in battle, O Grandfather.
"Overcome by our enemy, we have come to you for refuge;
therefore, I am reflecting on how Viṣṇu might provide protection for the inhabitants of heaven."
[402] By means of the banner bestowed by Śambhu, which has been raised aloft, there is no doubt;
thus have I spoken to the gods, including Indra: "Let the Lord Viṣṇu be propitiated."
He will give the Great Banner (Mahāketu), which deludes all the Daityas;
they have gone at my command to the Ocean of Milk where Keśava resides.
Abiding in the nature of both the supreme and the non-supreme, unborn, immutable, and eternal;
marked with the Śrīvatsa, long-armed, and adorned with the Kaustubha jewel upon his chest.
Then these gods, including Indra, being tormented by the fear of their enemy, offered praise; Keśava was pleased with them and said, "Choose a boon, O Purandara."
Then, being entreated by them, the God said, "Give me a banner that slays the enemies of the gods.
Having adorned it accordingly, He gave him that which dispels the fear of the gods.
The white parasol, of great splendor, adorned with beautiful garlands and bracelets,
possessed a radiance equal to ten thousand suns and was accompanied by the tinkling sound of small bells.
