Seeing that army equipped with yak-tail fans and marked by the signs of enemies, it was broken, and he too was struck down.
From that time forward, O Śakra, this banner has belonged to your lineage;
for other kings as well, its hoisting brings victory.
"Whoever shall take refuge in this king— whether it be I, or Lord Hara, or Viṣṇu, or Vāsava— will find him supported by us."
He shall become the subduer of all enemies and invincible upon the earth;
thus was the cause of Śakra’s banner explained by Brahmā.
"O Lord of Vidyās, I too have revealed all of that to you.
Nṛpavāhana said:
"Blessed One, I wish to hear how his elevation came about."
Now that the day and the lunar mansion have been established, tell me the ritual procedure for the substances.
Agastya said:
O Śakra, I shall explain the ritual for the elevation of Ketu exactly as it was told by Brahmā in the presence of Bṛhaspati.
On an auspicious day, under a favorable constellation and *karana*, at a propitious and auspicious moment,
the astrologer, accompanied by assistants, should go to the forest together with the master builder.

Having performed the installation of the Goddess according to the prescribed rite, and having undertaken the journey as enjoined by the rules for such a journey, he should proceed to the forest. Having gone there, he should observe an auspicious tree— such as a Dhava, Arjuna, or Priyaṅgu.
The Udumbara and Aśvakarṇa—these five, O King, are auspicious.

O child, for the purpose of the banner, one should avoid trees grown in divine groves, such as the *priyaṅgu*, *bījaka*, *aśvakarṇa*, and *sarja*. One should fashion the flagstaffs according to the cubit-measure (*karamāna*) in three sizes: small, medium, and great.
O child, one [lute] has eleven strings, while another has nine or five;
it is covered with leather, filled with insects, and resembles the nest of a bird.
One born from an anthill, a cremation ground, or a hollow tree;
likewise one who is humpbacked, blind, or barren, or one who has been sprinkled [with water]; and likewise, a woman whose name is not censurable.
One should avoid wood struck by lightning or burnt;
in its absence, one may use sandalwood, mango, sal, or even that made of śāka.

For the sake of the insignia of Śakra, it must be made; never should it be produced from any other tree. One should take that which grows in auspicious soil, with auspicious water, and which brings about prosperity.
Then one should worship the tree, facing either the east or the north.
Homage to you, Lord of Trees! O Tree, this king approaches you for the purpose of a banner; it is according to the truth, O Protector, and not otherwise—please grant him your consent.
This is the mantra for worship:
"O great tree, a bali offering should be given there at night, likewise upon a twin-tree; having made this for the sake of Vāsava, you may go elsewhere."
There is no fatigue for you there, even for the sake of the banner of the King of Gods. These are the *balimantras*;
and here also are the mantras mentioned in the *Varāhasaṃhitā*.
To those beings who dwell here in this tree, may there be well-being; let there be homage to you! Having accepted this offering, please depart and grant us a dwelling place.
"O best of mountains, tomorrow a king chooses you for the sake of Indra’s banner;
please accept this honor."
Having worshipped the tree, one should then cause an offering to be given to the spirits;
at dawn, one should cut down the tree provided that auspicious dreams and other such signs have been seen.
One should see a man in white garments, cross the ocean or a river,
climb trees, enter auspicious villages, see parrots, or ascend a temple.
Likewise, an image of a deity, a twice-born, a virtuous person, a symbol of Brahman, or even Hari,
when worshipped in a dream, swiftly bestows spiritual perfection.
Eating fish and meat, obtaining curd, [drinking] blood, weeping for the dead, and engaging in forbidden sexual intercourse— these grant the fruit of swift accomplishment.

Having seen in a dream the leaping over trees and mountains, the destruction of enemies, as well as inauspicious things, or having obtained fruit, flowers, white objects, and dūrvā grass, one shall conquer the earth.
A conch shell, cows, and likewise the acquisition of ivory bestow a kingdom;
seeing a cow with her calf that has recently calved grants the fruit of sons.
Having seen such auspicious dreams as crossing a mudbank, being released from illness after a long time in a well, or cutting down a tree, one should then proceed.
Facing north or east, one should first offer the animal like honey;
falling toward the northeast is auspicious, provided it makes no sound and is without wounds—such an animal is favorable.
One should not discard those that do not have fire at their base; otherwise, one should abandon them.
One should discard eight finger-breadths from the root and cast half of the tip into the water.
One should cast half of the remaining tree, measuring four finger-breadths, into the water;
likewise, O child, one should bring it back by means of a cart or even with oxen.

One should lead that tree, which has been cast into the water, before the city by means of ropes provided with a hundred thousand [loops]. When the pole being led is level or square, [it is auspicious].
A square [diagram] causes the ruin of the king’s sons and domestic priests;
when the commencement is broken, one should destroy the sacrificial offering, and likewise, upon the destruction of the path, there is loss.

One should break or destroy the wooden rim belonging to the wheel of the king or others. However, in that case, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) due to the breaking of the chariot's axle,
using either the mantra "indrakṣatre" or the "jātavedasa" mantra.
Having led him thus at an auspicious moment, one should have him seated in front;
O Lord, one should cause the beautification of the gateway, the road, the carriage-way, and the house to be performed.
Prostitutes with the sound of small drums, conchs, and twice-born brahmins,
accompanied by auspicious rites and the chanting of the Vedas, should lead [the bride] to where the ceremonial canopy is raised.
With auspicious, smooth garments made from the feathers and wool of birds, in due order,
the maidens named Nanda and Upananda are the first portions.
The goddesses named Jaya and Vijayā are established in sixteen parts;
when there is an excess, the mother of Śakra and Jayanta are the presiding deities.

When there are more than sixteen [parts], this is the meaning: "Then, those exceeding sixteen" refers to the flagstaff (*dhvajastambha*) from the section of the banner. In that regard, on the first and second sections, two maidens (*kumāryau*) should be made in each direction, but only one on the third. Their length and width are these two parts; among them, the maidens situated in the first portion are, in each pair, Nanda and Upananda; those in the second portion are Jaya and Vijayā; and those in the third portion should be known as the goddesses who are the mothers of Śakra. On the top of the banner are the deities Datta, Upadatta, and Ātreya. The circumference of the first [ornament] is one-third of the measure of the banner; the wise man should make the remaining ones with circumferences diminished by sixteen parts [each]. This is the measurement for the ornaments to be described hereafter. Having divided the banner into three parts, having determined the circumference of the first ornament by the length of one part, he should make the remaining ones with circumferences successively diminished by sixteen parts. Thus, it is implied that the thickness of the banner must be made suitable for the insertion of the ornaments. One should place the ornaments of variegated colors upon the first [section] for the sake of the Self-born One (*Svayaṃbhū*).
On the eighth day, Śakra himself should cause a second one to be presented— square, deep red, and blue-red in color— crafted by Viśvakarman.
The [discs] of Yama are black, those of Varuṇa are hexagonal, and the god Vāyu has a peacock as his vehicle;
they are the color of madder and clouds.
One should give that blue-colored [image], highly variegated, to Skanda;
one should give a circular, gold-hued [image] to Agni on the eighth lunar day;
and one should personally cause a necklace resembling lapis lazuli to be given to Indra.
The sun is in the shape of a half-moon, while the Viśvedevas are like lotuses;
the Ṛṣis, dwelling there, should give [offerings] resembling dark blue sapphire.
Then, by the Guru, by Śukra, and by the constellations from all sides,
as well as by the many Mothers, a variegated [offering] was placed within the house.
Whatever is given by whomsoever, whatever banner is his ornament,
and whichever deity he raises on the day [of the rite], one should know that to be his deity.
The meaning is that one should worship each respective deity on the day of its erection.

First, the staff enters the ground; I, the kingdom, and the person [of the king] enter first. Merely by being raised, it is prior to all exertion. Through the sounds of clapping hands (*tāla*) made by children, it announces the destruction of the region. If broken, it causes the imprisonment of the king; however, if it is completely intact, it brings auspiciousness and universal peace. To Śambhu, Sūrya, Yama, Śakra, Soma, Dhanada, Varuṇa, Vahni, Īśa, and the sages, oblations of curd, honey, and unbroken rice (*akṣata*) should be offered with mantras.
Śambhu, Brahmā, and Īśvara should be offered oblations mixed with curd and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). One should worship Śukra, Skanda, Guru, Rudra, the Apsarases, and the others.
Having performed the fire sacrifice according to the rule, the wise man should observe the flame of the fire.
Possessing great splendor, a beautiful radiance, blazing, compact, and shining with the luster of the sun;
having the appearance of red garments, he was auspicious with the sound of chariots and kettledrums.
The sounds of conchs, drums, and clouds are auspicious when the fire is kindled;
thereafter, one should raise plantain trees, sugarcane stalks, and banners.
And various other beauties were displayed upon the raising of Śakra’s banner on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, under an auspicious constellation.
One should uproot [the tree] during the bright fortnight of Āśvina or Śrāvaṇa,
accompanied by groups of citizens and woodsmen, while the sound of sharp-sounding drums provides entertainment.
Abundantly adorned with the splendor of canopies and banners, and brilliantly illuminated by flags,
it was consecrated with the mantras of Viṣṇu, Īśa, and Śakra, as well as those for the accomplishment of perfected protection.
The protection, having produced an extraordinary efficacy when employed for its purpose, is firmly established;
it is an auspicious gateway-arch (*toraṇa*) of the Mother’s staff (*mātṛkadaṇḍa*).
The two pillars of the gateway-arch are the two staves of the Mothers.
O Lord, having raised the banner and the dwelling (Vāsava) neither slowly nor too hastily, but with an even and unbroken seat—
the seat being an ornament—
[one should proceed].
In the *Varāhasaṃhitā*: "With an umbrella, a banner, a mirror, a plow, a half-moon, a variegated garland, plantain trees, and stalks of sugarcane..."
It was adorned with windows featuring lions and elephants, and the guardians of the quarters were stationed in all directions.

One should raise up the banner of the One whose eyes are the thousands of marks, [the banner] which has its ropes uncut, its wooden frame firm, and its top-pole and arch firmly joined by well-fastened mechanisms.
"Like young girls submerged in a tree of heartwood."
A wise man should recognize a site as ruined if it is frequented by crows, owls, and pigeons;
nor should he provide a place for sitting for other birds either.
Then one should perform the formal assignment of the path (pathoddeśa) with unbroken [mantras] according to the rule.
"Assignment" (uddeśa) refers to the portion of ground.
Having worshipped it as it is situated, one should [place the disciple] well-restrained by a comfortable mechanical device.
One should keep a vigil at night by reciting the mantras of Indra;
the domestic priest, always knowledgeable in astrology and ever devoted to auspicious rites of pacification, [should do so].
By the falling of a mechanical device, one should kill the king; by the death of a buffalo, the queens;
by a boil, the crown prince; and by a canopy, the minister.
In the kingdom, by the falling of a gateway, there shall be a loss of food;
when a festival for the banner is being performed,
one should predict the king’s wrath from the falling of the Indra-pole (the staff).
There is danger from swarms of insects, locusts, and thieves.
When it is established in harmony, there is peace for both the king and the city;
as long as it remains elevated, the citizens are always joyful.
The daughters of Brahmins who are devoted to the sacrifice of the banner should eat;
they should eat and [he] should feed them.
A banner that is struck down or torn remains for as long as eight days.
One should perform the same kind of worship at the time of striking, falling, or raising [the image] as was performed for its installation.

If one causes such a banner to be made, he who does so goes to the king along with his kingdom, even if it falls at night while performing auspicious rites and remains unpecked by crows, pigeons, and other such birds.
Whether in a village, a city, or a market town, if the citizens act in this manner,
one should again raise a banner at the gate of the city or town that touches a bull, a lion, or a bird.
This [mantra] is equal [in power], the destroyer of defects, and the supreme bestower of victory.
Thus, in former times, Hari obtained the banner from the bull-vehicled Lord;
likewise, Brahmā, the Brahmin, attained Indra by means of this very same [mantra].
He was given by him to Soma; thereafter he came to Dakṣa.
From that time until today, kings continue to celebrate his festival.
Thus, the king who causes such a victory-bringing banner to be made shall have the earth, together with its forests and islands, come under his control.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Puṣkara said:
"In the eastern direction from Śibi, on a portion of ground that is thus auspicious and radiant..."
One should construct an auspicious palace for Indra on ground that slopes toward the northeast.
With bright garments and likewise with beds of various colors,
he then carefully established the site of Śakra’s banner in the center.
One should depict Maghavan on the cloth; on its right side, one should likewise depict the goddess Śacī on the left side of the cloth.
In the bright fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, beginning from the first day of the lunar cycle,
the worship of those two [deities] must be performed constantly by the lords of the earth.
Then, according to the ritual for entering the forest, the king should have the Indra-pole brought by means of an ox-cart,
or else he should have it brought by men.
Of *arjuna*, *ajakarṇa*, *priyaka*, and *vacā*; *priyaka* is the same as *vījaka*.
Likewise of *suradāruka* and of *udumbara*.
Or else, O Rāma, [use] sandalwood or lotus in case of an emergency.
In the absence of any other trees, one who knows the Dharma should make a staff of bamboo, bound with gold, and he should cause it to be properly entered [into the ritual].
O destroyer of enemies, O best of the twice-born, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Prauṣṭhapada, the sacrificial pole of Śakra is to be known as being of a specific measure.
Reduced by four finger-breadths, including the tip, it becomes a giver of happiness;
likewise, having cut it at the base with eight [finger-breadths], one should cast it into water.
Having raised the city out of the water, one should cause it to enter [the city] properly;
having raised the city out of the water, together with its garlands of banners and flags.
One should have the royal road sprinkled with water and likewise decorated with young trees;
it should be crowded with actors and dancers, and likewise honored by the deities.
O Rāma, the king, whose home had been honored and whose speech likewise revered,
was followed by the citizens, well-dressed and carrying fruits in their hands.
On the eighth day, one should cause that staff to be brought in amidst the sound of musical instruments;
thereafter, one should have it placed upon a mechanical device between the two cloths.
On that very day, O knower of dharma, one should have it placed there covered with cloth;
first covered [with earth], one should then have it completely covered with beautiful cloths.
One should continue to worship her while she remains in the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī). On the eleventh day (ekādaśī), the king, having observed a fast,
should keep a vigil (prajāgara) together with his ministers and his family priest for the duration of a year.
The night-keeping vigil should be performed by the people of the city;
in various places, the illustrious ones should provide swings as well as honey.
A *preṅkhā* is a swing; *madhu* is wine. On the twelfth day, having bathed his head and being purified, the king, the lord of men, should then worship Śakra at night with dance and song.
With a concentrated mind, one should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*) for the banner of Śakra with the mantra.
However, since the *Devīpurāṇa* states that the concluding rite takes place on the eighth day, there is an option between these two dates.
One should construct four well-secured pillars for its pavilion.
O highly fortunate one, one should worship him with perfumes, garlands, and an abundance of food.
One should constantly perform worship of the two cloths and worship of the staff,
with various kinds of offerings as well as the honoring of Brahmins.
He should constantly offer oblations with Vaiṣṇava mantras and puronuvākyas;
he should also perpetually worship Śakra with song and dance.
On the twelfth day, O knower of dharma, the king should honor the Brahmins with stores of wealth,
especially the astrologer and the domestic priest.
[413] At both the rising and the entry, the king, who knew the proper time, honored Śakra with the mantra that is about to be recited by his domestic priest.
The king, being self-restrained, should perform worship for four days;
when the fifth day arrives, he should dismiss the banner of Śakra.
Having worshipped them, O illustrious one, with an army and cavalry, and having led the triad by means of lordly elephants, one should then cause them to flow away into the river.
The triad consists of two cloths and a banner;
there, a musical performance is proclaimed with the great sound of instrumental music.
There, the people of the city and the countryside should enjoy themselves in the water,
and likewise, a great festival should be celebrated by those situated on the riverbanks.
Having performed this ritual, O Rāma, the king attained great prosperity for his people and vehicles,
as well as the destruction of the host of his enemies.
He received a great gift from the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods.
If the top of Indra’s banner should break, or if Indra’s banner should fall,
or if the staff of Śakra should be eaten [by animals], the death of the king is certain;
the same should be understood in the case of the breaking of the mechanism, as well as in the case of the severing of the ropes.
Likewise, O twice-born one, when the *mātṛkā* is broken, there is fear of an enemy army;
for the *mātṛkā* constitutes the arches and pillars [of the city].
Indeed, divine, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents will always occur there.
For them, because of their intense fear, this result is extremely terrible.
And likewise, O twice-born one, when carnivorous beasts take refuge upon Indra’s staff,
either the king dies there or the entire country perishes.
O best of the twice-born, whatever damage occurs to the construction of Indra’s banner should be understood as a source of suffering for the city-dwellers resulting from some other destruction.
This expiation is prescribed for any one of these occasions, except when it is caused by the Indra-banner; in that case,
one should perform the Indra-sacrifice again in the golden Nandaka forest.
Having given the kingdom to his preceptor, he should release those in bondage;
and having worshipped for seven days, he should bestow banners upon the twice-born.
Peace for the sake of the Brahmins should be performed daily;
and cows, accompanied by gold, garments, and silver, should be given to the most eminent of the twice-born.
When this is done, evil comes to peace,
and likewise there shall be prosperity for the lord of men.
Śrī Rāma said: O best among all upholders of dharma, I wish to hear those mantras for the elevation of Śakra which a king, while fasting, should recite.
Puṣkara said:
Listen properly to these mantras that destroy all sins,
which a king, being self-restrained, should recite when the raising of Indra’s banner has arrived.
O conqueror of enemies, subduer of Paraśu, destroyer of Vṛtra’s slaying;
O God of gods, O highly fortunate one, for you have attained the state of being the most abundant.
You are the Lord and indeed eternal, devoted to the welfare of all beings;
you possess infinite splendor, are free from passion, and increase glory and victory.
O Lord worshipped by the gods, arise always with self-restraint;
you are Brahmā, the self-existent, the Blessed One, the grandfather of all the worlds.
Rudra, the bearer of the Pināka bow, proud and accompanied by the Śatarudriya, is the leader and performer of the sacrifice; likewise is Viṣṇu of the wide stride.
The mighty sun constantly increases that splendor;
O Lord of Gods, uphold your splendor; be victorious, O Śakra, bestower of good rain!
The glorious Viṣṇu, wielder of the mace, bearer of the conch, discus, sword, and Śārṅga bow, bestows his splendor upon you today; be victorious, O Śakra of great strength!
The god without beginning or end, the eternal body of Brahmā,
possessing the brilliance of fire, O mighty-armed one, is Rudra himself, the son of Pārvatī.
Kārttikeya, wielder of the spear, six-faced, and bearer of the mace— may he,
the most excellent giver of boons, increase your splendor, O Lord.
Skanda, the commander of the divine army, honored by the foremost of the gods;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, and likewise the two Aśvins;
Bhārgava and Aṅgiras, as well as the Viśvedevas and the hosts of Maruts.
The three world-protectors, as well as the moon, the sun, wind, and fire;
the gods, the sages, and the yakṣas, gandharvas, and rākṣasas.
The oceans, the mountains, the rivers, and all living beings;
as well as splendor, attainment, truth, Lakṣmī, Śrī, and fame itself.
May your splendor prevail; be victorious, O Śakra, Lord of Śacī!
May victory and constant auspiciousness be yours here.
Be gracious; through the worship of kings and brahmins in every way, by your favor may the earth always be rich with crops.
May there be auspiciousness, free from obstacles; may the sages be thoroughly pacified.
Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods; homage to you, O slayer of Bala!
Homage to Vighna! Homage be to you, O thousand-eyed Lord of Śacī;
you alone are the supreme refuge for all the worlds.
You alone are the supreme vital breath of this entire world, O Lord;
for you are the joyful Sovereign, the infinite Purandara.
You alone are the cloud, you are the wind, you are the fire, the lightning, and the sun;
here, through dense cognition, you are Meghabāhu, once again the cloud.
You are the supreme and terrible splendor; you are the thundering cloud;
you alone are the creator of the worlds and their unvanquished destroyer.
You are the light of all the worlds; you are the sun, the source of radiance.
You are the wondrous great element; you are the king, the supreme among gods.
You are Viṣṇu, you are the thousand-eyed one, you are the god, you are the supreme refuge;
you alone, O God, are the nectar of immortality, you are liberation, most highly honored.

You are the moment (muhūrta), you are the entire duration, and you are indeed the man (nara) who is the instant (kṣaṇa); you are the semen (śukra), the non-abundant, as well as the digits (kalā), the measures of time (kāṣṭhā), and the minute divisions (trūṭi).
You are the year, the seasons, the months, the nights, and the days; you are the moments, the best of mountains, the earth,
and likewise the sun and the sky free from darkness.
The great ocean, containing timi and miṅgila fish, possessed of waves, and crowded with many mines of gems;
O you of great renown, you are always to be honored here by the great seers of joyful mind and noble soul;
praised by them, you drink the soma at the sacrifice.
And even the oblations consecrated with the cry of "vaṣaṭ" lead to prosperity.
You are constantly worshipped here by the Brahmins for the sake of fruitful results,
and you are praised with incomparable power in the meanings of the Vedas;
the foremost of the twice-born are devoted to sacrificing to you through the Vedas.
They apply themselves to the Vedāṅgas through all the Vedas.
The destroyer of sacrifice, the protector of the world,
the slayer of Vṛtra, the killer of Namuci,
and the Great-Souled One who always dwells within Kṛṣṇa.
He who discriminates between truth and falsehood in the world.
To that vigorous one, the embryo of the Asuras,
who approaches Vaiśvānara as his vehicle— to him, the lord of the thirty gods, be constant homage.
To the lord of the three worlds, to Purandara.
Unborn, immutable, eternal, and of single form, Viṣṇu is the Boar, the Ancient Puruṣa;
you are the sacrifice, the consumer of all, and the fire Kṛśānu.
Indra, the thousand-headed, whose weapon is the thunderbolt.

May the poet, the seven-tongued one, the protector Indra, Savitṛ, Indra, the Lord of Gods, the Moon, Śaṅkara, the enemy of Śaṅkha, the slayer of Vṛtra, and he of the excellent army— may our heroes be superior. May the protector Indra, the soul who is the cause of the senses, and Hiraṇyagarbha, the primary source of the world, [protect us].
I perpetually bow down to Lokeśvara, the most excellent of gods, the most preeminent, who is eternal bliss.
Thus, through the praises of that great-souled lord of the gods, the best of deities, he who was well-restrained obtained the desires that were pleasing to his mind.
And he returns from the heavenly worlds through various bodily transformations.
In the *Varāhasaṃhitā*: "Whether at the completion, the raising, the entry, the bathing, or the offering of garlands, [one should perform] the rite of dismissal."
The king, having observed a fast, should recite these auspicious mantras of the banner of Indra (Puruhūta).
The completion [of the rite] consists of the hoisting of the banner, for which there is a specific mantra:
"With Hara, Arka, Vaivasvata, Śakra, Soma,
Dhaneśa, Vaiśvānara, and Pāra, [I offer] with the Ṛg-verses."
[419] He was honored by hosts of great ṛṣis together with the gods and apsarases,
and by Śukra, Aṅgiras, Skanda, and the hosts of Maruts—
just as Arjuna is worshipped by those whose sole form is their hands.
And he was adorned with magnificent ornaments.
"Likewise here, O Lord, take these auspicious ornaments with a joyful mind.
Thus ends the procedure for raising the banner of Śakra.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other vow, the Pañcamūrti-vrata.
The year is remembered as Vahni, and likewise the Arkaparivatsara.
Likewise, Prajāpati is declared to be preceded by *iṣṭāpūrta* and *soma*,
and the God of gods, Maheśvara, is likewise said to be preceded by *ut*.
The arrangement of their mandalas is prescribed exactly as before.
"As before" means that the mandala arrangements should be made with blue, white, red, white, yellow, and black [powders].
As before, worship should be performed; likewise, the fire sacrifice (homa) and the ritual procedure should be carried out.
With sesame seeds, rice, barley, ghee, and white mustard seeds.
With the mantras of the chariot and the names of its talliṅgas,
one should likewise remain eating only at night for five days in succession, as previously described.
Beginning from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra,
one should perform this vow in due order during the year known as Saṃvatsara.
O Yādava, at the conclusion of the worship, five gold pieces should be given;
O Yādava, it should be given to one who knows the four Vedas according to the specific Vedic recension (śākhā).
One should offer each one as the fifth; thus shall one become a knower of time.
Moving through the air at will, one attains whatever world one desires.
O knower of dharma, one who is honored by gods and asuras through this vow,
upon attaining human birth, becomes free from disease and endowed with excellence of form, beauty, and strength.
Either a multitude of enemies endowed with a king’s majesty,
or an eminent brahmin who has performed many sacrifices.
Thus ends the vow for the year as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Brahmā said:
Furthermore, I shall explain to you the supreme worship of the Goddess.
By performing which, there shall be the attainment of all desires and complete satisfaction.
With staffs made of ivory, beautifully adorned with golden bands,
and exquisitely decorated with various gems such as rubies, it was most splendid.
In that manner, one should have constructed for the Goddess a beautiful, all-surpassing temple,
covered with fine silk garments and adorned with a crescent moon.
O Śakra, one should worship that chariot, which is richly adorned with bells and tinkling ornaments and graced with mirrors, with *jātī* flowers and *mallikā* jasmine.
Having perfumed the place with pārijātaka flowers, yakṣakardama, and sandalwood, one should cause the goddess to be seated there.
O child, one should worship the beautiful image, which brings about the destruction of the great Daityas,
when it is placed upon a chariot and established as the source of all auspiciousness.
Goddess Durgā, Kātyāyanī, the bestower of boons, dweller of the Vindhya mountains;
the slayer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
May Umā, the patient mother who forms half the body of Śaṅkara, be gracious to me;
may that which is desired in our hearts always come to pass.
Having worshipped with this [mantra] preceded by the bali offering and joined with prostrations,
the king then pervaded everything on all sides with songs.
On the fifth, seventh, and full moon days, as well as on the ninth and eleventh;
on the third, and on the days of Śiva and Vighneśa, and during festivals.
And on the banks of great rivers, in forest glades, and at mountain springs,
one should construct there a large pavilion built of bricks.
Having fashioned [an image] either of stone or of clay, one who knows the divisions of the site should have it complete with all auspicious characteristics and endowed with every beauty;
first he should have Śakra installed, and afterwards he should commence the procession.
One should worship it with all kinds of food, drink, and offerings, [a place] filled with great populations and crowded with large throngs of women.
And then, O Śakra of good vows, one should offer the directional oblation equally to the hosts of bhūtas and vetālas in the eastern and other directions with this mantra.
Victory to you, O Kālikā, surrounded by all beings! Protect me from your own spirits and always accept this beloved offering.
O Mother, O Mother, O excellent Durgā, who fulfills all desires!
By this offering of a bali-oblation, grant me all my wishes.
Having thus offered the bali-oblation, O Śakra, one should likewise cause the goddess to descend;
one should then place her upon the auspicious throne, adorned with mandalas.
One should cause the Goddess, residing therein, to be reached by means of eight thousand jars made of gold, silver, and copper, well-filled with scented water.
Then, with sacrificial twigs complete with all their fruits,
one should bathe [the deity] while subsisting on a single meal, using new and sturdy vessels filled with gems.
With the auspicious sounds of the Vedas, the resonance of conch trumpets, flutes, lutes, and mṛdaṅga drums, and the ringing of bells and small tinkling bells;
Having bathed the goddess, one should then adorn her with auspicious pigments;
a man should worship [her] with lotuses made of cow dung and the like, illuminated by lamps, wicks, and so forth.
With svastikas, nandikāvartas, conch shells, blue lotuses, and water-born flowers.
One should churn it with barley-grass mixed with sprouts of barley and śāli rice.
With *udaja* lotuses, with barley-straw, and with barley-grass—
one should burn incense for each and bathe each jar;
likewise, with camphor powder and sandalwood and saffron.
Having smeared the Goddess with a mixture of *gorocanā*, one should worship her with golden ornaments,
jasmine garlands, and various offerings of gems.
One should lift both feet with garments and flowers;
the meaning is that one should cause them to walk upon the clothes and flowers.
Likewise, one should gratify maidens, the twice-born, and the poor, the blind, and the suffering.
There, one should satisfy everyone with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as drinks.
Having fed her, he should ask for forgiveness, saying, "May the Goddess be pleased with me.
Then, having placed the Goddess upon a chariot, he should lead her back home once again.

With a great multitude of people endowed with all kinds of wealth, the entire area around the chariot was strewn with flowers, *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice grains, and water, while maidens, women, and those chanting auspicious verses offered their blessings.
Then, having sprinkled dust on the road with water in five successive stages,
he created the splendor of the city, the splendor of the road, and the splendor of the gateways at every house.
O Śakra, one should have it constructed in such a way that it wards off all afflictions;
the trees therein should be indestructible, and one must avoid harming living beings within it.
O Śakra, one should release those enemies such as anger who are bound and condemned to death;
however, one should not perform the Kaumudī festival or the chariot procession at an improper time.

"At an improper time" refers to the Kaumudī festival, the Festival of Lights; the meaning is that one should perform [the rite] at that improper time. Furthermore, the chariot procession (rathayātrā) was always established by all the gods beginning with Śaṅkara, and likewise, O Śakra, it is always performed by the gods in heaven.
Likewise, by the power of the chariot procession, the deities in heaven rejoice along with the Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and those dwelling on the earth and in the netherworld.
O King of Kings, by means of a chariot belonging to the Ādityas, one may traverse the sky in a chariot;
by the power of the chariot procession, the divine Ādityas stationed in their celestial palaces [are moved].
They sport with various enjoyments, free from all afflictions;
likewise, O Lord of Gods, you too should become a performer of the chariot festival.
To Śivā, the bestower of auspiciousness, with supreme meditative absorption.
Agastya said:
"The merit of the chariot procession for Vāsava was indeed equal to that of Brahmā."
O dear one, all of that has been related by me to you in its entirety, just as it was told before.
The supreme majesty of the Goddess has been established here; of this there is no doubt.
O best of kings, whoever—whether reading or even listening to it—with devotion, [shall attain the highest goal].
"He shall obtain happiness, fame, good fortune, and the desired attainment of a son;
of this there is no doubt—thus spoke the Brāhmaṇa."
In ancient times, the attainment of the city of Śakra was recounted by Suvala for his benefit,
as well as the arrival at the city of Dhanada and Varuṇa by means of Vāyu.
Having heard this, he established them in that hateful place among the Nairṛtas;
yet they enjoy the auspicious city of Nāgavatī with supreme satisfaction.
Thus ends the description of the chariot procession as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
Rudra said:
"How should the chariot procession of Bhāskara be performed here by human beings?"
And what indeed would be the fruit for those who perform their journey there?
O Supreme among Gods, by what rite and at what time should it be performed? And how, O Lord, should one cause the Sun-god, mounted upon his chariot, to circumambulate?
What fruit is declared for those men who, out of devotion, cause this chariot of the God to be wheeled about and offer it, as well as for those who perform the necessary services?
Men devoted to dance and song worship him as he wanders;
filled with faith and devotion, they keep a vigil.
And what fruit is declared for those who provide a chariot for the Sun,
as well as for one who with devotion provides ten portions of food every year?
"O best of gods, tell me all this in full detail: what is the annual food, the rice-gruel, the snacks, and the solid foods? O Lord, for the welfare of the worlds, my curiosity is great."
Brahmā said:
Well asked, O Lord of Beings, O Lord of Gaṇeśas, O Three-eyed One!
Listen with a focused mind; I shall speak at great length according to what has been asked.
This is the chariot procession of the high-souled god Bhāskara;
likewise, O Rudra, the festival of Indra— since these two are equal in the opinion of the wise—
they are honored throughout the world of mortals for the sake of peace.
In that land, these two great festivals proceed in every region—
these being the festival of Indra’s banner and the festival of the Sun’s chariot.
There, no calamities arise from kings or thieves.
Therefore, these two tasks must be performed with devotion for the sake of pacifying the famine.
O Hara, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should indeed anoint the God with ghee and worship the five elements.
He who, endowed with faith, daily anoints the Lord of Planets with clarified butter when the Sun has entered the color-pigment, [attains his desires].
In the *varṇaka* hall, the chamber for anointing,
he shall go mounted upon a vehicle covered with red chalk and small bells,
to the divine city of Vaiśvānara, adorned by Gandharvas and Apsarases. [426]

Whoever offers daily to Bhāskara rice cooked with milk (śālyodana) mixed with sugar-candy and accompanied by many *vajras*— the meaning being that it is accompanied by *vajras* [i.e., diamonds] and clarified butter (*ājya*)— and served with various colored portions;
Having ascended a beautiful celestial chariot adorned with garlands of banners,
O God, you shall go to my city while being praised by the great seers.
Therefore, with every effort, men should [worship] the Sun-god together with [the others].
One should offer colored rice and establish various pigments here;
and he who offers *ghṛtapūra*, *khaṇḍaveṣṭa*, *kāsāra*, and *modaka* [cakes];
Those who offer here to the god Bhāskara curd-rice, milk-rice, wheat-cakes mixed with sugar, and molasses-buns as a colored offering;
Those men who, day after day, offer [a gift] with devotion to Bhāskara, go to my abode; of this there is no doubt.
O Lord, he who offers ghee for anointing attains the supreme goal;
likewise, he who daily offers food of various colors with devotion.
Having obtained auspicious desires in this world, he too shall go to my abode—
he who daily offers auspicious powder and unguents to the Sun.
He goes to the supreme abode where the divine Sun-god dwells;
thereafter, one should satisfy that deity according to the prescribed rite in the month of Pauṣa.
Listen with a one-pointed mind to what should be done on the seventh day of the bright fortnight:
having brought water from a sacred ford (tīrtha), or otherwise pure and auspicious water.
The wise one should bathe the image according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas;
indeed, the wise one should recite the names of the sacred fords while mentally recollecting them.
Prayāga, Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra together with Naimiṣa,
Pṛthūdaka, Bhadravaṭa, Soma, and Gokarṇa as well.
Brahmāvarta, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, the Nīla mountain,
the holy Gaṅgādvāra, and likewise the confluence of the Gaṅgā with the ocean.
Kālasūrya, Mitravana, and likewise Muṇḍīrasvāmin;
the highly meritorious Cakratīrtha and the auspicious Rāmatīrtha.
The Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, Candrabhāgā, along with the Narmadā; the Vipāśā, Yamunā, Tāpī, Śivā, and likewise the Vaitaraṇī.
The Godāvarī, the Payoṣṇī, and likewise the river Kṛṣṇaveṇī;
the Śatarudrā, the Puṣkariṇī, the Kauśikī, and likewise the Sarayū.
Likewise, let other oceans also provide their presence;
as well as the most holy hermitages and divine shrines.
Having thus performed the ritual bath, having worshipped and prostrated,
and having offered incense and the water-offering (arghya), one should consecrate the image.
For three nights, seven nights, half a month, or even a full month,
a person should devotedly feed the deity residing in the house while staying there.
Then, O Destroyer of Tripura, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, one should cause a well-enclosed square altar to be erected.
Having performed the fire-ritual according to the rules and having provided a feast for the Brahmins,
[he should proceed] with the sounding of conchs and kettledrums and with abundant recitations of the Veda.
Then, with various proclamations of an auspicious day and the recitation of benedictions by Brahmins,
he should cause a procession to be made for his sake and for the peace of the people.
On the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, one should cause the Sun to mount a beautiful chariot adorned with a network of small bells.
Having performed the fire-ritual according to the rules, as well as the feeding of Brahmins,
he gratified all the people with sacrificial fees, food, and other gifts.
Having honored the divine Brahmins and the reciters during the fire-offerings,
the reciters— the most excellent of Brahmins— proceeded with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

He is considered a god and has been seen; therefore, he should always be worshipped on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, while observing the practice of eating only once a day.
On the fifth day, eating only what is unasked for is prescribed; on the sixth, eating at night is proclaimed;
on the seventh, there is fasting; and on the eighth, one should cause the sun to rise [after having fasted].
Then, having performed the fire-rite (agnikārya) in front of the chariot, O Śiva,
Lord of Beings, the consecration (adhivāsana) of the chariot shall take place here on the sixth night.
Having fed the Brahmins, both celestial and terrestrial reciters,
he should place the God, the creator of all beings, upon the chariot on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, in front of that temple.
One should keep a vigil at night right there in the presence of the deity,
with various kinds of performances and adorned with rows of lamps.
With the sounds of conchs and trumpets, and with abundant recitations of the Vedas,
one should keep a vigil before that deity during the night.
Then, on the eighth day, one should lead the deity Āyatana, mounted upon a chariot.
The northern gate of the city resounded with the blare of conchs and kettledrums;
then likewise the eastern, the southern, and the other gate as well.
When the journey is conducted in this manner until the end of the year,
men prosper in happiness and the king conquers the army.
May all people be free from disease, and may there be peace for the cows;
indeed, those who perform this pilgrimage shall become partakers of heaven.
"And likewise, O Rudra, those who bear it go indeed to the world of the Sun.
Rudra said:
"And how, O Brahmin, is it moved, having been established once and for all?"
Speak thus to us, O Lord of Gods; I have a very great doubt in this matter.
Brahmā said: Long ago, I fashioned for that high-souled thousand-rayed one a chariot composed of the constituent parts of the year.
Indeed, that chariot is considered the foremost of all chariots;
having seen it, the other vehicles were then fashioned by Viśvakarman.
O Lord Śaṅkara, having obtained the chariot fashioned by Viśvakarman, [the gods] appointed many of all the deities, beginning with Soma.
Born from the wrath of Mānava, he was given for the sake of worship;
that Ravi is worshipped by mortals as one bestowed upon Mauneyakṣvāku.
Therefore, O wielder of the trident, the movement of the sun by means of a chariot has been ordained;
consequently, there is no fault in the sun's motion.
Therefore, the sun traverses this earth by means of his chariot;
as he moves, he never stands still, for such is the constant nature of the orb of the sun.
Because it moves as directed, it is indeed known as *cālana*;
thus it has been firmly established by the wise in the processions of the chariot of the Sun.
O beloved of Pārvatī, the displacement of other deities—
such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others— who have been installed according to the prescribed rites, is not desired.
Therefore, for the sake of the peace of the subjects here, the procession of the god by chariot must always be performed according to the prescribed rules every year.
It should be made of gold, or silver, or even of solid wood;
it must have strong axles, yokes, and wheels, and be well-constructed.
Having carefully placed the image upon that most excellent and beautiful chariot which has been prepared, one should yoke the auspicious horses.
[He should give] elephants endowed with auspicious marks, with beautiful faces, well-behaved,
having anointed them with saffron and adorned them with chowries and garlands.
Having honored the excellent horses with banners, garlands, and ointments,
and having also fed the best of the twice-born with various kinds of food;
Having satisfied all those who are distressed, blind, or miserable according to one's ability,
one should not treat anyone— whether superior, inferior, or middling— with duplicity.
Regarding the Sūryakratu sacrifice, the wise have said this concerning Savitṛ:
"He who sets out with broken hopes, afflicted by hunger and oppressed by disease..."
For by that act, he causes even the ancestors of the donor who reside in heaven to fall;
and a sacrifice devoid of sacrificial fees is not praised by the Sun.
Therefore, having gratified [the deity] with various kinds of desires provided with foods to be chewed and licked, one should recite this [mantra] for the sake of all fruit, addressing the Sun.
May the gods accept my offering— the Ādityas, the Vasus,
as well as the Maruts, the two Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, and the Grahas.
Against the Asuras, the Yātudhānas, those deities stationed upon chariots, and all others,
one should recite this verse concerning the black dust.
Then, with the sound of "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and the resonance of musical instruments,
he should perform the circling of the chariot by way of a level path.
It should also be carried by men endowed with devotion to the Sun,
who have performed meritorious deeds and are restrained in their conduct, or else by draft-oxen given as gifts;
so that it may provide relief for one traveling on a rugged path.
By Brahmins established in fasting, endowed with divine enjoyments and firm in their vows—
whether twenty or sixteen in number— an image of the Sun-god [should be fashioned].
O Rudra, one should bathe, wash oneself, and slowly mount the chariot;
and the queen Nikṣubhā is the wife of that great-souled one.
Then he should slowly place [the two] there on both sides:
Nikṣubhā on the right side, and likewise the Queen on the left.
At its entrance stood two divine Brahmins, and on its sides were two earthly ones;
likewise, Brahmā and Soma were situated above Kubera.
One should likewise imagine a Garuḍa being fashioned upon his back,
as well as a white parasol with a celestial handle that is beyond compare.
Variegated with golden spots, resplendent with jewels and pearls,
and then another one with a golden shaft resembling a rainbow.
O destroyer of desires, one should fashion for it a banner adorned with seven pennants of various colors and diverse patterns.
Above the banner is the great, excellent void, presided over by the letter *mukāra*;
having joined together on the main roads, the Vipra shall lead the excellent chariot of the Sun.

One who desires his own welfare should always ensure that a Śūdra does not mount a chariot occupied by [a member of] the Rathyā [caste]; if he wishes for his own well-being, he should never ascend such a vehicle.
The progeny of one who mounts that chariot goes to destruction;
that chariot of the God of gods must always be carried by Brahmins.
It is for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, and never for Śūdras;
nor for those who are devotees of other deities, nor for those who promote the consumption of liquor.

O Rudra, beloved of Pārvatī, it must not be carried by those Śūdras nor by men who are arrogant with pride; rather, it should be carried by those who are endowed with fasting. Once moved from its place, O Rudra, it shall indeed proceed to the eastern gate.
He shall dwell there for one day, being honored by the king with various kinds of spectacles and the hearing of the Purāṇas.
Having remained there on the eighth day with various sounds of Vedic chanting and offerings to the Brahmins, one should then depart on the ninth day.
O Three-eyed One, one should go to the southern gate of the city;
there too, O Destroyer of Tripura, one should stay for one day.
Being thus honored by the kṣatriyas, as well as by those kings,
he should then proceed quickly to its western gate.
Even there, O Madhusūdana, he remains for one day.
Just as a king is honored by those other than the kṣatriyas, so too is he honored by kings;
therefore, one should practice even beyond that, and thus proceed further toward Rudradvāra.
Nevertheless, O Rudra, he should be worshipped by Śūdras of pleasing appearance according to the prescribed rites; therefore, one should move him toward the center of the city.
Established there, the Brahmins, filled with faith,
worship him with the sounding of conchs and musical instruments, as well as with excellent spectacles.
With various sounds of Vedic chanting and lamps on every side,
and with diverse gifts of wealth and the gratification of the Brahmins.
O Destroyer of Tripura, having satisfied the poor, the blind, the wretched, and the helpless,
one should depart from the city and remain upon reaching one's own abode.
When the Lord has thus been brought and stationed before the temple,
he shall then remain there to be worshipped by all the citizens in their entirety.
Being honored day and night, he remains mounted upon his chariot;
on the following day, he proceeds to the bath, doing so continuously and with devotion.
O Three-eyed One, when the thirteenth day has passed, on the fourteenth day one should always cause the Lord, the Ruler of Planets who removes misfortune, to be paraded.
[He saw] the Supreme Lord Rudra, accompanied by his retinue and followers.
Rudra said:
"O Brahmin, how might one cause him, who stands upon his chariot and fasts, to move?"
And how did his followers follow Keśava in succession?
O best of gods, for my own welfare, please explain this further and in greater detail;
O Lord of the entire world, for I have a great curiosity.
Brahmā said:
O Rudra, one should move slowly along a beautiful path;
in this way, there will be no failure for one traveling on a rugged road.
First, one should lead the chariot of the gatekeeper for the sake of purifying the path;
immediately after that, O Rudra, one should respectfully lead the staff-bearer,
and then Piṅgala, following behind him with respect.
From that gate, he mounted his chariot and followed behind;
likewise, mounted on his chariot, he stood before Daṇḍideva.
Therefore, O Rudra, the scribe, who is dear to Bhāskara,
should also gradually move the chariot of the god Helina.
O Three-eyed One, just as there should be no breaking of the chariot wheel, so too [is it with the others]:
if the pole breaks, there is fear for the twice-born; if the axle, however, there is the destruction of the king.

If the balance is lost, there is danger for the Vaiśyas; if the sacrificial pin (śamyā) is lost, there will be fear from Śūdras. If the yoke-pin (yuga) breaks, there will be drought; if the pedestal (pīṭha) breaks, there is danger for the subjects.
One should recognize the arrival of an enemy army by the breaking of a wheel on a chariot;
likewise, one should indicate the wrath of the ancestors by the falling of the banner.
In the case of the Pratimādyaṅgikā, however, one should predict the death of the king;
and likewise when such initial portents, whether auspicious or inauspicious, have arisen.
The wise man should perform the *balikarma* and likewise the *śāntihoma*;
may there be peace for the cows, for the progeny, and indeed peace for the entire world.
May there likewise be peace for each and every one, and may there likewise be peace everywhere for the Sun;
for you, O Lord, are indeed the creator and the sustainer of the world.
O Protector of Creatures, Lord of Planets, Lord of Heaven, grant peace!
And I shall speak this other thing, which is the supreme cause of peace.

However, having recognized that the planets are malevolent toward one's own birth-constellation of the person who has become the cause [of the affliction], one should perform a three-day propitiatory rite.
Having thus ensured the peace of the subjects and performed the recitation for well-being,
O Hara, he should once again prepare his chariot and set forth on his journey.
Having passed the remainder of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should lead the Sun to the temple;
then, having worshipped all the deities as prescribed in the scriptures.
O Three-eyed One, just as all the planets have been declared worthy of worship,
so too are the deities of the chariot to be worshipped, who reside supported upon the chariot.
Milk and gruel are indeed my supreme food, O Lord;
but for you, O Lord of Beings, one should offer fruits in the month of Kārttika for the sake of your pleasure.
O Lord of the Gods, one should likewise offer meat and liquor to Vivasvat,
and edible foods to Puruhūta along with his followers.
One should offer sacrificial oblations to Agni; likewise, food fit for the thunderbolt to Viṣṇu;
and one should give meat-rice equally to the Rākṣasas, O Hara.
O destroyer of Tripura, one should offer refined meat and rice to Revanta, and one should give sesame and rice to the King of the Ancestors (Yama).
One should offer cakes to the Aśvins, meat-rice to the Vasus,
and milk-rice mixed with ghee and honey to the ancestors.
One should offer barley-gruel to Kātyāyanī, curd to Śrī,
the "three sweets" (honey, ghee, and sugar) to Sarasvatī, and rice cooked with sugarcane juice to Varuṇa.
O Three-eyed One, when Dhanapati is your friend,
the offering of satisfaction to the Maruts with curd-butter mixed with sugar is prescribed.
One should devotedly offer black gram and cakes to the Mothers;
one should offer *ullopikā* sweets to the spirits, and offer water for the sake of heaven.
O Destroyer of Tripura, the wise one should offer *modakas* to Gaṇapati;
*śaṣkulis* should be given to Nairṛta-Indra, O Leader of the Gaṇas;
and all kinds of edible foods should be offered on all sides to the Viśvedevas.
One should offer milk-rice to the sages and milk to the nāgas;
one should also present an offering to Sūryaratha, which is common to all beings.
O Śaṅkara, one should offer meat-rice, liquor, and clarified butter to those who carry burdens;
O Rudra, one should likewise give you cakes mixed with ghee and sesame seeds.
O Destroyer of Tripura, one should always offer parched grain (lāja) with the mantra "svāhā sutāya" to the Sun; O Three-eyed One, one should also give deodar (suradāru) to Bhāskara.
One should offer the *rājavṛkṣa* tree to Surendra, sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) to Pāvaka,
seven kinds of grain to the Wielder of the Discus (Viṣṇu), and meat, clarified butter, and fine ornaments [to the respective deities].
Various fragrances for the Yakṣas, resin from the Vetasa and Uṇḍaja trees,
and that which comes from the Vikaṅkata tree, O Rudra, are always proclaimed for Yama.
O Bull-bannered One, *karṇikāra* flowers should be given to the Aśvins;
lotuses should be given to Śrī, and sandalwood to Candrikā.
One should offer fresh butter to Sarasvatī, meat likewise to Vinatā,
and flowers of the mālatī to the Apsarases, O Rudra.
One should offer Agni to Varuṇa in this manner, fruit and roots to Nairṛti, a bilva fruit to Kubera, and likewise a kapittha fruit to the Maruts.
O Destroyer of Tripura, one should offer beautiful fragrance to the Gandharvas,
and one should offer fine camphor to the Vasus and to the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Offer the roots of the *piṇḍa* tree to the ancestors, the *vibhītaka* fruit to the elemental spirits (*bhūta*s),
barley to the cows, and bring unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) for the mothers.
Guggulu should be offered to Vighnapati, and boiled rice to the Viśvedevas;
to the Ṛṣis, the Brahmavṛkṣa tree, and to the Nāgas, the most excellent poison.
O lord of men, O three-eyed one, here one should offer to Bhāskara and Gaurika sacrificial portions smeared with honey and clarified butter, accompanied by formal resolutions (saṃkalpa).
O Hara, one should always offer a *nyagrodha* tree to Rudra with devotion from his two arms,

these two [proportions] destroy for men the suffering of birth, saṃsāra, and death.
For the lowest [grade of] sacred thread (*pavitraka*), twelve knots are prescribed; for the middling, they are remembered as being double that number; and for the highest, they are said to be triple.
One intent on the worship of Viṣṇu should, according to the prescribed rite, fashion one hundred and eight knots for the forest garland of the Lord of Sages.
In the *Adhivāsana-sūtra*, however, twelve knots are prescribed;
now listen, O best of Guhyakas, to the procedure for the placement of the principles (*tattva*).
This mantra known as "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" is for the twice-born;
for Śūdras, the twelve-syllable mantra is indeed the application of the principles (tattva-vinyāsa).
One should recite the mantra as many times as there are knots remembered,
whether once, twice, or even thrice, upon the purifying cord.

One should recite the mantra once for each knot on the wrist, twice in the middle, and thrice at the end. Then, having anointed the purifiers with saffron, ushira, camphor, sandalwood, and other unguents, one should perform the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should perform the purifications for the ritual acceptance.
Having worshipped with flowers and other offerings, one should then perform the deposition (nyāsa) within the city of Viṣṇu at night;

On the eleventh day and during that night, the devotee, with devotion,
[should worship] on the eleventh day with auspicious scents, flowers, incense, and ointments, using the root mantra.

accompanied by dance, song, auspicious recitations, and the performance of wrestling matches.

and one should offer to Hari an oblation consisting of milk, meat broth, barley gruel, *vaṭaka* cakes, *apūpa* cakes, *modaka* sweets, fragrant fruits, and other sweet offerings.
On the eleventh day, a man, having worshiped Madhusūdana with devotion,

should perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) for the Discus-bearer, the God of gods; he should do so while fasting, having bathed cleanly, performed his prayers, and subdued his senses.
Having given gifts to the foremost of the twice-born and having worshipped Janārdana,
one should properly take up the sacred thread (pavitraka) that was previously consecrated.
One should offer it upon the head of Viṣṇu with the mantra "ato devā.
This mantra is prescribed for the twice-born during the rite of placing the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa).
Or the *mūlamantra* of a Śūdra, by which one should indeed worship Hari;

Therefore, with every effort, he who worships the guru with joy just as he does Viṣṇu shall obtain the fruit of liberation.
As is Viṣṇu, so is knowledge; as is knowledge, so is the guru.
He who worships them without distinction is worthy of the fruit of liberation.
Having honored the betel leaf with flowers, perfumes, and other offerings, one should dismiss it;

O Hara, having thus completed the rite for the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa), one should feed other mendicants who have arrived according to one's capacity.

this very procedure is prescribed for the God of gods upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila).

whatever merit is traditionally declared for the proper performance of the Pavitrārohaṇa rite [is obtained].
