established in virtuous conduct, the practitioner of mantra has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
One who is gentle, free from harshness and slander, mild, and devoted to the welfare of all beings—
he indeed should be known as an Ācārya, for he is truly engaged in all [virtuous] actions.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya are worthy of sacrifice, O Madhusūdana;
likewise, the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, as well as women and Śūdras.
All those established in their own dharma and devoted to Madhusūdana,
having approached the previously mentioned guru, should satisfy him with devotion.
Afterwards, one should pray for the purpose of the sacrifice: "O Lord, grant me my share;
by means of this very purifier, Madhusūdana, who is to be worshipped through sacrifice, shall be worshipped."
When he has said, "I shall do so," one should gather the necessary provisions.
One should offer all of Hari’s thread and other items to the guru;
being pure and unwearied, one should perform the purification rite according to one's ability.
Likewise, knots are tied with the eight-syllable mantra;
[use] saffron and yellow pigment (rocanā) combined with camphor.
One should first scatter [the substances] with the mantra spoken individually;
thereafter, the wise practitioner, as a master of mantras, should recite it in its entirety.
One should avoid the *pavitraka* with the very mantra already mentioned.
Having sprinkled saffron with "Oṃ," galle (*rocanā*) upon it with "Namaḥ," and camphor upon that with "Nārāyaṇāya"—
having thus mixed them with the mantra split into its parts— and having consecrated them with the entire mantra, "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya," one should fashion the *mala* using that same entire mantra.
Thus ends the procedure for the offering of the *pavitra* as declared in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.
Brahmā said:
"O child, at the beginning of the month of Caitra, one should perform my worship according to the prescribed rite."
By means of offerings of perfumes, flowers, and garlands made from *damanaka* blossoms;
One should always worship the God; one shall obtain all desires.
O Dānava, one attains the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas).
On the first lunar day (pratipad), one should worship Umā, Śiva, and Agni;
on the second day, however, one should worship Pitāmaha with *damanaka* flowers.
O best of Brahmins, one who first offers fragrant worship and presents food fit for oblation as an offering obtains the fruit that was proclaimed by Umā.
On the third day, one should worship the Goddess together with Śaṅkara,
adorning her with saffron, agallochum, camphor, jewels, garments, and garlands.
O child, one should swing Śiva on a swing adorned with fragrant, meritorious incense, with *damanaka* and *sumālatī* flowers; thus he is always pleased with me.
A vigil should be kept at night, and in the morning, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given,
consisting of gold, garments, vessels of food, betel leaves, and garlands.
[454] Women who desire good fortune and the happiness of having sons should always perform worship of Gaṇeśa, offering him sweets such as *laḍḍukas* and other delicacies.
On the fourth day, for the destruction of obstacles and the fulfillment of all desires,
one should worship the Nāgas on the fifth day, and likewise offer gifts to the Mahoragas.
O Lord, milk and ghee offered as a food-oblation remove the poison of serpents.
On the sixth [lunar day], a worship of Skanda should be performed with all kinds of offerings;
one will obtain happiness and good fortune in this very life, and at the end, attain the state of Skanda.
By performing worship of the Sun on the seventh lunar day with *damanaka* and other offerings,
one who has performed great austerities and is free from enemies attains enjoyments and other rewards.
Furthermore, O child, by performing on the eighth day an offering to the Mothers consisting of all kinds of food and perfumes,
one obtains the desired accomplishment through *damanaka* flowers.
On the ninth day, one should worship the Goddess Mahāmahiṣamardinī with saffron,
agallochum, camphor, incense, food offerings, banners, and libations.
With *damanaka* flowers and *marupatra*, one shall attain the state known as Vijaya.
On the tenth day, however, worship of Dharmarāja should be performed with fragrant perfumes;
such a person becomes wealthy, possessed of sons, and beloved, and is glorified in the world of the Ṛṣis.
On the twelfth day, one should worship Viṣṇu with camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
O mighty-armed one, by offering oblations of sacrificial food, the performer shall attain the station of Viṣṇu;
on the thirteenth day, Kāmadeva should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
Endowed with passion and delight, adorned with the Aśoka-jewel,
he is remembered as holding a bow in his left hand and having five arrows in his [other] hands.
Whether on a water-pot or on white cloth, one should draw [the deity] with the five fruits and other offerings;
by offering pieces of sugar-candy and sugar, one shall obtain incomparable good fortune.
On the fourteenth day, having bathed the Lord of Gods, whose crest is marked by the crescent moon,
with ablutions of milk and other substances, [one should worship] him with incense and fragrant flowers.
O Śivā, one should worship according to the prescribed rule with intoxicants known as *madana*, and a grand offering of garments, food, and jewels should be performed.
One should provide canopies, banners, and parasols for the deity and perform a vigil;
one thereby attains great merit, such as the fruit of the horse sacrifice and other rewards.
Likewise, on the full moon day, it should be performed for the fulfillment of all desires;
by offering to Indra together with Sacī, one obtains the fruit of one's wishes.
Thus, those who perform worship for fifteen days obtain here the fruits of all sacrifices, austerities, and gifts.
O Queen, those kings sported at their own will amidst the various enjoyments of the gods;
indeed, upon the exhaustion of their merit, they have come here to this earth.
"His enemies have been overcome; of this there is no doubt," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of Damanaka as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
Sūrya said:
Those twice-born ones of excellent vows who shall worship Śiva and offer curd,
being liberated from all sins, will go to heaven.
Just as Paśupati, having given away this entire world,
is never again stained, so too he who constantly observes the vow remains unstained.
O best of the twice-born, by performing the vow known as Pāśupata, one destroys the sin committed in this life as well as that committed in previous lives.
On the twelfth day one should eat only a single meal; on the thirteenth, food obtained unasked;
likewise on the fourteenth, a meal at night; and on the following day, a fast.
On the following day, the new moon day,
one should have a bull made of gold, as well as [images] of silver and copper; furthermore,
one should have a golden leaf fashioned for each separately, weighing eighty *guñjās*.
Right there, one should delineate the forms of both Śivā and Śiva.
One should have a bull made of that same measure, using silver four times the amount of gold;
or one may have it made of copper eight times the amount of silver, or even half of that.

Its weight, however, should be eighty *guñjās*, or half of that; for gold, silver, and copper, three *vṛṣas* (bulls) appropriate [to the material] should be fashioned, according to the statement: "One should give the *vṛṣas*.
Having placed the leaf upon the pitcher along with an excellent cloth, one should observe a single meal on the thirteenth day and a night-fast (*nakta*) on the *riktā* lunar day.
This is the secondary rite (*anukalpa*):
having worshipped Gaṅgādhara with perfumes, flowers, all kinds of food offerings, garments, ornaments, and lamps, one should pray for a most excellent boon.
O Gaṅgādhara, Mahādeva, you who are the supreme and the inferior of all worlds;
O Śaṅkara, being worshipped here, destroy all my sins.
O Gaṅgādhara, sovereign of the earth, bestower of boons higher than the highest; O Śrīkaṇṭha, Nīlakaṇṭha, beloved of Umā—salutations be unto you!
Having thus performed the worship according to the prescribed rite on the first day of the lunar fortnight when the sun has risen,
one should present gold and other gifts, as well as a bull, to the Brāhmaṇas.
Just as you are all-pervading, all-encompassing, the abode of all, and the creator of all, yet remain unstained while manifesting your transformations— so too, O Śaṅkara, make me such.
Having heard this and having paid obeisance, one should give as many bulls as desired to the twice-born, beginning with the preceptor, saying, "May Śaṅkara be pleased.
Having thus performed this vow, one should give a bull to a member of the twice-born.
In this case, the bull is the image;
he never beholds the most terrible path of Yama.
Having heard this, that brahmin-sage returned once more to his own city.
Having beheld the realm of Yama together with the Sun,
the king then met with them and related everything exactly as it had occurred.
Then, having heard this, that lord of a thousand Akṣauhiṇīs, firm in his vows, made a gift of bulls for the destruction of all his sins.
Together with all those virtuous spirits, the pretas, and likewise another hundred others, that royal sage shall attain the world beyond.
He who performs this vow, which destroys all sins,
is not smeared by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.

A man is released from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, from approaching those who should not be approached, and from the consumption of forbidden food and drink, even if he has committed them but once.
O fortunate one, he who performs a gift that brings all happiness,
having destroyed all sins without exception, goes to the heavenly world.
Thus ends the Pāśupata vow as declared in the Vahnipurāṇa.
Maitreya said:
Tell me that which is capable of pacifying sins and increasing merit.
And let that vow which grants all desires be told to me.
Yājñavalkya said:
Whatever fruit is obtained by men through various sacrifices during the month,
that they obtain by worshipping Janārdana through fasts.
O knower of dharma, listen to me regarding this supreme vow among all vows, which brings about the fulfillment of desires and destroys evil.
Having performed which, no man becomes dull-witted, blind, deaf, or afflicted by suffering,
nor does anyone experience the pain of separation from what is dear.
He never becomes unpleasant to this world;
for seven lifetimes he experiences auspiciousness and is liberated from all evils.
This is known as the Viṣṇu-vrata, taught by Viṣṇu himself;
it begins on the second day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa and lasts for four days.
One should undertake this supreme vow, which consists of breaking the fast only after six months;
first, bathing with white mustard seeds is prescribed, and thereafter with black sesame seeds.
Then, on the third day, one should worship him with all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadhī) using the name Kṛṣṇācyuta. Thereafter, one should likewise worship him with that [name].
And likewise on the fourth day, having worshipped the god Hṛṣīkeśa Keśava with flowers, leaves, incense, and ointments, [459]
And as the young moon rises, one should, with a concentrated mind and devotion,
offer the *arghya* with flowers, leaves, fruits, and all kinds of grains.
One should recite these names of Candra according to the sequence of the days:
Śaśī, Candra, Śaśāṅka, and Niśāpati in order.
One should always eat only at night as long as the moon remains;
when it has set, one should not eat, O auspicious lady, for fear of breaking the vow.
O illustrious lady, in this manner, during all the months ending with Jyeṣṭha,
this most excellent vow should indeed be performed for four days, beginning from the second lunar day.
O illustrious lady, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin on the fifth day;
in this manner, one should complete the first breaking of the fast over the course of six months.

And at the conclusion of the fast, the gratification of the Lord should be performed with devotion using auspicious offerings according to one's capacity; one should avoid stinginess regarding wealth.
O Lord of Wealth, the breaking of the fast for this auspicious vow is declared to occur on the second lunar day of the month of Āṣāḍha, after six months have passed.
This vow was observed by Dilīpa, Duṣmanta,
Yayāti, and likewise by other protectors of the earth through the performance of fasting.
The fast at night was practiced by the foremost of sages, such as Marīci and Cyavana,
as well as by Sumitrā, Kaikeyī, Śāṇḍilī, and Dhūpapiṅgā.
And likewise it was performed by Sudeṣṇā, Devakī, and the wise Matimatī;
and by Sāvitrī, Pūrṇamāsī, Vīriṇī, and Subhadrā.
This vow was performed by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, as well as by women— specifically by Urvaśī, Rambhā, and Sīrabheyī.
It is frequented by the Apsarases of the earth who know the Dharma, out of a desire for merit;
in its first part one is worshiped as a foot, and in the second, as the navel.
In the third [verse] there is the worship of the eye, and in the fourth that of the head of Hari;
having recited this with faith, one is freed from all sins.
He is indeed liberated from impurities and attains his heart's desires;
for this is the supreme among vows, spoken by the Lord himself.
It is praised as the pacifier of sins and the bestower of the fruits of one's desires;
and whatever object one contemplates while performing it with fixed vows, that very thing is attained.
O highly fortunate lady, this vow fulfills the desires of men;
it grants their heart's wishes and dispels all evil.
And it bestows the state of having unimpaired faculties for seven births.
Whatever merit there is from bathing at Prayāga during the month of Māgha, which destroys all sins,
one obtains that entirely by hearing this vow dedicated to Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Viṣṇu-vrata as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
[461] Śrī Kārkaṇḍeya said:
"One should fast during the four months for the sake of Hari, the Lord who is the embodiment of Yoga."
If one should worship on the full moon day, he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
One who has become a yogin should worship her,
who is the embodiment of the full moon, on the new moon day while fasting;
he attains the Rājasūya sacrifice and uplifts his own lineage.
Brahman-like and partless;
by attending upon Keśava, who is thus become Brahman on the new moon and likewise on the full moon, and who has become Yoga, one shall attain the Great.
Hari, the best of gods, being honored with devotion and fasting by those two for months and fortnights, always attains extreme delight.
This is known as the Great Vow (Mahāvrata), which destroys all impurities;
by performing this for a year, one is glorified upon the back of the celestial vault.
This vow is proclaimed as the pacifier of all evils;
here, the power of one's own mind alone is the cause in all ritual actions.
Having observed the vow for twelve years,
one attains the world of Puruṣottama;
having dwelt there for a very long time, that high-souled one—
From that, this person attains the world.
Thus ends the Mahāvrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform it every day for seven days.
One should worship Hradinī, Hrādinī, and Pāvanī,
as well as Sītā, Ikṣu, Sindhu, and Bhāgīrathī, in due order.
One should likewise perform the external bath daily and subsist on food only at night; with a tranquil mind, one should offer milk as an oblation in the water day after day.
Water-jars filled with milk should be given to the twice-born,
and one should subsist on milk for seven days thereafter.
Having performed this for a year, when the year is complete,
the man should then give a pure pala of silver to the twice-born.
On the seventh day, in sequence, during the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna,
a man attains that world where there are mud-pools of milk-rice (pāyasa).
There are divine rivers flowing with milk that grant all desired fruits;
having dwelt there for a long time in purity, the high-souled one, upon attaining human birth, becomes free from disease.
Whether it be a king or a preeminent brahmin, one who is endowed with virtue, moral conduct, and wealth.
Thus ends the Nadīvrata as declared in the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara.
[463] Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe to you the auspicious Lokavrata.
The sacred utterances (vyāhṛtis) that are therein are proclaimed as the seven worlds.
One should perform the ritual bath outside every day without weariness,
beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra for a period of seven days in succession.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass,
along with a fast for one night— one should perform these in this very sequence.
Every day, an oblation of sesame seeds should be performed with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
and at the end of the year, one should likewise give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
O best of men, having performed this vow for one year, he [should give] a very large garment of gold, as well as a brass vessel and a cow.
The glorious one, the best in all the world, may become a lord of men by his own will,
as the supreme king at the beginning of a kalpa, remaining so until the end of that kalpa.
That wheel-turning monarch, honored by the best of kings and possessing power exceeding that of gods and asuras,
[reigned] for hundreds of ten-thousands of years.
He proceeds, delightful to the entire earth.
Thus ends the Lokavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe to you the auspicious Śailavrata.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimat, and also Ṛkṣavat.
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountain ranges (kulaparvata).
From the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra, for seven days every day, [the sun moves].
Having performed their worship with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food, one should perform the external bath.
One should likewise perform the fire-oblation with barley and give barley to the Brahmin;
one should eat barley-food daily and observe this vow for a year.
At its conclusion, one should give twenty *prasthas* of barley and gold of refined gold to the reciter, who is a preeminent among the twice-born.
By the performance of this vow, the king, having brought his enemies under subjection, enjoys the earth girt by the four oceans.
Having enjoyed the pleasures of the Lord of the Three Heavens and reached the earth as described,
one indeed attains everything that has been spoken by me.
The best of kings [recalled] his very previous births.
Thus ends the Śailavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe to you the Samudravrata.
Then, beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, for seven days every day.
One should worship with salt-water, milk with ghee, whey, wine, water,
as well as sugarcane juice and sweet water.
One should perform the ritual bath every day, having become pure both internally and externally;
one should perform a fire-oblation with clarified butter and cause it to be offered on the seventh lunar day.
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), he should observe this vow at night for one year;
at the end of the year, he should likewise give a milch cow as a gift.
By performing this vow, a king shall enjoy the earth, which is girdled by the seven oceans, for seven future births.
One who desires health should likewise observe this vow;
so too should one who desires dharma, one who desires wealth, and likewise one who desires heaven.
This is auspicious, supremely purifying, increasing prosperity, and causing the growth of dharma;
it should be performed by men who are self-restrained.
"And by those who desire clarified butter, it shall be attained without delay.
Thus ends the Samudra-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme Dvīpa-vrata;
beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, it is performed every day for seven days.
One should worship daily, in sequence, those known as Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmali, Gomeda, and Puṣkara islands.
At that time, one should always perform the bath in this manner outside;
one should likewise sleep on the ground constantly for those same seven days.
When a full year has passed, one should give silver fashioned [into the form of the fruit],
especially fruits, with the arrangement made like a lamp.
Having performed this vow for a full year, a pure man attains the heavenly world for as long as the dissolution of all beings.
Having taken up human birth, he enjoys the earth consisting of seven continents, having conquered the factions of his enemies,
and is always honored by the gods.
By the great seers and the preeminent brahmins.
Thus ends the Dvīpavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe to you the vow known as the Śrīvrata.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform a bath preceded by an oil massage.
Having dressed in white garments, O King, wearing white garlands and unguents,
he should subsist on rice with ghee and sleep upon the ground for that night.
On the fourth day, one should likewise perform the ritual bath outside;
and on the fifth day, being pure and wearing white garments, one should do so especially.
One should worship Lakṣmī with lotuses, whether in an artificial image or not;
or else with white perfumes, garlands, and ghee lamps.
The form of Lakṣmī is according to the Nāradīya Purāṇa:
Padmā should be depicted with a lotus in her hand, seated upon a lotus-flower throne,
possessing four arms, endowed with a beautiful form, and holding a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
[467] And with turmeric, grain, ginger, and molasses;
with products of sugarcane and with abundant salt.
And according to his own capacity, O Great King, having performed an extensive drawing out of the offering,
the pure one should then offer lotuses into the fire while reciting the Śrīsūkta.
One should offer its leaves and bilva fruits; in their absence, likewise ghee.
One should feed the Brahmins food consisting mostly of cow-products and abounding in ghee.
He should give a gold coin as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa;
thereafter, he should sleep in a clean place according to the prescribed rule while abstaining from food.
Then, having reached the fifth [day], one who has taken refuge there should likewise bathe in the previously mentioned lotus-water and perform worship just as before.
Furthermore, O twice-born one, he should give a full gold māṣaka coin;
or else, immediately thereafter, he should consume a lotus seed or a bilva fruit.
Then, O best of kings, that most excellent of men, having restrained his speech, should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) for one year after performing this vow.
One obtains the vast fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices by performing this vow even without the gift of gold.
At the conclusion of the vow, having worshipped on the fifth day of the bright fortnight while observing a fast, one obtains the entire fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for every māṣaka offered.
One who constantly worships the goddess Śrī attains unsurpassed prosperity,
as well as supreme strength, beauty, and health.
The king who, endowed with faith, worships here in this world Vibhāvarī— the foremost in the universe, the bestower of boons, meritorious, all-pervading— [attains the highest state].
He obtains all desires at all times.
Thus ends the Śrīvrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now I shall describe to you another vow, the Pañcamūrtivrata.
O mighty-armed one, [he holds] the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and the earth.
Having prepared a circular mandala with perfumes, a person should worship five [deities] at each [point],
beginning from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
Having fasted, bathed outside, and being pure in white garments,
he should offer perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and an abundance of food.
Having performed the worship of all [the deities], one should offer oblations into the fire;
likewise, one should perform the ritual for the house with the names of all the gods.
At that time, one should feed Brahmins with excellent food;
having performed this for a year, at the conclusion of the vow, [one should give] five garments.
O lord of men, one should give five [gifts] of five colors to those who know the Vedas;
by performing this vow, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Having attained human birth, he becomes free from disease,
endowed with strength, devoted to the Dharma, disciplined, and possessed of learning, beauty, and wealth.
Or perhaps he was a king of kings, or else a lord among the twice-born.
Thus ends the vow of the five forms as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O sinless one, I shall describe to you the greatness of the gift of food."
Listen now with a one-pointed mind to that which was proclaimed by the seers of old.
"Give food, give food, give food, Yudhiṣṭhira!
For something given by another provides immediate satisfaction in this world."
In the past, even while observing a vow, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, spoke out of despondency regarding his own younger brother; that too I shall relate to you.
On this earth, which is full of food, we are desirous of food;
by the son of Sumitrā, food has been offered by us into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa.
O Lakṣmaṇa, whatever seed of karma is sown by men, its fruit is inevitably obtained; we have not received that food which was offered into the mouth of a Brahmin.
That which is not to be attained cannot be attained through knowledge or human effort; this is a worldly proverb: "What has been taken up remains."
O Bhārata, compared to the consumption of food, the gift of that same food is supremely beneficial; other types of edible gifts yield results according to their specific nature.
In this regard, tell me the supreme gift; speak of the supreme word of truth:
the conquest of hunger and thirst is gain, and contentment is the supreme happiness.
For men who have bathed, anointed themselves, and adorned with ornaments,
there can be neither happiness nor contentment without food.
In ancient times, there was a sovereign ruler of the earth named Śveta.
By him many sacrifices were performed, battles were won by you,
gifts were bestowed, and the earth was protected in accordance with righteousness.
O King, having enjoyed vast pleasures while standing at the head of your enemies,
you renounced the glory of sovereignty according to the rules for forest-dwellers.
Having enjoyed her, he went to heaven while being honored by the hosts of Maruts;
there he dwells, taking delight together with the Vidyādharas and the Uragas.
Renowned, he is honored by the Siddhas, served by hosts of Apsarases,
praised joyfully by Gandharvas, and followed even by Śakra himself.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and adorned with celestial ornaments,
he would constantly descend from his preeminent celestial chariot to the surface of the earth.
O son of Kuntī, having first abandoned the body, he comes of his own accord;
yet that body remains exactly as it was, preserved by the force of past actions.
Once, while staying in the celestial realm, he approached Brahmā;
having prostrated and joined his palms in reverence, out of world-weariness he spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, by your grace, the happiness of heaven has been attained by me;
O bull among the gods, he is worthy of worship even by all the deities."
But, O Lord, hunger afflicts me exceedingly even though I am situated in heaven;
by it, I eat my own flesh in the absence of food.
Brahmā said:
O Śveta, you who are endowed with a pure lineage, listen to my words.
You have studied, heard the scriptures, given gifts, and satisfied your gurus.
[471] O best of the twice-born, you have granted destruction to one who was hungry,
yet who was endowed with Vedic study, learned in the scriptures, and possessed of restrained senses.
"By which you may attain satisfaction and that which is inexhaustible shall arise for you.
Having heard those words of Viriñci, the lord of the earth was filled with haste.
O best of the Bharatas, Śveta, having fed Agastya with devotion and having fulfilled his vow of giving food as a sacrificial fee, went to heaven satisfied.
After Paulastya had been slain and amidst the conflict between the gods and the dānavas,
Agastya joyfully bestowed the Ekāvalī upon Rāma.
I shall describe to you further the greatness of this vow;
truly, I have declared that there is no gift whatsoever superior to giving food to you.

and seeing this proof, they then felt great faith.
Having completed the vow according to the rules, he then gave various kinds of gifts:
cows, land, clothing, gold, fruits, betel, and garments.
Having given [the gift] to the Brahmins with faith, the two of them were filled with joy at their birth;
by the power of this vow, supreme prosperity abounded in their home.
[490] Endowed with sons, grandsons, and others, and possessed of wealth and grain,
that merchant’s son came to be so through the power of his own vow.
Having enjoyed pleasures on the surface of the earth for more than a full hundred years,
that merchant then brought about the end of his body and met his death.
Messengers dispatched by Yama, with nooses and mallets in their hands,
red-eyed, clad in red garments, with red hair, and terrifying to behold.
With parched bellies and massive bodies, adorned with red flowers,
they seized the merchant's son and bound him with numerous snares.
Then the messengers, bound by nooses, spoke to Śrīkara.
The messengers said:
"If, according to the course of time, you have obtained this human body..."
Why was the realm of Yama acquired by you through the power of evil?
"A human being performs that which cannot be accomplished even by gods and asuras"—
speaking thus, those messengers held hammers raised in their hands.
Desiring to strike him, the merchant’s son drew his sword;
yet by the power of that vow, he became free from fear,
and a beautiful, radiant spear emerged from his body.
I too have dispatched messengers from my own command to bring him back;
however, they engaged in a most terrible battle with the messengers of Yama.
By their own power, those messengers of Yama were repelled by my attendants;
and at that moment, O beloved, my auspicious celestial chariot arrived.
Surrounded by hosts of siddhas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and apsarases,
the merchant’s son ascended a celestial chariot that is available at all times.
O Goddess of the Suras, you have come to my abode through my grace;
by the very fact of your arrival, that place has been granted to you by me myself.
He shall dwell in the city of Śiva until the dissolution of all beings;
thereafter, having enjoyed the sovereignty over the earth girt by the oceans, he shall attain that state.
Having thus obtained the boon, he sported within the teaching of Śiva;
in this manner, O Goddess of the Suras, did this vow become manifest.
By the power of his vow, even a Brahmin, endowed with all virtues,
attains the most auspicious station and rejoices in the world of Śiva.
The greatness of the vow of silence— which destroys death and sin— is difficult for those of small intellect to attain, yet it is free from mental and physical afflictions.
This meritorious vow, which bestows all accomplishments, is auspicious and more secret than the secret;
it has now been told to you with affection and grace.
In the fierce Kali age, O Goddess, it is not possible to perform this vow;
for this vow has forbearance as its root, which is indeed difficult to attain directly in the Kali age.
For this reason, I did not reveal this previously;
for this vow of silence, which accomplishes all goals, is indeed difficult to fulfill.
But for them, upon reaching that day, all evil is destroyed;
he shall have no sorrow, and it will be a constant cause of happiness.
Out of devotion, men perform this vow which delivers them from sin;
indeed, by the power of silence, they dwell in the auspicious abode of Śiva, their bodies pure and cleansed.
Being attended by throngs of apsarases, they roam through various delightful worlds.

And this vow must be performed on the very day [of the lunar date] that is joined with the previous [tithi], because it is a vow dedicated to Rudra; it is not to be performed on the subsequent [tithi] in the forenoon as a rite for the gods. For there is a statement in the *Brahmavaivarta* Purāṇa: "In all vows dedicated to Rudra, the lunar day (tithi) that is facing [the previous one] should be observed. Thus ends the Dīpa-vrata as described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Now follows the conclusion of the Mauna-vrata as described in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of Gods, the greatness of the vow of silence and its narrative have been duly related by you in full detail, and they have been heard by me from your own mouth."
The conclusion of the vow follows immediately thereafter.
With garments, ornaments, umbrellas, sandals, garlands, and so forth,
it is taught that the gift for the preceptor (*ācārya*) is double [the standard], and likewise half of that for the *brahman*.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), equipped with its girdle (mekhalā) and provided with the sides of the sacrificial pit.
Having fashioned an image of Śiva, one should likewise have an image of Pārvatī made;
free from deceit, one should have them made of gold, silver, or copper.
[493] One should fashion a four-armed deity according to one's wealth;
however, even for a poor person, it is prescribed that it be made from gold weighing at least one *māṣa*.

[He holds] a trident and a rosary, adorned with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; the remainder [of the description] is that he bears a rosary. And the goddess is likewise two-armed, auspicious, and with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having bathed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five auspicious decoctions (kaṣāya),...
Then, with fruits and earth, and then with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one should perform the rite with the mantra "Namo ’ghorāya," and thereafter with water from the Gaṅgā.
Likewise, on a sixteen-spoked wheel or even upon a lingodbhava,
one should firmly place a flawless water-pot together with a copper vessel.
There, having been initiated, he should cause the God, together with the Goddess, to sleep according to the procedure taught in the Āgama; he should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa) for the God.

The placement of the limbs (*aṅga-nyāsa*) is taught with the long-voweled *prasāda*. [This means] by means of *prasāda*, that is, by means of the seed-syllable *prasāda*. One should first perform it within oneself and afterwards apply it to the deity.
Thereafter, one should perform [the rite] for the Goddess according to the true principle by means of the seed-syllable of Māyā.
Then one should give two garments, and after that a sacred thread;
likewise, sandalwood paste, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings to the Mothers.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods with betel-leaf mixed with camphor and various kinds of fruits, one should then commence the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña).

The thirty-two deities are to be worshipped in sequence with flowers, incense, and other offerings according to the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the planets (grahayajña); thereafter, the establishment of the fire (agnisthāpana) is prescribed.
One should perform a fire sacrifice there with auspicious fuel-sticks having many feet— that is, with fuel-sticks from the *vaṭa* tree—
and likewise with clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter.
And by performing one hundred and eight oblations with the Tryambaka mantra.
Having completed the Śiva-sacrifice, one should then begin the oblation for the planets (graha-homa);
having performed the worship of the planets once more, one should then begin the offering of the bali-oblation.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should worship the preceptor;
thereafter, one should give a cow, gold, as well as food and garments.
And one should give clothing and other gifts to other Brahmins as well;
one should present sixteen water-pots adorned with garlands and cloths.
One should present the deity together with the goddess to the preceptor;
furthermore, one should act in such a way that the preceptor is fully satisfied.
When he is satisfied, the Lord of Gods is satisfied; it cannot be otherwise.
If he is dissatisfied, the sacrifice is fruitless in this world; of this there is no doubt.
One should give food along with a sacrificial fee to the poor, the helpless, and distinguished persons;
food together with clothing should also be given even to those whose limbs are smeared with ashes.
Or, according to one's means, even if devoid of abundant wealth;
having thus completed everything, he should eat while remaining pure and restrained in speech.
Accompanied by learned and beloved ones, with cooked foods prepared with ghee,
the commencement of this [rite] is prescribed when the night has turned to dawn.
The conclusion is prescribed for the evening, but the meal follows thereafter; having clothed the preceptor together with his wife according to the rule.
"O Goddess, he who thus performs the auspicious conclusion of his vow of silence, saying with restrained speech, 'May Rudra together with Pārvatī be pleased'— [attains the fruit]."
In birth after birth, he shall possess many offspring and great wealth;
thereafter, having gone to the city of Śiva, he shall dwell in the presence of Śiva.
Thus ends the conclusion of the vow of silence (*maunavrata-udyāpana*).
Sūta said:
[He spoke] to the God of gods, the Teacher of the World, who was seated upon the peak of Kailāsa.
Having prostrated, Pārvatī spoke to Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world.
"Tell me of some vow that bestows beauty and good fortune.
Īśvara said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim a vow renowned throughout the three worlds."
It is known as Mahālakṣmī, auspicious and the bestower of all prosperity.
Formerly, in the city of Virāja, there was a king named Śivaśāda;
in that very city, the king had a brahmin who possessed a young daughter.
Then, from afar, he saw a large lake full of water;
having drunk the cool water there, he beheld [the serpent] dwelling within the water.
Having gone to the shore of the Lavaṇa ocean, he saw the splendor of the Apsarases and their host;
approaching them, he asked, "O auspicious ones, why is this being worshipped?"
They said: "O one of great splendor, at our word, manifest in the mortal world as the goddess of the twice-born, known as Mahālakṣmī."
"Even for you, all that is auspicious shall come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Having spoken thus, all the hosts of apsarases vanished on the spot.
Then the king also, intent on hunting, entered the forest;
seeing the young student, the monarch, being hungry, asked for food.
When asked for the reason, he then gave food to the king;
having explained the greatness of the vow, he also communicated the vow to him.
O Great King, understand this auspicious Mahālakṣmī-vrata;
O best of men, it is performed on the eighth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Bhādrapada.
Having praised and worshipped Mahālakṣmī and having offered her a meal of single-grain rice,
one should [offer] a thread smeared with saffron and ghee, provided with sixteen knots.
One should tie a cord of threads of that same length to the hand,
consisting of sixteen strands of dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and young sprouts.
Furthermore, on the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Āśvina,
one should perform a festival for the Goddess, resounding with the music of hundreds of musical instruments.
And having made his own home divine, adorned with an excellent canopy,
its edges hung with pearls and decorated with garlands of flowers.
It was accompanied by *svastika* symbols, *vardhamāna* motifs, and full water-jars;
furthermore, it was fashioned from wood, clay, or sandalwood, or else depicted in a painting.
One should likewise meditate upon Mahālakṣmī with four arms, seated upon the back of a horse,
holding a staff and a rosary in her hands, while her other two hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Seated in the lotus posture, holding a lotus in her hand, she is Padmā, whose eyes are like lotus petals;
she is being bathed by the elephants of the quarters with excellent golden jars.
Then, when she has descended into the vehicle or likewise into the house,
he should perform the bath without agitation, accompanied by the mantra and ritual service.
Having gratified the gods and the ancestors, one should then proceed to the temple;
having bathed [the deity] with the Śrīsūkta, one should thereafter perform the ritual of worship.
Rice flour, barley food, and wheat powder,
along with milk-rice mixed with ghee, in the measure of five handfuls (prasṛti).
Or one may cook auspicious modakas with pure triphalā;
these should be given to Brahmins, and then one should consume them oneself.
Having gathered fruits and prepared eight lamps,
and having thus assembled the necessary materials, he should then begin the worship.
[The image] should have its limbs anointed with white sandalwood paste and be adorned with garlands of white flowers.
Covered with a pair of white garments, one should worship her with white flowers:
"Salutation to Capalā" for the feet, and "Salutation to Cañcalā" for the knees.
Salutations again and again to the hips for Kamalavāsinī, to the navel for Kṣānti;
salutations to the two breasts for Manmathavāsinī, and to the two arms for Lalitā.
One should offer salutations to Utkaṇṭhinī for the throat and to Māyā for the circle of the face;
then, one should respectfully present the food offering (naivedya) to Śrī upon the head.
One should offer the *arghya* according to the prescribed rite with coconuts and other such fruits, with pumpkins, clusters of *karkaṭī*, and other seasonal fruits that are available at that time.
Then, sixteen or eight [offerings] should be given according to one's capacity;
thereafter, at the rising of the moon, one should devotedly offer the *argha* to the Moon.
With flowers like coral fruits, shining with sixteen petals,
you are ever new at the end of each month, being born again and again.
United with the Ocean of Milk, you, Hari, nourish the gods;
O you who have become the very essence of the Milky Ocean, born from the eye of Atri!
"O younger brother of Ramā, salutations to you who illuminate the expanse of the quarters!
O best of kings, a wise man should perform this very rite for a period of sixteen years;
every year, he should worship a Brāhmaṇa together with his wife."
For one who performs [this rite] with devotion in this manner, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees consisting of gold, garments, and gifts of cows, Prosperity shall dwell in his home.
Having heard this, the king respectfully undertook the vow as prescribed;
however, as time passed, he forgot about that cord.
Then his queen, taking [the milk], cast it into the blazing fire;
having placed other [milk] into the vessel, she held it in her own hand.
By the ripening of her karma, misfortune thus fell upon her;
otherwise, she would have received honor from her husband and the prosperity arising from the king.
Whoever performs this great festival for the Goddess year after year.
Fortune never abandons him for three lifetimes;
he obtains long life, health, sovereignty, wealth, and honor.
If one who lacks wealth should especially perform the auspicious Lakṣmī-vrata,
he shall obtain through that vow the fortune born of the grace of Vāsudeva.
Any woman who performs this, having obtained permission from her own husband,
becomes fortunate, beautiful, and possessed of many sons.
He who, having honored the daughter of Bhṛgu, performs with devotion this beloved and purifying vow dedicated to the Enemy of Mura,
shall enjoy sovereignty and prosperity on earth fit for noble people.
Having eaten, he goes to the abode of Madhusūdana.
Thus ends the Mahālakṣmī-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe to you the Caturmūrti-vrata.
But the form of the God of gods, O Yādava, is twofold.
She is fierce, gentle, auspicious, and non-terrible;
she becomes the purifier, cool, and the mistress of fire, for the world consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
The fierce [planets] are declared to be of two kinds, and likewise the gentle ones;
the fierce are Fire and the Sun, while the gentle are the Moon and the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa).
O best of the twice-born, their worship should be performed in sequence beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna.
O King, being supremely pure, one should worship Āditya on the first day,
Vahni on the second day, and Jalādhipa on the third day.
On the fourth day, that best of men, being wise, should duly fashion the forms of the Moon and those [other deities],
and then worship them.
On the first day, one should perform a bath with *vacā* and *haridrā*, accompanied by perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food offerings.
O tiger among the Yadus, on the second day there is a bath with auspicious *āmalaka* fruits;
on the third day with *priyaṅgu*, and on the fourth day with white mustard seeds.
The knower of dharma should perform the fire-oblation day by day with wheat, sesame, grain, and barley; now hear also about the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should wear garments dyed with saffron, use sandalwood and an umbrella,
and sustain one's life every day with milk alone.
O best of men, having performed this vow for a full year,
one enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
He goes to the heavenly world in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun;
having dwelt there for a very long time, he is born into a great family.
Having attained human birth, he becomes free from disease, a lord of the earth, and one who has conquered the faction of his enemies;
established in righteousness, devoted to truth, and disciplined.
He has conquered his senses and is beloved by all people.
Thus ends the Guṇāvāpti-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
O best of the Yadus, Śakra, Kīnāśa, Varuṇa, and Dhanādhyakṣa—
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe, is declared to have four aspects;
having fashioned their forms, the wise man should worship them.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship the Lord of the Thirty-three with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food.
On the second day, one should bathe before the god Yama; on the third, before the lord of the waters;
and on the fourth day, before the presiding deity of wealth—one should perform the bath every day in this manner.

Having reached a riverbank, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with barley, sesame seeds, clarified butter, as well as sesame and rice, following the flow of the water toward the direction of the gods.
Red, yellow, black, and white are the garments according to the sequence of the days;
having performed this auspicious vow for a full year, a man [attains the fruit].
He attains the world of the gods until the dissolution of all beings;
having returned to human birth, he becomes free from disease, a lord of the earth, and a conqueror of his enemies' factions.
Charming to people and fortunate by nature, he then attains the state of a Brahmin once again.
Thus ends the vow for attaining Brahmanhood as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
Viṣṇu, the earth, the sky, and Brahmā constitute his fourfold form;
having fashioned these forms, the wise man should worship them.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship the deity Viṣṇu with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food.
O knower of dharma, in the second and subsequent [offerings], the entire procedure for the earth, the gods, and the Grandfather (Brahmā),
as previously described, shall be performed again.
Having performed this vow for a kalpa, a man shall attain heaven;
having returned to human birth, he becomes free from disease, devoted to dharma, and endowed with wealth.
Endowed with wealth, beauty, and happiness, he was beloved by the people and had conquered the ranks of his enemies.
Thus ends the vow for the attainment of wealth as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
O joy of the Yadus, [I possess] strength, knowledge, sovereignty, and power.
The fourfold form of that God of gods is renowned;
indeed, it is exactly as the form of Kūrma has been described for Bala.
O King, the form of knowledge has been described to you as Narasiṃha;
likewise, the form of Rudra and his sovereignty have been explained by me to you.
His eastern face is Balarāma, and his western face is Vāsudeva; they know his southern face to be the deity Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is Knowledge.
The western face is Īśvara, and likewise the Raudra face removes sins;
the Varāha face is proclaimed as Aniruddha.
Having fasted for three nights, one should first worship the eastern face in the month of Caitra;
then, on the first day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the southern face.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, the western face [of the house] should be given, and likewise the northern in Āṣāḍha;
in the month of Caitra, that which is useful for the household should be given to a twice-born man.
O best of the Yādavas, that which is useful for battle should be given in the month of Vaiśākha;
that which is useful for yoga should be given to the twice-born in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Likewise, in the month of Āṣāḍha, that which is useful for sacrifice should be given;
having performed this vow for four full months, a man [attains the fruit].
Having performed the first breaking of the fast, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
the second breaking of the fast shall take place during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa.
Having enjoyed heaven for ten thousand years as described,
the third breaking of the fast shall take place amidst enjoyments such as good fortune and the like.
Having performed the third breaking of the fast, the pure person should feed the Brahmins a meal consisting mostly of dairy products,
accompanied by grapes and sugar.
Upon reaching the second breaking of his vow, he attains residence in the same world as the God,
and remains in the world of Indra in heaven for the duration specified.
One who desires all prosperity enjoys happiness.
Thus ends the Sarvāpti-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturyuga-vrata.
One should worship the four ages, beginning with Kṛta, with a well-concentrated mind.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the Kṛta Yuga was worshipped with a pair of white garments, as well as with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.
On the first day at the commencement of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform worship.

O twice-born one, one should worship with all kinds of white offerings, such as perfumes and garlands, on the first day; likewise, on the second day, one should worship with red offerings, and thus perform the Tretā sacrifice.
On the third day, the wise man should worship the Dvāpara age with yellow [sandalwood];
on the fourth day, he should fully worship the Tiṣya (Kali) age with black [sandalwood].
One should bathe with *siddhārthaka* seeds, saffron, and likewise turmeric,
and similarly with *āmalaka* fruits, becoming pure day by day.
One should sustain one's life with milk alone every single day;
having performed this vow for one year, which is equivalent to a cycle of four yugas, one rejoices upon the back of the celestial realm.
Having fully worshipped the deity known as Yugamūrti,
he rules over the entire earth throughout the four ages.
Thus ends the section on the cycle of the four yugas as spoken in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another matter, the vow of the four forms (caturmūrtivrata).
And likewise Īśāna, Vahni, Virūpākṣa, and Samīraṇa.
Know, O tiger among the Yadus, that there are four divine forms;
having fashioned their images, the wise man should worship them.
O highly fortunate one, with offerings of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food,
[one should worship] from the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra onwards in due order.
One should perform a ritual bath with water from a well, a lake, or a pond.
Likewise, there should be an oblation (homa) performed with curd, sesame seeds, barley, and ghee;
as well as camphor, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood.
O King, it should likewise be given to Brahmins according to the sequence of days;
for three days, one should eat only what has been honored [as an offering], both at evening and at dawn.
The best of men, observing the vow, should eat for only one day;
having performed this vow for a year, O most excellent of persons.
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled;
having attained human birth, he becomes free from disease, a lord of the earth, and one who has conquered the ranks of his enemies.
"In another birth, he shall become a preeminent leader among the best of the twice-born,
devoted to the Vedas and a performer of many sacrifices.
Thus is described the Devamūrti-vrata as stated in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Hereafter, I shall describe to you the Saptamūrti-vrata,
beginning from the first day (pratipad) of the month of Caitra and proceeding in due order.
The Subhāsvaras, the Barhiṣads, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas;
the Kravyādas, the Apahatas, the Ājyapas, and the Sukālins.
O King, one should worship [the deity] every day with perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
one should offer rice mixed with sesame (kṛsara) as a food offering and perform oblations of sesame seeds into the fire.
O lord of men, one should feed the Brahmins kṛsara and give sesame seeds as a sacrificial fee; likewise, one should remain eating only at night and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Having performed this vow for a year, O best of men,
one should give a pala of silver to a brahmin at the conclusion of the vow.
By the performance of this vow, one shall attain passage through the seven worlds;
honored by the thirty gods, one becomes a bird capable of moving at will.
O lord of men, having completed the twelve years in this manner, a person indeed attains liberation from saṃsāra at the end of his life.
Having attained human birth, he shall become a lord of the earth.
Thus ends the Pitṛvrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Beginning from the month of Caitra, day by day during the dark fortnight...
One should perform the worship of the netherworld (pātāla) in sequence, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad).
The earth may be rough, or moist, or from the netherworld (pātāla), or consist of blue clay;
it may also be red earth, yellow earth, or even white or black soil.
With gold, perfumes, garlands, and abundant food offerings,
by the offering of lamps filled with ghee, and by the satiation of the fire;
Having thus observed the vow of eating only at night for a full year,
one should, at the conclusion of the vow, present lamps in the houses of the twice-born.
O Indra among kings, whether wearing white garments or those of various colors,
a man who performs this vow shall become a sovereign lord of half the earth.
O Great King, thousands of Daitya maidens delight that man who has gone to the netherworld for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
In due time, having descended here into the world of men,
he shall become a king who crushes the hosts of his enemies,
endowed with strength, beauty, and wealth.
He is the great destination, the foremost of all the world.
Thus ends the Pātāla-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform it every day for seven days.
Suprabhā, Kāñcanākṣī, Viśālā, and Mānasodbhavā.
One should always worship Meghanādā, Suveṇu, and likewise Vimalodakā with devotion, and perform the ritual bath outside.
Every day, one should perform a fire-oblation for them by name with curd;
and on this occasion, one should feed Brahmins an excellent meal accompanied by curd.
Likewise, he should eat rice with ghee only once at night;
having thus performed the Sārasvata vow for a year, the man [attains his goal].
Having dwelt there for a very long time, when he is born again in the human state, he becomes either a lord of men who has conquered the faction of his enemies,
or an excellent brahmin who performs many sacrifices.
Endowed with beauty, grain, and wealth, he shall be possessed of sons and be dear to the people.
Thus ends the Saptasāgara-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śrī Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform this daily for seven days.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.

One should worship the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha day by day with fruits and flowers produced in season, along with milk and other seasonal fruits. One should perform the ritual bath outside every day and observe the practice of eating only at night.
One should daily perform a fire-oblation with sesame seeds accompanied by the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
furthermore, one should satisfy the Brahmins there with fruits, roots, and dairy products.
And water-vessels filled with milk should be given to the twice-born;
having performed this for a year, [one should give them] to a wandering ascetic who maintains the sacred fires.
O King, one should give a black antelope skin as previously instructed by me;
having performed this vow, a person finds the means to liberation.
Having attained the means to liberation, one undoubtedly attains liberation;
or else, one attains the world of the gods,
or that of the god Viṣṇu, or that of Īśvara.
By that vow of his grandfather or great-grandfather, he quickly became one of great majesty.
Thus ends the Saptarṣi-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
[509] Īśvara said:
The ninth, the eighth, the full moon day, and the fourteenth;
O Goddess, the man who eats during these auspicious days does not attain equality with them.
"He attains the status of a Gaṇapati, free from rivals and beyond reproach.
Thus is described the vow of fasting on the ninth lunar day and subsequent days as stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
He who observes the fast on the eighth day of the dark fortnight by eating only at night, and likewise on the seventh day of the dark fortnight— the word "should fast" being understood here—
attains happiness in this very world and an auspicious state in the next.
Thus ends the Sukha-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa.
Āditya said: "On the seventh and likewise on the sixth lunar day of both fortnights..."
He who, for one year, eats only at night, self-restrained and with senses conquered.

Whatever supreme merit is said to belong to those who constantly perform sacrificial sessions (sattra), whatever merit belongs to those who speak the truth, and whatever merit belongs to those who approach their wives during the proper season; [all that is attained by him].
"Having obtained that entire fruit, he comes to my world"—
thus is the Arkavratam described in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
On the eighth and the ninth day of both fortnights as well, [one should observe this vow].
He who, devoted to the worship of Caṇḍikā, does not eat for one year;
"He goes to the supreme abode where that Caṇḍikā resides.
Thus ends the Caṇḍikā-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Atri said:
And for those women devoted to the vow who worship Lalitā, the bestower of all happiness,
widowhood shall never occur.
Whatever deities there may be— whether humans, serpents, or rākṣasas—
they all come under one's control when the worship of Lalitā has been performed.
In ancient times, Daśāśva, Yayāti, Mucukunda, Janaka, and Purūravas performed this for the sake of the continuous increase of their lineage.
These and many others attained a kingdom free from thorns;
therefore, with every effort, one should worship the auspicious Lalitā.
Anasūyā said:
O Brahman, in which month and on which lunar day is this excellent vow performed?
What are the mantras? To whom does this worship belong, and for whom is the gift prescribed?
Atri said:
Listen, O lady of faultless limbs, to the ritual for the worship of Lalitā:
on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvina, one should observe the practice of eating only at night.
A divine image made of gold, adorned with all ornaments, should be placed in an auspicious location; in its center, a beautiful bathing pool and a splendid altar should be constructed.
One cubit in length and half a span in width, provided with ten grains [of rice],
five earthen deities should be placed in the corners of the altar.
Having sprinkled it with water, the Goddess should be carefully installed in its center;
[therein] a flawless, water-filled jar accompanied by a copper vessel.
There, an auspicious golden image of the goddess Lalitā should be installed;
furthermore, one should have a silver image of the Moon joined with Rohiṇī made and placed in front.
Having established Hīśvara on the right and Vighnanāśana on the left,
one should worship everything there with the root mantra and the Gāyatrī.

The wise one should worship the image, which displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and the boon-granting gesture (varada) in its right hands, while holding a citron (bījapūraka) in its left hand, and which is placed upon a jar and draped with cloth.
Having placed a water-pot nearby, along with fine flowers, fruits, and sandalwood,
one should place cakes filled with ghee upon the pot during the first [offering].
One should worship the auspicious image with perfumes, flowers, and food offerings;
with *śatapatra* flowers on the first day, with *jāti* flowers on the second,
with *campaka* flowers on the third, and likewise with *pāṭala* flowers on the fourth.
In the seventh [day] with bilva leaves, and in the eighth with those produced from the yūthikā flower.
In the ninth [month], with *kūṣmāṇḍikā* flowers; in the tenth, with golden flowers:
"Oṃ! You are the Goddess of the gods of gods; you are the Mother, you are the Father of the world.
By your grace, O Goddess, may widowhood not befall me in this life."
The prayer mantra:
"O Goddess Lalitā, you are always to be worshipped by gods and asuras;
by your grace, may beauty, good fortune, and long life ever be mine."
The mantra for worship:
O you who are dark as the petal of a blue lotus, O you with a face as beautiful as a white lotus!
Accept this flower, fragrance, fruit, and water; accept this *arghya* offering. Homage, homage!
The Arghya mantra:
Having worshipped the head with "Lalitā," one should worship the feet as "Umā. Having worshipped the knees as "Girijā," Rati is prescribed for the region of the face.
One should worship the goddess Candrikā at the navel,
Lakṣmī in the region of the two sides of the belly, and the daughter of Menakā on the breasts and the two arms.
She is named Subhagā on the face and Śaṅkarapriyā on the forehead;
having thus worshipped that goddess, one should present the food offering.
Such an image should be worshipped daily for ten days; ten *ghṛtapūra* cakes should be offered as *naivedya*, and one should consume them.
The second [tithi] should be worshipped with sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka) that cause the clear manifestation of the Somāli [deity],
as well as with nectar-like fruits, sugar-coated cakes, and pieces of fried pastries wrapped in dough.
One should worship with *udumbara* wood and *kokarasa* every day; one should cause ten offerings of food (*naivedya*) to be presented in each vessel (*karaka*).
One should worship with fruits and flowers produced in their proper season for ten days;
one should offer oranges, coconuts, and citrons.
She should be worshipped for ten days with dyed cloths, all kinds of ornaments and decorations, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
When the tenth day has arrived, at night during the rising of the moon,
having worshipped the Goddess according to the prescribed rites, one should offer an oblation (arghya) to the Moon.
Taking water in a conch shell together with flowers, fruits, and sandalwood:
"You are ever new, being born again and again at the end of each month."
"Accept this arghya from me, O Moon, together with Rohiṇī.
This is the mantra for the arghya offering to the Moon.
[Offer] water-pots filled with water and provided with fruits and foods.
By acting thus with resolve, a man shall become one who has fulfilled his duty.
By this method, a woman shall never encounter widowhood.
O best of sages, this vow was previously performed by me:
that one should cause a water-pot filled with food to be given to a woman who has recently given birth.
On the tenth day, one should present the image to the preceptor for two watches;
one should honor the preceptor, together with his wife, with garments and jewels.
"O lovely-eyed one, an image should be offered every year;
whoever performs this according to the rite for ten days,"
For as many years as the Lord has been worshiped by gods and asuras,
O auspicious one, you have obtained such a fruit for each single year.
All this has been told to you, O auspicious lady, regarding what was done in another birth;
indeed, even sins equal to the killing of a Brahmin do not touch you.
Wealth, grain, good fortune, sons, and grandsons increase for that man who,
having risen early in the morning, recites or likewise listens to this.
"Completely liberated from all sins, one shall attain supreme perfection.
Thus ends the Daśarathalalitā-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Furthermore, O Lord of the Gods, my mind has been purified by devotion to you;
I am here to hear the great words of Dharma as they are being spoken.
O Janārdana, whether even a tiny portion has been given, or a great sacrifice performed, or whether the sacred narrative has been heard or even recounted, it becomes a source of merit.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pāṇḍava, I shall tell you a secret ordained by the gods,
which has never been spoken by me to anyone, O Bhārata, even to one who is very dear.
The third day of the month of Vaiśākha, the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
and the [ninth] day of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya.
The thirteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Māgha.
The third day of Vaiśākha is equal to the Kṛta Yuga;
and that ninth day of Kārttika is indeed equal to the Tretā Yuga.
The thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya is considered equal to the Dvāpara age;
O King, the fifteenth day of Māgha is said here to be the beginning of the Kali age.
"O King of kings, these four are remembered as the origins of the Yugas;
for this reason, they are called 'the beginnings of the Yugas' by the ancient sages.
Thus [it is said]. Fasting, austerity, charity, as well as the performance of recitation and fire-offerings—
But when anything whatsoever is performed, it shall become ten millionfold.
On the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, you should worship Nārāyaṇa, the Teacher of the World, together with Śrī, using flowers, incense, and ointments.
Then, with an abundance of garments, ornaments, and various kinds of food offerings,
a cow made from one āḍhaka of salt should be placed before him.
O best of the Kuru lineage, O calf, it should be prepared with a fourth part [of the materials],
having been placed upon a goat skin and fashioned according to the prescribed rite.
One should present it to a Brāhmaṇa according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures, saying:
"May Śrīdhara, the Lord of Śrī, the Auspicious One, the Master of Śrī, be pleased."
O descendant of Bharata, by giving a cow to a Brahmin according to this rite,
one obtains without doubt the fruit of gifting a thousand cows.
In the same way, on the ninth day of the month of Kārttika, a man who observes the *naktabhuk* fast,
having bathed in a river, a pond, or even in a natural pool dug by the gods;
Then one should worship the blue-throated Lord, accompanied by Umā and the bestower of boons,
with flowers, incense, and other offerings, as well as food offerings, lamps, perfumes, and so forth.
One should give a cow made of sesame seeds according to the procedure prescribed in the Purāṇas, and should proclaim:
"May Nīlakaṇṭha, the eightfold-formed one, be pleased."
Following that, O Pārtha, merit is attained; it is described as being gained by eating only at night.
By giving a cow made of sesame seeds, one shall reach the world of Śiva.
On the thirteenth day of the month of Nabhasya,
one should worship the ancestors there with milk-rice (pāyasa), flowers, and ghee.
One should devoutly feed Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
for the sake of the ancestors, a cow with her calf and a bronze milking vessel should be given.
O illustrious one, here before your eyes is a young, prolific cow;
likewise present are her father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.
"In the same way, let my three ancestors beginning with the maternal grandfather be pleased by this gift of a cow"; having said this, he should dismiss them.
O Indra among kings, the merit that is obtained by performing this cannot be described by anyone else even in hundreds of years.
A man obtains here itself sons, grandsons, and all his great desired wealth, as well as the supreme goal in the world beyond.
On the fifteenth day of the month of Māgha, having worshipped the Grandfather (Brahmā),
the God accompanied by Gāyatrī and adorned with the Vedas and Vedāṅgas.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa a cow made of fresh butter, accompanied by various kinds of fruits, along with gold and her calf.
One should recite: "May the lotus-born Grandfather be pleased with me today!
Whatever is difficult to obtain in heaven, in the netherworld, or in the mortal realm—that one obtains without doubt through the grace of the lotus-born."
And whatever other gifts are given,
O Great King, even in great abundance on the first days of the eons, they indeed become inexhaustible.
Even if one devoid of wealth gives a small amount of property according to his own power, that too becomes inexhaustible; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Whether wealthy or even destitute, one should give according to one's means;
for if anyone should give something else, however small, even while being poor.
All that shall become inexhaustible during the beginnings of the Yugas, without a doubt,
through the application of wealth according to one's means and by means of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) accomplished through the *Ṛgveda*.
Land, gold, a house, clothing, beds, seats,
umbrellas, sandals, and vehicles should be given by one who desires auspiciousness.
Having thus given according to one's ability and having fed the twice-born as well,
one should afterwards eat with a joyful mind, restrained in speech, together with one's kinsmen.
Whatever sin there may be— whether verbal, mental, or likewise physical—
all that goes to destruction through the worship performed on the lunar day marking the beginning of a Yuga.
Then, being sung of by the Gandharvas and honored by the gods and asuras, O Pārtha, he shall dwell for one kalpa in the world of Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever is given, they say that becomes ten millionfold;
likewise, bathing and recitation are all certainly inexhaustible,
O King, on the Yugādi and Parva days which are themselves inexhaustible.
Vyāsa and the other eminent sages have stated this; it is not otherwise.
Thus ends the vow for the beginning of the Yuga as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Janārdana, on the third day of the bright fortnight in the month of Vaiśākha...
He brought forth the Yugas and initiated the Kṛta age;
he brought the triple-pathed river from the world of Brahmā down to the surface of the earth.
And King Bhagīratha, who brought happiness to the sons of Sagara, [is honored] therein;
one should perform a fire-oblation with barley grains and worship Viṣṇu with barley grains.
One should give barley to the twice-born and, being self-restrained, consume barley;
likewise, bathing, giving gifts, recitation, ancestral rites, as well as fire-offerings, chanting, and so forth [are performed with barley].
Whatever is performed there with faith leads to infinity;
especially at the confluence of rivers, everything is said to be inexhaustible.
Thus ends the rule for the beginning of the Yugas as stated in the Ādipurāṇa.
Brahmā said:
"On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Prauṣṭhapada..."
The Yuga has descended into that Tretā, and he remains concentrated therein.

The connection is that when this Tretā age has ceased, the Yuga has descended on this lunar day; thus, "the latter half" is understood. On that lunar day, being composed in mind, one should bathe in a lake or a pond after having smeared oneself with cow’s urine, cow dung, dūrvā grass, and clay.
He who bathes the Lord of the Three Worlds, whose banner is Garuḍa, at the beginning of a Yuga, has undoubtedly performed a Śrāddha at Gayā.
Bathed with holy water, milk, and clarified butter, and then anointed, worshipped, and saluted, he shall indeed go to the city of Viṣṇu.
At the beginning of the Yuga, Hari, the creator of the Yuga and the bestower of liberation upon men,
indeed exists with every effort as the Lord of the World at the start of the age.
Hari, the remover of all suffering, is to be worshipped by people with devotion.
Thus ends the vow for the advent of the Yugas as declared in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.

Thus concludes the section on vows for various lunar days (*tithi*) within the Vrata-khaṇḍa of the *Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Hemādri, the sovereign over all faculties, proficient in all branches of knowledge, and the supreme king of great kings under the illustrious Mahādeva.
[520] Now begins the twenty-second chapter. Now, the observances dedicated to the days of the week (vāravratas).

Now, following the sequence beginning with the Sun, the learned Hemādri, whose playful speech brings joy to the virtuous, speaks of the vows for the seven days of the week while his mind remains attentive.
May Lakṣmī be ever with him, who is purified by the friendship arising from the hymn to the deeds of his beloved.
In that regard, first are the Āditya-vows.
Ḍihī said: "O Brahmin, those who worship the Sun-god according to the Āditya-vow..."
Tell me, what fruit do they obtain through bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts?
Brahmā said:
Those men who perform the śrāddha ceremony when the day of the Sun (Sunday) has arrived,
having reached seven births, become free from disease.
Having indeed attained dispassion in this world, they go to the realm of the Sun.
Those who always observe the fast according to the Āditya-vrata and recite the Mahāśvetā mantra obtain their desired fruit.
Especially on Sunday, while reciting the six-syllable mantra of Mahāśveta, one who recites [it] for the lords of the Gaṇas attains the state of Vairocana.
The Ādityahṛdaya is the yantra. And its great six-syllable mantra is: *hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ*. [The invocation is: *hrāṃ sīṃ sa śūryāya namaḥ*.
Whosoever, endowed with faith, worships the Sun on a Sunday and observes the night-fast (nakta), that person goes to the world of the immortals.
Thus ends the Ādityavrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Āditya said:
"The man who performs the *nakta* fast for one year on my day (Sunday)..."
O bird, he is a celibate student who has conquered anger and is devoted to my worship.
Having reached the end of the year and having fed my devotees and the best of the twice-born, he should say with joy: "May the Sun be pleased with me."
And whoever is endowed with devotion goes to my world;
that man shall certainly attain the world created by Bhānu.
Thus is described the Āditya-vrata as stated in the Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa:
On a Sunday coinciding with the Hasta constellation, one should observe the saura-nakta-vrata;
having bathed and honored the brahmins, that man shall indeed become free from disease.
Thus ends the solar *naktavrata* as declared in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*.
[522] Now follows the procedure for the *nandā* and other days on Sundays.
Brahmā said:
On the twelfth lunar day, under the asterism Hasta, on the day of the great-souled Sun,
there were Nanda, Bhadra, Saumya, Kāmada, Putrada, Jaya, Jayanta, and Vijaya; thus did he attend upon the Sun and the other deities.
It is a heart-remedy that destroys disease and eliminates great ailments;
here, jasmine flowers and excellent white sandalwood [are used].
Having offered incense made of the finest guggulu and an offering of cakes to a brahmin, one should then eat those cakes while remaining silent.
One should prepare an excellent cake measuring one *prastha*,
made either from wheat or from barley, and mixed with fragrant mustard seeds.
One desiring welfare should give gold along with [the gift] to the Brahmins;
whether on earth or in the divine realm, one should bestow it as a fulfillment for the Sun.
The gods are the Brahmins of the earth, as well as those others who are Brahmins.
A cake (*pūpa*) or a fried pancake (*maṇḍaka*) should indeed be given with the recitation of mantras; such offerings as cakes should be presented with devotion, dedicated primarily to Āditya.
The mantra for the gift:
"O Brahmin, may this most excellent cake from the western direction, produced by the splendor of the sun and fashioned by the hand of the queen, lead to my welfare."
The mantra for receiving [the gift]: "I always bestow upon you this *maṇḍaka*, beloved of the Sun, which grants desires, bestows happiness, confers merit, grants sons, and likewise grants wealth."
"These two great mantras, O best of the Gaṇas, are dear to Ravi for the giving and taking of the cake; of this there is no doubt today."
O Lord, this procedure for mantras has been proclaimed for the welfare of men;
whoever worships the god Ravi according to this rite, [attains success].
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of the Sun;
neither poverty nor diseases shall afflict the family of that high-souled one.
Whoever honors this mantra always expands it inexhaustibly;
having taken refuge in the world of the Sun, he becomes a king upon the earth.
"Endowed with many kinsmen, that man shall be like the sun.
Thus is the ritual for Nandā as declared in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*.
O Hero, it occurs in the month of Bhādrapada during the bright fortnight.
O best of the Kuru lineage, that sixth [lunar day] is proclaimed as Bhadrā;
whoever should observe a vigil or even a fast on that occasion, [attains great merit].
One who has mounted a laughing vehicle goes to the world of laughter;
likewise, one who offers jasmine flowers and white sandalwood here [attains the same].
