And likewise, victory-incense and an offering of milk-rice (pāyasa) are supreme.
Regarding victory-incense and incense, as stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"O Brahmin, [the incense should consist of] flawless silhaka, śrīkhaṇḍa, and likewise aguru."
O twice-born one, camphor, as well as the root, sugar, and cinnamon bark;
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, the Sovereign of the World, at midday,
and having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should then eat while remaining restrained in speech.
One should offer milk-rice with jaggery, and jaggery together with clarified butter;
one obtains all desires, such as sons, wealth, and so forth.
Thus ends the procedure for Bhadrā as declared in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"O Hero, when the asterism is Rohiṇī and the day of the Sun (Sunday) occurs..."
O Hero, he who possesses gentleness by birth is proclaimed as truly gentle;
likewise, bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, and the worship of deities and others [are his duties].
There is no doubt that it shall be inexhaustible for that high-souled one on whose day a man, being composed, worships the Sun at night.
He goes to the world of the high-souled god Bhāskara;
there indeed are red lotuses as well as red sandalwood.
Fragrant incense should also be offered here, along with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) as the supreme food offering (*naivedya*).
"He is Brahman"—thus has my mind been resolved.
O son, when the Sun-god (*Bhāskara*) is thus worshipped, he shall become the bestower of sons.
Therefore, this lunar day of the god is proclaimed as one that bestows sons.
Thus is the rite for obtaining a son described in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*;
that which occurs during the southern transit of the sun is proclaimed as the *Jaya*.
O Lord, fasting, as well as bathing, giving gifts,
and performing penance on the day of the Sun, shall become a hundredfold more meritorious when performed here.
Therefore, one should perform [the rite] at night and so forth; from this, the prescribed rule is a hundredfold more meritorious.
Thus ends the procedure for victory as declared in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
[525] Jayanta is situated under the constellation Uttarā; Āditya is the leader of the host, and on this day the Lord, the Master of the Gaṇas, is to be worshipped.
The Lord of Gods, being worshipped there, bestows a thousandfold fruit for acts such as bathing and giving charity.
In this case, bathing with ghee, milk, and sugarcane juice is prescribed;
likewise, an ointment of saffron paste is highly recommended, as it is pleasing to the Sun-god.
O Dear One, the incense rite should be performed with guggulu resin and the food offering (naivedya) should consist of black gram;
having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should indeed perform [the remaining rites] with the mantra.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins with sweetmeats (modaka), sesame cakes (tila-śaṣkulī), and other foods;
he who worships the Sun in this manner when the moon is in conjunction with the Rohiṇī asterism (Prājāpatya-ṛkṣa).
That [place] is named Śokavijaya, which removes all sins and fears;
there, every fruit of meritorious action possesses the quality of a jewel.
The Blessed Lord, the God who is the leader of the hosts, grants [the fruits of] bathing, giving, recitation, burnt offerings, and the worship of the ancestors and the gods when he is honored.
Whether by night or while fasting, the Sun-god should be worshipped here;
having become the sovereign of all worlds, one attains the state of the Lord of the Seven Suns.
Thus is the Tripurasūdana-vrata for the day of the Sun, as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
Having performed the morning ablutions and worshipped the Maker of Day,
one should stand facing the Sun until the setting of the Sun.
Reciting prayers with devotion, he leaned against a pillar,
out of devotion to Mahādeva and to Divākara, the God of gods.
Beholding and reciting the Mahāśvetā mantra, one should remain until the setting of the sun,
having worshipped the Sun-god with offerings of fragrances and flowers.
One should give a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin and then eat while restraining one's speech;
in this very manner, a person should observe the vow for the pleasure of Bhāskara.
"Bhānumān, being pleased with him, shall grant all his heart's desires.
Thus is described the ritual for facing the Sun as stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*. For when there is a transit of the sun (*saṃkramaṇa*), O Lord of Gaṇas, it is the day of the Sun (*ravivāra*).
He is named Ādityahṛdaya, the one dear to Ādityahṛdaya.
Having taken refuge with me there at night and having worshipped the deity with diligence,
you shall afterwards go to my city and become a lord of men upon the earth.
Standing facing the sun, the wise man should go to the abode of the Sun and recite the Ādityahṛdaya one hundred and eight times.
The person who worships the Sun with devotion, endowed with faith,
attains all desires while remaining established in the Ādityahṛdaya.
Thus ends the procedure for the Ādityahṛdaya as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
When a Tuesday falls on a Saturday,
that is indeed proclaimed as a most excellent conjunction (vara), which removes all diseases and fears.
Pūrvāphalgunī has Bhaga as its presiding deity;
whoever worships the Sun there with auspicious perfumes and ointments, [attains prosperity].
Freed from all diseases, he goes to the abode of the Sun;
having placed an arka leaf in a fold [of cloth] on a Sunday coinciding with the Puṣya asterism, O observer of good vows.
A wise man should worship with devotion before the Deity at night;
indeed, he should worship the twice-born here with devotion according to this ritual procedure.
Freed from all diseases, one shall go to the abode of Ādityakāla;
from there, one shall proceed to the world that is devoid of the sound "huṃ."
"A twice-born man is the Sun; a Brahmin is one devoid of the sound 'huṃ'.

Thus is the procedure for the *rogahavis* (oblation for disease) as stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*. O observer of good vows, [this applies] on the day of the Lord who is the master of the solar eclipse.
He, renowned as Gośrutibhūṣaṇa, would constantly worship them together with one another.

Gośruti is Cakṣuḥśravas; he whose ornament is that [serpent] is "Sarpabhūṣaṇa" (one adorned with serpents)—this is the meaning. Whoever should constantly worship Pataṅga, the lord of the pannagas, with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, or likewise with various hymns of praise.
Having fasted and being purified during a solar eclipse, O best of the Gaṇas,
one should recite the Mahāśvetā mantra and the lord of the planets as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch.
O Destroyer of Tripura, having fed the Brahmins, one should then eat while restraining one's speech on this day, which is joined with the Sun and the planets.
O Bull-bannered Lord, whatever merit is produced by these actions— such as bathing, giving gifts, and recitation— all that shall become auspicious.

O best of virtuous ones, there is no doubt that for those who perform [meritorious acts] on this day, the fruit is infinite, just as the word of the Sun-god declares. Therefore, wise men should perform meritorious deeds on the day of the Sun.
Having thus eaten at night, or likewise observed a fast,
those who perform this on a Sunday attain the supreme goal.

Whatever other gift is given during that [time] is considered equal to the gift of a cow; it is auspicious, meritorious, conducive to fame, and likewise bestows long life and the fulfillment of desires.
O mighty-armed one, these twelve [names] of the high-souled Sun have been declared; when performed through speech, they remove the fear of all sins.
Having performed this for them according to the rules during the watch of the Bull-vehicled One,
one may then go to the supreme world of the high-souled Vṛṣaketu.
Thus ends the procedure for the Nandā and other vows as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Śrī Nārāyaṇa said:
Having prepared the ground, one should draw a beautiful lotus adorned with a pericarp.
It was endowed with twelve petals, beautiful and delightful to the mind.
Among those, however, one should place four [petals] and in their midst the Sun;

that is to say, of those twelve petals, four petals connected to the pericarp (*karṇikā*) should be made in the center of the lotus, while eight are outside of that—meaning [one petal each] on the twelve petals. One should place Sūrya on the eastern petal and Divākara in the southeast.
One should place Vivasvat in the southern direction and Bhaga in the south-western direction.
One should place Varuṇa on the western petal, Indra in the northwest,
Āditya in the north, and Savitṛ immediately beyond that.
One should place the pericarp upon the eastern petals of the horse;
with the southern [petal], one should place the thousand-rayed Mārtaṇḍa on the western petal.
[529] But having thus placed the god Ravi in the north and Bhāskara in the center, the worship of Sūrya shall take place in all directions.
One should worship the All-facing One with karavīra and arka flowers, or with sandalwood, aguru, and campaka, as well as with whatever flowers are available in season.
O glorious Divākara, bring about the destruction of birth, death, old age, sorrow, and the fear of saṃsāra; destroy poverty and calamity!
With the mantra of salutation, with the vyāhṛtis beginning with the praṇava, [one should say]:
"I praise Agni; homage to you, O Jātavedas; let there be homage to you."
I am able for you; homage to you! I am able for strength; homage, homage!
O Agni, come hither for the feast; O you who contain Agni within, let there be homage to you!
"Be gracious to us, O Goddess; salutations to you, the eye of the world, salutations again and again!
O Pāṇḍava, first seize the day of the Sun with your hand."
Thereafter, one should worship for seven days starting from Sunday;
eating only once a day or at night, one should honor Brahmins during the day and devoutly give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to a Brahmin according to one's ability.
O Bhānu, you are the eye of the world; you are [the eye] of all of us who possess bodies.
You are the goal of all followers of Sāṃkhya, and you are the supreme refuge of the yogins.
You are the unbarred gate for those seeking liberation;
by you the world is sustained, and by you the world is illuminated.
By you it is purified; by you the seedless [state] is protected;
for at the proper time, the Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas attend upon you.
Worshipped by hosts of sages, may the Protector, who is to be honored with the mantras prescribed in one's own Vedic branch,
protect you as you travel upon your divine chariot while seeking a boon.
The Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Guhyakas, and Pannagas;
and indeed the thirty-three gods, and the hosts of Vaimānika deities.
Both Sopaṇḍra and Mahendra have attained their desired success;
indeed, by worshipping you, they have reached their heart's desires.
Adorned with divine mandāra garlands, resembling the vidyādharas of heaven,
there were the divine hosts of ancestors, as well as those who were like the sun and those who were human.
Having worshipped you, they quickly attain preeminence—
namely the Vasus, Maruts, Rudras, and the wise Sādhyas.
The Siddhas, such as the Vālakhilyas and others, have attained preeminence among living beings;
for you are equal to them in all the worlds, including those where the sound of the Vedas resounds.
I do not consider that to be truly great which surpasses the sun;
there are other beings who are both powerful and mighty.
But their brilliance or power is not such as yours;
for you are all the luminaries, you are the Lord of all lights.
In you reside both truth and untruth, and all states of being characterized by goodness (sāttvika).
You are the wheel made of adamant by Viśvakarman with its excellent hub;
you are Bali, intoxicated with pride, who was destroyed by Śārṅgadhanvan.
Taking you up with your rays during the summer, you [withdraw] the vital heat of all embodied beings;
and again, during the rainy season, you release it along with thundering and discordant sounds.
Some great clouds scorch, others burn, and others roar;
some flash with lightning and others pour down rain—such are your rays during the rainy season.
Neither fire, nor outer garments,
nor woolen blankets bring such comfort to people afflicted by cold winds as do your rays.
The lord of thirteen islands illuminates the earth;
you alone act for the welfare of all three worlds.
If you were not to arise, this world would be consumed by ruin,
and wise men would not engage in the pursuit of virtue, wealth, and pleasure.

Through your grace, the primary sacrificial rites— consisting of animal sacrifices, the Bheṣṭi-mantras, and the performance of ascetic penances— are attained by the multitudes of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes.
The day that is proclaimed as belonging to Brahmā is equal in duration to a Yuga;
you are declared by those who know time to be both its beginning and its end.
The fire of universal destruction remains after having reduced the three worlds to ashes;
yet from your rays are born various-colored and highly precious [gems].
Accompanied by Sairāvatī and Aśanī, they perform the consecration of all beings;
having divided himself twelvefold, he has attained the state of the twelve Ādityas.
Having withdrawn everything into the single ocean, you dry it up with your rays;
they call you Indra, you are Rudra, you are Viṣṇu, and you are Prajāpati.
You are Agni; you are the subtle mind; you are the Lord, the eternal Brahman. You are Haṃsa, Savitṛ, Bhānu, Aṃśumālin, and Vṛṣākapi.
You are Vivasvat, Mihira, Pūṣan, Mitra, and likewise Dharma;
you are the thousand-rayed Āditya, you are austerity, and you are the Lord of Cows.
Mārtaṇḍa, Arka, Ravi, Sūrya, Śaraṇya, Dinakṛt,
as well as Divākara, Saptasapti, Vyomakeśin, and Virocana.
You are celebrated as the swift-moving, the destroyer of penance, and the one with green horses;
whoever performs worship with devotion on the seventh or the eighth lunar day, [attains the fruit].
Fortune attends that man who acts without despondency; for them, there are various calamities, yet no mental anxieties nor physical diseases.
Even one who performs this prostration with a distracted mind while reciting the verse shall be freed from all diseases and rid of all sins.
Those devoted to your being become happy and long-lived;
you, moreover, are here for me who desires to achieve the fulfillment of all my wishes.
Out of faith, you ought to give immeasurable food to the Lord of Food,
as well as to all his other attendants who have taken refuge at the edge of your feet.
Māṭhara, Aruṇa, Daṇḍa, and the others,
together with Nikṣubha and Kṣubhā, were filled with loving-kindness and paid due respect to those who stood by their side.
I pay homage to all of them; may they protect me who has come for refuge.
Whoever else, with a purified mind, should recite this hymn here while focused in meditative concentration, shall obtain their desired boon.
The Sun shall grant him his heart's desire;
he shall obtain it, even if it be exceedingly difficult to attain.
Whether it be a woman or a man, whoever recites this daily at both twilights shall be liberated from calamity upon encountering it; a barren woman shall obtain sons and wealth.
Whether born of desire or anger, or likewise born of intoxication or pride—
even sin arising from a thousand lifetimes— is destroyed at that very moment.
Endowed with wealth and grain, that man enjoys good fortune for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Having ascended a supreme celestial chariot, she is honored in the world of the Sun;
yet, a woman who may be childless and destitute of wealth and good fortune—
"A woman of beautiful form obtains sons, wealth, and good fortune. Thus is described the Divākara-vrata as stated in the Bhaviṣyapurāṇa.
Skanda said:
Listen to this supreme, divine, and most meritorious method of worshipping the Sun,
by performing which one shall obtain the complete fruit of all desires.
On the shore of the ocean was the auspicious city of Dvāravatī,
while Vāsudeva, the best of the Yadus, governed as the crown prince.
Durvāsas, an emanation of Śaṅkara, arrived as a visitor;
there he was honored by Kṛṣṇa with offerings of water for the hands and feet, a seat, and other honors.
Whatever food was given to that sage according to his desire,
he was honored by Kṛṣṇa as that sage departed.
It is said that when Śambu’s son suddenly spoke thus to him,
that tiger among sages, though already enraged, himself gave way to further anger.
"How can it be right for me to feel resentment now that I have been honored by him?
Having gone there, he said to Nārada, "O sir, I have been laughed at by Śāmba."
"In another manner, you must provide him with instruction.
Having been addressed thus, Nārada departed for Dvārakā to the presence of Kṛṣṇa.
"O son of Devakī, show me your own army;
O Lord, I shall know it once I have seen it, crowded as it is with elephants, horses, and chariots."
Released by Nārada himself, the powerful one acted exactly as instructed;
but when Bala was shown to him, he said, "Śāmba is not to be seen here."
"I myself shall quickly bring you from Dvāravatī to your presence.
Having been addressed thus by the sage, O son of Jāmbavatī, listen!
Thus was Śṛṅgāra brought there by the sight of Makaradhvaja;
having gone there, the gopīs, who were under Kṛṣṇa’s protection, embraced and kissed him.
O sinless one, the blessed Nārada spoke thus regarding that misconduct.
"O lord of men, become a leper," was the curse uttered by the enraged son of Sura;
as soon as this was said, the son likewise became afflicted with the disease of leprosy.
Śāmba, having prostrated, said: "O Father, for what reason have you cursed me?
Examine the matter with certainty through the vision of your own power and knowledge."
Through meditation, Durvāsas learned that his transformation was indeed the cause;
"O son, you must perform a favor for me during this bright fortnight."
"Perform the vow of Āditya, which indeed destroys leprosy.
Śāmba said:
"How am I to perform this vow that bestows all fruits?"
What is the ritual procedure, what are the mantras, what is the gift, and what is the worship?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: When the month of Āśvayuja arrives, on whichever day it may be the day of the Sun (Sunday), then this vow should be undertaken by men and especially by women.
O son, for as long as a year, one should again prepare a circular maṇḍala on the ground with cow-dung according to this ritual; there,
one should offer an oblation (arghya) with red flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).
With this mantra, one should daily worship the radiant Ācārya,
so that all directions may become stainless through the rays of the Sun, Bhāskara, and Bhānu.
"Likewise, grant me all my desires; you have been constantly worshipped by me.
This is the *arghya* mantra.
In this manner, one should worship him until the year is completed.
O child, when the vow is completed, one should perform the rite of formal conclusion (udyāpana).
On ground smeared with cow dung, one should draw a mandala using lines of red sandalwood and especially with saffron.
In the center of that, the wise one should fashion a twelve-petaled lotus,
its petals filled with vermilion and as red as the hibiscus flower.
In the center of that, one should place a water-pot resembling a sprout of coral,
filled with śāli rice and provided with sugar and sandalwood.
Upon that, one should place a vessel made of copper or fashioned from gold according to one's means;
having fashioned the Sun-god with a lotus in his hand, according to one's capacity.
The form of Āditya, however, should be understood as described in the Nikṣubhā-bhāskara-sapatamī-vrata;
one should place it upon a vessel, accompanied by a pair of red garments.
Having first bathed [the deity] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), [one should worship it] smeared with hibiscus flowers,
along with red flowers, food offerings, and fruits produced in season.
One should worship the Lord of the worlds with lamps and the finest incenses.

"Salutation to Sūrya! Salutation to Varuṇa! Salutation to Mādhava! Salutation to Dhātṛ! Salutation to Hari! Salutation to Bhaga! Salutation to Suvarṇaretas! Salutation to Aryaman! Salutation to Divākara! Salutation to Tapana! Salutation to Bhānu! Salutation to Haṃsa! With these twelve [names], the worship should be performed.
"Salutations again and again to the Destroyer of Sin."
Salutations to Savitṛ, the soul of the universe, who possesses seven horses, the storehouse of the Sāma, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas, the Ordainer, and the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
This is the prayer-mantra. With this mantra, one should offer the *arghya*.
Having thus worshipped the Sun, one should eat at night while maintaining silence;
then, having honored the preceptor with garments and auspicious ornaments.
To him, one should cause that image and a water-pot devoid of gold to be given, [with the prayer]:
"May the Blessed Lord, the deity who delivers me from saṃsāra, be pleased."
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins with an abundance of twelve kinds of food and other offerings;
to them, one should give water-pots and a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity.
Thus, for one who correctly observes this unsurpassed vow known as Āśāditya, the fruit of merit is great.
Free from disease, skillful, and long-lived, endowed with sons and grandsons,
he shall enjoy stainless pleasures that are difficult even for the immortals to attain.
At the end of the body, you shall attain the supreme union with the Sun;
freed from the disease of leprosy, you will obtain the highest prosperity.
He shall never experience the frustration of his hopes throughout birth after birth;
for this reason, my child, perform this supreme vow.
Having heard these words spoken by his father Kṛṣṇa, Śāmba,
having performed the vow, attained all perfections that are very difficult to obtain.
The man who hears this with devotion, or likewise causes it to be heard,
both of them, being performers of meritorious deeds, shall attain the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the Āśādityavrata as declared in the Skandapurāṇa.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain this supreme secret,
by which Lakṣmī, fortitude, contentment, nourishment, and splendor are produced.
By whose grace all planetary influences always become auspicious—
having previously taken it with devotion on a Sunday coinciding with the Hasta constellation.
A person devoted to faith, having performed seven nights of fasting for each [deity], should perform all the worship and other rites for the Sun according to the procedure prescribed in the mantra.
Then, when the seventh [day] has arrived, a person should perform the recitation by Brahmins;
having carefully fashioned an image of the Sun out of pure gold.
The form of Āditya is to be understood as being like the Ādityavrata;
having placed it in a copper vessel, one should worship it with red flowers.
Covered with a pair of red garments and provided with an umbrella and a pair of sandals,
one should bathe it with ghee and offer sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas).
The knower of mantras should perform the homa with ghee and sesame seeds while reciting the name of the Sun;
he should offer one hundred and eight, or twenty-eight, fuel-sticks.
It should be offered with honey and ghee, or indeed with curd or clarified butter;
the fuel sticks here are of *arka* wood.
One should present these to a learned Brāhmaṇa with this mantra.
O Primordial God, O Seven-Horsed One, O Maker of Day, salutations to you!
O Ravi, deliver us from this ocean of saṃsāra;
O King of Kings, by means of this vow, supreme health shall be attained.
The knowers of the Purāṇas declare that this brings about the attainment of wealth and sons;
and this peace and prosperity are always unfailing for human beings.
Thus ends the Āditya-śānti-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Nārada said:
[I shall describe] that which brings about health for men and bestows infinite fruit.
O Nandin, tell me that vow which destroys all sins.
Nandikeśvara said:
That which is the abode of the Universal Self, the supreme, eternal Brahman,
exists in the world in three forms as the sun, fire, and the moon.
By worshipping him, O Brahmin, one always attains auspiciousness and well-being;
therefore, one should always eat only at night on Sundays.
When the day of the Sun coincides with the Hasta constellation,
and when a constant devotion toward the Sun arises,
then, free from envy, one should observe the practice of eating only one meal on that Sunday.
From that time forward, one should always perform the rite at night on Sundays;
having fed the best of the twice-born at night on a Sunday.
Then, at the time when the sun has set, having drawn a twelve-petaled lotus made of red sandalwood paste and having worshipped it, one should first worship with the mantra "Sūrya."
Likewise, one should place Divākara in the southeast, Vivasvat beyond that,
the god Bhaga in the southwest, and Varuṇa on the western petal.

One should place Mahendra on the petal of the Maruts and Āditya likewise in the north; one should assign Śānti in the northeastern quarter with a gesture of salutation. One should then place the horses of the Sun upon the eastern part of the pericarp.
On the southern petal is the one named Yama; on the western petal is Mārtaṇḍa;
to the north is the god Ravi; and on the pericarp is Bhāskara.
Then, O Brahmin, having offered the *arghya* consisting of red sandalwood mixed with sesame seeds,
along with barley and unbroken rice (*akṣata*), one should recite this mantra:
You are the soul of time, the soul of all beings, the Sun facing every direction;
since you possess the forms of both fire and the moon, protect us, O Maker of Light.
I praise Agni; homage to you! For strength, for vigor, [I praise] Bhāskara.
O Agni, come hither, O giver of boons; homage to you, O Lord of lights!
Having offered the *arghya* and performed the ritual dismissal, one should then eat at night— avoiding oil—
with a purified mind, while repeatedly recollecting the Sun-god.
On the previous day and on a Saturday, one should avoid an oil massage;
at the end of the year, having fashioned an excellent golden lotus, one should perform [the rite].
One should likewise have a two-armed male figure fashioned according to one's ability;
[one should also give] a brown cow with golden horns, highly precious,
with silver hooves, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel and her calf.
Having placed [the image] upon a copper vessel filled with guṣa, one should offer it along with a lotus and a man.
Having worshipped the twice-born with red garments, garlands, and incense— or indeed with red or tawny ones—
and having washed his hands, he should [draw] the Puruṣa together with the lotus.
One should give to one who has performed many vows and acts of giving.
Salutations again and again to the one of unimpaired form, who has conquered his senses,
who is a householder, pure and free from arrogance;
salutations to the destroyer of evil.
To the soul of the universe, who possesses seven horses.

Salutations to the Ordainer, the storehouse of the abodes of the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajus Vedas; to the Creator who is the boat for the ocean of worldly existence; to the Progenitor of the universe, whose nature consists of the three Vedas and the three qualities.
Homage, homage to you, the Lord of the Three Worlds!
By this rite, the man who observes a fast at night on every Sunday for one year shall become free from disease.
Endowed with wealth and grain, and accompanied by sons and grandsons,
he shall remain in the mortal world for a long time and thereafter attain the realm of the Sun.
Having attained the exhaustion of karma, the king— freed from suffering, grief, fear, and disease—
became the lord of the seven continents again and again.
He was the embodiment of Dharma, endowed with immeasurable splendor.
And she who, devoted to gods, gurus, and her husband,
practices day and night according to the Veda—
she too, honored by the Lord of the Immortals, attains the world of the gods.
O Nārada, he goes to the Sun; of this there is no doubt.
The Sun is the embodiment of the Vedas; therefore, the meaning is that one should observe a fast (nakta) on that day.
Furthermore, the man who recites this, or hears it, or beholds it, or even rejoices in it—
He too rejoices among the gods in the abode of Śakra for a hundred koṭis of kalpas.
Thus ends the Sūrya-nakta-vrata as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa. Now follows the Veśyā-vrata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
I have heard from the Purāṇas about the origin of the castes and stages of life;
now I wish to hear, in accordance with reality, the proper conduct of courtesans.
Who indeed is their presiding deity, O Kṛṣṇa? What is their vow, what is their fast, and by what dharma will they attain the unsurpassed heaven?
Kṛṣṇa said: "O Pāṇḍava, I have one hundred and sixteen thousand wives— auspicious ones who are abodes of the god of love, endowed with beauty, generosity, and virtue."
By them, during the spring season, on the bank of a lake filled with blooming white lotuses and surrounded by flowering groves teeming with cuckoos and swarms of bees;
Then, adorned with drinking parties and social gatherings,
the glorious one, whose eyes were like flowers, placed a *mālatī* flower upon his crest.
Śāmba, the conqueror of cities, should go into their presence,
manifest in the form of Kandarpa and adorned with all ornaments.
Gazed upon with longing by those women tormented by the arrows of the bodiless god of love,
his passion increased and brought a trembling to all their limbs.
Having perceived all that transformation with the eye of meditation, I, filled with wrath, cursed them all: "Thieves shall seize everything here."
Hearing these words— “When I have reached heaven, you will be deluded by passion”— his eyes became clouded with tears.
They said to me, "Speak, O Govinda! How will this come to pass?
Having abandoned our husband, the Lord of the worlds, we shall go to the presence of the other."
The city possesses divine splendor, and the houses are filled with jewels;
all the inhabitants of Dvārakā are like gods, and the youths have the forms of deities.
O Blessed One, how may I enjoy the prosperity of the entire world?
"How shall we come to be reduced to the state of slaves?
What will our duty be, what our conduct, and how will our livelihood be?"
As those young women were thus lamenting, their eyes clouded with tears, I said to them: "Abandon this anguish."
In the *Padma Purāṇa*, in the dialogue between Dālbhya and the Gopīs:
Dālbhya said: "Formerly, during sporting excursions in the water at Lake Mānasa..."
And Nārada came into the presence of all of you.
"All of you are Apsarases, the daughters of Hutāśana, in your former lives;
because you did not bow out of arrogance, that knower of yoga was questioned by you."
"Instruct us on how Nārāyaṇa might become our husband;
therefore, in the past, both this boon and this curse were granted."
Because this Dvādaśī of the bright fortnight in the months of Madhu and Mādhava is preeminent for the gift of golden vessels,
her husband will surely be Nārāyaṇa in another birth.
"O Lord, because you asked me questions out of envy for my beauty and good fortune, without first paying homage to me, you shall suffer separation from your own."
"By the curse of Nārada and of the wise Keśava, you shall all be carried off as prostitutes by thieves."
"All of you have become courtesans, deluded by a curse.
Now listen, O beautiful women, to what I shall say:
long ago, in the war between the gods and the asuras, when hundreds had been slain by the gods..."
Among the armies of the gods and asuras, and among the rākṣasas here and there, they were born from among thousands of their women— by the hundreds and by the thousands.
O Lord of Gods, best among speakers, he declared that all those [deeds] which had been performed by force and those which had been spoken by force were likewise [invalidated].
Now, following the profession of courtesans, you beautiful women should conduct yourselves with devotion in the king’s palace as well as in the temples of the gods.
Kings are equal to masters, as are Brahmins who are deeply learned;
you should stay in their houses, for impurity (sūtaka) regarding them is likewise the same.
And through devotion to me, all of you shall possess good fortune;
never should affection be placed in a man who is destitute of wealth.
One who is estimable, pleasing, and always a payer of taxes— whether handsome or ugly— is the one for whom wealth is required there, just as with a deity.
In this place, which is entirely free from deceit,
anyone at all— even one as eminent as a sage— shall always come to your home for the sake of receiving material offerings.
He alone, being free from guile, should be served by you; one should never practice deceitful conduct toward the Master, even in other circumstances.
Whether out of pride in her beauty and youth, or through greed for wealth, any woman who, even toward a beloved husband, always commits adultery;
On an auspicious day when the deities and ancestors have been honored, the most wicked man goes to a low state along with his master.
Gifts of cows, land, and gold should be bestowed according to one's ability; O lady of beautiful limbs, Brahmins should be honored with excellent vows and rites.
Furthermore, I shall correctly instruct you in another vow according to its true nature;
that, moreover, must be practiced by all of you without hesitation.
Those who know the Vedas understand that this is sufficient for crossing over saṃsāra:
when the Hasta, Puṣya, or Punarvasu nakṣatra occurs on a Sunday.
One should properly perform a bath with all medicinal herbs;
then, the presence of the one who pervades the five arrows (the God of Love) is desired.
One should worship the lotus-eyed Lord, even while reciting the names of Anaṅga;
having worshipped the feet for Kāma, one should worship the thighs for Manmatha.
Salutation to Kandarpa-nidhi at the penis;
salutation to Prītipati at the waist; salutation to Saukhya-samudra at the navel; and likewise to Vāmana at the abdomen.
He offered his heart to the Lord of the Heart, his breasts to the Source of Delight,
his throat to Utkaṇṭha, and his mouth to the One Born of Bliss.
The left shoulder to Puṣpacāpa and the right to Puṣpavāna.
One should worship the forehead with "To Puṣpabāṇa," the head with "To Pañcaśara," the crown of the head with "Salutation to Anaṅga," and the two shanks with "To Vilomāya."
One should worship the head of the God of gods, who is the soul of all, as worthy of worship:
"Obeisance to the Lord of Śrī, who bears the banner of Tārkṣya and the goad."
Salutation to the one who holds a lotus in his hand, to the one who holds a conch, to the one whose hand bears the discus;
salutation to Nārāyaṇa, salutation to him whose self is Kāmadeva.
Homage to Peace, homage to Contentment, homage to Delight, homage to Prosperity;
homage to Contentment, homage to Nourishment, and homage to the Bestower of All.
Having thus worshipped Govinda, the Lord whose essence is the god of love,
with perfumes, garlands, incense, and food offerings, O beautiful lady, in nine ways;
Then, having summoned a Brahmin who knows the Dharma and has mastered the Vedas,
and whose limbs are unimpaired, he honored him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
One should give a *prastha* measure of śāli rice, combined with a vessel of ghee, to a brahmin, saying, "May Hṛcchaya be pleased. Then,
eating whatever food one desires at night, one should attend upon that very best of the twice-born.
"She should be held in the mind with the thought, 'This is Kāmadeva for the sake of the road.
Whatever the eminent Brahmin desires, that the playful woman shall do."
And with her whole being, she should satisfy herself while speaking with a smile;
thus she should always perform that vow on Sundays.
From the gift of a prastha of rice and so forth, up until the thirteenth month;
then, when that thirteenth month had arrived, his beloved wife—
One should give to a Brahmin an exquisite bed, furnished with all its accessories,
provided with pillows for rest, well-spread with excellent coverlets, and beautiful.
Having adorned him together with his wife with a lamp, shoes, an umbrella, sandals, and a seat, and having decorated them with golden threads and rings;
One should worship Kāmadeva together with his consort, seated upon a jar of molasses, adorned with fine garments, bracelets, incense, garlands, and ointments.
The form of Kāmadeva, however, should be understood as that described for the Madanatrayodaśī vow:
seated upon a copper vessel, with eyes covered by a golden cloth,
accompanied by a fine bell-metal bowl, and provided with a stalk of sugarcane.
One should likewise give a single milch cow according to the prescribed rite,
so that I may never perceive any difference between Kāma and Keśava.
In that very way, O Viṣṇu, may I always attain all desires;
just as Kamalā never departs from my body, O Keśava.
In the same way, O Lord of Gods, make me also have my husband residing within my body.
In that very manner, having accepted the golden deity, the best of the twice-born should recite the mantra "Who gave? while meditating on Mādhava in his heart.
"From whom [should one give]?"— this is a mantra well-known in the branches of the Yajurveda.
Then, having circumambulated him clockwise and dismissed that bull among the twice-born,
one should lead the entire bed and other furnishings to the house of the Brāhmaṇa.
From that time forward, whoever else comes to the house seeking pleasure shall be properly honored according to one's desire on Sundays.
In this manner, O best of the twice-born, he should remain for one month, up to the thirteenth day,
satisfying his desires while dwelling in the abode of the Sun.
One should follow his instructions until his return;
in this way, [one should serve] a single twice-born man who is peaceful, knows the proper conduct, and is discerning.
One should worship the four wise ones according to the command of the Bestower of Boons,
even when one's own obstacles arise from birth, pregnancy, or the period of impurity following childbirth.
Whether by fate or by human agency, or even through an eclipse,
O Lord, Lakṣmī is never separated from you as she is from you.
My bed, O Madhusūdana, is likewise empty;
one should cause the sound of singing and instrumental music to be made for the God of gods.
For this has been correctly explained especially for you ladies: this is the supreme, sacred dharma and the ultimate state of courtesans here in every respect.
That which was previously proclaimed by Puruhūta to the Dānavas through me—
now all of that is likewise applicable even to you.
It pacifies all sins and bestows infinite fruit;
one should worship eighteen or twenty practitioners of good conduct according to one's ability.
O King, this has been declared by me among the Dānavas;
furthermore, this entire vow has been revealed by me concerning courtesans.
This auspicious woman, residing in the world of Mādhava, makes complete and unbroken this Purāṇa— the essence of all dharma and the bestower of happiness upon the people of the courtesans' quarter.
Worshipped by all the hosts of gods,
she goes to the abode of Viṣṇu, which bestows bliss.
Thus ends the "Vow of the Courtesan" (Veśyāvrata) within the "Bestowing of Desires" (Kāmadāna) section of the glorious Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Sūta said:
[To the World-Teacher] seated comfortably upon the auspicious throne on the side of Mount Meru...
[He saw] Kaśyapa, the creator of the world, an ascetic of pure mind.
Nārada, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas and one who delighted in wandering through the three worlds,
once having fallen into a state of misfortune, went to Kaśyapa for refuge.
Nārada said: "O Creator of all beings— gods, dānavas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, serpents, and humans— you indeed know both dharma and adharma."
O you who are compassionate toward those who have come for refuge, tell us the means for those who are overcome by evil planets and whose minds are struck down by misfortune.
Kaśyapa said:
O best of Brahmins, tell me how they are liberated so that those bonds may be severed.
Well asked, O highly fortunate one, you who bring joy to the world!
I shall describe the meritorious solar vow (sauravrata), which is supreme in bringing an end to misfortune;
for it bestows the [proper] periods (daśās) upon living beings and is the highest fulfiller of one's desires.
O Nārada, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight falling on a Sunday,
one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules in the morning as well as at midday.
One should meditate upon Bhānu, who indeed possesses a triple form and is the destroyer of all Daityas;
likewise, all forms of worship should be performed with fragrant unguents and ointments.
One should worship Durdaśā there with the sixteen types of offerings together with food-oblations containing fruit, having drawn ten little figurines there.
One with a foul mouth, a dejected face, impure, speaking untruths,
a destroyer of good intellect, cruel, and a source of much anxiety—
these women of dark complexion should be honored with a mind full of devotion.
At the outset, one should worship with effort and smear [the ground] with cow dung;
she is eternally a doer of evil, sinful, and an adversary of the gods and the twice-born.
Go away, O goddess Durdaśā, you who constantly increase the power of one's enemies! I entreat you with this [mantra]; lick [the offering] and dismiss her with effort.
Then worship should be performed upon the sun in the form of a cord,
provided with ten knots and adorned with ten threads.
Having established the cord and performed worship, one should place it in the hand;
thereafter, one should cause the worship to be performed, beginning with the invocation and ending with the offering of gifts.
There, having first asked the deity for forgiveness, one should then commence the ten-fold worship (daśāpūjā),
having drawn the ten figurines either on a portion of the ground or upon a pedestal.
Bestowing wise intellect, bringing happiness, and granting all prosperity—thus Lakṣmī bestows the eight enjoyments; she grants renown and destroys suffering.
The tenth lunar day bestows intelligence, brings happiness, grants all prosperity, provides security for one's children, confers victory, and bestows righteousness.
These [deities] are to be worshipped individually with these names and mantras;
the ritual installation, worship, and the offering of food (naivedya) should be performed according to the prescribed rules.
One should meditate upon the Goddess, whose garment is pure, adorned with all ornaments,
the tenfold goddess of the ten stages, who bestows boons and fearlessness.
Thus, one intent on attaining the state should perform meditation;
as for the fruit, one should enjoy it for ten days, provided it is free from oil.
"In this manner, the supreme vow that brings about the attainment of the [final] stage should be performed.
Nārada said:
"O Kaśyapa, by your grace, I have indeed heard of this most excellent vow."
By whom was the Daśāvrata performed, and with whom was the Sun-god pleased?
Kaśyapa said: "O Nārada, in former times there was a righteous king named Nala, a sovereign of the earth; yet he was deprived of his kingdom and lost his ten wives through gambling alone."
Having also worshipped the Sun with diligent effort and observed his vow,
he destroyed his misfortune and regained his kingdom along with his wife.
Then, during the Dvāpara age, the brahmins, afflicted by suffering and beset by misfortune,
while wandering in a terrible forest, reached the son of Satyavatī.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By what action did I, a king, fall from my kingdom and lose my ten-fold fortune?
Now tell me that which is most beneficial for me, which will bring about the recovery of my kingdom."
Having meditated upon Ghṛṇi and having seen Daśākara as well, that best of sages,
the preeminent among ascetics, gave him instruction on the vow.
By the power of this vow, a kingdom free from all thorns was obtained;
and having performed the vow according to the prescribed rites together with his four brothers.
Having heard these words, Nārada questioned Kaśyapa once more.
Nārada said:
"By the ripening of what karma is a man struck by misfortune?"
O tiger among sages, it arises; you ought to explain that reality to me.
Kaśyapa said:
Listen, O Nārada, knower of reality; a miserable state is encountered by men such that they might perhaps leap over chaff, ashes, bones, or a pestle, but never over this.

One who has intercourse with a maiden, a washerwoman, or an old woman; those who take pleasure in animal wombs; one who penetrates the non-vagina or the anus; and one who has sexual intercourse with a Brahmin woman—[these are all equal].
He who takes pleasure in women during the twilight hours or on festival days, or with a woman in her menses;
he who abandons his father and mother, or his master in the midst of a battle.
He who abandons his own lawful wife meets with misfortune;
therefore, with every effort, one should not follow another path.
Therefore, that vow must be performed for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
Thus ends the Daśādityavrata in the Śrī Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, within the dialogue between Kaśyapa and Nārada.
In the Sauradharma, within the dialogue between Māndhātṛ and Vasiṣṭha, Māndhātṛ said:
O Blessed One, best among the wise, please speak out of your grace;
I desire to hear from your own mouth the vow that destroys all sins.
It bestows all desires and destroys all diseases;
it includes the offering of worship and the presentation of the *arghya*, as well as the food offering (*naivedya*) accompanied by its consumption.
"Tell me all of this, O Lord, if you are pleased with me.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Listen, O King, I shall proclaim that which is a secret and supreme vow."
It bestows all desires upon men and destroys diseases such as leprosy.
O King, it brings satisfaction to the Sun and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
at its rising, the hosts of gods, groups of sages along with the Cāraṇas,
as well as the Devas, Dānavas, and Yakṣas, constantly perform worship.
O best of kings, I shall describe in detail the vow of that deity, upon whose rising there is awakening for all beings, O King.
Listen now to the truth regarding the worship, the offering of arghya, the consumption [of the remains], the gift, and the food offering (naivedya):
whatever merit exists in all sacred fords and whatever fruit exists in all sacrifices [is obtained through these].
Whatever merit is obtained through all forms of giving and austerity,
and whatever merit is gained by bathing at dawn or on a Sunday— [all that is attained by this].
O Lord of the Earth, O Divākara, I shall perform the Sūryavrata throughout all twelve months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, for the duration of one year.
"O Prabhākara, by your grace, may my vow reach completion. [This is the mantra for the observance.
Then, having risen at dawn, one should go to a river or other pure water.
Having bathed, O lord of the earth, one should offer libations to the gods and the ancestors.
Having smeared a clean place, one should worship the Sun there;
one should draw a twelve-spoked lotus with a pericarp.
Likewise, in a copper vessel with river water mixed with red sandalwood water,
one should worship there the Lord, the Master of the Gods, the Lord of Day.
And as for those specific offerings, O King, which are made month by month, listen indeed to them:
in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship Mitra with an excellent offering of coconuts.
The food offering is prescribed as rice mixed with ghee and jaggery;
having consumed three leaves of Tulasī, one should remain with the senses subdued.
O King, one should give food along with a sacrificial fee to a Brahmin;
likewise, having worshipped Viṣṇu in the month of Pauṣa, one should offer kṛśara as a food offering.
One should offer an *arghya* oblation with a citron (*bījapūra*), consume three *palas* of clarified butter,
and give clarified butter along with food to a Brahmin.
In the month of Māgha, having worshipped the one named Varuṇa, one should offer a meal of jaggery with sesame seeds,
as well as a plantain fruit as the food offering and a sacrificial fee.
Having offered the *arghya* with that same [mantra], one should consume three handfuls of sesame seeds;
in the month of Phālguna, having worshipped the Sun, one should present an *arghya* of citron fruit.
One should consume three mouthfuls of curd; the food offering (naivedya) consists of curd mixed with ghee;
and the gift of rice mixed with curd is prescribed for the meal.
In the month of Caitra, having worshipped the Sun, one should offer ghee-filled *pūrikās* as the food offering (*naivedya*);
the fruit prescribed is the pomegranate, and three *palas* of milk should be consumed.
One should give food to a brahmin, specifically sweet food along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). In Vaiśākha, the Sun is said to be the deity; beans with ghee are prescribed as the offering.
One should offer the *arghya* with grapes and perform the consumption of cow-dung;
this should be done month after month, accompanied by ghee and ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

O King, one should worship Indra during the month of Jyeṣṭha; the food offering (naivedya) is karambhaka, the respectful offering (arghya) is with a mango, and one should consume three handfuls of water as a draught.
Having worshipped the Sun in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should likewise offer food consisting of curd and rice to a Brāhmaṇa, as well as perform worship with the Vibhītaka fruit.
One should give food to a Brahmin and cause him to eat three grains of black pepper;
and in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Bhagasti and likewise offer a cucumber fruit.
And three handfuls of flour are prescribed for consumption;
O King, one should give a meal to a Brahmin along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
When, in the month of Bhādrapada, the venerable Kūṣmāṇḍa consists of rice,
cow’s urine is prescribed for consumption, and likewise a meal for a Brāhmaṇa.
For Hiraṇyaretas and Āśvina, the food offering (naivedya) is prescribed as sugar;
for Dāḍima, however, there is no offering of arghya, but rather three palas of candied sugar (khaṇḍa) are to be consumed.
To a Brahmin with supreme devotion, [one should offer] rice and sugar for a meal;
and in the month of Kārttika, the fruit is indeed the same as that of consuming plantains.
Milk-rice (pāyasa) is prescribed as the food offering (naivedya), and milk-rice is likewise prescribed for consumption;
having thus completed this vow, one should then perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
Then, having gone to the teacher's house, one should grasp both his feet [and say]:
"I shall perform the concluding rite; please come to my home."
One should have an image of the Sun made from a māṣaka of gold;
a chariot made of silver should be fashioned, complete with all its necessary equipment.
Having fashioned a twelve-petaled lotus from red rice grains,
one should place there a flawless jar endowed with the five jewels.
Upon that, one should place a copper vessel filled with rice,
covered with a red cloth and encircled by a garland of flowers.
One should bathe [the image] with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), preceded by the recitation of my mantra;
then, having performed the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and established it, one should cause the worship of the deity to be performed.
With sandalwood, various flowers blooming in season,
and uncut silk cloths, as well as a water-pot and sandals;
O Lord of the Earth, one should place three *vardhanīs* there in the presence of the deity,
along with a pair of saffron-dyed garments under that name.
On the first lunar day, he should be fully worshipped with the twelve names of the Sun.
Mitra, Viṣṇu, Savitṛ, Varuṇa, Sūrya, and likewise Bhānu;
Tapanendra, Ravi, Gabhasti, and Śamana are to be worshipped.
Hiraṇyaretas, Dinakṛt, and Pūṣan—these should be worshipped with effort;
in their midst, the Thousand-rayed One (the Sun) should be worshipped together with Saṃjñā.
With betel nuts, incense, lamps, garments, and food offerings,
as well as with a coconut, one should devoutly present the arghya water-offering to the God.
O King of kings, with this mantra for the fulfillment of the vow:
"Homage to the thousand-rayed one, the destroyer of all diseases!"
"O Ravi, together with Saṃjñā, accept this water-offering (argha) given by me.
This is the mantra for the arghya.
Then, having performed the waving of lights (ārātrika) as well as the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the worship.
Then, having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), the Śrāddha rite dedicated to the Sun-god should indeed be performed.
O Lord, one should devoutly feed twelve Brahmins with sweet foods;
a meal consisting of excellent rice should be given to a married couple.
Then, having worshipped [the preceptor] with garlands and other offerings, one should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
all that, including the ritual gifts and so forth, should be presented to the guru.
Having satisfied the preceptor right there, one should dismiss the Brahmins;
whatever has been performed that is deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in procedure [is thereby rectified].
May all that reach fulfillment through the grace of the gods of the earth;
having followed the preceptor and the Brahmins, one should then partake of a meal.
Having bowed to the aged along with his kinsmen and to the god Divākara,
that mortal who acts in this manner, free from the stinginess of wealth, [attains the fruit].
O Great King, hear now the fruit of the merit of the Sūryavrata:
a Brāhmaṇa obtains knowledge, and a Kṣatriya shall attain sovereignty.
The Vaiśya shall obtain abundance of wealth, and the Śūdra shall attain happiness;
the sonless man obtains a son, and the maiden obtains a husband.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease; one who is bound is released from bondage.
Whatever desire one contemplates, that shall certainly be his.
O best of kings, that supreme ruler who hears this with devotion and a one-pointed mind shall obtain all desires through the grace of the Radiant One, O King.
Thus ends the Sūryavrata as declared in the Sauradharma. Now follow the Somavāravrata observances.
Hereafter, I shall fully proclaim that unsurpassed secret.
By which prosperity, fortitude, contentment, nourishment, and splendor are produced.

Having observed the Monday falling on one of those various [auspicious] lunar days, the wise practitioner should perform all the rites, such as the worship of the Moon, according to the procedure prescribed for the night vigil.
Then, when the seventh [day] has arrived, having provided a feast for the Brahmins,
one should place Soma, produced from silver, within a bronze vessel.
The form of Soma, however, as described in the Mahārāja-vrata performed on the fourteenth day, should be understood as follows:
having placed King Soma in a vessel, worshipped him with white garments, and provided him with sandals,
shoes, an umbrella, a vessel, and a seat.
The knower of mantras should perform the homa with ghee and sesame seeds using the mantra named Soma;
he should offer one hundred and eight or twenty-eight fuel sticks.
It should be offered with honey and clarified butter, as well as with curd and ghee.
[558] Palāśa wood fuel-sticks are to be known;
having placed them upon a peak of curd-rice, one should present them to a Brāhmaṇa,
O King of Kings, being fully endowed with devotion and reciting this mantra.
O Mahādeva, white as the flowers of the matted locks and cow’s milk, O Soma, may you be gracious to us; salutations, salutations to you at all times!
When this is done, O gentle one, it will bring satisfaction to Soma;
when the son of Atri is satisfied, all the planets shall become auspicious for him.
Thus concludes the propitiatory rite for the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Īśvara said:
Now, I shall describe the procedure for the vow (*vrata*) in brief.
Just as men act so that all their purposes and desires may be fulfilled,
so it shall be on the day of the bright path when the month of Kārttika has passed.
On the first Monday, however, one should worship him with the *nakta* rite whenever the performer has faith regarding the Monday vow (*somavāravratam*).
Then, having had everything prepared, one should commence with the Brahmins and others;
one should observe the Monday fast during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Caitra.
In whichever month one should begin it, in that same month one should bring it to completion;
having bathed well and become pure, the man should wear white garments.
Free from desire, anger, egoism, hatred, and all such defects,
he should gather white flowers— mallikā, mālatī, divine white lotuses, campaka, bilva, and pāṭala.
One should smear [the image] with flowers born of the *kunda* and *mandāra*, as well as *punnāga* and *śatapatraka*,
and then fumigate it with sandalwood and divine incense.
One should cause all those foods that are desired to be given;
one should worship Somanātha, the Lord of the World, with a spirit of devotion.
One should offer everything to Maheśvara with the *kāmika* mantra, which is generally used; listen now to this excellent and beneficial mantra.
Oṃ, homage to the ten-armed, three-eyed, five-faced wielder of the trident,
mounted upon a white bull, adorned with all ornaments!
"Salutations to You who abide as half of Umā’s body, the embodiment of all forms.
With this very mantra, one should perform the worship and the fire-oblation."
All undertakings, even those merely conceived in the mind, are accomplished;
one should perform worship during the night hours upon the appearance of the constellations.
Having first offered food with great devotion to the Brāhmaṇa,
as well as vegetables, betel-leaf, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
Endowed with this procedure and free from passion and hatred, [he attains success].
I shall describe in brief the merit of eating but one meal a day:
it destroys the unbearable sin accumulated over a hundred lifetimes, which would otherwise be irresistible even to gods and dānavas.
[560] Indeed, one perishes by eating but once a day; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Listen, O beautiful one, to the merit of one month as it truly is.
Misfortune becomes fortune, and the unfortunate become fortunate;
one desiring a son obtains sons, and the poor become wealthy.
O lady of excellent hips, in his house there shall be various kinds of happiness;
as a portion of Rudra, he shall possess wealth and, free from obstacles, traverse the earth.
A person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices;
having enjoyed all pleasures in heaven, he is born as the best of men.
O Maheśvarī, I shall describe before you in brief the meritorious fruit of those nights of Monday in the month of Pauṣa.
The fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice shall be a hundredfold;
O Goddess, endowed with the aforementioned deities, one obtains that fruit.
One should worship specifically on a Monday in the month of Māgha;
likewise, one should bathe [the deity] with honey, milk, and sugarcane juice.
It shall destroy all those sins, such as the killing of a twice-born;
purified and endowed with splendor, one becomes utterly stainless.
The merit that belongs to one who possesses much gold—which is difficult even for the gods to attain here—one who is impelled by devotion to me obtains it; of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Phālguna, O auspicious lady, I shall describe the beneficial results of Monday; and when the fast (nakta) is observed, its virtues will be explained to you in detail.
Four thousand five hundred and ten Vedic hymns were performed by those most excellent among various officiating priests, who were knowers of all the scriptures.
O beloved, one obtains even greater fruit than that from giving a hundred thousand cows during a lunar or solar eclipse; of this there is no doubt.
O auspicious one, listen also to my words regarding Caitra:
O beautiful goddess, by performing a night-meal on a Monday, [great merit is gained].
O Pārvatī, whatever fruit a woman obtains by bringing a hundred thousand measures of Gaṅgā water to a confluence such as that of Somanātha, [she obtains that same fruit by other means].
Indeed, the fruit of [an offering] made with ghee or honey is a hundredfold;
likewise, O Supreme Goddess, that of guggulu is five thousandfold.
In this way, this man shall undoubtedly gain merit;
he who observes the *nakta* vow on a Monday during the month of Vaiśākha will undoubtedly do so.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship with white flowers as they may be obtained;
indeed, cakes made from plantain fruit should be offered.
With a single-minded disposition that is stainless, O illustrious one,
for a thousand kalpas suitable for the gods, O lady of beautiful countenance.
O Goddess, by means of this gift according to the prescribed rite, a man on earth who possesses a beautiful form obtains that merit which belongs to men of handsome appearance.
O Great Goddess, one truly obtains that fruit by performing the Monday vow (somavāra-vrata) during the month of Jyeṣṭha.
O beloved, I shall tell you all the merit that arises from performing this rite according to the rules for cows with golden horns at Puṣkara.
A human being obtains the fruit of ten thousand gifts bestowed,
and attains that merit which is difficult even for gods and dānavas to reach.
O beautiful one, he sports there with the Lord for ten thousand kalpas;
on a Monday in the month of Āṣāḍha, one who has purified his soul should observe this vow.
But listen, O auspicious lady, as I tell you what is beneficial according to the prescribed rule.
O Goddess, the merit endowed with all auspiciousness that results from performing a hundred human sacrifices according to the prescribed rites shall belong to that man.
O Goddess, because these cannot be accomplished at night,
this vow is essential, since it is achieved only with great difficulty.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Mahādeva on a Monday;
at night, one should take a meal, free from intoxication and crookedness.
O Maheśvarī, as long as a living being remains alive, he may become a leader of the Gaṇas;
such is his activity in this world, while in the other world I shall tell you.
A human being obtains the merit of more than a hundred horse-sacrifices;
he dwells in my world as long as the moon, sun, and stars endure.
And in the month of Bhādrapada, one endowed with devotion should worship the Supreme Goddess;
O Goddess, listen specifically to the unsurpassed merit that belongs to such a person.
A man obtains that very fruit which results from the gift of ten million well-behaved cows together with their calves; of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Āśvina, I shall describe the hundredfold fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice,
as well as that of a thousand cows of nectar and a hundred cows of molasses.
During a solar eclipse at Kurukṣetra, a human being obtains the fruit of what was given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, O Supreme Sovereign, in the month of Kārttika, it is the granter of boons, the fulfiller of desires, the bestower of liberation,
and the destroyer of multitudes of sins through mere remembrance.
Devoted to the Monday vow, one should worship Śiva according to the rules,
eating only at night, endowed with faith, compassion, and truthfulness.
To one who has mastered the Vedas, he gave a hundred chariots yoked with horses bearing auspicious marks and skilled in the recitation of the Vedas.
O Goddess, a human being endowed with devotion obtains that same fruit which is the reward for what is given to the four classes of Brahmins.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should fashion a silver image of four-armed Soma,
along with thirteen water-pots accompanied by pairs of white cloths.
O Pārvatī, one should carefully place bamboo vessels filled with excellent foods upon them for the sake of accomplishing all aims.
With food that was very beautiful, fragrant, very succulent, and radiant,
as well as with mung beans, śāli rice, and ghee cooked in clarified butter.
Then, having honored the Brahmins with a mind full of devotion,
one should give thirteen water-pots and beautiful white cows.
Likewise, O Brahmins, according to this procedure, they should be adorned with various garments and provided with sandals, in accordance with one's intention and wealth.
One should give to Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with good conduct and are wise;
one should honor them with the essence of one's household wealth and then ask for their forgiveness once again.
Then, with devotion, one should cause the Guru to sit upon a seat and worship him with perfumes,

"O Pārtha, formerly in the Tretā Yuga, Indra did not send rain."
In some way, due to the king's misconduct, [misfortune] spread throughout his kingdom on all sides.
Then the kingdom became exceedingly harsh, overcome by hunger;
it was swarming with locusts and rats, and agitated by the fear of thieves and predatory beasts.
During that terrible and tumultuous time, Kauśika, together with his wife and children, abandoned his own home and slowly went to a foreign kingdom.
And as he was traveling along the road, he was left behind by whichever great seer it might have been;
for that boy alone was difficult to support as a member of a household.
At that time, when the collection of medicinal herbs had indeed become especially depleted,
Kauśika departed after having committed that merciless deed.
That fool, distressed by hunger and looking about in every direction with his eyes,
rose up and began to eat the roots of the peepal tree that were facing downward.
He drank water from the well daily within that very circle of hermitages;
having established himself there, he resorted to the fierce Rudra and performed extensive penance.
Then the blessed Nārada, who had mastered the Vedas, arrived;
he saw that young brahmin boy with a dejected face, overcome by hunger.
Then he performed for him the purificatory rites, including the binding of the girdle of muñja grass;
he taught him the Vedas according to the methods of *saharasa*, *pada*, and *krama*;
and he bestowed upon him the infallible twelve-syllable Vaiṣṇava mantra.
For this Pippalāda, who was devoted to the study of the Vedas and intent on meditation upon Viṣṇu,
Viṣṇu became manifest before his eyes every single day.
Mounted upon Vainateya, with the luster of the petals of a blue lotus,
four-armed, clad in yellow garments, and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
He then said, "Being pleased, choose whatever boon you desire."
Having heard that and looking toward the face of Nārada, the child then,
being permitted by Nārada, attained the science of yoga.
Having bestowed knowledge along with its instructions and the stainless practice of yoga,
Viṣṇu, who moves upon the back of the enemy of serpents (Garuḍa), vanished right there.
Then, having become a great sage of vast knowledge even as a child, he questioned Nārada: "O Muni, by whom am I being tormented?"
Seized by a planet in the form of a planet, appearing as a child and exceedingly distressed, he cried:
"I have no father, I have no brother; I live only through the suffering caused by this [planet]."
"O best of the twice-born, by fate you have bestowed the status of a Brahmin upon me."
Having heard these words, Nārada then spoke:
"Indeed, you are afflicted by the cruel planet Śanaiścara."
And this entire land has been oppressed by that slow-moving one;
likewise, this Saturn (Sauri), the son of Sūrya, has obtained his due reward.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Having spoken thus, all the gods returned as they had come;
Śanaiścara, too, was established in his own place as a planet.
The Brahman-sage Pippalāda, observing the command of Brahmā,
worshipped Śanaiścara and praised him with palms joined in reverence.
May the Sun, who stands in the corner, who is tawny, crooked, black, fierce, and like the Ender (Yama);
may Sauri, Śanaiścara, the slow-moving one, the best of planets, be pleased with me.
Having praised Śanaiścara in this way, the great sage Pippalāda is seen even today by human beings, blazing as he remains in his celestial chariot belonging to the Sun.
O best of the Kuru lineage, those men who shall read this narrative of Śanaiścara will not again be afflicted by suffering.
Whoever, with devotion, places an image of the King of Planets (the Sun) fashioned from black iron into a copper vessel filled with sesame oil and gives it to a Brāhmaṇa;
The affliction caused by Śanaiścara does not indeed trouble him.
[587] Thus ends the vow of Śanaiścara in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare this supreme secret,
by which prosperity, fortitude, contentment, nourishment, and splendor are produced.
O bull among the Bharatas, having observed the son of the Sun (Saturn) by means of its root mantra,
one should worship that triad of planets with devotion on that day.
O King, the knower of mantras should perform oblations with ghee and sesame seeds, in due order for Śanaiścara, Rāhu, and Ketu, using the names of the planets as mantras.
One hundred and eight, or indeed twenty-eight oblations,
should be offered separately with honey, clarified butter, curds, and ghee;
and the sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) for these should be, respectively, of śamī, dūrvā grass, and kuśa grass.
And when the seventh lunar day of the son of the Sun (Saturday) arrives at night,
O King, auspicious images of the three planets should be fashioned out of iron.
O best of the Kurus, O King, all of these should be placed in either iron or golden vessels;
one should then give a pair of black garments to each one in succession.
In this context, the form of Śani described in the continuous vow (nirantaravrata) should be understood:
he has a formidable face, holds a sword, a shield, and a trident, grants boons, and is seated upon a blue lion-throne; Rāhu is thus praised here.
All smoke-colored, with two arms, wielding maces, and having distorted faces;
seated eternally upon vultures, these banners shall be bestowers of boons.
Having anointed [the image] with musk and offered black agalloch incense,
one should present the essence of the food offering (naivedya) to a Brāhmaṇa.
O Śanaiścara, salutations to you; likewise, salutations to you, Rāhu;
and salutations to you, Ketu—may you grant all peace.
O best of the twice-born, listen now to what occurs when this has been performed.
If Mars is joined with the Sun, the Sun is with Rāhu,
and all the Ketus are situated at the head, these planets cause affliction.
By the mere performance of this, all calamities are pacified.
O King, for one who always acts in this manner, endowed with devotion, all [the deities], being favorably disposed toward him, grant victory and happiness.
O King, whoever hears this peace-chant of the planets, or even recites it, all the planets, being well-disposed toward him, shall grant him peace.
Having worshipped the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, together with the constellations beginning with Hasta, in their order of rising,
[one should offer them] fashioned of gold to an eminent brahmin.
Having given it, a person is not afflicted by seizure here.
One should offer Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu, placed in a vessel of iron; black aloe is prescribed as the incense, and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be according to one's own capacity.
Thus ends the propitiatory rite for Saturn and other planets as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
Now, according to the conjunctions of lunar mansions and lunar days, and through the conjunctions of the planets with those lunar days,
I shall once again explain the vows exactly as they are established.
When the conjunction with the eighth lunar day occurs on a Monday during the Rohiṇī asterism,
a special worship must be performed with diligence by one who desires a son.
When the conjunction of Jupiter occurs on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Puṣya,
or alternatively when there is a conjunction with the Moon, one should especially worship Śaṅkara.
One should offer milk-rice mixed with ghee to Śiva,
and worship Śiva as before with incense, lamps, offerings, and other articles.
The consumption of clarified butter should be performed; this vow bestows all desires.
When the Āditya-Revatī yoga occurs on the fourteenth day,
or when there is a conjunction with Maghā on the eighth day, one should worship Śiva as previously described.
Sesame seeds are recommended for consumption; this is declared to be the Ādityavrata.
Health arises for him, together with his sons and his circle of kinsmen.
When the conjunction of Rohiṇī and the Moon occurs on the fourteenth day,
or through its union with the Moon on the eighth day, then one should perform the Candravratam.
Having diligently worshipped Śiva according to the procedure previously described,
with curd and milk as the food offering and consuming milk alone,
one shall obtain fame, health, and sovereignty; this word is not false.
When there is a conjunction of Aśvinī and Mars on the fourteenth lunar day,
or a conjunction of Bharaṇī and Mars on the eighth, one should then perform the Bhauma-vrata.
Having worshipped Śiva with supreme devotion through the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra),
one who consumes the red lotus shall attain auspicious sovereignty.
When there is a conjunction of Rohiṇī and Mercury on the fourteenth day,
or on the eighth, one should briefly perform the Budha-vrata.
Śiva is to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite, preceded by a great ceremonial bath;
one should partake of milk-rice and ghee accompanied by a great wick-offering.
For him, sons, wives, and fame increase; it cannot be otherwise.
When there is a conjunction of Revatī and Jupiter on the fourteenth lunar day,
or a conjunction of Tiṣya and Jupiter on the eighth, one should then perform the Guru-vrata.
By consuming tawny clarified butter combined with the juice of the Brāhmaṇī plant,
one attains mastery over speech through the power of this vow.
When the fourteenth lunar day falls on a Saturday conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, know that to be the Śukra-vrata; likewise, when the eighth lunar day falls on a Sunday conjoined with Punarvasu.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord with extensive offerings according to one's means,
one should partake of honey here with a self-restrained mind;
by the power of this vow, one obtains great fruit.
When the conjunction of Śani with Bharaṇī occurs on the fourteenth day,
and likewise the conjunction with Ārdrā on the eighth day, then one should perform the Śanivrata.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rites, one should consume grain;
for Saturn, situated in the eleventh house, bestows auspicious results.
O child, that which is forbidden is yet auspicious; therefore, one should observe the vow for that purpose, [offering] gold, base metals, coral, and woolen blankets in due order.
O child, one should carefully cause a conch shell and sharp iron to be given to the preceptor in due order, according to what is available, with great effort.
Thus are the vows regarding lunar days, asterisms, and weekdays as declared in the *Kālottara*.
Indra said:
"How may great merit be attained even with very little material wealth?"
Therefore, O Lord of the Gods, I wish to hear about the conjunctions of the planets.
Brahmā said:
Listen, my child, I shall explain according to what you have asked—
the conjunction of planets, asterisms, and lunar days, which yields great merit with little hardship.
The conjunction of the eighth lunar day with the asterisms of Bhṛgu (Śravaṇā) and Pauṣṇa (Revatī), as well as the Śiva-yogas, is most excellent;
likewise, the group of soft (mṛdu) nakṣatras, the Saubhāgya yoga, and the Bhadrā yoga on a Friday are auspicious.
When, by the conjunction of fate, the sixth lunar day falls on a Sunday under the Puṣya asterism,
then the Skanda-sacrifice should be performed, which accomplishes all desires.
When the seventh lunar day, Vijayā, falls on a Sunday,
then that conjunction is auspicious and brings about all virtues.
O Lord of the Gods, when the moon is in its waning phase, there is a conjunction with the Ārdrā constellation.
When there is an auspicious conjunction on the ninth lunar day with the Sun being present,
or when the Moon is in conjunction with Śravaṇā on the eighth day, it brings happiness.
On the day of the Lord of the Gaṇas (Gaṇeśa), which falls on the fourth lunar day (kujāha) during the month of Āśvina (ahivradhna).
On the twelfth lunar day under the asterism Śravaṇā, when the day of Jupiter coincides with the Punarvasu nakṣatra,
one should then perform the sacrifice to Somaśambhu, which accomplishes all the goals of Viṣṇu.
On the second lunar day, whenever the constellation Kṛttikā occurs in the north,
then the sacrifice to the planets (grahayāga) should be performed, which bestows all peace.
On the day of Svāti, on the fourth lunar day of Śani, and during the Umā-yoga, [this practice] is remembered as most excellent.

By performing rites for the pacification of planetary afflictions and other such acts on the Uttarās, the Pūrvās, the full moon days, and the eighth lunar days (aṣṭamīs), one shall attain all desires.
On the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of Jupiter, or under the asterisms of Puṣya or Rohiṇī when Saturn is present, [one should likewise act].
For one who desires the good fortune of offspring, there is the sacrifice to Raudra-Vināyaka.
O great sage, on all full-moon days, as well as on the eighth and twelfth lunar days,
on the fourteenth and third days, and under auspicious planets and asterisms,
the sacrifice for all beings may be performed preceded by devotion.
Through the sacrifice to Rudra, the desired lifespan resulting from mantra practice is obtained.
O great sage, from Mahādeva one may obtain prosperity, wisdom, longevity, freedom from deceit,
the knowledge of yoga, fame, and perfection.
Health and the state of observing excellent vows are certainly obtained from the Sun;
Trivikrama bestows the desired goal according to one's wish.
But for one who beholds the Leader (Vināyaka), consciousness shall arise.
By beholding Skanda on the sixth day, one becomes free from enemies at that very moment.
Through the sacrifice to the Mothers, great accomplishment arises for everyone.
On the first day, by means of the fire-oblation, a man shall become wealthy.
The perfect attainment of heaven and liberation arises from the sacrifice to Durgā,
performed by those most excellent in the knowledge of Brahman on the day of Jyeṣṭhā, with Māyā and other [mantras], and Maṅgalā and others.
O Sage, the goddesses beginning with Kālikā should be worshipped according to the rite of Īśa and the others.
Thus ends the glorification of the greatness of the planets, lunar days, asterisms, and sacred observances (*yāga*) in the *Devīpurāṇa* and other sources.

This concludes the section on Vows according to the Days of the Week (*vāravratāni*) within the *Vrata-khaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Hemādri, the sovereign of all sovereigns, the great king, master of all faculties, and expert in every branch of knowledge.
[593] Now begins the twenty-third chapter: Next, the observances (vratas) associated with the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
The wise Hemādri is an abode of statesmanship and humility,
