a twice-born man skilled in traversing the stations renowned on the path of the righteous;
he is the architect who fashions the series of unimpaired fruits for the inhabitants of the three worlds.
Now he unfolds a diverse array of constellations and lunar observances.
Puṣkara said:
"O sinless one, hereafter I shall describe to you the ritual for specific desires.
On every full moon day, both the sacrificer and the domestic priest should fast."
Listen now to that: they should perform an auspicious bath under the asterism Aśvinī.
On ground free from obstacles, having prepared two jars filled with madhūka flowers and combined with aśvagandha, one should then always place them evenly.
Then the wise man, dressed in clean garments, should worship the two Aśvins, as well as the Moon, Aśvinī, Varuṇa,
and Hari, with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, and an abundance of lamps, incense, and food.
Then, having fashioned a pair of horses out of clay mixed with all medicinal herbs,
he should, bowing his head, present them to the two Nāsatyas.
O best of the twice-born, one should offer eight-ingredient incense to the gods.
Alternatively, one should always place horse-hair together with the fruit and root of the *aśvattha* tree in a single secret location and wear that beautiful gem.
A man who, being self-restrained, performs this very bath while offering an oblation to the Aśvins,
obtains horses beyond all counting.
Those born of noble lineage and endowed with heroism and strength.
Thus ends the ritual bath on the day of Aśvinī as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Brahmā said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, these lunar-day conjunctions have thus been described by me to you."
All the deities of the lunar mansions are established within those lunar mansions.
O Lord of the Gods, they bestow desired objects according to their respective places;
whenever the moon presides over a particular lunar mansion,
then that sacrifice to the gods becomes fruitful, as has been declared.
And I shall declare, according to the truth, the deities of the lunar mansions,
as well as all the lunar mansions themselves and their respective sacrifices individually.
By worshipping the two Aśvins under the asterism Aśvinī, a man becomes long-lived;
and he who is excessively afflicted by diseases is quickly liberated from them.
Yama, the lord of death, is worshipped under the asterism Bharaṇī with auspicious black flowers, as well as with pure perfumes and other offerings; thus, one shall be liberated from untimely death.
Agni, when worshipped with red garlands and other offerings on the day of Kṛttikā, bestows supreme prosperity; he certainly grants success through oblations of clarified butter.
When Prajāpati is pleased and has been worshipped, he likewise bestows cattle;
O tiger among gods, Lord of the World, I have thus declared the birth of cows under Rohiṇī.
Likewise, under Mṛgaśīrṣa, one obtains Soma, as well as high birth and health.
By worshipping Śiva under Ārdrā, one obtains cattle and victory;
by offering divine white lotuses and the like, as well as milk, one attains divinity;
and under Punarvasu, Diti, when gratified with *caru* oblations, bestows sons.
Under Tiṣya, Jupiter grants intelligence and abundant happiness;
under Āśleṣā, the Nāgas, when duly worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, bestow enjoyments.
And when satisfied with auspicious, sweet foods and other offerings during the Maghā asterism, the ancestors bestow nourishment, being themselves gratified by ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
To the east, Bhaga, the god, when well-satisfied, bestows victory.
Likewise, Āryaman, when duly worshipped with devotion in the Uttarā,
shall grant a desired husband to a woman and a choice wife to a man.
Likewise, the treasury of splendor, when worshipped with flowers and garments, should bestow freedom from disease, long life, prosperity, and a beautiful form into the hand.
When worshipped under the Citrā asterism, Tvaṣṭṛ bestows health;
and when Vāyu is worshipped under Svātī, he grants the desired offerings for the ancestors.
Having worshipped Indra and Agni under the Viśākhā constellation with yellow and red offerings,
one shall obtain wealth and sovereignty in this world and dwell forever as one endowed with splendor.
Having thus honored a friend with jewels under the asterism Anurādhā with devotion,
one becomes dear to all people and lives long at all times.
By worshipping Indra under Jyeṣṭhā as before, one shall obtain prosperity,
being fully endowed with all virtues through both action and speech.
Having worshipped Nirṛti at the base with offerings such as meat and other delicacies,
one obtains the fruit as before and shall become firmly established in one's own place.
Having performed the sacrifice with these waters and offered oblations right there as before,
one is swiftly liberated from both physical and mental torments.
Likewise, by worshipping Śrī during the Āṣāḍhā constellation through the conjunction with Viśva, Viriñci, and Turaga, one attains prosperity as well as supreme victory.
Viṣṇu, when worshipped under Śravaṇā, bestows all desires;
having sacrificed to the Vasus under Dhaniṣṭhā, one shall encounter no fear anywhere.
Having crossed over even great fear by worshipping Varuṇa under the Śatabhiṣaj asterism with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, a man is liberated from diseases.
By worshipping the unborn one on the day of Bhādrapadā, who resembles pure crystal, one attains liberation; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
In the north, one attains the supreme peace of Ahibradhna.
When Pūṣan is worshipped under Revatī with white flowers, lamps, and incense that increases victory, he bestows various kinds of livestock.
These sacrifices have indeed been fully described by me in brief for the benefit of practitioners of the lunar mansions and their deities;
therefore, according to one's wealth, they become bestowers of fruit.
And whenever one wishes to go elsewhere, or even at the very commencement of an undertaking,
one should perform a sacrifice to the lunar mansion deity and carry out all of that.
"For when this is done, one shall obtain the entire fruit of the pilgrimage;
indeed, the fruit of the ritual act will be complete," so was it said by the Sun himself.
Thus ends the procedure for the worship of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-pūjā-vidhi*) as declared in the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Does one attain the divine state of Agni, or perhaps the destruction of enemies?"
By what action of your own will, O bull among men, do you always [act thus]?
One should worship Vāsudeva with fragrant saffron,
with pleasing white flowers, and one should offer guggulu incense.
One should offer a lamp with ghee and likewise a red cloth;
one should present everything as an offering to the deity.
O bull among the gods, the oblation must likewise be offered into a well-kindled fire,
and weapons should be given as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
Having performed this foremost rite that destroys enemies and always crushes the hosts of foes,
one quickly achieves the destruction of adversaries through this preeminent act.
A mortal attains it; there is indeed no doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the vow for the destruction of enemies as spoken in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Śrī Rāma said:
"I desire to hear about the optional rites (*kāmyakarmāṇi*) intended for householders."
O omniscient one, knower of dharma, son of King Yagogaṇa!
Puṣkara said:
O Bhārgava, having observed a fast under the asterism of Yāmya (Bharaṇī),
the priest of the one who has fasted should perform the ceremonial bathing according to the rules under the asterism of Kṛttikā.
With jars of various kinds— some made of clay and others of gold— their mouths wide open,
filled with all varieties of medicinal herbs as well as the auspicious waters of sacred fords.
O best of the twice-born, [one should offer] fruits of the agni, aśvattha, śirīṣa, and nyagrodha trees,
as well as vessels filled with black sesame seeds.
With his neck likewise bound with a red garland and a thread,
the best of the twice-born, dressed in blue garments, should be bathed while facing the southeast.
One should worship Vahni, Kumāra, Śaśin, Khaḍga, and Varuṇa during the Kṛttikās with perfumes, garlands, and an abundance of food.
Likewise with yellow and red garments, as well as with lamps of ghee,
with cow’s curd, with parched grain, or even with fire and mantras.
Then, one should offer priyaṅgu seeds into the fire for the aforementioned deities, along with kṛśara, apūpikās, and various kinds of cakes.
O best of men, one should properly wear the hair of donkeys, horses, and peacocks on the right side, and according to one's ability, gold as well.
Thereafter, clad in white garments, one should worship Madhusūdana;
having constantly performed this rite, one shall always go to the city of Agni.
Thus ends the ritual bath under the asterism Kṛttikā as described in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Nandi said:
"The asterism Rohiṇī is the birth constellation of the Discus-wielding God himself."
Having fashioned it from copper or gold, and endowed it with the five precious gems.
One should establish [the image] with a pair of garments and worship it with flowers and incense,
along with divine offerings of seasonal fruits and oblations cooked in ghee.
Having completed this on the second day, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa who is learned in the Vedas,
handsome, a mendicant, and a householder.
One should eat only at night oneself when Rohiṇī is seen;
such a divine vow as this was performed by the gods in heaven.
As each year arrives, even today the gods perform [this rite];
whatever desire one contemplates, that very thing one obtains without a doubt.
Thus ends the Rohiṇī-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Puṣkara said:
Having fasted under the Kṛttikās, the sacrificer and the domestic priest [should proceed].
O Bhārgava, one should perform the ceremonial bath for the patron on the day of Rohiṇī.
One should prepare five jars adorned with garlands of white flowers, smeared with the sap of milk-trees and ghee, and provided with *priyaṅgu* and sandalwood.
Facing east, one should consecrate Viṣṇu, Śaśānka, Varuṇa, Rohiṇī, and Prajāpati with those jars placed upon a heap of rice.
Restrained and adorned with a garland, one should worship him with perfumes, flower garlands, and ointments;
incense should likewise be offered to Prajāpati, as well as to Viṣṇu and the Moon.
One should offer five divine flour-bulls and incense;
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for the deities once the worship has been accomplished.

With clarified butter and all kinds of seeds, dressed in white garments and with senses subdued, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the preceptor: a bronze vessel, a cow, and two auspicious garments.
And then, O illustrious one, gold was offered with devotion to the brahmins,
along with dust and mud, as well as horse-hair and hoof-dust.

Having fashioned a horn of *trivṛt* [grass], it should be worn as a jewel that bestows auspiciousness; this is for the sake of adornment. Furthermore, whether a man or a woman, one should always perform this ritual bathing.
One obtains sons as desired,
as well as nourishment and vast, preeminent fame.
Thus ends the bath on the occasion of Rohiṇī as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Manu said:
For a king or a prince who is afflicted by the evil influence of the planets...
Or a chief queen whose children have died, or among people such as the twice-born and others.
Where the fruit fails despite diligent effort and exertion,
and where the loss of elephants, horses, cattle, and bulls occurs;
O highly fortunate one, wherever an affliction is observed on earth or in the atmosphere, there one should perform the sacrifice of the flower-consecration.
He is known as the Root King (Mūlarāja); his progeny and so forth constitute the Branches (Śākhā).
This applies during the rite of final dissolution (upasaṃhāra-saṃskāra), whether it be auspicious or even inauspicious.
[601] O child, effort must always be applied to the root; for it is from the root that the branches and so forth arise. When the root is destroyed, the branches and the abundance of fruits perish.
Therefore, O Great Sage, one should strive for the protection of the root;
for that indeed is the cause through which one attains virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.
O Śaunaka, listen now as I proclaim to you that peace which was formerly explained by Brahmā for the sake of Mahendra through Bṛhaspati.
The Puṣya-bath is of great merit, the destroyer of all sins, and a divine pacifier of portents; perform it wherever you may be.
On ground free from anthills, husks, hair, bones, pungent substances, and thorns; devoid of the foul odor of *śigru* and *śleṣmātaka* trees;
and avoided by herons, doves, vultures, owls, and crows.
In a place flooded with Campaka, Aśoka, Vakula, Āmrāta, and Śādvala grass,
overspread with young creepers and endowed with unblemished leaves.
It abounded with very sweet trees, was adorned with fruits and sprouts,
was crowded with flocks of fledglings, graced by cocks,
and filled with jīvajīvaka birds, hārītas, woodpeckers, and parrots.
It was filled with *cakora* and *cāsa* birds, adorned with *cakravāka* ducks,
and resounded with the cries of peacocks, pigeons, *aśrīka*, *kokaka*, and cuckoos.
One should perform the sacrifice in a field or a beautiful forest that is filled with honey-flowers, wine, liquor, and madhūka blossoms, at a designated time of day.
On the Himalaya, or at Ujjayanta, on the Sahya or the Vindhya mountain range,
or on the sandy banks of rivers, or at a delightful confluence.
One should perform it on the shore of the ocean, or in a hermitage, or even in a house, which is beautified by yellow pigment, lac, gold, conch shells, and saffron.
On ground where there is an abundance of grain, water, and floating vegetation, following a clockwise path, in water free from dogs, rats, and mice, and devoid of the dwellings of crabs.
The earth, endowed with excellent color, fragrance, and taste, thick, smooth, and level,
has been thoroughly examined many times for such things as the sprouting of seeds when sown.
Then, having gone there at an auspicious moment,
one should consecrate it in the northern direction and present an offering of oblations and flowers accompanied by mantras.
Let all the gods who desire worship here come forth,
as well as those from the quarters, the mountains, the twice-born, and whoever else shares in the portions.
Having thus invoked them all, the domestic priest should then speak as follows:
"Having received this worship, may you depart after bestowing peace upon the king."
Having performed worship to them, the observer of the vow should then dwell there for that night;
having bathed, he should behold auspicious horses, cows, calves, curd, and mustard seeds.
The sight of flowers, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, fruits, and parched grain,
as well as the sight of an umbrella, chowries, a conch, a lotus, white garments, and so forth,
or the attainment of all desired objects, is proclaimed to lead to the fulfillment [of one's aims].
Trees that bear fruit and flowers and yield milky sap are considered to bestow auspiciousness;
climbing upon them is highly recommended for temples, palaces, and similar structures.
An eclipse of the moon or sun is auspicious; climbing a mountain is favorable;
and seeing oneself bound in shackles in a dream brings victory over enemies. One should circumambulate a mountain or conceal one's voice with a loud shout.
He who enwraps a temple in a dream shall attain victory;
he obtains everything desired, and indeed, gain shall be his.
Sexual union with a woman who has wept over the dead brings good fortune;
likewise, crossing over wells, mud, and pits in a dream is auspicious.
Crossing rivers as well as crossing the ocean is auspicious;
having conquered the enemy army, a human being attains victory.
Bracelets and other ornaments bestow the happiness of sons and sovereignty;
they bring about the acquisition of friends and people of excellent conduct, and grant women and wealth.
If one who has begun the slaughter of blood should drink it, or if he ever crosses over [the river],
he gains profit from the eating of flesh and bones, or obtains a beneficial fruit.
Causing laughter, dancing, wandering, enthusiasm, and falling, they are the bringers of strife.
In the south, there is coming and going, being dragged away, and the arrival of fear and death;
in the west, there is traveling by vehicle and likewise entering a well;
in the north, the appearance of red garlands and garments in a dream brings fear.

Upon seeing inauspicious omens such as a donkey, camel, monkey, pigeon, boar, snake, or night-stalker (a ghost), one should perform a rite for victory, as these portend the fruit of being struck down or falling.
For those suffering from disorders of wind, bile, and phlegm, for those traveling by vehicle or crossing fire,
and during the summer, autumn, and spring, they who give water-stalls and gifts of fruit [attain merit].
Whether it be the recitation of what was heard, that which was seen, experienced, or censured,
or even if such deeds were not observed, they are likewise [manifested] at the onset of the first watch of the night.
All those seen in the middle yield middling results, while those at the end bestow swift results;
likewise are those described who have witnessed the release of the cows.
Having seen auspicious dreams, one should perform a sacrifice or have one performed;
one should undertake bathing, worship of the deities, fire offerings, rites for victory, and rites for peace.
Having performed all these, O child, one should then draw the mandala,
beginning at four cubits and extending up to a hundred cubits.
A mandala should be constructed there; from that point upward, one should not cause it to be made.
It should be stainless, victorious, auspicious, a celestial palace, bestowing welfare, and propitious.
Vardhamāna, Deva, the one called Latā which grants desires,
and the one called Svastika with its wheel— these are the twelve maṇḍalas.
And the most beautiful powder of white and green colors should be prepared.
Having prepared a powder made from *śāli*, *ṣaṣṭika*, safflower, turmeric, and *haripatra* flowers,
as well as gems, coral, and red minerals,
consecrated with ashes and enriched with the incense of white mustard seeds, one should cause it to fall.
The mantra-practitioner should place the king of weapons, or the syllables that arise from it;
having made an auspicious and pleasant spot smeared with cow dung.
The ground, previously prepared and measured correctly toward the east, west, and north, should be perfumed with powdered sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, incense, and other fragrant substances.
In the southern direction, one should draw a swastika, a conch, and other such figures using threads adorned with knots;
in the center, eight lotus petals are drawn, tripled and then tripled again.
The doors have their lines aligned; likewise, there are lotuses radiant with buds and filaments, as well as svastikas and blue water-lilies.
Supporting [the vessel] with the right hand, one should begin the scattering of the colored powders (rajas) from above as desired,
using the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
Having turned the fingers downward, the wise one should cause them to fall;
the line should be made straight, unbroken, and free from clusters.
It should be made as thick as the joint of a thumb and even by one who knows.
One should never draw [a line] that is attached, uneven, thick, broken, thin, covered, terminated at the edge, or short.
One should know that when [the lines] are joined there is quarrel, and when they are curved there is conflict;
when they are excessively thick there will be disease, and when they are intermingled there is constant suffering.
Through dots, one incurs fear from the side of the enemy; of this there is no doubt.
If the line is thin, there will be loss of wealth; if it is broken, death is certain. Or else, there may be separation from beloved objects and children.
But whoever should draw the mandala according to their own whim without knowing [the rules],
incurs all the faults that have been previously described.
One should draw the supreme mandala, square with four gates;
in accordance with the dimensions of the mandala, one should draw a lotus at each gate.
O Brahmin, one should never draw a lotus with fewer petals than eight;
nor should a wise person draw more than four above [the center].
Prowess, longevity, prosperity, dharma, sovereignty, women, excellence of form,
and the attainment of wealth are obtained in the eastern gate and the [eastern] mandala.
Intelligence, memory, fame, happiness, health, being beloved by people,
and the accomplishment of all desires and aims [are attained] in the mandala at the northern gate.
In the western gate-maṇḍala, there is a son, as well as longevity, strength, good fortune, the crushing of enemies, and the increase of sacrificial rites.
In its center, O Brahmin, there is again a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp,
measuring four *vitastis* for a Kṣatriya, three *vitastis* for a Vaiśya,
and two-and-a-half *vitastis* for a woman or a Śūdra.
Following the sequence of the lotus itself, one should likewise arrange the stalk;
having taken recourse to the western direction, one should fashion the stalk accordingly.
Its stalk is proclaimed to extend through the seven netherworlds and reach to the end of the universe.
The pericarp shall be Meru, situated with the seeds as the hosts of planets;
the filaments shall be the rivers, and the mountains are situated within the pericarps.
The eight petals are said to be the directions, and the sages are established upon the lotus.
The seven netherworlds and the world of the earth are proclaimed as the stalk;
such is the lotus imagined by Śambhu, the God of gods.
It is joined with banners and archways and adorned with flags;
the world of the earth (bhūrloka) is to be known as its petals, while the directional self is the sphere of the void.
The heavenly world (Svarloka) is known as the pericarp, and the three worlds are designated as the lotus;
one should place the Lord Maheśvara, the object of worship, within that pericarp.
The Mothers, the Grahas, the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, the Rākṣasas, the Divākaras, the Vasus, the Sun, the Lords of the World, the Rudras, and the Sovereigns of the Universe.

One should likewise draw upon the lotus the units of time: the *kalās*, *kāṣṭhās*, *kṣaṇas*, watches (*yāmas*), nights and days— both bright and dark— the fortnights (*pakṣas*), months, seasons, divisions, years, the intermediate *yugas*, the ends of the *kalpas*, and the great *mahākalpas*.
In the first circle, one should worship the god Śiva together with Vighneśa;
in the second enclosure, one should worship him together with Gaṇanāyaka.
The sun with Rāhu in the east, and Pinākin in the northeast.
One should place Keśava facing the east and Pitāmaha facing the west;
in this manner, one should arrange them upon the ground in the third enclosure.
In an area strewn with various mines of jewels, one should further depict the gods,
the priests in their proper places, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, ancestors, and deities.
One should cause the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the Munis, and the Siddhas to be placed there;
as well as the Planets together with the Constellations, the Rudras, and the Mothers.
Having fashioned images of Skanda, Viṣṇu, Viśākha, the world-protectors (Lokapālas), and the celestial women out of various kinds of gold, endowed with pleasing qualities of fragrance;
Just as a wise person should worship with perfumes, garlands, and ointments,
as well as with various kinds of foods, fruits, roots, and so forth.
In the past, during the sacrifice to the planets, I performed a special worship with various delightful drinks, such as wine, milk, and fermented liquors.
The offering for the Mothers and the gods is also prepared right here;
one should worship the Piśācas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas with meat and liquor.
The ancestors [are satisfied] by ointments, collyrium, sesame seeds, and meat;
likewise, the sages [are satisfied] by the Sāman, Ṛg, and Yajur Vedas, by garlands, and by the three sweets.
One should worship the *nāgas* with all kinds of jewels and pigments;
and one should worship the gods with incense, offerings of oblations, jewels, and circumambulations.
One should worship the Gandharvas and Apsarases with perfumes, garlands, and flowers; likewise, one should honor all the remaining deities with offerings and fragrant blossoms.
Banners, garments, and ornaments bearing their respective names,
as well as sacrificial threads provided for the excellent sacrifice, were to be given to all of them.
Either to the south, the west, or the northwest of the mandala,
one should perform the fire offering (homa) as prescribed for the sacrifice to the planets, according to the ritual for the Mother-sacrifice.
O child, having prepared these substances as described and endowed with the proper characteristics—
namely parched grain, unbroken rice, ghee, honey, curd, milk, and mustard seeds— [608]
Siddhārtha seeds, fragrant flowers, incense mixed with sugar,
gorocanā, sesame seeds, darbha grass, mung beans, and nutmeg fruits.
One should present shallow bowls completely filled with ghee and milk-rice;
on the western altar, however, the one performing the worship should be a *snātaka*.
One should make the jars very firm; I shall tell you their defining characteristics.
O Great Sage, I shall explain the knowledge of the characteristics of their origin, by which jars are celebrated in the world as "vācakas" (proclaimers).
While the nectar was being churned by all the gods together with the Dānavas,
having made Mount Mandara the churning rod and Vāsuki the rope, they stirred it.
There, the nectar has arisen, possessing great potency and prowess;
for the purpose of containing it, the flask is proclaimed.
Because this was fashioned by the gods through Viśvakarman, taking a portion from each of them, it is therefore called a *kalaśa*.
Brahmā is at the mouth of the jar, Maheśvara is at the neck,
Viṣṇu is stationed at the base, and the hosts of Mothers are situated in the middle.
But all the remaining deities surround them on the four sides.
Within his belly are the seven oceans and the seven continents in their midst;
likewise, all the lunar mansions, the planets, and the principal mountain ranges.
Himavat, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha,
Meru, Rohita, Mālyavat, and Sūryakānti are the mountains.
The Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, the auspicious Sindhu, and the river Yamunā;
the Airāvatī and the Śatadru, as well as the river Vaitaraṇī;
the Godāvarī, the Narmadā, and the great river named Mahī.
Kurukṣetra, Prayāga, Ekahasta, Pṛthūdaka, Amareśa, Puṇḍarīka, and the Gaṅgā-sāgara.
Whatever sacred fords exist upon the earth truly reside within the water-pot,
as do Svāhā, Śānti, Puṣṭi, Prīti, and Gāyatrī herself.
The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and likewise the Sāmaveda,
together with the Atharvaveda— all are situated within the pitcher.
There are nine auspicious jars originating from the forms of Śambhu:
Gobhya, Upagobhya, Maruta, and another, Sumanda.
Manohara is indeed proclaimed as the auspicious fifth;
Virūja and Tanadūṣa are both the sixth and seventh;
the eighth is Indriyātīta, and the ninth is remembered as Vijaya.
The pitchers are indeed known to be nine; learn from me their presiding deities.
Listen, my child, to how the directions are established in their assignment.
The ninth, which is known by the name Vijaya,
is there Śiva himself, the auspicious remover of all sins, who dwells in person.
He is renowned in the world as five-faced, the accomplisher of all aims;
because he consists of the nature of the five Brahmās, he is remembered as five-faced.
One should know that Sadyojāta is in the western face, Vāmadeva likewise in the northern,
Tatpuruṣa in the eastern, and Aghora in the southern.
Īśāna is the fifth, situated in the center above all;
these five faces, O child, destroy sins and annihilate the malevolent planets.
Sadyojāta is white, while Vāmadeva is yellow;
Tatpuruṣa is to be known as red, and Aghora is indeed black.
Īśāna is at their western side, endowed with all colors;
he is the granter of desires, capable of assuming any form at will, the support of knowledge, and identical with Śiva.
Kṣitindra is the first jar; the second is Jalasaṃbhava;
the third is Pavana; the fourth is Hutāśana;
the fifth is Yajamāna; and the sixth is Ākāśasaṃbhava.
Soma is declared the seventh, and Āditya likewise the eighth;
these divine beings were produced in the past and presided over by Śiva.
There are eight forms of Indra and nine of Sūrya established;
Kṣitīndra is to be placed in the east, and Jalasaṃbhava in the west.
Having assigned Vāyu in the northwest, Agni-born in the southeast,
the Sacrificer in the southwest, and Kāma-born in the northeast.
One should place the Saumya [vessel] to the north and the Saura [vessel] to the south;
having thus placed the jars, one should contemplate their primordial form.
Brahmā is indeed at the mouths of the jars, Viṣṇu at their necks;
in the middle are all the hosts of Mothers, as well as the gods led by Indra and the serpents.
Within their bellies were the oceans and the earth with its seven continents;
likewise, Śrī, Umā, the Gandharvas, the Ṛṣis,
and the terrible five elements stood beneath them.
Filled with pure water, they are white and entirely radiant;
whether with water from rivers,
lakes, dug-out ponds, or reservoirs, or with water from tanks, wells, and the like, or even with ocean water, they bring happiness.
Auspicious in every way, the most auspicious of all, and destroyers of all sins—
such auspicious jars should always be taken for the consecration ceremony.
During a journey, at the time of marriage, or during the rites of consecration and sacrifice,
these [mantras] should be especially employed, for they accomplish all desires.
For a woman whose children have died, one who is proclaimed barren,
one with a dead fetus, one who has never conceived, one who is unfortunate, or one afflicted by disease— for these,
the ritual bathing within the Puṣya-maṇḍala should always be performed.
Provided with all kinds of jewels, medicinal herbs, fragrances, fruits, and flowers,
these [images] should be fashioned during planetary afflictions, as well as for auspicious and propitious occasions.
Because they cause the planets and likewise various mothers to move,
as well as most terrible misfortunes, they are therefore known as *cārakas*.
Because each individual digit (kalā) is withdrawn in due order by means of the embodied principles beginning with earth (kṣiti), they are therefore known as *kalaśas*.
They may be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, endowed with the proper characteristics;
five finger-breadths wide and sixteen finger-breadths in height.
As for the measurement of the jars, the mouth should be eight finger-breadths wide;
he who is established as the eightfold form is that Śiva born from the lotus.
His eight forms are the Gaṇas; Śiva is situated in the pericarp.
Those who are the Gaṇas are the petals, and those who are the Nāgas are the jars.
The jars are said to be the planets, and the directions are the world-protectors;
by these, this entire world, up to the realm of Brahmā, is pervaded.
One should place jewels, seeds, flowers, and fruits— belonging to beings who are invincible, great-souled, and purifiers of all sins—
into the vase, along with flower garlands, garments, food, and white sandalwood paste.
With diamonds, pearls, lapis lazuli, and great lotuses, as well as with crystals and all auspicious fruits such as the *bilva*, orange, and *udumbara*;
With citron, jambīra, mango, āmrātaka, and pomegranate; with barley, śāli rice, nivāra rice, wheat, and white mustard seeds.
With saffron, agallochum, camphor, madana, gorocana, sandalwood,
māṃsī, cardamom, kuṣṭha, camphor, patra, caṇḍā, and surājala;
Niryāsa, ambuda, śaileya, sarjja, devadāru, and phala; jātīpatra, kanāgāhva, pṛkvā, gaurī, and parṇikā.
Vaca, rātri, samañjiṣṭhā, turaṣka, and maṅgalāṣṭaka;
durvā, mohanabhṛṅgāra, śatamūlī, and śatāvarī.
Bālā, nāgabalā, the goddess (devī), sahadevī, jayā, akṣumā, punnāga, umā, sitā, pāṭhā, guñjā, and the surasikā creeper.

Having collected the *bālaka*, elephant tusk, *śatapuṣpā*, *punarnavā*, *brāhmī*, *devī*, *śivā*, *rudrā*, all fragrant substances, and gold— all these auspicious items— one should place them within the jars.
One should offer auspicious, victorious incense, the moon, and all that is auspicious;
as well as ornaments made of every kind of jewel and a cloth known as *rocanā*.
Increasing by two finger-breadths at a time up to thirty-six finger-breadths,
it may be circular or square, lotus-shaped, or consisting of three inner chambers.

One should fashion a two-cubit lotus in the center of which is Vāsava, accompanied by the Bhaga, Svastika, and Vināyakas; it should be graced by all the auspicious deities such as Śrī and the growth of the Śrīvṛkṣa, and endowed with all kinds of jewels.
One cubit in height, beautifully adorned with ten finger-breadths,
the part called the "bath" (snāna) should be one and a half cubits, together with a leaf and its stalk.
One should provide a double-layered bed known as a *śayyā*, measuring one bow (*dhanus*) in length and equipped with a frame;
it should be strewn with the footprints of elephants and lions and adorned with gold and jewels.
It may be called "Lion" with a width of one and a half [units], or it may be a "Staff-seat" (daṇḍāsana),
or a "Planet" (graha) with feet set evenly, adorned with golden leaf-patterns.
It should be known as having the color of a great sapphire, adorned with precious jewels;
it may have four legs or be made equal to the three mandalas.
One should have pillows made with tiger skins, leopard skins, or lotus-patterned cloths;
or else with other dyed fabrics filled with soft cotton.
The bed should be long and wide, measuring four cubits, and endowed with auspicious marks;
its feet should be shaped like those of a lotus, a horse, an elephant, or a lion.
Or, they should be made variegated with ivory and adorned with gold and jewels;
the female elephants should be fashioned with beautiful woolen cloths and their trunks raised aloft.
Kinnaras and others should be fashioned, endowed with all beauty;
likewise, birds and various collections [of beings], provided with auspicious fragrances.
The place for holding the head should indeed be made like a *śivopala* stone;
it should be joined with a lotus, a *svastika*, a water-lily, and a bird.
Adorned with a crest of leafy creepers, well-crafted with golden tusks,
and embellished with diamonds, rubies, emeralds, and lapis lazuli.
Having a form like the frontal globes of an elephant, or indeed marked with a half-moon,
it measures one thousand *kinnarīs*, or even seven hundred and five.
For the lord of men, the sovereign of all worlds, two hundred and thirty [palas] more than that [two hundred] should be used;
the bed should be made like a cotton mattress, filled with soft wooden blocks. A soft, circular, and variegated pillow should also be prepared.
The excellent narrative known as Śravaṇa is circular in shape like a water-chestnut (śṛṅgāṭaka).
The vehicle, bed, and seat should be made with beautifully adorned circular bases;
the well-decorated foot-rest should be made one span (vitasti) high.
Having thus prepared the entire bed, seat, and so forth,
adorned with the splendor of garments and ornaments, one should perform the consecration.
Then [he gave] the inexhaustible hide of a bull, of a warrior, and of a roe deer; then that of a lion, and after that, of a tiger.
One should spread those four skins upon that sacrificial altar when an auspicious moment has arrived and the moon is endowed with merit.
A beautiful throne-seat (bhadrāsana) should be constructed, made of gold, silver, copper, or from the wood of a milk-exuding tree, measuring one and a half cubits in height.
The royal mandala for kings should likewise measure one and a quarter cubits;
then, with a well-joyful mind, the king should enter it at the conclusion of the fire oblation.
Surrounded by astrologers, ministers, chamberlains, bards, citizens, and friends,
accompanied by the sound of the twice-born reciting the Vedas and the resonance of auspicious musical instruments;
With the sounds of mṛdaṅgas, conchs, and cymbals, and with auspicious noises,
one should bathe the king— who is dressed in unwashed linen and reclining on a woolen blanket— with jars containing offerings, flowers, and the like, and filled with clarified butter.
One hundred and twenty-eight, increased by eight, shall be the number of jars;
it is declared that each subsequent one is greater than the preceding.
O Lord, one should bathe with auspicious mantras, or with sacred water,
or with the water from the sacrifice for the Goddess and Śambhu, or even with clarified butter.
Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is auspicious and removes sin.
Clarified butter is the food of the gods; in clarified butter all worlds are established.
Whether terrestrial, atmospheric, or celestial, whatever [sin] exists that destroys all impurity—
may it all go to destruction through contact with this clarified butter (ājya).
Then, having brought forward a woolen blanket, the preceptor should bathe the king with jars filled with flowers and water while reciting this mantra:
"May the gods and those who are the ancient Siddhas consecrate you."
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Sādhyas together with the hosts of Maruts.
The Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two excellent Aśvins;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, Svāhā, Siddhi, and Sarasvatī.
Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Śrī, Sinīvālī, Kuhū, as well as Diti, Surasā, Cinatā, and Kadrū.
May the wives of the gods mentioned before, as well as the mothers of the gods,
and all the auspicious throngs of Apsarases, consecrate you.
The lunar mansions, the auspicious moments, the fortnights, the junctions of day and night, the year, the sun, the divisions of time such as kalās, kāṣṭhās, kṣaṇas, and lavas.
May all the auspicious divisions of Time consecrate you,
as well as the hosts of gods in their celestial chariots, the Manus, and the oceans.
And the highly blessed rivers, the nāgas, and the kimpuruṣas,
as well as the illustrious vaikhānasa hermits together with the twice-born forest-dwellers.
The twice-born ones, those moving through the air, the hours, and those fixed stars;
Marīci, Atri, Pulaha, Pulastya, Kratu, and Aṅgiras.
Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, Sanaka, and Sanandana;
Sanātana, Dakṣa, and likewise Sanakanandana;
Ekata, Hitaka, Trita, Jābāli, Kaśyapa, Dūrvāsas, Durvinīta, Kaṇva, and likewise Kātyāyana.
Mārkaṇḍeya, Dīrghatapas, Śunaḥśepha, Vidūratha,
Dvaipāyana, Yavakrīta, and Devarāta with his younger brother.
May these and other sages, devoted to divine vows,
together with their disciples and wives, who are rich in asceticism, consecrate you.
Mountains, trees, creepers, sacred shrines,
Prajāpati, Diti, and cows are the mothers of the universe.
And divine vehicles, all the worlds with their moving and unmoving beings,
the fires, the ancestors, the stars, the clouds, and the water in its various forms.
May these and many other auspicious ones, whose merits are celebrated,
consecrate you with waters that destroy all portents.
"May they bring you prosperity, as well as long life and health.
Then Maghavan was consecrated by these beings of joyful minds.
Thus, by means of these auspicious mantras— divine and otherwise—
belonging to Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, Rudra, and those originating from Brahmā and Śakra.
With the mantras "āpohiṣṭhā," "hiraṇya," and likewise "śambhave," one should wear a cotton garment that is the most auspicious among all auspicious things.
[617] Having sipped water for purification amidst auspicious sounds of conchs, flutes, and musical instruments,
the king should then worship the gods, his teachers, the Brahmins, and the banners and weapons.
The king should cause the parasol, musical instruments, elephants, and horses to be held while consecrated with mantras;
and by means of the Veda, he should achieve victory over his ornaments.
Then, on the second day, having bowed to the Vidyā, one should offer oblations into the fire;
one should observe the omens situated in the mouths and locations of the deities.
Svāhā to Rudra, to Candra, to Viṣṇu, to Brahmā, and to Śiva;
to Prajāpati, to Kumāra, to Vighnahā, and to Vināyaka.
"To Sūrya, king of the planets; to Varāha, who took three strides;
to the Mother of the Mothers, the boon-granting Cāmuṇḍā—svadhā!"
Then the king should have it brought from the Naga king Ananta;
once the hide has been properly prepared in sequence, the lord of men sits down upon it.
Above the bull, the wild cat, the donkey, the horse,
and the ram, there are those of the lion and the tiger beyond them.
Once he has sat down again, having performed the oblation with those mantras using sesame seeds mixed with ghee,
and having brought the remainder of the rite to completion, he should stand with palms joined in reverence and speak as follows.
May all the hosts of gods depart, taking the worship from the king,
after bestowing abundant success and for the sake of returning once more.

The remainder is that while being bathed, one should recite the three verses beginning with *āpo hiṣṭhā*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the mantra beginning with *namo saṃbhavāya* and *mayo bhava*. As Garga says:
"The king, having been bathed, should recite the three verses of *āpo hiṣṭhā* and the four verses of *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, accompanied by the sounds of auspicious proclamations and conch shells."
And having donned two new garments consecrated with mantras, he should wear the pair of clothes.
Thus, one should wear [the cloth] washed with all-auspicious substances such as sandalwood and the like, together with cotton.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Having bathed in this manner, one should likewise look at one's face in a mirror smeared with ghee."
Having performed the auspicious rites of grasping, wearing clean garments and being composed in mind, he should proceed.
Then one should perform the worship of the deities and others individually;
likewise, having performed the worship of the weapons, one should perform the worship of the vehicles.
Having performed the worship of the royal insignia, one should indeed adorn one's own body;
one should apply unguents consecrated with the Śrīsūkta.
"O Creator, bestow prosperity upon me; may he obtain the favor of the wise. This mantra is prescribed for the act of adorning oneself with the words, "Granting long life and splendor."
Then, having anointed himself with fragrant unguents, wearing garlands and beautiful ornaments,
and having performed the worship of Keśava, he should proceed to the place of the fire.
In the *Atharvaparisiṣṭa*:

"Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) to be made, the wise man should cause the commencement [of the rite] during an auspicious lunar day, asterism, muhūrta, and karana."
Having consecrated the musical instruments with the mantra "uccairghoṣa," the domestic priest,
adorned for the consecration, [should proceed] amidst the sound of all the musical instruments.
Then he should perform worship—this is the ellipsis.

Immediately after the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), having washed his clothes and sipped water for purification (*svācānta*), he should worship the gods, the preceptor, and the Brahmins. As for the banners, weapons, and so forth, having worshipped them and consecrated them with their respective mantras, he should wear them at the appropriate time following another *puṣya* bath. The wearing of ornaments is performed with the mantra of the Goddess known as *Vijayā*, beginning with the words "daivena," which is well-known in the Śaiva Āgamas.
The mantras for the banner and other items, however, are found in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Rāma said: O sinless one, tell me the mantras for the parasol, horse, banner, elephant, flag, sword, shield, as well as for the drum and the bow.
Puṣkara said: Listen, O highly fortunate one, to those mantras which the blessed Parāśara,
the best among all upholders of dharma, formerly spoke to Gālava.
Just as a cloud covers this earth for the welfare of all,
so do you cover the king for the increase of his victory and well-being.
The parasol mantra:
"O King of the Gandharva feathers, may you not be a defiler of your lineage,
by the word of truth of Brahmā, and of Soma and Varuṇa."
And by the power of the sacrificial fire, speak, O horse,
and by the splendor of the sun, as well as by the asceticism of the sages,
by the celibacy of Rudra, and by the strength of the wind!
Remember that you are a prince; remember the Kaustubha jewel!
Consider the fate that awaits the slayer of a Brahmin, as well as the slayer of a father or a mother.
One who speaks falsehood for the sake of land, and a Kṣatriya who turns his back in battle—
as far as the sun, the moon, and the wind perceive that evil deed,
one shall quickly go to that same destination; and that sin shall be yours.
O horse, if you do not meet with death in that battle,
then, having conquered your enemies in the fray, may you live happily together with your master.
The mantra for the horse:
"O great hero, banner of Śakra, the Suparṇa has taken refuge in you;
likewise, the banner of Nārāyaṇa is yours by virtue of half of the purifier."
He is measurable by his strides, the bringer of the nectar of immortality, the enemy of the Nāgas, and he whose vehicle is Viṣṇu;
he is all-pervading, invincible, and the slayer of the enemies of the gods in battle.
Garuda, possessing the speed of the wind, is present and stationed within you;
burn our enemies, the warriors along with their horses, armor, and weapons, wherever they may be.
The mantra of the banner:
Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, Vāmana, Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla— these eight are of divine origin.
Their sons and grandsons have taken refuge in eight forces:
Mada, Manda, Mṛdu, Gaja, and Saṃkīrṇa.
O great elephant, remember that you were born from a bamboo stalk in the forest;
may the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts protect you. O lord of serpents, protect your husband; let your agreement be observed.
Attain victory in battle; may there be well-being for us on your journey—depart!
May you have beauty from Soma, strength from Viṣṇu, splendor from the Sun, and speed from the Wind.
May the stability of Mount Meru, victory from Rudra, and glory from the god Purandara protect you in battle, O Naga! May the quarters of the world, together with the deities,
and the Ashvins along with the Gandharvas, always protect you, O Mountain.
The mantras of the elephant:
the Fire-god, the Vasus, the Rudras, Vāyu, Soma, the great ṛṣis,
the nāgas, kinnaras, gandharvas, yakṣas, hosts of bhūtas, and grahas.
May the Pramathas together with the Ādityas, Bhūteśa together with the Mothers,
Śakra, Senāpati Skanda, and Varuṇa— having taken refuge in you—
burn all enemies; may the king attain victory.
Those terrifying weapons discharged by the enemies from all sides—
let them fall upon the foes themselves, destroyed by your splendor!
Just as at the slaying of Kālanemi, as at the destruction of Tripura,
and as at the killing of Hiraṇyakaśipu and all the other Asuras, so too,
upon seeing this blue and white [image], the enemies of kings perish instantly.
Defeated in battle by various terrible diseases and weapons,
she who is known as Pūtanā, Revatī, and Kālarātri—
may she, having taken refuge in you as a banner, swiftly burn all enemies.
The mantra of the banner:
O sword, the slayer, the scimitar, the sharp-edged, the unassailable;
the womb of glory, victory itself, the protector of Dharma—homage be to you!
Thus these eight names of yours were spoken by the Creator himself;
your constellation is named Kṛttikā, and your presiding deity is the Great Lord Maheśvara.
Rohiṇī is your body, while Janārdana is your deity;
he is your father, your grandfather, and the God—protect us always.
The Sword Mantra:
"O giver of armor, you are indeed like an army of shields in battle;
protect me, for I am worthy of your protection, O sinless one! Homage be to you!"
The Mantra for the Drum:
O drum, may you increase the victory over our rivals,
just as aquatic creatures rejoice at the roar of the thundercloud.
"May it be so; by your word, may joy bring us delight."
Just as terror arises among women at the sound of a thundercloud,
so too may our enemies tremble at your voice in battle.
The Dundubhi Mantra:
O great sovereign of all weapons, destroyer of all enemies of the gods,
O bow, protect [us] always together with excellent arrows at all times!
The mantra of the bow.

Regarding the phrase "on the second altar" (*dvitīyāyāṃ vedyām*): it has already been established that three altars must first be prepared. Among them, bathing takes place on the western altar; the sacrifices to the planets (*grahayaṣṭi*) take place on the southern altar. However, this [altar]—which is the northwest altar in relation to the previously mentioned *graha-homa*, or because of its connection with the second *homa* to be described—is called the "second" by the word *dvitīyā*, even though it is actually the third. In the phrase "in the mouth, the station of the gods" (*devānāṃ vadane sthāne*), once the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*) has been prepared according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-kalpa*, one should offer twenty-eight or one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta-āhuti*) into the fire for each of the deities, beginning with Rudra and the other deities of the previously worshipped maṇḍala, using their names preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), ending in the dative case, and joined with *svāhā*.

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*: "Then, for those very [deities], the domestic priest should offer abundant clarified butter into the fire with their own names ending in the dative case, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*."

Regarding the passage beginning with "nimittāni" and so forth: while the fire-oblation (*homa*) is being performed, one should dissolve into the fire those auspicious signs (*nimitta*) that indicate good fortune, such as the flame turning clockwise, intense brilliance, auspicious sounds, and the absence of smoke.
Garga says:
"Then the domestic priest (*purohita*), while the king holds on to him, should perform the sacrifice in the fire."
We worship Tryambaka, from whom we partake of Indra.
"Bṛhaspate pari dīyase," "Idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame," and "Ā vāyo bhūṣa śucinā"— with these mantras, one should adorn [the deity] in due order.
The oblation (homa) should consist of one hundred and eight offerings each of *samī* wood, sesame seeds, clarified butter (*ājya*), *dūrvā* grass, and also *bilva* fruits; or it may be at least ten.
In the *Atharvaṇapariśiṣṭa*:
"The domestic priest should offer oblations according to the procedure of the *Caturhotṛ* formulas,
while stable Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas stand in the four directions."
One should subsist on bilva fruits, or on other fruits, or even on milk;
or one may subsist on ghee for seven nights, and thereafter perform the fire-oblation (homa).
One should prepare milk-rice with cow’s products using a golden ladle,
accompanied by the mantras that begin with the Vedas and preceded by the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
The group known as Śarma-varma-gaṇa, as well as Aparājita; the Āyuṣya group, the Abhaya group, and likewise the Svastyayana group.
Having offered oblations to these five groups, one should cause the best of the twice-born to recite.

The *śarmavarma* group begins with "May he be victorious today" (*adya śarma-varma*) and so forth; the *aparājita* group begins with "He who is unconquered" (*aparājitaḥ viśarasyamānaḥ*) and so forth; the *āyuṣya* group begins with "Life-breath and downward breath" (*prāṇāpānau*) and so forth; the *abhaya* group begins with "Bestower of well-being upon the people" (*svastidā viśām*) and so forth; the *svastyayana* group begins with "May there be a good landing" (*sūpārepātam*) and so forth. Then, according to the procedure prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, the declaration of the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) is performed. Then follows the "King’s Seat" (*rājāsana*). Thereafter, following the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should spread upon that very altar (*vedi*), in the northern part of the fire, the ox-hides previously mentioned; having brought a lion-throne (*siṃhāsana*) as the king’s seat, one should place it upon them. Having spread in successive order over each of those the skins of the cat and other animals, one should cause the king to sit down. Once the king is seated, the domestic priest (*purohita*), having offered oblations of sesame seeds soaked in clarified butter to those same deities with their respective mantras, should complete the sequence ending with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, the expiations (*prāyaścitta*), and the final full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Finally, with palms joined in reverence, he should perform the dismissal of the deities (*devatāvisarjana*) with the mantra beginning "May the hosts of gods depart" (*yāntu devagaṇāḥ*).
Thus it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"To the north of the fire, one should place a lion-throne upon the hide previously mentioned, with its back toward the fire and provided with an auspicious covering."
Then, however, one should arrange the skins there with their necks facing forward.
Above those of the bull, the wildcat, the ruru deer,
and the spotted deer, there are those of the lion and the tiger after that.
With the mantra "Thou art firm, thou art the sky," he should cause the king to sit down there.
A bull (*vṛṣa*) is a draft ox; a *vṛṣadaṃśa* is a cat; a *ruru* is a white deer; a *pṛṣata* is a spotted deer. The king and likewise the domestic priest should have *darbha* grass in their hands.
The twice-born man should tie two blades of darbha grass together with their ends held in their hands.
At the time of the oblation, another twice-born man should tie the two *darbha* blades held in the hands of the king and the domestic priest together at the place of the planets.
Then, the pure priest, being purified, should offer clarified butter with Vedic mantras dedicated to Rudra,
Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Indra, Soma, and Varuṇa.
Then one should perform the ritual procedure known as the "Northern" (uttara) according to the Bārhaspatya tradition.

The Brāhma mantras begin with "brahma jajñānam" and so forth; the Raudra mantras begin with "asme rudrāḥ" and so forth; the Vaiṣṇava mantras begin with "viṣṇor nu kam" and so forth; the Vāyavya mantras begin with "āvāyo" and so forth; the Śakra mantras begin with "trātāram indram" and so forth; the Saumya mantras begin with "āpyāyasva" and so forth; the Varuṇa mantras begin with "imaṃ me varuṇa" and so forth; and the Bārhaspatya mantras begin with "bṛhaspate atiyat" and so forth. Then the king should worship the astrologers and the domestic priest with cows, land, gold, and jewels, as well as others who have descended through his lineage in due order.
One should offer protection to the deities of the locality, the deities of the household, the riverbanks, and crossroads;
one should grant safety to people and perform the ritual release of a bull.
Having adorned them both according to rule with white garments and ornaments,
and having informed the god and the goddess, he should release those held in bondage.
One who has entered the inner apartments of a king should not release those who are ill-disposed toward him;
rather, he should initiate worship in the city with gestures appropriate to his wealth.

Having ascended the lion-throne, illuminated by lamps placed on four-legged stands and contained in silver vessels, and having offered water, respectful oblations (*arghya*), and clarified butter as worship, one should likewise gaze upon yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and other auspicious items, as well as a mirror.

[626] Then, having honored the astrologers and the domestic priest with cows, land, gold, and other gifts, and having likewise worshipped other learned Brahmins (*śrotriya*) and those of hereditary lineage, he should worship the household deities, the city deities, the riverbanks, and the crossroads with offerings of worship. "The release of a cow" (*gogotsarga*) means a pair of cattle; that bull and cow should be white in color and adorned with garments, ornaments, and the like. He should release them after making this declaration: "I release these for the pleasure of the god Maheśvara and the goddess Bhagavatī. Having released those who have committed offenses against the king’s person or within the inner apartments from their bonds, he should perform worship in the city with banners, arches, and other decorations. "Fourfold enclosure" (*catuṣkī*) refers either to the arrangement of colored creepers or a special kind of assembly hall. The phrase "illumined by lamps" (*dīpair nīrājitaḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sense. "Vanditam" (worshipped) is used with the instrumental case in an adjectival sense. Then, he should look upon yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), curd, *dūrvā* grass, and so forth, as well as a mirror and auspicious objects.
In the *Atharvaparisiṣṭa* it is said:
"The eight auspicious things are declared to be: a Brāhmaṇa, a cow, fire, the earth, white mustard seeds, clarified butter, the *śamī* tree, and likewise rice and barley."
Constantly beholding, touching, and even worshipping these,
a king does not encounter calamity and attains unsurpassed prosperity.
Likewise, one should arrange a lion-throne, or a hereditary banner,
accompanied by chowries and a parasol, adorned with door-keepers,
and four intoxicated elephants positioned in the four directions.
Then, having sat down, the king should promote the welfare of his subjects;
[exempt from taxes are] mines, Brahmins, cows, women, children, the dull-witted, and the sick.
Then the king should grant an audience to the Brahmins,
as well as to the leaders of the guilds and other dignitaries, and he should pay homage to the womenfolk.
And when the people of the realm on earth are satisfied, they shall bestow their blessings upon you;
thus the subjects will be devoted and the earth will come under your control.
The domestic priest, the minister, and likewise the commander-in-chief;
the superintendent of horses, the superintendent of cattle, and the master of the storehouse.
The king should honor the master of the treasury, the physician, and the astrologer in their proper order,
according to their respective merits.
The domestic priest should place upon the head dūrvā grass, white mustard seeds, clarified butter, śamī wood, rice, barley, and white flowers.
For this is the ritual prescribed by the Atharva Veda for the consecration under the Puṣya asterism;
having bathed therein, the king enjoys the earth and goes to the world of Śakra.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "Thus, under the Puṣya asterism, the performer obtains kingdom, long life, and prosperity;
even without [the full ritual], the meritorious Puṣyābhiṣeka yields half its fruit."
During national calamities and portents, upon the appearance of a comet,
and during the affliction of the planets, one should perform the Puṣya-bath.
There is no calamity in the world that is not pacified by this;
nor is there any other auspiciousness that surpasses it.
For a king desiring supreme sovereignty and longing for the birth of a son,
this procedure is praised as being prior to his consecration.
It was given by the god to Brahmā, and by him again to Uśanas;
it was obtained from the preceptor Uśanas and then went to the assembly of the gods.
Bṛhaspati, of great renown, spoke this to Mahendra:
"This bath is supreme, bestowing long life, increase of progeny, and good fortune."
With this very water, the king should bathe his elephants and horses;
thus freed from disease, they shall attain supreme prosperity.
O King, the consecration ceremony must be performed every year for the sovereigns of the mandalas,
as well as for the lords of the vassals.
The neighboring kings should always perform the auspicious sacrifice to Vighneśvara for that woman endowed with auspicious marks who finds no happiness in her home;
they should cause this bath to be performed for her, which grants the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the Puṣya-bath.

During the northern course of the sun, having fasted for at least one night during the waxing fortnight, one desiring prosperity should cook a *sthālīpāka* under the asterism Tiṣya (*Puṣya*). Having worshipped Mahārāja (Kubera) and fed the Brahmins with that [offering] mixed with clarified butter, he should have them pronounce success (*siddhi*) by means of the *puṣyārgha* rite. In this manner, starting from each subsequent Tiṣya, he should feed two Brahmins on the second [Tiṣya], three on the third, and so on, increasing progressively for a year; thus he nourishes great prosperity. The fast is to be observed from the very beginning. "At least" (*avarārdham*) means the minimum. It is called "at least" because, compared to the alternative of many fasts for a man who has not yet performed the full purification, this involves fasting for only one night. "Mahārāja" refers to Kubera. With the remains of that oblation (*caru*), he should have them pronounce success through the *puṣyārgha*; he should have them say, "May there be prosperity and success. In this way, as before, the rites of worshipping Mahārāja and feeding the Brahmins with the *caru* are to be performed. "Two on the second" means he should feed two Brahmins on the second [Tiṣya]. Likewise, for a year, increasing progressively as before, the Brahmins are to be fed on the third and fourth Tiṣyas with a greater number. "From the very beginning" means on the first Puṣya, both on the preceding day and the following day.
Thus ends the Puṣya-vrata as declared by Āpastamba.
Dālbhya said:
"O best of the twice-born, [I shall describe] the duty of women arising from fasting."
Tell me according to the truth what the procedure for the fast is.
O most excellent one, O Blessed One, please explain in its entirety the dharma that brings joy for a maiden living in her own home and for a widow.
Pulastya said:
"Listen, O Brahmin, to all that you have asked,
which is renowned throughout the three worlds for the benefit of women."
O Brahmin, in former times the goddess, daughter of the king of mountains, asked this very question of her husband Śaṅkara while he was staying on the peak of Kailāsa.
The Goddess said: O Lord of Gods, O Keśava, tell me how [the deity] is to be worshipped by maidens, by housewives, and likewise by widows and women.
Īśvara said: "Excellent, excellent! You have asked well regarding this refuge of Nārāyaṇa.
Listen now to the rule for the rites such as fasting and so forth."
Having completed the sacrifice, a woman prospers in happiness here;
for even if her husband is ill-behaved, a woman obtains both pleasure and wealth from him.
How can a woman, being without a support, attain Hari, the Lord of the World, the Sovereign of all worlds, who is endowed with all worldly virtues?
Therefore, O lady of excellent complexion, one should perform this vow which bestows satisfaction upon Acyuta;
hear now its characteristics.
By reciting this, every woman undoubtedly attains her welfare;
having obtained happiness in this world, she shall also enjoy the pleasures of heaven after death.
Having obtained permission from her father and mother,
the young maiden should worship with devotion Hari, the Lord of the World, who removes all sins.
Furthermore, during the three subsequent lunar mansions, a maiden desiring a husband should daily recite the name "Mādhavāya" without weariness.
Having worshipped Acyuta with priyaṅgu flowers, red blossoms, and madhūka flowers,
one should offer anointment with saffron.
Having bathed well with all medicinal herbs and having propitiated that Lord of the World, one should perform oblations of honey and clarified butter while reciting: "Obeisance to Mādhava."
Having thus always worshipped Janārdana during the Uttarā-yoga,
she obtains a handsome husband and goes to heaven after death.
And whatever sin she committed in her extreme childhood,
from that sin she is liberated and shall indeed become happy.
O slender-limbed one, whatever vow she desires to undertake within a single year,
that very thing she shall attain, O blessed lady, if she is devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
One should perform the propitiation of Hari for six months according to one's ability;
O highly fortunate lady, at the conclusion of the fast, one should feed the most excellent Brahmins.
Thus concludes the vow for obtaining a virtuous wife as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. Now follows the Jyeṣṭhā-vrata.
The sages said:
We have heard of the illusory power (*māyāvitva*) of Viṣṇu, the god of gods, the wielder of the discus.
You ought to tell us, O Romaharṣaṇa, according to the truth: how did the birth of Jyeṣṭhā come about from Janārdana, the god of gods?
Sūta said:
Having meditated upon the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning or end, the Master,
the Supreme Being in the world, fashioned this manifold universe for the sake of deluding it.
Viṣṇu indeed established the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the eternal Vedic duties;
having likewise joined Śrī Padmā, he assigned her a single share.
The one of great splendor caused the eldest sister, Alakṣmī— the inauspicious one who stands outside the Vedas— to take her portion among the lowest of men and unrighteousness.
Having first created Alakṣmī and afterwards Padmā, Janārdana [did so];
therefore, O best of the twice-born, she is known as Jyeṣṭhā (the Eldest), for she is Alakṣmī.
At the time of the emergence of the nectar, she arose immediately after the Sudhā;
she appeared before them and was indeed known as Jyeṣṭhā.
Śrī, known as Padmā, was born immediately thereafter as the consort of Viṣṇu.
Then the brahmin-sage named Duḥsaha married Aśubhā;
having fully attained his purpose, he gazed upon her with his mind as she stood there, perfectly formed.
Then that sage wandered through the world with her, his heart filled with joy.
In that place resounded the voice of Hari and of the high-souled Hara,
as well as the chanting of the Vedas by the brahmins and likewise the smoke from the sacrificial offerings.
Or wherever a learned Vedic scholar might be, there she goes, afflicted by fear,
covering her ears and running hither and thither.
Seeing Jyeṣṭhā in such a state, Duḥsaha was overcome by delusion;
having gone to the forest with her, that sage then practiced his austerities.
There he saw the great-souled Mārkaṇḍeya approaching;
having prostrated before the great-souled sage, Duḥsaha said:
"O Blessed One, this wife of mine will not remain with me by any means."
O brahmin-sage, what shall I do with this wife?
Where shall I enter with her, and where indeed shall I not enter?
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen, Duḥsaha, to all this: she is ill-repute, endowed with inauspiciousness, and this peerless Alakṣmī is designated as Jyeṣṭhā.

Where people are devoted to Nārāyaṇa, followers of the Vedic path, high-souled devotees of Rudra with their bodies smeared with ashes, and where such people dwell eternally— you must not enter there under any circumstances.
Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Mādhava, Acyuta, Ānanda, Govinda, Vāsudeva, Janārdana!
O Nṛsiṃha, O Vāmana, O Inconceivable One, O Rāghava— those people who shall constantly and joyfully utter these names, you must by no means enter their wealth,
houses, gardens, or cow-pens.
The exceedingly fierce discus of Viṣṇu, formidable with its mass of flames and resembling a thousand suns, always destroys their inauspiciousness.
Go elsewhere to that house where the utterances of "svāhā" and "vaṣaṭ" prevail, or to where the chanting of the Sāmaveda resounds.
Those who are constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas, dedicated to their daily rites,
and intent on the worship of Vāsudeva— dismiss them from afar.
In whosever home the Agnihotra fire is maintained, or where there is the worship of the Liṅga,
or where Vāsudeva’s form or Caṇḍikā resides;
Go far away, abandoning those who are free from all sins;
go elsewhere, O Duḥsaha, leaving behind those who worship Maheśvara with constant and occasional sacrifices, along with this woman.
Dismiss those by whom Vedic scholars, Brahmins, cows, teachers, guests, and devotees of Rudra are always and eternally honored.
Duḥsaha said:
"O best of sages, tell me that place where my entry is appropriate;
freed from fear by your word, I shall always enter their house."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Where a wife and husband are in mutual conflict,
you, accompanied by your wife, may enter that house free from fear."
The God of gods, Mahādeva, Rudra, the Lord of the three worlds—
the Blessed One who is free from sleep and devoid of fear— should enter there.
There is no devotion to Vāsudeva where Hari is never present;
there is no chanting, fire-offerings, and the like, nor is there sacred ash in the homes of those men.
There is no worship on a festival day, especially not on the fourteenth day;
nor on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, nor at twilight for Rudra, unless one is free from fear.
And where indeed they do not worship Mahādeva on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight],
by those evil-minded ones whose faces are devoid of Viṣṇu’s name and whose faces are tearful.
And [they offer] salutation to the All-pervading Śiva, the Supreme Lord;
yet those deluded and evil-minded men do not speak it before a Brāhmaṇa.
In that regard, my son, you should always enter there together with your wife.
Enter that place where the sound of the Vedas is not heard, where there is no worship of the guru,
and which is devoid of ancestral rites— even with your wife.
"Enter, free from fear, this house night after night where mutual quarreling occurs; dwell there with her constantly."
O Viśa, enter without fear that very place where there is no worship of the Liṅga, where there is neither austerity nor self-restraint, and where there is even derision of devotion to Rudra.
Whether it be a guest, a Vedic scholar, a guru, or even a Vaiṣṇava—
if there are no cows in one's house, you may enter that home along with your wife.
While the children look on, where the elders indeed devour the eater,
enter there with your wife, filled with joy.
Without having worshipped Mahādeva or Vāsudeva,
and without having offered substances according to the prescribed rule, enter wherever you may be.
Enter that place where, in a nearby house, there are fools who delight in evil deeds and are devoid of compassion toward one another.
That housewife who breaks down the walls and the dwelling—
having reached that house, dwell there forever with a mind focused on nothing else.
Where there are thorny trees, where there is the niṣpāva creeper,
and where the brahmavṛkṣa tree is located— enter that place together with your wife.
"Enter the house of those who have Agastya, Arka, and other plants, or indeed Bandhujīva; especially Karavīra, or Nandyāvarta, or Mallikā— enter with your wife into the home of such people."
Where there is a maiden and a creeper, where Rohita and Jaṭī are in the house,
and where there is a Vakula tree and a plantain tree— there you, together with your wife, should enter.
Enter the tāla, the tamāla, the bhallāta,
the grove of tamarinds, the kadamba, or even the khadira tree, together with your wife.
"O you who have a banyan tree in your house, and likewise a holy fig tree, a cluster fig tree, and a breadfruit tree— enter together with your wife!"
"Enter that house where a crow may find you, whether in a garden or even in a dwelling; or else, enter it with your wife, shaven-headed by a child."
Enter the assembly hall together with your wife, bringing one goat, two sheep, three oxen, five buffaloes, six horses, and seven elephants.
Enter that house where the goddess Kālī, in the form of a preta or a ḍākinī,
or a kṣetrapāla together with his wife, resides.
And in whose house there is an image of a monk, or likewise an ascetic,
or a joyful image of the Buddha— enter there quickly.
Those whose speech never utters the names of Hari during times of lying down or sitting, nor while engaged in eating or sitting at meals—
that house is described as such; enter it along with your wife.
Where there are heretics devoted to [prohibited] practices, excluded from the Vedas and Smṛtis, devoid of devotion to Viṣṇu, revilers of Mahādeva,
and atheists who are like corpses— enter that place together with your wife.
And those evil-minded ones do not say that Brahmā, the Blessed Viṣṇu, and Śakra, the lord of all the gods, are born from the grace of Śiva.
The foolish, with deluded minds, claim that Brahmā and Lord Viṣṇu are equal to Śiva, just as they might speak of a firefly as being equal to the sun.
Enter their house, field, or dwelling together with her;
eat sweet food in their home with a single-minded focus on no other.
Only fools and the senseless eat cooked food without performing ritual bathing or auspicious rites; enter their homes.
Enter the abode of that woman who has fallen from purity, who is devoid of bodily refinement, and who is constantly devoted to eating all kinds of food.
O sinful one, enter the homes of those mortals who delight in drinking liquor, who are intent on eating meat, and who take pleasure in the wives of others.
Enter the houses of those who take no delight in worshipping on sacred festival days, or who indulge in sexual intercourse during the day,
or even at the time of twilight.
He who engages in sexual intercourse with women from behind like a dog or a deer,
or who performs sexual intercourse in water— enter into him along with your wife.
If that lowest of men should go to a woman in her menses, or to a Caṇḍāla woman,
or even to a maiden, a cow, or a goat, you must enter the fire together with your wife.
What is the use of much talk? Enter the house of those who are excluded from their daily rites and devoid of devotion to Rudra.
Having smeared the penis with divine herbs, honey, and [other substances] from the tips [of the plants], he departs;
he causes the discharge of semen for him—enter into him together with your wife.
Having spoken thus, that illustrious sage,
a Brahman-seer resembling Brahmā himself, then closed his eyes and vanished right there.
Even Duḥsaha, having reached the aforementioned places, [remained there].
O tiger among sages, because her soul was devoted to the disparagement of Viṣṇu, the God of gods,
she became known as Jyeṣṭhā, along with her wife.
Duḥsaha said this to her on the grassy bank by the pond:
"Stay right here; I shall go and see the netherworld (rasātala)."
Then, having observed our dwelling place, for the purpose of residing there once again—
Having been told, "I shall come to your side," she said to him:
"What shall I eat, O illustrious one? Who indeed will give me an offering?"
Thus addressed, the sage said to her: "Do not enter the houses of those women who indeed worship you with offerings, flowers, and incense."
Having spoken thus, he entered and went to his dwelling in Pātāla;
even today he has not returned, and so she remains constantly in that village of Karkaṭavāhya upon the expanse of water, ever inauspicious.
In this context, Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods and sovereign of the three worlds, was attended by Lakṣmī;
likewise, Alakṣmī spoke to that Janārdana.
"O mighty-armed Lord, my husband has departed after leaving me as an offering;
I am without a protector, O Lord of the World! Grant me a means of subsistence; salutations be unto you."
Thus addressed, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu,
Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, Mādhava, and Madhusūdana, forcibly spoke to Jyeṣṭhā Alakṣmī.
Those who [worship] Rudra, the sinless, the all-pervading, the benefactor, the blue-and-red one;
or also Ambā Haimavatī, the mother of the worlds as well.
My devotees revile them here; their wealth belongs to you alone.
In this very way, even those who are my devotees, being foolish and unfortunate, perform sacrifices while reviling Mahādeva; their wealth belongs to you.
Indeed, by whose command and grace this Brahmā always dwells—
those who, having reviled him, perform sacrifices, are the ones who cause me to fall from my station.
Those who act thus in arrogance are not my devotees;
their wealth, home, field, and their merit from sacrifices and charitable works belong to you alone.
Having spoken thus and abandoned that Alakṣmī, the Blessed Lord Janārdana attained Rudra for the sake of achieving the destruction of Alakṣmī.

Therefore, an offering should be presented to her by lords of men and by devotees of Viṣṇu at all times and with every effort; of this there is no doubt. She should always be worshipped with various offerings by women and by the twice-born.
From the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"As for the woman whose children die, as well as the one who is barren like a crow..."
The third is characterized by miscarriage and is afflicted by various defects.
There are men free from passion, yet they remain afflicted by poverty;
tell me that, O Janārdana, by what action are they liberated?
O Lord of the World, tell me all of that: by what vow, when practiced, does a human being attain all that happiness?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When the constellation Jyeṣṭhā occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada,
one should perform a night vigil accompanied by the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
In this manner, according to the prescribed ritual, one should perform the worship well with these mantras.
Come, come, O highly fortunate one, you who are saluted by gods and asuras!
You are the eldest of all the gods; remain forever in my presence.
The invocation mantra:
Salutations again and again to her who is seated upon a white lion-throne, adorned with white garments, and who bears a boon-granting gesture, a book, and a noose.
The mantra for the seat:
O eldest, most excellent, devoted to austerity, most established in Brahman, speaker of Brahman, born from the ocean of milk—homage be to you, the eldest; accept this water of honor.
The Arghya-mantra: "O Jyeṣṭhā,
endowed with the Śārṅga bow, arrows, swords, gateways, mirrors,
and other weapons as well, I worship you."
The prayer mantra:
O Goddess, who are to be venerated by gods, asuras, and humans, and worshipped by yakṣas and kinnaras;
you have been honored by me, O Jyeṣṭhā, and now I worship you.
For the sake of the prosperity of sons and wife, for the increase of fortune,
and for the destruction of misfortune, I worship you, O Jyeṣṭhā.
The mantra for worship:
Whether it be a woman or even a man, one should worship Jyeṣṭhā with this mantra;
thereby one shall obtain Lakṣmī, increase of progeny, and the supernatural powers such as aṇimā.
O best of kings, at all times, one should honor and worship the eldest sister with devotion, as well as the preceptor, with garments, ornaments, and other offerings.
She should be worshipped with diligence for exactly twelve years;
likewise, she should be worshipped by human beings according to this rite until the end of their lives.
A woman who is worthy of worship always bestows wealth and sons upon that man who,
joined with this ritual method, performs her worship.
A woman should worship the eldest [image], and her prosperity increases;
a barren woman obtains sons, and an unfortunate woman becomes fortunate.
