Whether she has lost her children, whether her children are living, whether she is barren like a crow, or whether she has many offspring— a man who is otherwise suffering indeed dwells forever in happiness.
Whoever always worships Jyeṣṭhā according to such a procedure,
his obstacles shall perish just as salt dissolves in water.
This vow is most excellent, meritorious, and destructive of sins;
thus I have related to you in its entirety this great vow of Jyeṣṭhā.
O best of the Kurus, just as the most auspicious Jyeṣṭhā-vrata is to be observed, so too,
when the Nīrājana rite has been performed, a lamp should be accepted with great devotion.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having consumed the food offering together with the remainder of the vow,
one should always receive from the hand of the preceptor a great, blazing lamp.
Established in the vow, endowed with devotion, pure, and with a restrained mind,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the vow should be undertaken according to this very procedure.
The supreme goddess named Jyeṣṭhā bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O King, she grants heaven to whoever worships her.
In the Skanda Purāṇa,
Īśvara said:
"In the month of Bhādrapada, during the bright fortnight, when it is conjoined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism..."
On that day at that time, one should perform the complete worship of Jyeṣṭhā.
In that regard, when the eighth lunar day coincides with a Sunday and the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, it is called Nīlajyeṣṭhā; it is said to be rare and of great duration.
On that day, or on another day, a man who has performed his ritual ablutions should perform [the rites].
Endowed with devotion and purified, one should perform the worship of the Goddess Jyeṣṭhā;
having collected sand from a pure location on the eastern bank of a river during the day.
Having meditated upon the form of the Goddess right there together with the Brahmins,
he should then install that golden image of the Goddess within the mandala.
O best of the twice-born, one should have it established on a silver plate, a copper plate, or written down;
then one should invoke the Goddess, or even upon a manuscript.
I invoke Jyeṣṭhā, who possesses three eyes, white teeth, and a radiant body; she is expansive and has red eyes.
Come, come, O illustrious one, you who are saluted by gods and asuras!
You are the eldest of all the gods; come into my presence.
Having invoked that goddess with this mantra,
the twice-born who has well-performed his vows should offer water for the feet, mixed with fragrant substances, at both her feet.
One should offer water for worship mixed with sandalwood and camphor.
With devotion and effort, whatever is offered here to you by me, please accept it, O Sovereign of the Gods; salutations, salutations to you, the eldest and most excellent.

Having uttered this, and having offered the *arghya* with a vessel of gold or the like, or even with cupped hands (*añjali*), one should meditate upon the Goddess and likewise worship her with perfumes and incense. In the same manner, one should offer well-prepared food consisting of wheat, barley, rice, and other such substances.

With those [offerings] measuring five handfuls, one who is firm in his vow should present pūrikās and other foods with clarified butter, and with those very same [ingredients], he should offer them to the Goddess.
Then, having praised the Great Goddess, the bestower of the fruits of all desires:
"Salutations to you, the eldest; salutations again and again to you, the most excellent."
O eldest, most excellent, foremost, best, and speaker of truth!
Come, come, O illustrious Sarasvatī; accept this water of honor (arghya).
The *arghyamantra*:
Having offered hymns of praise, recitations, dances, and songs before him,
one should then give that which is mixed with *sauvīra* even to the *śūdras*.
One who has successfully observed the vow should give that [gift] to married women according to his ability;
then, having worshipped the Goddess with her permission, he should eat while remaining silent.
Having eaten food together with his friends, the observer of the vow who has performed his duties well,
having drunk and sipped water (ācamana), and having bowed to the Goddess again and again,
he should sleep according to the rules of celibacy (brahmacarya) and perform the ritual dismissal in the morning.
In this very manner, one should indeed perform the vow every year;
then, at the conclusion of the dismissal ceremony, one should cast that auspicious [image] into the water.
Then the twice-born man should give cakes and dumplings to the Brahmins;
he should do so with diligence, either in the evening or at the time of dismissal.
A seeker of knowledge shall obtain knowledge; one desiring a wife shall obtain a wife;
and he who performs the rite of crossing over [the river] by means of his head shall undoubtedly offer it to the Goddess.
Then, having performed the rite with gold, silver, or copper, one becomes successful;
for one has personally observed the vow and attained perfection through the completed offering.
The greatness of the Goddess has thus been told,
as well as this ritual procedure conjoined with the worship of the mantra;
for the mantra, when one is established in its vow, brings about union [with the deity].
In her, those of virtuous conduct always abide. To that auspicious goddess, whose chariot is yoked with a lion and also a mighty tiger, I go for refuge as my supreme resort.

"I take refuge in that Goddess Durgā, who is the color of fire, blazing with ascetic power, the daughter of Virocana, and who delights in the fruits of ritual actions. Saying "Homage to her whose chariot is easily crossed," he should invoke her. Then, with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are most beneficial" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*) and the three verses beginning "The golden-colored, pure, purifying ones" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ*), he should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

Then, having offered a seat by name, he should offer water for the feet (*pādya*), the respectful offering (*arghya*), a seat, clothing, water for sipping (*ācamana*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and so forth, in their entirety.
Having likewise offered perfume, flowers, incense, a lamp, and food offerings,
and having again provided water for sipping, one should perform the ritual dismissal.

Oṃ, obeisance to Jyeṣṭhā; Oṃ, obeisance to Satyā; Oṃ, obeisance to Kālī; Oṃ, obeisance to Kapāla; Oṃ, obeisance to Kalipriyā; Oṃ, obeisance to Vighnā; Oṃ, obeisance to Vināyaka; Oṃ, obeisance to Bhāgyā; Oṃ, obeisance to Tāpī; Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī; Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇā; Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛṣṇapiṅgalā. With these names, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Being well-restrained, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with curd, honey, milk, and ghee.
One should eat sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) oneself and feed the Brahmins with that same food.
He who, according to this procedure, for a period of four years,
should at the conclusion of the vow have a golden image made, proportionate to the fruit [of the rite],
and present it to the preceptor together with a black cloth.
Having prostrated before the twice-born who has been honored with garments, ornaments, garlands, and ointments,
one should thereafter offer everything to him.
Once the Brahmins have eaten, they should perform the *svastivācana* (recitation for well-being).
When the vow has been properly performed in this manner, complete peace arises;
there is an abundance of wealth and grain, and health is indeed produced.
Thus ends the Jyeṣṭha-vrata.
Puṣkara said:
O Śakra, the wise man, having fasted, [should approach] the sacrificer who has also fasted.
One should daily bathe [the deity] with the root mantra, while standing facing the direction in which that deity's abode is situated.
Facing the direction of its owner— that is, facing the southwest—
or facing the direction previously mentioned, one who has bathed should worship Madhusūdana with two full and very firm jars.
[He worshipped] Virūpākṣa, Varuṇa, Candra, and likewise Śūla,
with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food.
A twice-born man, having then put on yellow garments, should likewise offer oblations of clarified butter to these very deities by their names, as well as to Matsya, Kūrma, and Śūkara.
Standing facing the eastern direction as prescribed for the ritual bath, one should place one's knee upon the ground and offer strength to the king with offerings of liquor, *kṛsara*, and *saṃyāva*.
Then, with eighteen flowers and five roots,
the wise man should place the Suvarṇagarbha jewel upon his head.

Having performed all this ritual, one shall obtain a harvest of abundant fruit. Furthermore, those who give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) here— whether roots or fruits, white garments, gold, or silver— [shall likewise attain great reward].
And here, food should be given to the Brahmins according to their desire.
Never transgressing this root and always performing this bath, the foremost of the Mārgava lineage attains ever-increasing success in his agriculture.
There is no deliberation here regarding what is desired.
Thus ends the "Root Bath" (mūlasnāna) as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
[645] Bhārgava asks Garga, the most excellent of the best sages:
"What is the result for a child born under the constellation Nairṛta?"
"O you of noble vows, tell me that which has been proclaimed for every step;
how may the bathing, giving of gifts, fire-offerings, and other rites become worthy of being seen?
Garga said:
In the first [case], one kills the father; in the second, one kills the mother;
in the third, one destroys wealth; and in the fourth, it will be auspicious.
In the first [stage], having performed the incision, the flow of blood is prescribed;
in the second, the child of another man’s wife or of a man is given.
Or else, on the third day thereafter, one should perform a rite for peace;
and on the fourth day, the child’s father, having performed a ritual bath, is recommended [to do so].
A wise father himself should uproot a hundred [other] roots;
I shall now describe the auspicious and purifying medicinal herbs.
Lakṣmaṇā, śatamūlā, śirīṣa, and likewise vetasa;
siṃhakā, śvetamūlā, viṣṇukrāntā, and śaṅkinī; sarpākṣī, mīnanetrā, putrā, parikṛtā, and añjalī.
Palāśa, bilvaka, rocanā, the two types of sandalwood,
kṛṣṇamāṃsī, uśīra, dhavaka, and likewise āmalaka.
Gojihvā, tulasī, dūrvā, śatapuṣpā, śatāṅgulī,
brahmadaṇḍī, droṇapuṣpī, priyaṅgu, and white mustard seeds.
Pippala, kākajaṅghā, trāyamāṇā, and likewise ḍuhu; jyotiṣmatī, gāndhārī, nirgandhā, and pūrṇakauśikā.
Bhagakṣumā, Subhadrā, Guḍucī, Indravāruṇī, Alambukā,
Dantī, Kadalī, and likewise Ketaka.
Gokṣura, śatapatrī, ariṣṭaka, aparājitā,
citraparṇī, śatapatrā, nikumbha, and suvarcalā.
Aśvagandhā, hastikarṇī, the two types of haridrā,
uṣṭraka, madhukāra, aśvattha, and likewise vakula.
Sarjarāja, apāmārga, mandāra, atimuktaka, mālatī, svarṇapuṣpī, śrīkarṇī, and likewise śrīphala.
Darbha-root, karavīra, madayantī, vikaṅkata,
pāṭalā, suradāru, and likewise ardhāsūdanikā.
The fruit of the manmatha tree and the sprout of the palāśa;
rāsnā, the root of the nandīvṛkṣa, devadāru, and vidārikā.
One should place śvetavīthī, śvetapākā, blue lotus,
as well as nāgakeśara, sindūrī, and kumārī.
Water from sacred fords, the five products of the cow, all medicinal herbs, gold,
and as many of the hundred auspicious roots as are available—
these, together with the bark of the *vīra* tree, should be placed in a jar with a hundred holes.
Those situated on both banks of a river, those dug out by the horns of cattle,
those located at the roots of *barhis* grass, as well as those originating from a mother’s house,
those situated on an anthill or in a marshy place, and those which are dusty or red; [these are to be avoided].
"Red with dust" means colored by the dust of cows; that is to say, clay from the road.
At the time of bathing, however, that clay is said to be the destroyer of sins.
At that time, eight jars filled with water were used for the sake of peace.
Or else, having given four [threads] wrapped three times for the ritual head-bath,
he should then perform [the rite] upon a beautiful, anointed mandala together with the young girl.
Then, having consecrated a divine pitcher with the auspicious sounds of the Vedas and with mantras for the Puṣya-consecration, the preceptor should bathe [the king].
At the end of the birth-impurity period, this divine bath should be performed for the infant;
thereafter, one should bathe the mother and then have the worship of the planets performed.
Having honored the teacher, one who is endowed with virtuous qualities should also honor the Brahmins and present a golden image of a man to the teacher.
One should likewise give a cow, grain, and a śatamāna as a sacrificial fee;
then, having performed a circumambulation and prostrated, one should ask for forgiveness.

Indeed, for a child born under those [inauspicious] vows, or one afflicted by the evil influence of a planet (graha-riṣṭa), or during the junction of a lunar mansion (gaṇḍānta), this rite is prescribed for the infant:
sixty black sesame seeds are said to constitute the measure of a gold coin (hiraṇya).

The measure of gold is sixty black sesame seeds. *Nikumbha* is a type of *dantī*. *Suvarcasā* is attached to a winnowing basket (*sūrpa*). *Hastikarṇī* is *eraṇḍa*. *Uṣṭravaha* is *pīlu*. *Madhukāra* is *madhuka*. *Sarjarāja* is *bījaka*. *Apāmārga* is *ghāṭaka*. *Atimukta* is *mādhavī*. *Malati* is *jāti*. *Svarṇapuṣpī* is *muṣalī*. *Śrīphala* is *bilva*. *Madayantī* is *pūtikā*.

*Ardhasudanikā* is *pālaṅkī*. *Manmaśravṛkṣa* is *āmra*. *Suradāru* is a variety of *devadāru*. *Vidārikā* is *kuṣmāṇḍī*. *Śvetavīthī* is *girikarṇikā*. *Śvetakākā* is *guñjā*. The remaining [terms] are well-known by their own names.

[648] *Svāhā to Indra! Svāhā to Agni! Svāhā to Soma! Svāhā to Pavamāna! Svāhā to Marut! Svāhā to Yama! Svāhā to Mṛtyu! Svāhā to Antaka! Svāhā to Tattvāya! Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt!* *Trātāram indram* (Indra, our protector); *Tvan no agne* (Thou, O Agni, for us); *Sugannu panthām* (May the path be easy to traverse); *Asunvata* (Against him who does not press the Soma); *Tattvāyāmi* (I approach thee); *Ā noniyuddhiḥ*; *Vayaṃ soma* (We, O Soma); *Tam īśānam* (Him, the Lord); *Asmai rudrā* (To him, the Rudras); *Syonā pṛthivī* (May the earth be pleasant)—these and other such mantras. Thus ends the Mūlaśānti. Rāma said:
Explain to me the optional rite (*kāmya-karman*) by which trade succeeds, as well as agriculture;
and by what action does one obtain abundant results?
Puṣkara said: O knower of dharma, the domestic priest, having fasted at the roots [of the trees], should perform this rite for the sacrificer who has likewise constantly observed the fast.
When the Pūrvāṣāḍhā constellation has arrived, one should bathe the man facing east,
using [substances] joined with roots of vetasa and likewise with conch shells and pearls.
And with gems as they were obtained, and likewise with gold,
O descendant of Bhṛgu, [he performed the rite] with four jars containing *akālamūla* plants.
With fresh *akālamūla* flowers,
one should then worship the God who bears the conch, discus, and mace;
likewise, one should worship Varuṇa and the Moon here in the courtyard.
With an abundance of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and food,
the twice-born should likewise offer clarified butter into these very fires by their respective names;
then, having dressed in blue garments, he should cast it into the water with a concentrated mind.
Blue garments of various kinds should be given,
as well as sandalwood, liquor, and various types of maireya wine.
The observer of the vow should likewise offer white garlands and incense;
he should wear the bone of a full-grown crocodile, as well as conch shells and pearls,
having set them within gold, and likewise a gemstone.
Having performed this, one attains success in trade; of this there is no doubt.
One does not fail in sea voyages nor in agriculture;
seven blue garments are the sacrificial fee prescribed here.
Conch shells, gold, silver, and likewise pearls—
all these are prescribed for both the one who steals them and the one who makes them;
furthermore, one should feed the Brahmins here with well-prepared *paramānna*.
Having worshipped each of the eight forms individually, that man of blameless soul performs this rite;
he never turns back from his pursuit of gain.
They are indeed like rivers compared to the ocean voyage.
Thus ends the vow for the attainment of profit in trade as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Sūta said:
"The mind-born son of Brahmā is renowned as Vasiṣṭha."
Śakti was his son, and Parāśara was his son.
Desiring a son, he performed very great and difficult penance, which was hard even for gods and dānavas; as a celibate student, he then obtained a boon.
"You shall obtain a virtuous son"— thus addressed by those great-souled beings,
O Sage, perform the ritual bath for one year on every occasion of the Śravaṇā asterism.
He too, endowed with faith, obtained eight sons;
and Pārāśarya obtained a son through the power of this very vow.
In this way, any other lord of kings may likewise attain perfection;
he obtains sons and grandsons and enjoys ultimate happiness.
Thus ends the vow for the birth of a son as declared in the *Āditya Purāṇa*.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Among all the baths prescribed here, which bath excels them all?"
Tell me all of that, which destroys every impurity.
Puṣkara said:
Listen, O twice-born one, to the bathing in the water from the feet (pādodaka), which destroys all impurities; it is there that Hari, the fourfold self, has become present.
In that regard, this bathing rite is the destroyer of all impurities.
Now, under the constellation Uttarāṣāḍhā, one should remain without food and with senses subdued.
With all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances, according to his ability, the wise man should wash the feet of the God of gods, the fourfold Self, in due order.
Then one should prepare four very firm and new water-pots (kalaśas),
made either of gold, silver, copper, or even of earth.
Then, having ceased his walking, he should wash [himself] with the waters from the well.
With those [waters], a jar should be filled and placed in front of it.
Then, the feet of Pradyumna should be washed with the waters from the springs;
with those waters, a full pitcher should be prepared and placed before him.
The feet of Saṅkarṣaṇa should be washed with waters from the Saras lake;
a jar filled with those waters should then be placed before him.
A wise person should wash the feet of Vāsudeva with water from the Nādī rivers;
a pitcher filled with that water should then be placed before Him.
Then, indeed, worship should be performed for the Four-Selfed One;
one should fill those water-pots with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and unbroken grains.
Then, when the second day has arrived, having bathed and previously fasted,
he (the officiant) and Aniruddha, facing each other, should bathe while remaining in the utkaṭuka posture.
And then [he described] the god Pradyumna, and then Saṅkarṣaṇa,
and then Vāsudeva, the abode of all, who bears the discus.
O best of the Bhārgavas, the consecration of all the jars must then be performed by a pure person belonging to a noble lineage, using purificatory mantras.
Now I shall proclaim for you the mantras for the four jars—
those which are auspicious, conducive to fame, and which instantly destroy all evil.
With his path unobstructed everywhere, all-pervading and unconquered,
having the wind as his form and an inconceivable nature, he is Aniruddha, the self-existent Lord.
With divine, auspicious water from his feet, which destroys all evil,
the Lord himself quickly bestows growth upon the one who has thus presented the first offering.
May that radiant Lord Pradyumna, who illuminates the worlds like the sun and is like the sacrificial fire in his brilliance, grant you auspiciousness.
May Kāmadeva, the source of the world, the progenitor of creation, the Lord, the Sovereign, the remover of disease, and the Master of the universe, grant me auspicious blessings.
The Lord who draws forth the worlds is the Master Saṅkarṣaṇa;
he is the form of Rudra, whose nature is inconceivable, all-pervading, and the savior of all.
May Kāmapāla, the subduer of enemies, the one who brings all beings under his control,
the source of the universe, and the one of great splendor, grant me auspiciousness.
Vāsudeva is the abode of all, the self of all beings, the creator of all beings;
he is omnipresent, immeasurable, the Supreme Person, and the Supreme Lord.
May Ananta, the Lord of all gods, the cause of the world’s deliverance,
the remover of sins, and the bestower of boons, grant me prosperity.
Having bathed in this manner, offered praise, and put on two fine garments,
one dressed in white should sip water and perform the worship in due order.
With fragrant scents, flowers, and auspicious fruits; with lamps, fragrant incense, and various kinds of food offerings, such as milk-rice (pāyasa), through these acts of worship.
Having thus performed the worship of the gods, being humble, having attained blessings, and having dispelled all inauspiciousness,
he should partake of a meal consisting mostly of dairy products and remain vigilant.
One should hear of the principal incarnations of Keśava,
and likewise, one should avoid the sight of heretics and those who have fallen from their religious duties.
Thus has been declared to you the ritual bathing with the water from the feet;
it is a destroyer of demons, auspicious, a pacifier of sins, and the supreme eradicator of misfortune.
It pacifies all obstacles, destroys all afflictions,
subdues all malevolent beings, and is the supreme remover of all diseases.
It brings success to journeys, is meritorious, and causes the accomplishment of one's actions;
it destroys enemies, bestows intelligence, and in its midst increases strength, longevity, and memory;
it grants good fortune, fulfills desires, and augments fame and progeny.
This foot-bath of the Supreme Person is of unfailing efficacy;
it is the most excellent bath for you, O Raṇacandravega.
But what may I do for you, O Rāma?
Thus concludes the ritual bathing with water from the feet as described in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Śrī Rāma said:
"The second lunar day (dvitīyā) as well as the first (pratipat) are likewise bathings that bring about health."
Tell me about health and the Vaiṣṇava vow.
Puṣkara said: O highly fortunate one, under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā, the priest should cause the sacrificer to fast and perform a Varuṇa-bath.
Having prepared a hundred jars filled with water containing conch shells and pearls,
he should sit upon an auspicious throne, having bathed and being dressed in unwashed garments.
O Rāma, being self-restrained, one should worship Keśava, Varuṇa, Candra, Nakṣatra, and likewise Vāruṇa with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Then, with lamps, incense, prostrations, and likewise an abundance of food,
one should perform the invocation of the deities as they have been described.
The wise man, according to his ability, should offer all medicinal herbs as well as clarified butter;
he should give two garments to the preceptor, along with liquids, a cow, a water-pot, and gold;
furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins without any stinginess regarding wealth.
A three-stranded cord made from the leaves of the śamī and śālmalī trees, as well as from the tip of a bamboo stalk, should be worn as a jewel that destroys all diseases.
Having offered vegetables, green garlands, all kinds of grain,
and two garments to Varuṇa, one should present perfumes and incense.
For by properly performing that Varuṇa-bath for one who has not transgressed [the rules], along with the giving of gifts,
all diseases come to complete pacification.
Thus, one who is bound shall likewise attain liberation.
Thus ends the ritual bath under Śatabhiṣā as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Hereafter, O sinless one, I shall describe to you the optional rites (kāmyakarman).
In that regard, both the performer and the agent of the rite should observe a fast.

One who knows the scriptures should perform a bath at the end of the night during the conjunction of the month of Bhādrapada and when the sun has entered the constellation Āśleṣā, specifically on the second day.
A wise person should place udumbara leaves, the five products of the cow, kuśa water, yellow pigment (rocanā), sandalwood, and cloth into two jars.
Then one should prepare two jars, firmly provided with perfumes, garlands, and collyrium;
having bathed the performer with the Akālamūla plant, he shall then become [purified] by that means.
Having bathed and being composed in mind, he should put on garments that are white and free from hair,
and he should likewise worship both Ahibradhna and Āditya.
And he honored Varuṇa and Śaśāṅka with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, and food,
as well as with lamps, incense, prostrations, and likewise with the offering of bali-oblations.
Then, O Rāma, one should offer fourteen vessels of unbroken rice,
along with *sapharī* fish, to Rudra, the slayer of Ahi.
The best of the twice-born should indeed offer incense with the six-fold mantra;
thereafter, worship should be performed for the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus.
Then, preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, one should offer clarified butter for all the aforementioned deities,
one hundred oblations for each.
One should have an amulet made from the hooves and horns of a cow;
it should be worn on the hand, on the head, or on the arm.
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's ability to the performer and the instructor,
as well as to all the Brāhmaṇas, duly and in proper order.
He who, never transgressing the month of Bhādrapada, always performs this bath,
for him there shall be ten thousand cows.
In that very way, he attains supreme prosperity.
Thus ends the ritual bath for Ahibradhna as described in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Valaghu said:
"O bull among the twice-born, tell me of other optional vows."
Since you are omniscient to me, [you know] both women and men.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should worship the Lord under the Kṛttikās, beginning from the full moon of Kārttika,
fasting while observing Narasiṃha until the next Kārttikī full moon.
With ointments, flowers, and so forth, as well as with all kinds of jewels, he should always,
at the conclusion of the vow, give a white cow to a twice-born man.
O King, one who has fasted should always offer a cow with a white calf as well as silver; by this vow, he shall be forever free from enemies.
Then, beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, under the asterism of Mṛgaśiras, a person should worship Ananta, who is seated upon his infinite bed and grants all desires.
O Supreme Person, grant me the attainment of my every desire— that which is an accumulation of infinite flowers and bestows infinite happiness.
Having spoken thus and honored him, the man intent on the fast should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin, saying, "May Ananta be pleased."
Then, beginning from the month of Pauṣa, having fasted regularly during the Puṣya constellation,
one should worship Baladeva again until the month of Pauṣa arrives once more.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give ointments, flowers, and the like, as well as all kinds of gems, along with bell-metal and gold,
to a Brahmin with devotion; such a man shall always be endowed with prosperity.
Starting from the month of Māgha, a man should constantly worship the Lord Varāha under the Maghā asterisms, remaining perpetually observant of the fast.
By anointing with ghee according to the rules, with fragrant sandalwood,
and likewise with excellent food or even by an oblation of ghee;
At the conclusion of the vow, however, the lord of men should give a cow of ghee;
by performing this supreme vow, he obtains the favor of the ancestors.

Starting from the full moon of Phālguna, one should worship the deity Nara-Nārāyaṇa during the Phālguna months until the Phālguna full moon occurs again. At the conclusion of the vow, one should provide a well-spread bed.
By this vow, a woman shall become well-adorned together with her husband;
likewise, a man obtains a wife endowed with beauty and wealth.
O King, this great vow always brings about a favorable and beloved wife who is likewise endowed with brothers; it ensures that she shall never be separated from him and shall never suffer widowhood.
Then, beginning from the month of Caitra, one should constantly worship Citrā;
fasting regularly, one should continue until the full moon of Caitra once again.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a variegated garment to a twice-born man;
by this vow, a person obtains his desired sons.
Whether it be a woman or a tiger among men, O noble one, there should be no hesitation in this matter;
likewise, one should worship Viṣṇu during the month of Vaiśākha under the Viśākhā constellation.

Furthermore, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, that best of men, having observed a fast, should give gold at the conclusion of his vow to Pṛthu the All-pervading Lord, thereby attaining preeminence among his kinsmen.
Likewise, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, under the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, a man who always observes a fast should worship the Lord Kṛṣṇa with garments, ornaments, and decorations.
At the conclusion of the vow, one hundred unsurpassed cows, garments, and abundant gold should be given; [the donor] shall attain union with Kṛṣṇa.
Having likewise fasted for two days starting from the full moon of Āṣāḍha,
one should worship the god Pradyumna Aparājita under the Āṣāḍhā asterisms.
Furthermore, when the full moon day of Āṣāḍha occurs, one should then give a bed;
by that, one obtains spacious and beautiful women for eternity.
Then, beginning from the Śrāvaṇī full moon, one should worship Hari while he is conjoined with the planet [Jupiter],
observing a fast as before until the next Śrāvaṇī arrives.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give much ghee to a Brāhmaṇa;
by the performance of this vow, one shall attain long life.
Beginning from the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, one should constantly worship Saṅkarṣaṇa during the two Bhādrapadas until the [next] Bhādrapadī full moon.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a pair of excellent cows;
by this vow, a man becomes eternally endowed with sovereign authority.
Beginning from the full moon of Āśvayuja, one should constantly worship Padmanābha Vāsudeva during the Aśvinī constellations while observing a fast;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should likewise give gifts of bell-metal, silver, and ghee.
O lord of men, these vows which I have proclaimed to you are eternally destructive of sin;
they grant the celestial realm to the most excellent of men.
Those which grant the attainment of desires are indeed those that grant whatever one wishes.
Viśvakarman has described these forms:
Balabhadra is blue-robed, holding a plow and a club, and is radiant;
Nara and Nārāyaṇa are blue, appearing as the personifications of Śukla with matted hair and deerskins.
Standing upon a chariot, each with one foot placed in the middle, their bodies identical in form,
equipped with arrows and bows, and bearing two and four arms respectively.
Pṛthu has four arms and is marked with the characteristics of royalty;
Pradyumna is said to bear the conch, the kaumodakī mace, the lotus, and the discus.
Sankarṣaṇa holds the conch, the lotus, the discus, and the kaumodakī mace.
The remaining [details] regarding the Dharaṇīvrata are to be sought elsewhere.
Thus ends the vow for the attainment of all desires as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of men, just as suffering arises from not attaining sovereignty and other such things,
so too does suffering come to men from the loss of what was gained through their desires.
Either through the loss of sovereignty, or through the falling away from it, or even through the interruption of the lineage.
Tell me, O Umā, that vow by which neither a man nor a woman suffers a fall from their own station, whether from their desired goal or from any other.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O highly fortunate one, this is true: there is indeed the attainment of suffering and the destruction of sovereignty, wealth, kinsmen, and sons."
Listen to that very point, O Pārtha:
how it is that for men who properly observe the vow of fasting, there arises no falling away from their desired goal, such as heaven and the like.
O Indra among kings, those twelve lunar mansions which indeed occur month by month [should be honored] with flowers, incense, water, and other desired offerings.
O best of kings, beginning from the Kṛttikā constellation in the month of Kārttika,
one should offer kṛśara as the food-oblation for the first four months.
One should first offer saṃyāva at the beginning of the month of Phālguna;
thereafter, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) to the God starting from the month of Āṣāḍha.

With that, one should first offer *kṛśara* (rice and sesame) as food-offering during the four months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa; thereafter, during the four months beginning with Phālguna, one should offer *saṃyāva* (sweet cake); and from the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should offer *pāyasa* (milk-rice). With that very food, O King of Kings, the wise man should feed the Brāhmaṇas.
By bathing in water mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and consuming that same mixture, he becomes pure.
Having worshipped that very Puruṣottama perfectly, O Indra among kings,
the wise man, purified and having bathed according to the rule, should bow down and make his request.
Homage, homage to you! May my evil be destroyed, may my merit reach full increase,
and may my sovereignty, wealth, and so forth, always remain inexhaustible.
And may my lineage be undecaying and imperishable.
Likewise, O Acyuta, you are the Supreme Self beyond the supreme, the Self that has become Brahman, the Supreme Self beyond the supreme;
therefore, O Acyuta, fulfill that desire of mine.
O immeasurable Hara, may you take away my sin.
O Acyuta, O Ānanda, O Govinda, be gracious! O Immeasurable Self, O Supreme Person, grant that which is desired, making it inexhaustible.
Having thus worshipped the Lord and made supplications according to the prescribed rule,
one should always partake of the food offering oneself, endowed with faith.
Then, at the end of the year, when Acyuta has risen from his comfortable sleep,
one should present a copper vessel filled with ghee to a Brāhmaṇa.
One should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, saying, "May Acyuta be pleased.
Then, in the twenty-first year, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana) in this manner.
In front of that, an elderly Brāhmaṇī woman from Śāmbharāyaṇa should be placed;
she is a great chaste lady, made of silver, and she is always worthy of that mind.
Then, O King of kings, having honored them with garlands, garments, and ointments, and having prostrated according to the prescribed rite, they [should worship] with this mantra:
Every year, one should give food and drink to the twice-born;
one should give sesame seeds to a Brāhmaṇa together with gold and clarified butter.
Then one should give cows with their calves and bronze milking vessels to a brahmin;
and according to one's ability, one should devoutly offer a bed, for Keśava remains therein.
Seven jars, filled with bright water, are prescribed here as the objects to be established.
Having given along with an umbrella and a pair of sandals, a man does not fall from his state;
therefore, with every effort, one should dismiss the Brahmins after making these gifts.
O Indra among kings, through dance and song, a man obtains his desire,
as well as progeny, heavenly fortune, and sovereignty.
In that same way, a man who is completely absorbed in it does not fall away from it thereafter.
Therefore, one should worship everything with all effort and by means of the self alone;
O Supreme Person, one whose desire is for the imperishable should always strive in this manner.
Kṛṣṇa said: In this regard also, a certain woman is heard of who, having been an ascetic and observer of great vows, became a renowned perfected one (siddhā) in heaven known as Śāmbharāyaṇī.
Always removing all doubts and ever beneficial to the dwellers of heaven,
O King, at one time the king of the gods, Śatakratu,
asked Bṛhaspati this concerning the former conduct of Indra.
O best of the Aṅgirases, I desire to hear the accounts of those lords of the gods who existed in the east prior to the present Indra.
Thus addressed by that lord of the gods,
the supreme rishi Bṛhaspati, the best among the upholders of dharma and possessed of stainless luster, then spoke.
"O Lord of the Gods, know me to be contemporary with yourself;
after that, this lady, accompanied by Bṛhaspati,"
She went to where the highly fortunate ascetic lady was properly seated;
she saw that the King of the Gods and Bṛhaspati had arrived together.
Having worshipped him properly according to the Dharma and prostrated herself, she of virtuous vows said:
"Homage be to the King of the Gods, and likewise homage to Aṅgiras."
Or whatever task there may be for those of great fortune, let it all be stated here;
if it is possible for me to perform, I shall do it without hesitation.
Bṛhaspati said:
"O blessed lady, we two have come here desiring to ask you something.
O highly fortunate one, tell me that which is the matter you wish to inquire about."
If you remember, O auspicious one, the former deeds of Indra, then tell them, O highly fortunate lady, for the Lord of the Gods is full of curiosity.
Śāmbārāyaṇī said:
"That which was yours formerly from the Lord of the Gods, and that which was first [from him],
and those who were even earlier than he, and that which was the very first even for him."
O best of the Aṅgirases, I know all those who were their predecessors, and I know their entire history in its entirety.
O Brahmin, I know many Manvantaras, the creations, the inhabitants of heaven, the Seven Sages, and those who are the sons of the Manus.
Having spoken thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods, that Śāmbarāyaṇī named her teacher; I shall tell you about him as well.
Listen, my child: Nakukarṇa, who was difficult even for the gods and their deities to conquer,
having defeated the world-protectors along with their divine attendants in battle,
subsequently entered Indra’s abode quite fearlessly.
Seeing him suddenly arrived, Śakra, rolling upon the surface of his bed,
quickly protected the exhausted [demon] from the fear of Nakukarṇa;
he then addressed the Dānava on Śakra’s bed with a prostration.
But Vāsudeva, seeing that wicked one who was a thorn in the side of the gods, performed the seizing of his throat; Vāmadeva was delighted by that.
Then Kṛṣṇa, seizing him with his two arms by force, slowly began to crush him as he was uttering terrible cries while laughing.
That lord of the Dānavas died, his cage of ribs shattered by force;
he too then emerged from the base of the bed with his head hanging down.
Seated there, he praised Hari, who held the conch, discus, and mace;
having seen this, Śakra, the king of the gods, spoke to him.
Then, O King of the Gods, he said to the ascetic woman: "O daughter of Śambarāyaṇa, how do you know this? Perform fierce penance."
Śāmbharāyaṇī said:
"O Lord of the Gods, indeed all those lords of the gods who dwell in heaven—
I have heard of their conduct and likewise seen it."
Indra said:
"O knower of dharma, O sinless one, tell me what was seen by you by chance,
whereby you have attained a residence in the heavenly world according to some righteous principle."
Oh, among all vows,
this fast is indeed considered the most preeminent and supreme, bestowing an eternal residence in heaven.
Having been addressed thus by that lord of the gods,
the illustrious ascetic Śāmbarāyaṇī replied to him exactly as she had done.
O Lord of the Gods, the deity was worshipped by capable men every month;
having undertaken the prescribed vow, he was honored for seven years.
O King of the Gods, this is the extent of the fruit of my action in propitiating Acyuta: that I have not fallen from this desired world of the gods.
Whatever a man constantly desires—whether heaven, wealth, or sovereignty—he attains all that; therefore, the Lord must be propitiated.
I have related to you this entire account of your former conduct as the Lord of the Gods,
as well as the imperishability of your residence in heaven resulting from the month-long worship of Acyuta.
And as it has been told, O Lord, to you who inquire, O Ruler of the Thirty-three:
there is nothing else that is a cause for supreme success in attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— as desired by the lords of the gods— other than the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Having heard those words of hers, Devarāja and Bṛhaspati said to that virtuous woman, "So be it," and they both performed that vow as well.
Therefore, O Pārtha, with effort and concentrated mind,
you should worship Acyuta month after month, being then entirely focused on him.
Those wise ones who, having undertaken the vow, pass seven years according to the prescribed rule following the narrative of Śāmbarāyaṇa,
attain the heavenly world and dwell there for a long time.
Even with hundreds of sons, they do not fall away for ten thousand eons.
Thus ends the Śāmbharāyaṇī-vrata in the glorious Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O protector of the earth, to the vow known as Viṣṇupadatraya.
That which Hari spoke of long ago as the pacifier of all evils.
In former times, the capable Prajāpati Dakṣa, having propitiated Viṣṇu many times when his creation had repeatedly failed, questioned that slayer of enemies.
Dakṣa said: "O Blessed One, O Keśava, by your command, the status of being the creator of all has been ordained for me by the Self-born Brahmā, the God of gods."
O Lord of the World,
O Infallible One, tell me how this creation of yours was brought about by that which has gone astray through attachment to sense objects.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus by Dakṣa, Janārdana, the God of gods,
explained the vow of the three steps of Viṣṇu, which brings about the destruction of suffering.
It brings about the accomplishment of all undertakings, destroys evil,
and is [practiced] as desired by the steadfast ones of firm intellect who have severed the cycle of existence.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, I shall tell you of that which is the most excellent of all vows; listen as I describe it to you briefly, just as it was in the past.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, O Indra among kings, O Ruler of the earth, under the Pūrvāṣāḍhā asterisms,
one who is self-restrained and pure should worship Acyuta,
the Lord of the World, with flowers, incense, and pleasing fragrances such as aguru and sandalwood.
And likewise, according to one's means, the three steps of Viṣṇu should be established with other jewels or even garments, using substances situated in milk or oil.
Having worshipped according to one's ability, one should place [the offerings] before Keśava and give barley to a Brahmin, saying, "May Śrīpati be pleased."
O Indra among kings, a person should eat auspicious sacrificial food (haviṣyānna) at night during the month of Śrāvaṇa under the constellation Uttaraṣāḍhā.
Having likewise worshipped Govinda and the three steps of Viṣṇu,
and having given ghee to the brāhmaṇa, he gratified the Lord of the Earth.
A man, observing silence, should eat food consisting mostly of cow's products;
or likewise, O King of kings, a woman [should do so] under the Pūrva-phalgunī and Bhādrapada constellations.
O King, when the constellation Phālgunī (Pūrvaphalgunī) occurs during the month of Phālguna, it is so called.
Then one should worship the god Trivikrama according to the previously mentioned procedure;
O King, having worshipped the three steps of the god.
One should give gold as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), saying, "May the path to heaven be pleased.
O King of kings, one should eat at night, avoiding food cooked with clarified butter.
This very same rite is prescribed for the Uttarā-yoga in the month of Caitra;
one who is childless obtains a son, and one who is husbandless obtains a husband.
By worshipping these three steps, a man or a woman obtains reunion with their kinsmen after living abroad,
as well as prosperity, sovereignty, and health;
whatever desires they long for in their hearts, those they shall attain.
Free from desire, he attains those various states and reaches the world of Viṣṇu.
O lord of men, even if they have previously committed sins, a man or a woman is liberated from all taints by performing this three-step vow here.
Thus ends the Viṣṇupada-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Dakṣa said:
"Childlessness is a great sorrow; having wicked sons is an even greater sorrow."
Since this wicked son has become the cause of all my sufferings.
Blessed indeed are they who, being freed from all suffering, have obtained a son who is capable,
tranquil, powerful, devoted, and discerning of virtues.
He was constantly devoted to his own duty, dedicated to the gods and the twice-born,
skilled in weapons, knowledgeable in the Vedic dharma, and a refuge for the poor and the helpless.
He who, endowed with favor from the gods and possessed of perfect virtue,
obtains a son such as we are— there is no one more fortunate than he on earth.
Therefore, O great sage, I desire to hear from you that ritual by which men in this world may obtain a son endowed with those characteristics.
Pulastya said:
"It is even so, O illustrious one; this which I relate to you is the alleviation of all suffering arising from the birth of a son for parents."
In ancient times, there was a protector of the earth named Kṛtavīrya among the Haihayas;
he had a wife of excellent complexion named Śīlavatī.
That highly fortunate woman, being childless, took her seat and questioned Maitreyī about the virtues of obtaining a son;
then Maitreyī spoke of the auspicious vow known as Ananta.
Maitreyī said:
Whatever desire a man or a woman of dark complexion may wish for,
by properly propitiating that all-pervading Lord Keśava, they obtain it completely from him.
On whichever day in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa the lunar mansion Mṛgaśiras occurs,
having bathed on that day with a restrained mind, one should consume cow’s urine.
O lady of excellent complexion, one should worship the left foot of Ananta with flowers, incense, perfumes, and offerings according to one's ability.
May Ananta grant infinite fruit for every desire; may the Blessed One grant that infinity again both in this very life and in another birth.
This great vow brings about an infinite accumulation of merit;
O Supreme Person, grant that I may likewise attain my heart's desire.
Having thus uttered this, one should perform his worship according to the rules and prescriptions,
with a concentrated mind, preceded by prostration.
One should give sacrificial fees to a Brahmin, saying, "May Ananta be pleased";
having spoken thus, one should likewise eat at night, avoiding oil.

In the same manner, during the month of Pauṣa, under the Puṣya asterism, one should worship the left hip of the Blessed One as Puruṣa; thereafter, the consumption of cow’s urine should be performed, and one should further recite:
"Ananta [is the fulfiller] of all desires."
And having caused the best of the twice-born to recite [the mantras], he should eat according to the rule;
likewise, during the Maghā constellation in the month of Māgha, he should worship the two arms of the God.
And one should perform the Skandha rite under the Phālgunī constellation in the month of Phālguna, O beautiful lady;
in these four months, the consumption of cow's urine is prescribed.
Likewise, one should give sesame seeds and grains to a Brahmin;
in the month of Caitra, under the asterism Citrā, one should worship the right shoulder of the Deity.
In the same manner, O Lord of the Earth, one should partake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) here,
and should give a small amount of gold for as long as four months.
In the month of Vaiśākha, under the Viśākhā constellation, having worshipped his right arm,
he should likewise give gold and eat at night while remaining restrained in speech.
O observer of auspicious vows, having worshipped the waist in the month of Jyeṣṭha under the Jyeṣṭhā constellation,
one should likewise perform the worship of the feet of the Lord in the month of Āṣāḍha under the Āṣāḍhā constellations, O All-pervading One.
One should worship the two feet during the month of Śrāvaṇa;
ghee should be given to a Brahmin and consumed according to the prescribed rite.
In the months ending with Kārttika, one should perform the ritual consumption of food and indeed the giving of gifts;
one should worship the mouth during the conjunction of the Prauṣṭhapadā constellation in the month of Bhādrapada.
In the same manner, one should worship the two Aśvins and [the deity] Hṛdaya under the asterism Aśvinī;
with a concentrated mind, one should perform the ritual bath, the consumption of the sacred food, and the worship.
One should perform the worship of Anantaśiras during the month of Kārttika under the asterism Kṛttikā;
on whichever specific day the worship occurs, it should be performed on each and every such day.
However, his name should be recited when one sneezes, falls asleep, or in similar circumstances;
having first offered ghee for four months on behalf of Ananta.
Then, O delighter of the clan, for four months beginning with Caitra, the oblation is offered with honey,
and for four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, it is offered with milk.
Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) is recommended in all months;
thus, over the course of twelve months, there shall be three occasions for breaking the fast.
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should have an infinite, auspicious golden image fashioned.
One should place a silver pestle beside it;
worship should be performed according to the prescribed rules with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
One should worship Hari upon the seat (pīṭha) with these mantras in their proper order:
"Salutation be to Ananta for the head; salutation to the Soul of All for the feet."
One should worship the pair of knees with "Salutation to Śeṣa," the hips with "To Kāma,
salutation," and the two sides of Hari with "Salutation to Vāsudeva."
One should worship the abdomen with "To Saṅkarṣaṇa," the two arms with "To the bearer of all weapons," the throat with the name "Śrīkaṇṭha," and the face with "To the moon-faced one."
A wise person should worship the plow and the pestle by their own names;
having thus worshipped Govinda, who is adorned with white garments.
Equipped with an umbrella and sandals, and likewise adorned with garlands and wreaths.
The deities of the lunar mansions and the lunar mansions themselves should be worshipped in every respect,
as well as Soma, the king of the lunar mansions, the months, and likewise the year.
The deities of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), however, are according to the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa:
the two Aśvins, Yama, Agni, Dhātṛ, Candra,
Umāpati, Aditi, Vākpati, the Sarpas, the Pitṛs, Bhaga, and Aryaman.
Ravi, Tvaṣṭṛ, Marut, Śakra, Agni, Mitra, Maghavān,
Nirṛti, Toya, the Viśvedevas, and the Lord of Śrī.
The Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan—
these indeed have been described to you as the deities of the lunar mansions.
In this rite, twelve jars filled with water and provided with food should be prepared.
Having thus worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, according to the prescribed rites,
and having honored the Brahmins with garments and auspicious ornaments;
Or [he may invite] one who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, whose senses are restrained,
who knows the Purāṇas, who understands the Dharma, who is free from physical defects, and who speaks kindly.
To him, all that should be given, concluding with the words, "May [the deity] be pleased";
but to other Brahmins, gifts should be given according to one's wealth.
O auspicious lady, by this method this vow is completed;
and once it is fulfilled, one attains all of one's heart's desires.
O highly fortunate lady, for those in this mortal world who desire sons, wealth, servants, wives, health, strength,
and prosperity, this vow is the supreme merit and source of well-being.
"Perform this very vow, which is joined with infinite observances, which destroys all sins,
and which bestows the wealth of virtuous conduct;
it is the most excellent in all the world, if you desire a son."
Thus ends the Ananta-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Purūravas said:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the Rūpa-satra, which yields great fruit."
O Sage, at its completion, I shall become one who bears a divine form.
Atri said:
Therefore, one who desires to observe this vow should seek out two Brahmins as gurus—
one who understands astrology and another who knows the Itihāsas in their entirety.
Following the procedure prescribed therein, beginning with the feet and the eyes in due order,
when the full moon of Phālguna has passed and the eighth day of the dark fortnight arrives, a person should undertake the vow on that very day, including its preparatory rites.
A person should observe the fast on the lunar mansion and its presiding deity;
likewise, one should worship Varuṇa and the Moon according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship Janārdana, the Blessed One, the God of gods;
having fasted, one should diligently worship the limbs of the God as well.
Then, O King, having performed the fire-ritual and likewise honored the preceptor,
one should observe a fast on the second day.
Having observed the fast when the lunar mansion has passed, and having bathed and worshipped Keśava,
one should perform the fire-oblation according to one's ability and honor the best of the twice-born.
One should eat sacrificial food (haviṣyānna); hear from me the sequence of the limbs:
the root-mantra is assigned to the two feet, while the Prājāpatya mantra is for the two shanks.
O King, the two Aśvins are known as the pair of knees, and the two Āṣāḍhas are likewise the pair of thighs; the Guhya is also recorded as being joined with them.
The two Phālgunīs and Kṛttikā constitute the hips;
on both sides, together with the flanks, there are three equal lunar mansions;
O King, both Proṣṭhapadas as well as Revatī likewise form [the thighs].
The chest is proclaimed to be under Anurādhā, and the back under Dhaniṣṭhā;
the two arms are to be known as being under Viśākhā, and likewise the hands are said to be under Hasta.
Likewise, O lion among kings, the fingers are said to be in Punarvasu;
the nails are said to be in Aśleṣā, and the neck, O King, is in Jyeṣṭhā.
The two ears are to be known as being in Śravaṇa; the mouth is proclaimed to be in Puṣya;
O King, the teeth are said to be in Svātī, and the jaw likewise in Śatabhiṣaj.
Maghā is said to be the two nostrils, and Mṛgaśīrṣa the two eyes;
Citrā should be known as the forehead, and likewise Bharaṇī as the head.
O lord of men, at the conclusion of the vow, when the hair is still moist,
the sacrificial session (satra) is completed at the end of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
If no obstacle should arise, one who has fasted through the entire series of lunar mansions in their proper order shall achieve complete purity born of the [auspicious] signs.
At the conclusion of the vow, having bathed with self-restraint, one should worship Madhusūdana with sandalwood,
agallochum, camphor, musk, kuśa grass, and saffron.
With nutmegs, kakkola berries, and likewise with cloves and flowers,
with the resin of young guggulu, and with auspicious flowers produced in their proper season.
O King of kings, incense should be offered with the noble agallochum and fragrant sandalwood;
and lamps filled with sesame oil should be presented.
All the wicks should be prepared and dyed with great silver;
likewise, the food offering should be made with *paramānna* (milk-rice) mixed with honey.
With curd, milk, ghee, honey, and jaggery, as well as with sugar, and likewise with various foods, fruits, and roots, according to the prescribed rule.
With cakes, and with delightful, cool, and fragrant drinks.
O King of kings, one should offer vessels of salt, rice mixed with sesame (kṛśara), all kinds of seeds, and ornaments according to one's ability.
And with devotion and a disciplined mind, one should offer costly garments;
immediately thereafter, the oblation should be performed with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ param."
The twelve-syllable mantra is prescribed for women and Śūdras.
One should offer oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains mixed with ghee and honey;
then, O best of kings, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) must be given to the preceptor.
And elephants are to be given, as well as various villages,
foremost horses, and diverse kinds of jewels.
The Brāhmaṇa should be known as the father, the exhibitor of the sacrifice of form;
he is the bestower of beauty, fortune, charm, birth, and health.
Whether it be of a kingdom, of the status of a twice-born, or of great wealth,
there is no atonement for one who bestows such things that can be achieved through abundant giving.
In this matter, the grace of the Guru alone is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), and nothing else is the cause;
therefore, one who wishes to behold the Rūpasattra should desire his grace.
A vessel filled with ghee must certainly be given to him:
four palas of bell-metal, and gold of the finest quality.
Thereafter, according to his capacity, he should feed the most excellent of the twice-born with salt,
milk, curd, clarified butter, molasses, various foods, and white sugar.
Food accompanied by a drink should be offered, followed by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
A pair of new and auspicious garments should be given to the Brāhmaṇa,
as well as a highly valuable and beautiful ornament dyed with great silver.
The seven types of seeds should be given, as well as salt and base metals;
and whatever else may be desired, such as an umbrella and sandals.
O Lord of the Earth, one must not practice stinginess regarding wealth when giving an umbrella;
however, in this sacrificial session, a vessel filled with ghee must certainly be given.
By offering four palas of brass, gold,
or refined gold through the performance of this vow, one shall go to heaven upon the abandonment of the body.
Having remained there for a very long time, if he is born again in the human state,
he becomes either a king who knows the Dharma or a Brāhmaṇa endowed with wealth.
Born into a great family and peerless in beauty on earth,
he attains great health as well as the highest good fortune.
He possesses beauty, intellect, wisdom, and an exceedingly constant devotion to Dharma;
resembling the full moon, he brings all sentient beings under his influence.
O Indra among kings, such a man becomes like a woman, and a woman becomes equal to an apsaras—
fortunate, beautiful to behold, and endowed with the quality of loveliness.
Possessing abundant grain, abundant wealth, and many ornaments,
she was exceedingly beloved by her husband and renowned in the world for her virtuous qualities;
she was ever healthy, lovely, and free from all defects.
With a moon-like face and eyes like blue lotuses, beloved by the three worlds and cherished by her husband,
she will certainly be fortunate and virtuous in character.
Endowed with loveliness, fame, and splendor.
Thus ends the Rūpasattra-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follows the procedure for the Nīrājana rite.
Rāma said:
"O most excellent one, I desire to hear from you the ritual for the *nīrājana* ceremony.
O Lord, how should the king perform the *nīrājanī* rite for the sake of peace?
Puṣkara said:
[676] O King, in the north-eastern direction, within a charming city,
one should cause a vast and most beautiful hermitage to be constructed.
One should have three auspicious archways constructed there, facing east, protected by mats, spread with kusha grass, and adorned with banners and flags.
O best of the Bhṛgus, one should raise a gateway (toraṇa) sixteen cubits in height,
and its width should likewise be made ten cubits.
To the south of the gateway, one should then construct a hermitage;
there, the worship of the deities should take place, as well as the ritual of carrying the sacred fire.
O descendant of Bhrigu’s lineage, a pile of eight cubits in length and height, consisting of dry firebrands, should be prepared on the left side.
One should fashion a beautiful garland of one hundred knots with a five-colored thread,
placing the hundred loops in the middle of the central archway;
having covered it with *kuśa* grass, one should then cover it again with earth.
Therefore, all living beings must avoid transgressing [this boundary] once it has been established;
and it must not be crossed until it has first been trodden by the king's elephant.
When the sun, having left Citrā, enters Svātī,
from that time onwards the rite should be performed as long as the sun remains in Svātī.
O best of the twice-born, in the hermitage the gods must be worshipped every day:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śambhu, Śakra, as well as Vāyu and Agni.
Vināyaka, Kumāra, Varuṇa, Dhanada, Yama,
the illustrious Viśvedevas, and Uccaiḥśravas as well.
[677] Eight great elephants are to be worshipped; hear their names from me:
Kumuda, Airāvaṇa, Padma, Puṣpadanta, and Vāmana.
Supratīka, Añjana, and Nīla—these eight are the origins of the gods;
likewise, worship of the planets and the lunar mansions should be performed by the domestic priest.
Then, the domestic priest, being well-composed, should offer oblations into the fire with mantras bearing the names and characteristics of the deities who have been invoked.
And likewise, O mighty-armed one, for those who are devoid of mantras, [the rite is performed] with the Praṇava.
Having offered oblations of fuel-sticks from milky trees as well as white mustard seeds,
one should prepare water-pitchers filled with water and mixed with sandalwood paste.
Having honored them with garlands and perfumes and adorned them with trees, one should likewise provide a pair of garments bound with a five-colored thread. [One should also prepare] marking-nut,
rice, white mustard, *vacā*, *kuṣṭha*, and *priyaṅgu*.
On the western side of the bank, having bathed with jars previously prepared and purified by mantras, the best of elephants should be duly bathed.
And then, O illustrious one, having adorned those horses,
he likewise performed the consecration of the elephant and that horse.
Then, after the priest has consecrated it with mantras, a morsel of food should be offered;
upon the king's acceptance of it, his victory is proclaimed.
And upon his departure, one should recognize that a great danger has arrived;
therefore, one should first lead the elephant out through the arched gateways.
In that case as well, O Rāma, one should first indicate the death of the king by means of the preeminent elephant consecrated at the beginning, and then by means of the horse.
Famine should be recognized there when the hoof of a cow or the foot of a camel leaves a mark.
O King, if one should leap over that elephant with the left foot,
it will bring harm to the queen, the domestic priest, the minister, and the prince.
One should announce the death of the king when one treads upon him with the foot;
one announces the victory of the king when one steps over him with the right foot.
When the royal elephant has emerged, there shall be the destruction of his lineage;
therefore, all the elephants should emerge from the archways facing the east.
Then, O highly fortunate one, the horses appeared; then, O best of men, the parasol and the banner, and whatever other insignia of royalty there were.
Then, having established those [images], one should worship the weapons as well,
along with those *pratisarā* cords made of five-colored thread.
O Bhārgava, O King, the domestic priest should bind all the elephants and horses with the mantra beginning with "dūṣyādūṣya."
Then those elephants, together with the horses, should be led to their own stables while they remain there until the sun has reached its meridian.
One should always honor them, O Rāma; one should neither revile nor strike them.
One should always honor all the royal insignia within the hermitage.
One should constantly worship Varuṇa and likewise the twice-born according to the proper rites;
then, at night, the sacrifice to the spirits (bhūta) should be performed with excellent offerings.
The hermitage should be guarded by men with weapons in their hands;
the king and the domestic priest should always reside together in the hermitage.
He was preeminent as a veterinarian for horses and likewise the best of physicians for elephants;
he should also be consecrated and remain a celibate student.
When the sun, having left Svāti, enters Viśākhā,
on that day one should especially adorn the vehicle;
and royal insignia, having been worshipped, should be placed in the hands of men.
O knower of dharma, one should consecrate with mantras the elephant, the horse, the parasol, the sword, the bow, the drum, the banner, and the flag.
Having consecrated them all with mantras, he should then place them upon the backs of elephants;
the royal priest and the family priest should both be seated atop the elephants.
There was a preeminent veterinarian for horses as well as a supreme physician for elephants;
then the king, having mounted the horse consecrated with mantras, [set forth].
Having gone out through the archway, one should mount the consecrated elephant;
having gone out through the archway, one should perform the rite devoid of deities.
Having distributed the sacrificial offering according to the prescribed rites, the king, mounted upon the back of an elephant,
adorned with all kinds of jewels and fanned with chowries, [proceeded].
Then, with a mind well-composed, the king should circumambulate three times the unlit heap of flowers immediately thereafter.
Endowed with the fourfold army and accompanied by his entire host,
O best of men, he saw them as the citizens raised shouts of joy and the sounds of all musical instruments, and as the foot soldiers cheered.
Having done this, he should go home preceded by the king’s army;
and having honored the great multitude of people, he should dismiss them all.
O Rāma, this propitiatory rite known as *nīrājana* should be performed by kings;
it brings about security and the increase of men, elephants, and horses.
Blessed, bringing fame, destroying enemies,
conferring happiness, and unsurpassed peace—
this should be performed by kings for the sake of the prosperity of their kingdom.
With every effort, O hero of Bhṛgu's lineage!
Thus ends the procedure for the *nīrājana* rite as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Bhīṣma said:
For one who is unable to observe fasts but desires that very same fruit [of fasting], [there is this alternative].
Is it due to a lack of practice or because of illness? Tell me, what is your desired vow?
Pulastya said:
For those who are unable to observe fasts, eating at night is prescribed.
Listen now to that great vow regarding which this is taught.
The worship of Śaṅkara known as Ādityaśayana,
which those learned in the Purāṇas declare should be performed according to rule during specific conjunctions of the lunar mansions.
When the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) falls on a Sunday,
or during the sun's transit (Saṃkrānti), that lunar day fulfills all desires.
One should worship the image of Umāmaheśvara with the names of the Sun;
therefore, one should worship both the image of the Sun and the Śiva-liṅga.
O best of kings, no difference whatsoever is admitted between the Lord of Umā and the Sun; therefore, one should worship Śambhu in the home.
*Arcā* means an image. The form of Umā-Maheśvara, however, should be understood as that described in the vow for the first *kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*.
With the hand [one worships] the Sun; with the feet, the one called Arka;
and on the *citrā* [constellation], the region of the ankles.
On the Svātī asterism, one should offer the shanks to the supreme deity Dhātṛ; and on Viśākhā, the region of the knees.
Likewise, during Anurādhā, one should worship the two thighs of the god who possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns, saying: "Homage be to him!
During Jyeṣṭhā, one should worship the private parts, saying: "Homage be to Anaṅga!"
To Indra and Soma, the hips and the root.
And on the pair of Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, [worship] the navel;
"Salutation to Tvaṣṭṛ" for the seven-horsed one (the Sun);
and on Śravaṇa, the chest for the sharp-rayed one (the Sun).
Under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā, one should perform the rite for cutting.
The Vakasthala [mantra] should be worshipped during the constellation of the Lord of Waters (Jalādhiparkṣa) for the destruction of darkness;
the constellation of the Lord of Waters is Śatatārā.
And in both Pūrvā- and Uttarā-Aṣāḍhā, the two arms are to be worshipped with the mantra "namaś candrakarāya."
O King, one should worship the Lord of the Sāmans with both hands under the asterism Revatī;
likewise, the nails should be worshipped under Aśvinī.
Homage be to the one who bears the yoke of the seven-horsed chariot!
One should worship the sun with the words "Salutation to the one of fierce radiance" when the moon is in the Bharaṇī asterism; the back [should be worshipped] in Bharaṇī,
the neck in Kṛttikā, and the lower lip in Rohiṇī.
One should worship [them] during the Rohiṇī constellations in the month of Bhādrapada.
The fire-star is Kṛttikā; O Enemy of Pura, the teeth are located on the head of Mṛga;
you are to be worshipped, salutations to you, Hari!
"Salutation to Savitṛ"—thus [it is said] in the Śāṅkara [tradition]; then the nose and eyes are to be worshipped during Punarvasu.
To Śaṅkara, the Ārdrā;
to the Beloved of the Lotus (Brahmā), the forehead under Puṣya; to the Wind of the Vedas, the locks of hair.
Then, under Ārdrā, one should offer a crown to the beloved of the gods (Viṣṇu), and under Maghā, two earrings; thus says Gogaṇeśa.
Ārṣyā is Āśleṣā.
In the Pūrvās (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā), the eyes of Śambhu are most worthy of worship for the delight of cows and Brahmins.
Then, under the Uttaraphalgunī asterism, the two eyebrows are to be worshipped with the mantra "To Viśveśvara."
Homage be to him who holds the noose, the goad, the lotus-stalk, the skull-bowl, the serpent, the moon, and the bow;
[the destroyer] of the elephant-demon, of the bodiless god of love, and of the city of Andhaka.
Salutations to Śiva, the root of destruction.
Having thus daily worshipped the weapons and so forth,
one should worship the head with the mantra "To Viśveśvara," and here itself one should eat food together with oil.
It is meatless, free from alkaline substances, and not the remains of a meal.
Having performed such rites at night, he should further give a bull,
a prastha of śāli rice, and ghee in a vessel made of udumbara wood.

Having placed [the offering] in a vessel made of udumbara wood or copper, one should present it to a brahmin along with gold. On the seventh day, a pair of garments should be given, and on the day of breaking the fast (pāraṇa), there should be even more.

When the fourteenth fast-day (pāraṇa) of the Bhārata-year is reached— that is, the annual or yearly one— since there is one breaking of the fast every twenty-seven days, there will be fourteen such breakings of the fast in a year plus eighteen extra days.
One should devoutly feed the Brāhmaṇas with molasses, milk, ghee, and other offerings.
Then, having fashioned a golden lotus with eight petals and a pericarp—
pure, measuring eight finger-breadths, and endowed with petals of ruby—
Having prepared a distinctive bed, free from conflicting knots,
provided with a pillow for rest, well-spread, and serving as a support for the feet;
She is endowed with wooden sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a throne, and a mirror,
as well as ornaments, fruits, garments, and unguents.
Having placed that lotus upon it and adorned it with its excellent qualities,
[he should offer] a tawny cow, accompanied by a garment, possessing supreme character and yielding milk.

One should give away a cow with silver hooves, golden horns, accompanied by her calf, and provided with a bronze milking vessel, reciting the mantra during the forenoon; thereafter, one should cross over the fire.
Just as your bed is never empty of splendor,
fortitude, glory, and delight, even so may all spiritual accomplishments be mine.
"Just as you know of no one other than yourself who is more worthy of receiving blessings, O Sinless One,
so do you lift me up from the ocean of saṃsāra with its endless sufferings.
Then, having circumambulated him and prostrated, one should dismiss him.
One should bring all that— beds, seats, and so forth— to the house of the twice-born;
those who know the Vedas declare this to be the destruction of the sin of those whose minds are shattered by great crimes.
One who is appointed with sons, wealth,
and wives brings joy to the gods;
he does not encounter disease, nor does he suffer pain or grief.
Or whatever woman performs [this] with devotion.
Whoever thus recites or hears this account of Hari’s reclining shall become beloved by Puruṣottama;
he shall [deliver] even all his ancestors who have gone to hell.
He who performs [this] here brings even heaven itself down to this world.

Thus ends the Ādityaśayana-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. By [observing this] for one day and night under the asterism Aśvinī, or for twenty-three days, disease arises. The two Aśvins are the presiding deities. The food offering (naivedya) consists of milk and sweetmeats (laḍḍukas). The flower is the blue lotus (nīlotpala). The incense is guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter. "Devasya" is the mantra for worship. The sacrificial fuel (samidh) for the oblation (homa) is from a milk-tree. 1.

Under Bharaṇī, there is death or doubt; the duration is twenty-one days. Yama is the presiding deity. The offering consists of molasses-cakes and Arka flowers. Black fragrant flowers and fragrant Tulasī are used. Incense made from Putrakeśa and molasses is offered. "Tryambakaṃ yajāmahe" is the mantra for worship. One should offer oblations of ghee, honey, and sesame seeds. || 2 ||

[685] Under Kṛttikā, there are seven days. Agni is the deity. The food offering (naivedya) is rice cooked with ghee. The flower is the yūthikā. The incense is clarified butter (sarpiḥ). "May the divine beings purify me"—this is the mantra for worship. Ghee is the primary substance. 3.

In Rohiṇī, there are eight deities; Prajāpati is the presiding deity. The food offering is milk-rice (kṣīrodana). The flower is the lotus. The incense is sarala. Worship is performed with the mantra: "Obeisance to Brahmā, obeisance to Agastya. One should offer all kinds of grains as oblations. 4.

In Mṛgaśiras, there are five days; Soma is the presiding deity. The food offering is milk-rice (pāyasa); the flower is saffron; the incense is ten-ingredient (daśāṅga). "New and ever new he becomes"—this is the mantra for worship. Cow's milk is the principal substance. || 5 ||

In Ārdrā, death [is the obstacle]; Rudra is the deity; *sauhālika* is the food offering (*naivedya*); *vīrikā* flower; *jīvaka* incense; "Obeisance to Śambhu" (*namaḥ śambhavāya*) is the mantra for worship; honey and clarified butter are the primary substances. || 6 ||

In Punarvasu, there are seven days. Aditi is the deity. The food offering is rice with jaggery. The flower is the jasmine. The incense is sandalwood. The mantra for worship is: "Aditi is the sky, Aditi is [the earth]... The primary substance is ghee and rice. (7)

In Puṣya, there are seven days. Jupiter is the presiding deity. The food offering consists of pieces of *maṇḍaka* cakes. The flower is the lotus. The incense is *ṣaṭhikā*. Worship is performed with the mantra "bṛhaspate atīya. Ghee and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) are the principal substances. Thus ends [the eighth section].

In Aśleṣā, there are ten days. The Nagas are the presiding deities. The food offering consists of ghee. The flower is the Agasti flower. The incense is ghee and molasses. "Salutation to the serpents" (namo 'stu sarpebhyaḥ) is the mantra for worship. Curd, ghee, rice, and barley are the principal substances. || 9 ||

Under Maghā, there is death or doubt; the duration is twenty-one days. The ancestors (Pitṛs) are the presiding deities. The food offering (naivedya) consists of ghee-filled cakes (ghṛtapurāṇa). The flower is the campaka. The incense is guggulu. The mantra for worship is: "May there be satisfaction for the father. The primary substances are vessels of sesame seeds, rice, honey, and ghee. || 10 ||

For Pūrvaphālgunī, there are fifteen days; Bhaga is the deity. The food offering is *kṛśara* (rice and sesame); the flower is white *karavīra*; the incense is *bilva* fruit. "That which dwells within my womb" is the mantra for worship. The seven types of grain are the principal substances. || 11 ||

Under Uttaraphalgunī, there are twenty-one days. Aryaman is the presiding deity. The food offering consists of red śāli rice. The flower is the red lotus. The incense is guggulu mixed with clarified butter. The mantra for worship is "ahaṃ rudrebhir vasubhiḥ. Priyaṅgu seeds are the principal substance. || 12 ||

There is a danger of death within fifteen days. The deity is Savitṛ. The food offering is a cake (apūpa). The flower is red karavīra. The incense is śallakī. The mantra for worship is "ud u tyaṃ jātavedasam. Curd is the principal substance. 13.

In Citrā, there are ten days. Tvaṣṭṛ is the deity. Sweetmeats (modaka) are the food offering (naivedya). Jayā flowers are used. Incense made from yūthikā leaves is offered. "citraṃ devānām" is the mantra for worship. Variegated rice (citrodana) is the principal substance. 14.

In the month of Svāti, there are nine divisions. Vāyu is the presiding deity. Curd-rice is the food offering. The *damana* flower is used. Black agallochum incense is offered. "Like a father to his sons" (*sanaḥ piteva sūnave*) is the mantra for worship. Ghee and barley-rice are the ritual substances. (15)

In Viśākhā, there are twenty-five days. Indra and Agni are the presiding deities. Dhuṇaka is the food offering (naivedya). Tumbarikā is the flower. Devadāru is the incense. "Indrāgnī āgatam" is the mantra for worship. Curd-rice is the principal substance. 16.

Under Anurādhā, there are ten days. The deity is Mitra. The food offering (naivedya) is kṛśara (rice and peas). The flower is the pauṇḍarīka. The incense is sandalwood and sihlaka resin. The mantra is "deva savitaḥ prasuva yajñam. The primary substance is the sūraṇa tuber. || 17 || Under Jyeṣṭhā, there are fifteen days. The deity is Indra. The food offering is citrodana (variegated rice). The incense is camphor and aguru. The flower is the pāṭalikā. The worship mantra is "indro māyābhiḥ. The substance to be offered is the root of the sūraṇa tuber. || 18 ||

At the root is Death; the deity is Rākṣasa. The offering consists of cooked meat, liquor, and fried cakes. The flower is the black Sombarikā; the incense is ram-horn; and the ritual arrangement involves a Brāhmaṇa and fire—this is the mantra for worship. The primary substance is the radish-root (mūlakanda). || 19 ||

In Pūrvāṣāḍhā, there are twenty-seven days. Water is the deity. A small cake is the food offering. The *kahlāra* flower is used. Incense made from *śailaja* is offered. Furthermore, "O Varuṇa, what is this? is the mantra for worship. Red rice is the principal substance. (20)
