In Uttarāṣāḍhā, there are twenty days. The Viśvedevas are the presiding deities. The food offering consists of five *bilva* fruits. The flowers are of five colors. The incense is *bālaka*. "O Viśvedevas, come hither" is the mantra for worship. Pieces of *śallakī* wood are the primary substance. 21.

For the Śravaṇa [nakṣatra], there are nine days. Viṣṇu is the deity. The food offering (naivedya) consists of milk, sugar, and ghee-coated cakes (maṇḍaka). The flower is the Jātī. The incense is ten-ingredient (daśāṅga). "ato devā avantu naḥ" is the mantra for worship. Red rice grains are the primary substance. 22.

In Dhaniṣṭhā, there are fifteen days. The Vasus are the presiding deities. The food offering consists of *vaṭavaṭaka* cakes. The flower is the *śatapatrikā*. The incense is guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter. "May the gods protect us here" is the mantra for worship. The primary substances are figs grown in water. 23.

In Śatabhiṣā, there are ten days; Varuṇa is the presiding deity. The food offering consists of fried cakes (vaṭakas) with ghee. The flowers should be those grown in water. The incense is camphor and agallochum (aguru). "imaṃ me gaṅge" is the mantra for worship. Water-born flowers and [water-born] substances are the primary materials. 24.

In Pūrvabhādrapadā, death is the danger; Ajaikapād is the deity. Curd and clarified butter are the food offering. The *śatapatra* flower is used. Incense made from all medicinal herbs is offered. "May Agni act with his fires for peace" (*śam agnir agnibhiḥ karat*) is the mantra for worship. Domestic *pūtikarañja* and *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourds are the primary substances. 25.

In Uttarabhādrapadā there are fifteen days; Ahivradhna is the deity. The food offering consists of jaggery, meat-paste, and cold rice. The flower is a leaf of camphor. The sacrificial cake is made of ghee and neem leaves. "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb" is the mantra for worship. Fresh goat blood and milk are the substances to be offered. (26)

In Revatī there are eight days; Pūṣan is the deity. The food offering consists of sesame balls and parched grain flour. The flower is the mandāra. The incense is guggulu. The mantra for worship is "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad. One should offer oblations of clarified butter, milk, and fruits. || 27 ||

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of whatever substance has been prescribed for whichever constellation by the aforementioned Brāhmaṇa, using the Gāyatrī mantra. This very procedure, as described, produces immediate conviction;
it is an offering to the constellations that likewise bestows health.

One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the previous *samidh* wood, sesame seeds, milk, and clarified butter. Having written the twelve names in the mandala, one should worship them. Having installed the deity of the lunar mansion in the center and wrapped it in a pair of garments, one should give it to a Brahmin. Thus there is the pacification of disease.
This is the procedure for the lunar mansion oblation (*nakṣatra-homa*) as spoken by Garga.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
For that from which something is born is traditionally held to be its progenitor;
thus, the fourth is the mental [creation], and the tenth is designated as the creative act.
The sixteenth is known as Sāṅghātika, the twentieth is remembered as Samudaya;
the thirteenth is the Nakṣatra called Vaināśika, also known as Karmarkṣa.
O Lord of the Earth, the person is said by all to consist of six constellations; the king consists of nine constellations. Now hear about the triad of constellations.
O best of kings, for a monarch there are always six [astrological factors] that are superior:
the region, the asterism of consecration, and the asterism of birth.
O sinless one, I shall now describe to you the asterisms associated with birth.
The three asterisms beginning with Pūrva-phalgunī, as well as Kṛttikā, are proclaimed for Brāhmaṇas; likewise, Revatī, Anurādhā, Maghā, and Rohiṇī are traditionally remembered [for them].
O lord of men, for Śūdras, the Āditya, Āśvina, Hasta, Abhijit, Sārpa, Viśākhā, Yāmya, and Vaiṣṇava [nakṣatras] are likewise [auspicious].
For all those born of inverse unions (pratiloma),
it is proclaimed that there shall be loss of body and wealth in this world if their birth star (janmarkṣa) is afflicted.
In the Karmarkṣa (the tenth house), there is loss of actions and mental distress;
when the Sāṅghātika (the eleventh house) is afflicted, there is loss of one's body, wealth, and kinsmen.
If the *sāmudayika* [ascendant] is afflicted, there will be the loss of friends, servants, and wealth;

if the *vaināśika* [ascendant] is afflicted, there will be the destruction of the body, riches, and prosperity. Furthermore, if the *abhiṣeka* asterism is afflicted, one should predict the fall from the kingdom.
If the lunar mansion of the country is afflicted, there will be suffering for both the country and the city;
if the birth-nakṣatra of the king is afflicted, one should predict disease for the king.
Having encountered suffering born of planets and constellations,
one should perform worship according to one's own prescribed rite;
thereafter, O lion among kings, one attains auspiciousness.
A person whose sins have been shaken off is always [pure].
Having collected the dung and urine of a white bull,
one should bathe with the milk of a white cow along with water infused with *kuśa* grass.
A person is liberated from that affliction caused by the suffering of their birth-star by means of water infused with *śirīṣa*, sandalwood, *aśvattha*, and *nāgadāna*.
But one who has bathed in the heated Mānasa lake is liberated from that fault;
likewise, [one is purified by bathing in] Siddhārtha, Priyaṅgu, Śatapuṣpā, and Śatāvarī.
O King, when the constellation Kṛttikā afflicts the ruler, one should bathe after casting into the water priyaṅgu,
bilva, siddhārtha, barley, aśvattha, and surāhvaya.
Surāhvā is *devadāru*.
A bath combined with sandalwood water is beneficial for one suffering from a combination of diseases;
likewise, a bath with all-fragrant waters and auspicious white mustard seeds [is beneficial].
When the collective asterism (samudāyarkṣa) is afflicted, there is the destruction of the sins of men by means of earth taken from the horns of a bull,
as well as auspicious bilva-water.
In the case of a *vaināśika* [planetary affliction], the bath should be performed with water mixed with *śatapuṣpā*;
likewise, when the asterism of consecration (*abhiṣeka-ṛkṣa*) is afflicted, it should be done with water containing all kinds of jewels;
and when the asterism of the region (*deśa-nakṣatra*) is afflicted, bathing with earth is prescribed.
And I shall now describe the clay; listen as I speak of it:
[it should be taken] from the middle of both banks of a river, from a confluence, or from the shore of a lake.
From a horse-stable, from an elephant-stable, from a cow-pen, from a mountain peak,
from the abode of Śakra, from an anthill, from a royal palace, and from a temple.
O King, one who has bathed with water from the horns of an elephant or likewise from the horns of a bull,
using all kinds of seeds and water during an affliction caused by one's birth star (*jāti-nakṣatra*),
is liberated from sin; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
This is proclaimed as the bathing mantra for the waters that flow away.
Having bathed in that manner, O moon among kings, one should thereafter perform the bath as instructed;
then, the rite for the [deity] who causes affliction should be performed.
The sacrifice to the constellations has been performed according to the rules.
Then, O moon among kings, one should perform worship of the lord of the planets who causes affliction;
or rather, one should worship him as conjoined with the Moon.
Thereupon, he abandons all defects.
Thus ends the rite for pacifying the nine asterisms as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Manu said:
"If you desire an excellent husband in this life or in another..."
O best of kings, a maiden should perform this vow as described by Viṣṇu.
The rite named Umāmaheśvara, which bestows all merit and grants the fruit of all desires, should be performed according to the prescribed rule.
O Sage, it should be performed in the months of Proṣṭhapada or Āśvina, or under the asterisms of Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, or Śravaṇa,
and on the eighth lunar day or the day of Śiva (the fourteenth).

Proṣṭha is the month of Bhādrapada; Mṛga is the lunar mansion Mṛgaśiras; Bhāgya is Pūrvaphalgunī; Maitra is Anurādhā; Śākra is Jyeṣṭhā; and Śāṅkara is Ārdrā. On the preceding day, O child, [one should invite] a Brāhmaṇa accompanied by his wife—a man with a single wife who is endowed with all righteous conduct and vows.
Having addressed me and my instruction, one should then joyfully perform the task of favoring others at dawn,
free from the dualities of the Kali age.
One should feed [the deity] with sweet food, milk, sugarcane, barley, and rice;
likewise, two auspicious garments, white and fine as well as red, should be offered.
O child, having bathed in the pure Sadaśa, which is the purifier of gods and goddesses, and having worshipped Umeshvara on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and in the images;
The characteristics and proportions of the images of Umā and Maheśvara are to be understood from the Aviyogadvādaśī vow.
Having offered oblations and presented the *bali* offering to the quarters,
one should spread a canopy over a square area with four doors, having smeared it with cow dung.
Having prepared a square arrangement adorned with rice, wheat, and *karṇaka* seeds,
and provided it with a garland of lamps, one should then feed a married couple.
Having meditated upon this conch, which has the face of Śakra and is adorned with auspicious marks,
it is perfumed with sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and agallochum incense,
and decorated with jasmine, punnāga, mandāra, and white lotus petals.
Having placed the pair well-covered and having circumambulated them three times to the right,
one should feed them with a pleasant ointment and meditate upon that Lord of Umā.
Having sipped water for purification (ācamana), one should offer water for honor (arghya) and water for the feet (pādya), as well as scented water;
then, having offered it again along with gold and gems, one should ask for forgiveness.
May the Lord of Umā, the husband of Umā, the lord of all the gods, be pleased with me; [I worship] Umā with the mantra of Umā, and Śaṅkara with the mantra of the Lord.
When worshipped, he indeed grants all desires without hesitation;
by this, O Lord of the Gods, a woman shall obtain non-separation [from her husband].
In this life, one attains good fortune, wealth, sons, and happiness;
and upon death, one goes to the supreme abode together with Śaṅkara and Umā.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there, she attains a body in a noble family;
endowed with prosperity and supernatural powers, she finds a handsome husband.
Endowed with beauty and grace, she should always act in accordance with her husband’s wishes.
Praiseworthy to all and to the entire inner court,
she possesses excellent sons and living offspring, and is free from mental anguish and physical disease.
O best of kings, she who has previously served her husband, who worships Śaṅkara and Umā, and who enjoys her desires as she wishes, goes to heaven in her old age.
By this method, a man becomes the husband of women;
being prosperous, he attains lordship over all beings.
O best of gods, the Śaṅkaromā vow was formerly performed by Śakralakṣmī,
by the goddess Rati, by Arundhatī, and by Rohiṇī.
It was performed for the sake of happiness, and they now enjoy its fruit.
Thus ends the Umā-Maheśvara vow as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
Indra said:
"The vow known as Śaṅkara-Umā, which grants satisfaction to the mind, has been described."
O Father, I desire to hear that which is designated as Viṣṇu and Śaṅkara.
Manu said:
"O dear one, this vow should be performed just as [the worship] of Umā and Īśvara is;
however, one should offer yellow garments to Keśava."
One should provide incense, flowers, and fragrant smoke for Janārdana; and for the materials of worship, one should include sweetmeats and other delicacies, as well as curd.
Having thus honored them, O child, at either an image or a sacrificial mound,
one should offer oblations to two Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Or one should feed two ascetics endowed with vows, wearing matted hair and saffron robes, according to the prescribed rite, as they are Śūlapāṇi and Janārdana.
O child, having propitiated them according to the prescribed rite, you should offer gold as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for Viṣṇu and a pearl for Śaṅkara, which fulfill all desires.

Having given [these gifts], he followed [the recipient] through both worlds in succession; then, upon the dissolution of the body, having enjoyed such pleasures, O Śakra, he became a lord of sages here on earth.
He is born into a family of kings, happy and endowed with sons and other blessings.
Due to his previous state of being, he possesses eternal devotion toward Śiva and Viṣṇu.
Having attained supreme yoga, he goes to that imperishable abode.
Thus has been described the Śaṅkaranārāyaṇa-vrata as taught by the Goddess Prāṇā;
by this very procedure, the Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa-vrata is performed,
O dear one, as well as those pertaining to Brahmā-Gāyatrī and likewise to Candra-Rohiṇī.
In accordance with one's mental disposition, one shall obtain the fruit that is truly real.
Thus ends the Brahma-Gāyatrī-Candra-Rohiṇī vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
O Sage, having taken a bull and a cow, both young and endowed with auspicious marks,
one should worship them with golden horns, silver hooves, and cloths.

Having worshipped Śiva and Umā on that day, one should bestow [the gift] upon a Brahmin who is a devotee of Śiva, under either the Rohiṇī or Mṛga nakṣatra. Śiva and Umā are "Śivome. (Śivome refers to Śiva and Umā. Upon such a Brahmin devotee of Śiva, under either Rohiṇī or Mṛga.
There shall never be separation for that twice-born man from his sons, wife, or master;
or, having ascended celestial chariots, he shall go to the city of Śiva.
Having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time, he returns here and is born into a family abundant with wealth,
grain, and other riches, and filled with sons and friends;
by the power of this Brahma-vow, he shall be free from enemies.
Thus ends the vow of the pair of cows as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
Or, O Sage, whoever should worship a pair of cows endowed with jewels,
Śiva and Umā grant [the fruit] to that one of purified soul, saying, "May they be pleased."
Or, by the alternative [reading] "endowed with jewels," because it is an option together with the previous vow, the time mentioned for the previous vow is understood here as well.
He, liberated from all sins and suffering, sports forever;
he shall be fortunate in this world and, at the end of the body, attain the supreme state.
Thus ends the vow of the cow-jewel as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
[696] Manu said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which brings about beauty and good fortune.
O child, by means of the rite of the constellations, Śaṅkarī is thus satisfied.

Beginning with the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa and ending with Mūla, one should first worship the feet with a garland of jasmine; observing a fast, one should break the fast at the conclusion of the lunar mansion.
One should worship the two shanks of Brahmā with barley-rice prepared as an oblation;
"brāhmya" refers to Rohiṇī.
[One should worship] with white water-lilies and *bhṛṅgarāja* plants, while subsisting on a meal of sesame and black gram.
With that same [mantra], O brahmins, one should first worship the two Aśvins at the knees.
With *kuṇḍa* flowers, white blossoms, food, curd, and sugar,
one should worship with beautiful *bilva* leaves during the two months of Āṣāḍha.
There, one should feed the Brahmins with milk-rice; that constitutes the breaking of the fast.
However, during the pair of Phālgunī constellations, while she is breaking her fast, one should worship the Secret One (Guhyaka).
Pārayantī is a specific flower.
One should offer curd-rice as the food offering during the Kṛttikā constellation and worship the waist [of the deity].
[One should worship] with damana plants, white flowers, sweetmeat balls, and offerings of curd.
On both sides, during the two Bhādrapadās, one should worship with hundreds of flowers.
At the end of the lunar mansion, the brahmins should be fed with milk-rice and curd;
one should worship the two breasts of the Goddess, adorned with a garland of mango blossoms, under the asterism of Revatī.
One should perform sacrifice during the conjunction of Anurādhā while consuming food consisting of ghee and mung beans;
with auspicious yellow karṇikāra flowers, one should partake of a meal cooked in ghee.
One should worship the region of the back under the asterism *ghaniṣṭhā* with golden flowers—namely, golden flowers and *nāgakeśara*.
Under *karṇapati*, food offerings (*naivedya*) are worshipped; under *viśākhā*, the arms are worshipped.
Fragrant *marupatra* leaves and milk-rice (*pāyasa*) should be offered as food.
One should worship the two hands with ushira, tagara, and other substances;
and in the Punarvasu asterism, one should offer molasses and milk as the food offering (naivedya) to the fingers.
One should worship the Goddess with saffron, and ṣaṣṭika rice should be offered as food;
for the deity of the nails, one should worship with punnāga and other flowers.
One should offer food made of pearls and worship the neck with the Jyeṣṭhā constellation;
one should offer white garlands and the like to the Goddess, and provide food such as ghee.
One should worship the ears with the petals of plantain flowers and offer curd as food.
*Rambhā* is the plantain tree (*kadalī*).

Under the asterism Puṣya, one should feed [the deity] with lotuses and other flowers along with rice mixed with sugar. Under Svāti, however, one should worship the teeth of the Goddess with very red lotuses.
One should worship Haṃsa under the Śatabhiṣaj asterism with nāgakeśara and sandalwood;
one should offer dates and sugar as food, and worship Nāsā under the Maghā asterism.
Likewise, one should offer food prepared with wheat and clarified butter along with *jayā* flowers.
In the month of Mṛgaśīrṣa, one should worship the two eyes of the Goddess with fragrant flowers;
one should then provide various kinds of food consisting of clarified butter and black gram.

One should worship the forehead of the Goddess, which is variegated and adorned with a colorful garland and variegated food offerings, under the asterism Bharaṇī; one should worship her head with a garland of five-fold and other flowers.
One should offer milk-rice as food and worship the hair while it is still wet;
one should honor the Goddess with jasmine and other flowers, and feed her all kinds of foods.

[698] Under the auspicious constellations, the noble Āryās should always be worshipped by those desiring beauty and sons; likewise, Śambhu or Viṣṇu should be worshipped with offerings of ghee, gold, food, and sacrificial fees.
A pair of garments should be given to a Brahmin who has conquered his senses, who is accompanied by his wife,
who is skilled in the meaning of the scriptures of the Goddess, and who is proficient in the knowledge of Śiva.
Her face was like the full moon, her eyes were as long as lotus petals;
her teeth were beautiful and white, and her ears were well-fleshed.
Her hair resembles a swarm of bees; she speaks with the voice of a cuckoo;
her lips are copper-colored; she has the luster of a lotus petal; she possesses beautiful hands; and she is bent by the weight of her breasts.
Her navel was spiraling to the right; her thighs were like the trunk of a plantain tree;
she possessed beautiful hips and a slender waist, and she was radiant with well-knit fingers.
The woman was fortunate, and her husband was a man of great arms,
with a broad chest and wide shoulders, his face resembling the full moon.
With white teeth and the gait of an elephant, possessing great strength and prowess,
beloved by all the world, he has eyes as long as lotus petals.
He was a knower of the meaning of all scriptures and a captivator of the hearts of women.
By this vow, one becomes equal to Kāma in great heroic power;
there is no separation from beloved things and the attainment of desired objects.
For the sake of the lunar mansions, it is a source of great merit—the supreme vow among all vows.
Even in times of adversity, a woman must not cause division; she does not incur fault even through dispositions that are inherently flawed, O best of sages. She must never be abandoned.
Thus ends the Nakṣatrārtha-vrata as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
Nārada said:
[Through this, one obtains] glorious health, beauty, long life, good fortune, and all prosperity.
O Rudra, how could a man become united with you or with Viṣṇu?
O Lord, please describe some vow here by which even a widow, endowed with all virtues and good fortune, may gradually attain the state of liberation.
Rudra said:
"O Brahmin, you have asked well regarding that which brings welfare to all the worlds.
O Nārada, listen now to that vow which, though already heard by you, leads to peace."
The supreme worship of Nārāyaṇa is known as the "Constellation-Man" (nakṣatrapuruṣa);
one should duly form his feet while reciting the names of Viṣṇu.
Having reached the month of Caitra and performed the recitation by Brahmins, one should worship the image of Vāsudeva beginning from the Mūla constellation.
At the root, one should pay homage to Viśvadharā; at the feet, to Anantadeva in the Rohiṇī asterisms;
and the shanks should be worshipped as Varada.
The two knees are in Vāśvi, Kumāra, and Karkṣa.
The pair of Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā,

Afterwards, his inner self was struck by the sesame seeds.

Barley, wheat, varana beans, flat beans, polished rice grains, salt, curd, milk, cloth, and gold.
A woolen blanket, a bull, an umbrella, a pair of sandals,

Dharaṇī said:
"What is the nature of that Vyatīpāta which has been mentioned by you?"
Whose son is he, how is he to be honored, and what is the fruit when he is honored?
Varāha said: When the Moon seized Tārā, the wife of Bṛhaspati, the Sun, out of friendship, said to him: "Abandon the wife of Bṛhaspati."
When Candra, though he was his disciple, did not accept those beneficial words,
Aditya then became enraged and gazed at him with a blazing look.
Meanwhile, Soma also became angry with him; then, as the two, Soma and Sūrya, looked at one another in their mutual encounter and grew enraged,
a terrible man with tawny eyes appeared with his mouth wide open.
With bitten lips and long fangs, his face was contorted by a frown;
his beard, hair, and the tips of his locks were tawny, his eyebrows hung low, and his belly was very thin.
Terrible, with a long tongue, resembling the sun, fire, and Yama, he desired to consume the three worlds but was restrained by the sun and the moon.
"Anger and hunger afflict me; where indeed shall I cast you? he asked.
The Sun and Moon said:
"Because you became [the cause] of various calamities seen through anger,
you shall therefore be known on earth by the name Vyatīpāta."
At the time of your birth, may those who do good fare well;
may he who does evil toward you meet with misfortune—blessings be upon you!
"Eat that food while you are hungry; let your anger be cast aside there.
Consequently, you shall become known on earth by the name Vyatīpāta."
Vyatīpāta said:
Homage to you both, my parents! This fall from the sky, accompanied by food, has been granted by you; now let favor be shown and forgiveness granted.
Ravi and Indu said:
"Whoever should perform [the rites] according to your tradition, preceded by bathing, giving gifts, recitation, and fire-offerings,"
By your grace and through your favor toward this child, may his merit here be infinite.
Whoever performs your worship at that time,
may their desire be fulfilled;
may there be an abundance of good fortune, sons, long life, wealth, happiness, fame, and nourishment.
Preceded by physical beauty, health, and being beloved by the people of one's own village.
Varāha said:
For this reason, Vyatīpāta is honored by men upon the earth;
and when it is honored, its fruit has been declared to you by those who are composed.
Who is able to describe in detail the fruit of such worship? Listen now to that procedure by which, when performed, even the *vyatīpāta* [yoga] is overcome.
On an auspicious day of Vyatīpāta,
he should plunge into the waters of a great river with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); indeed, he should observe a fast while reciting the Pavamāna hymns.
But one who is pure should mutter: "Homage to Vyatipāta!"
Having placed a golden eight-armed man upon a golden lotus inside a jar filled with sugar and covered with a copper vessel, [one should install him].

[He may have] eight arms or eighteen arms, because the form of Vyatīpāta has eighteen arms in its *utpatti-vākya* (originative statement), and because the *viniyoga-vākya* (application statement) follows the *utpatti-vākya*, just as there are four *manus* in the *Bhagavadgītā*. [One should worship him] with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), incense, lamps, garments, food offerings (*nivedana*), various kinds of snacks, meals, and fruits, month by month in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Salutations be unto you, O Vyatīpāta, Lord, son of the Sun and Moon!
Whatever [merit] has been performed by me through giving and other deeds, may that become infinite for me in this world.
Having spoken thus, by casting into [the fire] an añjali filled with the five jewels, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice,

If the earth should experience a Vyatīpāta on the second day as well,

One should perform the breaking of the fast by consuming cow dung at the end of the Vyatīpāta yoga.
However, if the Vyatīpāta should occur on that very same day,
then one should observe the fast on that very day after having made the offering.
One should perform this month after month; thus, thirteen *vyatīpāta* occasions shall pass.
When a *vyatīpāta* has arrived, the wise man should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*).
Saying "svāhā to Vyatīpāta," one should offer oblations of ghee,
