Having fashioned a golden image complete with all its ornaments and placed it within a jar filled with sugar, one should present it to the instructor of the vow.
I bow to the great Vyatīpāta, the son of the Sun and Moon, who grants all desired objects;
may there be the destruction of all my sins.
And may the fruit of my merit be infinite.
Having thus reflected, the teacher is honored with bracelets, earrings, golden ornaments,
and all other such things as prescribed.
One enjoys the earth that is perceived here.
One should indeed give a milch cow with gold as the most excellent sacrificial fee;
having provided him with a firm bed made of solid wood.
It was adorned with golden bands and provided with a canopy of fine cloth,
covered with swan-down cushions, and furnished with auspicious pillows for the cheeks.
It was provided with a curtain for concealment, perfumed with incense and fragrances,
and made beautiful with betel, powdered saffron, camphor, and agallochum.
One should give lamps, shoes, umbrellas, chowries, and seats;
at the end of the body, one goes to the world of the Sun by means of celestial chariots with the brilliant luster of jewels.
Having gone there, honored by the gods, he rejoices for hundreds of billions of eons amidst the enjoyments of throngs of apsaras, who delight in song, dance, and amorous play.
At its conclusion, one shall become a king of kings, endowed with beauty and good fortune;
rich in fame, possessed of virtues, sons, long life, health, wealth, and grain.
One who knows valor, possesses a state endowed with great sovereignty, is deeply learned,
and is blessed with the good fortune of the people, shall remain so for as long as eight births.
A gift given on the new moon day yields a hundredfold merit; that same gift at the end of the day (the solar transits) yields a hundred times that;
at the sun's passage into a zodiac sign it yields a hundred times that; and at the equinoxes it yields a hundred times that again.
At the beginning of a Yuga, it is multiplied by one hundred; at a solstice, it is multiplied by one hundred times that;
during a lunar eclipse, it is multiplied by one hundred times that; and during a solar eclipse, it is multiplied by one hundred times that.
Those who know the Vedas understand that a gift given during Vyatīpāta is incalculable;
it is a hundred-thousandfold at Utpatti, ten-millionfold during the Bhramaṇa nāḍikā, and multiplied by one hundred billion at Patana;
when Patita occurs, recitation, giving, and other acts become inexhaustible.
The movement through twenty-two nāḍīs during birth is twenty-one [nāḍīs];
they know the fall of Vyatīpāta to be situated in seventeen [nāḍīs].
That which was offered at the time of the *vyatīpāta* yoga, when given again and again to the Sun and the Moon,
[yields merit] for hundreds of billions of kalpas.
For that which is increasing does not diminish.
Therefore, if you desire infinite merit, perform worship through the transference of your greatness;
if constant stability is what you desire.
And it bestows everything that is desired and maintained.
For that man who knows the time of the *vyatīpāta* yoga by calculation,
the Sun and the Lord of the Moon (the Moon) shall become the removers of all his sins.
Whoever reads, writes, hears,
recites, sees, or causes this to be done will surely reach the world of the sun and moon.
He remains there, being fully honored by the assembly of the gods.
Thus ends the Vyatīpāta-vrata as declared in the Varāha Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By the performance of which vow shall one not behold the decree of Yama?"
O Brahmin, I ask about the supreme vow that destroys evil.
"O brahmin-sage, having shown compassion for the world, please tell me that vow.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Listen, O King, to this ancient vow of Haryaśva."
That very king gave it to a suffering pig.
Once, however, O King, that best of monarchs, Haryaśva,
while wandering within the state of existence (bhava) after having been patient, saw a boar right there.
With his feet, hips, neck, face, and belly all scorched.
Seeing him in such a state, he who was devoted to compassion felt pity, wondering: "By the ripening of what karma has this man fallen into such ill health?"
"Alas, what misery! Alas, what misery! It is being consumed by a pig. One must inevitably experience the results of the deeds one has performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious."
Having spoken thus, the king addressed that boar in his true form:
"O boar, tell me, how is it that you have come to such a state?"
Having heard those words of the king, the boar sighed repeatedly;
then, remembering his past deeds, he replied to that monarch.
The boar said:
Listen, O King; formerly I was a Vaiśya named Viśvasakha. I fulfilled expectations, yet I gave nothing at all to those who sought my help.
I have heard many teachings proclaimed in the Purāṇas and the Śrutis;
nevertheless, due to my sinful intellect, I do not perform what is beneficial for myself.
Having fallen into the snare of hope, they have departed with their hopes shattered;
I have done only evil, and no good deed at all has been performed.
Once, however, a certain brahmin came to my house during a Vyatīpāta conjunction and begged from me, yet I gave him nothing.
Then the Brahmin, enraged, pronounced a curse upon me,
which burned my limbs one by one like the fire of desire.
In that very same way, O lowest of men, the forest fire shall consume your limbs in a desolate wilderness, devoid of water and lacking even a single tree.
"In that regard, take birth in the womb of a pig.
Having been thus propitiated by me, the brahmin spoke again at that time,
saying, "May there be knowledge even in the state of being a pig," and then he departed.
By that curse, O Indra among kings, he attained the state of a boar;
I have become miserable here in this desolate, waterless forest.
The king said: "By what means, O boar, are you released from sin? Tell me here, so that I may effect the destruction of your curse."
Varāha said:
"Listen, O King of kings, to the means by which liberation may be attained through ritual action;
O King, the vow known as Vyatīpāta was performed by you in the past."
Just as a mother here provides for the welfare of her son,
so too, O King, does this vow provide benefit both in this world and in the next;
just as the risen sun indeed consumes all darkness without exception.
In this very world, this vow likewise dispels all evil;
just as Viṣṇu, when remembered even once, bestows supreme bliss upon men—
of this there is no doubt— so too does this auspicious vow.
A gift at the waning of the moon yields a hundredfold; at the end of the day, a thousandfold;
at the equinox, a hundred-thousandfold; but at the vyatīpāta conjunction, it is infinite.
Listen to the procedure for this Vyatīpāta vow according to its true nature:
it may take place in the month of Māgha, or Phālguna, or even in another month.
On whichever day the Vyatīpāta yoga occurs, one should begin this supreme vow;
one should then offer a shallow bowl filled with sesame seeds and jaggery to the preceptor.
In this manner, it should be given on the second day, but on the third day one should complete the rite;
furthermore, milk-rice with ghee should be offered at each subsequent stage.
Thus, at the end of the year, one should perform the worship of the God,
who is golden-hued, with a conch, discus, and mace in his hands, and a lotus in his hand.
Having wrapped an excellent bronze vessel with a pair of garments,
one should place it there and designate that very spot as the abode of the God of gods; and while recollecting the Lord, a bed should be placed in close proximity to Him.
One should worship with devotion the Guru, who is the auspicious Lord Viṣṇu reclining upon Ananta, the bestower of infinite fruits, accompanied by Lakṣmī.
One should worship with *jātī* flowers using the Vaideha mantra alone;
the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of milk-rice mixed with sugar.
Having offered the *naivedya* to the God, the observer of the vow should offer this prayer:
"O God, O Infinite One, the *vyatīpāta* vow has been dedicated by you."
"May it yield infinite fruit for me in birth after birth.
Having thus prayed to Hṛṣīkeśa, the God of gods, the observer of the vow [should proceed].
One should give all of that to a preceptor who is a learned Vedic scholar (śrotriya) with a family,
especially to a Brahmin who has instructed one in the vow and possesses knowledge of Brahman.
Either land or gold is prescribed as the sacrificial fee;
having fed the Brahmins, one should thus complete this vow.
O Lord, this auspicious vow, which bestows heaven and liberation upon men and grants infinite fruit, was taken by you in a previous birth.
"I shall release myself from this sin of being a boar; of this there is no doubt.
Released by that very [act], Haryaśva spoke these words to the boar:
"I have performed all this; I give you the fruit thereof.
Having spoken thus, the best of kings gave the fruit to the boar.
At that very moment, by that merit, the pig was freed from its defilement;
it was released from its porcine body and adorned with all kinds of ornaments.
Having described the divine celestial chariot, he spoke these words:
"O people, do you not know the supreme vow of Vyatīpāta?"

Having seen that I am liberated from sin through the power of this vow— granting happiness to men in this very world and the supreme goal in the next— let faith be placed in this most excellent Vyatīpāta-vrata.
Having spoken thus, he then ascended to heaven while the king was looking on;
seeing this, the king was struck with wonder and came to have faith in the vow.
Then the king, having returned to the city, caused the people to observe the vow;
he himself performed there the entire auspicious *vyatīpāta* vow.
Then, having ruled the kingdom for a long time, [he served] the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus.
By means of that, Haryaśva attained that supreme abode of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should perform this most excellent vow of Vyatīpāta.
It brings about the destruction of all evils for men and bestows happiness here in this world.
The mortal who performs this, endowed with a state of faith,
shall be liberated from all sins and attain union with Viṣṇu.
By that [mantra] called Purakāminī, one obtains sons;
by it, O dear child, one who desires a woman shall obtain an unsurpassed woman in this world.
One should perform this Vyatīpāta vow on the day of Vyatīpāta;
such a person shall become wise, wealthy, illustrious, and happy even in this very world.
Whoever hears this with devotion is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the vow of Vyatīpāta as declared in the Nāradīya Purāṇa.

Thus concludes the section on Vows associated with Astronomical Yogas (Yogavrata) within the Vrata-khaṇḍa of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Hemādri, who is the sovereign over all faculties, a master of all branches of knowledge, and the supreme king of great kings under the illustrious Mahādeva.
[718] Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now, the observances of the instruments (karaṇavratas).
He by whose innate majesty even the entire world is led to excellence from afar— he,
this very one, speaks for the sake of accomplishing every desired object.
Hemādri: The Vows of the Karaṇas. Sanatkumāra said:
Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the supreme vow of the Karaṇas.
Those who know the ancient lore have declared the Karaṇas to be: Bava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitilam, Vaṇija, and Viṣṭi.
When the month of Māgha has arrived and it falls during the bright fortnight, on the day when the Karaṇa is called Bava, one should observe a fast.
One should worship the god Acyuta with perfumes, garlands, and ointments;
a beautiful golden image of Viṣṇu, weighing one karṣa, should be fashioned.
The wise one should chant the eight-syllable mantra there day and night;
having brought a water-pot, he should likewise place a copper vessel upon it.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa), one should worship the deity with a golden lotus;
one should then offer a canopy, a fly-whisk, and a bell to the deity.
[719] Thus, seven [karaṇas] are to be performed, beginning with the one called Bava; now, when the seventh, Bava, has arrived as the karaṇa, one should perform each preceding rite first.
One should feed seven Brahmins here, accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Then, in this manner, [the rites] beginning with the Bāla and ending with the Viṣṭi should be performed in due order.
Having dwelt there for seven times seven days according to the previously mentioned rule, O King, one should complete the vow by giving abundant gifts of cows, land, gold, and other such things.
O King, when this vow has been performed, one obtains the entire fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, as well as happiness, fame, and great prosperity.
Thus ends the Karaṇavrata as declared in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, who is this whom all people call Viṣṭibhadrā?"
Whose daughter is she, who is the eldest, and how is she worshipped by men?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: In ancient times, the daughter of the Sun-god was born from his shadow;
she is the sister of Śanaiścara, born of the same womb, and exceedingly beautiful.
As soon as she was born, she began to swallow the world;
if anyone went out on business, she stood directly in front of them.
She creates obstacles for one who is sleeping, eating, or standing;
she is the fierce one who obstructs sacrifices and destroys communal festivals.
O Pārtha, she causes constant agitation and destroys the world;
to whom then shall I give this slender-waisted woman, who is so ill-behaved?
[720] Through the misconduct of a daughter, a father is held liable for fault in his household;
therefore, a daughter should be given away in marriage with every effort by one who understands this.
Having thus thought, whichever auspicious woman he bestowed upon anyone,
that very person— in an instant— [was transformed] by the gods, rākṣasas, and kinnaras.
At the commencement of the pavilion, they destroyed it at that very moment;
Vivasvān then reflected, "To whom is this [merit] to be assigned?"
Deformed, evil-hearted, donkey-faced, and three-legged.
With hair standing erect and large fangs, wandering and acting according to her own will,
she brings about misfortune for those to whom she is given here in any way whatsoever.
While the Lord of the Day remained thus reflecting, O King,
the entire world was assailed by that wicked woman.
Then he who was born from the cosmic egg came to the side of Savitṛ;
having reproached him, he granted him the sovereignty over the entire earth.
The Sun spoke these words to that self-born Lord of the World:
"You are both the creator and the destroyer; why then do you speak thus?
Thus was Brahmā, of immeasurable splendor, addressed by Bhāskara at that time.
Then he said: "O noble lady, O blessed one, listen to what is spoken by me:
conduct yourself with the Karaṇas—namely, Bava, Bālava, and Kaulava."
When the seventh half-day has arrived, do whatever you desire—
whether it be setting out on a journey, entering a new home, performing auspicious rites, agriculture, or trade.
"Consume those men who go toward the path of death and who travel upon the wrong path;
indeed, no person is to be disturbed by you for three days."
"O venerable one, you shall be worshipped by gods and asuras for half a day.
O noble lady, those fearless men who act in defiance of you—
destroy their virtuous undertakings with certainty."
Thus has this Viṣṭi arisen, which destroys sacrifices;
it has been declared, O son of Kuntī, therefore avoid it.
She has a lion’s neck, seven arms, three feet, and is endowed with a tail;
her face is like that of a donkey’s head, she is mounted upon a corpse, and she has a slender waist.
Bearing blazing eyes and holding in her hand a noose, a sword,
and a spear, as well as human skulls and garlands— this is known as the sevenfold mudrā.
Having the color of a water-laden cloud, with a long nose, thighs, and fangs, broad jaws and cheeks, and calves like thick bows,
she vomits forth hundreds of thousands of fires in every direction.
Viṣṭi falls in the middle of the world for the destruction of one's undertakings.
But the daughter of the Sun, born as the eldest of a hundred sisters, dark-complexioned, ill-formed, and always poorly dressed,
was appointed by the gods to reside within the sense organs.
But the Viṣṭi yoga must be avoided in all circumstances.
Five *ghaṭikās* are always situated in the mouth, two in the throat,
eleven are said to be in the heart, and four in the region of the navel.
Five lines on the hips should be known [as auspicious], while three on the tail bring victory;
a line on the mouth leads to the destruction of one's undertakings, and one on the neck causes the loss of wealth.
In the heart it should be known as life-taking; at the navel, it brings about quarrels;
at the waist, there is loss of wealth; and at the tail of Viṣṭi, victory is certain.
Whatever actions there are upon the earth, whether inauspicious or auspicious.
O best of kings, all those [rites] succeed during the tail of Viṣṭi, according to the sequence of the directions: water, fire, moon, cruel planets, Yama, wind, and Indra.
Because forced labor is harmful when the number of watches is equal to the number of days, starting from the first day,
they are Karālī, Mandinī, Raudrī, Sumukhī, and likewise Surmukhī.
Triśivā, Vaiṣṇavī, and Haṃsī—these eight are indeed the Viṣṭis:
Dhanyā, Dadhimukhī, Bhadrā, Mahāmārī, and Kharānanā.
Kālarātri, the most terrible Mahāraudrī, Viṣṭi, and Kulaputrikā;
Bhairavī and Mahākālī, the destroyer of the Asuras.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites these twelve names shall have no fear of disease; a sick person is liberated from illness.
All the planets shall be favorable, and no obstacles or the like shall arise;
one shall be victorious everywhere—in battle, in the royal court, and in gambling.
And for that man who constantly worships according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, the accomplishment of all his goals arises; there is no doubt in this matter.
This is the Bhadrāvratam, which was previously told to you by me.
Thus has this Viṣṭi arisen, which destroys one's desired objects.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, it should be avoided by a man who desires the fruits [of his actions].
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall now describe to you that very procedure for the fast and that vow by which, when she is worshipped, she attains satisfaction.
On the day when Bhadrā occurs, O Bhārata,
a woman or a man should observe the vow of fasting on that very day.
If Viṣṭi should fall during the night, one should eat only once for two days;
fasting must then be performed—such is the rule according to the Purāṇas.
When the *viṣṭi* occurs after the third watch of the day, one should observe a fast;
otherwise, one should take a single meal.
Bathing with water infused with all medicinal herbs, or with fragrant *āmalaka* fruits,
is recommended everywhere— whether performed in a river, a pond, or at home.
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors, one should then fashion an auspicious image out of *darbha* grass and worship it with flowers, incense, food offerings, and other such items.
O King, one should perform a hundred and eight oblations (homa) with the names of the Viṣṭi;
having given sesame seeds and milk-rice to a Brahmin,
and having eaten kṛśara with oil, one may thereafter eat according to one's desire.
O Goddess Chāyā, daughter of the Sun, you who are Viṣṭi and the destroyer of desired objects—you have been worshipped according to my ability; O Auspicious One, be the bestower of prosperity.
Having observed the fast according to this procedure for seventeen days in due order,
one should then perform the concluding rite (udyāpana), having worshipped the Goddess as before.
Having placed him upon an iron seat and offered him *kṛśara* rice,
he should again clothe him in a pair of black garments while reciting the mantra.
Furthermore, one should give to a Brāhmaṇa iron, oil, and sesame seeds,
as well as a single black cow with her calf and a black woolen blanket.
Having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, one should bid farewell to Bhadrā.
O Pārtha, for that man who thus correctly performs the Bhadrā-vrata,
no obstacle whatsoever shall arise at the commencement of his undertakings.
Neither Rākṣasas, nor Piśācas, nor Pūtanās, Śākinīs, or Grahas shall afflict that mortal who observes the Bhadrā-vrata.
There shall be no separation from what is dear, nor does any loss occur for him;
at the end of the body, he goes to the abode of the Sun, without a doubt.

Having fasted on that Viṣṭi, whose mouth is radiant with blackness, which is the sister of Saturn— the giver of fear born of the sun— who wanders incessantly among mortals according to the sequence of the Karaṇas;
And a person attains the constant accomplishment of their desired aims.
Thus ends the Viṣṭi-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Furthermore, I shall tell you another unsurpassed Viṣṭi-vrata.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having performed which, one shall have no fear anywhere, even in battle.
It is easy to perform, endowed with excellent qualities, and supreme; it bestows all desired objects upon men, brings great joy to the Sun, and grants the pacification of all obstacles.

O bull of the Bharatas, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a wise man should begin [the rite] after honoring an excellent Brāhmaṇa during the Viṣṭi yoga and other such auspicious times.
Having worshipped that goddess as previously described, one should utter this mantra:
"O auspicious lady, for the sake of auspiciousness, I shall indeed perform this auspicious vow of yours."
"O Goddess, make my undertaking free from obstacles and bring about its success.
Having bathed well, one should thus honor a Brāhmaṇa according to one's capacity;
then, O King of kings, one should eat until the auspicious moment (Bhadrā) has arrived.
Alternatively, even after vomiting, a wise man, being restrained in speech and pure, should not eat anything at will until the *bhadrā* [period] has commenced.
By this method, O Pārtha,
a man or even a woman should perform the Pratibhadra rite for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
Then, when a year has been completed, the wise man should have an image fashioned—
either of metal, stone, or wood— according to his own means.
Having performed the concluding rite according to his capacity and having installed [the image] according to the rules,
the devoted and noble-minded Brahmin should worship it with these mantras.
Just as you were worshipped in the past by Indra, by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera),
by Viṣṇu, and by Śaṅkara, so do I, O Commanded One, worship you now.
Just as you have ensured the unimpeded accomplishment of their goals,
so too, O auspicious lady, be a source of welfare to me, your devotee.
Whatever has been done by me in transgression of you, whether out of ignorance or through arrogance,
forgive that, O inauspicious mother, for me who am wretched and seeking refuge.
Thus one should perform [the rite] according to one's ability, avoiding stinginess regarding wealth.
An inferior person who is incapable [of this] might worship [an image] belonging to another;
however, in the absence of such [materials], a wise man should complete the ritual by performing it with a written representation.
For indeed, whatever man performs the Bhadrāvrata with devotion,
his undertakings will undoubtedly succeed even on an inauspicious day (bhadrā).
Having enjoyed happiness in this world, endowed with the sovereignty of his sons,
free from obstacles, long-lived, and devoid of disease, O tiger among men,
he then attains a heavenly state at the end and rejoices like the king of the gods.
In ancient times, this was practiced by Mahendra with the desire to slay Vṛtra;
it was carried away by Kubera, the enemy of the gods, for the sake of his celestial chariot.
By Śambhu for Tripurāntaka, and by Viṣṇu for Pāñcajanya— verily,
prosperity indeed always comes to men here who perform this vow with devotion and respect.
Those who, having uttered the name Bhadra which is pleasing to the mind, perform [this rite], indeed obtain everything in its entirety, O King.
Thus concludes the Second Bhadrā Vrata as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.

Thus ends the section on Karaṇa Vratas within the Vrata-khaṇḍa of the *Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Hemādri, who is the sovereign of all faculties, a master of all branches of knowledge, and the supreme king of great kings under the illustrious Mahādeva.
[727] Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter. Now follow the vows (vratas) for the solar transits (saṅkrānti).
He by whose deeds, surpassing all dust [in purity],
the world rejoices and is filled with wonder—
he is this very Hemādri-sudhī at present.
[He is] the one who has gone forth, who has transcended, and who has attained the flood of vows.
Vajra said: "O Blessed One, by what action is a person not born into the animal realm or in a land of barbarians? Tell that to me as I ask you."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O best of men, at the sun’s entry into Aries,
one who has observed a fast should worship the divine Bhārgava Rāma according to the prescribed rites and to the best of one's ability.
When the sun's transit into Taurus arrives, one should likewise worship Kṛṣṇa;
and at the transit into Gemini, one should worship the Lord who reclines in enjoyment.
Likewise, during the transit of Cancer, one should worship Varāha and Aparājita;
and during the transit of Leo, the omnipresent Lord Narasiṃha.
At the transit of the sun into Virgo, one should likewise worship the god Aśvaśiras;
and at the transit into Capricorn, one should worship Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.
O King, one should worship Rāma, the delight of the Yādavas, during the transit into Aquarius (Kumbha),
and Vāsudeva as the Fish (Matsya) during the transit into Pisces (Mīna).

O King, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with perfumes, garlands, and an abundance of food, using either a cloth painting or an image, while reciting the name of the manifestation [of the deity].
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-cow (jaladhenu) together with an umbrella and sandals.
One should offer [the deity] every month together with a pair of garments and gold;
at night, one should worship the God of gods with rows of lamps.
Having observed this desired vow for a year,
one does not take birth among the Mlecchas or even among animals;
rather, one attains and dwells in heaven for a long time.
He surely attains that which is pleasing to the mind.
Thus ends the vow for obtaining a good birth as described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Brahmā said:
"Saffron, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), spikenard (*māṃsī*), liquor, sandalwood, and *bālaka*..."
A bath with turmeric combined with wool removes the afflictions caused by the planets.

Rocanā is *gorocanā*. It removes the afflictions of the planets (*grahāpaha*). *Priyaṅgu*, *padmaka*, *kuṣṭha*, *tvac*, *māṃsī*, *niśākara*, combined with *rocanā* and *aguru*, constitute the "Bull's Bath" (*vṛṣasnāna*), which yields great fruit.
Priyaṅgu, phalinī, niśākara (camphor), uśīra, padmaka, kuṣṭha, rocanā, granthiparṇaka,
combined with kuṅkuma and aguru, is considered to bestow sovereignty when used during the month of Mithuna.
Uśīra and bālaka; rocanā, bālaka, musta, and urāśaileyadala (?);
the lion-bath [bestows] sovereignty, long life, sons, and wealth, O Lord of the Gods.
Turmeric, bālaka, kuṣṭha, māṃsī, sandalwood, and gorocanā—
bathing with these should be performed by the bridegroom’s bride to increase progeny and conjugal pleasure.
Rocanā, raṅga, kuṣṭha, sandalwood, uśīra, padmaka,
combined with haridrā and bāla— this [mixture] in the balance destroys evil deeds.
Priyaṅgu, sphaṭika, māṃsī, padmaka, rocanā, aguru,
along with mustā and kuṣṭha, is considered to bestow sovereignty when [administered] during the Vṛścika [nakṣatra].
Coral, pearl, kuṣṭha, rocanā, ghanasāra, padmaka, murā,
and māṃsī— these, when combined, are auspicious at the time of the sun's transition into Sagittarius (Dhanus).
Ghana, mustā,
rocanā, tāvaka, kuṣṭha, candana, aguru, kuṅkuma, and uśīra, combined with padmaka, bestow all happiness when placed in the Makara [yantra].
Granthiparṇa, bark, hair, filaments, and nutmeg leaves,
combined with yellow pigment (rocanā), placed in a jar, bestow sons and sovereignty.
Kesara is *nāgakesara*; or else, with the fruits and roots of camphor, *sāṃsī*, sandalwood, *padmaka*, *bālaka*, *ghana*, *uśīra*, and cinnamon— these bring auspiciousness in the month of Mīna.
These twelve have been fully described; they are bathed and honored by the best of gods, destroyers of misfortune, auspicious, and destroyers of great sins.
Devadāru, mahākuṣṭha, candana, śaileya, and kundura;
Padmaka, patrakambola, surasā, guggulu,
and likewise mahiṣākhyam— these are indeed the eleven substances.
"Candra" means camphor; "surasā" means *tulasī*.
On a lunar mansion presided over by Soma, these should be applied while remaining self-restrained.
Under the asterism Mṛgaśiras, whose presiding deity is Soma,
that which is recited with the Vijayā-vidyā, performed,
and applied to the body is renowned as "Vijaya" (Victory), the destroyer of all calamities.
This blessed bed of Alakṣmī wards off the evil influence of the planets;
it serves for the protection of children and grants success in royal affairs.
O Śakra, this has been told by me to you in brief:
the ritual bath and the incense for the transit of the sun, exactly as you requested.
Thus end the vows for the *saṃkrānti* days as declared in the *Devīpurāṇa*.
Nandikeśvara said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed vow of grain (*dhānyavrata*).
For by performing this, O King, a man shall indeed attain all his desires.
Having performed his bath during the solstices and the equinoxes, the wise man,
having meditated upon the Sun-god, should undertake the observance of the vow.
"O Lord, I shall observe this vow, devoted to you and having you as my supreme refuge;
may it be accomplished for me without obstacle through your grace, O God."
Having recited this, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with saffron;
Bhāskara on the eastern petals, and likewise Ravi on the southeast petal.
Likewise, one should place Vivasvat in the southern petal, Pūṣan in the southwestern,
Āditya in the western petal, and Tapana in the northwestern.
Having thus worshipped Mārtaṇḍa in the northeast and Bhānu in the northwest,
one should worship Viśvātman in the center according to this sequence.
Having joined his palms in reverence, he should offer everything accompanied by mantras:
"He who is the self of time, the self of all beings, the self of the Vedas, whose face is turned in every direction;
the destroyer of disease, death, old age, sorrow, and the fear of saṃsāra."
This is the *argha* mantra.
Having worshipped with flowers and incense, and having prostrated with the head bowed,
one should meditate upon the Sun and then give a *prastha* measure of grain to a twice-born man.
Furthermore, every month, that thousand-footed deity should be worshipped in the same manner;
thus, one prastha of grain should always be given to a twice-born man.
Thus, when the year is complete, one should perform the concluding rite (udyāpana).
One should indeed have a golden vessel for the respectful offering (arghya) prepared, as well as an auspicious mandala.
One should worship the two-armed Bhānu, provided with a pair of red garments,
together with one *droṇa* of grain, or half of that, according to one's capacity.
Having meditated upon the twice-born as the form of the Sun, one should give to that knower of the Vedas a milch-cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and a bronze milking vessel.
A person who offers all of that to a Brahmin who is a vessel of knowledge obtains the fruit of thousands of Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
"For seven thousand births, one is endowed with wealth and grain;
free from disease and pain, wise, and even handsome, one is born.
Thus ends the *Dhānyasaṃkrāntivrata* as declared in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Nandikeśvara said:
Hereafter I shall proclaim the excellent Lavaṇasaṃkrānti;
having reached the day of the Saṃkrānti, one should perform a bath with auspicious waters.
Upon one who is clothed in garments and ornaments and endowed with a spirit of devotion,
one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp using saffron.
One should worship Bhāskara with devotion according to the prescribed sequence;
before him, the wise man should place a vessel of salt together with jaggery.
Having worshipped [the deity] with flowers, incense, and various kinds of food offerings,
and having performed circumambulation, one should then sit down according to the prescribed rule.
One should meditate on the form belonging to the twice-born, conjoined with the Sun;
being worshipped according to one's ability, [one should pray: "O Bhāskara, be gracious unto me!"
One should present a vessel of salt together with jaggery to a Brāhmaṇa;
thus, when the year is complete, one should fashion a golden image of the Sun.
Covered with a pair of red garments, smeared with red sandalwood paste,
and accompanied by a cow, one should give a lotus, salt, and a vessel to a twice-born man.
One should offer [the gift] while dedicating it to the Sun, saying, "May the Soul of the Universe be pleased.
Indeed, such is the merit that is obtained by men on earth when this is performed.
A person obtains the fruit of the gift of a mountain of salt, which cannot be described even in hundreds of millions of years.
With all his desires fulfilled, dwelling in the midst of a most excellent celestial palace,
he shall reside in the world of the Sun for a kalpa, being honored by gods and asuras alike.
Thus ends the vow of the Saṃkrānti of Lavaṇa as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
I shall now describe the Saṃkrānti of Bhoga, which increases prosperity for all the worlds.
Having reached the day of the solar transit, one should summon women.
Saffron, collyrium, vermilion, flowers,
all fragrant substances, and betel leaf mixed with camphor.
The wise person should offer rice mixed with camphor and joined with the moon [symbol], as well as fruits;
indeed, he should also offer other objects that serve as means of enjoyment.
One should diligently give [gifts] to couples with a joyful mind;
having fed them according to one's ability, one should cause a pair of garments to be presented.
Thus, at the end of the year, having worshipped the Sun as before,
one should give to a twice-born man together with his wife a cow endowed with all requisites— having horns of gold and hooves of silver— along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thus, he who performs this transference of enjoyment with devotion and respect shall become happy among all mortals and an enjoyer of pleasures in birth after birth.
Thus ends the vow of the transition of enjoyment (*bhogasaṃkrāntivrata*) as declared in the *Skandapurāṇa*.
Nandikeśvara said:
Now I shall tell you of another, the supreme transition of form (*rūpasaṃkrānti*).
On the day of the solar transit, the wise man, having performed his ablutions, should apply oil.
Having placed ghee in a golden vessel and accompanied it with gold,
one should, after beholding that vessel of beautiful form, present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Then, having observed the practice of eating only one meal per day, endowed with devotion,
at the conclusion of the vow he should give gold together with a cow made of ghee.
A person obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices,
along with excellence of form and youth, and the perfection of long life and health.
And Lakṣmī obtains abundant enjoyments here in this world, of this there is no doubt;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the heavenly realm.
Thus ends the Rūpasaṃkrānti-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
Now I shall further describe to you the supreme Tejaḥsaṃkrānti.
Having reached the day of the solar transit (saṃkrānti), the wise man should perform his ritual bath.
One should have an auspicious vessel prepared filled with rice grains;
having placed a lamp blazing with its own luster in the middle of it,
and having placed a sweetmeat (modaka) at its opening, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
The offering of *arghya* should be performed as before, and likewise the practice of eating only one meal a day;
when the year is fully completed, the wise man should perform the concluding rite (*udyāpana*).
O Nārada, a beautiful lamp should be made of gold;
a water-pot should be made of copper, and one should place the lamp in its center.
O sinless one, a tawny cow together with a bronze vessel should be given to a twice-born; by that, the fruit of giving ten million pieces of gold is obtained.
Resplendent like the sun in brilliance, one shall obtain the power of the wind;
through the greatness of the Saṃkrānti vow, this is attained—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the vow of the transference of splendor (*tejaḥ-saṃkrānti-vrata*) as told in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
Nandikeśvara said:
Now I shall fully describe another, the supreme transference of good fortune (*saubhāgya-saṃkrānti*).
Listen with diligence, O Nārada, to that which bestows wealth and sovereignty.
On the solstices, on the equinoxes, during the Vyatīpāta yoga with the sun,
and on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti), one who is free from envy should observe the practice of eating only once a day.

Having worshipped the Sun as before, and likewise the young bridegroom and the young bride accompanied by their wives, he should offer a pair of garments together with the eight auspicious items (saubhāgyāṣṭaka).
One should devotedly present that to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas.
Thus, when the year is complete, having performed a feast for Brahmins,
one should fashion a mountain of salt according to the extent of one's wealth.
Having fashioned a golden lotus, one should likewise have an image of the Sun made;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should present it to a Brahmin.
And at Puṣkara and Kurukṣetra, one obtains the fruit of a thousand cows;
she who performs this vow is beloved in the worlds of mortals.
Just as Gaurī is to Śaṅkara, and as Lakṣmī is to Viṣṇu in heaven,
so too does she rejoice with her beloved in the world of mortals.
Thus ends the vow of Saubhāgyasaṃkrānti as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Skanda said:
Now I shall tell you of another, most excellent vow, the Phalasaṃkrānti.
Having reached the day of the solar transit (saṃkrānti), one should perform a ritual bath as previously described.
Having worshipped the Sun as before with flowers, incense, and other offerings,
[he should present] a vessel containing sugar along with eight fruits.
Having reached the day of the solar transit (saṃkrānti), one should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa;
and at its conclusion, O Nārada, one should fashion an image of the Sun out of gold.
Having placed it upon the water-pot (kumbha), one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
then, one should offer eight fruits together with various kinds of food and edibles.
Thus ends the vow of Phala-saṃkrānti as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O Skanda, listen to the greatness of Dhana-saṃkrānti according to its prescribed ritual."
By performing which one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
Having reached the day of the solar transit, being pure and composed,
one should take a flawless water-pot filled with water and set it down.
Having fashioned it with gold, one should cause it to be given every month;
by this rite, at the end of the year, may the Sun-god be pleased with me.
The procedure for worship should be performed everywhere just as in the case of the transit of the grain.
And I shall describe the concluding rite (udyāpana), the most excellent completion of the vow:
having fashioned a golden lotus, one should place the Sun-god upon it.
One should indeed offer a lotus fashioned of gold in the hand;
a gift of a cow should be given there for the fulfillment of the visualization.
When this has been performed, I am not able to describe the merit and its fruit;
such a man shall be endowed with wealth for hundreds of thousands of births.
Endowed with long life and good health, he is honored in the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the Dhanasaṃkrānti-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
Now I shall fully describe another excellent rite, the Āyuḥsaṃkrānti.
Listen, my child, to the method by which merit increases.
Having worshipped the Sun as before on the day of the solar transit (saṃkrānti),
one should give bell-metal, milk, and ghee, along with gold, according to one's ability.
In the case of a separate gift, the mantra itself is proclaimed to be that very worship;
it takes on a form identical to nectar, consisting of milk from a cow of the Surabhi breed.
"Grant long life, health, sovereignty, and great splendor offered to the twice-born;
according to this ritual, one should unweariedly bestow everything correctly."
The concluding rite and all other ceremonies should be performed just as they are for the transit of the sun into a new zodiacal sign (*dhānyasaṃkrānti*).
The merit that accrues when this is done is such that it cannot be fully described by me.
Free from disease and long-lived, he shall be radiant in all his births;
there is no fear of untimely death, and he shall live for a hundred autumns.
Thus ends the vow for the transition of longevity as spoken in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
O Skanda, listen according to the prescribed rule to the majesty of the transition of command.
By performing which, a man becomes one who possesses authority throughout all worlds.
On an auspicious day of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), one should begin the observance of the vow;
having drawn an eight-petaled lotus with saffron, one should [worship] the Sun.
One should worship by reciting the mantra according to the rules in the presence of the guru.
The Command (ājñā) bestows splendor upon the back; it brings forth radiance, brilliance, and fame.
"O God, grant me permission to go everywhere; salutations be unto you.
Having thus honored him with saffron, he should then provide a meal for a Brahmin.
At the conclusion of the rite (udyāpana), however, he should likewise offer a golden image of the Sun-god together with his chariot.
And whoever, according to this rite, should perform the supreme transmission of the command (ājñā-saṃkrānti) by means of the single wheel with seven horses accompanied by Aruṇa, [attains the goal].
Then, by the power of the Sun, his command arises in the world.
When the mantra is favorable to cattle, friends, sons, and desired goals, his command prevails everywhere;
his enemies go to destruction, and he attains unsurpassed happiness.
Thus ends the Ājñā-saṃkrānti-vrata as told in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O Skanda, listen according to the prescribed rules to the greatness of the Kīrti-saṃkrānti."
Having reached the day of the solar transit, one should draw the solar disc upon the ground.
One should worship the deity situated in its center with all mantras, according to the extent of one's wealth; thereafter, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
Every month, one should indeed cause a pair of white garments to be given;
at the concluding rite (udyāpana), however, one should cause silver to be given along with the Sūrya-mantra,
and present it to a Brāhmaṇa covered with a pair of white garments.
When this is done, O Fire-born One, supreme fame arises;
its fruit cannot be described even by the tongue of Brahmā.
Stainless fame and sovereignty arise; of this there is no doubt.
Endowed with long life and health, a man shall live for a hundred years.
Thus ends the vow of the transition of fame (*kīrtisaṃkrāntivrata*) as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O Skanda, listen to the rite for the transition to sinlessness (*apāpasaṃkrānti*) according to the prescribed injunctions."
Having become disciplined on the day of the solar transit, one should offer white sesame seeds.
One should offer a water-pot (*karaka*) and a *vardhamāna* vessel;
by the term *vardhamāna*, a shallow bowl (*śarāva*) is meant.
Endowed with a spirit of devotion, one should bathe with this mantra.
May sesame protect me from sins through your grace, O God;
and may you, O Lord of Gods, cleanse me from the impurities of speech, mind, and body.
And for the concluding rite (udyāpana) of the deity, an image with two arms should be made using a gold māṣaka, or one should have it made of silver.
In this vow, a sesame-cow (tiladhenu) should be given; there is no doubt about this—for the destruction of prior sins and for the sake of longevity and health.
All this was previously told by Brahmā to Viṣṇu;
Viṣṇu declared it to Indra, and likewise he spoke it to Śambhu.
Śambhu himself has declared this to me, and I have proclaimed it to you, O Lord:
on the day of every saṃkrānti, one should begin this supreme vow.
Regarding the transits at the solstices and "in all [circumstances]," by what means is it praised?
Because of the instability of the body and because of simultaneity, it is highly commended.

And in this case, there shall be no omission of the prescribed rule, for the deity is indeed one and the same everywhere; however, for those observing vows to various deities, it is not recommended that they perform them at the same time.
Thus ends the vow for the transition [of the sun] into a sign without evil, as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
Now I shall fully describe another unsurpassed vow known as Tāmbūla.
One should perform the ritual procedure as before, just like that for the transition of grain.
Having received betel, sandalwood, and other offerings, as well as the command from that best of the twice-born,
[he remained thus] until the year was fully completed, thereafter night after night.
One should offer betel-leaf to the Brahmins and cause them to eat it, without any interval;
and at the end of the year, having fashioned a golden lotus.
One should also prepare a leaf-casket, as well as a container for betel nuts;
one should likewise prepare a vessel for the lime powder and a device for breaking the betel nut,
O bull among the twice-born, as well as vessels for the powders such as *sukhavāsa*.
Having invited a Brahmin couple, one should worship them with devotion using materials provided with all necessary utensils,
and one should feed the twice-born with food of six flavors.
Whatever has been prepared, she should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa;
the woman who acts in this way performs the most excellent vow known as Tāmbūla.
O best of the twice-born, he obtains all desires upon being born into a mortal caste and family; he attains good fortune and incomparable splendor.
She rejoices with her husband, sons, and grandsons in every household;
after death, in the course of time, she is glorified in the world of the Sun.
O Brahmin, any young woman who listens to this with her husband like a god until the dissolution of the world (āhūtasaṃplava) also enjoys that same fruit;
she is liberated from all sins and is glorified in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the vow of the transference of betel-leaves as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said: Hereafter, I shall describe the Saṃkrānti known as Manorathā.
On the day of the solar transit (saṃkrānti), one should give to a Brahmin who has a family a water-pot filled with molasses and covered with cloth, according to one's ability.
Thus, when the year is complete, one should perform the auspicious concluding rite (udyāpana) according to one's capacity;
a mountain [of offerings] made of jaggery should be prepared, adorned with garments and jewels.
One should give during the northern course of the sun and must not practice stinginess regarding one's wealth;
whatever desire one prays for, that one obtains in abundance.
"Completely liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the vow for the *Manoratha-saṃkrānti* as declared in the *Skanda Purāṇa*.
[742] Nandikeśvara said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme transference of the sorrowless state:
if, during a meritorious solstice or equinox, there should occur the Vyatīpāta yoga.
A man should observe a single meal a day and perform his bath with sesame seeds;
he should fashion an image of the Sun-god out of gold, according to his own means and capacity.
One should bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), worship it well with perfumes and flowers,
wrap it in two red cloths, and place it within a copper vessel.
Salutation to Bhāskara for the feet; salutation indeed to Ravi for the shanks;
salutation to Āditya for the knees; and Divākara for the thighs.
One should worship Aryaman on the hips and Bhānu on the abdomen; one should worship Pūṣan with "Salutation to Pūṣan" on the two arms, and Aryaman again on the two breasts.
Salutation to Vivasvat at the throat; salutation to Sahasrāṃśu is prescribed for the mouth;
salutation to Prabhākara at the eyes; salutation to Tejorāśi at the head.
One should worship Varuṇa with a salutation on the hair and the Sun on the feet and other limbs;
the offering of water (arghya) and so forth should be performed as before, and one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
Thus, when the year is complete, one should worship the Sun-god with gold, holding a lotus in his hand, according to the extent of one's wealth and capacity.
One should have it made, worship it with devotion, and wrap it in red cloths;
then, O Nārada, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the mantras of the Sun.

One should give twelve tawny cows, provided with garments and ornaments; if unable, one should give a single tawny cow, free from deceit regarding one's wealth. This is to be given at the time of an eclipse in Kurukṣetra to a worthy recipient.
One obtains the fruit of having given ten million times ten million pieces of gold:
long life, health, sovereignty, together with a wife and sons.
Thus concludes the Viśoka-saṃkrānti-vrata as declared in the Skanda Purāṇa.

Thus ends the section on Saṃkrānti-vratas in the Vrata-khaṇḍa of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Hemādri, the sovereign over all faculties, an expert in all branches of knowledge, and the servant of the illustrious Mahādeva, the great king of kings.
[744] Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter. Now, the monthly observances (māsavratas).
By whom this earth of the three worlds has been made fragrant with glories equal to camphor—
that Hemādri-sūri of great majesty— [I praise].
He declares here that the vrāta is the month-long vow (māsavrata).
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action is a man born handsome?
Cut through this doubt of mine, for you are indeed said to be all-knowing."
Mārkaṇḍeya said: O great king, when the full moon of Phālguna has passed, one should bathe day after day in succession, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) until the full moon of Caitra.
One should worship the god Keśava, who reclines upon the serpent, outside;
one should always eat only one meal a day and likewise sleep on the ground.
Having fasted for three nights, one should likewise perform worship on the full moon day of Caitra;
according to one's ability, one should give silver as well as a pair of garments.
For those desiring form, I have declared this supreme vow, which is constant and undaunted in spirit;
by performing it, a human being indeed attains heaven.
And having attained human birth, one shall be possessed of beauty.
Thus ends the vow for the attainment of beauty as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
[745] Brahmā said:
O Dharmarāja, listen to this great festival beginning with the *damanaka* flower.
It is filled with excellent women in motion and made beautiful by the utterance of the fifth [vowel].
Accompanied by his noble wife in the Nandana grove,
Śiva wandered like one intoxicated, his eyes wide with wonder.
In that blossoming forest during the spring season, he beheld many hosts of Vidyādharas,
honored by the hosts of gods and asuras, performing a dance.
Having tied the Mādhavī creeper to the *santāna* and *pārijāta* trees,
they would sometimes swing while embracing their full-breasted consorts.
Mounted upon musical swings, those supreme women appeared so enchanting that they seemed to uproot even their own lord, the god of love himself.
Seeing that, Bhavānī, overcome with wonder, said to Śaṅkara:
"O Lord adorned with serpent ornaments, curiosity has arisen within me."
"O Three-eyed One, have a well-adorned swing made for my sake, so that I may swing upon it in the month of Caitra."
Having heard those charming words of Gaurī, the bull-bannered Lord summoned the great Asura and caused him to swing.
Having caused two pillars to be made of brick and wood, firm and strong,
he fashioned the upper one of the finest wood, which was indeed the Truth.
Having bound Vāsuki in the place of the staff,
he made that seat well-covered with a collection of jewels from of old, adorned with gems.
It was indeed wound with thousands of fine cotton cloths and silken fabrics;
its hands were adorned with hanging garlands and wreaths, and it bore crests of jewels and pearls.
Having caused that variegated swing, swift as lightning and fully completed,
to be brought, he presented it with reverence to the perfected Guru.
Having ascended there, the Blessed Lord Soma, adorned with the moon,
caused his ornaments to sway along with his attendants standing at his sides.
On the left side is Vijayā, while on the right is Jayā.
As Pārvatī swayed, her two breasts pressed against his shoulders upon which chowries rested, she sang that song with faltering syllables.
By which the women of the gods and asuras became filled with joy;
the lords of the Gandharvas sang and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
The bards played their loud-sounding instruments;
all the great boundary mountains shook, and the seven oceans were agitated.
Winds accompanied by thunderbolts blew while the god was on his swing;
seeing the world thus agitated, the gods, led by Śakra,
approached, prostrated themselves, and spoke to the supreme remover of all sins.
Cease, O Blessed One, from this play of yours;
O Lord, the world is being whirled about like a turbulent ocean.
Delighted by the words of the gods, Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the world,
rose from the swing with his eyes wide open in great joy.
While the host of gods looked on, Śakra spoke words that were compassionate, very graceful, and with clearly articulated meanings, phrases, and syllables.
Śrī Mahendra said:
"From this day forward, those who shall cause the swing-sport to be performed on the bank of the Puṣkariṇī pond during the spring season, when the courtyard of the gods has been adorned,"
[747] Covered with a silken blindfold, adorned with rubies,
provided with curtains, and furnished with a golden footstool.
She has a chain of jewels; she is adorned with various ornaments that illuminate the quarters of space with their abundant luster;
she is embraced by the Mālā-vidyādhara, and a mirror is placed at her side.
Then, having prepared [the image] covered with umbrellas and chowries according to one's capacity, or as is possible,
one should perform the fire-rite (agnikārya) and offer the directional oblation (dikpāla-bali) in each of the directions.
Upon that [swing] one should cause the deity to ascend, surrounded by beloved and distinguished persons;
for the deities, the mounting of the swing has been attained through the root mantra.
A learned Brahmin standing by his side should recite the supreme mantra:
"He whose eyes are on all sides, whose faces are on all sides, whose arms are on all sides, and whose feet are on all sides."
With his arms he bellows, with his wings he fans the heaven and earth, generating them as the one God.
It was filled with the deep resonance of musical instruments and the sounds of martial drums,
as well as the voices of hymns and auspicious chants, and was perfumed with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
The people, adorned with saffron powder, betel, flowers, and garlands,
abandoned that water-sport and engaged in other pastimes.
That people, struck by the impact of the yellow song-water, consider it happiness—
surely this is some power born of the bodiless god of love.
Thus, those women who shall follow [this practice] when the swing has been set in motion will be free from disease and happy for a hundred autumns.
Endowed with sons and grandsons, and possessed of wealth and grain,
they will experience happiness here in the mortal world through their virtuous conduct, and thereafter they shall go to that supreme state.
When the spring season arrives,
those who emulate the swaying of the best of gods obtain the fruits of the tree of human birth upon this earth.
Those afflicted by suffering rescue even hundreds of families.
Thus ends the procedure for the Āndolana festival as stated in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
In the *Mahābhārata*:
"He who, being self-restrained, passes the month of Caitra eating but one meal [per day],"
One is born into a great family, enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "He who, devoted to Viṣṇu, passes the month of Caitra eating but one meal a day,
shall attain the state of a householder enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls."
Non-violent toward all beings and devoted solely to Vāsudeva,
one should recite "Obeisance to Vāsudeva" eight hundred times during the day.
Thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating but one meal a day. Now follow the vows of Vaiśākha.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
By refraining from flowers and salt during the month of Vaiśākha and giving a cow as a gift, one attains the world of Viṣṇu; thereafter, one becomes a king here on earth.
This is called the Kāntivrata; it bestows beauty and good fortune.
Viṣṇu is the deity here.
Thus ends the Kānti-vrata as described in the Padma Purāṇa.
[From] the Mahābhārata.
Whether it be a man or a woman, one who has conquered the senses and observes a single daily meal without interruption throughout the month of Vaiśākha shall attain preeminence among their kinsmen.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "Whether it be a man or a woman, he or she who passes the month of Vaiśākha eating but one meal a day and worships Hari shall attain preeminence among their kinsmen."
Non-violent toward all beings and devoted solely to Vāsudeva,
one should mutter "Obeisance to Vāsudeva" eight hundred times during the day;
thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating but one meal a day.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action does a man become endowed with intelligence?"
This alone is what constitutes the true humanity of human beings.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the month of Caitra has passed, for as long as the month lasts, day by day,
one should worship the unconquered god Nṛsiṃha as before.

"According to the previous [rule]" means that one should perform the single-meal fast (*ekabhakta*), bathing outdoors, sleeping on the ground, and so forth— just like the vow for obtaining the form described in the month of Caitra.
Furthermore, O King, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) every day with white mustard seeds (*siddhārthaka*),
and likewise, O King, one should feed the Brahmins with the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*).
The "three sweets" are honey, ghee, and sugar.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, a man who has fasted for three nights should give gold;
this vow bestows the attainment of knowledge and increases the intellect.
Having observed this vow for a month as prescribed, a person reaches heaven and remains there for a very long time; then,
having returned to the human state, he becomes endowed with wisdom.
And likewise, one should be endowed with wisdom.
Thus ends the vow for the attainment of knowledge as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*. Now follow the vows of the month of Jyeṣṭha according to the *Mahābhārata*.
He who observes a single meal per day throughout the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūla—
whether man or woman— is born into incomparable and supreme sovereignty.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"He who passes the month of Jyeṣṭha with a single meal a day, his mind dedicated to Kṛṣṇa,
non-violent toward all beings, and devoted solely to Vāsudeva..."
One should recite "Namo 'stu Vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times during the day;
one shall obtain the complete fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating but one meal a day.
Vajra said:
"In this world, what is the fruit even of life for one who is bereft of prosperity?"
Therefore, explain the vow by which a man may become endowed with prosperity.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the full moon day of Vaiśākha has passed, one should worship the God accompanied by Śrī day after day, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) in the same manner as before.
"As before" means like the vow for obtaining the form of Caitrī and so forth.
One should constantly offer flowers, roots, fruits, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*) into the fire,
and one should feed the twice-born with milk products and *bilva* fruits.
Having fasted for three nights, O King of kings, one should present gold and a pair of garments to Jyeṣṭhā; by that, one attains success.
Having observed this vow for a month as prescribed, and having attained human birth after a very long time, a person, with his splendor increased, [attains the goal].
Endowed with glory, he shall become the foremost in the world.
Thus ends the Śrīprāpti-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Now follow the vows of Āṣāḍha.
In the Mahābhārata:
Having remained for the month of Āṣāḍha eating but one meal a day without sloth,
one is born with abundant grain, abundant wealth, and many sons.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "One devoted to Viṣṇu should worship [the month] of Āṣāḍha by eating only one meal."
Thus ends the vow of eating but one meal a day.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action does a human being obtain enjoyment?"
But for one deprived of enjoyments, O twice-born one, there is a purpose served by wealth.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the month of Jyeṣṭha has passed, one should worship the Lord Hari, who bears the universal form, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) in sequence, as previously described.
In this case as well, "as before" means as in the vow for obtaining a [specific] form;
and having performed the vow, at its conclusion, one should likewise give a well-prepared bed to a twice-born man for three nights.
Having reached the world of the gods for a long time, O lord of men,
and having returned to the human state, he shall be possessed of enjoyments.
Thus ends the vow for the attainment of enjoyments as declared in the *Viṣṇudharma*.
Now follow the vows of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Sañjaya said:
When indeed is the Śrāvaṇī festival to be honored, and when is the vow performed?
How was this established by Indrāṇī, and what is the fruit of that vow? Tell me.
Vijaya said:
When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, during its beautiful bright fortnight,
one should install the goddess Pārvatī and worship her according to the power of one's devotion.
For one month, recollecting Pārvatī in his heart with constant discipline,
[he should worship her] with white offerings, white flowers, and white sandalwood paste.
One should offer an *arghya* with perfumes, incenses, food offerings, and fruits produced in their proper season;
indeed, the *arghya* should be offered with fruit alone, along with flowers, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), and sandalwood paste.
Homage to the goddess Ardhaśrāvaṇī, who causes the destruction of all sins!
O Queen of the Gods, accept this water offering from me together with Śaṅkara.
The Arghya-mantra:
Salutations, salutations to you, O Goddess of gods, O Pārvatī who hears the offering of water;
let there be salutation to you, O Mother of the world, salutation to you, O beloved of Hara.
Homage to the Goddess! Homage to you, O Kātyāyanī; let there be homage to you.
Homage to Kālī, Mahākālī, Śivā, and Durgā; let there be homage to you.
Salutations to all the Rudrāṇīs, O Aparṇā, beloved of Śaṅkara! O Goddess who acts for the welfare of all beings, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
The mantra for worship:
This incense is indeed food for all the gods, comparable to nectar.
Accept this incense, O Goddess of Gods, O you who are celebrated in the month of Śrāvaṇa; homage be to you!
A white garment, washed, clean, and auspicious, should be offered;
thereafter, at the end of Śrāvaṇa, having completed the observance, one should remain pure.
One should feed married women according to one's ability with sweet food during the auspicious Jaya festival;
one should also feed the twice-born there and clothe them in garments.
Having performed the Ardhāśrāvaṇī vow according to such a procedure,
there shall be neither poverty nor separation from one's beloved for him.
A woman shall obtain eight sons and a husband who is preeminent in virtue—
handsome, virtuous, beloved, learned, and sweet-spoken.
One should perform this auspicious vow by eating only once a day or by eating only at night;
having performed this in former times, Indrāṇī obtained Indra as her supreme husband.
Rohiṇī obtained Candra as her husband by the observance of vows;
the goddess Raṇyā attained Āditya, her good husband and lord.
This, O blessed lady, has been told to you regarding the Ardhaśrāvaṇika vow;
for she who performs it fully indeed fulfills all her vows.
If, due to the faults committed by the planets, the god does not send rain,
then by the mere hearing of this narrative, Vāsava, the god of rain, shall pour forth.
During a famine, in a terrible upheaval, in a violent conflict, or in a war between kings—
one who listens to this narrative at night is swiftly liberated from all faults.
Thus ends the vow of Ardha-Śrāvaṇika as declared in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
[755] How may great affection arise toward one’s own husband even when there is a connection with dissatisfaction?
O Teacher of the World, likewise tell me the vow for women of noble family.
Kṛṣṇa said:
On the eastern bank of the Yamunā, there is the auspicious city of Mathurā;
in that city there was a king named Śatrughna, the joy of the Raghu dynasty.
His wife was named Kīrtimālā, renowned throughout the world.
Once, having bowed down to the venerable Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages—
"O best of sages, being thus questioned, tell me how one may obtain incomparable good fortune;
explain to me the connection with sesame seeds and the cause of this supreme vow."
Thus addressed by Kīrttimālā, the wise and self-controlled Vasiṣṭha meditated for a moment and then described the supreme Kokilā-vrata.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When the time of twilight has arrived on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha,
one should indeed form the formal resolve for one month, beginning from the full moon of Śrāvaṇa.
"I shall perform my ablutions, remaining self-restrained and established in celibacy;
I shall eat only at night, sleep upon the ground, and practice compassion toward all living beings."
Having thus formed this resolve, whether a man or a woman, and having obtained permission from a Brāhmaṇa, one should then, in the forenoon, be equipped with all the necessary materials.
At the time of the ritual observance, a person, preceded by the cleansing of his teeth,
should take Tulasī and earth from a pond or a mountain stream.
O Pārtha, the observer of the vow should perform his bath with fragrant *āmalaka* fruits and sesame seeds;
thereafter, for eight days, he should bathe again and again with all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhī*).
One should perform these separately for eight days with barley and flour;
having bathed, meditated upon the Sun, and likewise offered libations to the twilight deities and the ancestors.
Having gratified [the deity], one should draw a cuckoo in the form of a bird using flour-paste;
one should worship Kalakaṃbā with auspicious flowers produced from the Campaka tree.
One should worship her with vessels, incense, food offerings, lamps, lac, and sandalwood; with sesame seeds, rice, and tips of dūrvā grass, one should then ask for her forgiveness.
O Pāṇḍava, one should always and constantly perform this with devotion using this mantra:
"O you who are fond of sesame, O you of variegated hue, grant me oil from sesame and happiness from sesame!"
"O Kokilā, grant me good fortune, wealth, and sons; salutations to you!
Having uttered this, he should then go home with self-restraint.
Having taken food, O Pārtha, one should sleep until the month is completed;
at the end of the month, however, one should [offer] a cuckoo made of sesame flour in a copper vessel.
One should present to a Brāhmaṇa a bird with jewel-like eyes and golden wings,
provided with garments, jewels, and molasses, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or alternatively, two earrings.
Those observing the vow, desiring auspiciousness, should bestow [the gift] upon the group of mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law, or upon an astrologer, or a domestic priest, or Vyāsa.
Thus, the woman who performs the Kokilā-vrata with devotion attains extensive good fortune throughout seven births.
Having obtained on this earth a worthy husband who is free from rivals and full of affection,
she dies and goes to the city of Gaurī by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
This vow was proclaimed of old by the sage Vasiṣṭha;
and it was likewise performed in its entirety, O Pārtha, by Kīrtimālā.
By her, through the word of Vasiṣṭha and by the grace of Śatrughna, all prosperity was obtained here, including the good fortune and honor of having a son.
In this way, O son of Kuntī, another woman who performs the Kokilā-vrata with devotion will certainly attain good fortune.
Those who offer to the twice-born a *kokilā* made of sesame paste mixed with ghee, its throat-plate resonant with sweet warbling—
having wandered at will through the Nandana and other celestial groves, they [attain their desires].
Having come into contact with mortals, they become sweet-toned.
Thus ends the Kokilā-vrata as described in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
In the Mahābhārata: "He who, being self-restrained, passes the month of Śrāvaṇa eating but one meal [per day]..."
In whatever [place], one who increases his kin is joined with consecration.
In the Viṣṇudharma:
Devoted to Viṣṇu, non-violent toward all beings, and taking refuge in Vāsudeva, one should pass the month of Śrāvaṇa by eating only a single meal a day.
One should mutter "Namo 'stu Vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times during the day;
one then obtains the complete fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating but one meal a day.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action may one always be devoted to dharma?"
O fortunate one, the reality of phenomena is the cause for making one's birth fruitful.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the full moon of Āṣāḍha has passed, one should worship the God who assumes a form of dharma, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) in the same manner as before.
By the phrase "as before," this includes the specific details not previously mentioned regarding the attainment of form and the observance of vows.
O King, at the end of the month, on the full moon day,
one should observe a three-night fast and give gold as a gift.
The supreme vow that brings about dharma and bestows all goals has been declared by you; there is no room for doubt in this matter.
Thus ends the vow for the attainment of dharma as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follow the vows of the month of Bhādrapada, according to the Mahābhārata.
But the man who eats only once a day during the month of Prauṣṭhapada attains abundant wealth, prosperity, and incomparable sovereignty. —
*Viṣṇudharma*.
He who observes a single meal in the month of Bhādrapada and maintains the Kṛṣṇa-vow,
being non-violent toward all beings and devoted solely to Vāsudeva;
One should mutter "Namo 'stu Vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times during the day;
one shall obtain ten times the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating but one meal a day.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action does a man become wealthy?"
A man who has sons becomes worthy of honor in the worlds of the gods.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the full moon of Śrāvaṇa has passed, one should worship the Lord Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Saṅkarṣaṇa, from the first day of the lunar fortnight onwards in due order, as previously described.
But it should be understood that this is improper due to the vow for the attainment of form:
"O King, with the petals of blue lotuses, with leaves of *bhṛṅgarāja*,
with ghee, with *paramānna*, and likewise with *bilva* fruits, O King."
O best of men, having fasted properly for three nights on the day of Proṣṭhapadī, a person should then give a cow to an eminent brahmin at the conclusion of the vow.
Having observed this vow for one month as prescribed by you,
a person shall dwell in heaven for a very long time after a month,
and upon returning to the human state, shall be endowed with wealth.
By the observance of his vow, that lion among kings—
Thus concludes the vow for the attainment of wealth as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Now follow the vows of the month of Āśvina.
Brahmā said:
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āśvayuja,
one should undertake the most excellent vow called Kaumuda, which yields great fruit.
Having become non-violent and pure, wearing washed garments and with senses subdued,
one should bathe on the twelfth lunar day and worship Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world.
Having anointed [the image] with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, agallochum, and saffron,
and with lotuses, water-lilies, white lilies, and fragrant red lotuses;
One should constantly worship Acyuta with fragrant jasmine flowers;
one should fill the vessel with ghee, but not fill it with oil.
One should offer a lamp with a long-lasting wick, auspiciously, both by day and by night;
one should present as an offering milk-rice, cakes, and sweetmeats.
Having offered [the gift] to Vāsudeva with devotion and having conquered his senses,
a man who has performed this vow, meditating upon Dharma, should ask for forgiveness.
A wise person should constantly recite: "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva."
One should feed Brahmins with devotion and give them sacrificial fees;
by this very procedure, one should observe the vow for one month.
O Lord, as long as the Garuḍa-bannered deity remains awake during the month of Kārttika,
this vow is of great merit and the destroyer of great sins.
The fruit of this is equal to, or even greater than, that of fasting for a month;
it is a merit that grants all desires and brings sons, health, and wealth.
Having performed this vow, a man shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the Kaumudī-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇu-rahasya.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action does a man attain freedom from disease?"
The beauty, fortune, and charm of the body are useless for one who possesses hair on the palms and soles.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the month of Proṣṭhapada has passed, one should worship Aniruddha during the daytime worship for the sake of the Yādava, beginning from the first day (pratipad) in due order.
According to the previously described procedure, this should continue until the month of Āśvayuja arrives.
With the previously mentioned [method] described in the *Rūpāvāptivrata*,

One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire and give clarified butter to the twice-born;

Then, having fasted properly for three nights on the full moon day of Āśvayuja,
a man [should give] a bell-metal vessel together with ghee and gold to a twice-born man.
A man should give [these], O tiger among kings, for the increase of his health;
this auspicious vow is prescribed as bestowing the heavenly world.
O hero among men, this supreme vow has been declared to you as not only a remover of disease, but also a bringer of obedience and the increase of beauty.
It brings about the attainment of one's desired wishes in the world of men.
Thus ends the Ārogyavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
In the Mahābhārata: likewise, he who passes the month of Āśvayuja by eating only one meal a day...
One is born possessed of servants, rich in vehicles, and having many sons.
As stated in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:

Non-violent toward all beings, he is devoted solely to Vāsudeva.
One should recite "Namo 'stu Vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times during the day;
thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus concludes the vow of eating but one meal a day. Now follow the vows of the month of Kārttika.

The month of Kārttika belongs to all the deities, and Agni is the mouth of all the gods; therefore, during the month of Kārttika, one should bathe outdoors and remain devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
"By eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya) at all times, one becomes purified from the sin committed during a year.
Thus is the rule for the Kārttika bath as stated in the Viṣṇu-smṛti.
Maitreya said:
Indeed, the month of Kārttika is great, for it is honored by all the gods;
for whatever hardships have been prescribed are indeed removers of all sins.
O lord of men, those rites performed by the sages involve offerings of ghee and honey poured out for the gods, the ancestors, and human beings.
There, food is declared to be inexhaustible by Brahmā, the creator of the world.
Having worshipped Hari with devotion and having offered a lamp day and night,
O King, a man whose soul is purified of all sins goes to heaven.
Thus ends the Kārttika-vrata as declared in the Vahnipurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard the words of Dāmodara, he (the king) posed a question.
O Blessed One, by what means is that great darkness destroyed?
"How could there be happiness in the world of the pretas equal to that of the celestial realm?
To that question, the Blessed One, the son of Devakī, gave this reply.
He spoke these supreme secrets that grant the fruit of one's heart's desires:
"O one of great intelligence, listen to the words I shall speak to you."
On the full moon day of the month of Āśvayuja, being composed in mind, Pūrṇa—
At the beginning of the first watch of the night, restrained in mind, speech, and body, [he should say]: "Salutation to Yama, to the ancestors, and to the deceased; salutation to Dharma and Viṣṇu;
salutation to Yama, to Rudra, and to the Lord of the Wilderness."
One endowed with faith should offer a lamp with this mantra;
for him who maintains it throughout the entire month of Kārttika, there shall be prosperity.
When the sun had reached the crest of the western mountain, a man [beheld] nearby his house an ancient piece of wood from a sacrificial tree,

Having made four [petals] with holes of one barley-corn in width at their centers, two cubits in length, and well-formed ribbons, they take the shape of an eight-petaled lotus.
By means of which one may follow the eight directions.
Just as a finger-measure is measured by barley-corns,
so too should a lamp of great brilliance be offered upon the pericarp, and likewise eight lamps placed upon the petals.
Excellent lamps with wicks and openings, provided with oil, ghee, and so forth, as available.
Then, a piece of cloth not yet worn,
either fresh and deep red or very white.
It is not clinging to the body and is not worn out;
it is auspicious, functional, wealthy, heart-pleasing, smooth, comfortable, perfectly even, and complete in every respect.
