It should be placed upon rice flour in such a way that it neither perishes nor shakes.
One should make everything three times the size of the central king of lamps; furthermore,
one should make it exceedingly rich in beauty upon the petals.
And for the attainment of one's desires.
Having subsequently attached eight bells adorned with hanging flower garlands and beautified by fine cloth to this ground, one should then smear it with cow dung.
[She was] anointed with water mixed with sandalwood paste.
Then, having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus of appropriate size within the mandala using various colors,
one should place fruits, roots, and likewise unbroken grains.
Then, having offered curd and milk, as well as food and drink, [he should recite: "jālā."
Having offered various kinds of special foods, along with beautiful dancing, singing, and sweet instrumental music,
upon the ground for Dharma and Hara;
And then also to Dāmodara, the King of Dharma.
Then [offerings] for the Prajāpatis, then for the true ancestors, then for those who have passed away, and then for those established in darkness—
from the southwest corner to the southern end.
From the [beings] beginning with the Dharmas and ending with the Pretas.
Then, having brought cool water mixed with ghee and honey— extremely pleasing to the heart—
and having filled eight jars with that water;
Then, having brought it from the southwest corner.
One should give a vessel made of gold or other materials filled with sesame seeds, along with a lid, and accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
as well as cows, land, gold, silver, and clothing.
Fruits, roots, barley, and grain.
A house, a chariot, a bed, a vehicle,
or whatever else is pleasing to the heart—
one should offer these to the most excellent of Brahmins.
Then, from those situated in the southwestern corner...
Then one should perform the gratification for each individual,
starting from Dharma and the others down to those near the city of the departed;
one should perform all of this according to the prescribed ritual.
Having first examined one's own power and one's own wealth.
Then, having bypassed all the lamps, they might even lead away all the foremost brahmins,
yet they would circumambulate the forest lady.
From that, one should become a practitioner of self-restraint who eats only at night.

One should perform this very practice every day at the arrival of night, treating the woman of the forest as a forest deity and the lamp-pillar as her physical form, engaging in such conventional behavior.
Having completed it with supreme devotion for the entire month, it is concluded on the full moon day of Kārttika.
One should offer either a great festival of lamps for three days, or else a single excellent lamp,
as well as throughout the entire month beginning with Āśvayuja.
Every day at the arrival of night, with devotion.
Having spoken thus for the sake of peace in his own home, "Homage be to the deities of the wilderness," the woman or the man, being well-restrained, [should proceed].
Then, at night, one should partake of food endowed with devotion.
Excellent lamps should be offered during the three junctions of the day, and at night on the full moon of Kārttika; likewise,
they should be given in the homes of the poor and in cow-pens.
In cremation grounds, temples, and shrines;
on riverbanks or within one's own home; or at a solitary linga, on a path, or beneath a single tree.
In this case, one thousand or a hundred [measures] of oil, exceeding by eight, should be placed in a very beautiful vessel.
Those [lines] which are half of that, or even half of those again,
having been measured out, should be emptied and then filled;
and one's own hands are exactly fourteen.
Then, having prepared a wick from cloth and thread.
The wise one, having restrained it, should kindle that [lamp] after honoring it with hundreds of women's ornaments;
the goddess is like a great wick upon a river.
And this day is meritorious, illuminating the world.
If a fool does not do this,
how can there ever be an end to that darkness?
For this lamp is indeed like the wish-fulfilling tree.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the auspicious jar, and then the flute.
"There is no doubt that by means of this lamp, one's heart's desires will be attained.
Having spoken these few words, [768] he—
And Dāmodara became hidden.
Thus ends the procedure for the lamp as taught in the *Ādipurāṇa*.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action may one attain victory everywhere?"
O best of the twice-born, he delights in worldly affairs, gambling, and dispute.
O best of beings, there is no happiness in the worlds greater than the attainment of victory;
since the attainment of victory is the supreme happiness, let that vow also be described.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the month of Āśvayuja has passed, one should worship the Lord Trivikrama, the protector of the worlds, from the first day (pratipad) onwards in sequence, as previously described.
"As before" means as in the case of the vow for obtaining form (*rūpāvāpti-vrata*).
At the end of three nights, on the full moon day of Kārttika, one should give the supreme food-offering,
having made [the image] hold all kinds of grain and adorned it with jewels according to one's ability.
O hero among men, having observed this vow for a month as prescribed, one attains that world for a very long time;
having dwelt there for a very long duration, that person—
One attains victory everywhere throughout the three worlds.
Thus ends the vow for attaining victory as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Brahmā said:
"In the most meritorious month of Kārttika, which is honored by gods, sages, and ancestors..."
When a vow is being observed by men, even if it is very slight, there shall be a great fruit.
The entire year is meritorious; therefore, it is especially honored during the rainy season.
Of the rainy season, the month of Kārttika is meritorious, and within Kārttika, the Bhīṣmapañcaka is most meritorious.
By offering a single month of Kārttika to Viṣṇu with food offerings, flowers, incense, worship, and excellent unguents, one obtains the fruit equivalent to a year’s worth of devotion.
Therefore, having reached the month of Kārttika, those who always desire auspiciousness should perform,
according to their capacity, this easily achievable vow dedicated to Hari.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, a man who subsists on air alone,
having fasted with devotion, should worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
The fast must be observed while standing in the midst of water;
by performing this *jalakṛcchra*, a man shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
On the tenth day, one should consume the five products of the cow; on the eleventh day, having fasted, one should worship the god Acyuta and observe the vow with self-restraint.
Having observed the Devavrata vow during the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika,
a man who worships Dāmodara shall become a dweller of celestial chariots.
Having drunk water, milk, curd, and ghee on the four days beginning with the seventh [tithi] of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, one should fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
Performing the penance known as Kṛcchrapaitāmaha, one should worship Hari;
he attains the supreme abode of Viṣṇu, which is honored throughout the three worlds,
by drinking only milk for three nights while remaining devoted to fasting.
In the bright fortnight of Kārttika, beginning from the sixth day, the Māhendra-kṛcchra is prescribed;
having worshipped Dāmodara, one should perform the Māhendra-kṛcchra.
O Lord, he goes to the supreme world of Viṣṇu, which is difficult to attain;
thereafter, he should eat the food of sages for three days, and then barley-gruel for three days.
*Munyanna* is food consisting of wild grains; *nīvāra* is wild rice.
One should fast for three days at the end; this is remembered as the Vaiṣṇava *kṛcchra*.
Beginning from the third day of the month of Kārttika, one should worship the imperishable Viṣṇu.
In the bright fortnight, a person goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
Having drunk milk for five nights starting from the first day of the lunar fortnight in succession,
one should subsist on curd for five days and fast on the eleventh day.
Performing this during the bright fortnight of Kārttika, a person should worship the one whose banner is Garuḍa;
having performed this rite called Bhāskara, he shall go to Śvetadvīpa.
One should partake of gruel, barley-meal, vegetables, curd, milk, ghee,
and water during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika, beginning from the fifth lunar day.
Performing this Kṛcchra penance bestowed by the Seven Sages, one who is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu attains the realm of Viṣṇu, which is free from rebirth.
One should drink well-boiled milk with leaves of *palāśa*, *bilva*, *kuśa*, *padma*, and *udumbara*; on the sixth day, one should fast for the entire day.
For by performing the supreme Āgneya-kṛcchra penance during the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
and worshipping Janārdana with devotion, one attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Having partaken of milk, bilva fruits, lotuses, and mouthfuls of lotus stalks on the seventh day and the following days, a man should observe a fast on the eleventh day.
This vow, which bestows prosperity, should be observed during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika;
by worshipping Keśava, one shall attain the state of Vaiṣṇava.
All these difficult penances remove all sins;
they should be performed by men with devotion, especially during the month of Kārttika.
Whether a householder, a forest-dweller, one seeking liberation, or a mendicant,
by performing this vow, one attains the imperishable state of Viṣṇu.
Performing all the *kṛcchra* penances, with speech and mind controlled and the senses restrained,
wearing washed garments and having bathed with purity, one should worship the imperishable Lord.
Non-violent, devoted to giving, and dedicated to recitation and fire-offerings,
one should worship Viṣṇu, the granter of boons, and perform penances.
The observer of the vow should always eat all the substances for the vow, such as milk and the like, when they are offered by a Brahmin;
he should eat them according to his desire, but not to his heart's content.
Regarding those objects indeed said to belong to others,
the most meritorious gift among them is that which one gives to the best of the twice-born while being afflicted by hardships,
distressed by pain, or bewildered by hunger.
One should cause the afflicted man to drink the nectar that is the milk of cows.
These eight do not destroy a vow: water, roots, fruits, milk, sacrificial oblation, the desire of a Brahmin, the word of a teacher, and medicine.
One should perform the *kṛcchra* penances according to the prescribed method;
having worshipped Kṛṣṇa in the month of Kārttika, one goes to where Janārdana dwells.
Thus, by various names, they are eternally partakers of the fruit of liberation;
through vows, fasts, and observances, they are partakers of the fruit of liberation.
Thus end the *kṛcchra* vows as declared in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.
[772] Māndhātṛ said:
O Sage, having reached the month of Kārttika, King Rukmāṅgada—
Tell me, how did he enjoy the enchanting woman who was possessed by delusion?
Devoted to the praise of Viṣṇu, he was the most eminent among kings;
what did that monarch do during that month, the most meritorious of all, on that particular day?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reached the month of Kārttika, which marks the awakening of Hari,
even that king, though utterly bewildered, spoke these words to Mohinī.
O Goddess, for many years together with you,
out of fear of your disapproval, I have never once released you.
"Now, O fair-faced one, listen to this as I desire to observe a vow:
O Goddess, many Kārttikas have passed while my mind has been attached to you."
No one born in the month of Kārttika has ever observed a vow, with the single exception of the day of Hari;
therefore, I desire to traverse this month of Kārttika by means of a religious observance.
O daughter of the Lotus-born, for those mortals who have passed the month of Kārttika without observing vows, their sacrifices, charitable works, and religious merit are all in vain.
For those kings who were meat-eaters and excessively devoted to hunting,
having abandoned meat during the month of Kārttika, went to the auspicious abode of Viṣṇu.
For those who have been eating [forbidden] foods, if a restraint is observed during the month of Kārttika,
they will necessarily attain the nature of Viṣṇu, which is the means to liberation.
By giving lamps, which bring delight to the heart, one shall go to heaven;
in the absence of even that, O fortunate one, there is the lighting of another's lamp.
One who desires prosperity should always perform this, since it is superior to all other gifts:
on one side are all other gifts, and on the other side is the gift of a lamp.
In Kārttika, nothing is said to be equal to the lamp; indeed, it is remembered as superior.
Having performed the Kārttikī rite in Kārttika, [one honors] the lamp born from the navel of Viṣṇu.
One is liberated from sins committed since birth; of this there is no doubt, for him whose month of Kārttika passes with vows, fasts, and observances.
Having become a celestial deity dwelling in a divine mansion, he goes to the supreme state;
therefore, O deluder, abandon your delusion toward me.
O lotus-eyed one, may you be devoted to the worship of the Mountain-Dweller (Śiva),
and I, too, shall be a bearer of vows in the worship of Hari.
Mohinī said:
O best of kings, tell me in detail the greatness of the month of Kārttika;
for this month has been declared to be superior to all merit.
Having heard the greatness of the month of Kārttika— [which is] proclaimed specifically at Puṣkara and at Saukara in Dvārāvatī— I shall perform whatever I desire.
Rukmāṅgada said:
O fair-faced one, I shall proclaim the majesty of this month,
by which devotion arises in you, and through which devotion Hari is worshipped.

O fair-complexioned lady, he who practices the *kṛcchra* penance during the month of Kārttika— whether for six days, twelve days, a fortnight, or a month— even if he is devoted to his wife and children.
Having exhausted [the results of his karma], that man goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu—
whether by eating once a day, or by eating only at night, or likewise, O fair-browed one, by eating only what is unasked for.
By performing a circle of lamps, men indeed attain the earth;
on that day of Hari, there is merit equal to that of the Bhīṣmapañcaka.
Having performed the Prabodhinī rite accompanied by a vigil,
even a man burdened with sins does not enter his mother’s womb again.
O beautiful lady, whoever beholds the mandala on that day attains the supreme state, even without the practice of Sāṃkhya or Yoga.
Having seen the Maṇḍala in Kārttika, and having seen the auspicious Śūkara at Saukara,
and indeed having seen Kokavarāha, one shall never again be a suckling infant.
But having seen the threefold liberation from sin for men at Mandāra,
O fickle-limbed one, and likewise at Kubjaka and Śrīdhara;
In the month of Kārttika, one should avoid oil; in Kārttika, one should avoid honey;
in Kārttika, one should avoid bell-metal; and in the month of Kārttika, one should avoid fermented liquids.
Oil is a preparation involving black mustard and other such ingredients.
O Goddess, if one devoted to Viṣṇu eats flat beans (*niṣpāva*) in the month of Kārttika,
he suffers the immediate loss of the merit accumulated over a year.
That person of evil intellect who eats pork in the month of Kārttika, due to that single act of consumption, attains birth in the womb of a king.
For sixty thousand years he is cooked in the Raurava hell;
once released from there, that sinner is born as a village pig that eats excrement.
One should not eat the flesh of fish, nor that of tortoises, nor indeed any other;
O King, by eating meat in the month of Kārttika, one is born as a Caṇḍāla.
The month of Kārttika destroys all sins for one who observes even a small vow;
that righteous person who passes it in this way need not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
Initiation performed in the month of Kārttika cuts through the cycle of human rebirth;
therefore, one should undertake initiation with every effort during Kārttika.
O lady with beautiful thighs, everything performed by one who is uninitiated is fruitless;
such a person enters the womb of an animal, whereas through initiation one attains birth in a noble family.
One should not perform the Kārttikī rite at home, especially the Kārttikī;
O beautiful lady, one should perform the Kārttikī at sacred fords with every possible effort.
Having observed the Ekādaśī of the bright fortnight of Kārttika, a man who gives auspicious water-pots in the morning goes to the abode of Hari.
For the completion of the year-long vows is traditionally held to occur in the month of Kārttika,
when five days remain of the period following Viṣṇu’s birth from the navel-lotus.
O lady of excellent complexion,
even when the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa) is lacking, there is auspicious purity for four days, provided that the ascendant is avoided.

"Since in you are seen these relationships that increase with sons and grandsons, therefore, O enchanting one, for the destruction of all my sins and for the increase of my love for you, I shall perform the Kārttika vow."
Thus ends the vow for the month of Kārttika as spoken by Nārada.
Brahmā said:
"That man who, devoted to the Goddess, subsists on milk during the month of Kārttika..."
One who cooks vegetables, eats only at night, bathes in the morning, and is devoted to Śiva.
One should perform worship with sesame oblations using honey, milk, ghee, and so forth;
this should be done with the mantra of the Goddess. Listen now, O Hari, to the meritorious fruit thereof.
One who is joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) or even joined with minor offenses (upapātaka) is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter, because Śivā is omnipresent.
Or another, endowed with meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), [is liberated] by this rite through Śivā.
One should worship it oneself, or have it worshipped by another.
No disease shall befall him, nor fear caused by enemies;
neither portents nor domestic calamities shall arise, nor shall his kingdom perish.
The seasons, endowed with their great inherent nature, bestow auspiciousness; there is the full ripening of all crops, and no thieves appear.
The cows yield abundant milk; the Brahmins are devoted to performing sacred rites;
all the women are faithful to their husbands; and the kings have subdued their enemies.
Through the ritual worship of Caṇḍikā, the goddess Earth becomes possessed of fruits and flowers and abounding in trees; of this there is no doubt in one's home.
O Jayantī, Maṅgalā, Kālī, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Durgā,
Kṣamā, Śivā, Dhātrī, Svadhā, Svāhā— homage be to you!
With this very mantra, one should perform recitation and fire-offerings;
O child, when properly remembered in the morning and duly worshipped, she is the slayer of the buffalo-demon.
"It quickly destroys evil, just as the rising sun destroys darkness.
Thus ends the Devī-vrata as declared in the Devī-purāṇa.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, I desire to hear the procedure for the month-long fast, which is the highest among vows, as well as its fruit as it has been declared.
In what manner the practice of the vow should be performed by men, how it may come to be,
how it should be commenced as before, and how it must indeed be completed according to the prescribed rule.
"O Grandfather, tell me how many times this must be performed; O sinless one, best among the gods, explain this vow to me in detail."
Brahmā said:
"Excellent, Nārada! Since you have asked this, O ascetic, wander as you wish;
listen, for I shall tell it to you, O best among the wise."
Just as Viṣṇu is among the gods, as the Sun is among the luminaries,
as Meru is among the peaked mountains, and as Vainateya is among the birds;
Just as the Gaṅgā is among sacred fords, and just as the merchant is among people,
so too is the month-long fast the most excellent among all vows.
One who observes the month-long fast shall obtain whatever merit exists in all vows, whatever fruit exists in all sacred fords, or whatever arises from all acts of giving.
One does not attain that merit through sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, performed according to rule with abundant sacrificial fees, which one attains by fasting for a month.
Whatever gift is given, oblation offered, mantra recited, bath performed,
or ancestral libation (svadhā) made by that man who observes the month-long fast according to the prescribed rule, [all becomes infinitely multiplied].
Having entered the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice and worshipped Janārdana with that,
and then having obtained the permission of his guru, he should perform the month-long fast.
Having performed all the Vaiṣṇava vows as prescribed,
such as those on the twelfth lunar day and others that bring merit, one should then observe the month-long fast.
Having performed the *atikṛcchra* and the *parāka*,
one should then perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* and the month-long fast, having ascertained the strength and weakness of one's body.
O Sage, whether he be a forest-dweller, an ascetic, or even a widow,
she should then perform the month-long fast with the permission of her guru and the Brahmins.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āśvina,
one should undertake this vow for a duration of thirty days.
That man who, dedicating it to Vāsudeva, fasts throughout the entire month of Kārttika, shall partake in the fruit of liberation.
With devotion, at the abode of Acyuta, one should worship three times a day with auspicious flowers—
mālatī, blue lotuses, and fragrant white and red lotuses.
Having anointed [the image] with saffron, ushira, camphor, and excellent sandalwood,
one should worship Janārdana with offerings of food, incense, lamps, and so forth.
With mind, action, and speech, a man whose senses are conquered by great devotion should worship the one who has Garuḍa as his banner and perform the three daily ablutions.
One should engage in such recitation of Viṣṇu’s names day and night;
with devotion, one should utter the praise of Viṣṇu and avoid false speech.
Endowed with compassion for all beings, peaceful in conduct, and non-violent—
whether asleep or established in his latent impressions— he should glorify Vāsudeva.
One should avoid recollecting, looking at, smelling, tasting, or praising [the food], as well as all longing for morsels of food.
One observing a vow should avoid anointing the limbs, anointing the head, betel-leaf, and fine unguents; indeed, he should avoid everything else that is prohibited elsewhere.
One established in a vow should not covet anything, nor should one disturb those engaged in improper acts;
one should remain in a temple, for a householder should not practice a vow.
Having observed a month-long fast, with his self composed and his senses conquered,
he should then worship the Meritorious One who has Garuda as his banner on the twelfth lunar day.
A person should worship with flower garlands, perfumes, incense, and ointments;
and with garments, ornaments, and musical instruments, he should satisfy Acyuta.
One should devoutly bathe Hari with water from sacred bathing sites mixed with sandalwood paste;
his limbs should be anointed with sandalwood and adorned with flowers and incense.
One should feed the best of the twice-born with gifts of clothing and other such items,
give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), prostrate before them, and ask for their forgiveness.
Having asked the Brahmins for forgiveness, and having honored and worshipped them, one should dismiss them in this manner,
according to one's means and with devotion, to the best of one's ability.
Having thus observed the month-long fast, having worshipped Janārdana,
and having fed the twice-born, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having thus correctly performed thirteen month-long fasts, one should then cause them to be concluded according to this rite; listen to that.
Having fasted on the eleventh day, one should indeed perform a Vaiṣṇava sacrifice,
or worship Hari, the Lord of Gods, with the permission of the preceptor.
Having worshipped Hari with devotion and likewise having saluted his guru,
he should then feed the Brahmins and cause them to eat according to the prescribed rule.
Having properly honored thirteen twice-born men of pure lineage and conduct who are devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, and having fed them well;
There were as many pairs of garments, vessels, and seats,
as well as pure meditation-bands and sacred threads.
And having honored and bowed down to the foremost of the twice-born, he should give [the gift],
and thereafter he should prepare a bed furnished with excellent coverings.
Having had a golden image of himself made according to his means— excellent, well-covered, provided with a pillow, and adorned—
Having worshipped that bed with garlands and other offerings,
one should place upon it a seat, two sandals, an umbrella, a pair of garments, and shoes.
One should also arrange purifying flowers upon the bed;
having thus prepared the bed and prostrated before those twice-born ones, one should proceed.
And for the sake of approval, he should pray: "I am going to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus honored, the Brahmins should always say to the observer of the vow:
Go, go, O best of men, to the healthy abode of Viṣṇu—
the divine Vaiṣṇava celestial chariot, prepared with a couch.
By that [merit], go to the abode of Viṣṇu, which is eternally blissful and free from ailment;
then, having prostrated and followed them, one should dismiss the brahmins.
Then, with devotion, one should worship the guru who bestows knowledge,
as well as that prepared bed upon which the guru has completed the vow.
Having bowed with his head, the peaceful one should present [the offering] to the Guru;
thus, O Brahmins, having worshipped Hari, the Brahmins, and the Guru who illuminates knowledge.
Having observed month-long fasts, a man shall enter the body of Viṣṇu;
likewise, one who has completed month-long fasts and is devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu [attains the same].
And if, O Sage, one who abides in the Dharma has conquered his senses and, having performed month-long fasts, passes away with a tranquil mind according to the prescribed rites;
Having uplifted a hundred lineages, that man shall go to the world of Viṣṇu,
having performed the month-long fast in a family of great merit born therein.
Freed from all sins, that man who performs month-long fasts becomes a man among the meritorious and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Together with both her father’s and mother’s families, she shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
or even a woman of great fortune, established in the vow as prescribed,
having performed month-long fasts, shall go to the eternal Viṣṇu.
Nārada said:
O Lord, this vow known as the month-long fast is extremely difficult for men to perform; it causes fainting and exhaustion, yet it generates devotion toward Acyuta.
O Lord, O Grandfather, what indeed should be done— either abandonment or favor— toward one who is thus severely afflicted, desiring death, and observing a vow?
Brahmā said:
O ascetic, having seen one who is observing a vow or one who is about to die,
a Brāhmaṇa, upon seeing him, should properly bestow his grace.
One who desires it should drink nectar-like milk once at night,
so that the observer of the vow, though afflicted by hunger, may not be deprived of life in this world.
One should protect a patient who is afflicted by fainting, emaciated, on the verge of death, and tormented by hunger,
by having him drink milk and giving him fruits.
And he who constantly protects one established in the vow throughout day and night,
having offered milk, roots, and fruits, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, when one who has undertaken a month-long fast finds himself in a life-threatening danger,
he should seek to preserve his life through two types of qualities that do not violate his vow, by the command of a Brāhmaṇa.
Milk, medicinal herbs, water, roots, and fruits [should be offered] according to the command of the Guru.
Having done this, he should then consume milk-rice with jaggery;
for, being thus protected, he may drink it and thereby regain his vow.
Now, Viṣṇu is the vow, Viṣṇu is the giver, and likewise Viṣṇu is the one who observes the vow;
having realized that everything is composed of Viṣṇu, one should uplift the one established in the vow who has become exhausted.
Just as one who is about to die is motionless, utterly exhausted, and deeply unconscious,
so too should one rescue a person who is wasted away, desiring [liberation], yet standing with his face turned away.
Having protected his body while observing the vow, the practitioner should complete the remainder of the vow;
as declared from the mouths of Brahmins, his fruit shall be as previously stated, but doubled.
A mind that is always unstained by the objects of the senses and remains pure pleases Viṣṇu; fasting does not [please Him] for those who have not conquered their selves.
What need has he for many sacred fords, baths, fire-oblations, recitations, and vows,
by whom the terrible host of the senses has been conquered with a joyful heart?
One who has conquered the senses, who is ever tranquil, who is devoted to the welfare of all beings,
and who is constantly intent upon Vāsudeva, does not deserve to suffer affliction.
Having performed the Vaiṣṇava vow dedicated to Puruṣottama as prescribed,
one attains the world of Viṣṇu, from which a return is difficult to find.
Those who always remember Viṣṇu with a pure inner self go to the stainless world of Viṣṇu, having cast off all fear.
Those who recite the praises of Acyuta at dawn, at midnight, at midday, and at the close of day, cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
Whether joyful, afflicted by sorrow, angry, or peaceful,
whoever indeed glorifies Hari with devotion shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
A person who constantly remembers Vāsudeva is never afflicted by the bonds of saṃsāra— the sufferings of conception, birth, old age, and disease.
He who perceives Viṣṇu everywhere— in stationary and moving beings, in the gross and the subtle, and in the auspicious and the inauspicious— that person is Viṣṇu himself.
Having realized that the entire three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, are pervaded by Viṣṇu—
he whose mind is tranquil has thereby worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa.
Through the *atikalpa* and *anukalpa* methods, as well as by means of the highest vows,
one attains the world of Viṣṇu through the grace of the Wielder of the Discus.
O best of the twice-born, the rule for the month-long fast has been duly proclaimed out of affection for your son and for the welfare of all the world.
Having performed [this] and having heard it with devotion, one shall thereafter go to the city of Viṣṇu;
it must not be given to one who lacks devotion, nor should it be given to one of wicked mind.
Thus ends the vow of fasting for a month as declared in the *Viṣṇurahasya*.
In the *Mahābhārata*: "The man who observes eating only once a day during the month of Kārttika..."
He is born brave, highly fortunate, and indeed possessed of fame.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "The man who, devoted to Viṣṇu, eats [only once] on a certain Ekādaśī day in Kārttika,
is born brave, learned, and possessed of many sons."
Non-violent toward all beings and devoted solely to Vāsudeva,
one should recite "Obeisance to Vāsudeva" eight hundred times during the day;
thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus concludes the vow of eating a single meal a day. Now follow the vows of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, as described in the Mahābhārata.
He who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa by eating but one meal a day and feeds the twice-born with devotion is liberated from diseases and sins.
Having observed the fast, one is born endowed with all that is auspicious, free from all suffering, devoid of disease, and possessed of vigor;
one becomes a sharer in the fruits of agriculture, possessing great wealth and abundant grain.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "He who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa by eating but one meal a day,
while performing service to Viṣṇu, is born in an auspicious land."
Non-violent toward all beings and devoted solely to Vāsudeva,
one should mutter eight hundred times during the day the mantra "Obeisance to Vāsudeva.
Thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating a single meal a day.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action does a man obtain beauty?"
To me, form devoid of beauty appears fruitless.

Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the full moon day of Kārttika has passed, one should worship the Lord Pradyumna, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) in due order, either upon a cloth painting or in a physical image.

Then one should perform an external bath; at night, being restrained in speech, one should eat a single meal, O Great King, always consisting of sacrificial food (haviṣya) while remaining self-controlled.
Then, having reached the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, being pure and having fasted for three nights,
one should worship the god Pradyumna and offer clarified butter into the fire.
One should feed the Brahmins here a meal rich in salt;
then, one *prastha* of powdered salt should be given to the twice-born.
O King, one should likewise give to the preceptor a pair of garments dyed with great silver-red lac,
as well as gold and a bronze vessel.
O Yādava, this supreme vow, which bestows beauty and grants access to the celestial realm within a month, fulfills not only all desires, but [all else as well].
One should give the Puruṣapradhāna to a man.
Thus ends the vow for attaining beauty as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
[786] Now follow the vows of the month of Pauṣa.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O son of Kuntī, he who passes the month of Pauṣa with a single meal becomes fortunate,
handsome, and a partaker of glory."
*Viṣṇudharma*:
O Dālbhya, that man who passes the month of Pauṣa by eating only one meal a day,
being intent on serving Śauri, becomes free from disease.
Non-violent toward all beings and devoted solely to Vāsudeva,
one should recite "Obeisance to Vāsudeva" eight hundred times during the day;
thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating a single meal a day.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action does a man become possessed of virtuous conduct?"
But among noble birth, lineage, and learning, virtuous conduct alone is preeminent.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: After the month of Āgrahāyaṇī has passed, for one month, day by day,
he should worship the unconquered Lord Varāha as before.
One should bathe the deity with ghee, offer oblations to Hari with ghee,
give ghee to the twice-born, and indeed present ghee as an offering.
Having fasted for three nights on the full moon day of Pauṣa, O lord of men, one should honor a twice-born man with a vessel of ghee and gold according to one's ability.
Having observed this vow for a month as prescribed, a person reaches heaven and remains there for a very long time;
and having returned to the human state, he shall be endowed with virtuous conduct.
One attains nourishment and long life.

Thus ends the vow for attaining virtuous conduct as declared in the Viṣṇudharma. Now, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Pauṣa, one who is composed should undertake the Cāndrāyaṇa vow for a month, which conquers all sins.
On the full moon day of the month of Pūrṇimā, however, one should worship [him] daily with water offerings.

The locative case in "Pauṣe" is used in the sense of proximity; this is because the fourteenth and fifteenth days belong to the preceding month. One should always satisfy Agni with these three [mantras]: "To Manoratha, svāhā!", likewise "sante payāṃsi," and "agnir etābhiḥ."
And having offered eight oblations of food to the Moon with these four supreme mantras beginning with "yad devād deva."
One should satisfy the arm with clarified butter for the pacification of all sins;
likewise, one should always perform this with sacrificial fuel-sticks while reciting the mantra beginning with "devakṛtasya."
Rice-porridge, alms-food, as well as barley-meal, buttermilk, and barley-gruel;
vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, fruits, roots, and water.
The meaning is that, beginning on the full moon day, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the fire-oblation (homa) every day;
thereafter, one should respectfully consume the food remaining from the oblation.
One should eat morsels of food the size of hen's eggs on the full moon day,
and having first taken fifteen, one should then reduce them by one each day.
By which [count], when combined with twenty, there shall be one hundred in the dark fortnight;
on that very day of the new moon, the Brahmin should then observe a fast.
Starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, according to the sequence of the moon's increase,
there shall again be one hundred and twenty morsels.
Within a month, two hundred and twenty [verses] may be mastered;
for one, the *praṇava* shall be the mantra, and it shall also be the mantra for both.
*Bhuvaḥ* belongs to three [worlds], *svaḥ* also to four, and *mahaḥ* likewise;
furthermore, *janaḥ* is declared to belong to five or six.
For seven [deities], austerity and truth are proclaimed; for eight, the syllable *oṃ*;
for nine, the sacrificial fuel (*iṣā*); and for ten, the mantra itself.
"Yoke the eleven; be victorious, and you shall become supreme. Beyond the thirteen is the Puruṣa; from that, Dharma is proclaimed."

Śiva is said to be the mantra for the fifteen morsels. Having consecrated each morsel individually with mantras joined by the utterances *svāhā* and *namas*, one should consume the morsels according to the sequence of the days.
The mantras begin with "Oṃ namaḥ svāhā" and "Bhūr namaḥ svāhā," and so forth.
Upon the completion of the vow, one should give a cow and a bull to a twice-born man;
by a single Cāndrāyaṇa penance, the destruction of all sins occurs.
Having performed this for one year, one shall attain the world of the Moon;
in this world, one obtains wealth, health, happiness, and the perfection of good fortune.
One would attain a place in the world of the immortals and in the abode of Śakra;
through that practice, there would be auspiciousness and birth in a brahmin family.
Thus ends the Cāndrāyaṇa vow as described in the Brahmapurāṇa. Now follow the vows for the month of Māgha,
according to the Nāradīya Purāṇa.
Kāṣṭhakīla said:
This month of Māgha has arrived, which is dear to those who practice austerities;
in this month, sins always cry out against those who perform ritual ablutions for sacrifice.
Even those acts committed against all bodies that are equal to the murder of a Brahmin [are purified];
for the month of Māgha, which bestows many gifts, is indeed difficult to encounter.
In the month of Māgha, the gods always infuse splendor into the water;
therefore, O fair-faced one, whether one has bathed or not, one should never resort to fire.
One should attend to the fire for the sake of the fire-sacrifice, never for the sake of warding off cold;
O lady of noble limbs, it is traditionally held that [the fire] lasts as long as its radiance remains after sunrise.
In the absence of river water and the like,
they know that water kept in a new jar and struck by the wind at night is equal to the water of the Gaṅgā.
There is no sin in the world that is not destroyed by bathing;
O fair-faced one, the Māgha bath is superior even to entering the fire.
[790] While living, one experiences suffering; once dead, one does not see suffering.
For this reason, O fair-browed one, the Māgha bath is preeminent.
Every day, sesame seeds mixed with sugar should be given;
indeed, three parts should be sesame seeds, while the fourth part is mixed with sugar.
O lady of beautiful hips, the observer of the vow shall spend the entire month without anointing his body, [thinking]:
"May the god Sūrya, the stainless embodiment of Viṣṇu, be pleased with me."
At the conclusion of the month of Māgha, O fortunate one, he should cause to be given food of six flavors,
as well as two white garments for the couple, together with the seven types of grain.
Thirty auspicious sweetmeats made of sesame should be offered; they should be finely prepared with black pepper, and one should also cause oranges to be given.
For you are the source of rivers, my supreme abode within the water;
by your splendor, may my sin be shattered into a thousand pieces.
O Divākara, Lord of the World, Maker of Light, homage be to you!
O Lord of the Dawn, may you cause this Māgha bath to be perfectly fulfilled here.
In this way, the boat of Māgha proceeds, having pierced the orb of the sun;
likewise the wandering mendicant engaged in yoga, or one slain facing the enemy in battle—
the third here, O lady of excellent limbs, is proclaimed as one who has performed the Māgha bath.
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
Yudhiṣṭhira said,
"O scion of the Yadu lineage, tell me about my ritual bath in the month of Māgha."
By which they cross over the ocean of existence from the flood of the mire and waters of suffering.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
The Kṛta Yuga is declared to belong to the Brāhmaṇas; Tretā is remembered as belonging to the Kṣatriyas;
they say Dvāpara belongs to the Vaiśyas, and likewise Kali Yuga to the Śūdras.
O King, although there is laxity among men regarding the act of bathing in the Kali age, nevertheless, I shall speak under the pretext of Māgha; listen to that.
He whose hands, feet, speech, and mind are well-restrained,
and who possesses knowledge, austerity, and renown, enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
One who lacks faith, one whose soul is evil, an atheist, one whose doubts are not severed,
and one who delights in reviling the reasons [for dharma]— these do not partake in the fruit of the sacred fords.
Having reached Prayāga, Puṣkara, or even Kurukṣetra—or wherever else one may be—one should bathe during the month of Māgha; such is the established rule.
Rivers that do not flow to the ocean yield their fruit after three nights;
those that flow to the ocean, however, yield it after a fortnight, and the lord of rivers (the ocean) yields it after a month.
Bathing near water at twilight when the sun has risen is equal to the Prājāpatya penance; it destroys even the most heinous sins.
The Brahmin who, having risen early in the morning, always performs his morning ablutions,
is liberated from all sins and attains the Supreme Brahman.
Bathing in hot water is in vain; reciting non-Vedic prayers is in vain;
a Śrāddha performed for one who is not learned in the Vedas is in vain; and a meal eaten without witnesses is in vain.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who know the rules of bathing have declared that there are four kinds of baths;
listen now to each one separately: the Vāyavya, the Vāruṇa, the Brāhmya, and the Divya.

The Vāyavya bath consists of dust from a cow; the Vāruṇa bath is performed with the waters of the ocean and other such bodies; the Brāhmya bath is that prescribed by the mantras of the Brahmins; and the Divya bath is the water of wisdom obtained from the sun.
Among all types of ablutions, that of Varuṇa is said to be the most excellent;
whether one is a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant.
All these—children, the elderly, and the young; men, women, and eunuchs—always praise immersion in the waters during the month of Māgha.
Having bathed in the auspicious Māgha month at a sacred ford, one obtains the desired fruit;
for the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, bathing accompanied by mantras is prescribed.
For Śūdras, O joy of the Kurus, it should likewise be performed in silence, or by means of a salutation; this brings about the destruction of the entire mass of their sins.
In the month of Māgha, when the sun has slightly risen, the waters cry out:
"Whom among us shall we purify as he falls—whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin or a drinker of liquor?"
Where the palaces are made of gold and the women are equal to the Apsarases;
where the rivers flow with curd and milk, and whose mud is made of milk-rice.
There they go and sink who [bathe] at sunrise during the month of Māgha;
one should walk on the path like an ascetic, observing silence and avoiding backbiting.
He who desires vast enjoyments comparable to the moon, the sun,
and the planets should bathe in the morning during the interval between the Puṣya and Phālguna constellations.
One should perform ritual bathing beginning from the full moon or the new moon;
these thirty days are meritorious while the sun resides in Capricorn.
Then, having risen, he should take up the vow according to the prescribed rite:
"O God Mādhava, during this meritorious month of Māgha, I shall perform my ritual bath."
Having formed the mental resolve, "I shall always bathe in a sacred ford with cool water," he who performs the actual bath with his body uncovered;
At every step, a person obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Then, having bathed in that auspicious tīrtha and having applied clay to his head,
O King, he should offer the arghya to the Sun according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
Having satiated the ancestors while remaining there, and then descending from that water,
one should bow to one's chosen deity and worship Puruṣottama.
One should worship the god named Mādhava, who bears the conch and the discus;
having offered oblations into the fire according to the prescribed rite, one should thereafter eat but a single meal.
One who is capable should perform bathing while observing the practice of sleeping on the ground and celibacy;
for one who is incapable of such practices as celibacy, his own preference is prescribed.
"The Māgha bath must certainly be performed"—such is the sacred revelation (śruti).
According to the Lord's will, dharma follows after strength.
One who bathes with sesame, one who rubs himself with sesame, one who performs oblations with sesame, one who offers water with sesame,
one who eats sesame, and one who gives sesame— these six types of "sesame-people" are destroyers of sin.
Oil and *āmalaka* fruits should always be offered at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*);
likewise, one should kindle a fire and have a windless hut constructed.
Thus, during the month of Mādhava, one who is capable should provide unrestricted food;
or else, according to one's ability, one should do so while remaining free from stinginess regarding wealth.
The couples of the foremost brahmins should be honored with garments and ornaments,
and various gifts should be bestowed upon them.
Blankets, skins, and garments, as well as various jewels according to one's ability,
should be given, along with bodices and covering cloths.
Sandals for the protection of the feet, and slippers that release one from sin;
likewise, whatever else is dear should be given during the Māgha bath.
That should be given to Brahmins who have performed the Māgha bath by one desiring prosperity. [794]
Even when the gift is very small, one should say, "O Mādhava, may you be pleased."
By performing the ritual bath, one is liberated from the sins of approaching those who should not be approached, from theft, from accepting gifts from the wicked, and from sins committed in secret.
Having performed the rites according to the prescribed rule in the month of Māgha while fixing his mind on Mādhava,
he shall rescue his ancestors on the father’s side and then his ancestors on the mother’s side;
together with twenty-one generations of his lineage, he shall enjoy pleasures as he desires.
Having bathed at dawn during the month of Māgha, one is indeed glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
He who performs his ablutions at dawn in the month of Māgha in the beautiful current of the river, while it is reddened by the rays of the sun,
rescues his ancestors, both paternal and maternal.
That man, assuming a divine body, goes to heaven.

Thus ends the ritual for the Māgha bath. Having performed the bath at dawn during the month of Māgha, one should honor a married couple by feeding them according to one's ability and honoring them with fine garments and ornaments.
One attains the state of good fortune and supreme physical health;
this is indeed remembered as the Sūryavrata, which bestows the world of the Sun.
Thus ends the Sūryavrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
During the Hemanta season, one should diligently observe the Kṛcchra penance and eat only a single meal throughout the month of Māgha.
And at the end of the month, one should have a chariot made, adorned with variegated cloths.
It was yoked to four white horses and beautifully adorned with white banners and flags, as well as a parasol, chowries, and a mirror.
O lord of men, having fashioned the Sun out of a measure (āḍhaka) of ground rice,
O king, place him upon the surface of the chariot together with Saṃjñā.
Having paraded him slowly through the royal highway at night with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, he should subsequently lead him toward the sun’s course.
And there, having gradually extinguished [the lamps] with powdered aloe-wood, adorned with lamps and other such things, and with beautiful objects to behold;
Having performed the ritual bath at dawn with either milk or ghee,
one should offer a chariot equipped with a vehicle to the Sun-god, along with a sacrificial fee according to one's ability for the sake of the poor, the blind, and the miserable.
Having eaten together with the Brahmins, one should bow to the Sun and go home.
Established forever in the dharma of Śakra, he is supreme among all observers of vows;
therein lies the vow known as Sūryavrata, which accomplishes all desires and aims.
O King, whatever merit is found in all vows and whatever fruit is found in all sacred fords—
all that merit one obtains here by means of the Sun’s chariot.
Together with those born of twenty-one lineages, he is honored in the world of the Sun by means of celestial palaces that resemble ten thousand suns and fulfill all desires.
Having enjoyed vast and unsurpassed pleasures in all the worlds for more than a hundred thousand aeons, he shall thereafter become a king upon the earth.
Thus ends the Sūryavrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa. [796] In the Mahābhārata:
"He who passes the month of Māgha subsisting on a single meal per day..."
But he who possesses wealth, noble lineage, and kinsmen attains greatness.
*Viṣṇudharma*:
O best of the twice-born, he who passes the month of Māgha eating but one meal a day,
devoted to the service of Viṣṇu, is born into a virtuous family of the righteous.
One who is non-violent toward all beings and devoted to Vāsudeva should mutter "Obeisance to Vāsudeva" one hundred and eight times during the day;
thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating but one meal a day.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action does a person become possessed of knowledge?"
The person should be understood as possessing knowledge; otherwise, he is a bound soul (paśu).
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the Pauṣī day has passed, from the first day (pratipad) onwards in due order,
one should worship the horse-headed Lord Hari as before.

"As before" means according to the procedure stated for the vow of attaining form (*rūpāvāpti-vrata*): one should offer sesame seeds into the fire and worship the deity Hayagrīva, who has the head of a horse, with sesame seeds. Having fasted for three nights during the month of Māgha, one should likewise offer sesame seeds and gold.
With a perfectly disciplined mind, one should give to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa excellent sacred threads and abundant sandalwood paste.
Having observed this vow for a month as prescribed,
a man shall always be endowed with knowledge; having reached the celestial realm, he shall enjoy pleasures.
And a person enjoys his desired objects of pleasure.
Thus concludes the vow for the attainment of knowledge as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Now follow the vows of the month of Phālguna,
according to the *Mahābhārata*.
But whoever passes the month of Bhagadeva eating only one meal a day,
that person— whether man or woman— attains incomparable and supreme sovereignty;
he or she becomes beloved among women, and they indeed become his or her devotees.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*: "One who is intent on service should pass the month of Phālguna by eating only one meal a day;
'intent on service' means devoted to the service of Viṣṇu."
There shall be good fortune for his own kin and exaltation for all;
he shall be non-violent toward all beings and devoted solely to Vāsudeva.
One should mutter "Namo 'stu Vāsudevāya" one hundred and eight times during the day;
thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
Thus ends the vow of eating but one meal a day.
Varāha said:
In the month of Phālguna, fragrant flowers [should be offered].
A devoted person, having taken up these auspicious and effective rites here in this world, [attains success].
Then, from the teacher described in the verse to be cited:
"But he who knows the rituals, being well-versed in all rites,
recites the mantras while remaining established in the observances such as fasting at night."

Having gone to the ground on his knees and having formed a hollow with his fingers by means of both hands— the word "having formed" being understood as having formed a hollow that is a vessel filled with flowers—
he should utter this mantra after saying, "Homage to Nārāyaṇa."
Homage be to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, who churns with the wheel;
homage be to you, the Protector of the world, O great hero; homage be to you!
No one here knows your beginning, middle, or end.
O Supreme Person, take these flowers at the arrival of spring;
he who performs this rite during the month of Phālguna does not enter the cycle of rebirth, but goes instead to the highest world.
Thus ends the ritual for the month of Phālguna as declared in the Varāha Purāṇa.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, by what action may one attain great good fortune?"
Without charm, beauty, and good fortune, it should be known as useless.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: When the full moon day of Māgha has passed, one should always worship Kṛṣṇa, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) in due order, either on a cloth painting or in an image.
O lord of men, one should perform here the entire procedure as previously described.
"Previously mentioned" means that which was stated regarding the vow for obtaining beauty associated with the month of Caitra. One should perform the daily bath with fragrant *priyaṅgu* [rice],
prepare the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) with *priyaṅgu*, and perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) with *priyaṅgu*.

"Gandha" refers to a fragrant substance with a scent like that of *priyaṅgu*; "priyaṅgu" refers to a fragrant substance with a scent like that of saffron (*kuṅkuma*), or it may refer to the *kaṅgu* grain.
Then, on the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, a man who has fasted for three nights should offer these.
And when garments smeared with saffron are to be given, O King, as well as a vessel of bell-metal for the shaving water—
this is indeed unsurpassed and bestows good fortune upon you.
This vow of mine has been declared, O hero among men.
Thus ends the vow for attaining good fortune (*saubhāgyāvāptivrata*) as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

Thus concludes the section on monthly vows (*māsavratāni*) within the Vow Section (*vratakhaṇḍa*) of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Hemādri, the sovereign over all faculties, proficient in all branches of knowledge, and the servant of the illustrious Mahādeva, the supreme king of great kings.
[800] Now begins the eighteenth chapter:
On the various vows of the *māsava* (spirituous liquor).
Unwearied, with its lovely golden [peaks]... having gratified the multitudes of living beings, its fame sung by Kinnarīs upon the Tilaka trees growing on the banks of the celestial Ganges—
this Hemādri (Golden Mountain) is here now the sole cause for destroying the mass of shimmering, formidable sins.
Then, skilled in the arts, he sequentially arranges the various intoxicants and vows.
In that regard, the vows for the four-month period [Cāturmāsī] are described in the Viṣṇudharmottara. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, O righteous-souled one, Janārdana, the God of gods, accompanied by Lakṣmī and ever reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa,
goes to sleep on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.
Both the gods and the sages praise this five-day period.
Then, for four months, as he remained in the state of yogic sleep,
seven sages equal to Brahmā waited upon him.
During those same five days of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
the inhabitants of heaven, including Indra, go there and awaken the Lord of Gods.
Therefore, a man should observe these four-month festivals with great celebration.
From the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
But what is Govinda’s bed, and for what purpose does he sleep there? How is that bed of the Discus-wielder, the God of gods?
What are the mantras and the worship here, what are the rules for the purpose of giving,
what is to be accepted and what is to be abandoned while the Lord of the World is asleep?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O Pārtha, I shall describe the Govinda-śayana-vrata,
the Kaṭidāna, the Samutthāna, and the sequence of the Cāturmāsya vow.
O Great King, one should install Madhusūdana when the thousand-rayed sun is situated in Gemini,
and one should raise him up again when the sun has reached Libra.
The Lord exerts himself; this indeed is the sequence of the method.
O Kṛṣṇa, he would not establish it otherwise, nor likewise would he cause it to arise otherwise.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha,
one should install an image of Viṣṇu holding the conch, discus, and mace.
[One should worship her] made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise of brass;
wearing yellow garments, gentle, seated upon an auspicious couch,
covered with a cloth of white fabric, provided with a pillow, and well-adorned.
From the Brahma Purāṇa:
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the Lord Hari always lies upon his serpent-bed in the Ocean of Milk.
Then, an image of her, endowed with all the auspicious marks, should be fashioned—
either from stone, clay, or wood— depicting her asleep upon the couch of Śeṣa.
[802] Whether fashioned from copper, brass, or silver, or depicted upon variegated cloths,
she has her beautiful lotus-feet placed by Lakṣmī’s own hand.
She should be worshipped with various kinds of offerings according to the prescribed rites;
likewise, a fast should be observed and a vigil kept at night.
When that night has passed, on the twelfth day one should worship her;
then, on the thirteenth day, one should present songs, dances, and instrumental music.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "A man who knows the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, or one who is a knower of the Vedas,
having bathed [the deity] with curd, milk, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth..."
Having anointed her with auspicious perfumes and adorned her with incense, garments,
and garlands of *jātī* flowers, one should worship her with this mantra.
When you, the Lord of the World, are asleep, this world becomes asleep;
and when you awaken, it awakens. O Acyuta, may you be gracious unto me.
Having thus installed that image of Viṣṇu himself,
the man should likewise speak before Viṣṇu with his palms joined in reverence.
For the four months of the rainy season, until the conclusion of the deity’s festival, I shall observe this vow; O Acyuta, grant that it may be free from obstacles for me.
Whether a woman or a man, my devotee who is firm in his vows for the sake of dharma should undertake these observances, beginning with the cleansing of the teeth.
I shall describe the fruits for those who perform these acts individually:
by abstaining from molasses, a man shall become a king with a voice like honey.
By abstaining from oil, O Lord, one is born with beautiful limbs;
by renouncing pungent oil, one shall attain the destruction of enemies.
By abstaining from madhūka oil, one shall obtain incomparable good fortune;
moreover, through the practice of yoga and the Vedas, he shall attain the state of Brahman.
The pungent taste consists of a collection of bitter, sweet, alkaline, and astringent flavors.
He who avoids these shall never encounter deformity or foul odor.
A seeker of pleasure should avoid betel-leaf, for he will become one with a blood-red throat.
From the renunciation of ghee, one attains beauty and a body entirely supple;
from the renunciation of fruit, one becomes wise and is born with many sons.
By eating only śāka leaves and avoiding uncooked food, one becomes pure;
by renouncing foot-massage, one should likewise avoid head-massage.
Radiant with a glowing body, he shall become a lord of bees;
by restricting himself solely to curd and milk, and being devoted to cows, he shall become a lord of cattle;
and by avoiding the *sthālīpāka* offering, he attains the status of Indra’s guest.
By avoiding food fried in oil, he attains long-lasting association [with the virtuous];
and by sleeping on a mat upon the ground, a Brahmin becomes a preeminent sage.
A sage should always be a practitioner of yoga and should avoid honey and meat;
free from disease and illness, possessing vitality, he should strictly abstain from fermented liquor and intoxicants.
O son of Dharma, by such renunciations as these, one becomes established in Dharma;
by fasting on alternate days, one is honored in the world of Brahmā;
and by not clipping nails or hair, one obtains the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
It consists of the eight limbs of yoga, beginning with *dhāraṇā*. For one who observes the vow of silence, the Command becomes fruitful.
By chanting "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," one obtains the fruit of sacrifice.

[804] This commencement of the Cāturmāsya vow should be performed even when Jupiter has set and so forth. As Vṛddhagarga said: "A man should not consider childhood, nor the dullness of Venus and Jupiter, nor the fragmentation of the lunar day at the outset of the Cāturmāsya rite."
By bowing at the feet of Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit born of the gift of a cow.
He who always eats from the ground shall become the lord of the earth;
by chanting "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa," one obtains the fruit of sacrifice.
By the touch of Viṣṇu’s lotus feet, one is liberated from the sins of the day;
indeed, by the sprinkling of the water from His feet, one obtains the merit of bathing in the Gaṅgā day after day.
The man who eats from leaves shall obtain the fruit of Kurukṣetra;
and he who constantly awakens people through the recitation of the scriptures [attains the same].
Vyāsa is quickly pleased with him, and he goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
having performed a dramatic spectacle for Viṣṇu, he shall obtain the world of the Apsarases.
By bathing Viṣṇu with water from sacred fords (tīrtha), one obtains a stainless body;
by consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), O Pārtha, one gains the fruit of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Without even asking, he obtains righteous sons in their entirety;
he who eats at every sixth mealtime shall dwell in heaven for an eon.
Having observed a single meal on alternate days separated by two fasts,
and subsisting on gleaned grains, one obtains the merit of bathing at Prayāga;
furthermore, one should perform the smearing and sweeping of a temple dedicated to Viṣṇu.
That man who recites hymns of praise while performing a hundred circumambulations shall become a king who endures for an eon; of this there is no doubt.
He shall go to the city of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans;
one who performs song and instrumental music for Viṣṇu shall attain the world of the Gandharvas.

By abstaining from water for two watches of the day, one is not overcome by diseases. A man who avoids jaggery should give a copper vessel along with gold, O best of kings; this same rule applies to salt as well.
In the *Brahmavaivarta*: Nārada said:
"O best of gods, how can the practice of a vow be performed while Govinda is asleep?"
It should be performed with devotion by men who are intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu.
Which lunar days (tithis) are indeed meritorious and bestow their fruits in their entirety,
on which Hari is satisfied with even a small amount of penance performed by men?

O best of gods, having explained the giving of gifts, fire-offerings, recitation, ritual bathing, the performance of vows, and the worship of Hari, please now describe the procedure for the practice of fasting.
Brahmā said:
Listen, my child, I shall explain the ritual procedure for the Cāturmāsya;
by performing it with devotion, a person attains the supreme goal.
Having understood the procedure for the ritual worship of Hari according to the injunctions,
one should then perform the vows, worship, and other rites, endowed with devotion.
Even one who performs the ritual of worship of Hari with devotion, though unaware of the procedure as it is prescribed, attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
But he who is constantly devoted to Viṣṇu, firm in his devotion, and has conquered his senses—
he goes to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu even while dwelling in a house.
Whether devoted to Śiva, or to the Sun, or to Gaṇanāyaka,
by undertaking the observance of the vow, one shall partake of the fruit as described;
the sin of a man arising from a hundred births goes to destruction.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, having fasted,
the best of the twice-born, observing the vow, should take his meal at night and undertake the religious observance.
"One should perform"—the syntactical connection is that one should undertake the observance (*niyama*) at night.
"But one should undertake it on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) and during the transit of the sun into Cancer."
At the beginning of Āṣāḍha, a person should perform the observance of the Cāturmāsī vow with devotion,
and should undertake the formal preparation for the Cāturmāsī vows.
"O God, this vow has been undertaken by me in your presence;
may its fulfillment be free from obstacles through your grace, O Keśava."
O Lord Janārdana, if death should overtake me while this vow is being observed, may it be rendered complete through your grace.
O Lord Janārdana, if I should die while this vow is still unfulfilled after having undertaken it, may it be completed for me through your grace.
Having thus worshipped Govinda, one should undertake all [the rites] such as the vow, the worship, and the recitation,
so that they may become complete.
O best of the twice-born, having observed the Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva vows here,
a man who eats but once a day, bathes daily, and is firm in his resolve [attains the goal].
He who worships Vāsudeva for four months shall attain the celestial realm;
at the conclusion, he should feed the Brahmins with devotion and bestow sacrificial fees upon them.
But the practitioner who, while Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, observes the vow at night and gives a pair of garments, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
Having abstained from cakes, one should observe the vow during the meal;
by giving gold, wheat, and clothing in the month of Kārttika, one becomes as one who has performed the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By giving food to a Brahmin, one attains the world of Brahmā;
likewise, by giving silver to a Brahmin while observing a vow and with the mind fixed upon that goal, one attains the same.
One should observe the vow of giving food and perform the breaking of the fast by giving silver,
while remaining intent upon the worship of Viṣṇu through fasting on alternate days.
By giving a cow to Vāsudeva, a man is honored in his world;
likewise, the man who lies upon the bare ground while Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep [attains great merit].
Having given a bed together with its furnishings, one is honored in the world of Indra;
likewise, he who renounces liquor and meat for the four months of the rainy season [attains the same].

He who, for the sake of Viṣṇu, casts [himself] into gold and other such substances during the two seasons beginning with Āṣāḍha, having performed even a quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance, shall become a twice-born man learned in the Vedas.
The mortal who performs the worship of Viṣṇu shall attain his abode;
O best of the twice-born, he becomes [as if] a donor of cows when the year is completed.
He who eats but once every three nights, bathes daily, has conquered his senses,
and is devoted to the worship of Vāsudeva, shall go to the realm of Viṣṇu.
This refers to the previously mentioned conclusion of the cow-gift (godāna-pāraṇa).
That man who, having avoided rice during the month of Kārttika,
gives gold along with śāli rice, attains the station of Viṣṇu.
But that man who, devoted to Keśava, drinks with devotion the water from Viṣṇu’s feet for the duration of the rainy season, shall enter the abode of Viṣṇu.
A man should give a milch cow together with silver and sandalwood;
for the four months of the rainy season, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Upon completion, he should give a pair of cows and provide a feast for Brahmins;
the man who performs this Parāka penance once a year should do so constantly.
Having worshipped Acyuta with devotion, he shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
[808] The breaking of the fast is as previously described. He who subsists on cow’s urine and barley-meal (*yāvaka*) and worships for two seasons, [attains the same].
Having worshipped Viṣṇu with true devotion, a person shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
at the conclusion, one should give a bull and a garment together with gold.
A man may spend the rainy season even on vegetables, roots, and fruits;
upon its completion, by becoming a donor of a cow, he goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.
One who observes the milk-vow likewise attains the eternal world of Brahmā;
and at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a single milch cow.
He who, avoiding honey, gives fine garments accompanied by curd, milk, and ghee on the full moon day of Kārttika, becomes a giver of cows.
Having honored a Brahmin couple with the words, "May Gaurī be pleased with me," one should give gold according to one's ability; thus, one is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
The man who spends four months in celibacy and gives a golden image of a couple shall attain the world of Brahmā.
By abstaining from betel, one becomes possessed of a resonant voice and a red throat;
at the conclusion, one should give a pair of garments or a single garment to a twice-born man.
Then, having performed the twilight rites at the conclusion [of the ceremony],
one who has given a jar of ghee should present a pair of garments, sesame seeds, and a bell to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having performed an anointing before Śambhu and Keśava, one becomes possessed of knowledge and wealth, and attains the station of Sarasvatī.
During the four months of the rainy season, one should give a milch cow;
and, restraining one's speech, one should bow down to the Aśvattha tree, the Sun, the Gaṅgā, and the Lord.
If a man, free from sloth, observes the practice of eating only one meal a day throughout the four months of the rainy season, he should,
at the conclusion of the vow, honor a Brahmin couple together with a cow and offer golden trees; he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.

Having performed the ceremonial bathing with ghee for both Śambhu and Keśava, one should fashion a lotus out of unbroken rice grains upon a circle of cow dung, using *aśvattha* trees [as the material].
At the conclusion, the observer of the vow should give a golden lotus together with a sesame-cow to a Brāhmaṇa; he is then glorified in the world of Śiva.
O best of the twice-born, he who offers a twilight lamp in the courtyard and,
at its conclusion, presents a lantern in the four-cornered garden of his house;
O child, one who is endowed with a pair of garments shall become radiant in this world;
he shall become a god traveling in a celestial chariot, attended by Gandharvas and Apsaras.
He who makes the earth his vessel and eats from it for two seasons,
and gives a bell-metal bowl and a cow, that man becomes a lord of the earth.
O Brahmin, one who subsists on food from a bed of leaves and, upon its completion, gives away a bronze vessel, goes to heaven and is honored by the inhabitants of the celestial realm.

One who is devoted to Viṣṇu enjoys the fruit of the fast using leaves from the *rambhā* and *palāśa* trees; he should avoid all other things that are desired. O Brahmin, one whose mind is purified becomes entirely imperishable.
O best of men, by performing prostration at the feet of Keśava,
one attains incomparable and infinite [merit] when the Garuḍa-bannered Lord is pleased;
the inhabitants of heaven find satisfaction in that man whose mind is purified.
Thus, meritorious vows that remove the suffering of birth,
when performed with Hari in mind, bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
On the eighth and the fourteenth days of both fortnights,
whoever should observe the *nakta* fast and offer a lamp at a crossroads, [attains great merit].
Having likewise offered a lamp in the courtyard and provided daily fodder for cows,
and having observed the Cāturmāsya vow, one should be a donor of a bull at the conclusion of the vow.
O best of the twice-born, having performed a circumambulation of Viṣṇu or of Śambhu, he goes to the abode of Śambhu, honored by the most excellent gods.
At the conclusion of the vow, one who becomes a giver of garments and gives them shall attain heaven;
so too for him who performs [this rite] for the four months for the Lord of the World.
O most fortunate one, O best of the twice-born, he who performs the worship of Keśava’s feet goes indeed to the eternal world of Viṣṇu; there is no doubt in this matter.
But he who, dedicated to Keśava, constantly offers sesame seeds,
shall remain tireless throughout the four months of the rainy season, making the offering of sesame a perpetual practice.
Upon the completion of the vow, O Brahmin, one should give a sesame-cow;
liberated from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu,
and at the end of that time, he becomes a king, the best among rulers, in Bhārata.
A man who constantly sings the praises of Keśava, the God of gods, and of Śiva, indeed attains the fruit of yoga.
At the conclusion of his vow, that practitioner should offer a sweet-sounding bell to the deity;
furthermore, that man who has avoided pungent, bitter, and astringent substances [should do so].

He shall be endowed with beauty and will not be overcome by diseases; and at the conclusion of the vow, having honored the venerable twice-born one, he should give a sacrificial fee according to his ability.
One should avoid conversation with the fallen and falsehood for two seasons;
a man should offer foot-massage and food to Brāhmaṇas, and by giving a sacrificial fee according to his ability, he shall go to the abode of Viṣṇu. [811]
He who indeed avoids excellent ghee for four months attains great beauty of complexion as well as fragrance of the body.
At the conclusion of the vow, O best of the twice-born, having offered a meal to the Brahmins for the sake of Hari,
and having worshipped Govinda with fragrant scents, one should then give a pair of garments to a Brahmin; thus, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O Brahmin sage, by refraining from food cooked in oil, one is born radiant;
and by feeding the Brahmins, one goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whoever gives up bathing with warm water for the sake of Dharma has,
without a doubt, performed the bath in the Gaṅgā every single day.
But he who constantly remembers the auspicious Gaṅgā, the daughter of Bhagīratha, obtains the merit of a constant bath in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.
But he who, when Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, should offer flowers, shall become a performer of vows at the conclusion of the vow; therefore, he is one who has offered a golden flower.
He goes to the radiant world of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor;
when the Lord of the World is asleep, he should worship the courtyard of Śiva.
He who constantly [decorates] with five-colored svastikas and lotuses indeed goes to the world of Rudra and shall attain the state of a leader of the Gaṇas.
But he who, having eaten in the evening or in the morning, worships Madhusūdana while Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, shall indeed go to the city of Prajāpati.
But he who, on the third lunar day while Hṛṣīkeśa is asleep, offers sugar to the Supreme Person every fortnight, saying, "May Gaurī be pleased with me."
When the union of the Brahmin couple is completed, having honored that best of the twice-born with garments and ornaments, and having fed them, one shall become happy.
On the fifth lunar day,
however, at the conclusion of the vow, he who offers a jar filled with rice after having honored the most excellent of the twice-born;
By giving garments, ornaments, and a prastha of rice,
one goes to the station of Sarasvatī, honored by the Gandharvas;
he becomes a learned man of full prosperity, endowed with wealth and grain.
Having worshipped the omnipresent Lord Umāmāheśvara on the fourteenth lunar day, one is born handsome, virtuous, and with a melodious voice.
Having fully honored the Pratipakṣa deity with flowers, perfumes, and offerings, one should then,
during the Cāturmāsya period, fashion an excellent bull out of silver upon a tree,
and upon that, the all-pervading Lord Umāmāheśvara out of gold.
O best of the twice-born, having performed the worship, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa;
that observer of the vow indeed goes to the world of Śaṅkara by means of a celestial chariot,
and remaining there until the end of the kalpa, he shall become a protector of the earth.
From the *Bhaviṣyottara*: "O Pārtha, through such vows as these, Keśava— Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of afflictions, the slayer of Kaṃsa and Keśin— is gratified when propitiated."
When that [planet] is asleep, all auspicious activities cease:
the observation of marriage, the binding of vows, and other sacraments such as the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*),
the entry into a sacrificial hall, and the consecration of deities and kings.
Whatever meritorious rites there may be that do not exist while the Lord of the World is asleep,
likewise, a month during which the sun does not transit is ineffective for rites dedicated to the gods or the ancestors.
A wise man should avoid the intercalary month and periods of impurity;
when the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight.
The "turning of the waist" (*kaṭidāna*) of Viṣṇu brings about the destruction of great sins.
"Turning of the waist" refers to the turning over of the limbs of Viṣṇu as he lies down. Listen now to the reason for this "sleep of the God."
O mighty-armed one, in former times I was gratified by the power of his asceticism; at the request of Yoganidrā, I was entreated to take up my abode in the limbs for her pleasure.
Then I examined my own body for a place [for her];
my chest was occupied by Lakṣmī, but my heart by the Kaustubha gem.
My arms are obstructed by the conch, discus, mace, and Śārṅga bow; likewise my chest.
Below my navel, I am hemmed in by the bird Vainateya;
my head is blocked by his crown, and both my ears by his two earrings.
Therefore, O Pārtha, I have devotedly granted a place for you in my eyes;
for four months of the rainy season, Vasu shall be pleased with you.
Having heard those words of his, Yoganidrā too became pleased;
for that purpose, O Yudhiṣṭhira, she made her dwelling in my eyes.
