And having meditated upon her, I honor that Great Sleep, the Yoga-sleep, as she resides within myself while I lie upon the couch of Śeṣa,
my feet washed by the waves of the milk-ocean, composed in meditation.
With his two feet being gently massaged by the lotus-hands of Lakṣmī,
my devotee who passes four months at that time [attains this].
O sinless Pāṇḍava, by means of various vows and observances for the sake of spiritual welfare,
a man shall dwell in the world of Viṣṇu for one kalpa, being honored there.
Then the God, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, awakens;
from the *Brahma-purāṇa*.
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, one endowed with faith and devotion should awaken Keśava, who has been asleep, during the night.
With dances, songs, and instrumental music; with the auspicious recitations of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas;
with the sounds of lutes and drums; and by listening to the Purāṇas.
And with stories of Vāsudeva, other Vaiṣṇava hymns,
well-spoken words that were like Indra’s rain, and indeed with many splendors.
With flowers, incense, food offerings, lamps, and most beautiful trees;
with burnt offerings, edible foods, cakes, fruits, sugar, and milk-rice porridge.
With sweet preparations of sugarcane, small grapes, pomegranates,
the blossoms of *kuṭheraka*, jasmine, and lotuses;
With *kuṭheraka* (the black basil),
with white and red sandalwood which are pleasing to the heart,
and always with saffron and lac-dye, accompanied by red hymns and bracelets.
Likewise, O Hero, the initial grasping [of the deity] is performed with various kinds of flowers and liquids gathered according to the sequence, together with a red garland.
When that night had passed, at dawn on the twelfth day,
one should first bathe [the image] with ghee, then with sugarcane juice, and thereafter with honey.
Then, according to the scriptures, one should perform anointment with curd, milk, and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
likewise, an ointment made of mung-bean flour, lentils, and āmalaka fruits.
Mustard seeds, priyaṅgu, all kinds of seeds, gold, auspicious items according to one's desire, red objects, and water with kuśa grass.
Having thus purified the Lord of Gods, one should offer auspicious gorocanā;
thereafter, the water-pots should be offered, well-adorned as they were obtained.
[815] Adorned with *jātī* sprouts, bearing fruit, and encrusted with gold, they resounded with the sound of holy flutes and the resonance of lutes and pipes.
Having thus bathed Govinda,
and having anointed him well and adorned him with fine garments, one should worship him with flowers,
excellent saffron, lamps, delightful incenses, and abundant milk-rice.
By giving food to worthy recipients, by burnt offerings, by flowers accompanied by sacrificial fees,
by garments, ornaments, and other gifts, and indeed by swift cows;
The Brahmins are worthy of worship and are the very forms of Viṣṇu dear to his heart;
whatever remains as the nectar of the meal should afterwards be eaten together with the Brahmins.
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
O King of kings, a composed twice-born man should awaken the Lord with the mantra.
The mantras are those spoken in the Varāha Purāṇa:
Oṃ, he who is worthy of being saluted by Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Agni, Kubera, Sūrya, Soma, and the others.
Awaken, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the World;
by the power of the mantra, awaken easily, O God.
But this twelfth day,
O Lord, was ordained by you yourself while reclining upon Śeṣa for the sake of awakening, for the benefit of all the worlds.
O Lord of the World, while you sleep, this entire world sleeps; when you arise, everything becomes active. Arise, arise, O Mādhava!
The clouds have departed and the sky is indeed stainless; the quarters are clear.
O Keśava, accept these autumnal flowers from me.
When the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" is recited for the purpose of raising Hari,
and Viṣṇu has thus been raised, auspicious rites proceed.
In that very place, the bathing of the God of Gods should take place as before;
at night, with the sounds of great musical instruments, one should cause the risen deity to be circumambulated.
The king himself proceeded through the city in a vehicle shaped like a celestial chariot,
along a path illuminated by lamps and crowded with people engaged in dance and song.
O Great King, whoever beholds Dāmodara risen as the upholder of the earth— that very breath of life shall lead everyone toward heaven.
O Lord, having stayed awake at night on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) in the abode of the gods,
one should bathe in the clear morning light and worship Viṣṇu on the twelfth day (dvādaśī).
One should offer oblations into the fire, the carrier of sacrificial offerings, with substances such as clarified butter;
thereafter, O best of kings, one should feed the Brahmins with an abundance of food.
Being worshipped with ghee, milk, curd, honey, *kāsāra*, jaggery, and sweetmeats, he is satisfied; the sacrificer should avoid haste.
O best of the Kurus, one should honor eleven, ten, eight, five,
or two brahmins with sandalwood paste, fragrant scents, garments, garlands, and other offerings.
O Pārtha, by one who, intent on the injunctions, worships with faith according to the rules prescribed in the scriptures, the ancestors are gratified; and by him, Keśava is gratified.
For there is nothing equal in this world to the Dharma, O Pāṇḍava;
whatever is given with faith by those endowed with devotion for the sake of the ancestors,
that is undoubtedly enjoyed with pleasure by the gods, beginning with Brahmā.

Therefore, at the conclusion of the vow, one should worship the twice-born according to the procedure prescribed for the *śrāddha*. Once they have sipped water (*ācānta*), one should then give them whatever has been set aside.

Whatever vow has been undertaken by one for the four months of the rainy season— consisting of one's own spoken word and the desired objects of one's mind, such as food, grain, fruit, and so forth— [that is the rule].
Having narrated this to the twice-born, one should give it to them with devotion along with a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā).
Having given it, one should dismiss the Brahmins and then eat while remaining silent.
O Pārtha, one should cause the news of that which was given up for four months to be proclaimed;
whoever performs this for him shall become a partaker of infinite fruit.
And he who performs this every year remembers Lord Hari.
At the end of his body's life, he rejoices in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the dissolution of all beings lasts, traveling in a most radiant celestial chariot with the splendor of the sun.
O King, he whose four-month vow is completed without obstacles shall have fulfilled his purpose;
indeed, Janārdana is pleased with him.
Whoever performs this observance with devotion during the Devaśayana [festival] shall obtain a fruit equal to that of a pilgrimage to the Ganges and other sacred fords.

Or even by rising [to perform this rite] for Kṛṣṇa, one shall attain the world of Hari. The man who hears, meditates upon, praises, proclaims, or rejoices in this vow with devotion shall indeed go to the city of Viṣṇu.
On whichever day the Lord Ananta, reclining upon his serpent-bed in the Ocean of Milk, either sleeps or awakens,
for those who observe a fast on that day with undistracted minds—
The contact with the body of Garuḍa grants a happy rebirth to men.
Thus ends the procedure for the laying down and the rising of the Lord.
For four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, a person should avoid oil massage;
and when the period has concluded, one should again give a jar containing a pair of sesame oils.
He who offers food consisting of milk-rice and clarified butter goes to the abode of the Lord;
for this is called here the "Oily Vow" (snehavrata), which brings joy to the world.
Thus ends the Snehavrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa:
during the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha, one should avoid clipping the nails,
as well as eating eggplant, and [one should offer] jars containing honey and clarified butter.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, one should present that golden [image] to a Brāhmaṇa;
by this supreme Śiva-vow, one attains the world of Rudra.

Thus ends the Śiva-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. That man who, having renounced highly valuable objects during the Cāturmāsya, gives golden ones to a twice-born in the month of Kārttika along with a pair of cows, [attains great merit].
Then, with a pair of white garments and with fully prepared clarified butter,
this is called the *phalavrata*, which bestows the fruits of all desires.
Thus ends the Phala-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa:
"A man should bathe in the morning for the four months beginning with Āṣāḍha;
having given food to a Brahmin, he should become a giver of a cow on the full moon day of Kārttika."
Likewise, one should give a jar of ghee; thus one shall obtain all desires.
This is called the Vaiṣṇava vow, which bestows the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the Vaiṣṇava vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. Furthermore, he who, having duly worshipped Śiva, offers a horse made of flour in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, is glorified in the world of the Sun.
For a thousand divine years he shall rule, and at its conclusion, he shall become a lord of the earth;
in the month of Pauṣa, one should offer an elephant made of flour before Śiva.
Accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva for a thousand divine years; at the end of that time, he shall become a lord of the earth.
He who, in the month of Māgha, offers a horse-chariot to Śiva becomes a great hero, a universal monarch endowed with all sovereign powers.
He too shall deliver his ancestors from this Raurava hell;
he dwells in the world of Śiva for thirty thousand divine years.
At the conclusion of that, he enjoys the entire earth, yet not in fragments;
in the month of Phālguna, however, he offers a herd of bulls made from flour, numbering eleven, as prescribed for Rudra.
Having offered it before Śiva, one becomes the sovereign of the three worlds for a thousand divine years; at the end of that time, one shall become a lord of the earth.
The great hero, a universal monarch endowed with all sovereignty,
[gives] in the month of Caitra a house made of moonstone, together with male and female servants.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should offer it to Śiva with supreme devotion— a [palace] equipped with household furnishings and adorned with various courtyards.
For eight hundred divine years he is honored in the world of Rudra;
at the end of that time, remembering his past births, he shall attain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin). In the month known as Vaiśākha, [one should offer] seven bowls of grain.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should offer [the gift] to Śiva with a joyful heart;
that man, together with his kinsmen, attains union with Śiva.
If a wise person, endowed with devotion, burns two hundred palas of guggulu incense before Śiva at the conclusion of worship during the month of Jyeṣṭha, [he attains the aforementioned fruit].
Accompanied by twenty-one generations of his lineage, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
at the end of that time, he enjoys the earth, though not in its entirety with its oceans.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, a sacrificial mandala for the wielder of the trident (Śiva) should be prepared,
honored with various kinds of food offerings and provided with diverse edibles.
The bali-maṇḍala should be fashioned, strewn with various colorful offerings;
having worshipped the Supreme Lord, one should then present it to him.
Having uplifted his fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, he,
joined by his sons and grandsons, is glorified in the world of Śiva.
For a thousand divine years he remains there, and at its conclusion,
the lord of the earth [ascends] the flower-born celestial chariot of the God in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should give [an offering] filled with various artistic arrangements;
for ten thousand years, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
By this, one becomes a peaceful lord of yogis through whom he shall indeed attain liberation;
he who performs the worship of Rudra during the month of Bhādrapada at that time.
One should first burn guggulu incense, and then burn suradāru; likewise, one should burn bilva-yoga with ghee, as well as various other substances combined with ghee.
Indeed, one should offer aguru incense as the fifth with one's whole being to the All-pervading Lord.
He who burns [the body] with devotion continuously for one month goes to union with Śambhu, together with his sons and his kinsmen.
But he who, with devotion, fills a cup made of *arka* leaves with milk and ghee for the month of Āśvayuja, without interruption, for Śambhu—
O Six-faced One, I am not able to describe the fruit of his merit;
for even those children born in his lineage who have been killed by infants or the like [attain such results].
Those highly fortunate ones proceed at their pleasure to the world of Rudra.
For more than ten thousand times ten thousand years, and at the end of that period, they are born as lords of men, devoted to Śiva, possessed of knowledge, and free from all taint.

Having received initiation into Śiva, they attain the supreme goal. Whoever, when the month of Kārttika arrives, offers at the conclusion of the worship a basket covered with cloth containing sugarcane juice before Śiva, [attains that same goal].
At the end of his life, he rejoices in the world of Rudra together with his kinsmen,
having duly honored the devotees of Śiva at the conclusion of the vow.
"O son, with gold, garments, food, and drink, and without stinginess regarding wealth"—
thus is the Śiva-vrata described in the Kālottara.
O King, that woman who passes the month of Kārttika eating but one meal a day, [attains great merit].
Through the observances of forbearance, non-violence, and so forth, she became a practitioner of celibacy.
One should respectfully offer to the Sun rice of the śāli variety mixed with jaggery,
along with karavīra flowers and guggulu resin with clarified butter.
On either of the two fortnights, one should be devoted to fasting on the seventh or the sixth lunar day, endowed with supreme faith.
Resembling a sapphire, he is honored in the world of the Sun along with more than a hundred pairs of women and celestial chariots that fulfill all desires.
And so, having diligently acquired enjoyments in all the worlds,
she returns from there to this world and finds a husband according to her desire.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, charity, purity, restraint of the senses,
worship of the sun, fire-sacrifice, contentment, and avoidance of theft.
This rule is always established as common to all vows;
[the image] is fashioned from flour in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should offer it to Bhāskara,
together with red chalks, great minerals, and those frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
For eleven thousand months he is honored in the world of the Sun;
with great golden ornaments from the mountains,
having returned to this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband.
In the month of Pauṣa, however, having fashioned an image of Garuḍa, one should offer it to the Sun.
Having adorned Bhāskara, the foremost of the gods, with perfumes and garlands,
one should then present all of that in a copper or bell-metal vessel,
accompanied by the gift of a great lotus that emits a divine fragrance.
Then, for eleven thousand years, she is honored in the world of the Sun;
having thus reached that world in due order, she finds a husband according to her desire.
In the month of Māgha, having fashioned a chariot yoked with horses, adorned with lamps and garlands, made of flour and joined with an image of the Sun, one should bring it to the temple.
In celestial chariots resembling the sun and filled with the sounds of song and instrumental music,
she is honored in the world of the Sun for seventeen thousand years;
then, returning to this world, she finds a husband according to her desire.
Having fashioned an image of the Sun out of flour in the month of Phālguna,
and having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should announce it at the temple of the Sun.
In celestial chariots resembling the sun and filled with the sounds of song and instrumental music,
he is honored in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred thousand years.
Having arrived in this world in due course, she finds a husband according to her desire;
likewise, having spent a moment in the month of Caitra, adorned with perfumes and garlands.
Having placed it in a vessel as prescribed, one should offer it to Bhāskara;
[the donor shall ascend] celestial chariots resembling the autumnal moon that fulfill all desires.
For more than a full hundred thousand years, he is honored in the world of the Sun;
then, upon the exhaustion of his karma, having returned here accompanied by sons and grandsons.
Having obtained her desired husband, she enjoyed there pleasures that are very difficult to attain;
indeed, she fashioned mountains like Mount Meru out of flour made from an *āḍhaka* measure of rice.
It is joined with the Nikṣubhārga and adorned with all the elements.
Endowed with various ornaments, adorned with various garlands,
and furnished with all kinds of jewels, one should place it in the abode of the Sun.
Indeed, he who observes this Great Sky Vow (Mahāvyomavrata) in the month of Vaiśākha is honored in the world of the Sun by means of various celestial chariots.
Having arrived in this world in due order, he sports on Mount Mānasa;
having fashioned a lotus with its pedestal out of flour in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Having worshipped the lotus with vessels, perfumes, and various garlands and ornaments,
[he ascends] celestial chariots that resemble pure crystal and fulfill all desires.
He is honored in the world of the sun for more than a full hundred million years.
Having arrived in this world in due course, she shall obtain a king as her husband;
and likewise, having bathed in the month of Āṣāḍha, she should offer an excellent cake made of flour (*paiṣṭa*) to the lotus.
Having filled it with the essences of all seeds, possessing auspicious characteristics,
enriched with the fragrance of various filaments, and endowed with all kinds of jewels;
The remainder [of the sentence] is that one should offer it to Bhāskara.
O King, by means of great vehicles drawn by swans and endowed with all enjoyments,
one is honored in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred crores of years.
In the world of Vradhna, in the world of the Sun—
having reached this world in due order— one finds a king as a husband.
One should offer a mountain of sesame seeds to the Sun in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
By means of vehicles that travel at will and are adorned with various jewels,
one is honored in the world of the Sun for more than a hundred million years.
Having experienced various enjoyments endowed with many wonders, she will,
in due course, reach this world and obtain a king as her husband.
O King, having prepared in the month of Bhādrapada a pavilion made of rice,
adorned with canopies, banners, cloths, and various garlands;
By means of magnificent great vehicles as bright as the rays of the moon,
he is honored in the world of the sun for thousands of millions of years.
Having come in due course to this world, she finds a king as her husband; or, having fashioned a vast mountain of grain in the month of Āśvayuja,
she should offer it before the Sun, together with gold, garments, and perfumes.
In various magnificent Mahāyāna vehicles, endowed with excellent enjoyments,
she is honored in the world of the Sun for thousands of millions of years.
"Having reached this world, she obtains a king as her husband. Thus was described the vow for the attainment of the desire for sons and women, as spoken in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*.
Pulastya said:
At the end of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana honors his own Māyā, namely Yoganidrā, upon the body of the serpent Śeṣa.
He practices these four types of pride until the month of Kārttika;
for it is then that distinguished rites such as sacrifices are performed.
In that regard, a man who, at the end of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, sleeps on the ground, bathes outdoors, and avoids oil-massage for five days and for the entire month, [attains the fruit].
Avoiding all other temples, he should eat only at night once a day;
remaining celibate, having conquered anger, and devoted to recitation and fire-offerings,
he should constantly worship Hari with perfumes, garlands, and excellent food.
With songs, instrumental music, dances, and indeed with garlands of lamps,
as well as by the gift of water-cows along with their calves,
the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should likewise take place on the third day at the end of the bright fortnight of Kārttika.
O twice-born one, for ten days indeed during both his sleep and his awakening,
what need has that great-souled one for sacrifices characterized by violence?
By that man who has worshipped Keśava both at the time of his sleep and his awakening,
and who, being devoted to Viṣṇu, has performed this vow for ten days;
One obtains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage;
Agni is the mouth of the gods, and the Kṛttikās have Agni as their deity.
The month of Kārttika is presided over by Agni and is remembered as the mouth of the gods;
it begins when the month of Āśvayuja has passed and lasts until the full moon day of Kārttika, O twice-born one.
Having performed the vow prescribed for ten days, one is glorified in heaven;
one obtains the merit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice and uplifts one's own lineage.
By offering a lamp every day during the month of Kārttika,
one becomes endowed with sight, becomes the best of Brāhmaṇas, and is likewise honored everywhere.
Having avoided the sun and the month for such a length of time,
one who has fallen from the heavenly world shall obtain happiness among humans.
Endowed with health and perfection of form, one shall become fortunate;
this is the vow proclaimed for ten nights when the Lord of the Gods of gods is asleep.
Having stayed for four months while Madhusūdana is fast asleep,
one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and is glorified in the highest heaven.
Having performed the "sword-edge vow" (asidhārāvrata) for one year in this manner,
a man attains the merit of all sacrifices and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Whatever desire one may have while walking upon the edge of a sword's blade,
having attained that very desire, one is thereafter glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus he becomes capable both in granting boons and in pronouncing curses;
he possesses the splendor of the sun—of this there is no need for doubt.
Dālbhya said:
O you of great splendor, explain the procedure for the vow of the sword’s edge;
sever this doubt of mine, for you are said to be all-knowing.
Pulastya said:
Having bathed, adorned with ornaments and garlands, and having eaten food that is free from meat,
and having performed worship of the deities, one should sleep at night accompanied by a woman.
O best of the twice-born, a celibate student (brahmacārī) should observe the vow of the sword’s edge:
having embraced both a virgin and a married woman, he should sleep at night.
A celibate practitioner undoubtedly obtains a hundredfold fruit;
this vow known as the "edge of the sword" is considered exceedingly difficult to perform.
Having observed the vow for twelve years, one shall certainly attain sovereignty over the three worlds;
and having enjoyed that for a long time, O foremost of the twice-born, [one attains liberation] at the end.
He attains union with Janārdana.
Thus ends the Asidhārāvrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other vow, the Caturmūrtivrata.
That which ought to be done by a man of great discernment who desires knowledge.
Having performed his external ablutions and having performed the worship of the *Ṛgveda*,
a man should listen to the *Ṛgveda* daily for two months without weariness.
Beginning from the month of Caitra, the knower of Dharma should always eat only at night;
then, O best of kings, when the last day of the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, he should proceed.
A pair of garments, gold, as well as a milch cow,
a bronze vessel filled with clarified butter, and gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should observe the vow of the Yajurveda during the months beginning with Āṣāḍha;
one should observe the vow of the Sāmaveda during the months beginning with Āśvina.
Nevertheless, that which is called the Atharva-vrata is prescribed for the months beginning with Pauṣa;
however, everything proclaimed as the Ṛgveda-vrata must be performed by all in all cases.
Having performed the worship of Vāsudeva, who is the soul of the Vedas, for twelve years,
a man goes to the world of Viṣṇu, which is superior to all worlds.
Upon reaching which, one abandons all suffering.
Thus ends the Veda-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another observance, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
During the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, however, one who has conquered his senses should observe a fast.
Having worshipped Vāsudeva, the wise man, knowing what is appropriate for the ritual, should give wealth as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇa.
O lover of righteousness, having duly worshipped Saṅkarṣaṇa in the month of Vaiśākha,
one should likewise give auspicious war-materials to a Kṣatriya.
O best of the twice-born, having worshipped Pradyumna in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should give to a Vaiśya whatever wealth is useful for his trade.
Having performed the worship of Aniruddha according to the prescribed rite during the month of Āṣāḍha,
O Gārgava, one should give ritual implements and materials to a Śūdra.
O twice-born one, after four months, there is the first breaking of the fast;
having performed three such fast-breakings, a man attains the world of Purandara.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, O King,
and having attained human birth, one becomes prosperous.
Thus ends the vow regarding the castes as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
O Yādava, [this should be done] constantly during the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa.
One should worship the symbols of the four oceans and the full jars;
the wise should know that Hari is fourfold in nature and has the ocean as his essence.
One should always perform one's bath with river water as long as it is available,
and one should daily perform the fire-oblation (homa) constantly, using oil-free materials.
Having honored the best of the twice-born on the final day of the month of Kārttika,
and having given oil to a Brahmin, one is glorified in the vault of heaven;
one obtains the fruit of a sacrifice that fulfills all desires.
Having attained human birth and having ruled the earth bounded by the ocean's girdle,
even there he remained with his mind fixed upon the Dharma.
And he becomes free from disease and endowed with strength.
Thus ends the Sāgaravrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrtivrata.
Garuḍa is the drum-staff of Vāsudeva, and Tāla is that of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Likewise, the emblem of Pradyumna is a crocodile with its mouth wide open;
Aniruddha is proclaimed as the god who knows dharma and has a rishi for his banner.
O delighter of the Yadus, yellow, blue, white, and red— of these,
it has been declared that their cloth and their banner should be of the same colors.
Whatever the emblem of a deity may be, that deity is proclaimed by its own self;
his banner is of such a kind, and his garment is of such a kind.
In the month of Caitra, a person should worship Garuḍa every day.
O twice-born one, in the month of Vaiśākha, one should always worship Tāla with yellow perfumes, food offerings, garlands, garments, and other such items.
O twice-born one, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should always worship Makara every day with blue perfumes, food offerings, garlands, garments, and so forth.
O twice-born one, in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the divine Ṛṣya according to the prescribed rite with white perfumes, food offerings, garlands, garments, and so forth; O twice-born one,
[one should worship him] with red perfumes, food offerings, garlands, garments, and so forth.
One should likewise perform an external bath and the worship of the fire; O knower of dharma, one should daily provide a meal for Brahmins,
and for the sake of breaking the fast, one should likewise eat at night, avoiding oil.
He should likewise sleep on the ground and remain a perpetual celibate student;
a man should properly observe this vow for four months.
On the final day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability;
O knower of dharma, one should give garments and sacrificial fees to the learned Brahmins.
O King, by performing one fast-breaking meal [on this occasion], one is glorified in the heavenly world;
by performing a second fast-breaking meal, one is glorified in the world of Śakra.
Having performed the third breaking of the fast, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā;
having performed six breakings of the fast, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
O foremost of Bhārgava’s lineage, by performing the twelve-year vow of the banner (*dhvajavrata*) and completing the twelve *pāraṇas*, a man attains the world of Viṣṇu.
He attains union with the divine Janārdana, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.
Thus ends the Dhvajavrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrtivrata.
The conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus are proclaimed as his fourfold nature.
Vāsudeva is remembered as the conch, and Saṅkarṣaṇa as the discus;
Pradyumna is the mace and the lotus, and Aniruddha is the Teacher of the World.
Having bathed outdoors during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, one should partake of the night-meal;
one should perform their worship month by month in due order.
With offerings of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, lamps, incense, and excellent food, and then, when the month of Kārttika has ended and the vow is likewise completed;
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's capacity,
as well as a bell-metal vessel containing ghee and likewise gold.
Having observed the vow for four months,
one attains the world of the Lord of the Thirty-three;
and thereafter, having regained human birth, it is exactly the same.
In this world, the hero becomes a lord of the earth.
Thus ends the *Āyudhavratam* as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
[832] Brahmā said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim that which increases all prosperity.
O sinless one, by performing which [act] does one become a sovereign emperor here on earth?
When the month of Nabhas has arrived, one who has conquered the senses, eating only at night, bathing in the morning, constantly engaged in study,
and devoted to the fire-rituals, O child, should worship the Goddess with bilva flowers, nāga, and campaka.
One should offer guggulu as incense, and for the food offering (naivedya), that which is cooked in ghee—
either milk-rice, rice with curd, or alternatively, vegetables and barley-gruel.
One should perform the recitation of the mantra a thousand times or perhaps a hundred times;
there, it should be offered to the Goddess until the vow is fulfilled.

Then, O child, when the vow is completed, one should feed and honor the preceptor’s daughter, the preceptor himself, and the wives of the twice-born according to one's ability with gifts of gold, cattle, and ornaments.
O best of kings, even in the absence [of a teacher], the recitation of mantras must be performed daily;
whoever performs it with devotion a hundred times shall attain equality with that [teacher].
Neither disease, nor old age, nor death, nor fear arising from enemies occurs for the devotee, O Goddess; and in the end, there is imperishable fruit.
In this regard, there are these mantra words:
*Oṃ nandane nandani sarvārthasādhanī namaḥ*. This is the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).

Oṃ nandane, homage to the heart; the heart. Nandinī, homage to the head; the head. To Sarvā, homage; the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ arthasādhinī, homage; the armor (kavaca). Oṃ namaḥ, hūṃ phaṭ; the weapon (astra). Oṃ, homage to the eye. Oṃ nandinī, the heart-mantra of the offerings.
On the third and fifth, on the fourth and the eighth, on the ninth, the full moon, the eleventh, and on the twelfth days.
And on the sixth [tithi], that very Vidyeśā should be worshipped with special care.
He who, intending for Nandā, gives a white bull in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
shall obtain his desired objects and the eternal world of the Goddess.
In the month of Nabhasya, one should dedicate this [rite] and give a cow or even gold;
having shaken off his sins, he shall go to the fearless realm of Nanda.
Having observed the fast and the meal of unasked food during the nine nights of Āśvina,
one should then worship the Goddess on the eighth day and on the following day.
A golden flower, a jewel, a garment adorned with various colorful patterns,
and gold should be given as a gift to Nandā for the sake of accomplishing one's own purpose.
With the multitude of his sins shaken off and endowed with all desires,
he indeed goes to that world where the goddess, the slayer of the enemies of the gods,
dwells; there he remains for ten million kalpas, served by hosts of apsarases.
He rejoices, and having arrived here, he shall become the sole sovereign on earth;
for by worshipping the Goddess with jasmine and *gajāhvaya* flowers during the month of Kārttika, he attains this.
While giving food as a gift to a Brahmin, or even to maidens or women,
white garments should likewise be given as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One is indeed liberated from all sins, even those committed in other births;
such a yogi is born right here [in this life] and attains the imperishable state in the hereafter.
Having bathed according to the rules on the road and having worshipped the Goddess with saffron,
offerings of food and ghee-filled cakes should be given to maidens and to the twice-born.
O child, one should feed and honor [the Brahmins] with garments produced from silkworms;
thus one shall obtain all desires and be liberated from all sins.
In the month of Pauṣa, having established the Goddess in meditation, one should worship her with lotuses.
One should offer an oblation of cooked rice and, having fed a maiden, honor her with gifts;
likewise, a beautiful bed adorned with yellow cloths should be offered to the Goddess.
By this method, O child, the Goddess herself becomes propitious;
she bestows desired enjoyments and, in the end, leads one to her own city.
In the month of Māgha, one should reverently worship the Goddess with garlands of kunda flowers and with saffron mixed with camphor, having likewise smeared [the image] with it.
Having first bathed [the image] according to rule with [water] mixed with musk and saffron, one should then worship the maidens,
the twice-born, and Caṇḍikā with devotion, according to the prescribed rite, using ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and the oblation of sesame seeds (tilahoma) to be offered according to one's ability.
With his sins and afflictions shaken off, endowed with all enjoyments, free from enemies,
and possessed of many sons, he is born as the best of men.
At the end of the body, O King, one goes by this rite to the world of Nandinī, which is saluted by all the gods; of this there is no doubt.
In the month of Phālguna, one should worship the Goddess with mango blossoms,
and likewise offer edible foods together with sugar and honey.
One should feed young maidens and Brahmins, and give sacrificial fees and white garments;
by this one becomes an enjoyer of pleasures and goes to the world of the Goddess.
When the month of Caitra has arrived, the Goddess is to be worshipped with offerings of flowers.
Sweets such as *laḍḍukas* should be offered as food-oblations, and likewise, one should feed young girls;
women should also be honored according to the prescribed rite with red garments.
By this, indeed, one shall obtain all desires without hesitation;
O child, one shall go to the world of the Goddess, where enjoyments are uninterrupted.

In the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship the Goddess with flowers born of the *vaikarṇika* plant; the food offering (*naivedya*) should consist of barley flour (*saktu*) and sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*). Then, one should feed a maiden and honor her;
auspicious golden umbrellas should be given to the best of the twice-born.
But one should bow to the Goddess, O child, who is unsurpassed among all the gods;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, Śaṅkarī is to be worshipped with red aśoka and karaṇṭaka flowers.

Likewise, the sacrificial offering (naivedya) should be given, and the maidens should be fed with offerings of ghee-filled cakes; furthermore, the skillful ones should be honored with auspicious gifts such as cattle and land.
Likewise, water-pots filled with white water should be given;
by this, he quickly bestows upon them the enjoyments associated with Varuṇa.
In the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the Goddess with lotuses, blue water-lilies, and petals;
the food offering should consist of sugar, curd, cooked rice, and milk-rice.
Maidens, twice-born men, and women should be fed, and likewise honored according to the ritual of worship.
The Blessed Lady should be worshipped according to one’s capacity with various golden ointments and the like, sesame seeds, land, and pearls, for the accomplishment of all desires.
Nandā, Sunandā, Kanakā, Umā, Durgā, Kṣamāvatī, Gaurī,
Yogeśvarī, Śvetā, Nārāyaṇī, and Sunāśikā.
Those men who, having risen, recite these twelve names beginning with "Ambikā" in sequence, are cleansed of their impurities through that proclamation.
O tiger among men, there are those on earth who are abundant in wealth;
yet these [calamities] constantly arise on the road, in battle, and during afflictions by enemies.
O best of gods, Carcikā crosses over all difficulties;
one should perform this most excellent of vows for half or even for a quarter [of its duration].
"Or it should be given for one month, beginning with the month of Śrāvaṇa.
Thus is described the Nandā-vrata as stated in the Devī-purāṇa.
Gauramukha said:
O king of kings, Devakī was the daughter of Devaka;
being childless, that beautiful woman indeed performed austerities for the sake of obtaining sons.
That wife of Vasudeva was devoted to truth and righteousness, yet she was not satisfied with Govinda; Bhārgava said this to her.
Bhārgava said:
"For what purpose, O blessed lady, do you perform this most difficult penance?
What object do you desire? Tell me, where is your wish directed?"
The goddess said:
"O best of the twice-born, I am childless; my husband has no offspring.
Therefore, having propitiated Govinda, I desire a beautiful son."
I shall perform penance with supreme concentration until Viṣṇu, being propitiated, grants me the sky.
Bhārgava said:
"O delight of your family, if you have the effort to worship Govinda, then,
undertaking this vow, satisfy Janārdana."
[837] When the first day of the month of Kārttika arrived, Devakī herself performed her bath with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and partook of food made from the five products of the cow.
Having worshipped the unborn, all-pervading Vāsudeva with bāṇa flowers,
and having offered sandalwood paste and incense, one should present the finest rice-milk (paramānna).
One should offer clarified butter to the Brahmin and then undertake the vow:
"From this day forward, for one month, I shall abstain from the killing of living beings."
From speaking untruth, from theft, and from eating honey, meat, and the like— whether sleeping, waking, or walking— I shall remember Acyuta.
Slander of others, backbiting, as well as causing pain to others,
or the reviling of true scriptures, deities, sacrifices, or anyone else on this earth.
O illustrious lady, seeing Hari present everywhere in this world, I shall say nothing,
for he is ultimately incapable of being fully carried even by one who is most powerful.
One should undertake a restrictive vow for its renunciation, which leads to the increase of dharma.
Having thus performed [the rite] before Viṣṇu, O auspicious one, and having attained freedom from sin,
one should always eat the food offering (naivedya) oneself while observing silence and facing north.
Likewise, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having worshipped Janārdana with jasmine flowers,
one should again offer incense and sandalwood.
Having given excellent food, clarified butter, and likewise [other offerings] to the deity and to the Brahmin, he should accept whatever restriction pleases him.
In the same way, O delighter of the family, one should eat only at night as an offering;
during all four months, the consumption of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth is equal,
but there is a distinction regarding flowers, incense, offerings, and sacrificial fees.
The equality of bathing and sipping water, as well as eating at night, has been explained;
now hear from me which flowers one should worship with each month.
And whatever incenses are to be offered, as well as the food for the sacrificial offering,
[should be presented] to Bāṇa with jasmine flowers and likewise with those born from the Mukunda tree.
With red *kundātimuktaka* flowers, with red *raktavīra* and *raktaka* flowers,
and likewise with white, bright *mallikā* and *mallikā* flowers.
When Viṣṇu is worshipped in sequence with curd, a *padmābha* flower, a *ketakī*, and a red lotus, he grants whatever resides in the mind.
In the months of Kārttika and Mārgaśīrṣa, one should offer incense; in Pauṣa, sandalwood;
and likewise, in Māgha, Phālguna, and Caitra, one should offer a teacher to Viṣṇu.
O Devakī, one should offer camphor with devotion to the God of gods during the three months beginning with Vaiśākha, and guggulu resin during the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa.
In the three auspicious months beginning with Kārttika, one should offer milk-rice (paramānna);
in the three months beginning with Māgha, sweet porridge (kāsāra); and thereafter, in the next three months, barley-food (yavānna).
The observer of the vow, adhering to the auspicious observance, should likewise give clarified butter, sesame seeds, a water-pot, or gold to a Brāhmaṇa every month.
And while performing the monthly observance of the rules as they have been described, the human being should say: "May Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, be pleased."
Even a woman of pure wisdom who observes this vow according to the prescribed rules for all its months shall attain her heart's desires.
O beautiful lady, Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, being propitiated by him through this vow,
bestows his desired objects in a very short time.
This vow of the Unmanifest-born bestows grain, fame, long life, as well as good fortune and health; it is more beloved than all other vows.
By means of this vow, Mādhava— his soul purified by this single step—
is undoubtedly easy to behold, provided one remains silent while holding a lamp.
One performs this great vow with body, speech, mind, and intellect;
then Janārdana, the pure and stainless God, becomes truly visible.
O woman of excellent complexion, for those living beings whose minds are one-pointedly focused upon that [object],
the glorious attainments of those destined for liberation come forth through their diligent effort.
Just as one who has reached the wish-fulfilling tree obtains whatever fruit he desires with his mind, so too does one obtain it upon reaching that all-pervading Lord.
Therefore, O Devakī, perform this auspicious vow, which destroys great sins and purifies, for the propitiation of Kṛṣṇa.
When that has been performed, Hṛṣīkeśa will surely grant you his vision;
and once he is seen, whatever you desire shall be fulfilled for you in its entirety.
Thus ends the Viṣṇudevī-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the rites of bathing, giving gifts, and religious observances."
Just as Janārdana is to be worshipped during the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira.
Whatever fruit is obtained by men in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Puṣya, Māgha, and Phālguna by bowing down to the Slayer of Madhu; [that same fruit is obtained by others].
Brahmā said:
Listen, my child, to the great merit of both the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons;
when Kṛṣṇa is worshipped here, he is well-pleased even by a very small [offering].

In the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad), one should undertake the practice of the vow pertaining to the winter and the cool season in their proper sequence.
Having bathed, worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa, and prostrated,
the observer of the vow should then request a boon with devotion from the Teacher of the moving and the unmoving.
O Blessed One, this maintenance of the life-force of living beings is indeed fickle;
death is certain for humans, but it is difficult to discern when it will occur.
Therefore, O Adhokṣaja, I entreat you for this boon:
that my vow may not be rendered incomplete, since you, O Lord, have been pleased with me.
"O God, this vow has been undertaken by me at your command;
may it be fulfilled, whether I remain alive or have passed away."
Having thus worshipped Hari, the Lord of the World and the teacher of all that moves and is stationary,
the wise man should then perform the religious observances of the winter season.
From the first day of the dark fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa,
a man should always be non-violent, engaged in ritual acts, and perform his morning ablutions.
One should always worship Keśava, the Lord of the gods of gods, at midday,
having smeared him with saffron, uśīra, and sandalwood according to one's capacity.
One should worship with *mālatī* flowers, as well as with *ghṛṅgi*, *bilva*, and other offerings;
one should offer a lamp that is perpetually bright and burn *guggulu* resin mixed with clarified butter.
One should present as an offering rice mixed with curd,
and likewise, one should repeatedly prostrate with devotion, bowing the head to Keśava.
Having worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa according to this very rite,
one should mutter the mantra "Oṃ namo keśavāya" one hundred and eight times.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of the Gods in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
a man should then eat from a vessel of non-bronze after having given alms to a twice-born brahmin.
One should always avoid honey and meat, travel on long journeys, and bad food;
as well as falsehood, theft, harsh speech, and association with those who have fallen from their status.
One should always provide fodder for the cows and sleep on the ground at night;
one should always pay homage to the pipal tree and likewise to the guru who bestows knowledge.

In this manner, during the months of Puṣya, Māgha, and Phālguna, the man observing the vow should complete the rite according to his capacity and must not, under any circumstances, cause himself physical emaciation.
One should cause him to dance according to this vow during the four months of the winter season;
listen now to the specific rule regarding this, and the separate procedure for the twelfth day.
Having fasted on the eleventh day of the auspicious fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should worship Keśava, the Lord of the worlds and the remover of sins.
On the twelfth day, one should bathe the Lord Puruṣottama with milk,
with meat-broth, with clarified butter, and with the five products of the cow, in that order.
On the twelfth day of the month of Puṣya, Māgha, and Phālguna, one should bathe the Lord;
then one should worship Hari with food offerings, flowers, incense, and other articles.
Having bowed his head to the god Keśava, the slayer of Keśin,
and having joined his palms in devotion, he should pray for the most excellent boon.
O Keśava, whatever has been worshipped by me— whether deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion—
may that, O Lord, become complete.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods and prostrated before him again and again,
he should then feed the Brahmins and devotedly give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
By this very procedure, during the months of Puṣya, Māgha, and Phālguna,
one should prostrate to the Lord with his name and, having worshipped Hari, offer prayers.
One should feed the twice-born again and give them sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
furthermore, one should give rice, clothing, and sesame seeds along with respectful offerings (arghya) according to the sequence of the months.
On the twelfth lunar day, having dedicated [the gift] to the Lord with devotion before the foremost of the twice-born,
and having thus completed it with devotion, O Vraja, a man is indeed called "Anaraka" (one who is not subject to hell) by name.
One shall not go to hell where he whose banner is Garuḍa resides.
O Sage, this vow is of great merit, superior even to all other vows;
it is difficult for those of wavering minds to perform, yet it destroys even the most grievous sins.
A drinker of intoxicants, a killer of a Brahmin, a thief, one who violates the teacher’s bed, and one who is always untruthful.
Having performed this rite with devotion, a person is instantly liberated from sin;
it has been constantly practiced by the great seers, such as Bhṛgu, Atri, and the best of the Bhujagas.
This vow has been highly honored by the fortunate seekers of knowledge;
for they, having fully worshipped the one whose banner is Garuḍa, attained the imperishable heaven.
Then, having reached the earth, the Lord of Gods was [propitiated] by Dakṣa and other sages, as well as by Bhārgava, Akrūra, and Yayāti through this vow.
Having propitiated Keśava, the best of gods, by means of this vow,
one who always bows down attains the supreme station of Viṣṇu, which is characterized by liberation.
Having worshipped according to this rite with devotion when Sanaka and the others arrived,
and having performed, heard, and meditated upon this meritorious vow named Anaraka— which grants all desires— a man shall not go to hell.
Thus is described the Anaraka-vrata as stated in the Viṣṇu-rahasya:
"For the four months beginning with Caitra, one should observe the *ayācita* (eating only what is unasked) vow;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-jar (*maṇika*) together with a new cloth."
One who offers a vessel of sesame seeds and gold is honored in the world of Brahmā;
at the end of the kalpa, he becomes a lord of the earth—this is called the Ānanda-vrata.
Thus ends the Ānanda-vrata as described in the Matsya Purāṇa:
Having diligently worshipped Śiva on the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha,
one should offer a sacred thread to Śiva and feed those who are devotees of Śiva.
And again, on the full moon day of Kārttika, having worshipped Śambhu,
one should ask for forgiveness after giving a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the ascetics, consisting of sacred threads, garments, and other such items.
Whoever should perform this *pavitraka* rite even once during the four-month period (*cāturmāsya*) is honored in the world of Rudra for thousands of millions of eons.
Falling away due to the exhaustion of his merit, one who was a knower of the four Vedas is reborn;
however, by his own will, he may become a king endowed with the form of a preceptor.
Thus has been described the vow of the Śiva-sacred-thread as taught in the Śivadharma. Now I shall proclaim month by month the unsurpassed Śiva-vow,
for the sake of dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation for embodied beings such as men and women.
When the month of Puṣya has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night—
speaking the truth, having conquered anger, and subsisting on rice, wheat, and dairy products— [attains great merit].
One should diligently observe a fast on the eighth day of both fortnights;
one should worship the Lord at the three junctions of the day and perform the fire-ritual with devotion.
At the end of the month, on the full moon day, having slept upon the ground and performed a bath with ghee and other substances, one should diligently perform a great worship to Śiva.
One should offer as a food offering (naivedya) one prastha of barley-gruel cooked in milk;
having fed eight Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva with appropriate sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
one should also offer a pair of tawny cows to Śiva.
Listen now to the fruit of the merit of one who has adorned that beautiful form:
he shall travel in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires and are as radiant as ten million suns.
He was surrounded by Rudra-maidens and accompanied by great bulls;
attended by throngs of Apsarases with song, dance, and instrumental music;
and praised by gods and asuras with yak-tail whisks, incense, and garlands.
Three-eyed and holding a trident, endowed with divine sovereignty,
he shall go to the beautiful city of Śiva, where Śaṅkara himself resides.
For as many thousands of yugas as there are hairs on his body and as many praises he receives among families, for that long shall he dwell happily and go to the city of Śiva.
Together with those born of his twenty-one generations of kin, he enjoys desired pleasures;
having attained the yoga of knowledge, he is liberated right there.
Thus has been fully explained to you this means for attaining the liberation of Śiva, for those dwelling in the ocean of saṃsāra who observe the stages of life (āśrama) dedicated to Śiva.
When the month of Māgha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming *kṛsara* mixed with ghee while his senses are fully restrained;
One should observe a fast on the fourteenth day of both fortnights;
however, on the full moon day, one should offer a "blanket of ghee" to Śiva.
And here, one should present a pair of well-formed black cattle.
Having performed the remainder as prescribed, one shall obtain the previously mentioned fruit;
[one travels] in celestial chariots resembling sapphire, accompanied by peacocks.
Having gone to the beautiful city of Śiva and having enjoyed pleasures as desired,
he who performs the practice of eating only at night when the month of Phālguna has arrived [attains that state].
Having conquered anger and mastered his senses, he should subsist on śyāmāka grain, milk, and wild rice,
and be devoted to fasting on the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight.
On the full moon day, the great ablution is performed with the five products of the cow, clarified butter, and so forth;
with earth from the top of an anthill and other such sites, and with cow urine, cow dung, and the like.
With the barks of milk-exuding trees as well as with fragrances such as dhātrī,
one should devotedly offer a pair of copper-colored cows to the Supreme Lord.
The rest, as previously described, yields a very great fruit:
one obtains celestial chariots resembling rubies and accompanied by elephants.
Having gone to the beautiful city of Śiva as previously described, one obtains that fruit; moreover,
when the month of Caitra has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming flour-cakes mixed with milk while his senses are restrained, [attains the same].
In this rite, one should offer a pair of cows, a *pāṭala* tree, and a very handsome bull, all well-adorned, to Śiva; the remainder of the procedure should be performed as previously described.
Having traveled by means of divine chariots yoked with horses, radiant with the luster of topaz,
they went to the beautiful city of Śiva, which is difficult to attain even for the gods.
When the month of Vaiśākha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night—
consuming flour-cakes mixed with milk while his senses are restrained,
sleeping in a cow-pen, meditating on Śiva, and wearing but a single garment during the night.
One should perform all the general observances exactly as they have been prescribed;
and on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should perform a ritual bath with ghee and other substances.
One should offer to Śiva a pair of auspicious white cows, well-adorned;
[the donor shall travel] by means of magnificent, decorated celestial vehicles possessing the luster of swans, jasmine, and the moon.
Surrounded by all those women of every form, he proceeds to the abode of Īśvara, yoked with white bulls.
When the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night shall sport for an inexhaustible time with women fragrant as blue lotuses.
Having rice mixed with milk and combined with clarified butter and curd, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture for half the night; during the day, he follows a cow.
Sitting without reclining is the *vīrāsana*.
One who constantly benefits cows and is free from egoism should perform the aforementioned rite of bathing and so forth on the full moon day.
In this rite, a pair of smoke-colored oxen,
adorned and as beautiful as great blue lotuses, should be given as a gift.
He sports for inexhaustible time with those bound upon great lions,
he who, when the month of Āṣāḍha has arrived, observes the practice of eating only at night.
One should offer parched grain flour mixed with abundant pieces of sugar-candy and water, along with milk products;
and one should present to Śiva a pair of white cows, well-adorned and auspicious.
"One should perform the general rite; indeed, everything is enjoined by the *Prakhya* [text].
Thus it is stated regarding the month of Puṣya.
"By means of vehicles resembling pure crystal, with cranes as their mounts..."
Endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, he may himself move about like Śiva.
When the month of Śrāvaṇa has arrived, he who should observe the practice of eating only at night,
subsisting on milk and sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika), being devoted to the welfare of all living beings;
One should offer a white mango tree and a pair of cattle to Śivā;
one should perform all that has been prescribed according to the general ritual procedure.
Having traveled in various great vehicles yoked with diverse horses to the divine city of Śiva previously mentioned, one obtains the aforementioned fruit.
When the month of Bhādrapada has arrived, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming only the remnants of the sacrificial oblation, and taking refuge at the foot of a tree during the day;
Dwelling at night in a sanctuary, compassionate toward all beings,
one should offer a bull with blue shoulders and a cow to Śiva.
With celestial palaces that resemble the rays of the moon, adorned with diamonds and lapis lazuli,
joined by ruddy geese, and fulfilling all desires.
Having gone to the delightful city of Śiva, which is worshipped by gods and asuras,
he sports together with enjoyments until the dissolution of all summoned beings.
The illustrious one who, with a serene mind and senses subdued, observes the practice of eating only at night during the month of Āśvayuja, consuming only ghee;
Having released before the Blessed Lady a bull with a dark-blue luster and a high-arched chest, along with a single cow well-adorned,
one should perform all the remaining rites as previously described.
At the end of his life, the self-controlled one goes to the supreme abode like Śiva,
[adorned] with [rays] resembling clear pearls and graced by sapphires.
Jīva sports with the highly fortunate Jīvakas in celestial chariots that fulfill all desires, until the dissolution of the summoned world-cycle.
And he who, during the auspicious month of Kārttika, observes the practice of eating only at night,
should eat rice with milk, being truthful in speech and having his senses subdued.
One should give a pair of Kapila cows here, with a complexion like collyrium, having performed the rite according to the previously mentioned procedure; thus, one becomes equal to Śiva.
In magnificent Great Vehicle chariots, which resemble the crests of the fire at the end of an eon and are delightful to the mind,
he moves about happily with the majestic bearing of a great lion, acting like Śiva.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, he who observes the practice of eating only at night,
consuming barley-gruel mixed with milk while his senses are fully restrained;
One should offer a divine pair of white cows, well-adorned, to Śiva; the remainder of the procedure should be undertaken according to the previously mentioned rule.
Having traveled by means of vehicles resembling white lotuses and joined with chariots drawn by white horses,
one shall go to the divine city of Śiva and become equal in power to Śiva himself.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, forbearance, compassion,
bathing three times a day, offering oblations into the fire, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at night.
One should observe the Śiva-vow through such rules as fasting on both fortnights and passing over the fourteenth and eighth lunar days.
A woman who is a devotee of Śiva will certainly become a man;
if she desires the most excellent state of womanhood, she should listen to this vow.
Thus ends the Great Vow of Śiva as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
In the auspicious month of Kārttika, she who observes the vow should subsist on a single meal a day,
remaining self-controlled through the observances of forbearance, non-violence, and other such rules.
At the end of the month, one should offer oil-cakes mixed with molasses and clarified butter;
on the eighth and fourteenth days, one should remain devoted to fasting.
In palaces resembling sapphire that fulfill all desires,
he is honored in the world of Rudra for more than ten thousand years.
Having diligently acquired enjoyments in all the worlds as they truly are,
she shall come in due course to this world and obtain a husband according to her desire.
Thus, the same rule is proclaimed for all months;
the wise know that the fruit of a single meal and fasting is equal.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, compassion, generosity, purity, restraint of the senses, worship of Śiva, fire-offerings, contentment, and the cultivation of affection.
This common dharma for all vows is recorded as tenfold:
in the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, having adorned a very clean bull with perfumes and garlands, one should offer it to Śiva.
In great vehicles yoked with bulls and attended by hosts of celestial nymphs,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand years.
In the month of Puṣya, having fashioned a Pināka bow upon a trident for the sake of the Wielder of the Pināka,
one should offer it to the Wielder of the Pināka, either in a vessel of copper, bell-metal, or other such materials.
By means of the great Puṣpaka vehicle, through the power of its divine fragrance,
one is honored in the world of Rudra for more than ten thousand years.
In the month of Māgha, having fashioned a chariot yoked with horses, adorned with rows of lamps,
and provided with a linga made of flour, one should bring it to the temple.
In vehicles resembling great chariots and yoked with white horses,
he is honored in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred thousand years.
In the month of Phālguna, having fashioned an image made of flour accompanied by a sacrificial oblation (caru),
and having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, one should install it in the temple of Īśvara with incomparable divine vehicles, filled with the sounds of singers and other musicians.
He is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a full hundred thousand years.
Having adorned Bhavakumāra with flowers in the month of Caitra and having placed him in the vessel as prescribed, one should bring him to the temple of Śiva.
In celestial chariots resembling the autumnal moon and fulfilling all desires,
he is glorified in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred thousand years.
Having fashioned Mount Kailāsa out of a measure of ground rice,
adorned with all minerals and joined by Īśvara and Umā;
One should establish in the temple of Īśvara that which is variegated with various caves, joined with a mound of salt, and endowed with all kinds of jewels.
He who performs the Kailāsa-vrata on the full moon day of Vaiśākha is honored in the world of Śiva, traveling in celestial vehicles resembling Mount Kailāsa.
Having fashioned a linga made of flour along with its pedestal in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
one should worship it with devotion using perfumes and other offerings, wrap it in a pair of garments,
and perform a vigil there adorned with various special decorations.
At dawn, one should offer [the merit] to Śiva with banners, conchs, and other [emblems];
[Śiva], by means of celestial chariots resembling pure crystal that fulfill all desires, [grants the fruit].
Having fashioned a house made of flour for the ancestors in the month of Āṣāḍha, one is glorified in the world of Śiva for more than a hundred million years.
It was filled with the essence of all seeds and possessed auspicious characteristics;
it was equipped with household utensils such as mortars and pestles,
endowed with all kinds of jewels, and adorned with female slaves, beds, and other furnishings.
Adorned with these items made of flour, including the *sādya* offerings, and illuminated by lamps and other ornaments.
It was crowded with all kinds of devotees, adorned with perfumes and garlands,
and beautifully decorated with banners and cloths that were white, red, black, and yellow.
On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, one should place a vessel containing four kinds of food mixed with red mustard seeds before Śiva.
Having prostrated before it, one should offer [the gift], which is endowed with all requisites,
along with celestial palaces of the Great Vehicle that possess a hundred stories and fulfill all desires.
He is glorified in the world of Rudra for more than a full hundred million years.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should offer a mountain of sesame seeds to the All-pervading Lord— a mountain strewn with the substance of white lime and adorned with various banners.
In resplendent, peerless, and auspicious vehicles resembling clear sapphire,
he is honored in the world of Rudra for more than a hundred million years.
Having prepared a magnificent mountain of grain in the month of Bhādrapada,
adorned with canopies, banners, umbrellas, and other ornaments, one should offer it to Śiva.
By means of magnificent Mahāyāna vehicles that resemble the rays of the sun,
one is honored in the world of Rudra for thousands of millions of years.
And having fashioned a vast mountain of fire in the month of Āśvayuja,
adorned with gold and cloth, one should dedicate it to Śiva;
[he shall travel] by means of most wonderful great vehicles, provided with excellent enjoyments.
For more than a full hundred million years, he is honored in the world of Rudra,
provided with all kinds of grain, as well as all seeds, juices, and so forth.
It is joined with all the elements, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
endowed with four peaks, and beautified by canopies and parasols.
It was exceedingly beautified with perfumes, garlands, incense, and lamps,
as well as with various dances and songs, and with conchs, lutes, and other instruments.
It was accompanied by the sacred sounds of the Vedas, as well as particularly meritorious and auspicious chants;
it was adorned with eight great banners and radiant with various beautiful flowers.
One should place Śiva, accompanied by all the gods, upon the summit of that supreme support of the three worlds named Meru, the lord of mountains.
The Daityas, Gandharvas, and Bhūtas, as well as the hosts of Siddhas and Yakṣas,
the Vidyādharas, Apsarases, Nāgas, and especially the Ṛṣis.
Having fashioned an image of a linga made of rice-flour, the wise man should place in the right hand a trident worshipped by the thirty gods.
In this manner, one should perform the rite with the weapon-mantra for all the deities in due order,
after having performed the great worship of Śiva accompanied by the *caru* oblation.
One should worship all the gods and offer oblations in the ten directions;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should afterwards feed the devotees of Śiva along with sacrificial fees.
One should offer to Rudra during the month of Kārttika an excellent mountain, prepared according to one's means and accompanied by all the ritual undertakings.
Listen to the fruit of merit for one who should perform this even once:
having become a member of a host equal to the gods, he will be endowed with virtue and beauty.
One should always wander through the world as motionless as Śiva;
that merit which was formerly described by the sages in the eternal Āgamas [is attained thereby].
One shall obtain that merit multiplied ten millionfold; there is no doubt in this matter.
[One shall travel] by means of vehicles radiant with great jewels and endowed with every kind of gem.
Accompanied by songs, dances, and instrumental music, together with celestial nymphs,
they travel in aerial chariots born of the gods, possessing a brilliance equal to ten million suns.
She was likewise praised by hosts of gods, dānavas, and gandharvas, as well as by auspicious breezes filled with the fragrance of men and women.
Becoming autonomous and omnipresent, she proceeds to the abode of the Lord;
possessing great ascetic power, she rejoices there for a hundred divine millions of aeons.
Having thus enjoyed all desired pleasures among all the gods,
she will return here upon the exhaustion of her merit and obtain a king as her husband.
"One who is meditated upon by Īśvara always becomes beautiful and fortunate.
Thus is stated in the *Śivadharmottara* the other great vow (*mahāvrata*) of the Śaivas.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Beginning in the month of Caitra, while drinking water, one should cause a stream of water to flow;
at the end of the rainy season, one should give a new oil-lamp filled with ghee.
This is known as the Dhārāvrata; it is supreme in removing all distress, generating beauty and good fortune, and destroying the pride of rival wives.
Thus ends the Dhārāvrata as described in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
In the Devīpurāṇa it is said: "In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa one should give the finest juice, and in Pauṣa, ghee, which yields great fruit."
The best of liquids is salt.
O best of sages, one should give sesame seeds in the month of Māgha, the seven kinds of grain in Phālguna,
and various garments in Caitra to a twice-born man.
In Vaiśākha, O twice-born one, wheat should be given; in Jyeṣṭha, a jar filled with water;
and in Āṣāḍha, sandalwood mixed with camphor should be given, which yields great fruit.
Fresh butter is considered appropriate in the month of Nabhas;
sweetmeats (laḍḍukas) rich in the color of jaggery and sugar are intended for Pauṣṭhapada; and, O Sage, he who offers the gift of lamps in Kārttika acquires great merit.
It is declared that one attains all desires in due course. O Sage, at the conclusion of the vow, one should cause a garland to be given according to the prescribed rite to the Goddess,
Brahmā, the Sun, or Viṣṇu, as appropriate.
O best of the twice-born, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite that which is pure by its very nature,
it should be given to one who is free from passion and devoid of desire and anger.
To one who is humble, well-behaved, and endowed with discipline,
a donor of cows obtains his desires and delightful pleasures in the worlds of Goloka.
Thus ends the monthly vow as declared in the Devīpurāṇa.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O protector of the earth, to those vows by which Viṣṇu is propitiated by men.
And even by women who have fallen into this terrible ocean of existence,
having worshipped Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, through meditative concentration, [liberation is attained].
He who eats but one meal and offers a second to the Brāhmaṇas,
having attained the month of Kārttika, acts for the pleasure of Keśava.
Whatever evil was committed by him in his youth, whether knowingly or unknowingly, he is liberated from that; there is no doubt in this matter.

By this very same procedure, having worshipped Mādhava in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa as well, he who gives [the merit] to those of the religious orders while eating but one meal a day for the sake of pleasing the Lord—
listen to me regarding his fruit.
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man in their middle age—
from that, liberation has been declared by the Supreme Self.
Likewise, he who observes a single daily meal and offers it to cows,
having worshipped Puṇḍarīkākṣa in the month of Pauṣa, is glorified.
O King, whatever sin has been committed by that person in old age for the sake of pleasing him—
whether he be a man or even a woman— he is liberated from it,
O Lord of Men, who performs this three-month vow.
By pleasing Viṣṇu, one is liberated from minor sins;
in the second year, O King, one is also liberated from secondary offenses (upapātaka).
In the same way, this vow, when performed for three months by men and women alike, effects the destruction of even the most heinous sins.
O King, it bestows fruit upon men within three years;
likewise, O King, the three states [of punishment] for the three kinds of sins are realized within three months.
The three names of the god liberate [one] from the three-year-old [sins].
Therefore, this vow is declared as the Trivikrama;
it pacifies all sins and is the supreme means of worshipping Keśava.
Thus ends the Trivikrama-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharma.
Sumantu said:
Having worshipped the Lord of the World, whether he be the Sun-god or Viṣṇu, [856]...
He eats one meal himself, and the second is offered to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having reached the month of Kārttika, one should diligently perform [this rite] for the pleasure of the Sun,
whether in the first stage of life and whether knowingly or unknowingly.
Therefore, one is liberated from committed sin; of this there is no doubt, O Vibhākara, by this very procedure in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Listen to me regarding the fruit obtained by him who, having performed worship, gives a single meal to the Brahmins for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One.
Whatever sin has been committed by a woman or a man in their middle age—
from that, liberation has been declared by the Supreme Self.
And likewise, O lord of the earth, he who observes eating only once a day and bestows [a gift] upon a Brahmin,
having duly worshipped the Sun in the month of Pauṣa;
In the same way, this vow, which destroys even great sins, has been performed by men and women for three months in the third [lunar month].
O King, it bestows fruit upon men within three years;
however, for the three states resulting from the three kinds of sins, O King, it takes three months.
The three names of the God liberate those who have been struck by the triple-planetary affliction;
for that reason, this vow is called Trivikrama.
It is the supreme propitiation of Bhāskara, which pacifies all beings.

Thus ends the Saura-Trivikrama-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "O best of kings, one should subsist on water for four months beginning with Caitra, or likewise during the months of Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍha, Māgha, or Pauṣa."

At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a water-jar accompanied by food and clothing, as well as a vessel of sesame seeds and gold; such a person is glorified in the world of Brahmā. At the end of that, one becomes a king of kings; this is here called the Vow of Water (vārivrata).
Thus ends the Vāri-vrata in the Padma Purāṇa.

Thus concludes the section on monthly vows in the Vrata-khaṇḍa of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Mahādeva, the sovereign over all kings, the lord of all faculties, and the master of all branches of knowledge.
[858] Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter:
Next, the seasonal observances (*ṛtuvratāni*).
Now, for the benefit of his friends,
Hemādri Sūri makes manifest this series of seasonal vows, which is a treasure of ritual perfection.
The one who accomplishes [all goals] and dispels misfortunes.
Markandeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme worship of the Sixfold Form (Ṣaṇmūrti).
O bull among sages, one should constantly worship Vasanta for two months.
One should worship the summer season with fruits, flowers, and astringent decoctions;
and during the rainy season, O Great King, one should observe the seasonal rite with sweet substances.
One should always worship with this: with salt during the autumn, with pungent and sour [tastes] during the winter, and likewise with bitter [tastes] during the cool season.
Likewise, one should remain a night-eater and avoid the five kinds of flavorful food;
one should also feed Brāhmaṇas with abundant clothing and other gifts.
Having observed this supremely purifying vow for one year,
one obtains the merit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice and attains the Rājasūya.
One attains all desires; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O best of performers, one obtains imperishable fruit from this vow.
That man who, having undertaken a fast, worships for one six-month period beginning on the sixth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Caitra, as prescribed—
One shall quickly obtain the eternal fruit indeed.

Thus ends the Ṣaṇmūrti-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara: Having observed the practice of eating only one meal a day during the winter season in the month of Māgha with self-restraint, one should,
at the end of Māgha, have a chariot constructed, adorned with variegated cloths.
It was yoked to four white bulls, beautifully adorned,
and graced with rows of banners, variegated chowries, and mirrors.

Having fashioned a linga together with its pedestal from rice-flour paste and having placed it in the center of the chariot, one should worship it once it has been marked with the proper characteristics.
Then, having paraded him at night along the royal highway to the accompaniment of the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments,
he should subsequently lead him to the temple of Śiva.

There, one should gradually pass the night with wakeful worship, adorned with lamps and the like, and by the offering of spectacles; then, at dawn, having performed the ceremonial bathing, one should provide food for those devoted to him.
And to the poor, the blind, and the wretched, he should give sacrificial fees according to his ability;
then he should offer a chariot endowed with splendor to Śiva.
Having eaten together with his kinsmen and having bowed to the Lord, he should go home;
this dharma, the most excellent of all gifts, is thus completed.
The vow named Śivaratha is the accomplisher of all desires and goals;
it possesses the merit found in all vows and the fruit found in all sacrifices.
All that merit shall become complete by means of the Śivaratha alone.
Resplendent in celestial chariots that shine like ten thousand suns and fulfill all desires,
he is glorified in the world of Śiva together with twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Thus ends the Śivaratha-vrata as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Pulastya said:
"The observer of the vow should avoid flowers during the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons."
And having fashioned three leaves out of gold according to one's means on the full moon day of Phālguna, one should offer them.
One should indeed give it at the proper time; may Śiva and Keśava be pleased.
