It produces fragrance for the head and bestows constant joy upon men.
"Having performed this supreme vow of fragrance, one attains the highest state.
Thus ends the Saugandhya-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
The Brahmin who provides fuel for four seasons beginning with the rainy season,
and at the end gives a cow filled with ghee, goes to the supreme Brahman.
The Vaiśvānara-vrata, known as the destroyer of all sins,
is thus described in the Padma Purāṇa.
[861] He who, during the summer, [places] jars filled with pure water upon Śiva...
He who causes the stream of milk to flow attains the state of Brahmā.
Thus ends the Galatikā-vrata as described in the Śivarahasya.

Thus concludes the section on seasonal vows (ṛtuvratāni) within the Vrata-khaṇḍa of the Caturvarga-cintāmaṇi, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Hemādri, who is the sovereign of all faculties, a master of all branches of knowledge, and the supreme king of great kings under the illustrious Mahādeva.
[862] Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Now, the vows for a year:
that wondrous moonlight which [awakens] the buds of the minds of the wise.
By Hemādri, for the benefit of living beings,
this collection of various vows is now being set forth.
Pulastya said: Having performed the *nakta* fast for eight nights, one should give a golden discus and trident, along with two garments, to a brahmin who maintains a household together with a cow.
Having bowed with devotion to Śiva and Keśava, may they be pleased;
this very vow is indeed the destroyer of great sins.
Thus ends the Ḍhava-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having observed silence during the twilight prayers, at the conclusion of the year, a man [should give] a jar of ghee.
One should present a pair of garments, sesame seeds, and a bell to a Brāhmaṇa.
One goes to the world of Sarasvatī and is born again right here;
this is the one called Sārasvata, which bestows beauty and knowledge.
Thus ends the Sārasvata-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. That man who, for a full year, eats but one meal a day, practices non-violence toward all beings, and is devoted solely to Vāsudeva;
One should recite "Namo 'stu Vāsudevāya" eight hundred times during the day;
thereby, one shall obtain the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
For ten thousand years he is honored in the heavenly world;
having returned here from that state, he attains greatness through his actions.
Thus ends the vow of eating a single meal (*ekabhakta-vrata*) as declared in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Pulastya said:
Having performed the smearing [of the ground] before Śambhu and Keśava...
Furthermore, one should give as many as eight cows, along with water and ghee.
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
having been reborn, he becomes a sovereign king, a lord of the entire earth.
This is known as the Śraddhā-vrata, which brings about manifold auspiciousness.
Thus ends the vow of faith as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Pulastya said:
Having bowed down to the Aśvattha tree, the Sun, and the Gaṅgā, while remaining silent in one place—
A man, free from envy, should observe a single meal on the eighth day.
At the conclusion of the vow, having honored a Brahmin couple accompanied by three cows, one should give a golden tree; he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
[864] Abiding in a celestial chariot in heaven, he is praised by throngs of apsarases;
this is known as the Kīrtivrata, which bestows fame upon the earth.
Thus ends the Kīrti-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing with ghee for Keśava and Śiva,
as well as for the Brāhmaṇa, Bhāskara, Gaurī, and Lambodara;
One should fashion an auspicious lotus with unbroken grains upon a mandala of cow dung;
at the conclusion of the rite, a golden lotus accompanied by sesame seeds and a cow should be given.
It lasts for one year.
One should give pure [food] measuring eight finger-breadths; such a person is glorified in the world of Śiva. This is called the Sāma-vrata for one who chants the Sāman.
Thus ends the Sāma-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Regarding the consumption of betel and other such acts, she who gives the Gaurī-leaf—
the leaf of the betel vine— is meant.
Combined with betel nut powder, it is for women or for men.
At the end of the year, however, he offers a golden vessel with silver fruit and leaves,
or one filled with powder made of pearls.
She incurs neither misfortune nor the loss of happiness;
this is the vow of the leaf, which bestows the world of Gaurī.
Thus ends the Patra-vrata as described in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
[865] Having performed the ceremonial bathing of Viṣṇu or Śiva with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta),
one should, at the end of the year, again present a cow accompanied by the five nectars.
By giving gold, a conch shell, and a pair of white garments to a brahmin, one attains the divine world of heaven; this is remembered as the *dhṛtivrata*.
Thus ends the *dhṛtivrata* as described in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*.
Pulastya said:
"Having avoided meat throughout the year, a man should become a giver of a cow at the end of the year."
In the same way, by giving a golden deer, one obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
this is called the vow of non-violence (ahiṃsāvrata), and at the end of the kalpa, one becomes a lord of the earth.

Thus ends the vow of non-violence (*ahiṃsāvrata*) as declared in the *Padmapurāṇa*. Having renounced a life of ease, one who gives a cow at the conclusion of the year attains the sovereignty of the Yakṣas; this is here called the "vow of the mouth" (*mukhavratam*).

Thus ends the vow of the mouth (*mukhavratam*) as declared in the *Padma Purāṇa*. Furthermore, he who, eating only at night on alternate days, offers a golden blue lotus together with a vessel of sugar at the end of the year, accompanied by a bull—
"He should give"—this is the ellipsis.
He indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu; this is remembered as the Nīla-vrata.

Thus ends the Nīla-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. [866] One who eats but a single meal for a year and gives away vessels filled with various foods and fruits shall dwell in the world of Śiva for a kalpa; this is known as the Prāpti-vrata.

Thus ends the Prāpti-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. He who offers a lamp at the twilight rituals and avoids oil for an entire year should, at the conclusion of that year, present lamps, a golden discus, and a trident.
By giving a pair of garments to a Brahmin, one becomes radiant in this world and attains the realm of Rudra; this is known as the Dīptivrata.
Thus ends the Dīptivrata as declared in the Padmapurāṇa. One who subsists on air for a year should, at the conclusion, give a milch cow;
he attains the world of Śakra—this is remembered as the Śakravrata.

Thus ends the Śakra-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. He who passes a year eating only one meal a day and then gives away a cow together with a bull made of sesame seeds, shall attain the abode of Śaṅkara.
This is known as the Rudra-vrata, which destroys both sin and sorrow.
Thus ends the Rudra-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, he who burns two thousand palas of [incense] known as māhiṣa for a full year shall become equal to Nandin unto me."
Starting from nine palas, one should reduce the quantity of milk by one pala each day.
Thus ends the Śambhu-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. Furthermore, he who offers milk-rice with ghee to the southern image for one year shall become equal to Nandin.
Then, when the year was complete, having observed a fast and performed a vigil,
he worshipped Maheśāna with the great ablutions and other rites.

One should give land, a bed, and a milch cow to a Brahmin. This meritorious vow, which destroys all sins, was performed with devotion for one year by Nandin, and for that same duration it was offered [to the deity].
Thus is the Maheśvara-vrata described in the Skanda Purāṇa:
he who, for a full year, eats [only once] daily and remains ever vigilant,
having offered [the food] to the ancestors and the gods, shall become the sole sovereign on earth.
"He eats upon the earth"—this is the grammatical construction. Thus ends the vow of using the earth as a plate (*bhūbhājanavrata*) as declared in the *Padmapurāṇa*.
[This was composed] for the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Mahādeva, the sovereign lord of all faculties and master of all branches of knowledge...
In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri, within the section on Vows (*Vratakhanda*), the annual vows.
[868] Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Now, the miscellaneous vows (prakīrṇavrata):
Hemādri, whose devotion to the Lord of Murāri was fully awakened and who had studied all the Vedas and the treatises on Dharma;
Having descended to uplift the entire world without exception,
he describes the miscellaneous topics in sequence.
To Vāsudeva, the God of gods, the Teacher of the world, the Lord of the universe, the cause of its preservation and destruction, who was seated comfortably on Śvetadvīpa.
Having prostrated before Mahādeva, Hari, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary,
[one obtains] health of body, sovereignty, and a husband equal to the god of love.
Through that [practice], there is indeed constant ease of understanding and never a separation from it;
whether it be that gift, or that vow, or even worship, propitiation, and so forth.
The dark-eyed Lakṣmī spoke softly to her husband:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, out of compassion for the worlds, I wish to ask you something; please show me favor."
O Lord of Gods, tell me of some vow that bestows beauty and good fortune,
by the performance of which one may obtain the fruit of all sacred fords.
By which [means] sons and grandsons, a home endowed with all prosperity,
bodily health, sovereignty, and a husband equal to Kāmadeva [are obtained].
Indeed, through that, there shall be eternal non-separation from the vision of bliss;
whether it be that gift, or that vow, or even the majesty of the sacred ford.
O best of gods, tell me that which, as soon as it is performed, will surely bring about all success— a secret more secret than secrets.
Viṣ� out of affection for his son, has not even told this vow to Pradyumna. I shall tell it to you; of this there is no doubt—it is the most excellent of all vows.
O beautiful lady, just as the sun is among luminous bodies, Garuḍa among birds,
the Gaṅgā among rivers, and the Brāhmaṇa among the social orders,
so is this vow said to be the most excellent.
Neither the Ganges, nor Kurukṣetra, nor Kāśī, nor Puṣkara are purifiers, O noble lady, to the same extent as this supreme vow.
In former times, this supreme vow was performed by the goddess Gaurī together with the high-souled Śaṅkara;
it was performed by Rāma together with Sītā, by Nala together with Damayantī,
and by Kṛṣṇa along with all the Pāṇḍavas.
By Rambhā, Menā, Paulomī, Satyabhāmā, Śāṇḍilī, Arundhatī, Urvaśī, and Devadattā;
O Goddess, this most excellent and unsurpassed vow was performed by Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī,
and indeed by other women as well.
Therefore, I shall describe to you that which destroys all sins, which is pleasing to Viṣṇu, delightful, and the most excellent of vows; listen.
The killer of a Brahmin is released from sin, as are the drinker of liquor, the striker with a weapon,
the one who approaches the wife of his teacher, and whoever associates with these.
One who uses false weights and measures, one who sells a maiden through fraud,
one who has sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, one who eats meat, and the husband of a *vṛṣalī*— [870].
One who seizes land, a false witness, and one who defiles a maiden—by all these great sins he is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
Therefore, with every effort, this supreme vow should be performed.
The vow named Kāñcanākhyā-putrī, the purifying oil-vow (tailakya-pāvana),
the third day of the bright fortnight, the eleventh day of the dark fortnight, and the full moon day.
O illustrious lady, on the day of the sun's transit, on the new moon, or on the eighth lunar day—
on these festival days, the auspicious city named Kāñcana should be given as a gift.
O beloved, having bathed in the forenoon in pure water such as that of a river, one who observes the vow should perform the application of clay according to this procedure.

O Earth, you were formerly lifted up by Viṣṇu in his playful form for the benefit of the worlds; you are saluted as the bestower of success and the fulfillment of desires. Therefore, being thus saluted, take away my sin born of many lifetimes.
The mantra for touching the clay:
"O Waters, you are the source of all things, created by Viṣṇu himself;
together with the sacred bathing sites (tīrthas), grant me your presence now."
The consecration of water:
Having bathed according to this rite and returned home,
the observer of the vow should not speak with backbiters, the violent, the sinful, or those who associate with the wicked.
Having avoided heretics, those engaged in improper occupations, and those who revile the gods and Brahmins,
and having washed his hands and feet, he should indeed perform the cleansing of his teeth.
One should observe the rule for fasting or, alternatively, for eating only at night;
then, taking a preeminent conch shell adorned with gold, one should take water.
Having consecrated the water with the mantra "Namo bhagavate vāsudevāya" and becoming pure, one should worship the water while muttering the syllable "Hari."
An altar made of Śamī wood, provided with four pillars,
measuring four cubits in size, and very beautiful, should be constructed.
The pillars should be wrapped in cloth, adorned with excellent canopies,
provided with flower garlands, and consecrated with a divine form.
In the center, however, a mandala called "lotus" should be made with beautiful colors;
and in the middle of that mandala, there should be a most splendid and auspicious throne.
Having placed a seat there, one should place a lotus upon it;
above that, one should install the Lord Janārdana, joined with Lakṣmī.

One should place a beautiful water-filled pitcher in front; one should diligently designate it by the name "Ocean of Milk. [The other vessels] should be made of one *pala* each, according to one's own means.

The term *catvāripalāny asyām* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound used distributively (*vīpsā*), similar to the word *saptavarṇa*. Regarding this distributive usage, there are houses and houses falling into the sixteen [sections], making seventeen; this is according to the rule for the Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, the central house is the eighth, being the house of the Preceptor (*ācārya*). The outer arrangement is like that of the outer houses. Thus, there is gold weighing one hundred and forty-four *palas*, and an equal amount of silver.
The pillars should be made of jewels and provided with ten inner chambers (*aurasa*).
One should have a rampart constructed of gold, silver, or even of flour.
The lead should be made from flour; the wise man should place sweetmeats upon the pinnacles of the temple and should encircle that city on all sides with most beautiful cloths.
In front of that, one should construct an archway using plantain trunks;
it should be adorned with flowers, fashioned according to one's means and in great detail.
The auspicious city should be established by Brahmins who have mastered the four Vedas;
in its center, one should install Viṣṇu together with Lakṣmī made of gold.
The eyes should be made of jewels, and the teeth well-adorned;
one should fashion ornaments there consisting of pearls.
The limb should be fashioned from gold and endowed with a conch, discus, and mace;
having bathed it with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
The Brahmin, with Vedic mantras as well as those spoken in the Purāṇas and others,
[worships] the feet for Vāsudeva and the ankles for Saṃkarṣaṇa.

One should worship the two knees of Hari with the mantra "To the progenitor of the three worlds," the [single] knee with "To the Lord of the three worlds," and the secret place with "To the one consisting of knowledge."
"To Dāmodara" for the hips; "to Viṣṇurūpin" for the belly;
"to Padmanābha" for the navel; and "to Śrīvatsadhārin" for the chest.
The throat to the one whose navel is the Kaustubha gem, the mouth to the face of sacrifice (Yajñamukha),
the arms to the destroyer of the Daityas, and the weapons to his own names.
One should worship the crest-lock of the God of gods with the mantra of Īśāna;
having fully worshipped Śrī with her own mantras, one should then honor the world-protectors.
The nine planets should indeed be worshipped, and one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) for them;
Durgā and Gaṇapati should also be worshipped, and one should arrange a fire sacrifice for those two as well.
O Agni, one should cause to be offered incomparable food-offerings cooked in ghee,
as well as milk-rice, ghee-filled cakes, sweetmeats, and likewise small pastries.
One should arrange fruits and other offerings here according to the specific place and time;
one should offer lamps in the ten directions, adorned with flowers on both sides.
O large-eyed one, one should cause [the offerings] to be given with ghee while reciting the root mantra;
sixteen jars should be prepared, adorned with white cloths.
One should cause sixteen delightful cooked foods to be presented separately, each accompanied by sweetmeats and gold.
O beautiful one, various kinds of fruits should be offered there;
one should also place lamps made of copper within those jars.
One should diligently honor the Brahmins along with their wives with various ornaments according to the prescribed rule, and one should perform sixteen recitations of the mantra.
One should consecrate [the water] with the mantra beginning "Sahasraśīrṣa" and so forth;
regarding the Brahmin as Viṣṇu, one should worship women as being the form of Lakṣmī.
An umbrella, sandals, garments, ornaments, fruits, the seven types of grain, and food as desired should be given to those accompanied by their wives, with the thought: "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me."
There, the preceptor, having risen while the auspicious song is being performed,
should take the patron by the arms and lead him into the presence of the deity.
For the welfare of the patron, the wise and all-knowing preceptor, together with the assistant priest, should bind the eyes of the patron with a white cloth.
With his eyes bound, the wise teacher should say this:
"Behold this city named Kāñcanā, which grants all desires."
"Adorned with excellent garments, beautiful, and the destroyer of suffering and misfortune"—
having spoken thus, O illustrious lady, one should then cast off the garment.
Then, having cast a handful of flowers, he should behold the auspicious city;
O Goddess, having seen that city, the sacrificer and the priest [should proceed].
Taking a golden vessel, or one of silver or even copper,
or else taking a conch shell, O beautiful lady, in the event that no vessel is available.
O Dear One, one should cast the five jewels there, as well as water, perfumes, fruit, white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, dūrvā grass, yellow pigment, and curd.
Then, O lady of virtuous vows, the water of honor (arghya) should be offered with this mantra,
with a mind purified by devotion, to the two deities Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa.
Having gone to the ground upon his knees, he should utter this mantra:
"The Goddess was fashioned from gold by Viṣṇu and by Śaṅkara."
The Goddess was worshipped by Pārvatī, Gāyatrī, Skanda, Vaiśravaṇa,
and Yama, out of a desire for the victory of Dharma.

"O Goddess, being honored, grant me good fortune, sons, wealth, and beauty; accept this *arghya* offered by me and bestow happiness upon me. Having thus offered the *arghya*, one should then light lamps.
One should keep a vigil there with song, dance, and other such activities;
by keeping a meritorious vigil for Viṣṇu, one obtains the fruit of a hundred sacrifices.
When the pure dawn has arrived, having performed the daily worship and other rites,
one should likewise honor the preceptor with garments and ornaments.
Having diligently fed and honored him along with his wife and sons,
one should provide him with a bed equipped with its furnishings and accompanied by garments and sandalwood paste.
There, the one of good vows should give that golden city, complete with all its furnishings, to the preceptor while reciting this mantra.
May the divine couple Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa, who grant the fruits of all desires,
bestow my wish through the gift of this city of gold.
O Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa, you who are both knowledge and the object of knowledge, and who are stainless;
by the gift of this city of gold, grant me the supreme bestower of worldly enjoyment.
Having given [the gift], a cow should then be presented to the preceptor with this mantra;
furthermore, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to them so that they may be satisfied.
Having thus asked for their forgiveness and bowed down to them again and again—
especially to those who were helpless, deaf, lame, and blind—
One should diligently give a daily portion of fodder to the cows once;
there, one should utter these words: "May Viṣṇu be pleased with me."
Having performed all this in such a manner, he should then partake of the breaking of the fast there,
accompanied by his beloved mantras, his family, and his sons and grandsons.
When this has been performed, the merit that arises is impossible for me to describe,
even in thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Having reached the world of Brahmā, the observer of vows rejoices like Brahmā;
from the world of Brahmā, he goes to the world of Rudra, and beyond that, to the world of Indra.
Then, O Goddess, having exhausted worldly existence, he shall attain my own realm;
there, O beauty of the three worlds, he shall enjoy vast pleasures.
When the person dissolves into the *maddeha*, he attains immortality;
indeed, he is born as a sovereign king in a noble family.
Whoever should constantly hear this vow as it is being recited, having delivered a thousand generations of their kin, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
In the past, you performed this vow known as Kāñcanapurī;
by the grace of that vow, I have been obtained as your husband, honored by the three worlds.
Thus ends the Kāñcanapurī-vrata as declared in the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Janārdana, [please explain] the perfection of human vows."
Grant me this favor; you ought to tell me this secret meaning.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, King of the Kurus!
At the conclusion of these secrets, I shall declare to you this supreme vow."
That vow is indeed called "Complete," for it bestows its fruit perfectly when it is observed by men and women throughout its full duration.
That must certainly be performed by those who desire the full fruit,
should any part of their vow be broken through negligence.
O Pāṇḍava, all that shall become complete through this vow,
even if it has been marred by various calamities and great delusion, O King.
Whatever vow may have been broken by obstacles or Vināyakas, all that shall become complete; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt.
A skilled artisan should have an image fashioned from gold, silver, or bronze;
that divine form should be well-crafted for one whose vows have been broken.
Indeed, that vow was undertaken by a man and a woman in bodily form;
yet nothing at all was accomplished, for by fate everything remained just as it was.
[The deity is] two-armed, seated upon a lotus, gentle, and with a smiling face.

The description of the forms of the male and female [deities], beginning with "two-armed" and so forth, refers to that form which is known through vows performed in other lifetimes that have now been forgotten; and for those [vows] as well, this same expiation is to be understood.
And on that very same day, it was completed by the artisan;
then, when another month had arrived, the Brahmin [performed the rite] in his house according to the prescribed rule.
One should bathe [the deity] with milk, curd, ghee, milk-essence, and water;
one should worship with fragrant sandalwood, flowers, and other blossoms.
Having placed [the image] at the mouth of a jar filled with water, [one should worship it] with sandalwood paste,
incense, lamps, unbroken grains (akṣata), cloths, weapons, and offerings of oblations.
And one should offer the *arghya* by his name with this mantra, O Pāṇḍava,
while standing with palms joined in reverence, as an expiation for being deficient in the fast.
Furthermore, show compassion once more toward me who has sought refuge,
who am terrified by the fear of the next world, and whose broken vows have been cast aside.

Grant me your grace; may my vow be complete. Whatever flaw there is in my austerity, whatever flaw in my vow, or whatever flaw in this broken vow—by your grace, O God, may all that become flawless for me.
Svāhā! Salutation to [Name] Deva.
One should perform the rite in the east, south, and north.
To the world-protectors above and below, salutation!
"This is for the guest, this is water for the feet, and this is the food offering; salutations, salutations to you!
Having spoken thus, one should then touch the feet, the knees, the waist, and the head.
Then, O son of Kuntī, one should duly present to the twice-born the chest, the belly, the heart, the back, as well as the skin and the hair.
One should worship that deity and thereafter ask for forgiveness:
"You have been worshipped according to my ability; salutations be unto you, O Supreme among Gods."
"O Lord, grant me the accomplishment of this task pertaining to both this world and the next.
Having thus asked for forgiveness from that divine image according to the prescribed rite, [he should proceed].
Standing facing the east, the Brahmin should receive [the gift] with darbha grass in his hand;
the donor, facing north, should place it into the hand of the Brahmin.
The Brahmin should also bestow that vow with this mantra:
"Speech is complete, the mind is complete, and the body is complete through the vow;
by the grace of you who are complete, may my heart's desire be fulfilled."
Whatever the brahmins speak, the deities rejoice in;
for the brahmins consist of all the gods, and their word is never otherwise.
The water was turned into milk, fire was made all-consuming,
and even Indra, the thousand-eyed, was brought under control by the high-souled Brahmins.
By the word of the Brahmins, the sin of killing a Brahmin is destroyed;
one obtains the full fruit of a horse sacrifice—of this there is no doubt.
By the compositions of Vyāsa and Vālmīki, by the words of Parāśara and Vasiṣṭha,
and likewise by the utterances of Garga, Gautama, Dhaumya, Atri,
Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Nārada, and others, may my vow be fulfilled.
Having taken [the vessel] according to such a procedure, the Brāhmaṇa should depart;
the donor himself should send everything to the Brāhmaṇa’s house.
Then, the wise man who performs this vow even once with devotion should offer the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) by means of food and other offerings.
That vow which was previously undertaken attains completion;
even a broken vow reaches fulfillment when the presiding deity of the vow is pleased.
Then, when it is completed, the performer shall become a practitioner with all his limbs perfected;
he shall be an enjoyer of prosperity, possessed of radiant fame, and one whose desires are fulfilled.
Having remained in the mortal world for a hundred years, one shall thereafter become immortal in heaven,
acting according to one's own will and honored by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa.
Having remained for a long time in the heavenly world, one shall again attain liberation;
this expiation was proclaimed to me in the past by Garga, O Lord.
"In Gokula, which is crowded with herds of cows, I indeed observed this fast in my childhood;
in the same way, O son of Kuntī, you too should perform this vow in its entirety."
Those [roots of merit] which were broken by a person under the influence of pride and delusion,
even accompanied by envy, in other lifetimes as well;
For one who is devoted to complete worship,
all vows become givers of their full fruits.
Thus concludes the complete vow as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
"Excellent, excellent, O great Brahmin! You are a devotee of Śiva and one of noble vows."
O knower of reality, I shall speak of silence, which is practiced even by the gods.
Listen, my child, I shall proclaim the vow of silence (*mauna*), which accomplishes all aims.
This vow of silence is of great merit; therein, one should avoid uttering "huṃ" or "huṃ."
If a "huṃ" sound escapes from men at the time of eating, it is as if all of it were liquor and meat; therefore, one should avoid such sounds while observing silence.
One should avoid violence there through action, mind, or speech;
indeed, by the power of this silence, even the gods have gone to the third heaven.
Non-violent, patient, peaceful, and established in the vow of silence,
he who observes silence for eight months, or even for six months, [attains the fruit].
One should practice for three months, and likewise for one month;
then again for half a month, or else for twelve days.
A silent practitioner should eat with effort six, five, three, or even one morsel;
when that vow is completed, he remains concentrated in the observance of silence.
Having fashioned a linga made of sandalwood, one should sprinkle it with the six limbs;
then, beginning with yellow orpiment, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
One should offer agallochum incense and then again perform prostrations;
having bowed down with hands, feet, and head, one should present it.
According to one's means, one should cause a golden bell to be offered;
one should fasten it before Śiva, for it is exceedingly dear to Śiva.
It was adorned with rows of banners and five kinds of beautiful jewels,
and with many-colored flower garlands hanging down in various ways.
One should attach a bronze bell to the corners of the pavilion; one should likewise bind three at each of the four cardinal points and one at the center, according to one's capacity.
One should also present a very beautiful vessel made of bell-metal or iron before Śiva,
and feed Brahmins who are devotees of Śiva.
Milk-rice mixed with ghee, drenched in honey and meat, along with various kinds of foods— both solid and soft, as well as those to be licked and drunk, and thick gruels.
Having eaten well-prepared *maṇḍakas* mixed with sweet milk,
one should finish them completely, leaving no remainder, for those who have gone forth.
And one should give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, avoiding stinginess regarding wealth;
O Brahmin, that [fee] belongs to whichever [deity] it may be, in due order.
One should constantly and repeatedly utter words of peace before the devotee of Śiva;
having placed that liṅga in a copper vessel, it should be adorned with flowers.
Carrying that vessel upon his head, remaining silent and composed,
he should proceed by the royal road as far as the precinct of Śiva.
Having circumambulated Śivā three times in a clockwise direction,
one should enter the inner sanctum and place [the image] to the right of the deity.
Having worshipped him again and again from all sides with perfumes and flowers,
and having thereafter bowed with prostrations, he should pay homage with his head to the ground.
O great sage, I have declared to you the very rule of silence;
by the majesty of this silence, even the gods attained the state of Śiva.
For thousands of divine years and hundreds of divine years,
as well as for a hundred million divine years, he was surrounded by Rudra-maidens.
With millions upon millions of celestial palaces crowded together in countless tens of millions,
they were adorned with staircases of diamond and crystal, and pillars possessing the luster of emerald.
He was surrounded by tens of millions upon tens of millions of beings, all divine and made of gold, adorned with forest garlands, and with the tips of their hands grasping fly-whisks.
Filled with divine fragrances and endowed with garlands and fruits,
he dwells happily in the city of Śiva in such celestial chariots as these.
For at the end of his time, King Amitavikrama will indeed come here—
he who is eloquent, fortunate, glorious, handsome, and pleasing to behold.
Endowed with a righteous intellect and proficient in all the scriptures,
this vow of silence (mauna-vrata) has been proclaimed as the means for accomplishing all desires and goals;
it is revealed as easily performed by everyone on earth who possesses the necessary capability.
Knowledge is the destroyer of non-dharma; it is primordial, liberation, beginningless, immediate, and singular;
it is auspicious, the Lord of the entire world, and the bringer of peace.
The Lord, who is imperishable and subtle, yet possesses a body that is not subtle.
Wearing a garland of human heads hanging down,
bearing the half-moon upon his matted locks that are tawny all over,
possessing ten arms and three eyes, he is the remover of sins.
Wearing earrings radiant with gems and bearing serpents,
he possesses excellent feet graced by beautiful anklets; the soles of his feet rest upon a lotus.
I invoke Śiva, who is adorned by the jewels in the rows of crowns of the Suras and Asuras; salutations to the peaceful Śiva, the cause of the three causes.
It is recited in all the scriptures, and especially in the Vedas,
as the soul of meditation, concentration, and yoga, for the sake of attaining both the higher and the lower manifestations.
Whoever recites this hymn and worships it with devotion,
neither the malevolent planets nor even the most excellent of planets shall cause him any affliction.
Verbal and mental sin is destroyed; there is no doubt about this. Thus, he who extends the meritorious vow of silence to Maheśvara is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Rudra.
Thus ends the vow of silence as declared in the *Śivadharma*.
O best of gods, I shall tell you that which I have indeed ascertained from the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and *Purāṇas*; to whom else could it be taught?
Having bathed at the morning twilight and sipped water near a Pippala tree,
he who gives a vessel of sesame seeds need not grieve over what has been done or left undone.
For this is the highest of all vows, the destroyer of all sins;
known as the "Vow of the Son," it has not been revealed by me to anyone.
Thus ends the Putravrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.

At the conclusion of the Kṛcchra penance, one should give a pair of cows and provide food according to one's ability; one attains the station of Śaṅkara through the Brahmins. This is remembered as the Prājāpatya vow.
The grammatical construction is: "one goes to the state of Śaṅkara.
Thus ends the Prājāpatya vow as declared in the Padma Purāṇa:
having worshipped the divine couple at the three junctions of the day while fasting, one should honor them with ornaments.
By giving a cow, one obtains wealth; through the moon-vow (induvrata), one attains liberation in this world.

Thus ends the Indu-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. Having installed Śambhu accompanied by Gaurī, Janārdana together with Lakṣmī, and Sūrya accompanied by his queen, according to the prescribed rites—
Together with an incense burner, a bell joined with a bowl.
A vessel is a lamp-vessel.
He who gives one to the best of the twice-born, having honored it with white flowers,
and having given it along with a sacrificial fee while bowing down again and again;
Because of the plural number in the phrase "of the lords of the twice-born," there is a separate offering for each pair, as well as the triad beginning with incense for each pair.
This is the vow known as Devīvrata, which bestows a divine body.

Thus ends the Devī-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. He who, having fasted for a month, gives a beautiful cow to a Brahmin, goes to the station of the Lord of All; this is remembered as the Bhīma-vrata.

Thus ends the Bhīmavrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. Furthermore, he who performs the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and offers a golden moon shall attain this Candravrata, which bestows the world of the Moon.
Thus ends the Candra-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa:
He who, fasting for a fortnight, gives two tawny cows to a Brahmin,
attains the world of Brahmā, being highly honored by gods and asuras.
At its conclusion, one becomes a king of kings; this is known as the Prabhāvrata.

Thus ends the Prabhā-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. Having fashioned a golden Brahmāṇḍa accompanied by a heap of sesame seeds, one should become a giver of sesame for three days and satisfy the fire and the twice-born.
Having honored a Brahmin couple adorned with garlands, garments, and ornaments, one should say according to one's ability:
"May the Soul of the Universe be pleased," offering at least three palas.
On an auspicious day, he who gives [this gift] attains the Supreme Brahman and is not born again;
this is known as the Brahma-vrata, which bestows the fruit of Nirvana upon men.
Thus ends the section on Brahmāvarta as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
He who gives away a cow with two faces (ubhayamukhī) accompanied by abundant gold,
and remains for one day observing the milk-vow (payovrata), goes to the supreme abode.
This is called the Vasuvrata, after which a return [to worldly existence] is difficult to obtain.
Thus ends the Vasu-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa. Hereafter, O dear one, I shall describe the two feet of Goddess Nandā, by which she is quickly pleased through this great vow.
When wooden sandals are to be prepared for one suffering from hemorrhoids,
they should be worshipped with mangoes, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and bilva leaves, accompanied by the recitation of mantras, according to the prescribed rites for pacification.
Having worshipped the Goddess with devotion upon a sacrificial mound or in images,
one should offer her to a Brahmin or to virgins out of that same devotion;
thus one is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Durgā.
Then, upon his death, the one of great wisdom shall become a lord of the Vidyādharas;
in time, having returned here to this earth, he shall become the best of kings.
Thus ends the vow of the two Nandās as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
Having fasted for seven nights, one should give a jar of ghee to a twice-born man.
This is proclaimed as the excellent vow that bestows the world of Brahmā.
Thus ends the Varavrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa.
For seven days, she should eat only one meal a day and feed unmarried girls here;
having worshipped Pārvatī with devotion using perfumes, flowers, and ointments.
Having prostrated, one should bid farewell to the goddess Kumudā with excellent betel leaves, vermilion, and a coconut fruit, saying, "May she be pleased."
One should worship each goddess for as long as seven days;
then, when the seventh [day] has arrived, one should invite those same seven.
Having fed six [brahmins] with food according to one's ability,
and having adorned them with ornaments, garlands, garments, earrings, and finger-rings;
Having worshipped Kumudā, Mādhavī, Gaurī, Bhavānī, Pārvatī, Umā, and Ambikā, one should separately present a mirror to each.
One should honor a single Brahmin, saying, "May it be accomplished for me. By performing the auspicious vow named Saptasundaraka, which removes sin,
one attains beauty as well as incomparable good fortune.
Thus ends the Saptasundara-vrata as declared in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Nandikeśvara said:
"O best of sages, hereafter I shall declare this supreme secret."
Endowed with a preeminent merit, it is practiced by all the gods.
By Brahmā, Viṣṇu, the Goddess, Skanda, Indra, and Yama;
and by Varuṇa, Āditya, Soma, Agni, Marut, Dhanañjaya, and Nārada.
By Dharmarāja, Strī, Śukra, and the lunar mansions;
by Mars, Saturn, Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Bṛhaspati, Budha, and the others.
By Śveta, Agastya, Dadhīca, and all the other supreme sages;
by Bhārgava, Atri, Mahākāla, Caṇḍeśvara, and the lords of the Gaṇas.
By Vṛṣa, Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, Kulika, Ananta,
Takṣaka, Śaṅkha, Padma, Mahāpadma, and other great serpents as well.
By the Siddhas, Yakṣas, Kimpuruṣas, and the high-souled Vasus;
and also by the Apsarases, Daityas, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and hosts of Bhūtas.
Just as the auspicious state, which transcends all other states,
was attained by me through the grace of Śiva, so too listen now to that which is supreme among injunctions.
Having bathed the liṅga with water scented with white sandalwood and having smeared it [with unguents],
one should worship it with white, blooming lotuses and prostrate before it.
Having placed the smallest liṅga in the middle of a mass of filaments— within a stainless lotus, a spotless moon, a flawless, flowering, wealthy, beautiful, and delightful [space].
Having bathed an auspicious image made of all fragrances, the size of a thumb, according to the prescribed rite, one should worship it with bilva leaves before the Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Near Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
one should place aloe-wood on the right side, realgar to the west,
sandalwood to the north, and yellow orpiment to the east.
One should worship with auspicious fragrances and various flowers;
one should offer incense of black agallochum, as well as guggulu mixed with clarified butter.
One should also provide fine, bright, and new garments,
as well as milk-rice mixed with ghee, and one should cause lamps of ghee to be lit.
Having offered everything with the mantra, one should then proceed clockwise around [the deity];
having bowed with devotion to the Lord of Gods and praised him, one should finally ask for forgiveness.
And one who has taken refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti should offer that liṅga, accompanied by all ritual offerings, to Śiva with the Śiva-mantra.
To that Śiva who has taken refuge in Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
by this method, the gods attained the status of all deities,
the Goddess attained the state of being the Goddess, and Skanda attained lordship.
Indra attained the sovereignty over the gods, and the Gaṇas attained the status of Gaṇas;
even so, he who worships the auspicious lotus made of fragrance as a Liṅga.
Completely liberated from all evil, he attains Śiva alone.
This supreme secret vow, the great vow of the Śiva-liṅga, has been declared by me to you because of your devotion; it must not be given to just anyone.
Thus ends the Śivaliṅgavrata as declared in the Śivadharmottara.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O God of gods, O highly fortunate one, out of a desire for the welfare of children—
Tell me the ritual for a birthday celebration, especially that of kings.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: The great sage Pārāśarya, born from the rites of his ancestors,
went to Prayāga, that excellent holy site on the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Having performed his bath according to the prescribed rites and having also offered libations to the ancestors,
he bowed to the god Mādhava and beheld the great sage there.
Having worshipped Sanatkumāra, the lord of yogis who dwells in Satyaloka, according to the prescribed rites, he engaged in captivating conversations with him.
At the conclusion of the discourse, O illustrious one, the sage Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, respectfully inquired for the benefit of all the worlds.
Sanatkumāra said: Every month, the wise joyfully perform the rite of celebrating the child's growth; this is observed continuously until the completion of the year.
Kumudā, Mādhavī, Gaurī, Rudrāṇī, Pārvatī,
Umā, Kālī, Sarasvatī, and Sāvitrī, the beloved of Brahmā.
[890] Satī, Saṃjñā, and likewise Medhā, endowed with Puṣṭi and Tuṣṭi;
Jayantī by name is the eighty-sixth, who protects the children of kings from fear.
Having drawn them in the center of the sun, they should be worshipped with diligence;
one may draw them either with a paste of turmeric or with saffron.
With fragrant perfumes and flowers, with lamps, garments, and offerings,
with charming fruits and various kinds of cooked foods and edibles.
One should hold a great festival there with the sounds of musical instruments and the chanting of the Vedas;
having smeared a pure area, one should install the Sun according to the prescribed rite.
Having established Kumudā and the others individually with unbroken grains and sandalwood paste,
they should be worshipped by their names, and the boy should be bathed.
O best of sages, when the rite of blessing a child occurs, the mother and father should worship the Lord of Beings (Śiva), who is adorned with all ornaments.
O Brahmin, the family priest should perform the worship during the rite for the king’s prosperity;
he should prepare bamboo vessels dedicated to Kumuda and the other deities.
To each individual, one should give sixteen wealthy [attendants];
or half of that, or half of that again; or two, or even one to each.
One should, preceded by devotion, give to married Brahmin women food consisting of many cooked dishes, along with fruits and flowers.
May Kumudā and the others be pleased with me; may they, who increase the protection of children, nourish my child with fame and growth, and indeed cause my child to flourish.
"May they grant constant health, happiness, and good fortune.
With this mantra, "And may prosperity be yours," one should offer the *arghya* to them.
Having done this and paid homage, preceded by the benedictions of the Brahmins,
O King, one should eat together with one's kinsmen, with a heart full of joy and contentment.
On that day, one should offer garments, betel, flowers,
and so forth to married women and Brahmins, saying, "May Kumudā be pleased."
Now, in the Atharvaṇa Gopatha Brāhmaṇa:

Then, when a hundred years have passed and the year is increasing, one who wishes to cause the king to prosper in longevity, luster, splendor, fame, progeny, fortune, victory, and renown should sprinkle him with accumulated auspicious substances, honor him with gold ornaments, prepare an offering for Mahendra, and cause the guardians of the world (*lokapālas*) to partake of the sacrificial food. Having sacrificed to the guardians of the world with the verse "That which [is offered] to Mahendra with vigor" (*māhendro yat tujasā*), and having touched the king, he should offer oblations with the two verses beginning "O Indra, bring the protector hither" (*arvācam indra trātāram*) and "O Indra, increase the Kṣatriya" (*indra vardhaya kṣatriyam me*). Then, with the verse "May he live sharpened through many autumns" (*śitaṃ jīva śarado vardhamānaḥ*) and "Increase with progeny, O you who have grown" (*abhivardhasva prajayā vāvṛdhānaḥ*), and with the four verses beginning "May the mountains protect you" (*rakṣantu tvā girayaḥ*), he should perform the protection. He should adorn him with the *rocanā* ointment while reciting "They sit together with their qualities" (*saguṇa āsate*). Having performed the *sampāta* ritual with the hymn "Verily, he [weaves] the thread" (*nā vai sa tantum*), and having recited "The Creator [binds] your knot" (*dhātā te granthim*), he says "Increase! and "May he be without rivals. This is the ritual of Mausalaputra Paiṭhīnasi.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "In this manner, on the anniversary of the birth or the day of the birthday,
a celebration (vardhāpana) should be performed month after month for the sake of the growth of children."
No diseases of childhood afflict him, nor diseases of Skanda, nor those from Śākinīs;
there shall be no fear whatsoever from water, fire, or the cardinal directions.
This applies especially to a foolish king.
Having obtained the kingdom at the end of his term,
the king should perform this propitiatory rite and a great festival,
having thoroughly worshipped the planets and Vināyaka.
And the goddess Durgā, along with Kumudā and the other goddesses— he who worships them with devotion shall indeed,
endowed with strength and intelligence, be a conqueror of his enemies.
Thus concludes the ritual for the birthday celebration (*vardhāpana*).
Now, from the *Atharvaveda Gopatha Brāhmaṇa*:
next is the rite of gazing at the clarified butter (*ghṛtāvekṣaṇa*).

Every morning, awakened by the sound of conchs and drums or by the chanting of the Veda, the king shall rise from his bedchamber, proceed toward the unconquered (northeastern) direction, and await his preceptor. Then the domestic priest—having bathed, anointed himself, purified, dressed in white garments, and having put on a turban adorned with auspicious ornaments—shall enter the chamber of peace (*śāntigṛha*). Having paid homage to the gods and requested the recitation of blessings (*svastivācana*), he shall sit down humbly. Having performed the rite for well-being (*svastyayana*) with the mantra "From the world of Yama, that living soul which... at the appropriate time, and having drawn lines, sprinkled water, and spread sacrificial grass around the fire, he shall offer sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter while reciting the *Śāntātīya* hymn. He shall prepare a vessel made of gold, silver, or udumbara wood, filled with clarified butter and containing gold; having consecrated it with the mantra "O Agni, stride forth like Viṣṇu, the wide-strider," and reciting "The clarified butter is splendor," he obtains [the desired result] through that offering.
Clarified butter is declared to be splendor; clarified butter is the supreme remover of sin.
By means of clarified butter the gods are satisfied; in clarified butter all worlds are established.
Whatever impurity has come upon you— whether terrestrial, atmospheric, or celestial—
may it all go to destruction through contact with this clarified butter.

In that [fire], one should see everything as the Self with one's own eyes. One should touch the head and the heart with two verses beginning with "As it flies upward. Having turned clockwise with the verse "The turning of the Sun," one should complete the remainder of the rite.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
This is declared to be the procedure for the inspection of the clarified butter according to the Atharvaveda;
one should perform it correctly, being self-restrained and well-concentrated.
At the time of sunrise, that king, desiring victory, shall conquer the kingdom;
his enemies shall not even behold him.
Afterwards, having brought a tawny cow, the king should give it to a twice-born man,
and then hear the benediction issued from his mouth.
When this has been declared by the Guru, one shall obtain long life;
one gains sons, grandsons, and friends—of this there is no doubt.
Beholding the clarified butter is said to bestow long life, luster, good fortune, and the scorning of enemies; it destroys evil dreams and is conducive to merit.
Thus ends the procedure for gazing at the clarified butter.
Now follows the procedure for the *arghya* offering to Agastya,
according to the *Padma Purāṇa*.

Bhīṣma said: The world of the earth (bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), the world of heaven (svarloka), as well as Mahas, Jana, Tapas, and Satya— these seven are proclaimed to be the worlds of the gods.
But how can there be sovereign power over all things by turns? O Brahmin, honored by the gods, how may there be auspicious form, long life, health, and abundant prosperity in this world?
Pulastya said:
Within that water-pot, Vasiṣṭha appeared as before;
then, from it, there emerged the four-armed one, holding a rosary and a water-pot.
There was a most excellent sage named Agastya, whose soul was tranquil,
who lived in the region of Malaya according to the Vaikhānasa injunctions.
Accompanied by his wife and son, he performed extremely difficult austerities with the Brahmins;
then, after a long time, [the world] was oppressed by Tāraka and others.
Beholding the world with wrath, he drank up the ocean;
thereafter, Śaṅkara and all the other bestowers of boons appeared before him.
Brahmā and the Lord Viṣṇu went there to grant a boon:
"Choose a boon—may it be well with you—whatever is desired here, O sage."
Agastya said:
"For twenty-five crores of thousands of Brahmās,
I shall remain as a celestial traveler in the path of the southern sky."
"Whoever shall perform worship of me upon the rising of my celestial chariot, let that person alone attain merit; this is the boon chosen by me."
But those who perform the ancestral rite (śrāddha) with devotion, preceded by the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), for them the entire host of ancestors shall remain in heaven together with me.
"And let him remain for this length of time; this alone is my boon.
Having been told, "So be it," those gods departed as they had come.
Therefore, that arghya-offering should always be presented to Agastya by the wise.
[895] In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, the words of the Grandfather (Brahmā) to the great sage Agastya:
"O Brahmin, this auspicious work for the sake of the gods has been accomplished by you."
Therefore, I shall tell you the place that lies outside the path of Vaiśvānara.
There, possessing a divine body and seated upon an excellent celestial chariot,
you shall dwell in the southern direction, accompanied by the rising and setting [of the sun].
O one of stainless wisdom, upon your arising, the clarity, coolness, and freedom from poison of the waters shall exist forever through my grace.
O twice-born one, having risen in the autumn, set in the spring;
endowed with the power of irresistible will, traverse the entire earth in this manner.
Therefore, O Brahmin, having reached the autumn season at your rise,
you shall receive worship in the world through my grace, O best of the twice-born.
And those who shall worship you with perfumes, garlands, fruits, and unbroken grains,
as well as with curd, gold, jewels, and abundant supreme food—
With full jars, along with kūṣmāṇḍa gourds, umbrellas, sandals, and staffs;
with a cow, a bull, food offerings, garments, and gold.
Tell me the procedure for the worship of Agastya, which consists of a year-long renunciation of a single fruit, as well as the honoring of Brahmins and the recitation of your mantras.
Pulastya said: At the time of dawn, at the rising of this [star], a wise man,
dressed in white garlands and garments, should perform his bath with white sesame seeds while still at home.
At night, at sunrise, at night, or at the break of day, one should perform the ritual bath.
One should place a flawless jar, adorned with garlands and cloth.
It should be endowed with the five jewels, combined with a vessel of ghee and food,
provided with various kinds of edible fruits, and accompanied by a copper vessel.
Having placed a golden four-armed figure of a person, just a thumb’s breadth in size and with exceedingly long staff-like arms, within the mouth of a water-pot;
The seven grains together with the seven types of clothing.
Having raised his long-armed, pot-bellied form, he should present to the best of the twice-born a vessel containing flowers, unbroken rice grains, and a conch shell, accompanied by the mantra.
With a mind focused on nothing else, standing facing whichever direction he chooses.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having lifted up and offered the *arghya*—prepared with fresh flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) along with a conch shell—one should give it. "With very long staff-like arms" is an adverbial modifier for the action of lifting; "with a hanging belly and long arms" is an adjective qualifying the image. "The bull among the twice-born" refers to Agastya.
One should give a white cow that has a silver bell, silver hooves, and a golden face, together with her calf.
A man, having bowed to a milch cow adorned with cloth, bells, and ornaments, [should give her] to a brahmin.
And having had a very beautiful golden image made according to one's ability— representing a tranquil person wearing a mass of matted locks— from the *Bhaviṣyottara*.

One should then place upon that jar the Sage, who holds a water-pot in his hand, who is surrounded by disciples and celestial beings, who destroys the fierce poison of death, and who wears a garland of darbha grass and rosary beads; he should be depicted as clinging to the jar and smeared with sandalwood paste.
He was bathed and anointed with fragrant sandalwood,
honored with *jātī* flowers, and perfumed with delightful incenses.
Now, in the Viṣṇurahasya:
Having fashioned a beautiful image made of kāśa flowers, one should place it at nightfall in a well-adorned full water-jar, consecrated with the mantras of Varuṇa.
In this case, there is an option according to one’s capacity regarding the previously mentioned gold and silver. A full jar is a jar filled with water.
One should worship that which is situated in the jar with flowers, incense, and ointments; one should offer an oblation of curd and unbroken rice, and keep a vigil at night.
And the worship should be performed with the *arghya* mantras that will be described hereafter.
Having taken him [the image] at dawn, until reaching a sacred body of water,
he should gaze upon those [mantras] and the image of the Sage at the edge of the water at the end of the night.
Having fasted properly, one should devoutly offer the arghya water to Agastya with flowers,
roots, fruits, perfumes, and fragrant incenses.
With auspicious items such as grapes, dates, jujubes, and coconuts,
combined with the five jewels and accompanied by gold and silver.
Having prepared a vessel made of copper, filled with the seven types of grain, smeared with sandalwood paste,
one should offer it as *arghya* to a twice-born man.
O Sage, reciting this mantra beginning with "Agastyaḥ khanamāna," one should act according to whatever gain is obtained, or by all means possible, or according to one's own capacity.
They should offer the *arghya* to Agastya; this is the ritual procedure for a Śūdra:
"O you who resemble the *kāśa* flower, born from fire and wind, son of Mitra and Varuṇa, O Pot-born one, salutations be to you!"
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "Thereafter, the arghya offering should be presented; hear from me with which substances it should be made: with dates, bananas, pumpkins, and cucumbers."
With *karkoṭa*, *kāruvella*, *karmara*, and *bījapūraka* fruits; with eggplants, pomegranates, oranges, and plantains.
With sprouts of dūrvā grass, kuśa grass, kāśa grass, lotuses, and blue water-lilies;
with various kinds of food offerings, cows, garments, and auspicious juices.
With seven kinds of grains that have sprouted and been placed in bamboo vessels,
as well as in vessels made of gold, silver, copper, and bamboo.
O King, standing with his head bowed and touching the earth with his knees,
he turned toward the south and meditated upon Agastya for a moment.
One should diligently offer the *arghya* with a focused mind using *aguru* and sandalwood.
According to the statement, "The *arghya* vessel should be shaped like a conch shell, containing *kāśa* flowers, *akṣata* rice, and a conch shell," [the offering is made].
O you who resemble the *kāśa* flower, born from fire and wind!
O son of Mitra and Varuṇa, born from a jar, homage be unto you!
Salutations again and again to that glorious one, the husband of Lopāmudrā, by whom Vātāpi was devoured and the ocean was dried up in ancient times.
Salutations to that Agastya, who, along with his disciples and his son, causes sins and diseases to dissolve by his mere utterance.
O best of kings, the Brahmin should offer the *arghya* with a Vedic mantra:
"Agastya, desiring offspring, progeny, and strength, digs with his digging-tools."
The fierce seer nourished both castes;
he attained true blessings among the gods.
Having thus offered the *arghya*, O descendant of Kuru, one should prostrate and dismiss [the deity], saying:
"Honored according to my ability, salutations to the great seer Agastya;
having granted me success in my undertakings pertaining to this world and the next, please depart."
The mantra for dismissal:
Having dismissed that Agastya, one should present him to a brahmin who is an astrologer,
who has the form of Vyāsa, and who is a proponent of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
May Agastya, who is dear to my mind, be present; Agastya resides within this jar.
May Agastya, in the form of a twice-born, accept [this] with due honor.
May Agastya destroy the sin arising from seven births for us both;
O Great Sage, grant us incomparable and stainless happiness.
The mantra for receiving [the gift] is as follows:
"He who thus performs the Agastya-vrata with devotion and respect should likewise renounce one fruit, one grain, and one type of liquid."
And when the year is thus completed, one should begin the practice once again.
In the Viṣṇurahasya:
Having offered arghya according to the prescribed rite to Agastya, who was born from a jar,
a man should set aside a single grain of rice, a single fruit, or a single condiment in honor of Agastya.

Then, even during the month [of Kārttika], having offered the *arghya* to Agastya, and performing the renunciation of fruit (*phalatyāga*) every year in this manner, one does not suffer. After performing the fire-oblation (*homa*), a person should thereafter refrain from eating fruit.
The *homa* should be performed with clarified butter using the *argha* mantra, preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*.

Then, one should honor the Brahmins in due order with offerings of clarified butter, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and sweetmeats (*modaka*). One should also give them cows, gold, and garments as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
One should present that water-pot, its mouth covered with a vessel containing ghee and milk-rice, along with gold, to a Brāhmaṇa.
Before the sun has reached the sign of Virgo,
those who dwell in Mahodaya should offer the respectful water-offering (arghya) to Agastya within seven days.
The meaning is that the sun has entered the constellation of Pūrva-bhādrapadā; however, in Ujjayinī, this occurs earlier. As Varāhamihira said:
"Having understood its appearance according to each specific region through the prescribed enumeration, the wise man should give his instruction."
And that [longitude] of the true sun, when it has reached Ujjayinī, is diminished by the portions known as the vowels.
The meaning is: when the sun, having reached the seventh part or degree known as Svara, has entered the second quarter of Maghā;
likewise, while the nocturnal darkness is slightly illuminated by a mass of reddish rays in the southern direction.
Having determined the directions according to the year,
being supported by the arghya-plant, and being self-restrained, he should offer it.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*, there are these words of Kṛṣṇa:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira,
offer the *arghya* to that very Ṛṣi when the sun has entered the zodiac sign of Virgo, specifically on the seventh day prior."
When the maiden has arrived, the time for the guest-offering (arghya) comes to an end.

In the ancient city of Yudhiṣṭhira, the third quarter refers to the rising of Satyakarṇa; that is the meaning. In whichever region and on whichever day the sight of Agastya occurs, in that region and on that day the offering of *arghya* (water of respect) should be made—this is the summary. By the phrase "when the sun has entered Virgo" (*kanyāyāṃ samanuprāpte*) and so forth, it is shown that starting from the seventh day and taking the *saṃkrānti* (the sun's passage into the sign) as the limit, the offering of *arghya* is appropriate even within seven days of its rising.
And likewise, in the *Padmapurāṇa*:
"Until the seventh night from the rising of Yama..."
All of this must be given by a man.
"Of Yama and Agastya: from sunrise until seven nights have passed; having set seven nights as the limit, the meaning is that the *arghya* offering should be given on one day.
But after seven nights, the offering of the *arghya* is useless.
Thus [it is stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
Agastya,
the son of Varuṇa, a yogin who crushes the foothills of the Vindhya mountains, remains stationed in the sky, taking his resort in the southern quarter.
Starting from the six western portions of Virgo and continuing by count up to seventy-two degrees, the Sun traverses these degrees within the zodiacal signs.
The Lord Agastya, the bearer of light, now rises in the sky,
beginning from the western rays of the sun and proceeding in due order as before.
And for as long as the sun consumes [the netherworlds] thirty-six times in succession,
so long does he, being exhausted, descend toward Pātāla and reach his setting.

The bull (*ukṣā*) is the *vṛṣabha* (Taurus). The *aṃśa* is the *caraṇa* (quarter). A *rāśi* (zodiac sign) consists of nine *caraṇas*. This is because of the enjoyment of two and a quarter lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). Starting from the third *caraṇa* of Uttarā [Phalgunī], there are seventy [degrees] ending at the third *caraṇa* of Aśvinī; this much is the time of rising according to the solar division. The remainder here is the [remaining] time.
Having observed the fast, one should behold the sage Agastya when he has risen;
he grants all desires, is meritorious, and increases all fortune.
And the Blessed One should be worshipped by those endowed with faith and devotion,
with full water-pots, kushmanda gourds, barley, meditations, and clarified butter.
With *jāti*, *padma*, and *utpala* flowers, with white sandalwood,
with cows, clarified butter, as well as garments, and with jewels produced from the ocean.
With sandals, umbrellas, and staffs; with shoes, collyrium, and bark garments; with oblations, supreme food, fruits, and beautiful flowers.
With various kinds of food offerings, fire oblations, and the gratification of Brahmins,
one should invoke auspiciousness, directing the mind toward a single desired goal.
O Blessed One, if I should attain the desire residing in my mind,
I shall worship you once again without hindrance through your grace.
Having spoken thus, he should thereafter worship the astrologers as well as his gurus;
and after having fed the Brahmins, he should then eat himself while remaining restrained in speech.
Now, in the Padma Purāṇa:
"Until the rising of Yama on the seventh night,
all of this must be given by a man."
They may be as many as seventeen years, or even more than that, as some authorities maintain.
The man who offers the guest-offering (argha) according to this rite attains this world, endowed with beauty and health.
By the second [offering], one attains the Bhuvarloka;
thereafter, he who bestows seven arghyas attains all seven worlds.
Whoever should perform this for as long as they live goes to the Supreme Brahman.
In the *Varāhasaṃhitā*: "A king, offering this *arghya* with faith..."
If one who is free from the defects of pride and has conquered the faction of his enemies should indeed give [this] correctly for seven years,
he attains lordship over the earth girt by the ocean.
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa:
O Pāṇḍava, having offered the arghya for seven years in this sequence,
listen with a one-pointed mind to the fruit that a man obtains.
A Brāhmaṇa shall become a knower of the four Vedas and an expert in all the Śāstras;
a Kṣatriya attains the entire earth, girdled by the oceans.
For Vaiśyas, there will be the production of grain and they shall also obtain cattle-wealth;
for Śūdras, there will be wealth, health, and an abundance of crops and food.
Sons are born to women, and their homes become prosperous and blessed with good fortune;
for widows, O son of Pāṇḍu, great merit increases.
In those regions where this worship of the Arghya offering to Agastya is performed by people, a maiden obtains a husband and one who is suffering is freed from disease.
In those regions, the rain-god Parjanya pours down rain according to desire;
calamities are pacified, and likewise diseases perish.
Those who recite the vow of the seer Agastya, and others who listen to it;
All those best of men, freed from sin and having remained for a long time upon the earth,
go to heaven by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans.
If you desire in this mortal world a home endowed with supreme prosperity,
incomparable enjoyments, a body, and the flourishing of cattle and sons,
then, O beloved of jewels, [seek] that which is of great value at the rising of the Sage.
Offer the *argha* with fruits, garments, juices, and grains.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
"Whoever reads or hears this account of the gift of the one born from the body of the pair of Vasus..."
Even he who merely directs his mind toward Viṣṇu is honored by hosts of gods once he has entered a celestial abode.
Brahmā said:
Having established the sky [as the altar] with white sandalwood water and having smeared it,
one should worship with lotuses fashioned upon the pericarp and prostrate before it.
When the *vakula* tree— spotless, gentle, without gaps, and in full bloom— is adorned with its whorls (*karṇikā*) and decorated with its whorls;
"in full bloom" means having blossomed.
In the center of the mass of filaments, a very beautiful seat should be established.
O best of gods, having placed before the Sun a [liṅga] the size of a thumb-joint, endowed with all fragrances.
One should worship with oleanders and likewise with red sandalwood;
one should offer guggulu incense and bow with the head to the Sun.
One who is concentrated on the sky-like [void] should place saffron on the eastern side;
having placed agallochum on the south, one should place white sandalwood on the west.
Furthermore, one who is skilled in the science of space should place four equal parts in the northern direction;
one should reverently place auspicious and meritorious red sandalwood in the center.
One should worship with various flowers as well as with aguru and sandalwood;
one should offer incense made of black aguru, or else guggulu mixed with clarified butter.
One should offer very fine garments with their fringes intact,
and one should cause milk-rice mixed with ghee and ghee-lamps to be given.
Having offered everything with the mantra, one should then perform a circumambulation;
having bowed the head to the Sun, and rising up, one should ask his forgiveness.
One should present an offering (bali) accompanied by all ritual gifts to the deity Sūrya of immeasurable splendor, using the mantra "khakholkāya."
Having previously worshipped the god Ravi according to this rite,
I attained the state of Brahmā through the grace of Bhāskara.
Thus is described the Vyomavrata as stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
Having stayed in the water during the night, one should become a giver of a cow at dawn;
one attains the world of Varuṇa—this is here called the Varuṇavrata.
Thus ends the Varuṇa-vrata as declared in the Padma Purāṇa; he who performs the *nakta* fast on every *parvan* for one year— where "parvan" refers to the fifteenth day (the full moon or new moon).
A celibate student who has conquered anger and is always devoted to the worship of Śiva,
O best of Brahmins, [should honor] composed devotees of Śiva at the end of the year.
Having fed them, he should then say: "May the Blessed Lord, the Master, be pleased.
One who is thus endowed with this rite goes to the world of Śiva;
such a man does not again attain the unstable human state in this world.

Thus ends the vow of eating only on the lunar festival days (parvanakta-vrata) as declared in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "O Goddess, that man who always eats from an earthen vessel on the festival days obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice within a single day and night."
The meaning is that one should place food upon the earth as a vessel; Śiva is the deity here.
This concludes the vow of the Earth-Vessel on the festival day as described in the *Padma Purāṇa*.
He who, having fashioned a golden image of the earth weighing more than twenty palas, [performs this vow]...
One who observes a milk-vow for a day shall be honored in the world of Rudra;
this is declared to be the Dharā-vrata, which endures for seven hundred kalpas.

The day of the gods is the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*). Having performed the milk-vow (*payovrata*) immediately thereafter—this is to be supplied from the context—the deity is Rudra, and the breaking of the fast consists of the gift of earth.
Thus is the vow of the Earth (*dharāvratam*) as declared in the *Padmapurāṇa*.
Nandikeśvara said:
Likewise, O Nārada, hear the greatness of the renunciation of all fruits,
which is an inexhaustible vow that yields the fruit of all desires in the world beyond.
In the auspicious month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the third lunar day, one should undertake the vow of the sages;
or alternatively, on the twelfth, the eighth, or even the fourteenth day.
O best of sages, one should begin during the bright fortnight after having performed the recitation for the Brahmins,
or on an auspicious day in other months as well.
One should worship the twice-born according to one's ability with milk-rice and sacrificial fees;
and from among the eighteen kinds of grains, one may offer at least a small measure of fruit.
One should avoid [the meat of] eight [animals], with the single exception of the boar, except for the purpose of medicine;
one should cause an image of Rudra, together with a bull, made of gold, and Dharmarāja to be fashioned.
The kūṣmāṇḍa, the mātuliṅga, the vṛntāka, and likewise the panasa; the āmra, āmrātaka, kapittha, kāliṅga, and then the vāruka.
One should offer, according to one's ability, wood-apple, holy fig, jujube, citron, plantain fruit,
karmara, pomegranate, and sixteen pieces of gold.
Kaladhauta is gold.
Mūlaka, āmalaka, jambu, indīvarī, karañja, manda, kaṅkaila, tuṇḍīra, karīra, kuṭaja, and samī [are medicinal plants].
Elaka is the fruit of the *elā* plant;
*udumbara*, coconut, grape, and the two types of *bṛhatī*—
one should have these sixteen fruits made of silver according to one's means.
One should prepare copper, the fruit of the *tāla* tree, as well as the fruit of the *agasti* tree,
the fruit of the *piṇḍīraka* and *kāśmarya* trees, and the *sūraṇa* tuber.
*Kāśmarya* is *śrīparṇī*.
*Raktālukākaṇṭaka*, *ketaka*, *amlīka*, and *cirbhaṭa*: [908] *ketaka* is the fruit that clarifies water; *amlīka* is the tamarind (*ciñcā*).
Likewise, the fruit of the *citravallī*, the fruit of the *kūṭaśālmalī*—
the *kūṭaśālmalī* being the *rohītaka*—
as well as *grāmaniṣpāva*, *madhuka*, *vaṭa*, *iṅguda*, and *paṭola*.

Madhuka is the Madhūka tree; iṅguda is hiṅguṇa. A man should have these sixteen copper items made according to his capacity. He should also prepare two water-pitchers placed upon grain and covered with cloth.
Then, one should have a bed prepared upon which [an image of] Yama is placed, clothed in garments,
accompanied by two vessels of food, and attended by Rudra and his bull.
On an auspicious day, having honored a peaceful Brahmin who maintains a household along with his wife, one should present [the gift] together with a cow.
Just as the immortals dwell within fruits in the form of their essence,
so may devotion to Śiva arise in me through the vow of renouncing all fruits.
Just as Śiva and Dharma always bestow the fruit of eternal bliss,
may they both grant me that fruit by bestowing the results associated with them.
Just as fruits may always be obtained by the devotees of Śiva,
so may I attain infinite fruit in birth after birth.
"Just as I perceive Śiva, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Padmaja as distinct, so may Śaṅkara, the soul of the universe, be ever my benefactor. Having spoken thus, she adorned herself with all ornaments for a year.
After a year has passed,
if he is able, he should provide a bed equipped with all its furnishings;
but if he is unable, he should give the aforementioned fruits according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise, having given a pair of water-pitchers and two golden images of Śiva and Dharma to a Brahmin, he should eat while restraining his speech and avoiding oil.
O best of the twice-born, one should also feed others according to one's ability;
there is nothing superior to this, both in this world and in the next.
O best of sages, this vow of his yields infinite fruit:
however many atoms there may be in gold, copper, and silver, [so many rewards shall he obtain].
O best of sages, for as many thousands of yugas as there are grains of powder in those fruits, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
May this [work], which removes all impurities for people, serve as a means of livelihood among men forever;
and may there be no suffering from separation from one's children in future births.
And he attains the abode cherished by the god Purandara.
Thus ends the vow of the renunciation of fruits as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Pārtha, listen with a concentrated mind; I shall describe the ritual for the eggplant (vṛntāka)."
One should not eat it for a year, or six months, or three months.

Then, having observed a fast for one night under the asterism of Bharaṇī or Maghā, and having invoked the deity upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and worshipped with perfumes, flowers, food offerings, and so forth, one should—with *darbha* grass in hand—invoke [the deities] with scented water, saying: "I invoke King Yama; I invoke Kāla; I invoke Citragupta; I invoke Mṛtyu; I invoke Parameṣṭhin. Then, having established the fire, one should offer oblations of sesame and clarified butter, saying: "Svāhā to Yama! Svāhā to Nīla! Svāhā to Nīlakaṇṭha! Svāhā to Yamarāja! Svāhā to Citragupta! Svāhā to Vaivasvata! One should then offer the fire the eight *vyāhṛtis* one hundred and eight times.

Having himself administered the expiation, the Brāhmaṇa shall act as the preceptor for the others. Then, according to his capacity, he should present a golden eggplant (*vṛntāka*) to a Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, he should give a black cow and a bull, along with earrings and finger-rings, an umbrella and sandals, a pair of black garments, and a black woolen blanket. He should feed the Brāhmaṇas and cause them to pronounce blessings. Whoever bestows the eggplant according to this rite—
For three months, or six months, or one year, he should not eat [meat].

Furthermore, if one performs this rite and practices renunciation until the end of life, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu; he obtains the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka and Aśvamedha sacrifices. For seven thousand births he is glorified on the back of the celestial vault (nākapṛṣṭha), and as long as the seven worlds endure, he shall not behold the realm of Yama.
He who gives an unblemished eggplant, consecrated with excellent gold, together with ghee and cloth to a twice-born man—
whether for a year, a month, or even for just one day— [attains great merit].
A person never beholds the city of Yama.

Thus ends the procedure for the renunciation of eggplants as declared in the *Bhaviṣyottara*. Having observed the milk-vow (*payovrata*) for three days, one should offer a golden wish-fulfilling tree weighing more than one *pala*, according to one's means, together with rice placed in a winnowing basket.
Having given a winnowing basket containing two *droṇas*, one goes to the abode of Brahmā; this is known as the *Kalpavṛkṣa* vow.
[911] Brahmā is the deity here. Thus is the Kalpavṛkṣavrata (the Vow of the Wish-Fulfilling Tree) as declared in the Padmapurāṇa.
One should fashion a golden chariot, yoked with horses and so forth, weighing more than two palas.
One who gives [this] while having observed a fast shall dwell in heaven for a hundred kalpas;
at the end of that, he shall become a king of kings—this is remembered as the Aśvavrata.
Indra is the deity here;
thus is described the Aśvavrata as stated in the Padmapurāṇa. Likewise, one should further give a golden chariot accompanied by two elephants.
