Having observed this vow of the elephant, the protector of the earth shall dwell in the world of truth for a thousand kalpas, having remained fasting. This is remembered as the Karivrata.
The grammatical connection is that one should give [the gift] after having observed the fast. Likewise, this applies after two kalpas. Brahmā is the deity here.
Thus ends the Karivratam as declared in the Padmapurāṇa.
Furthermore, he who should perform the consecration with ghee for Śiva for a day and night...
In the month of Puṣya, he rises up with steady, smooth streams.
One should keep a vigil there with offerings of song and dance, the sounds of conchs and musical instruments, and the splendor of lamps and other illuminations.
Freed from all sins and accompanied by his entire family,
he [ascends] upon countless, blazing great vehicles that are like the best of mountains.
Endowed with yoga, he rejoices eternally in the city of Śiva, happy like Śiva himself,
especially during eclipses, equinoxes, and other auspicious days.
He who, having fasted, beholds the consecration with clarified butter until its completion,
shakes off all sins and goes to the world of Śiva.
One person worships with devotion, while another praises [the act] with devotion;
the fruit for both is exactly equal, for devotion alone is the cause in this matter.
Thus ends the procedure for the bath with ghee as declared in the *Śivadharma*.
Sūta said:
Indeed, that liberation which is attained by embodied beings without effort is difficult to obtain.
Listen, O best of the twice-born, to that action by which one is born.
Having drawn a mandala the size of a cow's hide with cow dung,
the knower of mantras should fashion it as a square according to the rules and sprinkle it with sacrificial porridge (caru).
Having adorned it with canopies and other ornaments, as well as with beautiful parasols,
and with golden bubbles, crescents, and leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
With white and blooming lotuses, as well as red and blue water-lilies,
with a variegated celestial chariot, with strings of pearls, O best of the twice-born,
and with very smooth full jars representing white dances;
With garlands of fruits and sprouts, with victory banners,
with silken cloths, with rows of fifty lamps, and likewise with various kinds of incense;
Having drawn an excellent lotus endowed with fifty petals,
using those respective colors and powders, or even white powder;
Having fashioned a lotus according to the prescribed rite with a measurement of one cubit,
one should place the deity upon the pericarp and offer Bhava, the Lord of Gods.
There, one who is firm in his vows should place the letters beginning with 'a' in the sequence starting from the east,
indeed placing all the letters beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
Having worshipped them in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, O best of sages,
one should feed fifty Brahmins there according to the prescribed rites.
A rosary of seeds, a sacred thread, earrings,
a water-pot, a seat, as well as a staff, a turban, and a garment.
Having given to those best of the twice-born, as well as to Śambhu, the God of gods,
the great caru-offering, the food offering, a black cow, and a bull;
Having offered food and other items of that same color to the God of gods,
one should present auspicious substances suitable for yoga.
The wise one should recite [the mantra] beginning with the syllable Oṃ, proceeding sequentially through each phoneme.
Having thus devoutly drawn this supreme mandala of colors,
I shall now tell you in brief what fruit a mortal obtains.
Having studied the Vedas together with their auxiliary branches according to the rule and in accordance with the prescribed ordinances,
and having performed sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others in due order and according to the rule.
Then, having performed the Viśvajit sacrifice and fathered such sons,
he entered the forest-dwelling stage of life (vānaprastha-āśrama) together with his wife and his sacred fires.
Having performed the Cāndrāyaṇa and other penances, and having duly renounced the world, the twice-born man,
having studied the science of Brahman and having attained knowledge through diligent effort, [should proceed].
Whatever fruit a yogi may obtain by perceiving the object of knowledge through gnosis,
he obtains all that fruit from the vision of the mandala of the castes.
O best of the twice-born, having written or smeared the basis of the abodes with whatever material available, whether on the north, the south, or even behind;
Or else, having adorned the four corners on all sides with colors,
and having scattered fragrant flowers and the four kinds of incense and lamps, one should pray to the Lord Īśāna; thus one goes to the world of Śiva.
Having enjoyed great pleasures there for hundreds of millions of kalpas,
that man shall fill the temple of Śiva with the auspicious fragrances of his own body.
Having gradually attained the state of a Gandharva and being honored there by the Gandharvas,
he eventually comes to this world and becomes a powerful king.
Thus ends the description of the circle of colors as stated in the Saura Purāṇa:
"In the bright fortnight, having recognized that the new grain has ripened auspiciously,
and when there is a favorable lunar day, a favorable asterism, and an auspicious moment (muhūrta)..."
One should go to the sacred field according to the prescribed ritual, preceded by song and instrumental music.
There, having kindled the fire and strewn it with fragrant substances according to the scriptures,
and having performed the *homa* sacrifice, one should thereafter lead forth the decorated grain.
Having gratified the gods, the ancestors, and his kinsmen in due order with flowers, garments, fruits, and roots, as well as with elephants, horses, and chariots;
Having divided [the harvest] according to his ability, the astrologers, protected by the crops,
should be clothed in new garments, wearing garlands, well-anointed, and well-adorned.
Previously established in the sacrifice, he was gratified by the sound of Vedic chanting;
or else, listening to it, he was supremely delighted and engaged in auspicious rites such as the touching of sacred objects.
One should consume it mixed with curd, consecrated with nine mantras;
having finished the meal, one should perform a great festival with songs and instrumental music.
Thus ends the description of the Sasyotsava as declared in the Brahma Purāṇa. Formerly, from the ancient Ocean of Milk while it was being churned,
the goddess Śyāmā emerged, endowed with all auspicious marks.
She who is called Nārāyaṇī is delicate and illustrious;
born from the body of Satī, she is Satī herself, supremely beautiful.
Seeing her, all the gods and asuras there were struck with wonder:
"Ah! She is so beautiful and fair-faced; indeed, we shall behold her."
Having spoken these words to her, they all beheld that very thing;
then they saw its four names spread abroad upon the earth as "drākṣā."
Therefore, when it is half-cooked, she should be diligently honored with flowers,
incense, ointments, and the like, as well as by the gratification of Brahmins.
Immediately thereafter, having honored his two young sons as well as his elders,
and with the aim of attaining dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, he— accompanied by his wife, joyful, and together with his servants, friends, and sons— [proceeded].

Having anointed oneself according to rule, wearing a garland and fine garments, one should eat what has been offered by the guru; it must not be otherwise. Furthermore, a festival filled with dancing and singing should be celebrated.
Thus ends the Great Festival of Śyāmā as declared in the Āditya Purāṇa.
Brahmā said:
O Sage, they know Soma-deva to belong to the Ṛgveda and the Ātreya gotra.
And the wise know Ugradeva to be Kāśyapa in the Yajurveda.
One should know that the Sāmaveda also has the Bhāradvāja and Purandara lineages as its presiding deity; now hear from me about its forms.
The Ṛgveda has eyes as broad as lotus petals and garments that hang down low;
his neck is well-proportioned, and his hair and beard are curled. In measurement, he is five *vitastis* long. He should be worshipped as made of silver or born of pearls.
The bestower of boons to the twice-born who is endowed with devotion.
The Yajurveda has tawny eyes, a neck and cheeks as thick as kusha grass in the middle, a copper-colored complexion, and measures one span and six finger-breadths in height.

Having worshipped [the deity] in a painting or in a linga, one shall obtain all desires. The Sāmaveda is eternally garlanded, firm in his vows, pure, dressed in clean garments, patient, self-controlled, bearing a staff, with golden eyes, and in color like the sun; he measures six cubits. Worshipped in a copper or iron image, or in a linga named after Indra and the other [deities], he bestows auspiciousness. The Atharvaveda is sharp, fierce, able to assume any form at will, the soul of the universe, the creator of the universe, cruel, possessing upward-flaming fire, performing minor rites, arising from well-performed lineages, blue-lotus colored in hue, satisfied with his own wife, and golden. He should be worshipped in a ruby or a rudrākṣa bead; having worshipped him, one shall obtain all desires.
Whatever sacred rites, Vedic hymns, meritorious sacrifices, and vows are prescribed in the Atharvaveda,
one who is permeated by devotion shall obtain the fruit of them all simply by hearing this.
One who is sonless obtains sons; one who is destitute shall acquire wealth;
the unlearned attains knowledge; and the sorrowful is liberated from sorrow.
Having recited it, one becomes esteemed by all the gods and beloved by the twice-born;
of this there is no doubt, and the Goddess is always the granter of boons.
Thus ends the Devavrata as described in the Devīpurāṇa. From the Saurapurāṇa: Furthermore, a man, standing upon his own feet, should dwell in a sacred field of Śiva.
At the end of the body, one attains union with Śiva; there is no doubt in this matter.
From the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"Even one who merely pierces two footprints [of Śiva] shall dwell in the realm of Śiva; he attains the state of Śiva during the month of Caitra—no doubt should be entertained in this matter."
Thus ends the section on intense vows.
Śaṅkara said:
O Rāma, during a solar eclipse and during a lunar eclipse, [one should perform these rites].
Through fasting, one attains the destruction of all conceptual constructions.

O best of the Bhārgavas, bathing, giving gifts, as well as the recitation of mantras, and likewise the performance of śrāddha and the worship of the fire, are all remembered as yielding inexhaustible merit at that time.
Thus ends the fast for an eclipse as described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Now, the vows of great austerity (*mahātapas*):
"The wise man who performs a three-night fast month after month,"
Having reached the world of Kuvera, he shall attain the supreme state.
The man who, observing his vows and being pure, eats on the fourth day,
attains the station of the Gandharvas and rejoices in heaven like Śakra.
He who, unwearied, eats on the fifth day every month shall be liberated from all sins and go to heaven with great splendor.
He who, being self-controlled and pure, always eats on the sixth day,
having reached the world of Varuṇa, shall attain the supreme state.
He who, firm in his vow and having conquered the pairs of opposites, eats on the seventh day,
reaches the world of the Sun and shall also attain great glory.
He who has conquered the pairs of opposites is patient;
he who eats on the eighth day, having conquered the pairs of opposites and being firm in his vow,
shall attain the world of Viṣṇu and become possessed of supreme splendor.
The man who, established in his vow, eats on the ninth day,
becomes dear to the Vasus and wanders together with them.
He who eats on the tenth day obtains the fruit of twelve days;
having become equal to the two Aśvins, he likewise sports in the imperishable.
The *dvādaśāha* is a specific type of sacrificial rite (*kratu*).
However, the man who remains pure and eats on the eleventh day,
having completed the eleventh-day observance, shall attain the status of a follower of Rudra (*rudragaṇatā*).
O Goddess, that man who always eats on the twelfth day,
having reached the twelfth day [of the vow], is glorified in the world of Śakra.
But the man who always eats on the thirteenth day shall dwell in the abode of Bhārgava, endowed with divine happiness.
But the man who always eats on the fourteenth day shall dwell in the world of Rudra and attain union with Śiva.
He who, having conquered his senses, practices this constantly for half a month becomes equal to the king of the gods and dwells in heaven.
But the hero who, having conquered anger and subdued his senses, spends a month [in this practice],
shall travel in a divine celestial chariot accompanied by Apsarases.
He dwells throughout all the worlds for eighty thousand births;
then, having attained the seat of Brahmā and being highly honored by Brahmā himself,
that best of men resides in the world of Brahmā just like Brahmā.
In the Mahābhārata:
"By observing three-night fasts month after month for twelve years,
one attains the leadership of the Gaṇas, free from rivals and unblemished."
But that man who eats but one meal a day for a full year obtains a fruit equal to that of the Atirātra sacrifice.
For ten thousand years he is honored in the heavenly world;
when that [merit] is exhausted, having returned here, he attains greatness.
But he who, for a full year, eats only every fourth mealtime,
being constantly devoted to non-violence, truthful in speech, and having his senses subdued;
He enjoys the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
for thirty thousand years, he rejoices in heaven.
If a man lives for a year eating only every eighth mealtime,
that person obtains the fruit of the Gavām Medha sacrifice.
He travels by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes,
and he rejoices in heaven for fifty thousand years.
O King,
the venerable Aṅgiras has declared that for one who eats only once every fortnight for an entire year, it is equivalent to six months of fasting.
And he dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years.
[920] He should eat during the second fortnight on all days; this is the distinction. He is awakened from his deep sleep by the sweet and resonant sounds of lutes, harps, and flutes.
If that best of men drinks milk here month by month for one year,
O dear one, he obtains the fruit of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
He travels in a celestial chariot drawn by lions and tigers;
and once he has arrived, eight divine maidens delight that man.
He rejoices in heaven for seventy thousand years;
O tiger among men, fasting is not prescribed beyond one month.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Lord, O Grandfather, tell me of that rite which can be accomplished even by the poor,
and which is equal in its fruit to that of a sacrifice."
Bhīṣma said: He who eats in the morning as well as in the evening, and does not drink in between,
who is constantly devoted to non-violence and offers oblations into the sacred fire;
He who would perform a sacrifice with abundant gold, dear to Vāsava,
being truthful in speech, generous by nature, and a proclaimer of the injunctions of Brahman;
Whatever fruit one who is patient, self-controlled, and victorious over anger may attain,
that is found in a celestial chariot resembling white light and marked with the sign of a swan.
"At dawn" means in the morning; "he should drink water" is the understood remainder of the sentence.
He attains perfection in exactly six years; there is no doubt about this.
He may even dwell among the women of the gods in a place resounding with dance and song.
One should dwell for a lotus-number of years (eighty-four million) in the world of Prajāpati, which originates from fire.
One who eats only a single meal daily for three years, constantly devoted to his lawful wife, shall obtain the fruit of a hundred koṭis of lotuses and the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
He who, for twelve months, always eats but one meal on every second day while offering oblations into the sacred fire;
He who would perform a sacrifice involving much gold, dear to Vāsava,
being truthful in speech, generous by nature, devoted to Brahmins, and free from envy;
Whatever fruit one who is patient, self-controlled, and has conquered anger may attain,
[he dwells] in a celestial chariot resembling pale clouds and marked with swans.
When two years have passed, he shall dwell together with apsarases in a lotus. "Passed" means fully completed. Furthermore, he who eats but a single meal on the third day [shall attain the same].
Indeed, for twelve months, he constantly offered oblations into the Jātavedas fire.
One who is constantly devoted to the fire-ritual and the awakening of daily duties attains the unsurpassed fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
He shall dwell forever in the world of the Seven Sages together with celestial nymphs;
they know that his stay there shall last for three padmas of years.
Having remained [in this state],
he who eats a single meal on the fourth day for twelve months, while indeed offering oblations into the fire (jātavedas), [attains the goal].
One obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
one shall establish [the recipient] throughout all the worlds, even to the very limits of the ocean.
He constantly observes the play of the king of the gods,
as well as the limits of the ocean and the specific measurements of the sea. He who eats but a single meal on every fifth day—
And he, indeed, for twelve months offered oblations into the Jātavedas fire.
One who is free from greed, truthful, devoted to Brahman,
non-violent, free from envy, and established in righteousness shall obtain the fruit of the twelve-day sacrifice.
He shall ascend a divine celestial mansion made of Jāmbūnada gold, marked with the sign of a swan,
radiant like a garland of suns, a white abode.
There are four rotations; twelve lotuses on the scales;
and for as long as the measure of five arrows [fifty], he dwells there for a long time.

The *āvartanas* are the *manvantaras*; the *tulāpadmas* are measured at one hundred. The measurement of "arrows and fires" (*śarāgni*) consists of five arrows and three fires; this measurement also pertains specifically to the *manvantaras*. On the sixtieth day, the sage should partake of food, constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months.
Bathing three times daily at all seasons, observing celibacy, free from malice,
and a sage with restrained speech,
he obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Gomedha sacrifice.
In that very same way, having fallen asleep on the lap of an apsaras, he awakens.
By the sound of anklets and the tinkling of girdles,
[he remains] for thousands of millions of years and hundreds of millions of yugas.
With eighteen lotuses, two banners,
and likewise fifty thousand [offerings], and equal in measure to the hairs on a hundred skins of trees, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
[923] *Patākā* refers to a specific number.
He who eats but a single meal on the seventh day,
constantly for twelve months while offering oblations into the sacred fire (*jātavedas*), [attains the fruit].
Protecting Sarasvatī, one should practice celibacy;
one should avoid flowers, cosmetics, honey, and meat.
The person goes to the world of the Maruts and to the world of Indra;
having achieved his purpose in each of those places, he is honored by celestial maidens.
A person obtains the fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold, or even a merit exceeding that number; he rejoices in those worlds.
"Exceedingly meritorious" (atiguṇa) refers to saffron and other such substances; it means possessing qualities that surpass others, that is to say, immeasurable.
But that man who, for a full year, eats only on every eighth day,
remaining constantly devoted to the service of the gods and offering oblations into the sacred fire;
He obtains the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice in due order and ascends a celestial chariot (vimāna) resembling the color of a lotus.
Women who are dark, golden-hued, or fair, as well as others endowed with youth and beauty—he obtains them; of this there is no doubt.
But he who eats on every ninth day for a full year,
constantly invoking Jātavedas for twelve months, indeed [attains his goal].
A human being obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice;
indeed, that man gains a celestial chariot (vimāna) as radiant as a white lotus.
By the splendors of the blazing sun and fire, and by divine garlands,
he is led through the eternal firmament by the daughters of Rudra.
For eighteen thousand years, as well as for a full kalpa and a hundred thousand times ten million [kalpas], he rejoices in those worlds.
But he who eats [only] after each ten-day period has passed for a full year,
constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire (jātavedas) for twelve months;
When it has arrived, the daughter of Brahmā,
adorned with chowries, performs her play there in that place which is enchanting to all beings.
He obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices;
and beautiful maidens always delight that man.
But he who, when the eleventh day has arrived, consumes the sacrificial oblation,
constantly offering oblations into the Jātavedas for twelve months;
One should not desire another's wife, either by word or even by thought.
One should not speak untruth even for the sake of one's mother or father;
one should approach Mahādeva, who is of great power and seated upon his celestial chariot.
He, whose splendor was like the fire at the end of an eon, [dwelt] upon that divine and enchanting upper garment of the Rudras in heaven, for a measurable number of years.
Honored by gods and dānavas, he constantly bows down to Rudra a hundred thousand million times and a hundred billion times.
He who obtains a vision of him day after day,
and on the twelfth day indeed partakes of the sacrificial oblation (havis), [attains his goal].
He who constantly offers oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months indeed ascends a celestial chariot that possesses the splendor of the twelve Ādityas.
Endowed with the eight great supernatural powers (aṣṭamaharddhi), it is established in the Brahma-world;
O King, it is a permanent residence, crowded with men and women.
On the arrival of the thirteenth day, he who eats the sacrificial offering (havis) [attains this].
By always [reciting it] for twelve months, a person shall obtain the fruit of a divine sacrificial session (devasattra) and achieve a celestial mansion named Ratnapadmodaya.
In that regard, one shall dwell for two periods of Śaṅkupatāka, as well as Yugānta and Kalpa,
and likewise for Ayutāyuta, Padma, and Samudra.

Śaṅkupatākā and others are specific types of banners. Always delighted by those celestial maidens, he is worshipped with songs and the sounds of Gandharvas, as well as the resonance of kettledrums and small drums.
He who always consumes the sacrificial oblation on the fourteenth day for twelve full months shall indeed obtain the fruit of a great sacrifice.
Celestial maidens, whose age and form are indescribable and who are beautifully adorned, travel through the sky in celestial chariots, wearing polished and refined armlets, to visit him.
There, she was awakened here and there by the cries of kalahamsas, the tinkling of anklets, and the jingling of waist-bands as they were drawn upward.
And that man who dwells in that abode of celestial maidens remains there for a full year, equal to the number of grains of sand in the Ganges.
But he who, having conquered his senses, eats only one meal when the fortnight has passed,
and constantly offers oblations into the sacred fire for twelve months;
He obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices;
he mounts a celestial vehicle frequented by swans and peacocks.
Variegated with circles of jewels, covered with gold,
and adorned by excellent women radiant with divine ornaments.
It had a single pillar, four gates, and seven stories; it was highly auspicious, adorned with thousands of Vaijayantī banners and resounded with the sounds of singing.
He ascends a celestial chariot endowed with divine and super-divine qualities,
adorned with jewels, pearls, and corals, and possessing the brilliance of lightning.
He shall dwell for a thousand yugas, mounted upon a sword and an elephant; he who,
when the sixteenth day arrives, takes but a single meal throughout the twelve months, shall indeed obtain the fruit of the Soma sacrifice.
He dwells eternally in the abodes of the daughters of Soma;
anointed with gentle fragrances, he moves according to his will.
Seated in his celestial chariot, he is indeed honored by beautiful and charming women, and served with all objects of sensual enjoyment.
That man shall attain the fruit of a hundred lotuses for more than ten great kalpas,
and he shall also accomplish four revolutions.
He who, having reached the seventeenth day,
always consumes the sacrificial oblation for twelve months while offering oblations into the Jātavedas fire;
He attains the abodes of Varuṇa, Indra, and Rudra;
he also goes to the world of Marut, Uśanas, and Brahmā.
There he was served with a seat by the daughters of the gods;
and Bhūḥ and Bhuvaḥ also gazed upon the celestial sage Viśvarūpa.
There, thirty-two maidens— sweet, well-adorned, and assuming thirty-two forms— delight that God of Gods.
O Lord, as long as both the moon and the sun move in the sky,
so long does that hero move, subsisting on the essence of nectar and ambrosia.
He who eats but one meal on the eighteenth day,
doing so consistently for twelve months, beholds the seven worlds.
He was followed from behind by chariots with joyful sounds,
drawn by celestial maidens who were radiant and beautifully adorned.
And Sumukhī ascends that supreme, divine celestial chariot, which is yoked with tigers and lions and resounds with a noise like the thundering of clouds.
There, for a thousand kalpas, he rejoices together with maidens and partakes of the supreme essence of nectar, which is like ambrosia.
He who eats but one meal on the nineteenth day,
doing so constantly for twelve months, beholds the seven worlds.
He attains the supreme station, frequented by hosts of Apsarases,
and a celestial chariot possessing the splendor of the sun, adorned with Gandharvas and the beauty of song.
There, free from all feverish distress, he rejoices with the most excellent women of the immortals;
clad in divine garments and endowed with splendor, he remains for ten million times a hundred years.
Furthermore, he who eats but a single meal on the completion of every twentieth day,
for twelve full months, being truthful and firm in his vow;
One who abstains from meat, practices celibacy, and is devoted to the welfare of all beings attains the vast and delightful worlds of the Ādityas.
He is followed from behind by Gandharvas and Apsarases, adorned with divine garlands and unguents, and by celestial golden chariots.
He who eats but a single meal on the twenty-first day,
doing so for twelve full months while constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire (jātavedas), [attains the highest state].
He goes to the divine world of Yama and to the realm of Śakra;
always delighting in the pleasures of the Aśvins and the Maruts,
he remains seated in a supreme celestial palace (vimāna), utterly ignorant of sufferings.
Served by excellent women, that lord sports like an immortal;
for twenty-two days he takes but a single meal,
constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire for twelve months.
The wise man who is devoted to non-violence, truthful in speech, and free from malice,
attains the worlds of the Vasus, possessing a radiance equal to that of the sun.
Moving at will and subsisting on nectar, seated upon a supreme celestial chariot and adorned with divine ornaments, he delights in the company of divine maidens.
He who eats but one meal on the thirteenth day,
always for twelve months, being moderate in diet and having his senses subdued;
He goes to the world of Vāyu and indeed to the world of Rudra;
moving at will and going wherever he desires, he is honored by hosts of apsarases.
Seated upon a supreme celestial chariot that possesses countless excellent qualities,
he rejoices with divine maidens, adorned with celestial ornaments.
But he who eats a single meal on the twenty-fourth day,
constantly for twelve months while offering oblations into the sacred fire (jātavedas), [attains the same merit].
Rejoicing, he shall dwell for a long time in the abode of the Ādityas;
he delights with thousands and tens of thousands of celestial maidens.
He who eats a single meal on the twenty-fifth day [attains this].
Indeed, throughout the twelve months of the year, he always mounted a magnificent vehicle,
followed from behind by chariots that resounded with joyful cries.
Mounted upon bright, stainless, and auspicious silver chariots together with celestial maidens,
he indeed delights there for a thousand kalpas, surrounded by hundreds of women.
He always obtains food and flavor that is like nectar,
he who eats but a single meal on every twenty-sixth day.
For twelve months, indeed, being self-restrained and restricted in diet,
with senses conquered and free from passion, he offered oblations into the sacred fire.
O highly fortunate one, being honored by hosts of apsarases,
he attains [this state] and enjoys the worlds of the seven Maruts and the Vasus.
Honored by Gandharvas and Apsarases,
he enjoys himself in heaven for two thousand yugas with divine splendor.
He who eats but a single meal on the twenty-seventh day,
while constantly offering oblations to the fire for twelve months, indeed [attains this].
He obtains abundant fruit and rejoices in the world of the gods;
dwelling there as one who feeds on nectar, he indeed remains satisfied and is honored.
Delighting with women who are beautiful to the mind, intoxicated with passion,
he dwells in happiness indeed for three thousand yugas and kalpas.
He who, for twelve months, always eats but one meal on the twenty-eighth day, being self-controlled and having conquered his senses;
He attains the vast fruit of the conduct of the divine sages;
endowed with splendor, he enjoys pleasures in heaven like the stainless sun.
And those women of delicate form and radiant splendor, taking delight with him,
gladden his heart in that celestial chariot as lovely as the mind desires and brilliant as the sun.
He who eats a single meal on the twenty-ninth day [of the lunar month] dwells for a hundred times ten thousand kalpas in a divine realm endowed with all desires.
For one who is constantly devoted to the vow of truth for twelve months,
his worlds are auspicious and divine, endowed with the quality of celestial fragrance.
There, beautiful celestial women, adorned with divine ornaments,
enchanting to the mind, sweet, and intoxicated with passion, delight him.
Possessing enjoyments and endowed with splendor, he was as radiant as Vaiśvānara;
divine in his celestial body, he shone like an immortal god.
He goes to the worlds of the Vasus, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the Aśvins,
as well as the worlds of the Rudras and the world of Brahmā.
But he who, being composed in soul, eats a single meal after a month has passed,
shall for twelve full months attain the destination of the world of Brahmā.
Taking nourishment from the essence of nectar, glorious and captivating to all,
he shone like the sun, endowed with splendor and a radiant body.
Seated in a celestial chariot, he is honored by women who are self-luminous.
He is constantly worshipped by the daughters of Rudras and devarṣis;
and for as long as a thousand years, he pours down rain upon Jambūdvīpa.
So many years are said to constitute the lifespan of the wise Brahmā in his world,
as many as the droplets that fall from the vault of the sky.
During the rains, he who possesses the splendor of an immortal dwells [in heaven] for as long as it rains, and so forth.

Furthermore, in Jambūdvīpa, during the rainy season, for every single drop or particle of water that falls from the sky while the wise deity sends down rain for a thousand years, for that many years does he dwell in the world of Brahmā; such is the meaning.
One who fasts for a month, however, attains the highest heaven after ten years.
Then, having attained the state of a great seer, he shall possess a physical form.
The sage is self-controlled, having conquered anger as well as his genitals and stomach;
he offers oblations into the fire according to rule and is devoted to the practice of the twilight devotions.
For that man who eats in this manner for a month according to many observances,
a dwelling is prepared for him who is habituated to living in the open air under the clouds.
Having gone to heaven with his own body, O King, like an immortal,
he enjoys merit in the celestial realm according to his desire and in accordance with the prescribed rites, O monarch.
Having observed the rules of fasting, one shall go to the supreme goal;
likewise, Vaiśyas and Śūdras also perform the fast.
For those two, nourishment is not found for three nights or two or three nights;
for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra, the practice of fasting until the fourth mealtime is prescribed.
"A three-night fast, however, has not been prescribed by those who know the Dharma, the exponents of the Veda.
Thus end the vows of great austerity.
Rāma said:
I wish to hear the names and likewise the procedure for the Kṛcchra penances;
tell this to me, for you, O knower of dharma, know it exactly as it is.
Puṣkara said:
"O Rāma, these penances (kṛcchras) are to be performed by the three castes;
it is ordained that a Śūdra has no entitlement to these penances."
O Bhārgava, at the outset, a mandala must be prepared in all difficult rites;
one should always perform ablutions three times a day and worship Keśava.
The fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with purificatory mantras, and likewise directed toward that very object;
furthermore, one should avoid conversation with women, Śūdras, and outcasts.
This should be performed without distinction in all hardships; furthermore, the vīrāsana posture should be maintained according to the rule whenever one acts out of desire.
"That which is devoid of the vīrāsana posture is proclaimed to be deficient in ritual procedure.
Rāma said:
"O observer of noble vows, I desire to hear the true nature of the vīrāsana."
When combined with the heroic posture (vīrāsana), the kṛcchra penance becomes manifold in its benefits.
Puṣkara said:
Having risen, one should remain standing during the day and likewise perform worship at night;
this is declared to be the vīrāsana posture, which destroys even the greatest sins.
For two months he subsists on *āmikṣā*, likewise for [two] months on cooked milk;
for eight nights on curd, and for three nights on clarified butter.
One should observe the Uddālaka vow for three nights without food;
it pacifies all sins and likewise grants all desires.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, one should bathe the fire for one's own sake;
thereafter, one should offer oblations into the fire with something that has not been struck by anyone.
Being consecrated with the mantra "brahmadeva," the wise one should indeed bind the *darbha* grass for the sake of protection; such is the praise.
O Rāma, a person should consecrate three times with this mantra that which has been placed [on the body], that which is being bathed, and likewise that which has been deposited in a vessel.
You are barley; you are the king of grains; you are the gift of Varuṇa mixed with honey;
you are the purifier that cuts through all evils, praised by the seers.
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, for barley is indeed the nectar of immortality;
may it purify all my evil, whatever misdeed has been committed by me.
Whatever deed has been done by speech, whatever evil dream has been experienced, whatever ill-thought has been conceived, and misfortune itself—barley grains destroy it all; may they purify me.
May the barley grains purify for me all that has been licked by dogs or pigs, or defiled by camels and the like, as well as my service to my mother and my teacher.

May all these barley grains purify for me: the food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or a period of impurity, the food of a thief, food from a recent funeral,
as well as that which belongs to children, the elderly, the unrighteous, and that which comes from the king’s gate.
May the barley grains purify for me all the sin arising from stealing gold, sacrificing for one for whom one should not sacrifice, and reviling Brahmins.
This mantra is to be placed in the vessel; thereafter, one should recite it.
Those gods who are born of joy, whose minds are concentrated, who are highly skillful, and whose father is Dakṣa—may they protect us, may they favor us; salutation to them, and salutation to you!
O knower of Dharma, one should always offer this into oneself;
one should not overeat, for this barley-meal is indeed the Brahman.

O subduer of enemies, it is declared that for those who have committed minor offenses (upapātaka), the period is three nights, or even six nights; for one guilty of a major offense (mahāpātaka), it is remembered as twice that amount, namely six nights. However, for those who have been made to wait for seven nights, they are considered eligible.
Within twenty-one nights, one obtains the desired objects of desire.

By means of barley grains obtained from cows that have been released from their stalls, one attains liberation from all sins within a month; of this there is no doubt. Indeed, by performing this very [rite] with those same grains, one achieves the same result.
O knower of dharma, one certainly attains ten times that fruit within a month;
by means of liberation, one beholds the thirty [deities], the Vedas, and the sciences.
And thus, O Bhārgava, he becomes capable of both bestowing boons and pronouncing curses;
for by eating the rice-balls, each one larger than the last, until they are the size of a hen's egg, he gains such power.
O fortunate one, one should decrease the intake by one morsel each day starting from the first day of the dark fortnight,
and one should not eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) when the moon has completely waned.
The great sage has declared this Cāndrāyaṇa to be "barley-shaped" (yavamadhya);
this same practice, when reversed, is proclaimed as "wheat-shaped" (vājimadhya).
One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance by taking eight mouthfuls of barley every day;
likewise, one may do so by some means or other with two hundred and forty morsels of food.
One should consume this for a month; it becomes the *suracāndrāyaṇa*.
[Furthermore,] one should drink cow’s milk for seven nights, and two *sure* and four *caṣṭayas*.
From three days of liquor [the effect lasts] seven nights; from seven nights, two days of liquor [lasts] six nights;
by means of three days of liquor, it becomes three nights through the wind.
This is the vow called Somāyana, which destroys all impurity:
for three days one should drink water silently, and for three days one should drink warm milk.
Having drunk hot ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for three days; this is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra*. When cold [ghee] is used, it is proclaimed as the *śītakaṛcchra*.
The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days,
consuming cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass.
A fast for one night is known as the *sāntapana* penance;
when this is practiced every day, it is known as the *mahāsāntapana*.
Then, practicing each one for three days is known as the Mahāsāntapana;
fasting for twelve full days is designated as the Parāka.
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for, and observing one full fast— this is proclaimed as the quarter-kṛcchra penance.
This very same [penance], when practiced three times over, is proclaimed as the *śiśukṛcchra*.
One should eat for three days in the morning, for three days in the evening, and for three days food that has not been asked for.
A twice-born man should not eat for three days thereafter, but should perform the Prājāpatya penance by consuming oil-cake,
curd-whey, water, and barley-meal on successive days.
A single fast for each day is proclaimed as the Saumya-kṛcchra;
likewise, subsisting for a month on water prepared with [herbs] or on water alone is the Vāruṇa-kṛcchra.
The wise have declared that the *phala-kṛcchra* consists of fruits for one month;
the *śrī-kṛcchra* is said to be performed with *bilva* fruits (*śrīphala*), and another is likewise with lotus seeds (*padmākṣa*).
Another *śrī-kṛcchra* is traditionally prescribed as being performed with *āmalaka* fruits for one month.
The Patrakṛcchra consists of leaves; that Kṛcchra is said to consist of flowers;
likewise, the Mūlakṛcchra consists of roots, while the Toyakṛcchra consists of water.
With curd, milk, buttermilk, oil-cakes, and chickpeas,
as well as with vegetables and meat, the wise should perform the rites according to their respective names.
A man who eats only in the evening and in the morning, and does not drink anything in between,
performs what is called the *ṣaḍvārṣika-kṛcchra* (six-year penance) by fasting constantly for six years.
Eating only once a day for a month is what is called the *ekabhakta* penance;
and he who eats only at night for a year performs the *naktakṛcchra*.
But he who knows the Dharma, having fasted at night— or indeed, eating but one meal—
should fast for three days and bathe at the three daily libations.
And likewise, submerged in water, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times;
its deity is Bhava, its conduct is that of the gods, and its meter is Anuṣṭubh.
Likewise, one should likewise recollect that sage and the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn;
on the fourth day, a milch cow should be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
For three days, being pure, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn according to one's ability; for the deity is remembered as being of the nature of intention, and likewise as the Supreme Puruṣa.
One should know that the hymn dedicated to that deity is the Aghamarṣaṇa;
it is like the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, which removes all sins.
Likewise, the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn is proclaimed as the destroyer of all sins;
then, having put on a black antelope skin, or a kutapa woolen blanket, or a garment of bark.
O Rāma Bhārgava, one should observe this vow for a year, including the Citra constellation;
during that time, one should not enter a house and should sleep in the open air.
Or, O Rāma, he may become incapable, dwelling in a cave of a great mountain;
he should bathe daily at the three periods of the day, and likewise, O twice-born one, he should have faith in him.
O best of the twice-born, he may eat alms, vegetables, or fruits at his pleasure;
likewise, he should practice the hero’s posture (vīrāsana) and observe silence like a piece of wood.
For this Vāyavya-kṛcchra-sūkta bestows all desires and destroys all impurities; it consists of eating only as much food as fills the palms of one's hands.
O knower of Dharma, the Agneya-kṛcchra is said to destroy all impurities when performed with sesame seeds for twelve nights, or for one month.
Likewise, for one who eats even a single *prasṛti* measure of food mixed with gold for a month, there is the *Kṛcchra* penance dedicated to the deity Candra.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, when one consumes barley flour mixed with *harītakī* entirely for a month, it is designated as the *yāmyakṛcchra*.
One should perform one's bath with cow urine and subsist on cow dung;
one should always stand in the midst of cows and lie down upon cow dung.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, one should not drink water while the cows are still drinking;
one should not eat while they have not yet eaten; and one should rise only when they have risen.
And when they have all sat down in that very manner, the man should sit down;
thus is described the month-long cow-vow (gōvrata), which destroys all impurity.
For one who dwells in the midst of the unborn, this [realization] occurs without difficulty;
yet for one who eats three times a day, the self is like chaff, and neither of the two fruits is attained.
When the [rite] that destroys all sins has been described as lasting twelve days,
one should fast on the fourteenth day and immediately thereafter on the fifteenth.
One should consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and thereafter eat sacrificial food (haviṣya);
one should indeed perform this Brahmakūrca rite for the pacification of what has been declared.
Whether it be performed at the end of a fortnight, or again in the middle of a month,
the man who always performs the Brahmakūrca rite on full-moon days—
his sin, including that resulting from improper eating, goes to destruction; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed the Brahmakūrca twice a month for one month with a concentrated mind, a man,
liberated from all sins, shall attain his desired goal.
By attending upon Keśava, who has become Brahman on the new moon day and likewise on the full moon day, and who has become Yoga itself, one shall suddenly attain [liberation].
Thus have these difficult rites been described by me to you;
here, O Bhārgava, they pacify sins and misfortunes.
The best of the twice-born should perform even a single *kṛcchra* penance for the sake of purifying food eaten unknowingly; however, for food eaten knowingly, a more specific penance is required.
Whether unknown or known, one may purify grievous sin through the *kṛcchra* penance;
for those whose sins are completely purified by the *kṛcchra*, rebirth in hell is not ordained.
One who desires prosperity, one who desires nourishment, as well as one who desires heaven,
and likewise one devoted to the propitiation of the deities, should perform the *kṛcchra* penance.
All elixirs, mantras, and medicinal herbs likewise attain success for that man who performs the *kṛcchra* penance.
And whatever Vedic rites there may be that are performed for specific desires,
O best of the Bhṛgus, they all attain success for one who performs the Kṛcchra penance.
Through that union with his great splendor, he attains all the desires of his mind; of this there is no doubt.
He becomes known among the gods as well as among the hosts of sages;
he is free from sin, free from darkness, and especially completely purified.
Having performed austerities for the sake of propitiating Madhusūdana, the Supreme Person,
he was liberated from sins and became pure in heart.
And he obtains all desires exactly as he wishes.
May the Blessed One Brahmā, that sage whose vehicle is a swan,
the four-faced god and the lord of asceticism, sacrifice, and vows, come here.
The knower of mantras should invoke Padmayoni with this mantra,
and he should worship him with devotion using the mantra "devasya ca."
With water for the guest-offering (arghya), incense, purifying substances, and in due measure with flowers, fruits, roots, offerings of food (bali), various kinds of sacrificial oblations (naivedya),
the giving of lamps according to one's ability, and through recitation (japa) and auspicious hymns of praise;
With a well-concentrated mind, one should prepare the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) before that.
One should take eight *māṣaka* measures of cow’s urine from a copper-colored cow;
it is meritorious, has Varuṇa as its presiding deity, and is consecrated with the *Gāyatrī* mantra.
One should slowly take four māṣakas of cow urine from a white-colored cow for the deity Agni with the mantra "Gandhadvārām."
Milk from a golden-colored cow, dedicated to the deity Soma,
should be offered with the mantra "Āpyāyasva," up to a quantity of twelve māṣakas.
They take curd produced from black-colored [milk], which has Vāyu as its presiding deity,
measuring exactly ten māṣakas, while recollecting the mantra "dadhi krāvṇo akāriṣam."
They take the ghee from the blue-colored vessel, measuring five māṣakas, while reciting in sequence the mantra: "Thou art the splendor whose deity is the Sun."
One should take three hundred and forty-five māṣakas of kuśa-water and recite the mantra "devasya tvā."
Having mixed that [mixture] in a copper vessel or a vessel made of *palāśa* leaves,
they stir it with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and drink it while reciting the *praṇava*.
Facing north, having sipped water three times, he should then go to that house;
having performed there the previously hidden fire-oblation, he should give a sacrificial fee.
One should provide delightful food to the Brahmins according to one's ability.

Regarding the colors of the cows, there are white and other colors; in whatever place they exist, one should collect the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) there, according to the classification of those colors.
There is no fault in [eating] what lacks color; one should avoid that which is deficient in measure.
And the excrement, urine, and milk of those who are defiled must be rejected.
And [food] that has been licked by a dog, or smeared with semen, or tainted by blood,
or eaten by a clothed woman, or likewise mixed with food not intended for consumption.
[940] And for those afflicted by disease, by means of full [vessels] and the like; for those who are inauspicious due to being dead embryos;
for the elderly because of their fruitlessness; and likewise for the emaciated because of worms.
Those given without excessive affection, those not produced by improper means,
kept in a clean and pleasing vessel, and those that have not fallen upon the ground;
These should be taken according to the prescribed rite, and one should not cause weariness for them;
this is the Brahmakūrca vow, which destroys all sins.
It bestows all desires upon men, brings about beauty, health, and fame,
destroys even the greatest of sins, and increases prosperity.
Thus ends the Brahmakūrca vow as declared in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
The sages said:
"By what action does a person obtain what, O Great-minded One?
Cut through this doubt of mine, O best of the twice-born among the twice-born."
The Haṃsa said: "O Brahmin, through giving one becomes an enjoyer; through austerity one attains greatness; and by serving the elderly, a human being becomes wise."
Through sacrifice one attains the worlds, and through truth, the supreme goal;
through ritual bathing one attains purity, and especially through breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Through meditation and through the dhāraṇās, one attains the unsurpassed state;
through self-restraint, one attains whatever resides within the mind.
The gods are pleased by purity and are pleased by fasting;
for those established in the vow of fasting, the attainment of their desires will certainly occur.
Vast enjoyments accrue to those who do not flee from battle;
for one who has desisted from honey and meat, all their heart's desires are fulfilled.
Even one who has merely desisted from eating meat experiences supreme happiness;
moreover, through non-violence one shall be free from disease, and through non-violence one shall also be long-lived.
O Brahmins, one who is always endowed with beauty, charm, good fortune, wealth,
and grain shall attain the destruction of all sins by following the path of the sacred fords (tīrthas).
But one who is free from all impurities attains an unsurpassed state by providing shelter, whatever worlds he desires in his mind.
O Brahmins, the man who honors those worthy of honor and who constantly practices salutation while serving the elderly becomes endowed with fame.
By acting thus, they increase their reputation, lifespan, fame, and strength;
likewise, one should avoid approaching one's wife except during her fertile season.
O best of Brahmins, by this very procedure, even a man who offers only water at the appropriate place and time goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
He obtains all his desires and attains his desired goal;
likewise, he who observes silence at the time of eating [attains these].
The fruit of his daily fast is obtained by one who observes silence and eats only at night once a day; he attains all his desires.
If a man bathes daily, he does not incur the suffering of hell,
provided that he gives unblemished food to one returning from a journey.
For one who has been peaceful and whom he has never seen before, his merit is great;
[he should offer] water for the feet, a seat, as well as a lamp, food, and shelter.
For the sake of honoring a guest, that Yakṣa gives five gifts:
he shall give his sight, he shall give his mind, and he shall give speech that is kind and truthful.
One who subsists on water follows [the deity] and bestows the fruit of all desires;
likewise, for those who eat flowers, there is sovereignty, and for those who eat vegetables, great wealth.
Those who subsist on milk go to heaven, and those who abstain from food attain the infinite goal;
so too does the brahmin who has given away his mortar, as well as he who lives by gleaning grains.
"May this pigeon obtain from me sustenance and its desired goal;
by fasting unto death (prāyopaveśana), sovereignty is said to be the fruit in every case.
By that which pleases one's father, Prajāpati is pleased."
By that which pleases one’s mother, the Earth is thereby honored;
by that which pleases one’s preceptor, one becomes honored by Brahmā.
All duties are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual action is fruitless.
Knowledge comes through service to the guru; progeny through the constant performance of śrāddha;
one becomes skillful by bathing daily; and one should always recite prayers during the two twilights.
Through service to the twice-born, one obtains either a kingdom or the full status of a twice-born;
through service to the gods, one thereafter attains every desire as wished.
One who bestows consolation upon all beings is honored by all the worlds.
One who properly attends to the sick is not overcome by diseases;
likewise, through service to cows, one attains the world of cows.
By removing the garlands from a deity, by washing the feet of a twice-born man,
and by massaging one who is weary, O Brahmins, one enjoys ultimate happiness.
Seven thousand [merits] are gained by [dying] in water, eleven in fire,
ten by falling from a precipice, and likewise twenty in battle.
Having cast off his body after thousands of years, a man rejoices;
however, O knowers of dharma, there is no such reckoning for one who practices fasting unto death.
One who accomplishes the rite at Mount Meru attains sovereignty on earth as desired;
having entered the station of merit, one shall attain whatever destination is wished for.
By entering the fire, one certainly attains the desired world;
by casting off the body in water, a man reaches the realm of Varuṇa.
He who, having been initiated, joyfully partakes together with deer in the young grass cast up from the mouths of those deer, goes to Amarāvatī.
He who practices that vow of eating only śaivala moss or withered leaves,
while constantly enduring the onset of cold, shall go to the supreme goal.
Whether subsisting on air, eating only roots, or even consuming fruits and roots,
one attains the sovereignty of a yakṣa and rejoices with hosts of apsarases.
In summer, during the period favorable for the application of fire, by means of the ritual prescribed by rule,
one becomes a sovereign king for twelve long years.
Having observed the restriction of food for twelve years, the sage,
upon completing his vow in due time, becomes a king, a ruler of the earth.
Having encompassed the pure space upon the sacrificial ground on all sides,
and having entered with joy, he undertook the twelve-year initiation.
He describes the fruits of the sacrificial mound: "O Brahmin, there are vehicles and couches, and houses as fit for a bed, white as the moon."
He who lives by means of his own self, being self-restrained and moderate in diet,
attains heaven after casting off the body through fasting.
He who lives for his own sake, having pressed his feet with a stone during a long twelve-year period, yet rejoices in worldly merits;
Having perfected the self by means of the self, free from dualities and without possessions,
and having completed twelve years of initiation directed solely toward the mind,
he attains the heavenly world and rejoices together with his ancestors.
He who, subsisting on his own self, abandons his body in a great battle after completing a twelve-year initiation, shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
He who, subsisting on his own self, undertakes the twelve-year initiation and casts off his body into the consecrated fire, is glorified in the world of Agni.
But that brahmin who, having been duly initiated and with his senses restrained,
has established the self within the Self, is free from the pairs of opposites and devoted to righteousness.
Having completed these twelve years of initiation in good health, he should, carrying the fire-drills upon his shoulder, undertake the practice of wandering to sacred fords.
Having traversed the path of heroes, always seated in the hero’s posture and constantly abiding as a hero,
he shall attain the destination of heroes.
When the hero has gone to the world of heroes, always practicing heroic yoga,
having renounced everything belonging to the self, initiated, self-controlled, and pure,
that glorious one goes to the world of Śakra and rejoices in heaven like a god.
Those who observe vows, are pure, self-controlled, non-violent, and speakers of truth,
having attained perfection, rejoice in freedom from suffering with the Gandharvas after death.
Lying upon a bed of frogs according to the proper place and according to the rite,
that righteous soul undergoes initiation and rejoices together with the Nāgas.
The man who, wearing wet clothes during the winter,
maintains this vow with self-restraint for twelve years, becomes a sovereign earthly king.
Likewise, one rescues from suffering the living beings dwelling in the trees and forests, as well as those seven generations of ancestors and descendants, and especially oneself.
Whatever action a person performs with whichever body,
they indeed experience that fruit with that very same body.
In whatever state one performs an action, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
in that very same state one experiences its fruit.
From the Mahābhārata: For those who subsist on fruits and roots, sovereignty is attained; for those who subsist on leaves, heaven shall be theirs;
one who subsists on milk goes to the celestial realm, while by standing in water, one gains wealth.

They say that those who subsist on grass attain heaven by means of the initiation consisting of grass, as do cows and other such creatures; by bathing at the three periods of the day, women may obtain the fruit of a sacrifice, and by drinking only air, one may likewise attain the merit of a rite.
A twice-born man who bathes daily shall obtain a kingdom, and by performing the two twilights, he attains victory;
one who practices fasting unto death conquers a kingdom including that of Indra and reaches the vault of heaven.
For those who sleep upon the bare ground, houses and beds are provided;
for those who abstain from flavors, good fortune is found.
If one provides sustenance with material gifts, the progeny shall be long-lived;
he who dwells in the water-retreat shall become a lord of men.
Withdrawal is renunciation; dwelling in water is living in the water.
The best of men who dwells in truth rejoices together with the gods.
Through the practice of perfumes and garlands, one gains abundant splendor;
by maintaining the hair and beard, one attains that supreme abode.
Having performed fasting, initiation,
and consecration for twelve years, the king excels even Vāsava.
He who hangs with his head downward, he who dwells in water,
and he who constantly practices a single austerity— he shall attain his desired goal.
Through giving one finds the supreme; through silence the self is attained;
through austerity one gains enjoyments; and through celibacy, long life.
Physical beauty, sovereignty, and health are said to be the fruits of non-violence;
through fasting unto death (prāyopaveśana), one enjoys the fruit of kingship everywhere.
One attains heaven through truth and an excellent lineage through initiation;
indeed, by studying all the Vedas, one is immediately liberated from suffering.
"One attains the heavenly world through the mental practice of the excellent Dharma.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
The sages said:
To which world does the best of men attain by what action?
Tell us that truth, for you are said to be all-knowing.
The Haṃsa said:
One should always worship with devotion one’s elder sister, father, preceptor, and mother; such a person is honored in the world of Yama.
One should honor the guest with food, lodging, and other necessities;
such a person rejoices in the worlds of the King of Kings—of this there is no doubt.
Just as those who are constantly devoted to giving and are tranquil go toward Meru and likewise to the Northern Kurus, so do they go to the world of the Moon.
Just as people go to the world of the Sun according to how they are situated,
so do those of purified intellect proceed to that world by means of the supreme pilgrimage to sacred fords.
Those slain in battle go undoubtedly to the world of Śakra;
likewise, by giving correctly, rulers of the earth go to the realm of Prajāpati.
Likewise, through devotion to cows, the best of men go to Goloka;
those who always speak the truth go to the world of the Sādhyas.
Those men who have desisted from accepting gifts and who attend to the sick are honored in the world of Vāyu, even if they possess wealth.
Those devoted to the service of the fire go to the world of Agni;
those intent on protecting others go to the world of Nirṛti;
and those who sleep in the open air rejoice in the worlds of the Bhṛgus.
Those who observe vows go to the world of Aṅgiras; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, men who give vehicles go to the world of the Maruts.
Those who give medicinal herbs rejoice in the world of the Nāsatyas; likewise, those who are affectionate toward cows, Brahmins, and the sick attain the world of Rudra.
Those men who are devoted to their own speech and are compassionate rejoice with the Ādityas; they undoubtedly attain the Vaiśvadeva realm.
The world of Brahmā, the world of Viṣṇu, and likewise the world of Rudra—
these are attained through devotion to Him, O best of the twice-born, and not otherwise.
Whatever devotion a person constantly bears toward whichever deity, that deity bestows upon him the state of residing in the same world; of this there is no doubt.
O Brahmins, I have described to you the course of a person through the divine worlds according to their karma;
what more than this shall I tell you?
Tell that to me, O you who are foremost in asceticism.
Thus end the various fruits of merit.
Now, the procedure for the renunciation of the body is described; these include fasting to death, entering fire, leaping from a precipice, and so forth. From the Viṣṇudharmottara:
A man, even if free from disease, should not abandon his own body;
for those worlds called "the lowest," shrouded in blind darkness—
to them go after death all those people who are slayers of the self.
Having realized that his own death was imminent through undesirable omens,
he was afflicted by disease and abandoned by physicians when his lifespan had reached its end.
Just as one should cast off one's own body in accordance with the [spiritual] age,
by abandoning the body at that time, one shall obtain the fruit as described.
The death of a Brahmin before his full lifespan has been observed,
as well as that of a Kṣatriya in battle, and of a woman whose husband has died.
For the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, one may sacrifice one's own body;
for everyone, even if it is not the appointed time [of death], shall attain the highest state.
From the Āditya Purāṇa:
"He who may be joined with great sins such as the *mahāpātaka*s,
or he who may be afflicted by incurable, great diseases."
When the time for the destruction of his own body has arrived,
even a highly intelligent Brāhmaṇa [should act] out of a desire to win great rewards such as heaven.
In the morning, he makes himself blaze forth, or likewise practices fasting unto death,
or else plunges into a bottomless mass of water or falls from a precipice.
One may go with devotion to the Mahāpatha or to the Tuṣāra mountain,
or one may cast off the body at the tip of the branch of the Prayāga banyan tree.
One shall attain the highest worlds and shall never be a slayer of a kinsman;
through the destruction of all great sins, one enjoys divine pleasures.
The eligibility for these [rites] among all living beings is through austerity;
this rule applies to men and women of all castes.
Having approached his mother-in-law, his own mother, a virtuous Brahmin sister,
a woman who fasts for a month, or likewise the wife of his teacher,
a Brahmin should enter a fire of dried cow-dung and undergo great penance.
Likewise, in the Revākhaṇḍa:
"Those who have died on the bank of the Narmadā, at the confluence, or upon seeing a Liṅga—
their houses shall be delightful and situated in the eastern region."
Likewise, at the confluence of the Sāvitrī in the middle of the Narmadā and the Medā,
and at the presence of Tripurā as well as in the presence of Viṣṇu.
On the southern side of Oṃkāra, at Marakaṇṭaka in the east,
at the reservoir of water known as Koṭitīrtha, those human beings who have died there [attain liberation].
And these most excellent men dwell in these delightful palaces;
whether on the Bhrigu mountain, in fire, in water, or at the confluence of all rivers.
And likewise at Ātreyī and Bhāratī, as well as in Vārāṇasī;
at Drumālaya, Gogṛha, Gokarṇa, and Mahālaya.
At Hariścandra, Purīścandra, Śīśila, and Tripurāntaka; at the Kṛṣṇā, the Tuṅgabhadrā, and the Mahārathyā, the great river.
O son, those who die at Svāmikuṇḍa in the month of Kārttika,
or who give up their lives at the Sarasvatī in Prabhāsa, which is adorned by the Moon;
[950] On Mount Pāriyātra, at Mahākāla, those who abide in reality are born. First, fasting is described according to the Viṣṇudharma:
"O Great-minded One, this which has been stated is the foremost of all austerities."
On account of his qualities, Brahmā declared fasting to be the most excellent.
Indeed, he who, while observing a fast, gives up his life-breaths while remembering Hari,
goes to the realm of Viṣṇu for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
O bull among men, by practicing fasting here, one purifies seven, seven, and seven families of the past and the future.
No other meritorious deed is declared to be superior to fasting for those who are afflicted;
I shall describe its characteristics, as well as that which is to be chanted by one who is about to die.
O great Asura, having recognized that his own time had come near, the wise Janārdana should be meditated upon in whatever form [is appropriate].
Having shaken off the impurities and defects, bathed, and with a restrained mind,
he likewise worshipped Hṛṣīkeśa with flowers, incense, and other offerings.
One should worship with prostrations, praises, meritorious acts, and the yoga of meditation; and likewise, having given gifts to the Brahmins, one should worship Vikalāditya.
In the assembly, among fellow Brahmins, among gods, in ascetic practice,
toward kinsmen, sons, and wives, and regarding fields, grain, wealth, and the like—
And, O Lord of Daityas, one should repeatedly turn away from the sense of "mine" regarding the circle of friends,
as well as toward friends, enemies, neutrals, and others.
One should seek forgiveness for one's own good deeds through the practice of humble entreaty;
thereafter, being purified, one should perform the ritual relinquishment of all actions.
O Lord of Daityas, one should utter this Vedic mantra of the Śunāśunās:
"I renounce this gift; I honor all my friends."
I have renounced food and the like, as well as betel, ointments, and services such as attendance; I have abandoned both giving and taking.

The ritual acts such as the fire-oblation (homa), whatever regular sequences belong to me, as well as those performed on specific occasions, those for desired results, and those prescribed for the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha).
The duties of the stages of life and likewise the beneficial duties of the castes have been abandoned by me;
wandering or acting as I please day after day with my feet and hands.
I shall not inflict evil upon any living being; may all creatures be fearless—those that dwell in the sky, those in the waters, and those upon the earth.
Those who dwell in holes in the earth, those who live among heaps of stones,
and those who reside in grain, clothing, beds, and seats;
Nothing given by one's own intellect to them brings fear;
I have no kinsman whatsoever other than Viṣṇu, the teacher of the world.
And may Viṣṇu be on my side as a friend—below, above, and likewise in front;
on my flanks, on my head, in my heart, in my two arms, and even in my two eyes.
"Viṣṇu is established within me in the ears and all other limbs"—
having thus abandoned everything and meditated upon the omnipresent Acyuta.
O Lord of Gods, one should constantly recite the name of Vāsudeva;
then, one should lie down upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing south, with the head directed toward the east.
Or, O Lord of the Daityas, with his head toward the north, he meditated upon Viṣṇu,
the Lord of the Universe— the victorious Jiṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, Keśava, and Madhusūdana.
Nārāyaṇa, Nara, Sauri, Vāsudeva, Janārdana, Vārāha, Yajñapuruṣa, Pauṇḍarīka, and Acyuta.
Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Kṛṣṇa, Nṛsiṃha, Aparājita, Padmanābha, Aja, Śrīśa, Dāmodara, and Adhokṣaja.
To Rāma, the Lord of all lords, the pure, the infinite, the Sovereign;
who bears the discus and the mace, who is peaceful, who holds the conch, and whose banner is Garuḍa.
I bow down to the imperishable one who wears the crown and the kaustubha gem;
may Janārdana abide in this Lord of the World, and he in me.
Let there be no difference between us, as there is none between the *śamī* tree and the sky.
This is Viṣṇu, this is Sūrya, and this Kṛṣṇa is my city;
he who is dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes as broad as lotus petals.
This Lord is indeed most visible; I behold Hari, from whom I am not distinct, who am the mind, and upon whom I depend.
Thus, with a one-pointed mind, he should mutter [the mantra] while remembering Hari, the Lord of All,
having transcended all sufferings and remaining equanimous toward both friends and enemies.
Homage be to Vāsudeva; one should constantly recite what is prescribed for the vow,
or recite whatever name one is capable of uttering,
and likewise meditate upon the beautiful form of the god Viṣṇu.
With serene eyes, eyebrows, and face, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, gracious-minded, four-armed, and wearing a crown.
One should always contemplate the form of Kṛṣṇa, wearing yellow garments and adorned with beautiful armlets, having fixed the mind with single-minded resolve.
Whatever form of the Discus-bearer the dwarf fixes his mind upon,
one should contemplate that very form and proclaim, "Vāsudeva. Thus, constantly reciting and remembering the true nature of the Supreme Self, [953] one should practice.
O bull among men, until the cessation of breath, a hero whose mind is fixed on Him and who has Him as his sole refuge— even if he is burdened with every sin—
attains dissolution in Acyuta, the most worshipful Lord of the gods of gods.
Just as fire, when joined with the wind, consumes masses of grass,
so too does the resolve for fasting completely burn away the sins of men.
Behind him, celestial maidens holding chowries follow him in aerial chariots;
and in that abode of divine maidens,
the man dwells for a full year, which is equal to the sands of the Ganges.
Bali said:
At the time of death, the mental faculties of living beings become deluded;
how much more so, then, for those afflicted by the defects of disease and the like, who are already devoid of youth?
If, being extremely advanced in age and afflicted by disease,
he is unable to remain on the ground upon a bed of darbha grass;
Therefore, O Grandfather, tell me if there is any other means for men in the performance of action by which it does not meet with failure.
Prahlāda said:
"In this matter, neither the ground, nor the kusha grass, nor the mat is the cause;
Viṣṇu alone, who has become the object of my meditation, is the cause here."
Whether standing, walking, sleeping, waking, or running here and there,
at the time of death, by remembering Govinda, one becomes absorbed in Him.
O best of Daityas, what is the use of recitations, or indeed what is the use of ritual acts, or even of *kuśa* grass,
for one in whose heart Janārdana does not reside, despite performing them?
Therefore, my son, you must always practice the meditation upon Vāsudeva;
O Lord of Daityas, through absorption in Him, the means for that shall be explained in detail.
Thus, O sinless one, everything that I was asked by you has been told;
now, what further shall I tell you regarding the remembrance [of the Lord] at the time of departure?
From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa: "Indeed, [the merit lasts] for seven thousand years in water,
eleven in fire, and sixteen in falling [from a cliff]."
O Bhārata, for sixty years in the house of cows, for eighty years in battle, and for an infinite duration in fasting, one attains an imperishable state.
And so says the Śatapatha Śruti:
"They desire to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through celibacy,
austerity, faith, sacrifice, and fasting."
From the Saura Purāṇa:
Having become fasting in a sacred field of Śiva, one should abandon one's life-breaths;
through the power of the Supreme Lord, one attains union with Śiva.
From the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"O best of sages, having remained without food for as long as it takes, one who gives up their life in a sacred field of Śiva shall attain union with Śiva."
Thus concludes the procedure for fasting.
Now begins the section on the Great Procession (*mahāyātrā*):
They sport in the celestial Ganges, in the eighth path of the winds.
By whom the lordly elephants, Kumuda and the others, were brought to Janārdana.
Therefore, the meditation on Vāsudeva is said here to be the primary [act];
it is stainless, born of Brahman, and by its rays it becomes the water of the Gaṅgā.
Having taken it, they release it with a "phut" sound while facing the south.
They were scorched on their backs by the falling rays and, due to proximity, by the sun's beams.
Possessing the power to awaken the pillar and to pacify the burning,
that water, blue-hued like a great waterfall, was falling down.
Being established by the wind, it attains stability;
and when that merit falls as snow upon the slopes of the Himalayas, it becomes solid.
First, Himavat and Śiśira are to be worshipped there,
as well as the nāga Hemanta, who is born from the blue-blue lotus.
The serpents of the site should be worshipped with vessels made of *kāla* wood, not those made from *meru* wood;
*arka* flowers should be offered, and the incense should be derived from *guggulu*.
One should offer a large amount of cold water mixed with ghee and sesame seeds for the ancestors;
however, in a region where there is no snow, one should say "snow, snow."
The Great Departure (mahāprasthāna) journey should be undertaken following the fire sacrifice;
relying on complete fortitude, it bestows immediate liberation.
As long as he has not reached Purandara in the world due to the gravity of his task,
he would rather venture to cast off his own body in the midst of snow.
But when one who is consumed by frost, losing consciousness and casting off his life-breaths,
sees a conch shell turning clockwise within a blazing fire—
that is the body of Viṣṇu, which draws all things toward itself and burns away the effects of the moon and fire.
Thus concludes the Great Departure as described in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
[956] Now follows the entry into the fire.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Whether one is a preeminent maintainer of the sacred fires or has set out upon the path of heroes,
having first composed the mind, one should slowly recite the mantra."
O Agni, you are Rudra; you are the vast heaven of great light;
you rule over the host of Maruts and over nourishment;
you travel with the ruddy winds, O wielder of the thunderbolt.
As Pūṣan, you protect the worshiper by your own self.
Thus, the twice-born who correctly recites the mantra with his mind and enters the fire goes to the world of Rudra.
The Lord Agni is Time; he is remembered as Rudra, who is Time.
Therefore, whoever enters the fire transcends Rudra.
From the Liṅga Purāṇa:
Having established the sacred fire in a field of Śiva and having worshipped the Supreme Lord, one should offer the lump of one's own body as an oblation; he goes to the supreme state.
From the Saura Purāṇa:
Having established a fire in front of Śiva and worshipped Keśava,
he who offers his own body as an oblation goes to the presence of Śiva.
Now, the entering of fire by women is prescribed. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"When he is distressed, she is distressed; when he is joyful, she is delighted; when he has gone abroad, she is soiled and emaciated;
when he dies, she should die—such a woman is to be known as a devoted wife (pativratā)."
Then Aṅgiras said:
"For virtuous women here,
once their husband has died, no other duty is ever to be known than following him by entering the fire."
A woman is not liberated from her female body in any way whatsoever.

For women who have entrusted their husbands with the state of virtuous conduct, separation from them is more unbearable than the earth itself; for when their husband has set, it would be as if [the world] had ended.
For the path is indeed free from fear through entering the fire.
Hārīta says: Listen now to the fruit obtained by that woman who, being virtuous and firm in her vows, follows her husband when he has died.
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on a human being— whether three and a half crores or however many— so long is one honored in the heavenly world.
She who follows her husband purifies three lineages: that of her mother, that of her father, and the family into which she is given as a bride.
Vyāsa says: Whether it be the sin of killing a Brahmin, being ungrateful, or killing a friend—
that woman who dies taking her husband with her purifies him.

"Having taken [her] and embraced her"—this is the meaning. Thus says the author of the Kalpasūtra: "They say that the wife lies down together with the body of the husband," as stated in the Ādityapurāṇa.
Whether she offers her body into the fire along with her deceased husband,
or whether she is one who possesses the great ocean-like depth of being through the excellence of her goodness— any such woman is a devoted wife.
This great sacrifice of the ancestral offering (pitṛmedha) is proclaimed for women;
therein the body, while still possessed of life, is the oblation, and the vital breaths are the sacrificial fee.
[958] However, the brother-in-law may at all times gratify his brother’s wife, provided he does so in a manner consistent with the meaning of the *Ṛgveda*, while remaining accompanied by her husband.
Placing these virtuous women, devoted to their husbands, upon the funeral pyre, the wise man has performed the highest and most extensive duty. These holy wives have been born as devoted spouses.
