Having attained a state free from widowhood, adorned with jewel ornaments,
anointed with saffron, clarified butter, and collyrium, they were honored with garlands and made beautiful with their finery.
May they obtain a firm union with their husbands by their own power;
free from malicious rumors, may they remain well and unafflicted by disease,
and enter the fire together with the bodies of their husbands.
Having heard this, a woman endowed with faith and devotion may then attain heaven through the Pitṛmedha sacrifice.
When her husband has died, for virtuous women there is no other course of action.
There can be no other pacification for the burning caused by the fire of separation from her husband;
according to the words of the Ṛgveda, a virtuous wife must not commit suicide.
This very same is the statement of the Ṛgveda:
"May these women, who are not widows and have good husbands, enter with ointment and clarified butter."
O Agni, let the wives, stainless, free from disease, and possessing excellent jewels, ascend to their place of origin.
If he dies in another land, that virtuous wife, having purified herself and placed his two sandals upon her breast,
may enter the fire.
Vyāsa says:
When a devoted wife hears that her beloved has gone to an unknown place, she ascends a blazing fire; learn now of her power. [959]
"Vṛtta" means dead.
Even if one has entered hell, bound by most cruel nooses,
having undergone tortures there, and seized by the servants of Yama;
Standing helpless and dejected, writhing under the power of his own past deeds, he remains;
yet, just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent by force,
so too does she take her husband and ascend to heaven through the power of her asceticism.
There, devoted supremely to her husband and being praised by hosts of apsarases,
she sports with her lord for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
In the Varāha Purāṇa: Then she beheld her husband, wearing divine garments, adorned with divine ornaments, and seated in a celestial chariot in the sky.
From the Kūrma Purāṇa: A woman may rescue her husband— even if he is a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, or defiled by a mortal sin— by entering the fire together with him.
The wise know this alone to be the supreme expiation for women;
there is no need for further deliberation regarding any sin that may have arisen.
From the Āditya Purāṇa:
"She who, upon the death of her husband, at any time ascends the fire,
being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world."
Whether from her mother’s side or her father’s side, the woman to whom a girl is given purifies three lineages— the one of her birth and the one of her husband— if she follows after her husband.
Where she sports with her husband for as long as fourteen Indras endure;
now follows the ritual procedure involving the fire of dried cow-dung.
The man who prepares a fire-pit of dried cow-dung in the Puṣkara forest,
having abandoned all worlds, goes to the world of Brahmā.
He shall dwell in the world of Brahmā for as long as the destruction of the kalpa occurs;
he shall not fall back among mortals, even while being tormented by his own karmas.
And his movement is unimpeded across, upwards, and downwards;
wandering at will through the worlds of the Seven Sages and all other realms, he is the master of himself.
He was skilled in the rules of etiquette, captivating to all the senses,
knowledgeable in dance, instrumental music, and song, fortunate, and pleasing to behold.
Being honored with flowers, adorned with divine ornaments,
dark as the petal of a blue lotus, and possessing dark, curly hair.
With unconquerable waists, they were honored for all their good fortune;
endowed with all sovereign qualities, they were exceedingly proud of their youth.
Women constantly attend upon him and delight him on his bed;
even when asleep, he is awakened by the sounds of lutes and flutes.

Through the grace of Brahmā, the god of gods and the performer of auspicious deeds, he enjoys the happiness of a great festival, which is difficult to attain for those who have not disciplined themselves.
Thus ends the method for preparing the kārīṣa fire as described in the Padma Purāṇa,
from the Revākhaṇḍa. [961]
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O great sage, to what destination do those heroes who fall from a cliff go? I truly desire to hear this; please tell me."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Listen now to the destiny of those heroes who give up their lives by fasting on alternate days and by restraining themselves from food during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
And their individual dwellings, according to their respective karma,
number twenty-four crores, as well as another seventeen.
But formerly, both the intermediate and superior kalpas were cursed;
however, that man who gives up his life according to this rite [attains the higher state].
That husband has indeed been granted by me to you through your grace;
and those who have died shall truly attain the status of husbands to you, [becoming] lords of the immortals.
By seeing Bhṛgu, the best of lineages, one is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin;
eighty-four Bhṛgus are proclaimed to exist in Jambūdvīpa.
Likewise, seven others are specified as the supreme stairways to heaven;
Bhairava and Bhṛguśreṣṭha are to be known [as such] at Amarakaṇṭaka.
O King, Śūdras, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and even those of the lowest castes may indeed give up their lives, provided they avoid a twice-born man.
Having fallen there, the Brahmin would become both a slayer of a Brahmin and a slayer of himself.
And when Rāhu and the Moon meet, O King, thirty-two thousand years pass; then one becomes a king in the city of the Vidyādharas.
When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, one enjoys double the fruit [of his merit],
whether he be helpless or self-controlled, even if destroyed by floods or fire;
O King, having reached Bhṛgu, he shall become a sovereign of the Vidyādharas.
"Know Bhṛgu, who originated from Kailāsa, to be Bhairava in form.
Those who revile Bhṛgu are proponents of the Brahman-linga;
Bhairava forgives them—thus it was proclaimed by Skanda."
A Brahmin who has fallen from renunciation (saṃnyāsa), as well as one who has killed his mother or father,
is freed from that sin by falling [into the fire], by the sacred cord (kāṣāgni), and by ritual purification; he goes to the world of Śiva.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, whoever indeed dwells here for a year, half a year, three months, or even a single month, or for seven or three days;
Indeed, by fasting on alternate days, he shall go to the abode of Śiva—
whether at Hariścandra, Purīścandra, Śrīśaila, or Tripurāntara.
By falling into the Dhautapāpa, the Mahāpuṇya, the Vārāha on the Vindhya mountain,
or likewise into the pool of the Kāverī, one shall attain heaven.
On the southern side of Bhṛgu, however, is the Liṅga known as Cāpaleśvara,
famous here for the protection of the sacred field and the destruction of sins.
Bhṛgu is at Bhṛtī with sixty [steps]; that indeed should be known as Cāpaleśvara. If a man ascends the mountain without having seen it, he undoubtedly takes away all the fruit of his merit.
Having painted the sun upon a cloth, adorned with banners and staffs,
and having placed a sacrificial offering in his hand while being fanned with chowries,
the hero, with a parasol held over him by Rudras, should ascend Mount Bhṛgu.
"At every step he shall obtain the fruit of a sacrifice; so Śaṅkara has declared."
Deluded by desire, the apsarases, mounted upon divine vehicles and adorned with celestial ornaments, await the time of the festival.
But a hero who has fallen there, having himself cast off his body,
shall at that very moment become equal to Śakra in the divine worlds, O King.
Having mounted the vehicle that grants all desires, he shall go to the city of Śiva together with celestial nymphs, filled with joy, even while engaged in mutual dispute.
For one who is impotent, devoid of strength, or who has leaped from a precipice,
there is no doubt that he incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin at every step.
Since a mortal does not have a long life, why does he fear death?
For who is capable of holding back a man who has fallen under the power of Time and Death?
That most wicked man of evil conduct, a social outcaste censured by the world,
is he who, having ascended to the state of renunciation and the like, falls away from it.
Upon seeing a Brahmin who has fallen from renunciation, a person should gaze at the sun with every effort; if he touches him, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should never speak truth or falsehood with him;
indeed, one should set out in silence, unless one would thereby incur sin.
When death has been determined to have arrived, how can one remain indifferent toward one's sustenance?
Since old age, death, and disease exist within the perilous ocean of saṃsāra,
O best of kings, having understood this, one should indeed ascend the supreme Bhṛgu.
[964] From the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. Kṛṣṇa said:
I shall tell you that procedure, O son of Pāṇḍu;
having performed which rite first, that [result] will follow immediately thereafter.

Having first performed three *kṛcchra* penances, a man who is pure, bathing at the three periods of the day (*triṣavaṇa*), subsisting on a diet of vegetables and barley-gruel, should recite [the mantra] ten hundred-thousand times.
One should worship the Lord, the God of gods, the three-eyed one, at the three times of day;
O King of kings, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) right there with a tenth part [of the offerings].
One should thus recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times and worship with perfumes and garlands;
then, at night in a dream, one will see oneself seated in a celestial chariot (vimāna). O dear one, one might then somehow feel that one has not yet achieved one's goal.
Whoever casts himself down according to this very procedure,
having reached the heavenly world, rejoices together with the thirty gods.
Having enjoyed various pleasures for thirty thousand years and likewise thirty million years, he would then go to the surface of the earth.
Honored by the twice-born, he shall enjoy the earth under a single umbrella;
freed from disease and sorrow, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
From the Devīpurāṇa: The Supreme Lord said:
"If indeed the Bhairava form has been assumed for the sake of destroying living beings..."
He shall become the king of mountains for the sake of favoring all living beings.
Those sons of mine who have entered into that state and have been meditated upon by me—
those husbands of mine fall [into it] as well, and they indeed become equal to me.
Having thus enjoyed the pleasures appropriate for a king by means of that [practice],
they gradually attain Anudbhava, which certainly bestows liberation there.
Brahmā said:
Thus were those words spoken by the trident-bearing God of gods,
which eternally bring joy to women who desire a husband.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Lord, what is this Bhairava form, and how did it come to be?
O God, please graciously tell me the fruit of the Pātālajatrā.
Brahmā said: Those who, endowed with such devotion, have fixed Śiva in their minds, go to Bhairava; they go to Rudra; they go to the supreme state.

O great sage, even those twice-born who go to Bhairava out of affection, fear, greed, or curiosity, attain the state of Śiva and the state of Rudra through that very grace and by the gradual application of yoga; such is the case for those brahmins across the worlds.
Alternatively, having fashioned the terrifying form— purifying and worshipped by the gods— which bestows all desires, as Bhairava upon a great vehicle in a vessel,
those twice-born ones attain the state of Rudra as the twenty-five-armed deity.
Alternatively, having fashioned the form of Bhairava upon a cloth— worshipped by the gods, the great vehicle, Bhairava who grants all desires— one should place it in a vessel.
The deity should be depicted with twenty-five arms, his body yellow, worshipped by the gods,
holding a sword and a shield, and with his supreme hand raised, brandishing a trident.
He wears an elephant hide, and likewise has an arm raised with a discus;
he holds a khaṭvāṅga staff, a skull-cup, a vajra, and a ḍamaru drum.
In such a form— with terrifying fangs and a face like the earth—
Śaṅkara, the three-eyed one, was piercing Andhaka.
Let them fashion the god Bhairava, who is worshipped by gods and asuras alike,
endowed with various auspicious and non-auspicious forms, and adorned with diverse ornaments.
The splendor of fresh youthfulness, which illuminates all beauty;
Vāsuki, the king of serpents, serves as the sacred thread for the razor-king.
The Kulika should be placed in the binding of the matted locks by Śaṅkhapāla,
and Takṣaka and Padmanāga should be made as ornaments for the armlets.
The two auspicious serpents Padma and Karkoṭaka, serving as anklets upon his feet—
thus one should fashion the god Bhairava, who grants all desires.
Two gatekeepers should be fashioned for him, with yellow limbs and all auspicious marks;
they are two auspicious deities holding tridents in their hands, possessing the sounds of elephants and horses.
The two gatekeepers there, Gaṅgā and the others, should be placed at the Bhairava gateway;
for if they are provoked by afflictions and the like, they will commit a transgression here.
Thus, O one of noble vows, has this been told to you here as an incidental discourse:
the two gatekeepers of the god should be depicted holding skull-topped spears and blue lotus sprouts, adorned with all ornaments.
One should visualize the form of Bhairava with an upward-facing face, accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the other gods,
bearing the appearance of having pierced Andhaka with his trident.
Having thus prepared [the image] on cloth and worshipped the supreme Lord together with his retinue and the mantra, one should honor him with red garlands, garments, and other offerings.
Having adorned oneself, with hands decorated by ritual mudrās,
one should reach that delightful abode which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having performed worship to the Lord of Gods, the remover of the pride of Gayāndhaka,
one shall ascend to the immortal abode that bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Having contemplated the form that bestows one's own desires,
one should perform the fire-offering (homa) into the fire of its mouth by means of the oblation of oneself.
The sacrificial fire is indeed the mouth of the gods; therefore, those who desire supreme accomplishment should offer sesame seeds and other substances with that very disposition.
Understand now the heroic *pātaṅgaka* according to its rotation:
he who casts himself like a moth into the fire of a lamp—this descent is called *pātaṅga*; now hear that which is known as the *haṃsa*.
Having restrained the assembly of its wings and made its body swift-moving,
that flight named Haṃsa bestows the fruit of the practitioner's desire.
Just as a deer in the herd might move by leaping over pits and such,
so too is that movement called the "deer-fall" (mṛgapāta) in which one places both feet together.
Just as one who has become a pestle might fall upon a mortar in the *mauśala* [yuga],
so too shall one obtain celestial chariots, garlands of banners, branches, swings, and the like.
O twice-born one, having performed the "shaking" (dhūnana) for a very long time like a bull,
you should recognize the "bull-fall" (vṛṣapāta), which bestows the fruit of the world of Rudra.
Just as a lion exerts its body in the destruction of a lordly elephant,
so too is the descent performed with that same intent considered the "lion's pace" (siṃhakrama).
Having assumed a terrifying form equipped with weapons and freed from all affliction, one should cast that body into the mouth of Śiva; that fall bestows the state of Bhairava.
Just as the birds beginning with the Pātaṅga, O twice-born ones, proceed toward their own essential nature,
so too do all those who bestow fruits advance toward the state of Bhairava.
The worlds are diverse and innumerable by count;
those foods and drinks which exist here, they too are limited in sequence.
Even those who are devoid of initiation and have fallen under the sway of transgression,
having experienced excellent enjoyments, proceed to the supreme state.
For even a sinful man there, though devoid of caste and stage of life,
enjoys excellent happiness through the very power of the God.
Likewise, Nandakedāradeva and Rudramahālaya are equal to Bhairava; they grant liberation at the end of worldly enjoyment.
O tiger among gods, there are four things that remove all misfortune;
even those men who are driven away from there by the angry [deities], if they are moved by mere association [with the devotees],
they too shall ascend the vehicle and come to the auspicious state.
Having gone to heaven in due order and enjoyed various supreme [pleasures],
they are endowed with diverse forms and bestow all desired objects and happiness.
Maidens of sixteen years, with full and elevated breasts, enjoy these most wonderful things; those men partake of the drink and apply themselves to the practice.
Or if women should cause [the ritual substance] to fall, then they enjoy terrible [rebirths];
yet, through their sovereignty, they possess divine enjoyments and the like, accompanied by throngs of apsarases.
Likewise, the Gāndharva, Yakṣa, Kinnara, and Vāruṇa [mantras],
as well as the Vidyādhara, Saura, and Raudra, are established in their respective order.
One shall obtain a celestial realm endowed with the perfection of one's own desired enjoyments;
having enjoyed that even according to one's own wish, one goes at the end to the supreme state.
One should always wear a rosary made of the bones of Viṣṇu and a conch-shell sacred to Śambhu,
for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds, [upon that devotee of] the Lord of the Gods.
Those who, having performed meritorious deeds, worship [images] made of various elements, wood, or even precious stones and mountains, they too go to the state of Śiva.
Thus, whether in a house, on a mountain, or in rivers, the Vindhya mountains, or forests,
whoever worships Bhairava shall obtain his desired fruit.
Having constructed these four— a leaf-hut, a flower-garden, a monastery, and a well— for Bhairava, they should be offered for the attainment of happiness.
Whatever fruit a human being obtains by giving to all the gods,
that same fruit one may obtain from Bhairava by giving to a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas.
Thus ends the procedure for leaping from a cliff.
Now follows the procedure for battle.
Dharmadhvaja said:
"The path to heaven for heroes has been described by you, O best of sages, through the context of the battlefield; therefore, you ought to speak further on this matter."
Maitreya said: One does not obtain that fruit by performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees which one might obtain in battle.
Thus have those who know the sacrifice and are skilled in sacrificial rites declared.
Therefore, I shall explain to you that fruit which belongs to those who live by the sword.
The gain of Dharma, the gain of wealth, and likewise the gain of fame belongs to that man who is a hero and has crushed the enemy host.

For him who mounts that vehicle after slaying one who was facing him in battle, there is indeed the attainment of dharma, artha, and kāma, as well as sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Striding like Viṣṇu, he thus exerts himself while fighting on the field of battle;
by that deed, he obtains the merit of four horse-sacrifices.
But that hero who, not casting aside his weapon, stands facing the enemy at the head of the army with valor— he does not return from heaven.
Whether it be a king, a prince, or even a commander-in-chief,
whoever is slain by a kṣatriya shall swiftly attain an eternal and certain world.
As many weapons as pierce his skin in battle,
so many inexhaustible worlds, yielding all desires, does he obtain.
The heroic posture, the heroic bed, and the steadfast persistence in remaining in a firm position—
those who are slain for the sake of cows, for the sake of Brahmins, or for the sake of their cowherds,
go to the stainless realm just like those of meritorious deeds.
He who strikes down an enemy while unbroken, protects one who is broken,
and guards those standing at his back— he too attains that same state.
Likewise, one who has not yet crossed over [the battle] may immediately give up his life in combat;
having fallen in battle with his horses slain, he does not return from heaven.
O King, those who have been killed by fanged or horned creatures, or by barbarians and thieves, for the sake of their master, attain heaven; of this there is no doubt.
O King, whether out of fear, shame, or affection, he who dies facing the enemy on the field of battle attains heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Celestial maidens follow and delight that hero whose body is marked with the wounds of arrows, spears, swords, and lances.
Thousands of celestial nymphs run swiftly toward that hero slain in battle, crying out, "He is my husband! He is mine!"
Wherever a hero is slain while surrounded by enemies,
he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not speak while intoxicated.
By conquering, one gains fortune; even by dying, one gains a celestial maiden. Since life is destroyed in an instant, what anxiety can there be regarding death in battle?
Whatever property is seized by others from one who has been slain, or is standing face-to-face with them, or has fallen, or does not retreat— that indeed is his own wealth, for it bears fruit.
From the *Viṣṇudharma*: "Indeed,
it is possible here for men endowed with righteousness— even by the hundreds— as stated,
to sacrifice their own bodies for the sake of a Brahmin in battle, though this is exceedingly difficult."
That very destination which Brahmins seeking heaven attain through attachment to sacrifice, through austerity, and through the performance of long sacrificial sessions,
they reach in a single moment.
In the great battle, they cast away their own bodies.
All the Vedas together with their six auxiliary limbs, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and the asceticism of men—
one may transcend all these qualities in a single step.
He who would sacrifice his own body for the sake of a righteous battle.

He of firm vows who remembers these well-spoken words— composed of variegated phrases and auspicious syllables, spoken by the slayer of Vṛtra for the sake of the gods— as he stands on the verge of battle;
He is not slain, yet he slays his enemies in battle.
This is the most meritorious heaven, a perfect sacrifice facing all directions;
it belongs to all castes indeed, but especially to the Kṣatriya.
Furthermore, I shall speak again these unsurpassed words of Bhīṣma:
one should avoid a striker exactly as he is.
Even if an assailant approaches on the battlefield seeking to kill him, one who has mastered the Vedānta may slay him with the intent to kill; by doing so, he does not become a killer of a Brahmin.
O Great-minded One, one who speaks of water when his horse has been killed should be slain; as should one who is afflicted by calamity while eating.
One who is intent on flight, who abandons his life-breaths in a pitiable manner,
who runs about with disheveled hair, and who appears like one insane;
One who carries leaves, branches, or grass, one who says "I am yours," and one who says "I am a Brahmin," as well as a child, an elderly man, or a eunuch—
one should avoid these individuals on the field of battle, as they have been specified.
From the Kālikā Purāṇa:
"In former times, the sages declared that there is no atonement for men who [kill] one who is afflicted,
terrified, agitated, a scribe (kāyastha), or one who has come for refuge."
Furthermore, [one should avoid killing] a woman, a child, a cow, a cripple, an ascetic,
one who is lamenting, one who is insane, one who is exhausted, and likewise a Brāhmaṇa.
[973] He fell, fleeing away, alone and weaponless;
naked, wretched, and likewise aged, he approached the vicinity of his shattered hopes.
Those fools who will slaughter one with disheveled hair, intoxicated, or sleeping like a beast in the forest, shall surely [emerge] from the ocean of hell.
Through lack of exertion, they fall apart like an elephant that has collapsed.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Rāma said:
"I wish to hear the great truth concerning the warfare of kings."
O illustrious one, O God, you know everything, like the Supreme Lord Brahmā.
Puṣkara said:
"When the battle takes place on the second day,
the king should then bathe his elephants with auspicious waters containing all medicinal herbs."
One should adorn and worship with perfumes and garlands according to the prescribed rule;
one should worship Viṣṇu as Nṛsiṃha and all the royal insignia in their entirety.
O mighty-armed one, the parasol, the banner, the flag, the Dharma itself,
and likewise all weapons must be honored by the king.
Having performed their worship and having conducted the first worship of the night,
one should pray for a dream regarding victory or its opposite.
And first, O great Pārtha, the lord of the earth should sleep upon the ground in the midst of his physicians, domestic chaplain, ministers, and counselors.
Self-restrained and practicing celibacy, while constantly remembering Hari, the Man-Lion,
he should undertake the commencement of battle when an auspicious dream is seen at night.
Having risen at the end of the night and bathed in water infused with all medicinal herbs,
he should worship Nṛsiṃha along with his vehicle and every other requisite without exception.
Beholding the sacrificial fire kindled and offered by the domestic priest,
the pure priest should there offer the mantras as before.
Then the lord of the earth should honor the brahmins with sacrificial fees;
thereafter, O King, he should anoint his limbs with the verse beginning "gandhadvārā."
Having anointed his head and throat with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and the auspicious kānta and kālīyaka, as well as auspicious yellow pigment (rocanā);
Having consecrated it with this mantra, "Bestowing long life and vigor," he should fasten the ornament; and with the mantra, "May she bestow fortune upon the wearer," he should place the garland.
Having meditated thus, "O herbs," one should wear auspicious medicinal plants;
and with the mantra "New, new," one should wear auspicious cotton cloth.
Then, with the mantra "aindrāgne," the wise king should take up the Dharma-staff; then, with the mantra "dhvanvanāga," he should take up the water-pot consecrated by the Sarasvant mantra.
Having mounted an elephant, a chariot, or a horse that has been consecrated with the mantra "May it yield [success]," the king, possessing accomplishment, should go forth into the equal radiance.
Visible to his enemies in the field, he should arrange his constituent elements;
he should fight a small number in a compact formation, but may extend a large number as he desires.
The *sūcīmukha* (needle-mouthed) array is formed when few troops are joined with many;
arrays are proclaimed to be both of the form of animal limbs and of the form of material objects.
The array in the form of Garuḍa, as well as the wheel,
the half-moon, the thunderbolt, and the wagon array.
The Sarvatobhadra array, the Sūcī array,
as well as the Padma and the Maṇḍala arrays, are proclaimed as the primary ones.
Now, for all military arrays (vyūha), there is a fivefold arrangement of the army:
two wings, two flanks, and the fifth shall be at the gate.
He should engage in battle with either one or two [of the enemy's divisions],
and he should set aside a third part for their protection alone.
A king should never engage in conceptual construction regarding military arrays;
he should not concern himself with the cutting of leaves, the cutting of fruits, or the cutting down of trees.
It sprouts again, but perishes when its root is cut;
therefore, even a king who is skilled in all weapons must not fight with his own hand.
For it is constantly observed in the world that those possessing greater power prevail over those with lesser power;
therefore, the lord of the earth should remain at a distance of one krośa behind the army.
In that situation, the rallying of broken troops is highly praised;
however, it is not prescribed for the main body of the army to remain stationed there.
One should not harass enemies who have been broken, for they are then on a single path;
all of them, being certain of death, might destroy the enemy host.
Even under the pretext of breaking a banyan tree, they lead others to their own territory;
for those established on their own ground, death is thus easily accomplished.
One should not arrange the warriors in the battle array too closely nor too far apart,
so that there may be no mutual clashing of their weapons.
And so, O descendant of Bhṛgu, a stratagem must be devised by warriors:
one who desires to break the enemy host should break it while they are still united.
Even one intent on the protection of the gods should likewise act with solidarity;
having understood the deployment of scouts, he should arrange his military formation according to his own discretion.
Then the king should form many arrays against the enemy’s array;
O twice-born one, four excellent chariots should be assigned for the protection of the elephant.
The chariot had four horses, and the armored warrior had as many;
it is proclaimed that there were an equal number of bowmen among those armored warriors.
First, those armed with shields should be stationed; after them, those with bows;
after the bowmen, the cavalry; and after them, one should deploy the chariots.
Elephants should be assigned to follow the chariots by the ruler of the earth; furthermore, armor must be provided with great effort for those designated as infantry and elephants.
Or that man who, having first subdued me, would arm himself;
for even heroes go to their death by virtue of their well-performed deeds.
Heroes should be placed at the front; cowards should never be placed there.
Or rather, when heroes are stationed at the front, it is merely a display of one's own physical presence.
An assembly of cowards must perform that which causes the enemy to flee;
for cowards, having fled before, now run even further ahead.
Those who knit their eyebrows together, who are prone to anger, fond of quarreling,
never satisfied even when constantly looked upon, and who are brave, should be known as lustful.
The Pañcālas and Śūrasenas are men skilled in chariot warfare,
while those from the South are known to be experts with sword and shield.
The Kaṅkalas and the Dhanvins are to be known as such, as are the mountaineers;
likewise, those who dwell in the mountains are skilled in fighting with stones.
The Kambojas and the Gandharas are skilled in horses;
furthermore, the Mlecchas for the most part should be known as those who employ spears.
The Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Kaliṅgas are to be known as warriors who fight from elephants;
their duty is to bring back those who have fallen in battle.
For those who are unacquainted with each battle, as well as for the bringing forth of clouds and other such things,
and for the bringing of weapons, the duties of the infantry are prescribed.
The protection of one's own army against enemies seeking to break it,
the breaking of those who are united, and the renown of the shield-bearer’s shield.
Turning one's back in battle is likewise described as the duty of archers;
retreating to a distance is similarly called the duty of horsemen.
The routing of enemy armies and the operation of chariots are likewise described;
as well as the breaking up of compact formations and the unification of those who are divided.
O Bhārgava, from the palace or from Gomukha,
the actions of elephants— such as the breaking of young trees— which are unbearable for enemies, have been described.
The uneven ground is known as suitable for infantry, while level ground is likewise for chariots and horses;
and ground consisting of Shaky trees is declared to be the battlefield for elephants.
Thus having arranged the array, with the sun behind him,
and likewise with Venus, fire, the guardians of the quarters, Rudra, and the wind blowing favorably from behind.

O twice-born one, they say that a warrior may conquer all his enemies not merely through the slaughter of his foes, but through the attainment of enjoyments and victory; and for one who has died, victory lies in the attainment of heaven. Indeed, they declare that auspicious omens portend victory.
The crushing of his auspicious limbs, the appearance of auspicious dreams,
and the sight of elephants and horses— every such omen is seen as auspicious.
Indeed, even the auspicious signs of enemies are seen by those who follow their own minds;
however, the enemy perceives everything here in a contrary way, and not otherwise.

Sirs, you too are born of noble lineage and have reached the further shore of all scriptures and weapons; surely you are always devoted to dharma and eternally established upon the path of the righteous.
Since I am forever incapable of being led astray by others, how could my victory not be certain?
The royal glory belongs to you alone; it is yours, and mine only through you.
Two additional yak-tail whisks for the brave, a parasol with the luster of the moon,
the attainment of a share of the spoils after victory, and the supreme destination for one who has died—
there is no atonement for the master’s funeral cake; there is no higher goal than battle.
When the blood of heroes flows from a narrow passage,
the righteous man casts off all his evil along with that very blood.
Likewise, for one who performs medical treatment or removes pain,
there is no affliction in this world more severe or more terrible than that [retribution].
For one who has died [in battle], there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water-libation rite;
yet what could be greater than this for one who desires to act here?
Ascetics devoted to charity and performers of sacrifices with abundant fees,
having seen unsurpassed enjoyments, desire the goal of the brave.
Thousands of excellent apsarases, afflicted by desire, rush toward a hero slain in battle, thinking, "He shall be my husband."
The master takes away the merit of those who turn back without having broken [the vow],
for it is said that they lose the fruit of their deeds at every step, as if they had performed a horse sacrifice at every station.
By conquering [the senses], one attains the enjoyment of enemies' wealth, and for one who has died, there is the supreme destination.
The gods, led by Śakra, perform worship for him;
the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice is said to accrue from turning back those who have been broken.
O illustrious one, at every step,
when a great battle is imminent, the celestial women, as well as Alakṣmī, Sin, and Disease, wait expectantly for high-souled men who face them in the fray. [979]
"Whether he lives or whether he dies, I must take back my debt"—
such a thought-illness remains within him along with his sin.
Prosperity attends him while he lives after having performed his duty;
and when he has died, celestial damsels seated in divine chariots wait upon him.
Having thus inspired them, he should desire victory in battle through righteousness;
for a king who achieves victory through unrighteousness, the world of Yama is terrifying.
Whatever flaw is said to arise from wealth gained through unrighteous victory, another flaw will surely follow from that very flaw; of this there is no doubt.

O Bhārgava, a warrior must not discharge an arrow that has no feathers, nor one that is smeared with poison, nor one that is half-shafted; nor should an arrow be discharged with its barb already removed, nor one whose barb has been fixed in place. O twice-born one, one should fight as an equal against an equal, employing various strategic means.
One who is armored should encounter one who is armored, a horseman a horseman,
a charioteer a charioteer, and a foot soldier a foot soldier.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, one mounted on an elephant must fight with one mounted on an elephant;
likewise, those who have turned their backs, those whose weapons are broken, and those protected by women or children [should not be attacked].
One who is disarmed, one whose limbs are broken, one who has come for refuge,
one who is fighting another, and one who is merely a spectator of the battle.
One who provides water to the distressed, as well as one who holds a staff in hand—
these must not be slain in battle by one who desires to uphold the dharma of the Kṣatriya. However, against a most wicked opponent who fights with deceit, one may employ a deceptive tactic.
O one of great strength, battles should not be waged when one's own side is exhausted, when the surety has fled, when half the army has been lost, or during foul weather.
When battle has commenced against the enemy for the sake of their name, O Rāma,
one should cry out while grasping the arms of those pursued by the foe— whether they are broken or unbroken.
He who had attained variegated power and was a leader of many has been struck down here;
that very general has been slain, as has the deformed general.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, one should thus form a variegated array against the enemy;
for it is prescribed as a means to effectively strike down fleeing warriors,
and the arrangement should likewise be made according to the rules of the science of archery (Dhanurveda).
And the *vapā* (omentum) should be offered by those who know the Dharma, as well as the most enchanting [offering];
by means of this, an auspicious elevation should be effected in its proper place.
Furthermore, an auspicious collection of musical instruments must be prepared;
O twice-born one, I shall explain all of this in the Bhavopaniṣad.
Having achieved victory in battle, one should perform the rites of worship;
one should honor the Brahmins here and also honor one's gurus.
Jewels that go to the king, the path, and the vehicle—
everything else shall belong to him by whom it was killed in battle.
O Rāma, noble women are to be known as such; they belong to no one, whether in their own country or in a foreign land, for a virtuous woman would never bring reproach upon anyone.
Otherwise, a terrible oath becomes a source of victory here;
one who has encountered an enemy in battle and is released is proclaimed as his "son."

Furthermore, one who knows the Dharma should not fight against that which is the local custom in each region, handed down through successive tradition; this is the opinion of those who know the Dharma.
That very country, once selected and acquired, must be protected;
even when the enemy has been slain in battle, the king should demonstrate this to the people.
He has not done what is pleasing to me by slaying him in battle;
rather, he is paying him honor without understanding my will.
This man has been slain for my benefit; even now he is dear to me. The king should protect the wives of those who have died childless.
Then, having reached his own city, he should enter his home within a muhūrta;
there, he should again perform the worship of the deities as prescribed by the rules for the expedition.
One should especially perform the worship of the twice-born,
and one should practice sharing one's wealth with people for the sake of attaining the supreme state.

Having conquered the earth through righteousness, marked by sacrificial posts and other temples dedicated to the gods, and likewise having performed other acts of victory according to his capacity, the king—
He conquers even the world of the Lord of the Immortals.
Parāśara said:
"If one falls upon the ground in battle with blood streaming from his forehead,
that itself constitutes for him the drinking of soma, and he becomes equal to the entire host of gods."
If blood flowing from a wound inflicted by a weapon enters the mouth at the region of the forehead,
that is equal for him to the drinking of soma.
In the sacrifice of battle, this very rule is observed.
Yājñavalkya:
Having brought back all the property of a Brahmin that was stolen or caused to be stolen,
one is purified even by killing those responsible with weapons for that purpose.
He who dies as a mount in battle attains purification;
or even while living, he is purified by wounds that are like the blows of death.
Wherever a hero, surrounded by enemies, is slain,
he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not utter words of cowardice.
Manu says: "These two persons in this world pierce the solar orb:
the wandering mendicant absorbed in yoga, and he who is slain facing the enemy in battle."
From the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"He who exerts himself for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa and is deprived of his life thereby attains the supreme abode where the divine Sun resides."
From the Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa:
Those men who, having cast away their bodies in the great ocean, offered protection from fear to cows, Brahmins, masters, and wealth;
Yogins who contemplate that Supreme Self do not obtain the fruit of tranquility through birth and other such means.
As Śālihotra said: "A man slain by the back of a horse shall dwell in heaven for as many years as there are hair-pores on that riding horse."
To whatever world men who have been slain on the backs of horses go,
to that same world also go those who have been slain by mares.
Pālakāpya said:
Those slain by the shoulder of an elephant go to heaven;
even in heaven, they remain intoxicated with pride, like the waves of the ocean reaching the triple-peaked mountain of Meru.
Men slain upon the necks of elephants by arrows, lances,
and discuses go directly to heaven in an instant, remaining there until the dissolution of all things at the end of the kalpa.
Thus concludes the procedure for battle. Now follows the ritual of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*).

It should be performed on the full moon day of either Kārttika or Āśvayuja. At the outset, one should examine the bull: it should be the son of a cow that has living calves, endowed with all auspicious marks, blue-black or reddish-brown, entirely white in its tail and feet, and capable of protecting the herd.

Then, having strewn grass around a well-kindled fire in the midst of cows, having cooked a *caru* offering for Pūṣan, and having offered oblations with the mantra "May Pūṣan protect our cows here and now," he should summon a bull and an ironworker. He should bathe the bull—marked on one flank with a wheel and on the other with a trident—with the four verses beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and with the verse "Śaṃ no devī. Having brought it, bathed and adorned, together with four young heifers likewise bathed and adorned, he should mutter the Rudra hymns, the Puruṣasūkta, and the Kūṣmāṇḍī mantras. He should recite the mantra "Pitā vatse" into the right ear of the bull.
For the Blessed Lord Dharma is proclaimed to be a bull with four feet;
I choose him with devotion, and may he protect me in every way.
"Thus I give you a young husband; sport with him, your beloved, and enjoy yourselves. Do not let us be separated from our kinsmen. For we are indeed great through our offspring and our own bodies.
O King Soma, you who hate the abode of Māra!
One should have a bull yoked with a heifer placed in the northeastern direction;
one should give the officiating priest a pair of garments, gold, and even bell-metal.
The blacksmith should be given wages according to his heart's desire;
one should provide him with food containing plenty of ghee and feed the Brahmins there as well.
In whatever reservoir a bull, having been released, drinks water,
and wherever that proud animal digs at the earth with his horns,
there abundant food, drink, and other offerings accrue to the ancestors.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
Furthermore, on the full moon day of Caitra or Kārttika,
the release of a bull should be performed with effort by the three twice-born castes, provided they possess a gentle mind.
The bull, however, was a black-spotted one, fresh and three years old,
pleasing to the mind, handsome to behold, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
It was yoked with eight milch cows, or alternatively four in sequence,
and was adorned with auspicious, well-formed three-year-old heifers.
Endowed with all necessary implements, great, and moving among all crops,
it has been released according to this rite and in accordance with the rules of the Smṛti.
In a region sloping toward the northeast, in a pleasing and secluded forest,
neither an outsider nor anyone else should ever drink that milk;
it is for the satisfaction of one's fathers, mothers, and kinsmen, offered with the exclamation *svadhā*.
Whosoever belong to the mother’s side, and those others born of the father’s side;
those who have arisen in the families of gurus, fathers-in-law, and kinsmen;
those who have fallen into the state of pretas, and others who have been deprived of the śrāddha rite.
Through the rite of releasing a bull, they all obtain supreme satisfaction.
With this mantra, one should offer water mixed with sesame seeds and unbroken rice grains to the ancestors, and likewise give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins in brief.
Then, filled with joy and accompanied by that bull,
the cows frolic in the forests for the successful completion of the rite of setting the bull at liberty.
When the rite of bull-liberation had not yet been performed, the donor spoke to the Brahmins with words of indirect speech: "Whatever has been released by me in this secluded place..."
No one else shall take that away; rather, it should be divided in due order.
Apart from the rite of releasing a bull, there is no other merit on the surface of the earth.
In the Matsya Purāṇa,
Manu said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear the characteristics of the bull."
As well as the ritual for the release of a bull, and likewise its great meritorious fruit.
First, one should examine a cow that is well-tempered and endowed with auspicious marks— free from physical defects, not emaciated, possessing a living calf, and free from disease.
She was of glossy complexion, with glossy hooves and likewise glossy horns;
she was captivating, exceedingly gentle, well-proportioned, and not over-exuberant.
She who is endowed with rightward curls on her right side and leftward curls on her left,
and whose hips and breasts are broad.
Lips that are soft and firm are highly praised; likewise, a tongue that is red, not too long, and clearly reddish when extended is auspicious.
And his eyes were copper-hued with thick lashes, while his hooves were dark,
dense, and the color of beryl or honey, resembling bubbles on the water.
With eyes that are red and glossy, and with pupils that are likewise red,
she has either seven or fourteen teeth and a non-dark palate.

She possesses six elevations, beautiful sides, thighs, and a broad [chest], endowed with the five equalities; she has a head and neck eight times [the length of] the face, and is thus possessed of auspicious marks.
In which five [parts] should there be six elevations and five lengths?
Likewise, eight lengths in the marks of cows bring about auspiciousness.
Matsya said:
O lord of the earth, the wise declare that cows have six elevated parts: the chest, the back, the head, the belly, and the two hips.
O son of the Sun, the two ears, the two eyes, and the forehead—these five are praised when they are long; likewise, a tail that resembles a chowrie is auspicious.
O King, there are four breasts; thus, the wise say there are eight [limbs] on the body of a king, including the head and neck, which are exceedingly long.
One should examine her son, a bull endowed with auspicious marks:
with elevated shoulders and hump, a straight tail, and a dewlap.
He has great hips and shoulders like riverbanks, eyes like lapis lazuli gems,
the tips of his horns colored like coral, and a very long, jeweled tail.
A peacock with nine, eight, or ten auspicious teeth with sharp points should be kept even in the home; it bestows wealth and grain.
In terms of color, a copper-brown horse is praised for a Brāhmaṇa;
white, red, fair (gaura), black, and pale-red (pāṭala) are likewise commended.
One with a back the color of sapphire, one who is brindled, one with five black spots,
one with large ears, one with a great hump, and one whose hair is like that of an eye— [these are the auspicious marks].
One that has red eyes and is tawny, one that has red horns,
one with a white belly and a black back— such a bull is recommended for a Brāhmaṇa.
A glossy red complexion is praised for a Kṣatriya;
one with a golden luster for a Vaiśya; and even a black one for one of the lowest birth.
He whose two horns extend forward and always face his own mouth is the accomplisher of all goals for all social classes alike.
One with the feet of a cat and tawny like Kapila is auspicious; one who is reddish-brown like Kapila is also auspicious;
and one who is white with the feet of a cat and eyes resembling jewels is likewise auspicious.
Karaṭa, Piṅgala, and likewise Śvetapāda;
he whose feet and head are clear, and Dvipāda who is entirely white.
One resembling a francolin partridge is auspicious, as is one resembling darkness;
however, he whose face shines covered up to the root of the ears,
especially if it is red in color, should be known as a Nāndīmukha.
O Lord of the Earth, that bull whose belly and back are white,
who has eyes like the ocean, is a constant increaser of his lineage.
The bull of the giver of land becomes variegated with jasmine flowers;
the giver of a cow becomes variegated with lotuses and mandalas.
And likewise, one with the color of an atasi flower is considered most auspicious;
these are the auspicious ones, O King, and I shall now proclaim to you those who are inauspicious.
Those with black palates, lips, and teeth; those with rough horns and hooves;
those with indistinct colors, who are short, and those resembling the color of tiger’s ash.
Those with the color of crows and vultures, as well as those resembling mice;
the dull-witted, the one-eyed, the lame, and those known as "kekakas"; those with uneven white feet, and likewise those with wandering eyes.
Those bulls must not be set free, nor should they be kept in the house;
I shall further explain the characteristics of those that are to be eaten and those that are to be kept.
Their horns were shaped like svastikas, their roars resembled the rumbling of a mass of clouds,
they possessed great vital strength, and they moved with the gait of elephants in rut.
They have broad chests, heavy breaths, and great strength and prowess;
their heads, ears, foreheads, tails, and likewise their feet [are vast].
The eyes, the flanks, and the ears are praised when they resemble the moon;
these are praised when white, especially in the case of a black horse.
A bull is praised when it drags its thick tail and long-haired tuft along the ground, with its penis held erect in front.
Those bulls whose row shines with the luster of spears, banners, and flags are blessed;
they bring about the attainment of wealth and victory.
Fortunate are those who increase the herd, their heads and necks held high, who turn back of their own accord when the circumambulation is completed.
One whose horns, humps, and eyes are red and whose body is white,
with hooves resembling coral— there is no one more blessed than such a person.
These should be maintained with effort, or else released if they are bulls;
for when maintained or likewise released, they cause an increase in wealth and grain.
O Lord of Cows, one should designate that bull as "Nīla" whose feet, face, and tail are white, while the rest of his body has the color of lac juice.
That bull alone should be released; it should not be kept in the house.
For this reason, there is this ancient verse well-known in the world:
"One should desire many sons, so that even if one among them goes to Gayā..."
Thus, O King, even if one has acquired a bull endowed with auspicious marks, whether born in one's own house or purchased,
a great-souled man who has renounced it does not grieve over death.
Or rather, he would not indeed prescribe a rule for one who is great.
From the Ādipurāṇa:
Bhānu said:
"Those who eat a bull that is blue and very beautiful..."
With its tail drawn back, its entire body covered in hair, possessing horns, and enchanting to the mind.
He who gives [these] on the full moon day of Kārttika, having performed worship, has no doubt [of the reward];
he should give cows that have calved three times and are with calf, as well as a bull.
One should recite the Sāvitrī there, as well as the Aghamarṣaṇa;
one should indeed provide the Karṇajāpya for the bull—of this there is no doubt.
One should give a bell made of iron, along with auspicious horns and bundles of grass;
and one should feed Brahmins in the presence of Rudra according to the prescribed rite.
O Sage, as many hair-pores as there are on the bull, and as much hair as there is on the cows while he lies down,
for that many thousands of crores of years he is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Whatever sin a man afflicted by the lack of livelihood may commit,
all of those go to destruction through the act of liberating cows, O Lord of Cows.
By the very sound of the bull, the ancestors together with their grandfathers are seen in the heavenly world by Ākhaṇḍala; of this there is no doubt.
[990] Having cast its tail into the water, the bull draws up the water;
by that act, the ancestors are gratified for ten thousand years.
Even if one merely piles up earth on the riverbank as high as the shoulder,
the ancestors are satisfied by that mountain composed of various kinds of food and drink.
And whenever a bull sports in the midst of cows,
the ancestors sport forever with a thousand apsarases.
As he sports in the water, releasing his tail,
the ancestors are then served by throngs of hosts of Apsarases.
The satisfaction that the ancestors truly derive from a pond constructed according to the rules after a thousand [cows] have been gifted is said to be equal to that derived from a bull.
From the Devīpurāṇa:
Manu said:
"Merit equal to that of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) is obtained through the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga)."
Or under the asterism Revatī in the month of Āśvina, or under Kṛttikā in the month of Kārttika.
A marriage for a cow should be performed either on the full moon day of Māgha or Phālguna;
likewise, the auspicious rite for Śiva and Umā on the third day of Caitra yields great fruit.
The ritual union of the *aśvattha* and *udumbara* trees should take place according to the marriage ceremony;
it may be performed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), on a lap, or even in a cow-pen.
There are four types of *vatsikā* cows, or two, or even three;
the one whose calf is complete in all its limbs—that cow is the *vatsikā*.
O Sage, having adorned it as beautifully as possible, one should perform the ritual offering;
by doing so, one always obtains marriage, prosperity for a year, and the color blue.
By means of a bull, one obtains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) rite;
even if only one son goes to Gayā, many sons will be born.
One should either perform the horse sacrifice or release a dark-colored bull.
A bull that is red in color, with a conch-like hue and voice,
and whose head and tail are white— that indeed is known as a *nīlavṛṣa*.
Having first released the sacrificial mark (*aṅka*) and having adorned the cow on all sides with hair-ornaments, one should proceed.
Then, on the left side of that [deity], one should draw a wheel, and on the right, a trident.
One should engrave it with mercury, gold-mercury, iron, or copper;
having done this, one obtains the fruit proclaimed for the horse sacrifice.
Whomever one may dedicate the calf for, that person shall obtain it without hesitation;
just as the worship of Śiva and Umā, when honored, grants all desires.
Having thus worshipped these three deities,
one obtains a fruit equal to that which one would attain by performing a thousand sacrifices through the rite of releasing a bull.
From the Varāha Purāṇa:
"But having released Nīlakaṇṭha at the arrival of the Kaumudī [full moon],
and having performed the Śrāddha and gratified the twice-born, O lady of beautiful hips..."
Having offered water with sesame seeds and the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the paternal and maternal ancestors,
[one honors] those men who dwell here as paternal uncles and paternal kinsmen.
They shall become their protectors according to the ritual for the release of a dark-blue bull;
having taken up an udumbara vessel and prepared water with black sesame seeds.
Having performed the recitation of the *vipāṇas* and having offered a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability,
if one should pour water upon the tail of a blue-necked [bull], [the rite is complete].
By that, his ancestors have been gratified for sixty thousand years.
O lady of beautiful hips, if the mud clinging to the horn were to be lifted up by the blue-throated bull with his horn as soon as it was released, it would remain upon that horn.
O beautiful one, his kinsmen and ancestors who dwell in hell are all delivered from hell and go to the world of Soma,
by virtue of the great merit of the liberated Nīlakaṇṭha.
For sixty thousand years and six hundred years,
they all enjoy the essence of nectar eternally in the world of Soma.
From the Kālikā Purāṇa:
Anilāda said:
"He has the luster of a blue lotus, a white body, and the moon upon his head."
The youth with beautiful eyebrows and red eyes is called the Blue Bull.
Alternatively, one should release a bull that is red, tawny, or very white;
this bull, the vehicle of Hara, is the entirety of Dharma in its four quarters.
Listen to the procedure by which one who is equal and free from envy may perform this rite for his sake:
having fasted, being pure, and having bathed, he should go to the temple of Hara along with cows.
Having covered the canopy-island, one should place it upon the head of Śiva;
one should perform the ceremonial bath for Śiva with auspicious-smelling products of the cow.
The wise man, having carefully extracted [the oil] with thirty-five ingredients using clarified butter,
should wash it with decoctions and then with lukewarm water.
Having again diligently anointed Śaṅkara with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should then bathe Śiva with devotion using camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
One should worship with the finest flowers and anoint with sandalwood paste;
a golden lotus should be fashioned, adorned with thirty-five petals.
One should place upon the head [of the image] a lotus adorned with jewels, rich in filaments, and complete with a pericarp;
likewise, one should offer a pair of white, fine, and very beautiful garments.
Having offered the *arghya*, one should then light the lamp with twenty-six [offerings];
then, one should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony using a vessel made of silver, copper, or other materials.
Then, one should diligently offer an oblation to the spirits (bhūtabali) in all directions;
at the conclusion of the worship, one should honor eight Brahmins and give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, one should prepare an altar and a canopy measuring four cubits;
having established the fire right there, the wise man should place three sacrificial oblations (carus).
Having offered a cooked oblation (sthālīpāka) to Rudra, as well as barley-gruel (yāvaka), sacrificial porridge (caru), and milk-rice (pāyasa),
he should then present the Raudra bali with these [substances].
Then, in all directions, he [should perform the rite] for Hari according to the mantra and the prescribed rules,
together with young cows and amidst the chanting of the Veda.
Having consecrated that bull according to the ritual procedure,
one should also adorn it with red, yellow, white, and black flowers.
Having perfumed two pairs of garments produced from gold and lapis lazuli, along with two small bells and two necklaces, one should adorn [the image] when they are joined together.
Then he should scatter parched grains (lājā) clockwise around Jātavedas;
with his joined palms, he should hold the tail together with gold.
Having lifted it from his hand with water mixed with flowers for Hara, the Supreme Lord, he should release it while reciting: "This has been given by me."
Having released the shins, the tops of the feet, and the buttocks upwards in a clockwise direction,
the wise one should mark them with a trident using saffron.
Having prostrated before the Lord, one should offer and worship a water-filled pitcher,
filled with sesame seeds and containing a piece of gold weighing half a karṣa.
And he should cause that [image] to be given to the preceptor along with a pair of garments,
especially to Brahmins who observe the Śiva-vow and are self-restrained.
Having fed those established in their vows with gifts of gold and clothing, one should honor them;
likewise, the feeding of the poor, the blind, and the suffering is not to be withheld.
One should release the bull in a forest, at a crossroads, or in a cow-pen;
a wise man should not release it within a house, for [the latter] yields the full fruit of one's desire.
From the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O lord of men, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja..."
Or else, one should perform the rite of releasing a bull in the month of Kārttika.
The two eclipses are of great merit, as are the two solstices,
the two equinoxes, and the anniversary of a kinsman's death.
On whichever day the anniversary of death falls, on that very day one should perform the rite;
having first established the Mother [image], one should worship her with flowers and unbroken grains of rice.
Thereafter, one should perform the śrāddha for the mother, which brings about the prosperity of the lineage;
[using] a water-pot with roots of the *akālamūla* tree and adorned with leaves of the *aśvattha*.
There, having invoked the Rudras, he should cause those deities of the Rudras to recite [the mantras].
Having well-kindled and widely spread the sacrificial fire in the midst of cows,
the wise and composed man should cook the *caru* offering for Pūṣan with milk.
In the same manner, he should recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta and likewise the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras;
thereafter, a skilled smith should brand the bull.
One should indicate the right side with a trident and the left side with a discus;
having marked him thus, one should subsequently bathe him while reciting the appropriate mantras for the bath.
O Lord of Men, [one should recite] the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇā," as well as the three beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," or also those beginning with "śaṃ no devī."
O lord of men, one should then decorate those four heifers and that bull with perfumes and garlands according to one's ability.
With beautiful tinkling bells and auspicious Chinese silks,
one should then recite this mantra with a disciplined mind upon that which is thus marked.
For the Blessed Lord Dharma is proclaimed to be a bull with four feet;
I choose him with devotion, and may he protect me in every way.
I give you this youth, a bull,
the lord of cattle, the leader of the herd, most precious;
roam with him as you desire.
May the heifers obtain their desire accordingly.
I give this young man to you as a husband; sport with him, your beloved, and dwell together with offspring, not with your own bodies.
Let us slay that King Soma for the sake of our enemy.
The father, well-known as "Vatsa," should whisper the mantra into the left ear of the bull;
he should then cause that bull to move about.
All the young cows, however, [should face] the eastern direction.
Then a pair of garments should be given to the Hotṛ priest,
along with gold and a bronze vessel filled with ghee;
likewise, a price should be paid to the chief artisan.
O King, that which is given likewise attains prosperity.
Likewise, the Brahmins should be fed with food mixed with curd, clarified butter, and milk;
they depart as soon as the bull has been released.
His ancestors attained supreme satisfaction.
O Lord of the Earth, that very lake from which he, afflicted by thirst, comes to drink, becomes for his ancestors a divine, full, and complete [reservoir].
In this world and in the next, he brings about satisfaction.
Then, overcome by thirst, he approaches a certain excellent river belonging to his ancestors.
The most excellent of rivers, carrying various waters, provides satisfaction for a very long time.
O King, when that elephant, full of pride, tears up the earth with the blows of his tusks,
his ancestors and others there [in the afterlife] are then [afflicted by] the trap.
They certainly obtain [it]; there is no doubt in this matter.
O King,
he who has fulfilled his desires shall likewise go to heaven, having been released for hundreds of years equal to those of the gods.
Being attended upon by the women of the thirty [gods].
Thus ends the procedure for the ritual release of a bull.
Śatānīka said:
"O Blessed One, by what rule should the Bhārata be heard by men?"
The life-story of Rāmabhadra and especially the Purāṇas.
O best of Brahmins, how are the Vaiṣṇava duties, the Śiva duties, and even those of the Sauras [to be understood] in their entirety? Please state the procedure for hearing them.
Sumantu said:
"Indeed, I shall tell you the rule for hearing the Purāṇas;
by listening to the Itihāsas and Purāṇas with devotion, one is liberated."
O Lord, one is liberated from all sins, including the killing of a Brahmin and others.
He who listens, having become pure, in the evening, in the morning, and likewise at night— for him Viṣṇu, as well as Brahmā and Śaṅkara, are pleased.
At dawn the Blessed Brahmā is pleased, and at the end of the day Hari is pleased;
likewise, Mahādeva is pleased at night. O Lord, may satisfaction come to those who listen to the eighteen Purāṇas as one.
O tiger among kings, listen to the Bhārata and its fruit;
O lord of the people, first hear this procedure for the reciter.
Having performed a circumambulation of the abode of the Śuddhavāsa deities and other places that are endowed with the proper ritual timing, she indeed becomes the deity residing therein.
O King, having honored that [scripture] according to the prescribed rite for all [beings] like an incomparable teacher,
one should cause it to be heard, concluding with "May there be auspiciousness";
O tiger among kings, O lord of the earth, it must not be heard from anyone else by any of the castes.
Vaiśyas always listen in the presence of Śūdras, Kṣatriyas likewise in the presence of Vaiśyas,
and Brāhmaṇas in the presence of Kṣatriyas.
Then, O King, standing in the middle of them all, the reciter should cause [the text] to be read;
and those born of mixed castes, O King, should stand at a distance behind the Śūdra.
One should know that the reciter must be a Brahmin, not one born of another caste, out of respect;
having heard [the scripture] from a reciter born of another caste, O King, one shall go to hell.
O King, descendant of Kuru, for those who listen to these syllables in their proper sequence, there shall be a breaking of the fast month by month.
O King, for the sake of one's own welfare, one should honor the reciter, O ruler;
at the end of each month, O best of kings, a gold masha should be given.
O mighty-armed one, two [gifts] are to be given by a Brāhmaṇa, but two by a Kṣatriya;
O best of kings, likewise three are to be given by a Vaiśya to the reciter.
Furthermore, O best of kings, even a Śūdra should give four gold māṣakas to the reciter with faith every month.
O King, at the first breaking of the fast, by honoring the reciter according to one's means,
a person obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O mighty-armed one, from the month of Kārttika until the end of Kārttika,
[one obtains the merit of] the Agniṣṭoma, the Gosava, and likewise the Jyotiṣṭoma.
O King, [one should perform] the Maitrāvaruṇa, the Vājapeya, and likewise the Vibhu;
as well as the Māheśvara, the Brāhma, and the Puṇḍarīka.
O Indra among kings, one obtains the fruit of the Āditya sacrifice, as well as that of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha, by means of these twelve months in succession.
Having thus obtained the fruit of sacrifice, he goes to the highest worlds.
When the festival is concluded, O King, one should satisfy the reciter and the Brahmins according to one's ability, honoring them with all desired objects.
One should present perfumes, garlands, pairs of garments, and ornaments to the reciter; thereafter, one should honor the Brahmins.
By giving gold, silver, clothing, cows, and brass milking vessels to the reciter here on earth, one obtains the fruit of the sacred learning heard.
The deities are pleased with him by whom the reciter is honored;
therefore, the wise know that wealth should always be given to him first.
O King, when a twice-born reciter, endowed with faith, eats at his śrāddha,
his ancestors remain satisfied for a hundred years.
O King, let him teach the text and its meaning to the Brahmins and the other castes;
O King, that Brahmin who teaches in this manner is called Vyāsa.
One who recites otherwise than this should be known by the name of his father;
such a reciter, equal to Vyāsa, may dwell wherever he is.
O King, among all lands and cities, that land is considered the most excellent;
for it is there that men obtain the fruit of bowing with devotion to the reciter.
That cannot be attained even by a thousand sacrifices, O joy of the Kurus.
Just as all the planets are on one side and the sun alone is on the other,
so too are all the twice-born on one side and that speaker alone is on the other.
[1000] O King, in rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors, these are the supreme purifiers:
a reciter, an ascetic, and likewise one who knows the six Vedāṅgas.
O best of kings, all these should be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanas).
One should know that speech is of three kinds, according to the distinctions of its inherent qualities.
And the Śrāvaka, O mighty-armed one, is of three kinds according to the distinction of his qualities;
listen as I describe these two to you.
Too rapid, as well as indistinct, devoid of all [proper] articulation (khara),
lacking the division of words (padaccheda), and bereft of the respective emotional states (bhāva).
O Lord of Men, that brahmin who causes such a person to recite— being ignorant of the meaning of the text, greedy, and devoid of enthusiasm— is himself a sinner.
One who is wrathful, speaks unpleasantly, is ignorant, and corrupts the texts,
yet does not abandon his hardships— he should be known as the lowest of reciters.
It was perfectly clear, wonderful, and peaceful, with distinct syllables and words; it was endowed with a resonant tone, yet devoid of emotional sentiment or dramatic expression.
O King, that reciter who causes [the text] to be recited without understanding the meaning of the book should be known as a Rākṣasa; now hear about the Sāttvika type.
But one who understands the entire meaning of the text in its completeness, O King,
should worship according to the rules among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, O King.
O King, he who recites [this] in such a manner should be known by the wise as one of sattvic nature;
whereas one who is devoid of faith and devotion, greedy, and likewise a detractor, is not so.
Devoted to the doctrine of causality and likewise possessed of envy, O King,
he gave sacrificial fees for the daily, occasional, and optional rites, O monarch.
O mighty-armed one, that man who merely listens to the reciter, O King, should be known as a *tāmasa* person; he is always a *tāmasa* human being.
O hero, a wise man indeed should not recite in his presence.
But he who, devoid of faith and devotion, listens merely out of incidental circumstance or mere curiosity,
should be known by the wise as one of a rajasic nature.
Having renounced all ritual actions, O King, one who is endowed with devotion and faith should constantly worship the reciter with sincere devotion.
Whether giving during obligatory rites, occasional rites, or rites for desired results, as well as when giving to a guru—
he who is thus a reciter, O Hero, is to be known by the wise as one of sattvic nature.
O King, just as Vyāsa is worthy of worship by the Śrāvakas, so too, O best of kings, the reciter (vācaka) should first be honored by the wise, according to the word of Vyāsa.
In times of distress and likewise upon his advancement in age, he is considered equal to a preceptor.
O Hero of noble vows, at the time of Vaiśākha on the third lunar day,
and likewise on the full moon days of Kārttika and Māgha, he should be worshipped first.
And on these festival days, O Lord, it is traditionally taught that one should worship according to the Dharma.
Gold, fine gold, wealth, grain,
as well as cooked food and meat, O joy of the Kurus—
these should first be given to him by the disciples with the utmost devotion.
Having given flowers, fruit, water, leaves, and even fuel,
as well as Sarasvata and whatever else is to be given, one should offer it to him from all sides.
Then, O King, all the disciples must perform worship in that manner,
so that the reciter may always abide in happiness, O lord of men.
O lord of men, one should act in such a way that one is not afflicted by the pairs of opposites;
in the winter, a woolen cloak should be given, and in the rainy season, an excellent umbrella.
At the proper time, he should indeed wear two sandals made of black, hairy leather.
O sinless one, when he is unable to give even a single *māṣaka* of gold,
then he should give that *māṣaka* for the sake of his own welfare.
In the absence of that, one should give gold, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
for even earth should be given by one who makes his learning bear fruit.
Thus has this perpetual [pūjā] been described;
thereafter, O King, there shall be the occasional [pūjā] on lunar days such as eclipses and other festival occasions.
O King, two garments, perfumes, garlands,
and ornaments should be given at the conclusion of the festival by one who desires prosperity, O Lord.
Having recognized the conclusion of a festival day, a wise person should worship the reciter;
even by selling oneself, one who desires that their study of the scripture be fruitful must give you both the occasional and the regular sacrificial fee.
And he who always hears it, O dear one, obtains that same fruit in its unmanifest form;
O King, O Lord, it becomes fourfold compared to the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) given regularly.
"One obtains whatever enjoyment one desires," so said the Blessed Lord Śiva.
Thus, O King, has this rule for listening to the Purāṇas been declared.

In the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi* composed by Śrī Hemādri— the venerable Hemādri, who is the sovereign lord of all offices and a master of all branches of knowledge— under the command of the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Śrī Mahādeva, this is the section on miscellaneous vows (*prakīrṇavrata*) within the Book of Vows (*vratakhaṇḍa*).
Now, regarding the rites for pacification and nourishment:

He has been led away by thousands of streams of water from his own giving, with a mind intent on peace, by whom the forest fire of poverty— which had excessively tormented the multitude of supplicants— was extinguished.
He whose compassionate heart constantly nourishes the world that is distressed like a blade of grass— this Hemādri is now prepared to expound upon rites for pacification and prosperity.
In that regard, the ritual bathing of Vināyaka is described.
Yājñavalkya said:
"Vināyaka has been appointed for the sake of accomplishing the success of one's undertakings."
And likewise, he was appointed to the lordship over the hosts by Rudra and by Brahmā.
Learn now the symptoms of one who is afflicted by that [demon]:
in a dream, he plunges excessively into water and sees trunks [of elephants].
"Excessively" means that he is carried away by the current or sinks; for even a mere immersion is powerful.
And one who wears saffron robes likewise ascends upon a corpse-eater.
He dwells together with flesh-eaters such as vultures, tigers, and the like,
and with outcastes such as donkeys and camels;
likewise, as he wanders, he imagines himself to be followed by others.

He considers himself being overwhelmed by enemies pursuing him from behind; he disregards celestial chariots that are about to yield their fruits due to some causal factor. Thus afflicted by him, the prince does not obtain the kingdom.
A maiden does not [attain] a husband, nor does one pregnant with a child [attain] offspring;
likewise, a learned Brahmin does not attain the status of a teacher, nor does a pupil [attain] the study [of the Vedas].
A merchant does not obtain profit, nor does a farmer gain from his cultivation;
for him, a ritual bathing must be performed on an auspicious day according to the prescribed rules.
On an auspicious day, one joined with favorable lunar mansions and so forth— not at night—
for one who has been rubbed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter.
"Utsādana" means rubbing or anointing.

Likewise, for one whose head has been anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances and who is seated upon an auspicious throne, the auspicious twice-born ones should be made to recite benedictions.

Auspicious and learned Brahmins—four in number—should be addressed with the words, "May you, sirs, pronounce a blessing. At this time, one should perform the *puṇyāhavācana* (declaration of an auspicious day) according to the rules prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*; this is the meaning.

One should throw earth from a horse-stable, from an elephant-stable, from an anthill, from a confluence of rivers, and from a lake, along with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), perfumes, and *guggulu*, into the water.
Having brought water from a lake in four jars of a single color,
and having placed it upon a red bull's hide, one should likewise establish the *bhadrāsana*.

Then, having placed four jars—filled with the aforementioned water and clay, adorned with sprouts of mango and other trees, their necks encircled by garlands, smeared with sandalwood paste, and decorated with fresh flowers—at the three directions starting from the east on a pure, well-smeared sacrificial ground marked with a five-colored svastika; and having spread upon it a red bull-hide with the hair on the outside and the neck pointing eastward, and having placed upon that a seat covered with a white cloth; the Guru should perform the consecration for the one seated there, after the recitation of auspicious verses and once the student has been blessed by women whose husbands and sons are living, who are endowed with beauty and virtue.
With that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, made purifying by the seers—with that I sprinkle you; may the purifiers cleanse you.
May King Varuṇa grant you fortune; may Sūrya and Bṛhaspati grant you fortune;
may Indra and Vāyu grant you fortune; and may the Seven Seers know [and bestow] fortune upon you.
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, whatever is at your parting,
and whatever is on your forehead, ears, or eyes— may the waters always destroy it for you.

Three mantras have been prescribed for the three jars, while the fourth is the consecration with all the mantras. For one who has bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood upon the head, while grasping *kuśa* grass with the left hand.
Holding kuśa grass in his left hand, he should offer oblations within the door with the following mantras:
"Mita and Sammita, as well as Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa,
Kūṣmāṇḍa and Rājaputra, together with Aśvavāha."
