With their names and with offering mantras accompanied by salutations.
The phrase "with the *praṇava* and so forth" is to be understood as the remainder [of the instruction].

Immediately thereafter, having cooked the *caru* in a worldly fire according to the *sthālīpāka* rite, one should offer oblations into that very same fire with those same six mantras. Then, one should present the sacrificial remains (*bali*) to them by means of the *bali* mantras, using the names of Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, Brahmā, and Ananta, in the dative case ending and followed by the word "namas.
One should carefully place the winnowing basket upon the *kuśa* grass at a crossroads and offer the gift there.
He also offered rice grains both husked and unhusked, as well as rice mixed with minced meat.

Rice that has been prepared and unprepared, rice that has been carried away once, *palala* (sesame paste), rice mixed with that, and *palalodana*; likewise, cooked fish as well as raw, and meat—just this much;
variegated flowers, fragrant substances, and the three kinds of liquor.
Radishes, fried cakes, and bread, as well as garlands of *uṇḍaraka*,
rice with curd, milk-rice, and flour mixed with jaggery along with sweet balls (*modaka*).
The *uṇḍarakas* are garlands made of flour and other such substances; they are strung together. "Guḍapiṣṭa" is rice-flour and the like mixed with molasses.
Having repeatedly brought all these and placed them on the ground, [he places] the head from there.
Having brought these, [he proceeds].
Oṃ, we know that Puruṣa; we meditate upon the one with the curved trunk; may that Dantī inspire us. Thus for Vighneśa. We know Subhagā; we meditate upon Kāmamālinī; may that Gaurī inspire us.
Thus one should pay homage to Ambikā.

Having likewise worshipped Vināyaka and his mother, and having spread out the remains of the offerings upon *kuśa* grass and placed them in a winnowing basket, one should set them down at a crossroads with the mantra:
"May the gods, the Ādityas, and the Vasus likewise accept this offering."
The Maruts, the Aśvins, the Rudras, the Suparṇas, the Pannagas, and the Grahas.
Asuras, Yātudhānas, Piśācas, Mātṛs, Nagas,
Śakinīs, Yakṣas, Vetālas, Yoginīs, Pūtanas, and Śivās.
The Jambhakas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Mālas, Vidyādharas, and the sinless ones;
the guardians of the directions, the protectors of the worlds, and those who are the Vighnas and Vināyakas.
May there be no obstacle, may there be no evil for me, and may there be no adversaries.
May the spirits and pretas be gentle, satisfied, and bringers of happiness.
These are the mantras for the offering of bali at the crossroads.
Thereafter, one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka,
by offering a full añjali of dūrvā grass, mustard seeds, and flowers as arghya.
Having offered an *arghya* of flowers and water, and having presented a full *añjali* of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, and flowers, he should stand in worship with the mantra to be recited hereafter:
"Grant me beauty; grant me fame; O Blessed One, grant me fortune.
Grant me sons; grant me wealth; and grant me all my desires."
"O Blessed One, [the modification] is 'in the service of Vināyaka'.
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents,
one should feed Brahmins and also give a pair of garments to the preceptor.
The giving of a fee to the preceptor is also implied by the word "api" (also). And [offerings] should be made to the Brāhmaṇas for the sake of Vināyaka.
Thus, having worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule, one obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.
By constantly performing worship of the Sun, as well as applying the *tilaka* of the Lord and wearing the great serpent-garland, one shall attain perfection.
In the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*, in the section concerning those afflicted by Vināyaka:

"O King, with his mind deluded regarding the means [of liberation], and likewise enveloped by the inner darkness of ignorance as well as by his ancestors, he goes to the vicinity of the cremation ground."

The meaning is that when an action is to be performed or accomplished, one who does not enter within the blue—that is, one who is unattached to the earth and so forth—travels through the intermediate space (antarīkṣa).
O tiger among kings, he sees this at the end of a dream; there is no doubt about this:
[he sees himself] with limbs smeared with oil and adorned with oleander flowers (karavīra).

At the end of the dream, that is, in the midst of the dream; likewise, his ceremonial bath (snapana) should be performed on an auspicious day according to the prescribed rules. The man should have his body scrubbed with a paste of white mustard seeds and parched grain flour (saktu).
O King, on the fourth day of the bright fortnight,
under the day of Jupiter and likewise under the constellation Vīraja, [he was born] in front of him.
He has been rubbed with unguents and massaged. Dhiṣaṇa is Bṛhaspati.
Thus, for one whose head is anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrances and who is seated upon an auspicious throne, the auspicious twice-born ones should pronounce the benediction (svasti).
Having worshipped Vyomakeśa, as well as Pārvatī and Bhīmaja,
and also Kṛṣṇa’s father, Akarmārambhin;
O Bhārata, [he saw] Dhiṣaṇa, Kledaputra, Koṇalakṣmī,
Viprastaka, Bāhuleya, and Dhāriṇa of the Navakas.
The passage beginning with "aśvasthāna-gajasthāna" and so forth is identical to that of Yājñavalkya. However, the mantra for the worship of Ambikā is as follows:
"O Blessed One, grant me form; grant me glory; grant me fortune."
Give me sons, give me wealth, and grant me all my desires.
"O Goddess, make my fame, which arises from abundance, unshakable.
Fame arising from abundance is *lakṣmī*.
Thus ends the ritual bathing of Vināyaka.
Puṣkara said:
I shall describe to you another bath that removes all evil.
O King, this is the meritorious and ever-victorious battle of Maheśvara.
In ancient times, Manu spoke this in the forest to the lord of the Dānavas—
a discourse that brings wealth, fame, and long life, and which causes the destruction of all enemies.
And when the night has turned to dawn and the sun has risen,
O best of Dānavas, one should bathe according to the ritual prescribed by rule.
Having prepared a vessel made of gold, silver, or even clay, filled with water from rivers or lakes according to the prescribed rite;
One should place there medicinal herbs that have been well-anointed and finely ground:
Jayā, Vijayā, and likewise Sūkṣmaphalā.
Incense, mukhavījā, bhaṇḍī, and flowers;
that which is produced from milk, the remains of leaves, and what has been discarded by the goddesses.
Phalinī, Varāṅganā, and Mañjarī of the lordly elephant;
those born from small creatures and sprouts; and two dense ones, each appearing at night.
Mahodya, Mūrtika, Tumba, Yajñabhū, Śaśāṅka, Mṛgadarpa, and Dānakariṇ—
these medicinal herbs have been described to you; now hear the mantra for the ritual bath.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Rudra, whose limbs are smeared with thick white and pale ash.
It is thus:
Victory! Victory! Be victorious, O you who completely overwhelm such-and-such a person in quarrels, conflicts, and disputes! Birth after birth, crush, crush all adversaries!
May he who, at the end of the age, desires once more to incinerate this world—
that thousand-eyed one in his fierce form— protect your life.
And that arrow, which is like the fire of universal destruction, the destroyer of Tripura,
and composed of all the gods— may it protect your life.
"Nikhilam ity ani svāhā.
Thus, with that very mantra, one who is self-restrained and pure should offer into the blazing fire oblations of sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with clarified butter.
Then one should perform the worship of the trident-bearing God of gods with an ablution of ghee and milk, and with perfumes, flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains of rice.
With lamps, incense, prostrations, and likewise with abundant food,
with sweet songs and instrumental music, and with the recitation of benedictions by Brahmins.
Indeed, by performing this Māheśvara bath,
which destroys Rākṣasas and annihilates enemies,
a man obtains all his desires.
"Whatever [names] indeed remain in one's mind"—
thus is described the Māheśvara bath as spoken in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Puṣkara said:
I shall describe other baths to you; listen as I speak of them, which are especially destructive of demons, conducive to fame, and auspicious.
Bathing with ghee is said to be the supreme increaser of longevity;
O Rāma, bathing with cow dung is the supreme increaser of prosperity.
Likewise, bathing with cow urine destroys all sins;
bathing with water mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) eradicates all diseases.
Bathing with milk is said to increase strength and intelligence;
bathing with curd is said to supremely increase prosperity.
Likewise, bathing with dharma-water destroys all sins;
bathing with the water of the five products of the cow accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings.
Bathing with water from the horns of cows destroys all sins;
bathing with *palāśa*, *bilva*, and lotus flowers is like having a domestic priest.
Vacā, haridrā, mañjiṣṭhā, and tagara are likewise prescribed for the reciter;
this bath is ordained as a destroyer of demons and a cleanser of sins.
A bath with vacā, the two types of haridrā, and musta is supreme for destroying malevolent spirits;
it promotes longevity, is as praiseworthy as grain, brings fortune, and increases intelligence.
The bath with golden water is purifying and auspicious;
thereafter, one should perform it in descending order with slightly less silver and copper water.
Likewise, perform a bath with jewel-water and achieve victory in battle;
having placed [the image] in the center of Vaikuṇṭha, one should attend upon it with young sprouts.
A bath performed with that vessel shall grant all desires;
likewise, a bath with water and flowers shall bring about good health.
Likewise, bathing with seeds and water brings clarity to all seeds;
similarly, bathing with *āmalaka* fruit is the supreme destroyer of misfortune (*alakṣmī*).
Bathing with sesame seeds and white mustard destroys inauspiciousness.
Bathing with sesame seeds alone, or with white mustard seeds,
or bathing with *priyaṅgu* is said to increase good fortune.
O twice-born one, it is traditionally taught that bathing with the root of the *vandhyākarkoṭakī*, *kumārī*, and *padmavāriṇī* plants, each used individually, leads to the destruction of disease.
Prepare [a mixture] with meat, *surā* (?), *coraka*, and *nāgapuṣpa*,
along with those having the same name, the destroyers of enemies,
and *kaṅkolaka*, *jātī*, and *pūga*.
And it shall bestow all happiness and grant sons.
Thus ends the various rules for ritual bathing as declared in the Viṣṇudharmottara.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Janārdana, please describe the ritual for the Rudra-bath according to its prescribed injunctions.
It pacifies all evils and bestows all peace upon human beings.
Kṛṣṇa said: Agastya, the tiger among sages, spoke to Skanda, the commander-in-chief of the gods, the son of Rudra with six faces, as he sat comfortably.
"O Kumāra, you are indeed omniscient through the grace of Śaṅkara;
tell us, for whom and how should the bath according to the Rudra-vidhāna be performed?"
Skanda said: For a woman who has lost her children, one who is unfortunate, one who is devoid of menstruation,
one who gives birth only to daughters, or one who is barren— a ritual bath is prescribed for them.
Devoted to fasting on the eighth or the fourteenth day,
she should do so when the fourth day of her pure menstrual period has arrived, or on a Sunday.
One should perform it at the confluence of rivers, especially of great rivers,
or in a temple of Śiva, or in a cow-pen, or in a secluded courtyard of one's house.
One should request a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires, who is tranquil, knows the Dharma, and is established in truth,
to perform the ritual bath for the sake of the deity during a skillful and fierce rite.
Then one should construct a pavilion that is square and sloping toward the north,
adorned with garlands of sandalwood and smeared with cow dung.
In the center of that, one should draw a lotus filled with white powder;
in its center, upon the pericarp, one should place Mahādeva.
One should duly place Nandin and the others upon four petals according to the ritual injunctions,
and one should assign the world-protectors, Indra and the rest, to the other petals.
O King, one should install the Goddess and Vināyaka there,
having offered arghya, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and rice with jaggery.
One should offer various kinds of foods and diverse fruits;
in the four corners, there should be ornamental offerings adorned with leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.
O Brahmin, one should place each [of these] provided with all medicinal herbs;
then, one should offer the bali-oblation to the spirits in the four directions of the pavilion.
In the southeastern direction, near the mandala,
the fire ritual should be performed in an auspicious sacrificial pit adorned with leaves and flowers.
One who has performed the fire-oblation for the nine planets should offer salt mixed with clarified butter and honey into the fire for one month using a small spoon.
And the performer of the second fire-rite should be a Brāhmaṇa.
The preceptor who performs the recitation of the Rudra-mantra should be anointed with white sandalwood paste,
dressed in white garments, and adorned with white garlands.
Adorned with bracelets, necklaces, earrings,
and rings, and standing near the pavilion, one should recite the Rudra hymns free from envy.
When they have reached eleven, one should recite those [mantras] once again;
the second auspicious mandala should be prepared like the divine mandala.
In its center, however, is a woman adorned with white flowers,
wearing white garments, and anointed with white perfumes.
Once the preceptor, who is a reciter of the Rudra-hymns, has seated her upon a comfortable seat,
he should then consecrate her with water from a vessel made of *arka* leaves.
There are eleven items among the sixty-four in number:

sacred grass (*pavitra*), earth from Indra’s ant-hill, from a cow-stable, and from the Godāvarī river; all medicinal herbs, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), and waters from rivers and sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*).
Having condensed this [mantra] into the jar well-worshipped as Śiva,
[one should place it] specifically in the region of the belly, from the soles of the feet to the tips of the hair.
A woman of virtuous character should devoutly smear all her limbs with it;
then, she should bathe that lady while reciting the Rudra-mantra.
Thereafter, one should place eight water-filled jars filled with *aśvattha* leaves, situated in all directions, along with jars containing unbroken rice (*akṣata*).
Having bathed in this manner, one should give a cow and likewise gold to the bath-attendant;
in this rite, a milch cow is specified as the sacrificial fee for the Hotṛ priest.
Then, O bull among sages, having given cows, clothing, gold, and other gifts to the brahmins and others according to his own ability, he should ask them all for forgiveness.
O best of Brahmins, O beautiful woman, by performing this Rudra-bath,
a woman becomes fortunate, endowed with splendor, and gives birth to many sons.
For indeed, in all months, provided it is auspicious and with the consent of the Brahmins, a woman must certainly perform this rite; thus she attains sons and happiness.
She who, endowed with faith and with her body bowed low, performs the bath known as "Rudra" with the approval of the best of the twice-born,
destroys all the defects residing within the body.
O Bhārata, she who has a living child becomes dear to her husband.
Thus ends the Rudra-bath as spoken in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Īśvara said:
Listen, O Ṣaṇmukha, to the supreme bath performed in a single ghaṭikā according to its true nature.
Those who shall hold, O child, this water-pot fashioned by the gods.
Their wealth, desires, good fortune, and prosperity will increase.
Having constructed the previously mentioned mandala, one should worship Gaurī right there.
One should smear [the vessel] with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood;
having placed the water-pot filled with honey in the northeastern direction,
one should adorn it with flower garlands and wrap it with a red thread.
The wise man should place gold there; he should not leave it empty.
Having covered it with a cloth, he should deposit fragrant scents right there.
One should smear [it] with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and sandalwood.
The wise man should cast uśīra, sandalwood, mustā, bālaka, and all medicinal herbs, as well as āmalakī, dūrvā grass, and gorocanā.
Having performed one hundred and eight recitations according to the root-vidyā of Gaurī,
O Guha, one should then consecrate a water-pot with the mantra of Gaurī,
having recited it one hundred and eight times; that is the consecrated water.

Then one should indeed perform the consecration for either a woman or a man. O Guha, that woman who has been consecrated with water-jars in the mandala shall always be fortunate, and so too, O Guha, shall the man according to the rule.
A woman without a son obtains a son, and one who is not living shall become alive;
if a pregnant woman should have this performed according to this very procedure, [the same result follows].
She gives birth to a son of great heroism and prowess;
by bearing him in a great battle, the king attains victory.
Whatever beautiful maiden does not obtain a husband,
she shall always obtain incomparable good fortune through the consecration of the water-jar (ghaṭikābhiṣeka).
By whatever means a wise man should have a water-clock (ghaṭikā) made—
whether it be something not mentioned by me or even something that has been mentioned— in brief,
he should have it made by relying solely upon this very root-text.
The meaning is that one should approach by relying on the previously mentioned root mantra.
Nothing other than the *ghaṭikā* is considered a means for producing good fortune;
nothing other than the *ghaṭikā*, O Skanda, bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
Whoever wears [this] for a ghaṭikā shall obtain all desires;
one without a son obtains a son, and one without wealth shall acquire wealth.
Thus ends the Ghaṭikā-abhiṣeka as described in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
Kārttikeya said:
"You have already known that there are indeed no women who are barren."
Barrenness arises in those women due to various types of defects born from planetary influences and imbalances of the bodily constituents; explain these to me with diligence.
Īśvara said:
"I shall describe the afflictions caused by the planets; listen, my son, according to the truth.
Thirty-two planets have been declared, and they are the ones who cause suffering to women."
The other grahas are the Kaumārikās, and they too are proclaimed to be thirty-two;
thus, the total number of grahas of cruel deeds is indeed sixty-four.
The extent of each one is sixty-four thousand;
among them, however, sixty-four leaders are proclaimed.
O child, the planets seize a woman through twelve defects:
by sharing a single vessel, by using the same vehicle, and by using another's bed or seat.
Through union with another man, and by means of the clothes and ornaments of others.
Nor with flowers from the remnants of a meal, nor by eating from a single vessel.
Due to being sprinkled with water used for washing hair, due to embracing another noble woman,
and because of all these faults, the planetary spirits (grahas) are known to cause affliction.
First the flower is grasped, and immediately after that the embryo;
afterwards the milk, and then the child—thus they say, without a doubt.
I shall state the names of the grahas: Sacarī, Revatī, Śivā, Sukhamandī, Lambā, Pūtanā, and Kaṇḍapūtanā.
Gomukhī, Biḍālī, and likewise Mahāchalā; Kākolī, Hasantī, Ahaṅkārī, and Jayā;
Muktakeśī, Tridaṇḍī, Ajāmukhī, and Rocanā.
Mukula, Piṅgalā by name, and likewise Piṭanāsā;
these, as well as other Skandagrahas, are remembered as the leaders of them all.
Rajanī, Kumbhakarṇī, Tāpasī, another Rākṣasī,
Modanī, Rodanī, Dhanadā, and likewise Kulā are also there.
The sixty-four Mothers, the protectors of children, have been fully enumerated:
Ārjaka, Jambhaka, Bhāsa, Upaskanda, and the fifth, Pañcama.
All these tormentors of children wander about desiring offerings;
one should give the offering according to the prescribed rite, for only then will they release them, and not otherwise.
Then, having made the sacrificial field square with its cords perfectly aligned,
the wise practitioner should divide it into seven equal parts and perform the fire offering.
In their intermediate compartments, O child, one should have nine lotuses made,
having carefully drawn the wheel both externally and internally.
An eight-petaled lotus, white and radiant, together with filaments and a pericarp;
and within those petals, all the Gaṇas [should be placed] in order for their satisfaction.
One should worship all [the deities] starting from the east and so forth, likewise in eight groups of eight;
Śiva, however, is situated in the center of the pericarp within the nine lotuses.
O child, having prepared the ritual substrate (vāsana), one should worship Śiva together with his limbs in the center of the lotus according to the previously described procedure.
I shall describe his actions by which women are released,
having understood their transformations even when they are adorned with all their ornaments.
One who knows the ritual procedure, being devoted to fasting, should install [the image];
and on an auspicious day free from the *vyatīpāta* yoga, he should perform the ceremonial bath.
In the three following [asterisms], in Revatī, in Punarvasu, in Aśvinī, then in Puṣya, and likewise in Rohiṇī; in these lunar mansions [the rite should be performed].
In a mother’s house, or in a house, or at a triple-pathway or a quadruple-pathway;
in an old well, or in a pond, or at the confluences of rivers.
Then, on the eighth lunar day, one should bathe the queen at midday at a solitary tree, in a cremation ground, or even in a temple.

A queen desiring a son should bathe at Gotīrtha; one desiring a son should bathe at the confluence (saṃgama); an unfortunate woman should bathe at Mātṛsnāna; and a woman whose children have died should bathe at the cremation ground (śmaśāna).

One should diligently bathe a woman who has borne only one child, a barren woman, a woman who has been subjected to malevolent magic, and a man who is devoid of semen, at the confluence of rivers or in the vicinity of a temple of Śiva, using the water from an old well or a lotus pond.
The preceptor, however, should always be well-composed, dressed in clean garments, and pure;
he should be eight cubits in height, or even four cubits.
One should cause a four-cornered pavilion with four doors to be constructed, adorned with arches and banners,
moon-bright, provided with lamps, and beautified with flowers and garlands; therein,
one should offer various oblations consisting of ritual baths, drinks, and food offerings.
Having drawn the mandala that fulfills all desires with three powders—
white, red, and black— in their proper sequence.
Īśa, Brahmā, and likewise Viṣṇu are remembered as the presiding deities of the qualities of passion (rajas).
On the northern side of the mandala, one should construct a bathing mandala measuring four cubits in size and adorned with colored powders.
Water-pots made from non-seasonal roots, measuring four or eight [in size],
provided with mango sprouts and likewise arranged as desired,
together with golden dūrvā grass and a collection of medicinal herbs.
Having taken a small amount of earth from both banks of a river, as well as from an anthill and from the root of a tree, one should place it into the first jar.
Having placed cow dung on the second day, scented water on the third,
gold and silver on the fourth, and all medicinal herbs on the fifth.
In the sixth [vessel], one should place the waters of sacred fords; in the seventh, the seven oceans;
and having placed Śaṅkara along with the Mothers in the eighth jar, the practitioner of mantras should cause the consecration to be performed according to this rite.
Whether she has had stillborn children, or whose sons have lived, or whether she is barren or has recently given birth;
whether she is seedless, this mantra shall cause her—be it woman or man—to attain the state of possessing seed.
This mantra shall destroy any defect caused by malevolent sorcery.
By this very primary yoga, which is the kinsman of all,
an unfortunate girl, or even a fortunate one, obtains a worthy husband.
Whether it be elephants, horses, chariots, or vehicles; crowns and earrings;
or wealth, grain, and gold—whatever indeed pleases the Guru, by whose satisfaction the deities, the Mothers, and the planets are satisfied.

Now follows the vidyā for consecration: Oṃ rauṃ hauṃ sauṃ vauṣaṭ. By this, the consecration is secured when the womb is fixed: Oṃ vraṅ kṣaḥ śrī svāhā. By this, a man shall remain firm at the end of the enjoyment of the consecration: Oṃ śrīlayuṃ svāhā.
Furthermore, at the end of the flowers, one should cause the consecration to be given to women.

Oṃ rauṃ hāṃ svāhā. When the womb has been secured by this [mantra], the consecration should be bestowed. By this, whether he be living or his husband be dead, [the result] is certain. Oṃ sāṃ phaṭ raiṃ svāhā.
One should strike that body of the child with mustard seeds or even unbroken grains;
if the child dies while remaining silent, he will certainly live if he cries out.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the consecration of barren women.
Manu said:
"And regarding the measurement that is prescribed during an eclipse of Indra (the moon) or Āditya (the sun)..."
I wish to hear all of that regarding the substances according to the ritual procedures of the mantras.
Matsya said:
I shall now describe the ritual bath, accompanied by mantras and medicinal herbs, for one who encounters the occurrence of an eclipse upon reaching a particular zodiacal sign.
Having encountered a lunar eclipse and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
he should honor four Brahmins with white garlands and unguents.
Having gathered all the medicinal herbs and other materials for the eclipse-rite,
one should place four unblemished jars filled with water.
Having brought earth from the vicinity of elephants, horses, chariots, anthills, the confluence of rivers, a pool, a herd of cows, and the area near a king’s gate, one should deposit it there.
And indeed, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the five jewels into the jars,
along with yellow pigment (rocanā), a lotus, and a conch shell, together with the five-fold cleansing substances (pañcabhaṅga).

Having placed crystal, sandalwood, water from a sacred ford together with mustard seeds, ivory, saffron, as well as uśīra and guggulu— all these together into the jar— one should then invoke the deities.
May all the oceans, rivers, sacred fords, clouds,
and streams come to the patron, bringing about the destruction of his misfortunes.
May that Indra, who is considered the most eminent lord of the Ādityas and possesses a thousand eyes, dispel all suffering here.
May he who is the mouth of all the gods, the seven-flamed one of immeasurable splendor,
dispel the affliction by fire arising from the lunar eclipse.
May he who is the witness of the deeds of all worlds, renowned as Dharmarāja,
the manifest lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas, possessing the brilliance of the fire of universal destruction,
holding a sword in hand and exceedingly terrifying, dispel the affliction caused by the Rākṣasas.
May the god who holds the serpent-noose, whose vehicle is always the sea-monster,
the lord of the waters and the moon, dispel the affliction caused by the planets.
May Dhanadeva— who is to be abandoned as that Lord of Treasures (Nidhipati) bearing a sword, a trident, and a mace—
dispel the impurity caused by the lunar eclipse.
May that Lord Śaṅkara— the moon-bearing deity, wielder of the Pināka bow, whose vehicle is the bull— destroy the sins resulting from the lunar eclipse.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both stationary and moving— those hymns dedicated to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun— may they remove your sin.
One should worship the Brāhmaṇas as one's chosen deity with gifts of wealth and cows;
then, accompanied by these very mantras and provided with gold,
having worshipped them while facing east, one should gaze upon one's chosen deity.
When a water-pot filled with ritual substances has been obtained during an eclipse festival,
and once the lunar eclipse has ceased and the auspicious milking of the cow has been performed,
one who has completed his ablutions should offer that jar to a Brāhmaṇa.
Whoever performs the ritual bath along with the planets according to this procedure shall suffer no affliction from the planets, nor shall there be any loss of kinsmen or wealth.
One attains the supreme accomplishment, from which return is difficult to find;
during a solar eclipse, one should always recite the name of the Sun within the mantras.
O upholder of the royal lineage, it is said that the bath should be performed with those very same substances;
moreover, there should be a ruby and a beautiful, well-proportioned Kapila cow.
The person who would constantly hear this, or even cause others to hear it,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Śakra.
O King, during a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse,
if a person of the twice-born caste consecrates auspicious water-pots with these mantras and performs the ritual bath according to the rules for a man, his suffering [is removed].
The suffering caused by that grasping does not afflict such a person.
Thus concludes the ritual bath during lunar and solar eclipses as declared in the Matsya Purāṇa.

Now, therefore, we shall explain the pacification rite for the birth of twins. If a wife, a cow, a female slave, or a mare should give birth to a deformity, one must perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). When ten days have passed, one should collect a decoction from four milky trees—*plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, *udumbara*, *aśvattha*, *śamī*, *devadāru*, and white mustard seeds—and fill eight water-pots with these, along with gold, sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, and leaf-shoots. Having bathed the couple with all medicinal herbs using the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," the five verses beginning with "kayā naś citra," the five verses addressed to Indra, the five verses addressed to Varuṇa, and the verse "idam āpaḥ pravahata" (RV 10.9.1), and having adorned them, one should seat them upon *darbha* grass. Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* offering for the Maruts and offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*), one offers oblations of clarified butter with the aforementioned bathing mantras. One then offers the *sthālīpāka* with the following: "To Agni, svāhā! To Pavana, svāhā! To Māruta, svāhā! To Yama, svāhā! To Antaka, svāhā! To Mṛtyu, svāhā! To Brahmā, svāhā! To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! In the event of portents in the house—such as an owl, a dove, a vulture, or a hawk entering; or if an anthill appears on a sprout or in the washing-water of the water-jar; or if a seat, bed, or vehicle breaks; or if a house-lizard, a chameleon, or a reptile crawls over; or if a parasol or banner is destroyed, or any other such portent—this very same expiation is prescribed. Having performed the pacification rite for planetary influences (*grahaśānti*) according to the stated rule, having given a gift to the teacher, and having had the blessings of "well-being" pronounced and received, peace is attained.
Thus ends the rite for pacifying the birth of twins as spoken by Kātyāyana.
Puṣkara said:
"Now learn from me the characteristics of those with large teeth at the time of their eruption."
For that infant whose teeth first appear at the top [of the mouth].
O best of the Bhārgavas, listen as I declare the pacification for one who, from birth, has teeth along with [his mother],
or who might devour his mother, his father, or even himself.
Listen to that as I speak it.
O twice-born one, O knower of dharma, one should place the child upon the back of an elephant or on a boat; in the absence of those, [one should place him] on an excellent seat made of gold.

O Bhārgava, one should then worship the donor with all kinds of medicinal herbs, all fragrances, seeds, flowers, and fruits, as well as with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), jewels, banners,
and an offering of cooked rice (sthālīpāka).
In this case, it should be performed for seven days, as well as the feeding of Brahmins;
on the eighth day, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be given to the Brahmins.
Gold, silver, cows, land, or even one's own self—
listen now to the rule for bathing when these are given at the common time of a child's tooth-eruption.
Having seated [the image] upon an auspicious throne, one should bathe it with earth, roots, fruits,
as well as all medicinal herbs, all seeds, and likewise all perfumes;
and therein one should worship Fire, Moon, and Wind.
First, one should install there Keśava, the God of gods;
he should then offer clarified butter into the fire for those very deities according to the prescribed rite.
Then, worship and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be given to the Brahmins;
thereafter, one should have the well-adorned child seated upon the seats.

Then, one should well-bathe with seeds the head of the reciting [preceptor] beneath the parasol; with those seeds that have been well-steamed, the children should perform worship. Furthermore, women whose husbands are living, Brahmins, and friends should likewise be honored.
Thus concludes the rite for the pacification of the eruption of teeth as described in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Now I shall proclaim the Vasantikā rite for the pacification of the birth of *janmāra* (the spirit of death at birth),
when one, possessed by greed, oppresses the subjects with [excessive] wealth.
The king sports about, rushing forward, and does not abide by righteousness;
his subjects follow his word, having abandoned dharma.
Overcome by anger and greed, and devoid of virtuous conduct,
they do not worship their beloved gods, the Brahmins, nor the ancestors.
When they were thus overcome by unrighteousness, Rudra then became enraged.
This Blessed One is the ender of all beings and their father as well;
acting as the cause, he brings about various kinds of transformations.
The stars, planets, and comets; Rāhu, Kāka, and Valāhaka;
the sun and the portents of the twilight; the terrible cries of dogs, beasts, and birds; earthquakes, meteors, and thunderbolts; and the selling of sesame seeds for cold or hot water.
Excessive rain, drought, and likewise the inversion of the seasons occur;
furthermore, during such an inversion, medicinal herbs become devoid of their potency.
Devoid of taste and potency, they give rise to diseases;
because they provoke Rudra, they are called "the slayers of people."
Therefore, with great care and being well-composed, one should propitiate Maheśvara, the God of gods,
according to the ritual prescribed by the knowledge of the divine sciences.
One should perform the propitiation in this manner according to the Gāṇapatya rite, as well as the Atharvaśiras, and the Yāmala procedure.
One should recite the Śivasūkta, the Umāsūkta, and the Śatarudriya;
one should offer various kinds of oblations and gifts at the crossroads.
One should, being pure, invoke Rudra along with his attendants during the day or at night;
one should honor the Brahmins with various kinds of food and sacrificial fees.
Then, when Rudra was propitiated, the plague of the people ceased;
and the king, with his senses restrained, remained devoted solely to the recitation of prayers.
Being disciplined, one should resort to the fire-oblation according to the rules and with regularity;
for a king who is thus disciplined, the accomplishment of his tasks is praised.
For it is held that the root of that ritual action is the faithful king;
the king, having fasted and bathed, should be composed, clad in white garments.
Having personally performed the protection of oneself, one should then employ the rite of pacification.
Where the king and the royal priest are righteous in soul and knowers of dharma,
and where the qualities of the royal lineage prevail, there prosperity increases.

Thus ends the rite for pacifying the death of people as taught by Garga. Now follows the rite for pacifying diseases of cattle as proclaimed by Garga: "Ten types of diseases are said to afflict cattle; I shall describe what they are like."
Agitating, heart-seizing, causing one to fall, and likewise enchanting— such is the manifestation of their forms; I shall describe that to you,
as well as the rite of pacification that was prescribed for them.
When cows in the cow-pens at night are terrified and flee hither and thither,
that disease is known as Udvega, and by it indeed [the affliction] is produced.
They shed tears and they fall from their eyes;
one should recognize that as heart-disease, and one should diagnose it as a disease among the cattle.
Where one passes blood, feces,
or urine while trembling, with wrinkled skin and fallen [limbs], it is called the disease.
In this regard, they utter the sound "huṃ" and likewise form mandalas;
the wise know that which is well-pleased in the future to be the consciousness of the deluded.
One should recognize that as the abode of Pūtanā, where foul-smelling excrement and honey-like fluid flow forth from the cows, and where disease has arisen among them.
If, having scorched its tongue, it rushes toward a cow,
then a disease called Kalila indeed occurs among the cattle here.
When blood-red eyes roll and discharge fluid,
and flies also settle upon them, one should know that a most dreadful disease is present.
When a cow rises and moves toward the circle [of the herd] and is tossed about by the wind,
it should be known as the "ear-tossing gait," a disease that has arisen among the cows.
That disease which has arisen among the cattle, known as *svairaka*, is such that it cannot be traversed even by a razor when it stands spread out.
One whose limbs tremble, whose body hairs stand erect,
and whose two ears hang down— know him to be a Karṇalambaka.
Thus these diseases have been declared, as well as others that are like sacrifices;
regarding each of them as prescribed, one who is patient and pure, having abstained from food and personally performed self-protection, should then apply the rite of pacification.
One should avoid from afar those who are naked, those dressed in saffron-colored robes, the foolish, attendants, the deformed, and those who have stumbled.
One should avoid from afar those who are one-eyed, those with variegated skin, those afflicted by leprosy, those paralyzed on one side, and likewise those of the lowest castes.
It may be at an *aśvattha* or a *palāśa* tree, on level ground that is not saline,
or at a great sacred site, a solitary tree, or even in a cow-pen.
The astrologer, having purified himself, should prepare the deities and other requirements;
then, having installed the deities, he should construct the altar according to the prescribed measurements.
First, [he should offer] water-pots, kuśa grass, garlands, parched grain, woolen cloth,
as well as meat, cooked food, and likewise balls of snow.
One should collect mustard seeds with ghee and mustard oil, as well as unbroken grains, perfumes from which the *pratisara* has been removed, and sacrificial fuel sticks.
One should prepare sacrificial fuel sticks from udumbara, palāśa, khadira, bilva, aśvattha, and śamī wood.
One should have four thousand pieces made, each the size of a joint;
one should collect horse bones, elephant bones, and owl bones.
One should collect all these bones and incenses;
together with the sacred words, one should bring the incense into the huts.
One should offer an oblation of meat mixed with wine and blood, as well as cooked flesh,
toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, while performing a circumambulation.
One should lead the cows from all the pens to the temple pen,
having caused them to accept clarified butter, incense, and perfumes, and having performed a circumambulation.
Having formally brought forth the fire and strewn it all around according to the rules,
one should cause the rite to be performed at an auspicious moment, even while seeking victory by means of power.
While applying this peace-mantra, one should mentally recite the Sāvitrī;
for she was indeed proclaimed by the twice-born in the past as the mother of the Vedas.
Having taken blood from the ears of a black goat with its body [as an offering],
one should offer oblations of sacrificial fuel sticks, along with snake-skin ashes and clarified butter, until [the deity] is pacified.
A Brahmin should likewise offer oblations of Rakṣoghna oil and rice mixed with meat, accompanied by red garlands; this brings about the destruction of heart disease.
Then, one should offer the blood of a goat with ears like flowers,
along with castor oil and pungent oil, having observed the disease and applied the subsequent treatment.

If the sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*) are made of *śamī* wood, and the offering consists of *kṛśara* and barley-gruel mixed with protective oil, there will be a deluding disease therein. Furthermore,
[one should offer] the fat and the heart of a pale goat.
One should offer honey, clarified butter, and the tongue as oblations into the house of Pūtanā.
The fuel should consist of *aśvattha* and *udumbara* wood;
with the flesh of *palāśa*, *khadira*, and *māṃsa*, even a terrible disease is pacified. It may likewise be performed with the [flesh] of a black-necked goat or a female goat.
One should offer blood mixed with clarified butter as an oblation in the case of a severe illness;
likewise, the fat, heart, and blood of a goat that has reached full maturity.
Clarified butter mixed with mustard oil and the heart of a cock, combined with the form of ariṣṭa, destroys itching and brings security.
O bull among the twice-born, he who has performed the prescribed rite for the peace of cattle should have the sacrificial fuel brought forward and offered into the fire at the center of the hearth.
One should have [this] done for the sake of cows, or they should recite it hundreds of times;
thus his sons and grandsons, as well as his wealth and grain, shall likewise increase.
And cows will increase properly in the world; one shall attain fame through the Śivadharma.
He is praised by Brahmā with the Brahma-foot, the Praṇava.
May that eternal god Śiva drive away the plague among the cattle.
May that eternal god Śiva, well-praised by the elephant-faced deity Lambodara, drive away the plague from the cattle.
May that eternal god Śiva— who is always worshipped with devotion by the powerful Viṣṇu— drive away the plague from among the cows.
May that eternal god Śiva, who is saluted even by the Sun, the remover of all diseases, dispel the pestilence among the cattle.
He who is constantly saluted with devotion by the illustrious Gaṇa Ghaṇṭākarṇa, whose limbs are radiant, who is joyful and whose mind is focused on no other.
May that eternal god Śiva dispel the plague among the cattle,
he who is perpetually endowed with the power of Rudra and possessed of devotion to Rudra.
May the divine Gaṇa Ghaṇṭākarṇa, the bestower of the knowledge of Śiva,
dispel the pestilence among the cattle through the power of Śiva-yoga.
Salutations to the auspicious god, to Mahādeva, the radiant one;
constant salutations to you, Rudra, the stable one, Hara, and Ugra.
Salutations again and again to the Supreme Lord, the perfected one, the bestower of mantra-perfection,
to the Three-eyed One, the Great Lord, the Infinite.
Having consecrated water with these mantras in their proper order at all times, one should pray to the god of cows; from that, success will arise.
Whoever recites this among cattle, at the start of a journey, or in an assembly, shall become long-lived, powerful, wealthy, illustrious, and a lord of riches.
At the end of his body, he shall go to the supreme state; of this there is no doubt.
For the sake of purification from all sins, one should recite this "Peace of the Cow."
Thus ends the pacification of cattle.
Suśruta, Radarāja, Garga,
and Mitrajit likewise questioned Śālihotra, the treasure-house of asceticism, concerning the stable for mounts.
O Lord, how indeed does the terrible disease known as Maḍaka arise among horses?
Or how may they be pacified? Having heard this, please explain it to me.
The highly effulgent Śālihotra, a treasury of asceticism, said to them:
"When horses are kept in an unsuitable place, or when they have a splinter, or when they are afflicted by disease..."
A terrible mortality of horses will arise; there is no doubt in this matter—whether it be for one whose birth-star, action-star, or mental-star [is afflicted].
Whether it be Maghā and the subsequent asterisms, or even those ending with Sānu,
the names Mānasa and so forth apply to the fourth, tenth, sixteenth, and eighteenth asterisms from one's birth asterism.
If these are afflicted by Saturn, the Sun, and others, or even by Rāhu;
Or, by means of three kinds of such portents, there may be the death of his horse.
Whether it be Brahmins, gods, or even ancestors who are angry with someone,
or one who is possessed by Vināyaka, or whose horses are enraged;
However, he may have a Hayamāra; that one will be a bringer of peace.
Sons are not born from the horse, and others are afflicted by diseases.
One should effect a change of location or perform the extraction of the foreign object;
having done so, one should perform the worship of the deity Vāsudeva right there.
Likewise, when there is affliction from a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), one should perform the prescribed ritual bath;
both the afflicting planet and the afflicting lunar mansion are to be worshipped.
One afflicted by Vināyaka should worship Gaṇapati;
likewise, Mitra, Saṃmita, as well as Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa.
Kūṣmāṇḍa, the prince, and likewise Ambikā are indeed to be honored;
for those against whom Brahmins are angry, these must be worshipped and not otherwise. One must perform the worship of the gods for whom the denizens of heaven are angry.
And at night, when the clearing of the courtyard in the stable is performed,
the worship of the Gandharvas must be carried out there.
In a place where no lamp has been set and which is likewise devoid of purity,
one should first remove the impurities from that spot and then perform the worship of Śrī.
Even Uccaiḥśravas and others are to be honored by one whose horses are enraged.
When Hayamāra has arrived, or when there is some affliction of horses, I shall proclaim this rite of pacification; listen to me as I speak it.
In an auspicious place smeared with cow dung, the domestic priest,
having fasted for a day and night, should perform the rite of pacification.
Wearing washed white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
and decorated with a turban, he [proceeded] according to his ability together with those pure horses.
And he had four Brahmin companions who were free from sloth:
one was a master of the Ṛgveda, the second was preeminent in the Yajurveda,
the third was chief among those learned in the Sāmaveda, and the fourth was likewise an expert in the Atharvaveda.
All [the participants] should be without physical defects, of noble birth, pure, and endowed with virtuous conduct;
they should be clothed in garments and likewise hold sacred grass (pavitraka) in their hands.
One should prepare a fire-pit in the center and a rectangular mandala.
One should place full jars filled with medicinal water in the three directions,
and within them, one should set down vessels of liquid in the sequence beginning from the northeast.
In the eastern part of the pit, one should prepare the station for the Lord of Gods (the Fire) in sequence with clarified butter, milk, curd, and honey.
One should place Yama in the south, and likewise Varuṇa in the west;
and in the northern quarter, one should place the lord Vaiśravaṇa.
O Brahmins, one should honor all of them with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, as well as with garments, incense, and ornaments; likewise, there is the honoring of physicians.
Having obtained that fire from them by means of the king of mantras,
the wise experts of the Yajurveda who lived of old should recite the Aindra hymns.
The Sāmavedin should recite the mantra dedicated to Soma in the south, and the Bahvṛca should likewise recite the mantra dedicated to Varuṇa;
furthermore, the learned Atharvan priest should recite the mantra associated with Kubera.
Having given as separate sacrificial fees gold, a wonderful garment, bell-metal, and a cow,
one is liberated from the horse-sacrifice.
When Hayamāra has arrived, or when there is some affliction of horses, I shall proclaim this rite of pacification; listen to me as I speak it.
Then, in the auspicious place previously described, according to the previously mentioned ritual for treasure,
one should construct a fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) in the northeast, in the east, or indeed in the southeast; furthermore, one should perform the worship of the deities within the mandalas upon the ground.
In this regard, three Brahmins of the Rigveda should be employed; however, one from the Atharvaveda should not be employed at all.
Furthermore, in the south-eastern direction, the worship of Agni is prescribed.
The worship of Vāyu is in the northeast, while that of Savitṛ should be in the east;
one who is learned in the Yajurveda should mutter the Sāvitra mantra.
In the southeast, one who is expert in the Sāman should place the Bahvṛca and Soma;
all other previously mentioned rites should be performed by one who understands them.
In the event of portents, omens, or the twitching of horses, one should perform an expiation; then everything will be pacified.
To the north of the horse-stable, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there;
having fasted for three nights, the domestic priest (purohita) should perform a rite of pacification (śānti) at that place.
The sacrificial ground, strewn on all four sides with new garments,
should have fourteen water-pots placed there.
Vessels of liquid should be given when the jar is full, O well-trained one;
having bathed his head and put on a turban, he should have duly prepared the mandala.
Clad in white garments, having conquered anger, and being preeminent in virtue,
he should offer oblations into the fire with wisdom, perfectly composed in mind.
To Pitāmaha, to Rudra, to Skanda, and to Varuṇa;
to the two Aśvins, to Sūrya, to Śakra, and likewise to Agni.
To Vāha, or to Hari, and likewise to the goddess Śrī;
to the Gandharvas, to Soma, and to Uccaiḥśravas as well.
Whichever deity was the cause of that portent there,
having identified her within the mandala, one should worship her with offerings.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations for each deity, the son, seeking his welfare,
should then perform the worship of the gods with special care.
With offerings of milk-rice, ointments, lamps, incense,
and unguents, the Brahmins should be fed with food mixed with honey and milk-rice, accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
Dedicated to each individual deity, one should give ten, seven, or five [cows],
along with gold, a garment, a cow, and a bell-metal vessel as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Then, for the sake of expiation, the king should give [the required amount] to the domestic priest for three nights,
so that this twice-born man may be satisfied.
One should worship all the vehicles after having the best of the twice-born recite benedictions;
for this rite of pacification is always to be performed constantly during times of portentous calamities.
It is a destroyer of demons, conducive to fame, and a destroyer of all portents;
it grants victory to kings, is meritorious, and increases wealth and grain.
Thus ends the *Śālihotra-aśva-śānti* (The Peace Rite for Horses according to Śālihotra). Now follows the *Gaja-śānti* (The Peace Rite for Elephants).
Regarding this, Pālakāpya speaks of the characteristics of elephant keepers (*pālaka*) and the characteristics of elephants kept by such keepers.
One should observe that there the *kṣara* moves for the sake of an obstacle;
carrying [the breath], it kills either the elephants or even the preeminent elephant.
A king seeking his own welfare should personally perform this rite there;
he should diligently worship Rudra, Viṣṇu, and all the deities.
At night, an offering to the spirits should also be made with flesh and blood in all elephant stables,
at crossroads, and in lower streets.
Having suddenly emerged from the city at night, he led the elephants outside;
in either the eastern or northern direction, there was a bath that was delightful to the people.
On the following day, O King, other elephants, whose feet were well-trained and who fed on tree-branches and grass, were led through most delightful regions.
According to the prescribed ritual, with great mantras, eating but once a day and remaining self-controlled,
they should perform the rite for exactly seven days, devoted to recitation and fire-offerings.
The family priest, however, should perform a propitiatory rite that destroys sin;
having gratified the twice-born there, he should honor them with sacrificial fees.
[1037] And those who have mastered the earth, being pure and firm in their vows,
should bathe at night for one hundred and one days and eat sacrificial food and boiled rice.
One should settle those who subsist on tree-bark, wood, and grass in a single location;
their status as forest-dwellers shall arise through a mental resolve.
In the places where the oblation is kept, young cows should be made to stay for seven days together with their calves and with bulls as prescribed.
Then, having established two arched gateways on both sides of the water,
there should be a single golden *droṇa* vessel upon each of those *svastikas*.
And the high ministers should remain right there, dwelling upon the sacrificial ground;
and here, O twice-born one, a hundred gold pieces and water should be deposited.
One should prepare the bath prescribed for ordinary sacrifices;
likewise, it should be performed at the gateway during the ritual of the four months.
A Brahmin who knows the ritual injunctions, having performed the common sacrifice as prescribed, should offer oblations with sacrificial fuel-sticks into the fire using mantras.
With these mantras, one should offer oblations of sacrificial fuel (samidh) into the fire (jātavedas),
[invoking] Indra together with the Maruts, and with the elephant Airāvata.
One should suppress portents by bathing elephants in the northern direction;
having done this, one should offer oblations with the remnants of the sacrificial ghee in every direction.
Then, with those very same mantras previously mentioned,
the Brahmin should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for those very gods in the southern direction.

O King, the twice-born man, reciting this mantra with controlled and melodious voice, offered a bali-oblation to Agni and to all beings on the south side, as well as a bali of turmeric-smeared rice to Varuṇa.

And those Rudras and Rudra-like humans who dwell in the western direction, as well as the fierce spirits, the body hairs, and the diseases—to them belongs this offering, for health, disease, and life itself are dependent upon them. Having offered in the northeastern direction, one should offer boiled rice to Indra.

Well-composed, one should offer the *bali* according to the rule; a Brahmin should apply this mantra with effort: "Homage to the Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Gandharvas, and Rakṣases, among whom there is contact with the ancestors and upon whom life-breaths depend—to them be this *bali*. With these words, he should offer the *bali* to all the quarters while reciting this mantra.
To Agni, the lord of all terrestrial beings, whether they belong to the earth or not—this is your *bali*. To Vāyu, the lord of the beings of the intermediate space—this is your *bali*.
And to Rudra, one should offer the *bali* in due order according to the rule.
To those Rudras who are in the trees, those in the sacred fords, and those in the streets—to them be homage; I carry this offering to them.
To those who are in the intermediate space, those established upon the earth, and those who have taken refuge therein—to those Rudras be homage; I carry this bali-offering to them.
Having repeatedly offered the bali-oblation correctly and having caused the twice-born to recite auspicious words,
he performs the lustration ceremony with lamps in due order according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having given them a bath, one should then lead them to the next archway;
at the second gate, they should again be consecrated with the lustration rite according to the prescribed ritual.
One should recite the *nīra* [mantra] for five days, and then,
on the seventh day, having caused the royal personage to enter those who have performed the auspicious *maṇḍala* rites.
Having caused the virtuous twice-born to pronounce blessings with the sounds of song and instrumental music,
they were honored with all kinds of seeds, fruits, flowers, and *śālagrāma* fragrances.
Then, one should place jars containing gold at the doors of the halls,
having rendered them well-prepared and adorned, and honored with all necessary materials.
O King, it is said that Bharadvāja was a lake along with the Maruts;
likewise, he was again in the hall, which was filled with auspiciousness and well-being.
Entering [the palace], Aniruddha remained standing by a pillar for a hundred autumns;
free from disease and possessing great strength, he brought victory to the king.
Likewise: King Aṅga, in Campā, asked Pālakāpya:
"How should one perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for elephants during all four months of the rainy season?"
"O best of sages, explain this which I have asked to me exactly as it is.
Thus questioned by the King of Aṅga, Pālakāpya then spoke.
Listen to this, O Great King, concerning that which you ask me:
diseases, the Nairṛtis, as well as Rākṣasas and serpents.
Piśācas and Guhyakas, Gandharvas and Rākṣasas as well,
Dānavas and Yakṣas, and those who are the Kaumāra Grahas.
Those who are non-terrible, such as Jaya and the others, and those who are the Rudra deities; whatever obstacles there may be, and those born from the afflictions of the constellations.
Some desire to consume the sacrificial offering, others likewise desire to kill, and still others desire to sport;
such are the great grahas of terrible form.
Whatever other calamities caused by the gods may occur there, they find peace;
for this purpose, O protector of the earth, the lustration of elephants (gaja-nīrājana) is prescribed.
O King, the first is on the full moon of Kārttika, the second likewise on that of Phālguna, and the third occurs on the full moon of Āṣāḍha; these three are remembered as the Nīrājana festivals.
One who desires the welfare of elephants should observe the four-month period;
he should offer oblations (bali) to the deities and the Siddhas as is appropriate.
Camels, cuckoos, and nets; grain, curd, ghee, and honey;
milk-rice, honeyed porridge, red rice, and rice with molasses;
a well-established auspicious throne, and divine garlands and ointments.
One should procure long-pointed green darbha grass, food for the brahmins,
and new, auspicious equipment for the elephant according to the prescribed rules.
One should consecrate tagara, uśīra,
and priyaṅgu with all kinds of jewels and medicinal herbs, as well as incense, garlands, and collyrium.
One should perform protective rites for the elephants accompanied by recitations for well-being;
furthermore, pacifying rituals should be performed both upon their departure and arrival, as well as at the two twilights.
The family priest should offer oblations into the fire on the south side;
the physician, dressed in clean garments and composed in mind, should offer them on the north side.
Having put on a new linen garment, having become pure, and with palms joined in reverence,
he should pay homage to the eight gods and pronounce a blessing upon the elephants.
And Prajāpati, Viṣṇu, Yama, and the Lord of Śacī;
Rudra, Baladeva, Varuṇa, and likewise the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
I pay homage to the commander-in-chief, the lord and master of elephants;
then, having brought the sacrificial vessels, one should prepare the sacrificial ground.
To the east or within the interior, with the permission of the Brahmins,
in an auspicious place that slopes toward the northeast, on level ground where the herbs are lush and the soil is rich.
In a place where the water flows clockwise and which is easily accessible from all sides,
one should smear the sacrificial ground with cow dung and then cause him to enter.
Therefore, one should avoid ground that is not free of pits, which is eight *aratnis* deep;
nor ground damaged by gardens or deities, nor ground that is parched above, nor ground that is hard or uneven.
A wise man should avoid trees that are newly grown, straight, or unstable, as well as those that are excessively tall or have twelve spokes.
One should smear all the elephant stables with cow dung;
having made them clean, one should adorn them with the six kinds of offerings.
At the various stations, flower garlands were placed, and at the crossroads, arches were erected;
then the king, taking all the subjects with him, held unbroken grains and water in his hands.
One should sprinkle the bases of the pillars, the ground, and likewise the surrounding area;
the attendants should be well-bathed, pure, and dressed in white garments.
Until the time of the final extinguishing, one should lead the elephant toward the water;
there, one should offer the oblation of peace, and the Brahmin should perform the ritual.
[He worshipped] the ritual substances, the elephant stables, as well as the water-spouts,
Varuṇa, the river Tīrthakanyā, the Nāgas, and the deities of the waters.
Pure, one should worship the oceans, the rivers, the wells, the lakes, and all the ponds, as well as the gods.
Having performed the expiatory rites, the wise king should then cause the elephant to set out,
filled with all kinds of gems, medicinal herbs, and seeds.
One should bathe the elephant with the aforementioned types of sandalwood according to the seasons; once it has been bathed, one should provide it with new, unwashed garments.
Then, having taken yellow turmeric paste, the wise man should fill the five fingers and perform all auspicious rites.
One should properly anoint the village with yellow pigment (rocanā) and whatever else is pleasing;
on that day, well-adorned and joyful, one should celebrate with musical instruments.
It was adorned with banners of victory, not with fivefold ropes;
it was made of gold or silver, and endowed with celestial garments.
Tied with linen thread and mixed with nagara and uśīra,
it was produced on a mountain peak and is honored by all the gods.
A hundred elephants, having been released after sitting down, shall bring well-being to the elephants,
health to the serpents, and victory to the king.
And one should draw a svastika in the center; thus the elephants proceed auspiciously, having scattered parched grain all around the sacrificial ground.
One should strike it on all sides with blades of *kuśa* grass and branches of the *udumbara* tree, as well as with sticks made of *palāśa* wood and likewise with those of the perfected *udumbara*.
One should produce the luminaries as long as the fire is kindled;
then, taking up the vessel containing water, one should sprinkle the bearer of oblations.
O Aditi, homage to you! O Sarasvatī, homage to you! O divine Savitṛ, homage to you!
Arise, increase, and quickly manifest your power for me!
The Apsarases and the Brāhmaṇas with auspicious hands awaken [you].
"O Havyavāhana, being pleased, grant me the yoga;
having taken the clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, may there be peace for the elephants."
Svāhā! To the fuel-stick, svāhā! To the dipping-spoon, svāhā!
Bhūḥ, svāhā! Bhuvaḥ, svāhā!
May the Awakened One awaken all beings and Brahmā of immeasurable splendor.
[1043] The thousand-eyed one, the Lord of Beings, Kubera, Varuṇa, and Yama.
And also the high-souled Viṣṇu, as well as Nārada and Parvata,
Uddālaka, Kāśyapa, Marīci, and Bhṛgu.
With palms joined in reverence, I bow to all the foremost sages;
having offered an oblation of clarified butter to them, may there once again be well-being for Gaja.
May the kings be free from disease, and may the sacrificial priests prosper;
may they bestow gifts upon the twice-born, as well as strength, health, and glory.
Svāhā!
To Dakṣa, the beings, the Gandharvas, the plants, and the hosts of the quarters;
to the Ādityas and the Maruts, as well as the two Aśvins and the planets.
They bestow upon elephants strength, health, and glory.
Svāhā! Airāvata, Puṣpadanta, Kumuda, Vāmana, Pauṇḍarīka, Nīlavant, Sārvabhauma, and Sutejas.
And to Supratīka, the lord of nāgas,
and likewise to Mahābali and other great elephants, I pay homage with palms joined in reverence.
Having poured an oblation of clarified butter over them once more for the sake of the elephant's well-being, [he says]:
"May the elephants be free from disease, may the officiating priests prosper,
and may the elephants bestow strength, health, and glory."
Svāhā! [I offer] to Atri, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Pulaha, Kratu,
Dīrgha, Varavara, Pulastya, and likewise Cyavana.
And Vedottamā, Svāhā, and Mount Mālin here,
as well as these seven principal mountain ranges headed by Himavat.
In the same way, with palms joined in reverence, I pay homage from all sides to the infinite nāgas who dwell throughout the ten directions at all times.
I bow with palms joined in reverence to the mountain-dwellers and the serpents;
having offered an oblation of clarified butter to them, may there once again be well-being for the elephant.
May the elephants be free from disease, and may the priests prosper;
may they bestow upon the elephants excellence of color, health, and glory.

Svāhā! Having become pure and with palms joined in reverence, [one should worship] the desired mountain-supporters, who possess great splendor and great strength, who grant the gods their enjoyments, and who are of vast majesty.
I first pay homage to Ananta, who is honored by all the worlds;
and to Karkoṭaka, Dhūmaviṣa, and the mighty Vāsuki.
And having also paid homage to Kālīya, Bala, Utpala,
Hari, Vidyujjihva, and both Kavaḷa and Aśvatara;
Then he licks the rising sun with his tongue,
and he also fondles him as he bows down with his tail.
The highly fortunate Anuru, the five-headed and mighty Naga Maṇigraha, and those others who support the earth;
May the nāgas grant well-being for the sake of nirvāṇa and for crossing over;
those nāgas who dwell within the earth, and those whose range is the cardinal directions.
Having poured an oblation of clarified butter over them once more for the elephant's well-being, [he says]:
"May the elephants be free from disease, and may the officiating priests prosper."
"May they bestow upon the Nāgas strength, health, and glory;
furthermore, O Brahmin, one should recite this eulogy while facing the north toward the commander of the army."
The commander of the army, the wielder of the spear, the lord and master of elephants,
beloved of the sixth [Skanda], the enemy of the crane, the six-faced one with twelve eyes.
Wearing red garlands and garments, adorned with bells, ornaments, and earrings,
the three-eyed, twelve-armed, and invincible Kārttikeya.
One should offer a red protective thread-garland naturally perfumed with *kāmacandana*, and worship with jaggery, wheat-flour cakes, milk-rice porridge, *svastika* sweets, and so forth.
I bow to the southeastern quarter, as well as the southern direction;
likewise, I bow to the southwestern and the western directions.
I bow to Vāyu’s quarter, to the northern quarter, and likewise to the north-eastern quarter;
thereafter, I worship Aditi, the mother of the gods, who occupies half of that quarter.
Dwelling upon the elephants, I bow to them with palms joined in reverence;
having offered an oblation of clarified butter to them, may there once again be well-being for the elephant.
May the elephants be free from disease, and may the priests prosper;
may they bestow upon the elephants excellence of color, health, and glory.
Svāhā! Svastika cakes, saṃyāva, honey, parched grain, as well as ghee,
gold, fine gold, and new garments.
Maireya, surā, and this excellent vāruṇī;
guḍodana, mālla, madya, and kalmāṣa as well.
All this has been set forth for the benefit of the planets in their entirety; now tell us, O Horse, about hunger that is hidden and well-guarded,
and may it bestow upon the Nagas excellence of color, health, and glory.
Svāhā!
May he dispel all evils for the king here for a hundred years;
may the forest-dwellers released by you remain unassociated with human beings.
There is nothing that has not been granted by you; O granter of desires, you ought to enjoy this food, which is free from putrid flesh, abundant, and devoid of deceit.
O General, may there be prosperity for you as you mount that which has not been mounted by men, and as you grasp it according to its true nature;
may the elephants bestow upon you beauty, health, and fame.
Svāhā! I present to you this cock, whose weapon is his feet, the copper-crested, the hundred-feathered, the enchanting one, with variegated plumage and red eyes.
"Accept this cock from me, O Senāni; may there be prosperity for you. Bestow upon the elephants excellence of color, health, and power."
Svāhā!
With a tail of abundant color and all my limbs perfectly composed,
I present to you this goat, its skin washed clean with the paste of *āmalaka* fruit.
O Senānī, may it be well with you; accept this goat from my house, and bestow upon the elephants excellence of color, health, and glory.
Svāhā!
I show you uśīra, the ointment of the king of gods, bent upon a thousand spikes, the most excellent of all roots.
"O Senānī, take this uśīra root from me; may it be well with you!
Bestow upon the elephants excellence of color, health, and glory."
Svāhā!
This garland, belonging to Nairājinī, was worn by the Thousand-eyed One;
it is produced from the deities and is most captivating even to the Rākṣasas.
The goddess who generates joy, frequented by spirits and nāgas,
[is to be invoked] during invitations, marriages, and the consecration ceremonies for fields.
At the entrances of the Nāgas, the auspicious Vāruṇī liquor is prescribed;
it is fragrant, delicious, intoxicating, and delightful.

Worshipped by gods and men, being pleased, I appear before you. O General, may it be well with you; accept from me this Vāruṇī [weapon], which bestows upon the Nāgas excellence of color, health, and glory.
Svāhā!
Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, in the battle concerning Tāraka,
he of immeasurable splendor was consecrated by the gods as the commander-in-chief of the divine hosts.
O Commander of the Army, may prosperity attend you; protect the host along with the king, and bestow upon the elephants excellence of color, health, and fame.
Svāhā!
These are the śaṅkhas, mṛdaṅgas, and whatever bronze instruments there are;
the vīṇās, sarpīs, praṇavas, godhās, and parivadantakas.
Invoked for the sake of auspiciousness, sweet-sounding musical instruments are indeed played here for one night and one day for the victory of the king.
Having correctly understood the various forms appearing in the sacrificial fire,
one who knows the signs of the oblation being offered should provide instructions for the sake of protection.
When it is being carried away, they go to destruction: the fire that is very firm, Citraghna, Puruṣa, and likewise Vasugandha.
A fire that is excessively colored, variegated, and shaped like an anthill,
or one that gives its share to the Hotṛ priest, portends the destruction of the twice-born.
One that crackles with sparks and the like, is harsh, or has a deformed appearance;
one accompanied by smoke and wind, or one that possesses the smell of its own constituent parts and is even—these are unfavorable.
One that has the shape and appearance of a cow's mouth portends the destruction of cattle;
likewise, one that rises slowly and subsides quickly [indicates the same].
When the fire being offered oblations is black in color, smokeless, and has the smell of kr̥sarā,
it foretells the death of the king.
Furthermore, one should predict the death of a king from a fire resembling a vulture or an owl;
a fire that is of indistinct color, foul-smelling, and with scattered flames.
When the fire has the odor of a corpse, it will swiftly destroy the kingdom along with its common people and the royal priest; indeed, it portends the death of the king himself.
When the fire has a weak sound and the consumer of oblations smells like a corpse, and it is discolored and emits a foul odor, it foretells the death of the king; likewise,
when the fire is dark brown or pale red, it indicates the destruction of the royal treasury.
With his crest disheveled and possessing a voice like that of a crow,
he portends the destruction of the king’s treasury and the death of the crown prince.
Such a fire produces excessive smoke and excessive sound;
it causes burning in the hands and chest, and it becomes one that carries away the sacrificer.
In that case, one should know there will be loss of wealth upon seeing such an omen:
[a halo] resembling the smoke of dried cow dung and possessing the brilliance of a rainbow.
A fire of that kind would quickly portend the destruction of elephants and horses;
it is tawny in color, deformed, and likewise smells of leather.
The sacrificial fire, being fed with oblations, proclaims the destruction of the progenitor,
just as the fire, when smeared with the oblation, takes on the hue of turmeric.
One should predict the imprisonment of a king when [the marks] have the shape of a shackle, or resemble a conch shell, or even resemble a noose.
He whose smoke, rising with a sound, moves to the left and then turns back, having passed over the forms of hundreds of severed suns; ||| 12 ||
When there is a high mound and a sacrifice for those who smell of fish and blood,
the twice-born should know, by these signs declared in the scriptures, that the king’s son will be slain.
O King, inauspicious things such as insults and the like should not be reported;
even a woman who resembles a mountain palace or has the shape of a water-jar [is auspicious].
The crest of his flame turned to the right; it possessed the sound of swans and the ocean of jewels.
Then there was the sound of conchs and the resonance of kettledrums from the horses, resembling gold and silver and bearing the fragrance of milk-rice.
O Lord of the Earth, when the weapons, armor,
and elephants of one side shine with great brilliance in battle, one should predict victory for him.
If those with joyful minds, wearing white garments,
should take control of a beautiful mansion, that would be a sign of victory.
When the preceptor, being displeased, should offer oblations into the fire,
one should recognize that there will be great danger to the king as well as to his elephants and other assets.
The wise one should bathe with distinguished water the maces and other weapons, which are worthy of worship, possessed of divine marks, and have no other vehicle.
The practitioner should there bathe all other vehicles— the elephants and horses—
equipped with that [mantra], using only the water from an external jar.
On those days, the knower of mantras should perform the *nīrājana* rite for the king;
on other occasions as well, it should be performed in this manner, for he is indeed a supreme mine of jewels.
The family priest, having prepared the king, his mounts, and others likewise,
all adorned with every ornament and accompanied by every auspicious rite,
should afterwards cause many blessings to be recited by the Brahmins.
The king should give incomparable sacrificial fees to the officiating priests and to the preceptor;
he should also cause a vehicle, richly adorned with ornaments, to be presented to the teacher.
Among the male and female slaves, servants, and in all the villages and other places,
the king [should see them] adorned with all ornaments and mounted upon horses.
He was also accompanied by mounted riders on excellent elephants and horses in rut,
together with Brahmins and officiating priests who were reciting benedictions.
The preceptor, knowing the mantras, should himself cause the king to enter the royal palace with the water from the pitcher distinguished by the previous bath.
Having sprinkled the elephant stable and likewise the horse stable,
and having scattered white mustard seeds, rice, sesame seeds, and flowers [therein].

In the middle of the hall, one should worship Nṛsiṃha and the flawless Sudarśana with perfumes, flowers, and all manner of ornaments. Outside, one should offer an oblation to the spirits (bhūtabali) consisting of parched grain flour and rice mixed with sesame.
Then, in all the halls, one should feed the Brahmins sufficiently;
thereafter, at the time of the departure, the preceptor should [perform the rites] for the elephant and the horse.
Thus, when an omen occurs, the preceptor who knows the mantras, being well-composed, should perform this rite of pacification for the king and his retinue.
Complete with every excellence and free from all afflictions,
the king is glorified by that well-nourished system of governance.
Thus concludes the ritual for the pacification of elephants.

If a pillar should break in the middle of the house, or a pigeon should alight in the middle of the dwelling, or a crow should enter the house; if a cow should climb onto the house, or a cow should gore itself; or if a bull should scratch himself joyfully, or smoke should arise where there is no fire, or an anthill should appear, or a mushroom-ooze should emerge; or if a frog should dwell in a place that has not been rained upon; or if in a dream one sees the falling of bones or teeth—the householder shall find his wife pregnant with twins—or in the event of other portents occurring in the house, he should perform the *agadayajña*. Having performed the *janollekhana* (the ritual tracing of the boundary) and facing the fire, he offers a *sthālīpāka* sacrifice. Reciting the *puronuvākyā*: "From whom we fear, O Indra... and offering the oblation with the *yājyā*: "The Lord of Blessings, the giver of well-being...", he offers additional oblations of clarified butter as previously explained for the separate offerings. He recites: "May Indra and Agni be gracious to us with their aids; may Indra and Varuṇa, whose oblations are unassailable, be gracious to us; may the two who are peaceful be gracious to us for our prosperity and glory; may Indra and Pūṣan be gracious to us in the struggle for booty. And: "With what [help], O wonderful one, will you come to us today? and "Be united here, O you two of like mind. From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, it proceeds until the gift of a cow as a boon.
Then, with the *āmr̥* verse, he places the remnants of the oblation upon *śamī* leaves:
"May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid, may they be auspicious for our drinking; may they flow toward us for our well-being."
