Thus, having poured the rinsings of the cooking pot, the remainder of the clarified butter, and the remainder of the water into a vessel, one should dispose of them when these portents have arisen; or one should sprinkle them with the mantra, "That auspiciousness which we choose" (*tac chaṃ yo āvṛṇīmahe*).
Having performed the final consecration, honored the Brahmins, and caused them to pronounce blessings, saying "Auspicious! Auspicious!", the extraordinary rite (*adbhuta*) is thus explained.
Aruṇa said:
For those struck by various diseases and likewise afflicted by enemies,
there is no other supreme means for securing welfare except the propitiation of the Sun.
Therefore, one should propitiate the Sun, the destroyer of all diseases,
the remover of planetary afflictions, and the eradicator of all calamities.
Worshipping the Lord of the World, the Sun who dispels darkness,
one should constantly perform the fire-ritual for the Sun for the sake of purity and happiness.
It is renowned as the Great Peace, the destroyer of all calamities;
it is the supreme remover of planetary afflictions and the maker of a firm body.
For which reason, in the past, the Sun-god out of reverence performed for me this meritorious rite that removes all sins and destroys great obstacles, for the sake of peace.
The Lakṣahoma is remembered as bringing great prosperity and bestowing peace;
salutations to you, who possess the palm-tree banner and flag, and who are clothed in magnificent garments.
And here, for the sake of giving, the wise man should release the oblation with the cry "Svāhā!
to Mahodara, Śveta, Piṅgākṣa, and Mahāmati.
The wise man should offer an oblation with "Svāhā" to the Lord of the Wing (Garuḍa),
who faces the northern direction here, and to Mahādeva, his beloved.
Salutations again and again to the White One, who is white in color, the god of the three deities;
salutations to the Peaceful One, whose form is peaceful, the bearer of the excellent Pināka bow.
O tiger among birds, O one who resembles fire, one should duly offer an oblation to Īśāna here with the words, "Svāhā to the one facing the direction of Īśāna."
O King, having duly offered oblations to the high-souled god Pāvaka—
the deity who is the mouth of the world-protectors— with devotion for as long as half a *viśā*.
O best of excellent birds, having thus performed the fire-rite at will,
one should then duly perform a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma) and subsequently carry out the rite of pacification (śānti).
"Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā"—this is recorded as the procedure for the Lakṣahoma;
and in the Mahāhoma dedicated to the Sun, this indeed is the supreme procedure.
O best of birds, having thus performed the fire-ritual for the Sun,
one should duly perform a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (lakṣahoma) and thereafter carry out the rite of pacification (śānti).
The god has a luster red as vermilion, with eyes the color of a lotus at its periphery;
he is the thousand-rayed deity whose vehicle is a chariot drawn by seven horses.
The Blessed One, garlanded with rays, who is honored by all the worlds,
bestows upon you great peace that wards off the afflictions of the planets.
Mounted upon a chariot with excellent wheels, the lotus-born Lord who consists of the essence of the waters,
whose vehicle is drawn by seven horses, is the Master of Nectar for the sake of peace.
May Soma, the cool-rayed one and the nectar-rayed one, who is subject to waning and waxing,
dispel the affliction of the planets through his gentle nature.
Resembling molten red chalk, a master of all scriptures,
the preceptor of all the gods, he was a brahmin and the supreme among the best of seers of the Atharva Veda.
He who was renowned as Bṛhaspati and devoted to the science of polity (arthaśāstra),
became profoundly composed through supreme tranquility with a peaceful mind.
Having completely overcome the affliction of the planets, may he perform pacification rites for you through the grace of the Sun, being constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun.
Having the luster of snow, jasmine, and the moon, worshipped by the Daityas and Dānavas,
praised by Maheśvara, he is a hero, a great Saura, and a great sage.
May Śukra, who is ever devoted to the worship of the Sun, who is always radiant like the planet Venus itself,
and who is eternally intent upon the science of ethics (nītiśāstra), dispel the affliction caused by the planets.
Resembling a mass of crushed collyrium, born of shadow, and possessing great splendor—
may the son of the Sun, who delights in the Sun, dispel the affliction of the planets.
He who assumes manifold forms, who is unmanifest, and who delights in the knowledge of sound—
his birth does not occur, nor is his emergence perceived even by the wise.
Having one root and two roots, three crests and five topknots,
and appearing with a thousand peaks, he stands like the banner of Indra.
May that banner with its many crests— the son of the Sun, the son of Fire, and the offspring of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva— dispel your ailment.
These high-souled planets are always devoted to the worship of the Sun;
being delighted and ever desiring my welfare, they grant me peace.
Seated upon a lotus, lotus-colored, with eyes like the petals of a lotus leaf,
holding a water-pot, glorious, and served by gods and gandharvas.
The four-faced lord of the gods, ever devoted to the worship of the Sun,
the best of deities, possessed of great splendor, and the progenitor of all the worlds.
May Brahmā indeed bring about peace through the divine word "Brahman"—
he who knows the reality beyond time, who understands time, and who is devoted to the principle of time.
The god wears yellow garments, is always the granter of boons to the daughter of Atri;
he holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, is dark-complexioned, and possesses four arms.
He by whom Bali was directly confronted in the forests as if by a supreme [power],
that god Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu, is the highest deity among those to whom sacrifice is offered.
May Viṣṇu, who is eternally endowed with devotion to the Sun, who is free from worldly attachment and fond of liberation,
and who is ever intent on meditation upon the Sun, grant me peace.
Resembling gold, the kunda flower, and the moon, adorned with the *gośruti* ornament, the slayer of enemies;
the *gośrutis* are serpents.
Four-armed, of great splendor, he has flowers as his moon and the moon upon his crest.
Four-faced, wearing ashes, he is eternally dwelling in the cremation ground.
He who is the restrainer of the elements, the destroyer of sacrifices,
the most excellent, the one worthy of choice, the giver of boons, the God of gods, Maheśvara.
The illustrious Trailokyana, who was devoted to the worship of Āditya,
always held Āditya as supreme and remained intent on meditation upon Āditya.
May he who was born from the body of Āditya indeed grant me peace.
The auspicious Goddess, resembling a ruby, with four lotus-like faces,
her hands holding a rosary and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu).
O bird, may this Brāhmaṇī, who has a gentle countenance and is devoted to the worship of the Sun,
bestow peace upon you with affection, being intent on granting her blessing.
She is always beloved by the Sun and is renowned as Mahāśvetā;
O bird, she has attained the fame of "Mahāśvetā" in this world.
Resembling snow, jasmine, and the moon, she is borne by a great bull;
she holds a trident in her hand as her ornament, and Satī is adorned with cow-earrings.
May Rudrāṇī— four-armed, four-faced, three-eyed, the destroyer of sins, whose banner is the bull, and who delights in vehicles— grant me peace.
The goddess has a peacock as her vehicle, yet her form is that of one mounted upon a lion;
she holds a spear in her hand, possesses a massive body, and is adorned with every ornament.
Red as the sun, of great heroism, always devoted to dwelling in the forest—
may that goddess Kaumārī, the bestower of boons, grant you peace.
O Bird, that goddess holds a lotus and a discus, is dark-complexioned, wears yellow garments, possesses four arms, and has four lotus-like faces.
Constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun, with her mind solely fixed on the Sun,
may she who crushes all asuras grant you perpetual peace.
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, holding a thunderbolt in her hand, she is of great strength;
the goddess has a thousand eyes, and in color she is like a campaka flower with eyes like lotuses.
Adored by the Siddhas and Gandharvas, and adorned with all ornaments,
may Indrāṇī always swiftly grant you peace, O Hero.
The goddess who has the form of a boar, who is formidable, who possesses the excellent complexion of a boar,
who is dark yet radiant, and who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace—
she who here threatens all without exception while always worshipping the Sun.
May the goddess Vārāhī, the bestower of boons, truly grant you peace;
she whose hair is half-disheveled, whose eyes are fierce, who is fleshless, and bound together by sinews.
With a formidable face, she is terrible, holding aloft a sword and a bell;
garlanded with skulls, she is fearsome, bearing a khaṭvāṅga as her supreme attribute.
With reddish-brown eyes, draped in an elephant hide,
the goddess dwells in the cremation ground; she wears singing ornaments and,
with her terrible form, she strikes fear even into the worshipers of Śiva.
May Cāmuṇḍā, in her fierce form, always grant me protection—
she who holds Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa in her hands, the goddess who has gone to Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
The goddesses who are the mothers of space, as well as the mothers of the world,
all the mothers of living beings, and likewise the mothers of the ancestors.
These goddesses are worshipped by the wise as the Vṛddhas, the Śuddhas, and the Tanmātras; they are called "Mātṛ-mukhas" because they consist of Mātṛ, Pramātṛ, and Tanmātṛ.
The paternal grandmother, her mother, and whichever paternal grandmother is elderly—these indeed are the grandmothers; may they grant you peace, as do your paternal mothers.
All the goddesses, headed by Mātṛkā, with weapons in the sky and missiles in their hands,
pervading the world, remain established there, desiring offerings and possessing great majesty.
May they, who are devoted to the worship of the Sun, grant you constant peace;
with a peaceful mind, O peaceful one, may you be at peace, bestowing peace upon all.
With a body possessing every limb and a slender waist,
she was as radiant as a painted picture, graced by a gentle complexion of yellowish-dark hues.
And Dhāriṇī bore the crescent moon adorned with a tilaka on her forehead;
the goddess wore variegated garments and was decorated with all kinds of ornaments.
The most excellent among those whose forms consist of women, auspicious and the great abode of virtues,
Goddess Umā, who grants boons, is well-pleased with every mantra.
May she who is devoted to the feet of Āditya, having come in person with a peaceful form and immeasurable splendor,
grant you peace out of affection.
In the form of a young woman and child, he is six-faced and has the peacock as his vehicle;
with a face like the full moon, glorious, three-peaked, powerful, and all-pervading,
he blazes forth in the form of the sons of Kṛttikā, worshipped by the gods.
Kārttikeya, possessed of great splendor, was honored with boons by Āditya.
May the Lord of Birds grant constant peace, the fruit of happiness, prosperity,
offspring, strength, and likewise health.
Clad in white garments, Tārkṣya possesses a golden luster;
the highly wise Nandīśa, meditated upon as the Sun, holds a trident in his hand.
May the peaceful one grant you peace; may he bestow upon your mind unsurpassed wisdom regarding the Dharma.
O, may you always cross over the Dharma and grant it to others as something unshakable.
Large-bellied and large-bodied, with the face of an elephant and great strength,
he is adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread and decorated with serpent ornaments.
The support for the attainment of all goals, the leader of the hosts, the bestower of boons,
the one with formidable limbs, Bhava the god, the Guide, and Vināyaka— may they, with a joyful heart, grant you great peace and delight.
The maiden wearing yellow garments, adorned with various ornaments,
Yamunā, the auspicious daughter of the Sun, is honored by all the worlds.
O Lord of Birds, may the Goddess, who grants all accomplishments, who is most supreme through her grace,
and who is the Mother of the world, bestow peace upon you.
She who crushes the great buffalo with her entire being composed of the three qualities,
bearing a bow, a spear, a sword, and a paṭṭiśa weapon.
May the divine and auspicious Durgā, the daughter of the Sun, who raises her hands with sincerity and destroys all calamities, grant you peace.
With a fleshless body, bound by the cords of sinews,
he is exceedingly subtle yet most manifest— the unshakeable, crowned one, the Great One.
Possessing the nature of the sun, of great heroism, and with his mind fixed upon the sun,
may he who is eternally devoted to the sun grant you peace.
This excellent Caṇḍeśvara has an army of fierce attendants, possesses great side-glances,
holds a rosary in his hand, and is three-eyed.

May he who constantly removes fierce sins and destroys even the slaughter of a Brahmin grant you perpetual peace; may that great yogi, devoted to the worship of the Sun, bring about those various kalpas for one another.
In the sky are the divine Mothers, as well as the mothers of the world;
they are all the mothers of beings and likewise the mothers of the god.
May the goddesses, devoted to the worship of the Sun, who abide pervading the entire world—
those Mothers honored by the gods— grant you perpetual peace.
Those who are fierce, whose deeds are fierce, and who dwell in fierce places;
the Mothers of fierce appearance, and those who are lords of the hosts.
Likewise, others who have become obstacles, residing in the heavens and in all directions—
may they always grant you success and protect you at all times from fears.
Those of great strength who have gone to the eastern direction, holding thunderbolts in their hands,
are white as snow, jasmine, or the moon, or are adorned with staffs, blue, black, or red.
May those who dwell in heaven, in the atmosphere, on earth, and in the depths of Pātāla—
those devoted to the worship of the Sun and followers of Indra— always grant you peace.
All those who stand in the southeast have scriptures in their hands;
they are devotees of the Sun, red in color, and adorned with red ornaments.
May those [deities] belonging to the heavens, the atmosphere, and the earth, who are of the nature of fire and beloved of the Sun,
and who are devoted to the propitiation of Āditya, grant you perpetual well-being.
Those who have gone to the southern direction are always staff-in-hand;
they have dark bodies, dark attire, and are indeed excellent, dark-red in hue.
O bird, may the followers of Yama— those dwelling in heaven, those in the intermediate space, and those on earth—
who are devoted to the propitiation of the Sun, always grant you well-being.
Those Rākṣasas who are gathered in the southwest, with death in their hands,
have dark-blue limbs, dark-blue complexions, and are likewise dark-blue and red.
May those who dwell in heaven, the atmosphere, and on earth, the followers of Virūpākṣa,
always grant supreme health during the worship of Āditya.
But those in the western direction are excellent, whose hands are always occupied with action;
they consist of action, have the form of action, and always perceive things as momentary.
May those belonging to heaven, the atmosphere, and the earth, who are devoted to the propitiation of Āditya,
and may those of Varuṇa who follow Varuṇa, always grant you peace.
Stationed eternally in the northwest are the swift-moving birds;
they have yellow eyes, appear yellow, and are likewise yellowish-red.
May those dwelling in heaven, the atmosphere, and on earth, who are devoted to the propitiation of Āditya,
who observe the solar vow, and who are well-disposed, always grant you peace.
In the northern direction, there are those who constantly hold treasures in their hands;
they are the Girikākṣas, as well as the Kastūrikās and the Kṛṣṇalohitas.
May those who dwell in heaven, the atmosphere, and on earth— the beloveds of the Lord of Alakā—
who are devoted to the propitiation of the Sun, always grant you prosperity.
And those who are situated in the northeast, peaceful ones bearing tridents,
their bodies smeared with ashes, blue in hue, and adorned with red bracelets;
May those dwelling in the heavens, the atmosphere, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld,
who are ever devoted to the worship of the Sun, grant you constant peace.
For these guardians of the world possess great strength and prowess;
having worshipped the Sun, one should offer them their sacrificial oblation.
Then, with tranquil minds, accompanied by the world-protectors and the wives of Atri, may they all, being duly honored, grant well-being.
In the eastern quarter stands the city named Amarāvatī,
crowded with hosts of Vidyādharas and frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas;
it is beautiful with jeweled ramparts and adorned with great gems.
There the glorious lord of gods, Vajrapāṇi of great strength,
shines resplendent with a thousand cows, like a lord of cattle.
Mounted upon the elephant Airāvata, white as a cloud, of great splendor,
the thousand-eyed Indra is devoted to the worship of the Sun.
Devoted solely to the meditation on the Sun, endowed with devotion to the Sun,
and intent upon prostrations to the Sun— may he swiftly attain peace.
In the southeastern quarter, however, there is always the city Tejovatī,
crowded with various hosts of gods and adorned with various jewels.
There, filled with flames and possessing the brilliance of glowing embers,
was the fire that formerly burned within the bodies of those possessing cattle, destroying their sins.
May the gods— who are devoted to the worship of the Sun and whose minds are fixed upon the Sun—
grant you peace and the complete destruction of your sins.
To the south of that great-souled one is the delightful city of Vaivasvata,
crowded with hosts of the lords of the gods and filled with throngs of ancestors and rākṣasas.
Therein [is he] resembling a sapphire, with long eyes red at the corners,
mounted upon a great buffalo, and adorned with red garlands, garments, and ornaments.
May Antaka, who possesses great splendor and is devoted to the dharma of Sūrya,
being intent on the propitiation of Āditya, grant me security and health.
In the northwestern quarter, however, there is a city renowned as Kṛṣṇā;
it is crowded with hosts of great rākṣasas and teeming with piśācas and pretas.
There, the god resembling Skanda appeared, adorned with red garlands, garments, and ornaments;
he held a sword in his hand, possessed great splendor, and was radiant with a formidable countenance.
May the Lord of the Rākṣasas dwell here eternally, devoted to the propitiation of the Sun;
may he diligently grant you great peace, as well as wealth and grain.
In the western quarter, however, lies the auspicious city Śuddhavatī,
crowded with hosts of sages and Siddhas and beautifully adorned with various jewels.
There, the god Hari, resembling a jasmine flower or the moon, with tawny eyes, wearing white garments, holding a noose in his hand, and possessed of great strength;
May Varuṇa, with supreme devotion and his mind fixed upon the Sun,
now extinguish this fever that resembles disease, cough, and other ailments.
In the northwestern quarter of the directions lies the auspicious city Gandhavatī,
crowded with hosts of sages and Siddhas, and possessing golden ramparts and gateways.
There, indeed, was the body of the Lord, dark-complexioned with tawny eyes,
extending to the very limits of the earth, and elevated by his banner-staff and weapons.
May the final, supreme deity, the lord of the planets, who is higher than the highest,
constantly grant you security, health, strength, and peace.
There is a city named Mahodayā on Mount Mandara; it is called Mahodayā because of its great prosperity, filled with various yakṣas, and adorned with various jewels.
There the god Hari stood, mace in hand, adorned with variegated garlands, garments, and ornaments;
he was short-armed, possessed of great splendor, and had tawny eyes.
May he, peaceful and pleased, grant you peace with his tranquil mind—
he who dwells in the delightful city of Yaśovatī, situated in the northeastern quarter.
It was crowded with various assemblies, its divine abodes fashioned in diverse ways;
it was bounded by a wall of splendor, incomparable, and most brilliantly radiant.
There, may the supreme god Īśāna— who resembles a jasmine flower or the moon, who is adorned with unguents, who possesses three eyes, whose nature is peaceful, who holds a rosary,
and who is the bestower of boons— always grant you peace.
May Umāpati, of great splendor, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon,
and those who dwell in the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvar, and Svar— may the Goddess, surrounded by goddesses, grant peace at all times.
May all those gods who abide in Maharloka, Janaloka, and Tapaloka be joyful and always grant you peace.
But those gods in the world of truth (Satyaloka), who possess radiant bodies, are devoted to the Sun and are well-disposed; may they destroy all fear.
May those gods who dwell in mountain caves, fortresses, and forests, and who are devoted to the worship of the Sun, always grant you protection.
May Sarasvatī, who is devoted to the Sun, bestow peace upon you always with her body, which is purer than the autumn moon and possesses stainless luster.
May the goddess Śrī, who possesses the luster of gold, whose hands are like lotuses,
and who is devoted to the Sun, always grant you peace.
Adorned with a most variegated necklace and a radiant golden girdle,
may Aparājitā, who is devoted to the Sun, grant you victory.
The supreme goddess Kṛttikā, the fair-faced Rohiṇī,
the glorious Mṛgaśiras, the auspicious Ārdrā, and the most radiant [Punarvasu].
Punarvasu, Puṣyā, and Aśleṣā as well, O bird,
are always devoted to the worship of the Sun, being permeated by the nature of the Sun.
May these, who abide in the eastern quarter, always grant you peace;
may these Mothers of the Constellations, impelled by the Sun, likewise grant it.
Then Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, and likewise Sūryapara;
Pūrvāṣāḍhā of great power, and likewise Uttarāṣāḍhā.
The constellation named Abhijit and Śravaṇa, which is rich in learning—
these shine resplendently in the west, appearing as radiant forms.
These well-cultivated women worship the Sun at all times;
may they grant you constant peace and great prosperity.
O Mahāmati, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, Uttarabhādrapadā, Revatī, Aśvinī, and Bharaṇī—
these great goddesses are eternally situated to the north.
Constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun, with their minds fixed upon Āditya,
may they always grant you peace and highly precious prosperity.
Taurus, the lord of Taurus, Leo, the best among the luminaries— may these auspicious ones, intent on union with the Sun, illuminate the east; may they,
who worship the lotus feet of the Sun, grant peace through their devotion.
Sagittarius, Virgo,
and Capricorn— these, being most prosperous, always worship the Sun in the southern quarter.
May Libra, Gemini, and Aquarius, situated in the west and devoted to the worship of the Sun’s rays, always grant you peace.
Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces—these are situated in the north.
They worship Mahākāla, the Sun, the leader of the planets;
may they, ever intent on the knowledge taught by their respective traditions, grant peace eternally.
May the ascetics who have performed meritorious deeds, who are constantly remembered by the wise—
the twenty-seven sages and others, peaceful and supremely radiant,
endowed with the grace of the Sun— grant you peace forever.
Kaśyapa, Gālava, Gārgya, Viśvāmitra, Mahāmuni,
Manu, Dakṣa, Vasiṣṭha, Mārtaṇḍa, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Nārada, Bhṛgu, Ātreya, Bharadvāja, the sage Aṅgiras,
Vālmīki, Kauśika, Kaṇva, Śālavya, and then Punarvasu.
O Lord of Birds, these sages known as the Śālaṅkāyanas were indeed solely intent on meditation upon the Sun and devoted to the worship of Āditya.
The Daityas Tāraka, Agnimukha, and the mighty Kālanemi—
these high-souled Daityas were conceived in the form of the sun.
May the enemies of the gods grant nourishment, strength, and likewise health:
Vairocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, Suparvan, and Vasulocana.
Madhukanda, Mukunda, and the Daitya Raivataka likewise,
with eyes as broad as the face, were filled with the highest devotion.
Possessing the grandeur produced by great wealth, he bears the marks established by the Destroyer of Śaṅkha.
May Ananta, the lord of the Naga kings, who is devoted to the propitiation of the Sun,
destroy the accumulation of your great sins and swiftly grant you peace.
With an exceedingly white body resembling shimmering pearls,
and eternally endowed with royal splendor, may Vāsuki attain peace.
With a garment of deep saffron hue, shimmering with the perfection of his enjoyments and marked by the auspicious svastika sign through his divine splendor.
May the glorious Takṣaka, king of the nāgas, accompanied by a multitude of leaders and the remover of all defects and poisons, grant you great peace.
With an exceedingly dark complexion and a head formidable with matted locks,
he was marked by three lines upon his neck and held upraised weapons with terrible fangs.
May the illustrious Karkoṭaka, endowed with power through the pride of his venom,
dispel all your distress and grant you peace.
With a body the color of a lotus and beautiful, lotus-like eyes,
he was marked with five spots on his neck, a sign of auspiciousness.
May the illustrious Vyomapadma, who is devoted to the worship of the feet of the Sun,
grant you great peace that removes the fear of great sins.
Though his body was like a white lotus and possessed immeasurable splendor,
he was always adorned upon his head with the marks of the conch, the trident, and the sprout.
May Mahāpadma, the great Nāga who constantly worships the Sun,
bestow upon you peace, prosperity, and a stainless birth.
Possessing a dark-blue bodily form, glorious, and lotus-eyed,
he was intoxicated by the pride of his own poison and strength, and his neck was marked with three lines.
May Śaṅkhapāla, endowed with splendor, a worshiper of the feet of the Sun,
the joyful remover of great poison, grant you peace.
With a body exceeding [the norm], white in color, and with his head fashioned like a half-moon;
possessing a majestic pride born of his radiant bulk, he was marked by auspicious characteristics.
The lord of serpents named Kuliśa, who is ever devoted to the heroic,
having removed your terrible poison, may he perform a rite of pacification for you.
May those nāgas who dwell in the atmosphere, those nāgas who reside in heaven,
and those nāgas who abide in the netherworld— all of them,
intent upon worshipping the rays of the sun, grant peace forever.
May the female nāgas, the nāga maidens, and likewise the young male nāgas—
who are devoted to the Sun and possess noble minds— always grant you peace.
Whoever should proclaim or likewise hear this description of the form of the Naga,
serpents shall never harm them, nor shall poison ever take effect upon them.
The Gaṅgā is a meritorious great goddess, as are the Yamunā and the Narmadā river.
The Gomatī, the Śoṇā, the Varuṇā, and likewise the Devikā [flow there],
toward the God who is the Lord of all grahas, the Lord of gods, and the Leader of the worlds.
The rivers, imbued with devotion like the sun, always worship him;
may they, whose minds are solely intent on meditation upon the sun, grant you constant peace.
The river named Nairañjanā, the great river Śoṇa,
the supreme Mandākinī, and likewise the auspicious Satyānvitā.
May these and many other rivers on earth, in heaven, and in the intermediate space,
being devoted to the worship of the Sun, perform your propitiation.
The god Mahāvaiśravaṇa is the king of sacrifice, possessed of great power; he is the preeminent lord of ten million sacrifices, accompanied by a multitude of yakṣas.
Endowed with great prosperity, he was devoted to the worship of the feet of the Sun;
intent solely on the abode of the Sun, he was permeated by the very nature of the Sun.
May he whose eyes are as broad as lotus petals, being pleased, grant you peace.
The great yakṣa Maṇibhadra, adorned with precious jewels,
shines with a captivating necklace hanging from his neck.
With his form surrounded by yakṣiṇīs and yakṣa maidens,
and engaged in the worship of the Sun, may he perform peace for you.
The lord of yakṣas named Suvīra, adorned with jeweled earrings,
shines resplendent upon his forehead with a broad band of gold.
The lord of yakṣas named Vāpika was adorned with a necklace and a variegated crown set with many jewels.
Surrounded by hosts of yakṣas and accompanied by ten million yakṣas,
the glorious one, devoted to the worship of the Sun, may he grant you peace.
The great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, lord of nāgas and yakṣas, is a bird-like being;
he is draped in divine silk, covered with agallochum, and adorned with jewels and gold.
Devoted to the Sun, delighting in the Sun, and dedicated to the worship of the Sun,
may he, endowed with the grace of the Sun, perform your rite of pacification.
The great yakṣa Pūrṇabhadra is adorned with all ornaments;
he shines upon his forehead with a broad band of gold.
Surrounded by many yakṣas and hundreds of millions of yakṣas,
devoted to bowing to the Sun and endowed with devotion to the Sun,
and engaged in the worship of the Sun, may he perform the rite of peace for you.
The lord of yakṣas named Virūpākṣa, clothed in white garments and possessed of great splendor,
his golden body was adorned with various garlands of gold.
Constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun, Kañcākṣa,
who resembles a water-jar and is like the sun in brilliance, may he perform peace for you.
The yakṣas dwelling in the atmosphere, those yakṣas who reside in the sun,
the yakṣas in mountain fastnesses, and those who dwell in the depths of the underworld—
yakṣas who assume various forms, devoted to the Sun and firm in their vows.
May those who are devoted to him, whose minds are fixed on him, and who are eager for the worship of the Sun—
may they, joyful, peaceful, and dedicated to peace, bestow peace upon us.
There were yakṣiṇīs of various forms,
as well as yakṣa youths and highly fortunate yakṣa maidens, all intent upon the worship of the Sun.
May they, being ever perfectly composed, swiftly bestow peace, auspiciousness, security, strength, supreme excellence, and success.
May all the yakṣas and great lords, who are worshipped everywhere and have always been devoted to the Sun, grant you supreme peace.
May all the oceans on every side and all the planetary jewels in every way,
being intent upon the propitiation of the Sun, perform your pacification.
And on all sides were Rākṣasas of terrible form and great strength;
there were also those Rākṣasas who were corpulent and those who roamed through the intermediate space.
Those Rākṣasas who dwell in Pātāla and are constantly devoted to the worship of the Sun;
all the lords of the Pretas and the Pretas facing in every direction;
those Pretas who are exceedingly radiant and those Pretas who feed upon blood.
There are pretas who move through the atmosphere, as well as others dwelling in heaven;
and those pretas who roam at will in the netherworld or upon the earth.
May the chariot of that god who has a single wheel, and whose banner bears the bull,
bring you constant peace through his splendor.
Those piśācas who possess great heroism, are endowed with supernatural powers, and have great strength—
all of them assume various forms and are distinguished by various superior qualities.
Those Piśācas who are in the intermediate space, those in heaven who possess great strength,
and those on the surface of the earth in the netherworld— who are multiform and swift as thought— [are all here].
O hero, may those gods, for whom I am always the charioteer and for whom you are the leader of the gods,
grant you peace forever through their splendor.
May all the spirits of epilepsy, or all the spirits of fever,
those who seize the fetus and children, those who afflict the teeth,
and those spirits of the intermediate space— may they always grant peace.
Thus may all the gods and others, who bestow the knowledge of the Sun,
always bring peace to the world through devotion to the Sun alone.
Victory to the divine Sūrya, the adversary of darkness and delusion;
salutations be to you, Bhāskara, the sole sun of the worlds.
Salutations again and again to the supreme among planets, to the peaceful one, to the victorious one who brings about auspiciousness,
to the destroyer of darkness, to the unconquerable and the unvanquished.
Victory to you, O Lord of the radiant one, blazing with a thousand rays;
salutations to you, who have conquered the worlds by your speed and possess manifold forms.
Salutations again and again to the Sun, who is the embodiment of the Gāyatrī and the Vedas, the beloved of Sāvitrī, the upholder of the earth, and Mārtaṇḍa.
Sumantu said: Thus, O lord of the earth, was this propitiatory rite performed by Aruṇa for the welfare of the great-souled Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā and Indra.
In this same way, O Indra among kings, other men who are afflicted by diseases of the limbs also become free from illness once this fire-rite has been performed.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, the fire-ritual must be performed with effort according to the rules; indeed, that which is characterized by peace must be accomplished.
In the event of planetary portents, famine, or all manner of calamities,
and when the rain-god fails to send rain, one should perform the rite accompanied by a hundred-thousandfold fire offering (lakṣahoma).
Having recited the Agnisūkta and meditated upon the Sun with diligence,
when this is performed, the god will certainly rain for humans according to their desire.
Whoever should read or even hear this chapter on pacification shall leave all worlds behind and be glorified in the world of the Sun.
One desiring a daughter shall obtain a daughter; one desiring victory shall obtain victory;
one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth; and one desiring a son shall obtain a son.
O King, whatever desire a man prays for, he hears and swiftly attains it all; he shall become beloved by the Sun.
O descendant of Kuru, having heard this entire sacred peace,
whoever enters into battle while meditating upon the Sun shall conquer all enemies in war and attain the highest joy.
He rejoices for an inexhaustible time, his commands unopposed;
he shall not be overcome by diseases, and he will be firmly established with sons and grandsons.
He would be like the sun in brilliance and splendor.
O Hero, for whichever person a reciter recites this on their behalf,
that person shall not be afflicted by the defects consisting of wind, trembling, and phlegm.
For him there is no untimely death, nor is he defiled by any sins;
poison does not affect his body, nor does there occur dullness, blindness, or muteness.
He shall have no fear of portents, nor shall there be any fear of enemies.
Whatever diseases, whatever great portents, whatever malevolent planets, and whatever potent poison there may be—
O Bhārata, all these come to complete pacification through the hearing of this [text].
Whatever merit is established in all the sacred fords, such as the Gaṅgā and others,
one obtains that merit multiplied ten millionfold through hearing [this teaching] and other such means.
By performing ten Rājasūya sacrifices and especially the Aneṣa sacrifice,
one shall live for more than a hundred years, free from all afflictions.
The swift-acting, the ungrateful, the slayer of a Brahmin, the violator of the guru’s bed,
the killer of one who has sought refuge, and those who are betrayers of trust.
Even one who has engaged in wicked and sinful conduct, such as being a slayer of father or mother,
is liberated from all sins merely by hearing and reciting this.
This meritorious history, the unsurpassed ritual of the fire-offering, was told of old by Sūrya; it should always be given to one devoted to Sūrya.
O mighty-armed one, in former times this was told by Aruṇa’s younger brother to his own younger brother, the high-souled Bhojakas.
In Śākadvīpa, it is honored by those headed by Sūryaśarman;
he, in turn, recounted it to me, which removes the fear of all sins.
Thus ends the Mahāśānti as declared in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa. Now follow the rites for pacifying portents (*adbhuta-śānti*). Regarding these, it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa:
O Keśava, I wish to hear about that peace which is prescribed for celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents during great calamities.
Matsya said:
O King, I shall now fully explain the pacification rites for the three kinds of portents, especially for those terrestrial ones; one should perform the propitiatory ceremonies, O lord of men.
O King, let there be fearlessness in the intermediate spaces, on earth,
and in the divine realms for one who desires victory and seeks prosperity.
When one is attacked by an enemy intent on conquest, or likewise by others;
when there is fear of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), or even for the destruction of enemies;
and when great danger has arrived—then the peace of *Abhayā* is desired.
When beings are seen to be violent, peacefulness toward them is thus desired; likewise,
when people have arisen who are afflicted by sensations and have become nihilists,
and when the honoring of those unworthy of honor occurs, Brahmic peacefulness is thus desired.
When an assault is imminent, when there is fear of an enemy army,
and when internal dissension within the kingdom has arisen, the Raudrī propitiation is praised as the means for pacification.
When there is an excess of wind, when it arises from all directions,
or when a morbid disease born of wind has occurred, the pacification of the wind-element is desired.
When the fear of drought has arisen, as well as during abnormal rainfall and disturbances of water reservoirs,
the pacification rite dedicated to Varuṇa is prescribed.
O twice-born one, when the fear of a curse has arisen, the Bhārgavī [is the remedy]; likewise, O mighty-armed one, when a deformity occurs at birth, the Prājāpatyā;
and when there is a defect in the ritual implements, O delighter of kings, the Tvaṣṭrī.
O King, for children and for one desiring peace, as well as for Kaumārī,
one should perform the fire-related rite of pacification when an abnormality of fire occurs.
When an order has been thus disobeyed, when there is the destruction of wives, servants, and so forth,
or when a disorder arises in horses that desire peace,
the Gāndharva rite is prescribed for those horses who long for pleasure and honor.
For one desiring the pacification of elephants when their agitation has arisen,
the Āṅgirasa rite shall bring peace to the desire and pride of the elephants.
O mighty-armed one, when fear of piśācas and the like arises, the rite for pacification is known as Nairṛtī; likewise when there is fear of untimely death or even upon having a bad dream.
One should likewise perform the Kāmyā-śānti when Capricorn arrives;
when the loss of wealth has occurred, the Kauverī-śānti is desired.
When a transformation occurs among trees or other objects,
one desiring prosperity and peace should likewise employ the Pārthivī rite.
O best of men, during the first watch of the day or at night,
under the asterisms of Hasta, Svāti, or Citrā, and likewise on Sundays or under the Aśvinī constellation;
O son of the Sun, [these effects occur] during the second watch of the day and at night in Āryamṇa, Sīmajāta, Vāyavya, and Adbhuta.

One should perform the Āgneyī rite during the asterisms of Puṣya, Āgneya (Kṛttikā), Viśākhā, Pitṛ (Maghā), Aja (Pūrvaphalgunī), and Bharaṇī, as well as during Bhāgya (Pūrvaphalgunī) and any other occasions involving portents.
And during the third watch of the day and at night, O son of the Sun,
[the time is auspicious] under Rohiṇī, Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), Brāhma (Jyeṣṭhā), Vāsava (Dhaniṣṭhā), and Viśvadaivata (Uttarāṣāḍhā).
O upholder of the lineage, when any wonders occur during the Jyeṣṭhā or Maitra [nakṣatras],
the Mahāśānti rite dedicated to Indra should be proclaimed in times of fear.
And during the fourth watch of the day and at night, O son of the Sun,
[these occur] under Āśleṣā, Revatī, as well as Ārdrā, and the terrible Ahibradhna.
[1075] Furthermore, regarding those portents that occur when the root asterism has Varuṇa as its presiding deity,
a great propitiatory rite dedicated to Varuṇa (vāruṇī mahāśānti) must be performed by the ruler of the earth.
Whenever extraordinary events occur at any time when the boundaries of the maṇḍala have been breached,
pacification or the two-fold pacification must be performed when such a portent exists, and not otherwise.
If pacification is performed without a portent, a portent will arise [as a consequence].
Just as arrows do not strike men who are possessed by delusions, O King,
so too do the blows of fate not affect them.
Of those whose nature is dharma and who are devoted to peace.
Manu said:
O God, tell me likewise of the fruits of extraordinary deeds and their pacification;
for you, O large-eyed one, know all that is to be known in its entirety.
Matsya said:
In this regard, I shall describe to you what the one of great asceticism said;
for here, Vṛddhagarga, the best among all upholders of dharma, spoke to me.
O descendant of Pṛthu, the highly effulgent Garga, who was dear to the best of sages, questioned Gārgya as he sat upon the banks of the Sarasvatī.
Atri said:
"Describe to me the former appearances of people, as well as those of cities and kings; for you are indeed called all-knowing."
Garga said:
Through the transgression of men's observances, the deities incur offense;
from that offense against the gods, calamity proceeds.
The threefold portents are proclaimed as celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial.
The celestial consists of abnormalities involving the planets and constellations; now learn from me the atmospheric ones.
The falling of meteors, the burning of the quarters, halos,
as well as cities of the Gandharvas, and any abnormal rain— one should designate such phenomena in this world as portents from the sky.
The fear residing in the earth, as well as earthquakes born from the ground,
and the abnormality of reservoirs of water— that too is proclaimed as terrestrial (bhauma).
A Bhauma [yoga] should be known as yielding little fruit and ripening slowly;
an Abhaya [yoga] gives middling fruit and ripens quickly after a moderate time.
But when a portent has arisen, if the rain should become auspicious,
it should be known that within seven days the inauspiciousness will become fruitless.
If the ripening of a portent is not seen without pacification,
it will become capable of causing very great fear within three years.
It ripens upon the king's person, in the world, in the city, in his wife, in the domestic priest,
as well as in his sons and in the transport of his treasury.
O Indra among kings, due to the very nature of the seasons, there occur phenomena designated as "marvels";
they should be understood as bringing about auspicious results—listen to me as I describe them.
The sounds of thunderbolts, earthquakes, twilight, and atmospheric explosions;
as well as halos, dust, smoke, and the sun turning red at its rising and setting.

In the months of Madhu and Mādhava (Caitra and Vaiśākha), trees become rich with sap and moisture, there is the emergence of abundant crops and fruits, and there is an increase in the passion of cows and birds; these are auspicious signs.
Turbid with the falling of meteors and stars, the orbs of the sun and moon turned tawny;
there was a bursting forth of fireless flames, struck by smoke and divine winds.
Seeing the twilight as red as a blood-lotus, the sky resembling an agitated ocean,
and the drying up of the waters of the rivers, one should predict a favorable summer.
A halo around Indra’s weapon, the sprouting of withered trees,
trembling, upheaval, and deformity, as well as the rumbling and cracking of the earth.
During the rainy season, rivers, wells, lakes,
and the overflow from the abundance of rain, as well as the heads of water-dams, bestow auspiciousness.
There was the wondrous sight of celestial women, forms, gandharvas, and divine chariots;
the vision of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars; and superhuman speech.
The sounds of singing and musical instruments in the forests and on mountain ridges,
the growth of crops, and the production of sap are recorded as auspicious signs during the autumn season.
The cool breezes and frost, the delight of the deer and birds,
and the sight of beings such as rākṣasas and yakṣas, as well as non-human speech— these were present there.
In the winter season, smoke, darkness, locusts, forests, mountains,
and the high rising of the sun are considered auspicious omens.
Having seen the sky, which was dark as collyrium and tawny with falling stars and meteors, appearing strange and marvelous due to the falling of snow and the rising of fierce winds;
The birth of variegated offspring among women, as well as among cows, goats, horses, deer, and birds,
and the transformation of leaves, sprouts, and creepers during the cold season are auspicious.
But for that which has arisen or is seen as a marvel without the nature of the seasons,
this pacification through scriptural authority occurs immediately thereafter.
The task was to be carried out as commanded by the lord of the earth.
Thus, regarding portents occurring during a miraculous pacification,
Garga said:
"The images of the deities dance, tremble, and blaze with fire."
They cry out and weep, they stand still and laugh.
They sit down at the time of the meal, run about, and stay there;
while eating, they scatter vegetables, weapons, or banners.
They stand with their faces turned downward, or they wander from place to place;
they vomit fire, smoke, fat, and blood. Such disorders as these are seen arising suddenly.
One should not take pleasure in dwelling there in sacred sites (liṅga), abodes (āyatana), or fields (kṣetra);
for either the king will meet his end there, or that country will perish.
If one observes portents during the processions of the gods, one should declare danger to the country;
in such a case, one should not recommend residing there, even if it be the ancestral home.
The brown one among the Vasus is to be known as born from a king and a world-protector;
and that which is born from Skanda and Śikhaṇḍin is to be known as belonging to the army commanders.
One should know that for the worlds, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Indra, and Viśvakarman are the source;
and likewise, Vināyaka is to be known as the leader of the Gaṇas.
O God of gods, O best of kings: among the wives of the gods, the wives of kings are to be known;
among the deities of the site, they belong to the houses themselves, and not otherwise.
In matters concerning the worship of deities, the domestic priest, who is a knower of the Vedas,
should go to the place of worship, cover those [images], and then adorn them.
O highly fortunate one, one should worship her with perfumes, garlands, and an abundance of food;
immediately thereafter, one should attend upon her according to the rule with the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
Merely by means of worshipping that linga, the domestic priest, remaining unwearied, should offer the *sthālīpāka* oblation into the fire according to the rules for seven nights.
O best of the twice-born, the brahmins should be honored for seven days with sweet food and drink along with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā);
and when the eighth day arrives, they should be honored with gifts of land and cows.
Through [the gift of] gold, one attains peace from evil.
Thus ends the pacification of portents and deformities in the *Adbhuta-śānti*.
Garga said:
"In that kingdom where fire blazes without fuel and with an exceedingly loud sound..."
That kingdom, though possessing fuel, does not blaze; it is oppressed, O King.
If a fire should blaze up anywhere— even where there are no trees— or in any way whatsoever upon a palace,
an archway, a gate, a royal residence, or a temple;
wherever these things are consumed by fire, there shall be danger from the king.
Or they may be consumed by lightning; even there, there is fear for the king. Unseasonable darkness shall arise, and a vast calamity will befall him.
Where smoke appears without fire, there is great danger to the sky-goers.
If lightning flashes in a cloudless sky, there will be danger; likewise, if the sky is devoid of rain during the day yet possesses stars, one should predict fear.
If there should be a defect in the weapons, one should predict a battle in that case.
There, the family priest, having fasted for three nights and being well-concentrated,
[should perform the rite] with fuel-sticks of milky trees, mustard seeds, and clarified butter.
One should likewise give gold, cows, garments, and land to the twice-born;
when this is done, sin goes to destruction.
O best of the twice-born, whatever fear there is regarding abnormalities of the fire—
Thus ends the section on portents regarding the anomaly of fire within the *Adbhuta-śānti*.
Garga said:
"In those cities where trees appear as if impelled by fate..."
Whether speaking, or laughing, or flowing with much essence.
Without obstruction, the branches shed their leaves;
likewise, those trees three years old display fruit and flowers out of season.
They manifest their former state as fruit, flowers, or even as they were;
or else they exude milk, oil, wine, blood, honey, or water.
Those who are diseased suddenly blossom, or those who are withered grow anew;
here, those who have fallen rise up, and likewise, those who have risen fall down.
In this regard, O Brahmin, I shall explain to you the very fruit of their maturation:
through weeping one encounters disease, and through laughing, the ruin of one's country.
By causing a branch to fall, one brings about the downfall of warriors in battle;
by means of the fruits and flowers of young trees, one brings about the death of children.
Immediately after the fruit and flowers, it causes dissension within one's own kingdom;
cow’s milk signifies decline everywhere, and oil is a sign of famine.
In dry conflicts, the mantra of valor does not take root;
O Great King, it will cause the disintegration of mountains through fear.
If [the bird] moves from one place to another, one should predict the ruin of the country;
likewise, if it chatters among the trees or cries out, there will be the loss of wealth.

If this occurs upon trees that have been worshipped, it portends the death of even a sovereign king; likewise, one should predict the king's death from the flowers and fruits of those trees specifically designated for him.
And likewise, being untiring among other trees or when trees fall,
one should cover them with a mat and perform the *chagraprāyaścitta* for the pacification of evil.
One should worship the god Śiva and offer an animal victim to him;
then, having performed these rites for the Mūla-mantras, one should mutter the Rudra-hymn.
Having honored the Brahmins with milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter, one should give land as a gift,
accompanied by song, dance, and worship.
To the god Hara, for the sake of the destruction of evil.
Thus ends the pacification of the portent of trees within the *Adbhuta-śānti*.
Garga said:
Excessive rain, drought, and the fear of famine and other such calamities are considered [portents].
But if rain occurs after midday during the non-seasonal period, it should be known as portending fear.
If these changes are not slight but indeed severe, they should be known as portending the death of the king;
likewise, an inversion of the cold and heat of the seasons brings fear born of enemies.
Where blood rains down, there shall be fear of weapons;
when there are showers of embers and dust, the city perishes;
and when there are showers of marrow, bones, fat, and flesh, there shall be fear of the destruction of people.
Garga said: When wild beasts and birds enter the village,
or when domestic animals go to the forest, or when creatures born of water go onto dry land;
Whether born on land or moving in water, whether they are formidable or remain fearless,
jackals at the king’s gate or the city gate bring about inauspiciousness.
Whether those who roam by day roam at night, or those who roam at night roam by day,
or whether domestic animals abandon their village— one should designate that as a portent.
If the twilight hours are blazing and they form circles,
and where they utter unpleasant sounds, then one shall obtain the fruit of a ghost (preta).
If a cock crows at dusk, or a cuckoo in winter,
or if a jackal howls facing the sun at sunrise, it foretells fear of Yama.
If a pigeon should enter the house, or a carnivorous bird alights upon the head,
or if a honeybee should make honey [there], death will befall the master of the house.
If a carnivorous bird alights upon the walls, gates, or houses, at the archways, marketplaces, or streets, or upon objects known as banners, umbrellas, or weapons;
If anthills arise, or if honey flows forth,
then the region will go to ruin and the king will die.
Upon seeing mice and locusts, there will be great fear of hunger;
woodpeckers, bones, and horn-faced creatures portend the death of dogs.
If crows that steal grain are seen, famine should be known to be impending;
people, becoming fearless and skilled in warfare, will overcome one another.
If a white crow is seen engaged in sexual intercourse,
either the king dies there or else the country perishes.
Wherever an owl alights— whether on a garment or in a house—
it should be known that there will be death for the master of the house, as well as the loss of wealth.
In the event of portents involving wild animals or birds, one should perform a fire sacrifice accompanied by ritual fees;
furthermore, the mantra beginning with "devāḥ kapota" should be recited by five twice-born men.
With one [verse] beginning "sudeva," he should recite the *Devagavya* hymn along with the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
as well as the *Śākuna-sūkta* and the "Heads of the Manas-veda."
The gods, such as the pigeon and others, are well known through the mantras in the Ṛgveda.
And cows, along with gold, a pair of garments, and upper robes, should be given to the twice-born according to the prescribed rules.
When this is done, whatever evil has been signaled by deer or birds comes to an end.
Thus ends the pacification of the portents concerning beasts and birds within the *Adbhuta-śānti*.
Garga said:
[One should perform the pacification] of the palace, the bridge, the roof-covering, the gates, the ramparts, and the dwellings.
But if an omen without a specific sign falls for those who are steadfast, it portends the death of the king.
Where the quarters of the sky were overwhelmed by dust and the smoke of tears,
and the sun, moon, and stars grew pale, portending an increase in fear.

Where *rākṣasa*s are seen, where *brāhmaṇa*s act contrary to the law (*vidharmin*), where the seasons are disordered, and where people honor that which is unworthy of honor; where the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) appear displaced— that is the sign of great danger.
During the rising of a comet and during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, there is a period of vulnerability;
yet, fruits, flowers, grain, gold, and ornaments [are auspicious].
If there is rain of dust, insects, or fruit, there is danger arising from disease;
however, excessive rain during a period of drought increases the joy of the crops.
When no shadow is seen in a dust-free sun or cloudless sky,
nor is it seen in a lamp, there shall be danger to the country.
Or likewise at night when the sky is cloudless, seeing a white rainbow to the south or north,
or similarly seeing the fall of a meteor;
One should predict a conflagration of the quarters, a halo around the sun or moon, and likewise a city of the Gandharvas; as well as fear of a foreign army and calamities afflicting the country.
O best of the twice-born, an oblation to the sun, the moon, the rain-god, and the wind should be performed according to the rules,
along with offerings of grain and gifts of cattle and gold.
It should be given to the twice-born for the sake of destroying sin.
Thus ends the pacification of abnormal rainfall within the *Adbhutaśānti*.
Garga said:
They either retreat from the city or approach its vicinity.
For the lakes and springs of a river indeed become tasteless.
If rivers carry water that is discolored, turbid, heated, devoid of foam, agitated,
and reddened by the fat of milk or wine, and if these waters are abundant,
there shall be danger from a foreign army within six months.
The reservoirs of water roar, blaze, or boil;
they murmur most crookedly and emit flames and smoke.
If water appears in a place where there is no ditch, or if reservoirs overflow their capacity,
or if sounds of singing are heard, a plague of people may occur there.
One should sprinkle divine water, cow's milk, ghee, and honey there;
the Varuṇa mantras are to be recited, and with them, oblations should be made in the water.
In this rite, excellent food mixed with honey and clarified butter should be offered to the twice-born for the purpose of feeding them;
and cows adorned with white garments should also be given as gifts.
Likewise, water-pots [are offered] for the pacification of all evils.
Thus ends the account of the portents in the waters during the time of the Adbhuta-śānti.
Garga said:
"Women give birth out of season, and likewise, offspring are born prematurely."
And there were those with deformed offspring, as well as those who gave birth to twins.
Non-human beings, eunuchs, and likewise those with sexual characteristics are born;
they are born with deficient limbs, with extra limbs, or even with three [limbs].
One should predict the destruction of that region and its people when beasts, birds, and likewise reptiles [appear in such a manner].
O best of the twice-born, the king should banish her from the kingdom, yet women are to be honored; likewise,
one should perform the satiation of Brahmins according to one's inclination.
Therefore, in this world, evil attains peace.
Thus ends the section on the pacification of portents regarding birth.
Garga said:
If vehicles proceed even when unyoked, or do not proceed even when yoked;
When they are thus urged on, a great terror arises there.
Musical instruments that are being played do not sound, or they sound even when not struck;
the immovable shake, and the movable do not move.
When there is a transformation of ornaments and such, there will be a terrible fear of weapons.
Having performed the worship of Vāyu according to the rites prescribed by the best of the twice-born, one should recite the mantras taught therein and offer abundant food consisting of *paramānna*.
Because he gave it with a sacrificial fee, there is peace for this king.
Thus ends the pacification of disturbances caused by household utensils.
[1087] Wherever there is an abnormality involving planets or constellations, one should predict fear;
women engage in quarrels and strike children with their words.
Where the performance of customary rites is seen to be suspended,
and where the sacrificial fire does not blaze even while the propitiatory offerings are being poured.
Ants and flesh-eating creatures then move about in the midst of it;
full jars leak, or the sacrificial oblation is scattered.
Where the auspicious blessings of one's master are not heard on all sides,
or where trembling afflicts one even when there is cause for encouragement, that is censured.
Neither among the gods nor among the brahmins do they behave as they ought;
musical instruments are played with dull sounds and out-of-tune melodies.
Where people hate their teachers and friends and are devoted to honoring their enemies;
where people treat Brahmins—who are worthy of honor as kinsmen—with contempt.
Where an irreligious person appears during rites for peace, auspiciousness, or fire-offerings,
the king dies there or the entire country perishes.
"Perceive for me the omens that the king's destruction has arrived:
first, he hates the brahmins and reviles the brahmins."
He shows contempt for brahmins and seeks to kill brahmins;
he does not remember them when he has need, and even when entreated, he remains indifferent.
He does not welcome praise, nor does he seek honor or fame;
yet, out of greed, he imposes new taxes upon the people who are thus oppressed.
And one should properly honor these most excellent brahmins together with their wives;
likewise, food offerings for the gods and sacrificial oblations (balis) should be prepared.
Cows should be given to the best of the twice-born, as well as land, gold, and garments;
furthermore, fire-offerings (homa) and the worship of the twice-born should be performed.
When this is done, evil comes to peace.

Thus end the rites for the pacification of portents as declared in the *Matsyapurāṇa*. Thus ends the section on the pacification of portents (*adbhutaśāntika*) within the *Vrata-khaṇḍa* of the *Caturvargacintāmaṇi*, composed by Śrī Hemādri— the illustrious Mahārājādhirāja Mahādeva, sovereign of all departments, and master of all branches of knowledge.
